The ratio matters too: one part dal to one part rice, and five parts water, gives the soft-set texture. Less water gives you pilaf.

  • Dry-roast the dal. It is two minutes and it changes everything.
  • Five parts water to one of grain, for softness.
  • A spoon of ghee poured over at the table, not stirred in earlier.

item.title: Vegetable Biryani
item.description: Layered vegetable biryani with basmati parboiled to seventy per cent, saffron milk, fried onions and a sealed dum steam.
item.content:encoded:
The rice is boiled to seventy per cent and not a grain more. It finishes in the steam of the sealed pot, and rice that went in fully cooked comes out as paste. Test by pressing a grain: it should break into three with a hard white core still visible. Seal the lid with foil or dough — the steam is the cooking, and a lid that lets it out gives you dry rice on top and wet underneath.

  • Seventy per cent rice: it breaks in three with a white core.
  • Seal with foil under the lid or the steam escapes.
  • Lift to serve, never stir, or the grains break.

item.title: Poha
item.description: Flattened rice rinsed and steamed briefly with mustard seeds, curry leaves, turmeric, onion and roasted peanuts.
item.content:encoded:
Rinse the poha in a sieve under running water for about fifteen seconds and then leave it alone. It carries on absorbing while it stands, so poha that felt right in the sieve is right in the pan five minutes later; poha soaked in a bowl turns to porridge. Use thick poha — the thin sort dissolves whatever you do.

  • Rinse in a sieve, never soak in a bowl.
  • Thick poha only.
  • Fold rather than stir, or it turns to mush.

item.title: Żurek
item.description: Żurek — Polish sour rye soup with white sausage, potato, marjoram and boiled egg.
item.content:encoded:
The soup is defined by zakwas, a rye flour starter fermented for five days — it is what makes żurek sour in a lactic, bready way that vinegar cannot imitate. The starter is stirred in off the boil, because boiling it flattens the sourness and can make it separate.

  • Make the zakwas. Vinegar żurek is a different, lesser soup.
  • Never boil after the starter and cream go in.
  • Crush the dried marjoram between your palms to wake it up.

item.title: Upma
item.description: Roasted coarse semolina cooked with mustard seeds, urad dal, curry leaves and vegetables into a soft savoury porridge.
item.content:encoded:
Roast the semolina dry until it smells like toast and no longer sticks together, then let it cool before it meets the water. Unroasted semolina turns gluey; roasted, the grains stay separate. Pour the semolina into boiling water in a thin stream with the other hand stirring, or you get lumps you will never break up.

  • Roast the semolina and cool it before it meets water.
  • Thin stream in, constant stirring, no lumps.
  • Rest covered for five minutes — it finishes swelling.

item.title: Medu Vada
item.description: Ground urad dal batter beaten until aerated, shaped into rings and deep fried until crisp outside and soft within.
item.content:encoded:
Grind the dal with as little water as you can bear and then beat the batter hard for five minutes, lifting it as you go. The beating is the whole recipe: it whips air into the batter, and a spoonful dropped into water should float. Batter that sinks makes heavy, oily vada no matter how hot the oil is. Wet hands, not floured, for shaping.

  • The float test decides whether they will be light.
  • As little water as possible in the grinding.
  • Wet hands for shaping, and work quickly.

item.title: Svíčková
item.description: Svíčková — Czech beef pot roast with a blended root vegetable cream sauce and bread dumplings.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is the dish: the root vegetables that cooked under the beef are blended into it, which is why it needs no flour and tastes sweet and savoury at once. A splash of vinegar and a spoonful of cranberry at the end are traditional and necessary — the cream and root vegetables are sweet enough to need cutting.

  • Lard the beef. It is the difference between moist and dry after two hours.
  • Blend the vegetables into the sauce — that is the thickener.
  • Balance with vinegar and sugar at the end, tasting as you go.

item.title: Uttapam
item.description: Fermented rice and urad dal batter poured thick and topped with onion, tomato and chilli, cooked on one side then flipped.
item.content:encoded:
Uttapam wants batter a day past its best — slightly sour and slightly thicker than dosa batter, which is exactly what a dosa cook throws away. Put the toppings on the raw upper surface and press them in with the back of a spoon; scattered on loose, they fall off at the flip. One flip only, and thirty seconds on the second side.

  • Day-old batter is better than fresh here.
  • Press the toppings in or they fall off.
  • Thirty seconds on the second side, no more.

item.title: Vegetable Momos
item.description: Nepalese steamed dumplings filled with finely chopped cabbage, carrot and spring onion, pleated and served with tomato achar.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the shredded cabbage and let it stand fifteen minutes, then wring it out in a cloth. Cabbage is mostly water and the filling turns the wrapper to paste from the inside if you skip this — you will be surprised how much comes out. The wrapper is rolled thin at the edge and left thicker in the middle, so the pleats seal and the base does not tear.

  • Wring the cabbage out or the filling floods the wrapper.
  • Thin at the edge, thicker in the middle.
  • Stand a minute after steaming before you lift them.

item.title: Jjajangmyeon
item.description: Korean noodles in a fried black bean sauce with pork belly, onion, courgette and potato, thickened and served with cucumber.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the chunjang paste in oil on its own for two full minutes before anything else goes in. Straight from the tub it is bitter and raw and tastes faintly of ash; fried, it turns sweet, glossy and about two shades darker. Every recipe that skips this makes a sauce people describe as "bitter" without knowing why. Fry it in more oil than feels sensible, then pour the excess off.

  • Fry the chunjang alone for two minutes. It is the whole dish.
  • Dice everything the same size so it cooks together.
  • Serve the sauce on top and let people mix it themselves.

item.title: Trdelník
item.description: Trdelník — Czech spit cake of sweet dough rolled in sugar and walnuts and turned until caramelised.
item.content:encoded:
The sugar coating goes on before cooking, not after: as the dough turns, that sugar melts and then caramelises into a thin glassy shell, which is what gives trdelník its crunch against a soft interior. Overlapping the dough spiral by only a couple of millimetres keeps the shape hollow instead of solid.

  • Sugar before cooking, not after. That caramel shell is the point.
  • Overlap the spiral by millimetres, not centimetres, or the middle stays raw.
  • Roll the wound spit on the worktop to seal the seams.

item.title: Kimchi Fried Rice
item.description: Cold rice stir-fried with aged kimchi, gochujang and sesame oil, topped with a fried egg and seaweed.
item.content:encoded:
Use kimchi that has gone properly sour — the fizzing, three-weeks-open kind that is no longer pleasant to eat raw. Fresh kimchi is crunchy and mild and makes a fried rice that tastes of not much; sour kimchi has developed the acidity and depth the dish is built on. Fry the kimchi in oil for three minutes on its own before the rice, and use its juice too.

  • Sour kimchi, not fresh. Three weeks open is right.
  • Use the juice — it is half the seasoning.
  • Cold rice, pressed and lifted rather than stirred.

item.title: Budae Jjigae
item.description: Korean stew of kimchi, gochujang broth, sausages, tinned luncheon meat, tofu and instant noodles, cooked at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles go in for the last three minutes and not a moment sooner. They are there to be eaten from the pan while still springy, and a block that has sat in the broth for ten minutes turns to sludge and thickens everything around it. Arrange the ingredients in wedges rather than stirring them in, so each person can see what they are taking.

  • Noodles in for the last three minutes only.
  • Arrange in wedges rather than stirring.
  • The cheese is not a joke — it rounds off the chilli.

item.title: Pelmeni
item.description: Pelmeni — small Siberian dumplings with a thin wrapper and raw meat filling, boiled and buttered.
item.content:encoded:
The filling goes in raw with a splash of iced water worked into it, which turns to steam inside the sealed dumpling and gives the juicy interior that cooked-filling dumplings never have. The wrapper is rolled very thin and the dumplings are small, so the meat cooks through in the four minutes the pasta needs.

  • Iced water beaten into the raw filling. It is what makes them juicy.
  • Press every bit of air out before sealing, or they burst.
  • Freeze them on the tray first, then bag. They cook straight from frozen.

item.title: Doenjang Jjigae
item.description: Korean fermented soybean paste stew with courgette, potato, tofu and green chilli in an anchovy and kelp broth.
item.content:encoded:
Dissolve the doenjang in a ladleful of hot broth before it goes into the pot. Spooned in as a lump it never fully disperses — you get salty pockets and a bland broth, and stirring harder only breaks up the tofu. Make the broth with dried anchovy and kelp if you can; it takes ten minutes and is what separates this from a bowl of salty water.

  • Dissolve the paste in broth first, never spoon it in whole.
  • Anchovy and kelp broth takes ten minutes and doubles the dish.
  • Add tofu last and stop stirring once it is in.

item.title: Gyeranjjim
item.description: Korean steamed egg custard whisked with stock and salt, cooked in an earthenware pot until risen and softly set.
item.content:encoded:
The ratio is one and a half parts liquid to one part egg by volume, and it decides everything: less and you get a rubbery omelette, more and it will not set. Strain the mixture — the chalazae, those white cords attached to the yolk, will not break down and show as threads in the finished custard. Cover for the first half so the surface sets before the middle rises.

  • One and a half parts liquid to one of egg.
  • Sieve it, or you will find white threads.
  • Stir for the first three minutes, then leave it entirely alone.

item.title: Bossam
item.description: Whole pork belly simmered with doenjang, ginger and coffee, rested, sliced and served with lettuce, ssamjang and radish salad.
item.content:encoded:
Rest the belly wrapped in foil for fifteen minutes before slicing. Straight from the pot the fat is molten and the slices fall apart under the knife; rested, the collagen firms just enough to hold. A spoonful of instant coffee in the water is a standard Korean trick — it does not taste of coffee, it takes the porkiness off and darkens the meat.

  • Rest wrapped for fifteen minutes or it will not slice.
  • The coffee is for colour and cleanness, not flavour.
  • Slice thin — thick bossam is heavy.

item.title: Chicken Paprikash
item.description: Chicken paprikash — chicken braised with onions and sweet Hungarian paprika, finished with soured cream.
item.content:encoded:
Paprika burns at a surprisingly low temperature and turns bitter, which is why it goes into the pan off the heat, stirred into hot fat and onions with the burner switched off. Tempering the soured cream with hot sauce before it goes back in is what stops it curdling into threads.

  • Heat off before the paprika goes in. Burnt paprika ruins the whole pot.
  • Fifteen minutes on the onions. They are the body of the sauce.
  • Temper the soured cream. Straight from the tub it will split.

item.title: Hotteok
item.description: Yeasted Korean pancakes filled with brown sugar, cinnamon and peanuts, pressed flat and fried until the filling liquefies.
item.content:encoded:
The filling turns to molten syrup at about 150C and will burn a mouth badly, so these want three or four minutes standing before anyone bites one. Press them with an oiled spatula or the bottom of a cup rather than your hand, and press once firmly rather than repeatedly — repeated pressing splits the seam and the syrup escapes into the pan.

  • Seal the parcel completely or the syrup runs out.
  • One firm press, not several.
  • Four minutes standing. The filling is hotter than it looks.

item.title: Korean Corn Cheese
item.description: Sweetcorn mixed with mayonnaise and spring onion, topped with mozzarella and grilled until browned and bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
Drain the sweetcorn properly and then dry it in the pan for two minutes before anything else goes in. Tinned corn carries far more water than it looks, and wet corn makes the mayonnaise split under the grill so you get an oily pool under the cheese. Use low-moisture mozzarella for the same reason — fresh mozzarella weeps.

  • Dry the corn in the pan first or the mayonnaise splits.
  • Low-moisture mozzarella, not the kind in water.
  • Straight from the pan — it sets fast.

item.title: Lángos
item.description: Lángos — Hungarian deep-fried flatbread rubbed with garlic and topped with soured cream and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
A little mashed potato in the dough is the market-stall trick: it holds moisture, so the lángos stays soft for longer instead of turning leathery within minutes. Stretching the middle thinner than the edges gives the classic shape — a puffed rim around a crisp centre that holds the toppings.

  • Potato in the dough. It is what keeps a lángos soft.
  • Thin middle, thick rim. Stretch, do not roll.
  • Garlic water goes on while it is still hot from the oil.

item.title: Tonkatsu
item.description: Pork loin scored, breaded in flour, egg and panko and deep fried at 170C, rested and sliced, with tonkatsu sauce and shredded cabbage.
item.content:encoded:
Score through the line of fat and sinew that runs round the edge of a pork loin, every two centimetres. Left whole it contracts in the oil and curls the cutlet into a dome, so the middle never touches the fat and cooks unevenly. Fry at 170C, which is lower than instinct says: panko browns fast and pork loin this thick needs six minutes to come through.

  • Score the edge or the cutlet curls.
  • 170C, not hotter — the crust will be ahead of the meat otherwise.
  • Rest on a rack standing on edge, so the underside stays crisp.

item.title: Onigiri
item.description: Seasoned short-grain rice shaped into triangles around salmon or tuna filling and wrapped in toasted nori.
item.content:encoded:
Shape them while the rice is hot enough to be uncomfortable — around 60C. Cool rice has lost the surface starch that makes the grains hold together and an onigiri made from it falls apart in the hand. Wet your palms and salt them; the salt seasons the outside, which is the only part that gets any, and stops the rice sticking.

  • Shape hot, around sixty degrees.
  • Wet, salted palms every single time.
  • Wrap the nori just before eating if you want it crisp.

item.title: Shoyu Ramen
item.description: Clear chicken and kombu broth with a soy tare, rolled chashu pork, marinated egg and thin ramen noodles.
item.content:encoded:
Shoyu ramen is a clear soup and clarity is the whole discipline: it must never boil once the bones are in. A bare shiver at the surface for ninety minutes gives a broth you can see the bottom of; one hard boil emulsifies the fat and it turns cloudy and cannot be brought back. Skim in the first ten minutes, when the grey scum rises.

  • Never let it boil. That is the entire technique.
  • Skim hard in the first ten minutes.
  • Strain without pressing, or you undo the clarity.

item.title: Sarmale
item.description: Sarmale — Romanian cabbage rolls of pork, rice and dill cooked slowly with smoked meat.
item.content:encoded:
Pickled cabbage rather than fresh is what makes these Romanian rather than generic stuffed cabbage — the sourness cuts the fat and seasons the pork from the outside in. Layering smoked ribs or bacon between the rolls sends smoke through the whole pot as it cooks, which no amount of paprika replicates.

  • Pickled cabbage, not fresh. It is the defining ingredient.
  • Roll firmly but leave the rice room to swell.
  • A plate on top keeps the rolls submerged and stops them unravelling.

item.title: Ebi Fry
item.description: King prawns scored along the belly to keep them straight, breaded in panko and deep fried, served with tartare sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Prawns curl in hot oil because the muscle on the belly side contracts more than the back. Three or four shallow cuts across the underside sever that muscle, and then a firm press to straighten before breading — after which they stay straight through the fryer. It is the difference between a prawn that looks like a restaurant made it and one that looks like a comma.

  • Three cuts and a firm press, or they curl.
  • 180C and two and a half minutes — prawns need very little.
  • Tails on, for something to hold.

item.title: Japanese Curry Roux
item.description: A homemade Japanese curry roux of butter, flour, curry powder and garam masala cooked to a nut-brown paste, then made into sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The roux is cooked for twenty minutes over a low heat, which is far longer than a French one, and the colour goes from pale to the shade of peanut butter. That browning is where Japanese curry gets its particular round, almost sweet depth. Take it further and it turns bitter; stop early and the sauce tastes of raw flour, which is the fault of nearly every homemade version.

  • Twenty minutes for the roux. Peanut-butter colour is the target.
  • Loosen the roux with hot stock before it goes into the pan.
  • The grated apple is standard and it is what rounds the edges.

item.title: Mici
item.description: Mici — Romanian skinless grilled sausages of beef and lamb with garlic and a springy texture.
item.content:encoded:
The bounce that defines mici comes from two things: bicarbonate of soda, which raises the pH so the proteins hold more water, and beating cold stock into the mince until it is emulsified and tacky. Both need an overnight rest in the fridge to take effect, which is why same-day mici are always disappointing.

  • Overnight in the fridge. Without it there is no spring.
  • Beat the stock in properly until the mince turns tacky.
  • Very hot coals. Mici want char, not a gentle cook.

item.title: Panang Curry
item.description: Thai panang curry of beef or chicken simmered in a thick coconut and peanut curry paste, finished with kaffir lime leaf.
item.content:encoded:
Crack the coconut cream first: fry the thick top of the tin, without the watery part, until the oil separates and pools. Then fry the paste in that oil for two minutes. Nearly every home version tips paste and liquid in together and produces a thin curry with a flat, raw edge — the separated oil is what carries the spice and gives panang its gloss.

  • Crack the cream before the paste goes in.
  • Panang is thick — do not thin it out with stock.
  • Shredded lime leaf at the end, not cooked in.

item.title: Thai Yellow Curry
item.description: Thai yellow curry of chicken and potato simmered in coconut milk with turmeric-based curry paste and fish sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Yellow curry has Indian ancestry — turmeric, cumin and coriander seed came through the Muslim trading routes — which is why it takes potato happily where a green curry does not. Cut the potato in three-centimetre chunks and give it fifteen minutes: smaller and it disintegrates into the sauce and thickens it to paste.

  • Three-centimetre potato, or it dissolves.
  • Crack the coconut cream before the paste.
  • Lime juice off the heat, or it turns bitter.

item.title: Moo Ping
item.description: Thai grilled pork skewers marinated in coconut milk, garlic, white pepper and palm sugar, basted while grilling.
item.content:encoded:
The coconut milk in the marinade is not for flavour so much as for basting — it keeps the surface from drying while the sugar caramelises, and it is why moo ping comes off the grill glossy rather than leathery. Baste every time you turn them. White pepper rather than black is the Thai signature and tastes distinctly different: floral and hot rather than woody.

  • Baste at every turn — that is what makes them glossy.
  • White pepper, not black. It is a different flavour.
  • Weave the meat so it lies flat and cooks evenly.

item.title: Adjaruli Khachapuri
item.description: Adjaruli khachapuri — a Georgian bread boat of molten cheese finished with an egg yolk and butter.
item.content:encoded:
The cheese blend matters more than the dough: sulguni alone is stringy and mild, so it is cut with a salty brined cheese and a little mozzarella for pull. The yolk goes in during the last two minutes of baking so it stays raw enough to become a sauce when you stir it through the hot cheese.

  • Yolk in for the last two minutes only. It should still run.
  • Salty cheese blend. Mozzarella alone gives you a bread pizza.
  • Very hot oven with a preheated tray, or the base goes pale and soft.

item.title: Pad Woon Sen
item.description: Thai stir-fried mung bean glass noodles with prawns, egg and vegetables in a soy, oyster and fish sauce dressing.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the glass noodles in warm water, not boiling, and stop while they still have a firm core. They finish in the wok by absorbing the sauce, and noodles that arrive fully soft turn to jelly and clump into one lump. Cut them through with scissors once soaked, or you will be fighting a single continuous noodle for the whole stir-fry.

  • Warm water, firm core. They finish in the wok.
  • Scissors through the noodles after soaking.
  • Everything out and back in, so nothing overcooks.

item.title: Crying Tiger Beef
item.description: Thai grilled steak rested and sliced, served with nam jim jaew of toasted rice powder, chilli, lime and fish sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Toasted rice powder is what makes nam jim jaew taste Thai rather than merely hot and sour. Raw sticky rice toasted dry until it is the colour of straw and then pounded gives a nutty, slightly gritty body that thickens the sauce without any fat in it. It takes five minutes and nothing else does the same job.

  • Toast and pound the rice. It is what the sauce is built on.
  • Rest eight minutes, then slice across the grain.
  • Make the sauce first so the flavours have time to meet.

item.title: Khinkali
item.description: Khinkali — large pleated Georgian dumplings with a soupy meat filling and a thick twisted knot.
item.content:encoded:
The soup inside is not stock added as jelly but water beaten into the raw mince, which renders and mixes with the meat juices as the dumpling boils. The thick knot at the top exists so you have somewhere to hold while you bite a hole and drink the broth — it is a handle, and leaving it uneaten is the convention.

  • The filling should look far too wet. That water becomes the broth.
  • Thin rim, thicker centre. It is what makes the pleating possible.
  • Stir the water before they go in, and never let it boil violently.

item.title: Bánh Xèo
item.description: Vietnamese crisp turmeric rice flour crêpes filled with pork, prawn and beansprouts, eaten wrapped in lettuce with nuoc cham.
item.content:encoded:
The batter must be thin as single cream and the pan properly hot, and you pour it in and immediately tilt to spread — hesitate and it sets in a thick patch in the middle. The crispness comes from a generous amount of oil round the edge and from leaving it alone: no poking, no lifting to check, five minutes uncovered and then a lid for one.

  • Batter as thin as single cream, and tilt the moment it goes in.
  • Oil round the rim is what crisps the edge.
  • Do not touch it for five minutes.

item.title: Phở Gà
item.description: Vietnamese chicken noodle soup with a clear broth of charred ginger, onion and toasted spices, poached chicken and rice noodles.
item.content:encoded:
Char the ginger and onion black in patches directly over a flame before they go into the pot. It is not decoration: the burnt sugars give the broth its particular smoky sweetness, and pho made with raw aromatics tastes thin and vegetal in a way people notice without being able to name. Blanch the chicken first and throw that water away — it is where the scum comes from.

  • Blanch and discard the first water — it takes the scum with it.
  • Char the aromatics black in patches.
  • A bare simmer keeps it clear.

item.title: Bún Thịt Nướng
item.description: Vietnamese grilled lemongrass pork served over cold rice vermicelli with herbs, pickled carrot and nuoc cham.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles are dressed with nothing and served at room temperature; all the seasoning arrives as nuoc cham poured over at the table. That is deliberate — the contrast between the hot charred pork, the cool noodles and the sharp dressing is the dish. Rinse the cooked vermicelli under cold water and drain it hard, or the bowl turns into a wet clump.

  • Noodles cold and drained hard.
  • Char the pork properly — the black edges are the flavour.
  • Dress at the table, not in the kitchen.

item.title: Lobio
item.description: Lobio — Georgian kidney bean stew with walnuts, coriander and blue fenugreek, served with cornbread.
item.content:encoded:
Blue fenugreek and dried marigold are what make this taste Georgian rather than generically beany, and both go in at the end because their aroma is volatile. Mashing about a third of the beans thickens the pot without flour and gives the two textures the dish is meant to have.

  • Salt only after the beans are tender.
  • Spices off the heat at the end. Cooking them dulls the whole dish.
  • Mash a third, leave the rest whole. Two textures, one pot.

item.title: Bò Kho
item.description: Vietnamese beef stew of shin simmered two hours with lemongrass, star anise, annatto oil and tomato, with carrots.
item.content:encoded:
Annatto seeds fried in oil for one minute and then strained out give bo kho its red colour without any heat or flavour of their own. It is the reason a proper bowl looks the way it does, and paprika is not a substitute — it muddies the broth. Beef shin, not braising steak: the connective tissue is what makes the sauce sticky rather than watery.

  • Annatto for colour — strain the seeds out after a minute.
  • Beef shin, not braising steak.
  • Carrots in for the last thirty minutes only.

item.title: Chicken Fajitas
item.description: Chicken thigh marinated in lime, cumin and smoked paprika, seared with peppers and onion and served with warm tortillas.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the chicken and the vegetables separately and combine them at the end. Together in one pan they release enough water to stew, and fajitas that have stewed are grey and limp — the whole appeal is char. Get the pan properly hot, work in two batches, and do not stir for the first ninety seconds of either.

  • Two batches. Together they stew.
  • Do not stir for the first ninety seconds.
  • The pan must smoke before anything goes in.

item.title: Greek Lemon Potatoes
item.description: Greek lemon potatoes — roasted in lemon juice, olive oil and stock until the liquid reduces to a glaze.
item.content:encoded:
These are braised before they are roasted: the potatoes sit in liquid for the first forty minutes, absorbing lemon and oregano all the way through, and only crisp once the liquid has boiled away. Cutting them into large wedges gives enough surface for the glaze without them collapsing during the wet stage.

  • One layer, always. Two layers gives you boiled potatoes.
  • Do not skimp on the lemon. It should taste sharp before it goes in the oven.
  • Scrape the tin at the end — that is the best part of the dish.

item.title: Carne Asada
item.description: Skirt steak marinated in lime, orange, garlic and cumin, grilled over high heat, rested and sliced across the grain.
item.content:encoded:
Skirt steak has coarse fibres running in one obvious direction and everything depends on cutting across them. Sliced with the grain it is inedibly chewy no matter how well it was cooked; across, the same steak is tender. Find the direction before you cook, because char makes it harder to see afterwards.

  • Across the grain, always. Nothing else matters as much.
  • One hour in the marinade, not overnight.
  • Rest eight minutes before the knife goes near it.

item.title: Pico de Gallo
item.description: Fresh Mexican salsa of diced tomato, white onion, jalapeño, coriander and lime juice, salted and drained briefly.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the diced tomato on its own for ten minutes and pour off what collects. Tomato is mostly water and unsalted pico turns into a watery bowl within half an hour — drained, it stays a salsa. Rinse the diced onion under cold water too: it takes the raw sulphurous bite off without losing the crunch.

  • Salt and drain the tomato, or it floods.
  • Rinse the onion to take the raw bite off.
  • Season harder than feels right — it dilutes on the plate.

item.title: Salsa Verde
item.description: Mexican green salsa of tomatillos, serrano chillies, onion and garlic charred under a grill and blended with coriander and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Char the tomatillos rather than boiling them. Boiled, they are sour and one-dimensional; blistered black in patches under a hot grill, the sugars caramelise and the whole thing gains a smoky sweetness that balances the acid. Blend it only briefly — a salsa blitzed smooth goes pale and foamy, and it should stay a little coarse and dark green.

  • Char, do not boil.
  • Pulse, do not blend, or it goes pale and foamy.
  • Keep the tray juices — they are concentrated flavour.

item.title: Dolmades
item.description: Dolmades — vine leaves rolled around herbed rice with pine nuts, simmered with lemon and olive oil.
item.content:encoded:
The rice goes in raw and only part-cooked in the pan first, so it swells inside the leaf and packs it tight — pre-cooked rice gives a loose, mushy roll. A plate weighing the dolmades down keeps them submerged and stops them unrolling as the rice expands.

  • Raw rice, part-cooked in the pan. Cooked rice makes mush.
  • Roll firmly, not tightly. The rice has to double.
  • A plate on top is non-negotiable or they will unravel.

item.title: Chile Relleno
item.description: Poblano chillies charred and peeled, stuffed with cheese, coated in whipped egg batter and fried, served in a light tomato broth.
item.content:encoded:
Whip the whites to firm peaks and fold the yolks in rather than beating them together. A whole-egg batter runs off the chilli and fries into a thin skin; a whipped one clings in a thick puffed jacket that is the entire character of the dish. Dust the chilli with cornflour first — the batter needs something to grip on a surface as slippery as a peeled poblano.

  • Whites to firm peaks, yolks folded in after.
  • Cornflour dust or the batter slides off.
  • Spoon hot oil over the top as it fries so the upper side sets.

item.title: Sopa de Fideo
item.description: Mexican soup of fideo noodles toasted in oil and simmered in a blended tomato, onion and garlic broth.
item.content:encoded:
Toast the noodles in oil until they are the colour of a digestive biscuit before any liquid goes near them. It takes about four minutes of constant stirring and it changes the entire flavour from bland to nutty — untoasted fideo makes a soup that tastes of tomato and nothing else. They go from golden to burnt in about twenty seconds, so do not walk away.

  • Toast to biscuit-brown and do not look away.
  • Stand back when the tomato hits the hot oil.
  • Lime at the table is not optional.

item.title: Greek Yoghurt with Honey and Walnuts
item.description: Greek yoghurt with honey and walnuts — strained yoghurt, thyme honey and toasted walnuts.
item.content:encoded:
Straining ordinary Greek yoghurt for a few hours takes it from thick to genuinely dense, which changes how the honey sits on it — it pools instead of sinking. Toasting the walnuts is what removes their tannic edge, and doing it in a dry pan rather than the oven lets you stop at the exact moment they smell right.

  • Strain the yoghurt if you have three hours. It is a different dish.
  • Toast the walnuts and cool them off the pan.
  • A pinch of salt on top makes the honey taste more like honey.

item.title: Arroz con Leche
item.description: Mexican rice pudding simmered on the hob with whole milk, condensed milk, cinnamon and lime peel, served warm or cold.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the rice in water with the cinnamon and lime peel first, until the water has gone, and only then add the milk. Rice started in milk takes twice as long and scorches on the bottom before the grains are through, because milk conducts heat badly and its sugars catch. This way the grain is already soft when the milk arrives and it only has to thicken.

  • Water first, milk second.
  • Scrape the bottom every few minutes or it catches.
  • Take it off looser than you want it — it sets as it cools.

item.title: Menudo
item.description: Mexican tripe and hominy soup in a guajillo and ancho chilli broth, simmered three hours and served with lime, onion and oregano.
item.content:encoded:
Scrub and blanch the tripe twice, discarding the water each time, before it goes anywhere near the chillies. Tripe carries a strong smell that will otherwise dominate everything, and two changes of water takes it out completely. After that it is only time: three hours at a bare simmer turns it from rubber to something that yields between the teeth.

  • Two blanches, both discarded. That is what takes the smell out.
  • Strain the chilli purée or the broth is gritty.
  • The table condiments are part of the dish, not a garnish.

item.title: Pot Roast
item.description: Beef chuck browned and slow-braised with onion, carrot, potato and stock until fork-tender, with a thickened pan gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Chuck, and only chuck. It is the cut with enough connective tissue to turn to gelatin over three hours, which is what makes a pot roast sticky and rich rather than dry — a leaner joint like topside will be stringy at the same temperature for the same time and there is nothing to be done about it. Add the vegetables in the last hour or they dissolve.

  • Chuck. A leaner joint will be stringy however long you give it.
  • Vegetables in for the last hour only.
  • Uncover for the last twenty minutes to reduce the gravy.

item.title: İskender Kebab
item.description: İskender kebab — sliced lamb over pide bread with tomato sauce, browned butter and yoghurt.
item.content:encoded:
The dish is assembled hot and eaten immediately because the bread has a short window between soaking up sauce and disintegrating. The butter is browned separately and poured over at the table for the same reason it is done that way in Bursa: the noise and the smell are part of it, and the butter has to hit while everything is still hot.

  • Sear the lamb hot and fast in batches. Crowded lamb turns grey and tough.
  • Brown the butter properly and pour it at the table while it sizzles.
  • Assemble and serve within a minute. This dish does not wait.

item.title: Sloppy Joe Skillet
item.description: Minced beef simmered with onion, pepper, tomato, brown sugar and Worcestershire into a thick sandwich filling.
item.content:encoded:
Brown the mince properly before any liquid goes in — spread it out, leave it four minutes, and only then break it up. Mince stirred from the moment it hits the pan releases water and simmers grey, and no amount of sauce afterwards puts back the flavour that browning would have made. The sauce wants to be thick enough to sit on a bun, not run off it.

  • Four minutes untouched before you break the mince up.
  • Thick enough to hold on a spoon, or it soaks the bun.
  • Vinegar at the end balances the sugar.

item.title: Potato Salad
item.description: Waxy potatoes boiled, dressed warm with vinegar then mayonnaise, mustard, egg, celery and chives.
item.content:encoded:
Splash the vinegar over the potatoes while they are still hot, before the mayonnaise. Warm potato absorbs it; cold potato does not, and a salad dressed only when cool tastes of mayonnaise sitting on top of bland potato. Use a waxy variety — floury ones break down into a mash the moment you fold them.

  • Vinegar on hot potatoes. That is the step everyone skips.
  • Waxy, not floury.
  • An hour in the fridge — it needs to settle.

item.title: Turkish Lentil Soup
item.description: Turkish lentil soup — red lentils blended smooth with a chilli butter drizzle and plenty of lemon.
item.content:encoded:
The soup itself is deliberately plain — the flavour arrives at the end with the chilli butter and the lemon, which is why a version tasted before those go in always seems disappointing. Blending it completely smooth is not optional in Turkey; texture is what separates mercimek çorbası from a lentil stew.

  • Blend for longer than you think. Silky, not grainy.
  • The chilli butter and the lemon are the recipe, not garnishes.
  • Rinse the lentils until the water is clear or the soup will taste dusty.

item.title: Coleslaw
item.description: Shredded white cabbage and carrot salted and drained, then dressed with mayonnaise, cider vinegar, mustard and sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the shredded cabbage and let it drain for thirty minutes, then squeeze it. Cabbage is about ninety per cent water and undrained coleslaw turns into a pool within the hour — this is why shop-bought slaw sits in liquid. Squeezed, it stays crisp for days and the dressing coats instead of being diluted.

  • Salt, drain and squeeze. That is the whole difference.
  • Sharp before sweet.
  • Chives at the end so they stay green.

item.title: Egg Salad
item.description: Hard-boiled eggs chopped and folded with mayonnaise, Dijon mustard, chives and celery for sandwiches.
item.content:encoded:
Chop the eggs by hand and leave the pieces uneven. Mashed with a fork it becomes a paste and tastes of mayonnaise; chopped, you get whole pieces of white and crumbled yolk, and the yolk is what thickens the dressing while the white gives it something to bite. Nine minutes gives a yolk that is set but still bright yellow rather than grey.

  • Chop, never mash.
  • Nine minutes for a yellow yolk, not a grey one.
  • Cool them properly or the shells will not come off cleanly.

item.title: Tuna Salad
item.description: Tinned tuna flaked and mixed with mayonnaise, celery, red onion, lemon and dill for sandwiches or salad.
item.content:encoded:
Drain the tuna thoroughly and press it in the tin lid — every spoonful of oil or brine left in makes the finished salad looser and blander, and you cannot correct it by adding more mayonnaise. Celery diced small is what stops the whole thing being one soft texture, and it is the difference between a good tuna salad and a paste. Tuna tinned in oil gives a richer result than the spring water used here, if you would rather use it — just drain it even more thoroughly, since oil clings harder than brine.

  • Press the tin lid down hard. Every drop matters.
  • Leave some flakes large.
  • Capers do the same job as pickle, with more edge.

item.title: Künefe
item.description: Künefe — shredded kadayif pastry around melting cheese, fried in butter and soaked in cold syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Hot pastry and cold syrup is the rule for every syrup dessert: the temperature difference makes the syrup absorb fast without softening the crust. The cheese has to be unsalted and low-moisture so it stretches rather than releasing water into the pastry, which is why fresh mozzarella is the wrong choice.

  • Hot pastry, cold syrup. Never the other way round.
  • Press it hard, twice. Loose kadayif falls apart when you turn it.
  • Serve within minutes — the cheese stops stretching as it cools.

item.title: Chicken Salad
item.description: Shredded cooked chicken folded with mayonnaise, yoghurt, celery, grapes and toasted pecans, seasoned with lemon and tarragon.
item.content:encoded:
Shred the chicken along the grain rather than dicing it. Shreds hold dressing in their fibres and read as chicken; neat cubes shed it and taste like something from a packet. Half yoghurt and half mayonnaise keeps the dressing light enough that you can still taste the meat, which a full-mayonnaise version buries.

  • Shred along the grain, do not dice.
  • Half yoghurt keeps it light enough to taste the chicken.
  • Pecans in last or they go soft.

item.title: Fudge Brownies
item.description: Fudge brownies made with melted dark chocolate and butter, whisked eggs and sugar for a crackled top, baked until barely set.
item.content:encoded:
The papery crackled top comes from dissolving the sugar into the eggs before the chocolate goes in — whisk them for four minutes until pale and thick, and a thin meringue-like layer forms on top during baking. Take the tin out when the middle still wobbles; brownies carry on cooking in the tin for another ten minutes and one baked until a skewer comes out clean is a chocolate cake.

  • Four minutes of whisking makes the crackled top.
  • Out while the middle wobbles.
  • Cool completely in the tin or they fall apart.

item.title: Shish Taouk
item.description: Shish taouk — Lebanese chicken skewers marinated in yoghurt, garlic and lemon, grilled and served with toum.
item.content:encoded:
Yoghurt marinades tenderise gently because their acid is mild and their calcium activates enzymes in the meat — unlike a lemon-only marinade, which turns the surface chalky if left overnight. The tomato purée is there for colour more than flavour: it is what gives shish taouk its characteristic orange edge under the grill.

  • Thighs, not breast. Breast dries out before it chars.
  • A small gap between cubes on the skewer, or the sides steam.
  • For toum, add the oil painfully slowly at the start. It breaks if you rush.

item.title: Fluffy Pancakes
item.description: Thick American buttermilk pancakes raised with baking powder and soda, rested briefly and cooked on a medium griddle.
item.content:encoded:
Stop mixing while the batter still has lumps in it. Every stir past the point where the flour is just wet develops gluten, and gluten makes pancakes chewy and flat — the lumps hydrate on their own during the rest and disappear in the pan. A rested batter also gives the raising agents a head start, which is where the height comes from.

  • Lumpy batter. Ten folds, then stop.
  • Medium heat — high heat browns them before they rise.
  • One flip only.

item.title: Garlic Bread
item.description: Baguette split and filled with a garlic, parsley and butter paste, wrapped in foil and baked, then finished uncovered to crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Bake it wrapped in foil first and only uncover for the last five minutes. Wrapped, the butter melts through the crumb and steams the middle soft; uncovered from the start, the outside is dark before the inside has taken up anything. Grate the garlic rather than chopping it — pieces of chopped garlic scorch and turn acrid in the oven, and a paste distributes evenly.

  • Grate the garlic — chopped pieces burn.
  • Foil on for ten minutes, off for five.
  • Cut almost through so it stays one loaf until it reaches the table.

item.title: Pesto Pasta
item.description: Fresh basil pesto with pine nuts, garlic and hard cheese, tossed with hot pasta and starchy cooking water off the heat.
item.content:encoded:
Pesto is never cooked. Add it to the pasta off the heat and loosen it with the starchy cooking water, which emulsifies the oil into a sauce that clings — heat it in the pan and the basil turns khaki and bitter and the cheese goes stringy. Keep a mugful of the cooking water back before you drain; it is the only thing that turns pesto from a paste into a sauce.

  • Never heat the pesto.
  • Keep a mug of pasta water back before draining.
  • Cool the pine nuts or they turn the basil dark.

item.title: Moutabal
item.description: Moutabal — charred aubergine whipped with tahini, lemon and garlic into a smoky dip.
item.content:encoded:
The smoke is the dish, and it only comes from direct flame — an oven-roasted aubergine gives you a sweet purée with no smokiness at all. Draining the flesh in a sieve for twenty minutes is the other essential step: aubergine holds a surprising amount of water, and left in, it makes the dip loose and bland.

  • Open flame or nothing. An oven gives you sweet purée, not moutabal.
  • Drain the flesh for twenty minutes. It is what concentrates the flavour.
  • Chop by hand. A processor makes it gluey.

item.title: Minestrone
item.description: Italian vegetable soup with a soffritto base, borlotti beans, tomato and small pasta, finished with olive oil.
item.content:encoded:
Give the soffritto — onion, carrot and celery — a full twelve minutes over a low heat before anything else goes in. It should collapse and sweeten rather than colour, and it is the whole foundation: rushed for four minutes, the soup tastes of stock and vegetables sitting separately in it rather than of one thing. The pasta goes in for the last eight minutes only.

  • Twelve minutes on the soffritto. It is the foundation.
  • Pasta for the last eight minutes only.
  • A Parmesan rind in the pot is free depth if you have one.

item.title: Spaghetti alla Puttanesca
item.description: Spaghetti in a sauce of anchovies melted in oil with garlic, chilli, olives, capers and tomatoes, cooked fast and finished with parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Melt the anchovies into the warm oil until they disappear completely — two or three minutes over a low heat, pressing them with a spoon. Left as pieces they are salty lumps that people pick out; dissolved, they are invisible and the sauce simply tastes deeper. Do not add salt until the very end: anchovies, olives and capers between them usually make it unnecessary.

  • Start the anchovies in cold oil so they melt rather than fry.
  • No salt until the end.
  • Toss the pasta in the sauce, never sauce on top.

item.title: Maamoul
item.description: Maamoul — semolina shortbread filled with dates or nuts, pressed in carved moulds and baked pale.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is made a day ahead so the coarse semolina can hydrate fully — mixed and baked the same day it stays gritty and the cookies crack. They are baked only until the base colours and the top is still pale, because a browned maamoul has gone from tender to dry.

  • Rest the buttered semolina overnight. There is no way round it.
  • Bake pale. A browned maamoul is a dry maamoul.
  • Cool completely before moving them or they will break.

item.title: Ragù alla Bolognese
item.description: A long-cooked Bolognese ragù of beef and pork with soffritto, milk, white wine and a small amount of tomato, served with tagliatelle.
item.content:encoded:
The milk goes in before the wine and before the tomato, and it must be absorbed completely before anything else joins it. The lactose and the fat tenderise the meat and round off the acidity that comes later — a ragù made without it is sharper and grainier. The tomato is a spoonful of purée and half a tin, not a whole one: this is a meat sauce, not a tomato one.

  • Milk first, and let it go completely before the wine.
  • Very fine dice on the soffritto — it should disappear.
  • Two hours at a bare simmer, uncovered.

item.title: Lamb Kleftiko
item.description: Greek lamb shoulder marinated with lemon, garlic and oregano, sealed in parchment with potatoes and slow-roasted until falling apart.
item.content:encoded:
The parcel must be genuinely sealed, and paper alone will not do it — line it with foil. Everything about kleftiko depends on the steam staying in: it is what cooks the lamb to falling apart without drying, and what makes the potatoes taste of lemon and lamb fat rather than of oven. If steam escapes you have a roast, which is a fine thing but not this.

  • Foil under the parchment. Paper alone leaks.
  • Crimp every edge — steam is the whole method.
  • Open it in front of people. That is the dish.

item.title: Tiropita
item.description: Greek cheese pie of feta, ricotta and egg layered between buttered filo sheets and baked until crisp and golden.
item.content:encoded:
Score the pie into portions before baking, cutting down through the top layers of filo but not into the filling. Baked whole and cut afterwards, the crisp top shatters and slides off in pieces as the knife goes through. Scored first, each portion keeps its lid. Keep the unused filo under a damp cloth: it dries to uselessness in about three minutes uncovered.

  • Score before baking, not after.
  • Damp cloth over the filo at all times.
  • A flick of cold water on top helps it blister.

item.title: Ghormeh Sabzi
item.description: Ghormeh sabzi — Persian herb stew with lamb, kidney beans and dried limes, cooked long and slow.
item.content:encoded:
The herbs have to be fried for a long time — twenty minutes or more, until they darken and the volume collapses by three quarters — because that is where the stew's depth comes from. Dried limes must be pierced before they go in, or they float and never release the sour, slightly fermented note that defines the dish.

  • Twenty-five minutes on the herbs. This is the step that makes the stew.
  • Pierce the dried limes or they will bob about doing nothing.
  • Wait for the oil to rise to the surface. That is when it is done.

item.title: Youvetsi
item.description: Greek beef and orzo baked together in a tomato and cinnamon sauce until the orzo absorbs the liquid, topped with kefalotyri.
item.content:encoded:
The orzo goes in raw and cooks in the sauce, absorbing it, so the liquid has to be measured — about three parts liquid to one part orzo by volume. Boiled separately and stirred in, it tastes of nothing and the sauce stays thin. Stir once at the halfway point and no more, or the starch releases and the dish turns claggy.

  • Orzo raw into the sauce, never boiled first.
  • Stir once, at the halfway point.
  • Rest ten minutes — the orzo keeps absorbing.

item.title: Adana Kebab
item.description: Turkish minced lamb kebab with red pepper flakes and fat, kneaded and pressed onto flat skewers, grilled and served with sumac onions.
item.content:encoded:
The mince needs to be at least twenty per cent fat and it must be kneaded hard for five minutes until it turns sticky and pulls away from the bowl in one mass. That is what makes it cling to a flat skewer over a fire instead of falling into it. Chill the kneaded mixture before shaping — cold fat holds, warm fat slides.

  • Twenty per cent fat, and knead until it is sticky.
  • An hour in the fridge before shaping.
  • Flat skewers, or it rolls and falls off.

item.title: Fesenjan
item.description: Fesenjan — Persian chicken braised in ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses until dark and glossy.
item.content:encoded:
The walnuts must be ground fine and then cooked long enough for their oil to separate and darken the sauce, which takes at least an hour and cannot be hurried. Balancing the pomegranate molasses with sugar at the end is a matter of taste and of brand: molasses varies enormously in sourness, so the recipe has to be adjusted by tasting rather than by measurement.

  • Grind the walnuts fine but stop before they become butter.
  • The long simmer before the chicken goes back is where the colour comes from.
  • Taste and balance at the end. Molasses brands are wildly different.

item.title: Manti
item.description: Tiny Turkish lamb dumplings boiled and served under garlic yoghurt with a paprika and mint butter poured over.
item.content:encoded:
Manti are meant to be tiny — the traditional test is forty in a spoon — and small is not just for show: the ratio of thin dough to filling is what makes them delicate, and a large manti is a heavy thing. Roll the dough as thin as you can see your hand through. Bring the yoghurt to room temperature before it meets the hot dumplings or it splits.

  • Tiny. Roll the dough until you can nearly see through it.
  • Room-temperature yoghurt, or it splits on contact.
  • Freeze them raw on a tray if you make a big batch.

item.title: Karnıyarık
item.description: Turkish aubergines fried whole, split and stuffed with minced lamb, onion and tomato, then baked with peppers and tomato sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Peel the aubergines in stripes rather than fully or not at all. Left whole-skinned they are tough to cut on the plate; peeled completely they collapse in the pan. Alternating stripes hold the shape together while letting the flesh soften. Salt them for twenty minutes first — it draws water out so they absorb far less oil in the frying.

  • Stripes, not full peeling.
  • Salt for twenty minutes so they drink less oil.
  • Split without cutting through, or the filling escapes.

item.title: Şakşuka
item.description: Turkish meze of fried aubergine, courgette and pepper in a garlic and tomato sauce, served at room temperature.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the vegetables separately and drain them properly on paper before the sauce goes anywhere near. Cooked together they steam and turn to a wet mush, and şakşuka is meant to be distinct pieces sitting in sauce. It is also served at room temperature, not hot — the flavours only come together as it cools, so make it an hour ahead.

  • Fry each vegetable separately and drain each one.
  • Room temperature, never hot.
  • An hour standing is part of the recipe.

item.title: Tahdig
item.description: Tahdig — the golden Persian rice crust, made by steaming parboiled basmati over yoghurt rice or potato.
item.content:encoded:
Parboiling and draining the rice removes surface starch so the grains steam separately, and it is the only way tahdig works — a pot of absorbed-water rice goes gummy against the base rather than crisping. The wrapped lid catches condensation that would otherwise drip back down and soften the crust.

  • Parboil and drain. Absorption-method rice will never make tahdig.
  • The tea towel round the lid keeps the crust dry. Do not skip it.
  • Cold water under the pot for a minute before you turn it out.

item.title: Turkish Pilav
item.description: Turkish rice pilav with orzo toasted in butter, rice soaked and rinsed, cooked with stock and rested under a cloth.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the rice in warm salted water for fifteen minutes and then rinse it until the water runs clear. That removes the surface starch that makes grains stick, which is the entire difference between pilav and a sticky pan of rice. Rest it under a cloth at the end: the cloth absorbs the steam that would otherwise condense on the lid and drip back in.

  • Rinse until the water is clear. That is the whole technique.
  • Toast the orzo brown before the rice goes in.
  • A cloth under the lid for the rest.

item.title: Albóndigas
item.description: Spanish meatballs of pork and beef in a tomato, almond and saffron sauce thickened with fried bread and almonds.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is thickened with a picada — fried bread and almonds pounded together — rather than with flour. It is the classic Spanish method and it does two jobs at once: it gives body and it adds a toasted, nutty flavour that flour cannot. Fry the bread and almonds until properly golden, because that colour is the flavour.

  • The picada, not flour. Fry the bread and nuts properly golden.
  • Small meatballs — this is a tapa, not a main.
  • Chill them before browning so they hold.

item.title: Joojeh Kabab
item.description: Joojeh kabab — Persian saffron chicken skewers marinated overnight and basted with saffron butter.
item.content:encoded:
Grated onion is the workhorse of Persian marinades: its enzymes break down the surface proteins far more gently than acid does, so the chicken stays juicy through a long marinade. Saffron ground with sugar and steeped in hot water gives four times the colour of threads dropped in whole.

  • Grate the onion, do not chop it. The juice is the point.
  • Grind saffron with sugar before steeping — far more colour.
  • Flat skewers. Round ones let the meat spin when you turn them.

item.title: Pollo al Ajillo
item.description: Spanish chicken browned in olive oil with whole garlic cloves and finished with dry sherry, bay and parsley.
item.content:encoded:
The garlic cloves go in whole and unpeeled, fried gently in the oil before the chicken and then returned at the end. Whole, they turn sweet and creamy inside their skins; sliced or crushed at that heat they burn black in ninety seconds and make the whole pan bitter. Squeeze them out of their skins onto the bread at the table.

  • Whole unpeeled cloves. Anything else burns.
  • Fino sherry, not cooking wine.
  • Squeeze the garlic onto bread at the table.

item.title: Tarta de Santiago
item.description: Galician almond cake made with ground almonds, eggs, sugar and citrus zest, baked and dusted through a cross stencil.
item.content:encoded:
Whisk the eggs and sugar for a full five minutes until they hold a ribbon on the surface. There is no flour and no raising agent, so every bit of the cake's lift comes from air beaten into the eggs — undermixed, it bakes into a dense almond slab. Fold the almonds in gently and stop the moment they disappear.

  • Five minutes of whisking. It is the only lift the cake gets.
  • Fold the almonds in, do not beat them.
  • Lift the stencil straight up or you smudge the cross.

item.title: Flapjacks
item.description: British oat flapjacks made with butter, golden syrup and light brown sugar, baked until golden at the edges and cut while warm.
item.content:encoded:
Cut them while they are still warm and leave them in the tin to cool completely. Cut cold, they shatter; lifted out warm, they fall apart. Score them at about ten minutes out of the oven and then do not touch them for an hour. Underbaking by three minutes gives chewy flapjacks and overbaking by three gives crunchy ones — both are correct, so decide which you want.

  • Score warm, lift out cold.
  • Press the mixture down hard or they crumble.
  • Twenty-five minutes chewy, twenty-eight crisp. Pick one.

item.title: Ash Reshteh
item.description: Ash reshteh — thick Persian noodle soup with beans, lentils and greens, topped with mint oil and kashk.
item.content:encoded:
Reshteh noodles are slightly salty and made to break down a little, thickening the soup as they cook — Italian pasta is a poor substitute because it stays separate. The three toppings are not optional garnish: fried mint gives bitterness, crisp onion gives sweetness, and kashk gives sourness, and the soup underneath is deliberately plain so they can do that work.

  • Mint into oil off the heat. Burnt mint is acrid and there is no fixing it.
  • Thick enough for a spoon to leave a trail. Ash is not a broth.
  • All three toppings, every bowl. That is where the flavour is.

item.title: Vegetable Stir-Fry
item.description: Mixed vegetables stir-fried over a high heat in a soy, garlic and ginger sauce thickened with a cornflour slurry.
item.content:encoded:
Cut everything to a thickness that matches how long it takes to cook, not to look tidy: broccoli in thin florets, carrots in matchsticks, peppers in wide strips. Then add them in order of hardness, thirty to sixty seconds apart. A stir-fry that goes in all at once is either raw carrot or grey broccoli, and usually both.

  • Cut to cooking time, not to neatness.
  • Hardest vegetables first, softest last.
  • The slurry goes into a boiling pan, moving.

item.title: Ras Malai
item.description: Homemade chenna kneaded smooth, poached in syrup, flattened and steeped in reduced cardamom and saffron milk with pistachios.
item.content:encoded:
Knead the drained chenna with the heel of your hand for a full eight minutes, until it stops being grainy and goes greasy and smooth. That is the entire difference between ras malai that stays soft and ras malai that sets into rubber. The discs also double in the syrup, so make them half the size you want and leave room in the pan.

  • Eight minutes of kneading. Set a timer.
  • They double in the syrup — leave room.
  • Squeeze the syrup out before they go into the milk.

item.title: Sabich
item.description: Sabich — pitta stuffed with fried aubergine, boiled egg, hummus, salad, amba and tahini.
item.content:encoded:
Salting the aubergine slices before frying draws out water so they brown instead of steaming and soak up less oil. The order of assembly is not arbitrary — hummus first insulates the bread, and the tahini and amba go on last so they run down through the filling rather than sitting on top.

  • Salt and dry the aubergine. Wet slices absorb twice the oil.
  • Hummus against the bread. It stops the pitta going through.
  • Amba is what makes it sabich rather than a vegetable pitta.

item.title: Kulfi
item.description: Whole milk reduced by half with sugar and cardamom, blended with nuts and frozen in moulds without churning.
item.content:encoded:
Kulfi is not churned, so the smoothness has to come from the reduction — boiling the milk down by half concentrates the solids until there is not enough free water left to form large ice crystals. Scrape the skin back into the pan as it forms; that caramelised film is where the flavour is, and left on the surface it becomes rubbery threads in the finished kulfi.

  • Scrape the skin back in as it forms.
  • Reduced by half, not a third — that is what stops ice crystals.
  • Ten seconds in warm water and it slides straight out.

item.title: Gajar ka Halwa
item.description: Grated carrots slow-cooked in whole milk with ghee, sugar and cardamom until reduced and glossy, finished with nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the carrot in the milk until the milk has completely gone before the sugar goes anywhere near it. Sugar added early draws water out of the carrot and stalls the whole thing — you end up simmering in syrup for an hour and it never darkens. Grate on the coarse side of the box grater; fine gratings turn to paste.

  • Milk gone before sugar goes in.
  • Coarse grate, not fine.
  • It is ready when the ghee separates at the edge.

item.title: Falooda
item.description: A layered dessert drink of rose syrup, soaked basil seeds, cooked vermicelli, chilled milk and ice cream.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the basil seeds in plenty of cold water for at least twenty minutes and they swell to eight times their size with a clear jelly around each one. Rushed, they swell in the glass instead and drink like grit. Everything goes into the glass cold — a warm layer melts the ice cream and the whole thing collapses into pink milk.

  • Twenty minutes for the basil seeds, in plenty of water.
  • Everything cold before it meets the ice cream.
  • Pour the milk down the side so the layers stay separate.

item.title: Malabi
item.description: Malabi — rose-scented set milk pudding with red syrup, coconut and crushed pistachios.
item.content:encoded:
Cornflour sets a milk pudding softly and cleanly where gelatine sets it rubbery, and the ratio matters within a tablespoon — too little and it will not stand, too much and it turns to paste. The rose water goes in off the heat because its aroma is driven off by any further boiling.

  • Dissolve the cornflour in cold milk first, thoroughly. Lumps never come out.
  • Rose water off the heat. Boiling it away is the most common mistake.
  • Strain into the glasses for a completely smooth top.

item.title: Shrikhand
item.description: Whole milk yoghurt strained overnight and whisked with icing sugar, saffron and cardamom into a thick set dessert.
item.content:encoded:
Hang the yoghurt overnight and you lose about half its weight in whey — that is not a loss, it is the recipe. Anything less and the shrikhand will not hold a shape on the spoon. Use icing sugar rather than caster: granulated sugar never fully dissolves in something this cold and thick, and you can feel it.

  • Eight hours of hanging, and expect to lose half the weight.
  • Icing sugar, not caster — you can feel caster.
  • One pass through a sieve makes it silky.

item.title: Rasam
item.description: A thin south Indian tamarind and tomato broth spiced with freshly pounded pepper and cumin, tempered with mustard seeds.
item.content:encoded:
Rasam is never boiled once the tamarind and rasam powder are in. Bring it just to the point where a froth rises up the sides and take it off — boiling drives off the volatile aromatics that are the whole point, and turns the pepper harsh and flat. It should be thin enough to drink, not a soup you eat with a spoon.

  • Never boil it after the tamarind goes in.
  • Pound the pepper for this pot; ready-ground tastes flat.
  • Thin enough to drink is correct.

item.title: Israeli Couscous Salad
item.description: Israeli couscous salad — toasted pearl couscous with roast vegetables, herbs, lemon and almonds.
item.content:encoded:
Toasting the pearls in oil before adding liquid keeps them separate and gives a nutty flavour that plain boiling does not — untoasted ptitim clump into a solid mass as they cool. Dressing the couscous while it is still warm means it absorbs the lemon rather than wearing it.

  • Toast the pearls until they smell like popcorn. Untoasted couscous clumps.
  • Dress it hot, then again cold. Two stages, better absorption.
  • Herbs at the very end so they stay green.

item.title: Coconut Chutney
item.description: Fresh grated coconut ground with roasted gram dal, green chilli and ginger, tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves.
item.content:encoded:
Roasted gram dal is what stops the chutney splitting into water and coconut within the hour. It has no other job and no substitute does it as well — it absorbs the water and holds the emulsion. Grind with ice-cold water: a warm grinder turns coconut oily and the chutney goes greasy and grey.

  • Roasted gram dal is what stops it splitting.
  • Ice-cold water in the grinder.
  • Temper last and pour it over hot.

item.title: Tandoori Roti
item.description: Wholemeal dough rolled thick and cooked on an inverted cast-iron pan until blistered and charred in patches.
item.content:encoded:
A tandoori roti is thicker than a chapati and cooked much harder, so it stays soft inside while the outside chars. Wet one face of the rolled dough before it goes on the metal — the water is what makes it stick to a vertical surface, which is how you get to blister the other side directly over the flame without it falling into the fire.

  • Thicker than a chapati, or it dries out.
  • Wet one face so it sticks to the metal.
  • Char in patches, not evenly — that is what tandoori means here.

item.title: Pani Puri
item.description: Crisp semolina puris filled with spiced mint and tamarind water, potato and chickpeas, assembled and eaten immediately.
item.content:encoded:
The puris puff because the dough is stiff and the oil is hot — a soft dough steams and stays flat, and oil under 190C lets them absorb rather than inflate. Roll thin, cut small, and fry in oil hot enough that they rise within five seconds. Then keep the pani ice cold and assemble one at a time: a filled puri has about twenty seconds before it collapses.

  • Stiff dough and 190C oil, or they will not puff.
  • Cool them completely before storing — warm puris go soft.
  • Fill one at a time. Twenty seconds is all you get.

item.title: Musakhan
item.description: Musakhan — Palestinian roast chicken on olive oil soaked flatbread with sumac onions and pine nuts.
item.content:encoded:
The onions are cooked down slowly with far more sumac than seems reasonable — the sourness has to carry the whole dish, and the volume of onion collapses to about a third. Good olive oil is used at a quantity that looks excessive on paper; the bread is meant to be saturated with it, and that is the texture the dish is built on.

  • More sumac and more olive oil than feels right. That is the dish.
  • Thirty-five minutes on the onions, minimum.
  • Soak the bread with the roasting juices before the onions go on.

item.title: Dhokla
item.description: Gram flour batter soured with lemon, raised with eno and steamed into a light savoury sponge, finished with a mustard and sugar tempering.
item.content:encoded:
The raising agent goes in last and the batter goes straight into the steamer — you have about thirty seconds of usable lift before the bubbles collapse. Have the steamer already boiling and the tin already greased before you add it. The tempering is poured over while the dhokla is still warm so it soaks in rather than sitting on top.

  • Steamer boiling and tin greased before the eno goes in.
  • Cut it in the tin while warm, not after it cools.
  • The sugar tempering is what makes it taste Gujarati.

item.title: Bhel Puri
item.description: Puffed rice tossed with tamarind and mint chutneys, onion, potato, tomato and sev, assembled immediately before eating.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is prepared separately and combined in the last thirty seconds. Half the sev is folded in for flavour in every bite; the other half is saved for on top, so at least some of it is still crisp by the time it is eaten. Puffed rice is hygroscopic to a degree that has to be seen: chutney-dressed bhel is crisp when you toss it and soggy by the time it reaches the table if you dawdle. Toss, plate, hand it over, eat.

  • Everything ready before the chutney touches the rice.
  • Fifteen seconds of tossing, then straight into bowls.
  • Refresh soft puffed rice in a low oven first.

item.title: Harees
item.description: Harees — wheat and meat cooked for hours and beaten smooth, finished with ghee and cinnamon.
item.content:encoded:
Harees is defined by texture: the wheat and meat have to be beaten until neither is identifiable, which only happens after long cooking has broken the wheat down and the meat has fallen into threads. Beating it hot, with a wooden spoon against the side of the pot, develops the wheat starch and gives the stretchy consistency the dish is judged on.

  • Beat it properly. Under-beaten harees is porridge with meat in it.
  • Keep topping up with hot water — cold water stalls the cooking.
  • The ghee at the end is not optional; the dish is deliberately plain without it.

item.title: Grilled Cheese Sandwich
item.description: A grilled cheese sandwich with mayonnaise and butter on the outside, two cheeses inside, cooked slowly over a medium-low heat.
item.content:encoded:
Cook it far more slowly than instinct suggests — medium-low, four minutes a side. High heat browns the bread in ninety seconds and leaves the cheese solid in the middle, which is the single most common failure. Mayonnaise on the outside as well as butter sounds wrong and browns more evenly than butter alone, because it contains egg and oil rather than water.

  • Medium-low and four minutes a side.
  • Mayonnaise as well as butter browns more evenly.
  • Cheese to the edges, so you get some crisped against the pan.

item.title: Perfect Scrambled Eggs
item.description: Eggs cooked over a low heat with butter, stirred constantly into soft curds and taken off the heat while still glossy.
item.content:encoded:
Take the pan off the heat while the eggs still look slightly underdone and glossy. They carry on cooking in their own heat for another thirty seconds, and eggs that looked right in the pan are dry on the plate. Salt at the end, not the beginning: salt added early breaks down the proteins and the eggs weep water as they cook.

  • Low heat, constant stirring, and lift the pan when it runs ahead.
  • Off the heat while still glossy.
  • Salt at the end.

item.title: Banana Pancakes
item.description: American pancakes with mashed ripe banana folded into the batter, cooked on a medium griddle and served with banana slices.
item.content:encoded:
The bananas must be properly overripe — skins going black, flesh almost liquid. An underripe banana is starchy rather than sweet and it makes the batter heavy without adding any flavour, so people end up adding sugar to compensate. Mash it thoroughly before it meets the flour, because lumps of banana in the batter turn to wet pockets in the finished pancake.

  • Blackening bananas, not yellow ones.
  • Mash smooth before the flour goes in.
  • They colour faster than plain pancakes because of the sugar — keep the heat moderate.

item.title: Knafeh Nabulsi
item.description: Knafeh nabulsi — orange semolina dough over fresh white cheese, baked and flooded with syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Nabulsi knafeh uses fine semolina dough rather than shredded kadayif, which bakes into a dense, sandy layer that holds syrup without going soggy. The cheese must be desalted by soaking, because the whole dessert is sweet and a salty layer inside it is jarring rather than balancing.

  • Soak the cheese to desalt it — two hours, three changes of water.
  • Cold syrup on hot knafeh, poured the moment it is turned out.
  • Serve within fifteen minutes. Cold knafeh does not pull.

item.title: Corn Chowder
item.description: A creamy sweetcorn and potato chowder built on a stock made from the stripped corn cobs, finished with cream and chives.
item.content:encoded:
Simmer the stripped cobs in the stock for twenty minutes and then throw them away. The cobs hold a great deal of starch and sweetness that the kernels do not, and it is the single cheapest thing you can do to make a corn chowder taste of corn rather than of cream. Blend a ladleful and stir it back in — that thickens it without flour.

  • The cobs make the stock. Do not skip it.
  • Blend a ladleful back in rather than adding flour.
  • Do not boil once the cream is in.

item.title: Loaded Baked Potato
item.description: Baking potatoes rubbed with oil and salt, baked at high heat until the skin crisps, split and loaded with cheese, bacon and soured cream.
item.content:encoded:
Rub the skin with oil and coarse salt and bake it directly on the oven shelf with nothing wrapped round it. Foil traps steam and gives you a soft, damp skin, which is the opposite of the point — dry heat all round is what makes the skin crackle. Prick it first, and split it the moment it comes out so the steam escapes and the inside stays floury rather than turning waxy.

  • No foil. Ever.
  • Straight onto the shelf, so hot air reaches all sides.
  • Split immediately or the inside goes waxy.

item.title: Chicken Tagine with Olives
item.description: Chicken tagine with olives — slow cooked with preserved lemon, green olives, ginger and saffron.
item.content:encoded:
Preserved lemon rind and olives are both already salty, so the tagine is barely salted at the start and adjusted only at the end — season early and it becomes inedible. Reducing the sauce hard after the chicken comes out is what turns a thin broth into the sticky glaze the dish is supposed to have.

  • Salt at the end, never at the start. The olives and lemons do that job.
  • Reduce the sauce properly after the chicken comes out.
  • Use the rind of the preserved lemon only — the flesh is bitter and salty.

item.title: Chicken Caesar Wrap
item.description: Griddled chicken, cos lettuce and parmesan in a tortilla wrap with a Caesar dressing of anchovy, garlic, lemon and mayonnaise.
item.content:encoded:
Dress the lettuce and roll the wrap at the last possible moment. Cos leaves collapse within about ten minutes of meeting a creamy dressing and a wrap made in advance is a wet parcel. The anchovies are not optional and they do not taste of fish in the finished dressing — they are where the savoury depth comes from, and a Caesar without them tastes like mayonnaise.

  • Dress and roll at the last minute.
  • Anchovies are the dressing, not an option.
  • Warm the tortilla or it cracks as you roll.

item.title: Ground Beef Tacos
item.description: Minced beef browned and simmered with cumin, chilli and oregano into a taco filling, served in warm corn tortillas.
item.content:encoded:
Bloom the ground spices in the hot fat for thirty seconds before any liquid goes in. Ground spice added to a wet pan tastes dusty and stays on the surface of the meat; heated in fat first, it dissolves and coats everything. A splash of water at the end and two minutes of simmering makes the difference between dry crumbles and a filling that holds together in the tortilla.

  • Bloom the spices in fat for thirty seconds.
  • Four minutes untouched to brown the mince.
  • A splash of water at the end so the filling holds together.

item.title: Spaghetti and Meatballs
item.description: Beef and pork meatballs bound with a milk-soaked bread panade, browned and simmered in tomato sauce, served with spaghetti.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the breadcrumbs in milk to a paste before they go into the meat. That panade holds water through cooking and is the difference between a tender meatball and a dense one — breadcrumbs added dry absorb the meat's own moisture instead. Brown them for colour only and finish them in the sauce, where they cook gently and give the sauce their fat.

  • A milk-soaked panade, always.
  • Handle the mixture as little as possible.
  • Brown for colour, then finish in the sauce.

item.title: Msemen
item.description: Msemen — Moroccan square laminated flatbread, folded and fried until it separates into flaky layers.
item.content:encoded:
Msemen is laminated the same way puff pastry is, but with oil and dry semolina instead of butter — the semolina keeps the layers physically apart as the dough is folded, which is why they separate rather than fusing. The dough is stretched on a well-oiled surface, never floured, so it can be pulled thin enough to see through.

  • Oil the surface, never flour it. Flour stops the dough stretching.
  • Dry semolina between the layers is what keeps them separate.
  • A dry pan, not an oily one — the dough already carries all the fat it needs.

item.title: Greek Chicken Traybake
item.description: Greek chicken thighs roasted with potatoes, lemon, garlic, oregano and olives in a single tin with stock.
item.content:encoded:
Pour a little stock into the tin rather than roasting dry. The potatoes need liquid to cook through in the same time the chicken takes, and the stock reduces with the lemon and chicken fat into a sauce that is the point of the dish. Start the potatoes ten minutes before the chicken goes in — they are the slower of the two.

  • Potatoes ten minutes ahead of the chicken.
  • Stock around the food, never over the skin.
  • Rest in the tin so the juices settle.

item.title: Chicken Karahi
item.description: Pakistani chicken karahi cooked fast in a wok with tomato, ginger, garlic and green chilli, finished with ginger julienne.
item.content:encoded:
There is no onion in a real karahi and adding one changes the dish completely — it turns a sharp, tomato-led curry into a sweet, thick gravy. The tomatoes go in whole or halved and are pressed against the side of the pan as they collapse, so the skins can be lifted out. Everything happens over a high heat in about thirty-five minutes; a karahi that has simmered gently is a different, duller thing.

  • No onion. That is what makes it a karahi.
  • Lift the tomato skins out as they loosen.
  • High heat throughout — it is a fried curry, not a stewed one.

item.title: Moroccan Mint Tea
item.description: Moroccan mint tea — gunpowder green tea with spearmint, sweetened and poured from height.
item.content:encoded:
