  • Split the cakes with a long serrated knife and a steady hand.

item.title: Colombian Empanadas
item.description: Colombian empanadas — corn dough shells filled with potato and beef, deep fried until crackly.
item.content:encoded:
The masarepa dough is stiffer and drier than a wheat pastry, so it is rolled between plastic sheets rather than on a floured surface — flour would only make it crack. Sealing them by pressing with a plate or a bowl rim gives a clean, tight edge, and any gap means oil gets in and the empanada bursts.

  • Roll between plastic sheets, never on flour.
  • Cold filling, always. Warm filling steams the dough open.
  • Patch any crack before frying or it will burst in the oil.

item.title: Obatzda
item.description: Bavarian obatzda of ripe Camembert mashed with butter, sweet paprika, onion and a splash of beer, served with pretzels.
item.content:encoded:
Use Camembert that is properly ripe — soft to the point of collapse and smelling strongly. Under-ripe cheese stays in rubbery lumps that no amount of mashing fixes, and it is the ripeness that gives obatzda its depth. Mash it with a fork rather than blending: the texture should be uneven, with some pieces still recognisable.

  • Properly ripe Camembert, rind included.
  • Fork, not blender — the texture should be uneven.
  • Beer a spoonful at a time.

item.title: Pierogi Ruskie
item.description: Polish pierogi ruskie of soft dough filled with mashed potato and twaróg curd cheese, boiled then fried in butter with onion.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is made with hot water rather than cold, which gelatinises some of the starch and makes it far more elastic and forgiving — it rolls thin without springing back and it seals without tearing. Keep it under a bowl the whole time you work, because pierogi dough dries in about four minutes and dry edges will not seal at all.

  • Hot water dough. It changes everything.
  • Keep the dough under a bowl at all times.
  • Boil, then fry. Both.

item.title: Sernik
item.description: Polish sernik baked cheesecake of twaróg curd cheese, eggs and sugar on a shortcrust base, baked low and cooled in the oven.
item.content:encoded:
Twaróg has to be pressed through a sieve or ground twice — it is grainy in a way cream cheese is not, and lumps that look small in the bowl are unpleasant in the finished cake. Bake it low and slow and then leave it in the switched-off oven with the door ajar for an hour: sudden cooling is what cracks the top, and this one cracks readily.

  • Sieve the twaróg twice.
  • Low oven, and cool it in the oven with the door ajar.
  • Four hours in the fridge before it will slice cleanly.

item.title: Causa Limeña
item.description: Causa limeña — cold layered Peruvian potato terrine with ají amarillo, lime and a chicken filling.
item.content:encoded:
The potato is mashed while hot but seasoned and worked until it is smooth and slightly elastic, then chilled — that structure is what lets it be sliced. Ají amarillo paste and lime go in generously because the dish is served cold, and cold food needs more seasoning than hot food to taste the same.

  • Rice the potatoes hot, season hot, chill after. Order matters.
  • Season harder than seems right. Cold mutes everything.
  • Overnight in the fridge gives clean slices.

item.title: Medovik
item.description: Russian medovik of thin honey biscuit layers stacked with a soured cream and condensed milk frosting and rested overnight.
item.content:encoded:
The layers come out of the oven as hard biscuits and that is correct — they are supposed to. The overnight rest is not for flavour but for structure: the moisture in the soured cream frosting migrates into the biscuit and turns the whole stack into something you can cut with a fork. Served the same day it is a stack of biscuits with cream between them.

  • The layers are meant to be hard. They soften overnight.
  • Trim while hot; cold layers shatter.
  • Keep the trimmings — they are the coating.

item.title: Varenyky
item.description: Ukrainian varenyky filled with sour cherries and sugar, boiled and served with soured cream and the cherry syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Drain the cherries and toss them with semolina, not flour or cornflour, half an hour before filling. Semolina absorbs the juice they release without going pasty, so the dumplings do not burst in the water — and any juice that does escape thickens rather than clouding the pan. Seal the edges with damp fingers and pinch twice.

  • Semolina with the cherries, half an hour ahead.
  • A gentle boil, never a rolling one.
  • Pinch the seal twice.

item.title: Pisco Sour
item.description: Pisco sour — pisco, lime, syrup and egg white double shaken to a thick foam, with Angostura bitters.
item.content:encoded:
The dry shake — shaking without ice first — is what emulsifies the egg white into a stable foam; adding ice at the start chills the protein before it can be whipped and the head collapses in a minute. Peruvian pisco is unaged and aromatic, and swapping in a barrel-aged spirit changes the drink completely.

  • Dry shake first, always. Ice first gives you a thin, short-lived head.
  • Double strain so no ice shards break the foam.
  • Fresh lime only. Bottled juice makes the drink taste flat and sweet.

item.title: Dobos Torte
item.description: Hungarian dobos torte of five thin sponge layers with chocolate buttercream, topped with a caramel disc scored into wedges.
item.content:encoded:
The caramel top must be scored into wedges while it is still liquid enough to cut and firm enough to hold the line — about forty seconds after it is poured, and the window is genuinely that short. Oil the knife first. Left to set solid, it shatters when anyone tries to serve it, which is why so many Dobos tortes arrive with a broken lid.

  • Score the caramel at forty seconds. Oil the knife.
  • Keep the flattest sponge for the top.
  • Cool the melted chocolate before it meets the butter.

item.title: Pkhali
item.description: Georgian pkhali of blanched spinach, beetroot and beans separately pounded with a walnut, garlic, coriander and vinegar paste.
item.content:encoded:
The walnut paste is made once and divided between the vegetables, which is what makes a plate of pkhali read as one dish in three colours. Squeeze the blanched vegetables far harder than feels necessary — anything left wet turns the paste to soup. Blue fenugreek and marigold are the authentic seasonings but ground coriander and a pinch of turmeric get close.

  • One walnut paste, divided three ways.
  • Squeeze everything much harder than seems reasonable.
  • Taste and correct each colour separately.

item.title: Jachnun
item.description: Yemenite jachnun of dough stretched paper-thin, spread with butter, rolled and baked slowly with eggs until dark and sweet.
item.content:encoded:
Stretch the dough until you can read through it. Every roll you make is one continuous sheet folded on itself a dozen times, and the layers are what turn to threads over three hours in the oven — thick dough gives you a solid, doughy log instead. Oil the worktop rather than flouring it and pull from the middle outwards with the flat of your hand; the dough is elastic enough to take it.

  • Oil, never flour, or the layers glue together.
  • Roll loosely; a tight roll steams into a dense middle.
  • Foil under the lid matters — it is what keeps the steam in for three hours.

item.title: Provoleta
item.description: Provoleta — a disc of provolone grilled in cast iron until crusted outside and molten inside.
item.content:encoded:
Provolone hilado, the aged Argentinian type, has a low enough moisture content to brown rather than collapse into a puddle — a young provolone dolce will simply melt and run. Drying the cut surface in the fridge for an hour is what lets the crust form before the middle goes.

  • Aged provolone only. The soft kind runs straight out of the pan.
  • Dry the surfaces in the fridge first.
  • Serve in the pan. Off the heat it sets within three or four minutes.

item.title: Sopa de Tortilla
item.description: Mexican tortilla soup of a pasilla and tomato broth topped at the table with fried tortilla strips, avocado, cheese and crema.
item.content:encoded:
The tortilla strips go into the bowl at the table, never into the pot. Cooked in the broth they dissolve into thickener within a couple of minutes and the whole point of the dish — crisp against hot liquid — disappears. Toast and soak the dried chillies rather than using powder; the smoky depth of pasilla is the flavour people remember.

  • Strips at the table, never in the pot.
  • Toast and soak whole dried chillies.
  • Strain the purée or the broth is gritty.

item.title: Camarones a la Diabla
item.description: Mexican camarones a la diabla of prawns in a blended guajillo, arbol and chipotle sauce with garlic, tomato and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the blended chilli sauce for five minutes before the prawns go anywhere near it. Straight from the blender it tastes raw and thin and no amount of simmering with the prawns fixes it, because prawns need three minutes and the sauce needs five on its own. Fry it until it darkens and thickens, then add the prawns and take the pan off almost immediately.

  • Fry the sauce for five minutes on its own.
  • Season the sauce before the prawns arrive.
  • Three minutes for the prawns, then off the heat.

item.title: Milanesa Napolitana
item.description: Milanesa napolitana — breaded beef cutlet topped with ham, tomato sauce and melted cheese.
item.content:encoded:
The cutlet is fried first and topped after, then finished under the grill only long enough to melt the cheese — build it raw and the crumb goes soft under the sauce. Beating the beef to an even 5 mm means it cooks in the three minutes the crust takes to colour.

  • Marinate in the garlic egg. It is what makes a milanesa taste Argentinian.
  • Fry first, top after, grill briefly. Never bake it all together.
  • Rest the coated cutlets 15 minutes before frying.

item.title: Esquites
item.description: Mexican esquites of corn kernels charred in butter with epazote, dressed with mayonnaise, lime, chilli powder and cotija.
item.content:encoded:
Char the kernels properly — leave them still in a hot dry pan until they blacken in patches and start popping. Corn stirred gently in butter is sweet and one-dimensional; charred, it develops the bitter, smoky edge that the lime and chilli play against. Dress it while hot so the mayonnaise loosens and coats rather than sitting in cold blobs.

  • Leave the corn still until it blackens.
  • Dress it hot so the mayonnaise loosens.
  • More chilli powder on top than feels right.

item.title: Paletas
item.description: Mexican paletas of fresh mango and lime blended with a light sugar syrup and chilli, frozen in lolly moulds.
item.content:encoded:
Chop a handful of the fruit and stir it in whole rather than blending everything smooth. Paletas de agua are meant to have pieces in them — that is what distinguishes them from a shop-bought ice lolly — and the chunks also break up the ice crystals so the texture is less solid. A spoonful of lime juice keeps the mango from tasting flat once frozen.

  • Season sweeter and sharper than tastes right — freezing dulls it.
  • Chunks stirred in, not blended.
  • Sticks in after an hour, when the mixture holds them upright.

item.title: Conchas
item.description: Mexican conchas of enriched sweet dough under a butter and sugar paste topping scored into a shell pattern before baking.
item.content:encoded:
The topping is a paste of equal parts butter, icing sugar and flour, and it must be rolled thin and laid on before the second prove, not after. It rises with the bun and the scored lines open into the shell as the dough expands underneath — put it on after proving and the pattern stays closed. Score firmly, most of the way through the paste.

  • Topping on before the second prove.
  • Score firmly, nearly through the paste.
  • Roll the discs thin or the pattern will not open.

item.title: Dulce de Leche
item.description: Dulce de leche — milk and sugar cooked down slowly to a thick amber caramel spread.
item.content:encoded:
The bicarbonate of soda raises the pH, which speeds up the Maillard browning and gives the deep colour that sugar caramelisation alone would not — without it you get sweetened condensed milk, not dulce de leche. It has to be stirred more and more often as it thickens, because the sugar catches instantly once the water is gone.

  • A wide pan. A narrow one takes twice as long.
  • Stop while it still looks slightly loose. It sets firm when cold.
  • Constant stirring in the last half hour, or it will catch and taste burnt.

item.title: Gorditas
item.description: Mexican gorditas of masa harina griddled thick until they puff, split and filled with beans, cheese and salsa.
item.content:encoded:
They puff because steam builds inside a sealed thick disc, and that only happens if the masa is the right wetness — it should feel like soft modelling clay and not crack at all when you press the edge. If it cracks, wet your hands and knead more water in. A cracked gordita lets the steam out and stays flat, and then there is nothing to split open.

  • Dough that does not crack at the edge. That is the whole test.
  • Dry griddle first, oil at the end.
  • Split them while hot or the pocket seals shut.

item.title: Marry Me Chicken
item.description: Marry me chicken: golden pan-seared cutlets in a creamy sun-dried tomato, garlic and Parmesan sauce. One skillet, ready in thirty-five minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Slicing the breasts through the middle gives eight thin cutlets that are cooked through by the time they are brown, so nothing sits in the sauce drying out. The flour dusting browns the surface and then dissolves into the pan, thickening the sauce without a separate roux. Sun-dried tomatoes are the second flavour that matters: their sweetness and acid stop the cream tasting flat, and the oil they were packed in goes into the pan with them.

  • Grate the Parmesan yourself. Pre-grated cheese carries anti-caking starch and turns the sauce grainy.
  • Keep the sauce at a simmer, not a boil, once the cream is in or it can split.
  • Cook the cutlets in two batches so they brown instead of steaming.

item.title: Pastel de Choclo
item.description: Pastel de choclo — Chilean beef and chicken bake under a ground corn and basil topping.
item.content:encoded:
The corn topping is cooked on the hob with milk and basil before it goes on, so it sets to a firm, sliceable layer rather than staying wet — raw ground corn spread over the filling will separate in the oven. The dusting of sugar on top is a Chilean habit that makes a lacquered, slightly bitter crust against the sweet corn.

  • Cook the corn topping on the hob first. Raw corn separates in the oven.
  • Twenty minutes on the onions for the pino. It is the base of the flavour.
  • The sugar on top is not optional — it makes the crust.

item.title: White Chicken Chili
item.description: White chicken chili with cannellini beans, green chiles, cumin and shredded chicken, thickened with cream cheese. One pot, fifty minutes.
item.content:encoded:
There is no tomato and no red chile, so the flavour comes from three things: cumin toasted in the oil, mild green chiles, and lime at the end. The chicken poaches whole in the stock and is shredded afterwards, which keeps it tender and seasons the broth. Mashing a cupful of the beans against the side of the pot thickens the chili with their own starch, and the cream cheese then rounds it out without making it heavy.

  • Mash some of the beans. It is the only thickener the chili needs.
  • Add the lime juice off the heat, or its brightness cooks away.
  • Use thighs if you prefer, and simmer them 5 minutes longer.

item.title: Lasagna Soup
item.description: Lasagna soup with Italian sausage, a rich tomato broth and broken lasagna sheets, topped with seasoned ricotta and melted mozzarella.
item.content:encoded:
Lasagna sheets break into ragged pieces that behave like pappardelle in a soup, and they are cooked directly in the broth so their starch thickens it slightly. Browning the sausage hard first and cooking the tomato paste in the fat until it darkens does the work that a long-simmered ragù would. The ricotta is seasoned separately and added at the table, which is the part that makes it taste like the baked dish.

  • Stir the pot often once the pasta goes in. The broken sheets stick to each other and to the base.
  • Cook the tomato purée until it darkens. Raw purée makes the broth taste tinny.
  • Add the ricotta at the table so it stays cool and creamy against the hot broth.

item.title: Air Fryer Chicken Breast
item.description: Air fryer chicken breast with a paprika and garlic rub: pounded even, 190°C for 12 to 15 minutes and rested. Juicy inside, browned outside.
item.content:encoded:
A breast is thick at one end and thin at the other, and in a fast, fierce oven like an air fryer the thin end is dry before the thick end is done. Pounding it to an even 2 cm fixes that. A little oil helps the rub brown, and a five-minute rest lets the juices settle back into the meat rather than running out on the board. The thermometer matters more than the timer: 74°C is done, and every degree past it costs moisture.

  • Even thickness is the whole trick. Do not skip the pounding.
  • Trust a probe thermometer over the timer, since fryers vary by 10 degrees.
  • Leave space between the breasts or the hot air cannot brown them.

item.title: Completo Italiano
item.description: Completo italiano — Chilean hot dog with diced tomato, mashed avocado and mayonnaise.
item.content:encoded:
It is called italiano because the three toppings are the colours of the Italian flag, which means the proportions matter: equal, thick layers of each, not a scatter. Mashing the avocado with lemon and salt rather than slicing it is what lets it sit in a band without sliding off.

  • Drain the tomato. It is the difference between a completo and a soggy roll.
  • Mash the avocado rather than slicing it, so it stays put.
  • Equal bands of all three. That is what makes it an italiano.

item.title: Air Fryer Pork Chops
item.description: Air fryer pork chops: thick bone-in chops with a smoked paprika rub, 200°C for 10 to 12 minutes to 63°C, then rested. Juicy, browned, fast.
item.content:encoded:
Pork chops dry out because they are lean and cooked past the point they need to be. Pork is safe at 63°C, well below the 74°C people were taught, and the chop keeps cooking as it rests. A chop at least 2.5 cm thick can take the air fryer's fierce heat long enough to brown before it overcooks, and the small amount of sugar in the rub caramelises in that dry heat to give it a crust.

  • Choose chops at least 2.5 cm thick. Thin ones overcook before they brown.
  • Pull them at 63°C. Past 70°C they turn dry and chalky.
  • Pat the surface dry first, or the rub steams instead of browning.

item.title: Crockpot Potato Soup
item.description: Crockpot potato soup: russet potatoes cooked low all day in the slow cooker, mashed in the pot with cream cheese and topped with bacon and cheddar.
item.content:encoded:
Russets are the right potato because they are floury and fall apart, so mashing them in the pot thickens the soup with their own starch and no flour is needed. Leaving some pieces whole gives it body rather than the texture of baby food. Cream cheese goes in at the end because it melts smooth into hot soup and carries the flavour of the bacon without splitting the way a lot of milk can.

  • Use russets, not waxy potatoes. They break down and thicken the soup for free.
  • Mash by hand. A blender turns potato starch gluey.
  • Add the milk and cheese at the end. Long cooking can make dairy grainy.

item.title: Coxinha
item.description: Coxinha — Brazilian teardrop croquettes of shredded chicken and cream cheese in a stock dough, fried.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is made by cooking flour into hot chicken stock like a choux, which gelatinises the starch so it can be moulded warm without cracking — a cold dough will split every time you shape one. The teardrop shape is traditional because it imitates a chicken drumstick, which is what coxinha means.

  • Shape the dough while it is warm. Cold dough cracks.
  • Cold filling in warm dough, never the other way round.
  • Chill the crumbed coxinhas before frying so they hold their shape.

item.title: Breakfast Casserole
item.description: Breakfast casserole with sausage, cheddar and bread cubes in a mustard-spiked egg custard. Assemble ahead, bake until puffed and golden.
item.content:encoded:
It is a savoury bread pudding, and the bread is what makes it work: stale cubes soak up the custard without collapsing, so the middle sets creamy instead of turning to paste. Standing the dish before baking lets the bread drink the custard evenly, which is why it is so well suited to the night before. A pinch of dry mustard sharpens the eggs and cuts through the sausage fat.

  • Use stale bread. Fresh bread turns to paste in the custard.
  • Press the bread under the custard so every cube is wet and none burns.
  • The centre is set when a knife comes out clean, not when the top looks done.

item.title: Garlic Knots
item.description: Garlic knots: soft pizzeria dough tied into knots, baked golden, then brushed with garlic butter, parsley and Parmesan while still hot.
item.content:encoded:
A pizza-style dough, kneaded for a chewy crumb, is the right base because the knots have to stay soft inside and hold their shape. The garlic butter is not baked in: it is brushed on the moment they come out, when the bread is hot enough to absorb it and the raw garlic softens without burning. Grated rather than chopped garlic dissolves into the butter so it coats every knot evenly.

  • Butter the knots the second they leave the oven. Cold bread will not take it up.
  • Tie the knots loosely. They expand and a tight one bakes dense.
  • Grate the garlic so it melts into the butter instead of sitting in lumps.

item.title: Protein Muffins
item.description: Protein muffins made with oats, banana, Greek yogurt and vanilla protein powder, studded with blueberries. Soft, lightly sweet, about 9 g protein each.
item.content:encoded:
Protein powder dries out baking, which is why most protein muffins are dense. The moisture here comes from ripe banana and Greek yogurt, both of which hold water through the bake, and the oats blitzed into flour give a tender crumb without wheat. Do not overmix: the powder absorbs liquid slowly, and a batter that looks slightly loose when it goes into the tin bakes up right.

  • Use very ripe bananas. They supply both sweetness and moisture.
  • Fold gently and stop as soon as the flour disappears.
  • Frozen blueberries go in straight from the freezer so they do not bleed.

item.title: Caipirinha
item.description: Caipirinha — lime muddled with sugar, topped with cachaça and crushed ice and stirred until frosted.
item.content:encoded:
The lime is muddled with sugar rather than juiced, so the sugar crystals scrape oil out of the peel — that oil is most of the aroma. Muddling too hard crushes the white pith and turns the drink bitter, which is why the technique is a press and twist, not a pounding.

  • Cut out the white core. It is where the bitterness lives.
  • Press and twist, do not pound. Six or seven presses is enough.
  • Crushed ice, not cubes. It dilutes at the right speed for this drink.

item.title: Sausage-Stuffed Bell Peppers
item.description: Sausage-stuffed bell peppers filled with Italian sausage, rice, tomatoes and herbs, baked until tender under a bubbling mozzarella crust.
item.content:encoded:
Peppers filled raw come out either hard or, if baked long enough to soften, with a filling gone dry. Baking the halves empty for ten minutes first starts them softening, so the second bake only has to heat the filling and melt the cheese. Sausage supplies the fat and seasoning, so the rice and tomato need almost nothing added, and cooked rice is used because raw rice steals moisture from a filling this small.

  • Pre-bake the empty peppers so they finish tender, not crunchy.
  • Drain the tinned tomatoes or the filling turns wet and the peppers slump.
  • Cut a thin slice off any pepper that rocks so it sits flat.

item.title: Chicken and Dumplings
item.description: Chicken and dumplings: bone-in thighs simmered in a rich vegetable broth, shredded, and topped with buttermilk drop dumplings that steam fluffy.
item.content:encoded:
Dumplings steam rather than boil, so the lid has to stay on for the whole fifteen minutes: lift it and the steam escapes and the tops turn gummy and flat. Cold butter grated into the flour leaves pockets that puff as it melts, the same trick as a biscuit. The broth is thickened with a roux first because the dumplings sit on top of it rather than in it, and a thin broth lets them sink and go soggy.

  • Keep the lid on for the full 15 minutes. Steam is what cooks the tops.
  • Grate the butter while it is very cold so it stays in pieces.
  • Do not overmix the dough. Shaggy and sticky makes light dumplings.

item.title: Rice and Peas
item.description: Jamaican rice and peas — rice cooked in coconut milk with kidney beans, thyme and scotch bonnet.
item.content:encoded:
Cooking dried beans from scratch gives you their cooking liquid, which is what colours the rice and carries most of the flavour — tinned beans make a paler, blander pot. The scotch bonnet goes in whole and unpierced so it perfumes the rice without making it hot, and it must come out before it splits.

  • Cook the beans from dried and keep the liquid. That liquid is the recipe.
  • Whole scotch bonnet, never pierced, out before it splits.
  • Do not lift the lid during the twenty minutes.

item.title: Stuffed Shells
item.description: Stuffed shells: jumbo pasta shells filled with ricotta, mozzarella, Parmesan and parsley, baked in marinara sauce under melted cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Ricotta on its own bakes into a grainy, bland filling, so the egg binds it, the Parmesan salts it and the mozzarella makes it stretch. Cooking the shells two minutes short matters more than anything else: they finish in the oven under the sauce, and a shell cooked through first tears when you fill it and goes limp when it bakes. Covering the dish for the first half keeps the sauce from drying into a crust before the pasta softens.

  • Undercook the shells. They finish in the oven, and a soft shell tears when filled.
  • Fill them with a piping bag, or a freezer bag with the corner snipped off, to save time.
  • Whole-milk ricotta gives a creamier filling. Drain it in a sieve if it looks wet.

item.title: Beef Enchiladas
item.description: Beef enchiladas: tortillas dipped in a homemade red chili sauce, rolled around spiced beef and cheddar, and baked until bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is a chili gravy, a quick roux of flour and chili powder loosened with stock, and it is what separates an enchilada from tortillas baked with taco meat. Dipping each tortilla in the warm sauce before filling softens it so it rolls without cracking, and seasons it right through. The rest of the sauce goes over the top and has to cover the tortillas completely, or the exposed ends dry out in the oven.

  • Dip the tortillas in the sauce before filling. Dry corn tortillas crack when rolled.
  • Cover the tortillas completely with sauce or the exposed ends turn hard.
  • Cook the flour in the oil for a full minute so the sauce does not taste raw.

item.title: Taco Casserole
item.description: Taco casserole: seasoned ground beef, black beans, corn and salsa layered with tortilla chips and melted cheese, baked until bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
Layering with tortilla chips rather than soft tortillas gives the casserole two textures: the chips at the bottom soften into something like a tamale while the ones on top stay crisp. The spices are cooked into the beef with a little water, so they become a sauce that soaks the chips instead of leaving dry seasoning on the surface, and salsa does the work of tomato, onion and heat in one stir.

  • Crush the chips only lightly. Bigger pieces stay crisp on top.
  • Simmer the beef until the water has reduced or the casserole turns soggy.
  • Add the cold toppings after baking, not before.

item.title: Jamaican Beef Patty
item.description: Jamaican beef patty — turmeric pastry folded around spiced beef and baked until flaky.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry is laminated with cold suet or butter and turmeric, which gives the colour and, more importantly, the flake — patties made with plain shortcrust are a different, duller thing. The filling is bound with breadcrumbs so it stays moist in the oven without leaking through the seam.

  • Cold butter, folded twice. That is where the flake comes from.
  • Breadcrumbs in the filling keep it saucy without leaking.
  • Seal the edge properly with a fork, all the way round.

item.title: Tater Tot Casserole
item.description: Tater tot casserole: ground beef, green beans and cheddar in a creamy mushroom sauce, topped with rows of crisp golden tater tots.
item.content:encoded:
It is a Minnesota hotdish, built on the idea that everything comes from the cupboard and the freezer: the soup is the sauce, the frozen beans need no prep and the tots are the crust. The cheese goes under the tots as well as over them, because a layer of melted cheese between the filling and the potato keeps the tots from going soggy from underneath. At a high heat they crisp on top while the filling bubbles around them.

  • Drain the beef well. Extra fat pools in the dish and greases the tots.
  • Pack the tots tightly so the filling is covered and steams less.
  • Put the tots on frozen, straight from the bag.

item.title: Chicken Spaghetti
item.description: Chicken spaghetti: shredded chicken and spaghetti in a creamy cheddar sauce with peppers, onions and spicy tomatoes, baked until bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
This is a baked pasta with a cheese sauce rather than a tomato one, and its character comes from a tin of tomatoes with green chillies, which adds heat and acid to a sauce that is otherwise cheese and milk. The spaghetti is cooked two minutes short because it keeps taking up sauce in the oven. A rotisserie chicken is the traditional shortcut and gives a better-seasoned meat than poaching breasts.

  • Undercook the spaghetti. It keeps absorbing sauce in the oven.
  • Drain the tomatoes, or the sauce thins as it bakes.
  • Grate the cheddar yourself so the sauce melts smooth.

item.title: Trinidadian Doubles
item.description: Trinidadian doubles — soft fried bara filled with curried chickpeas, tamarind and pepper sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Bara has to stay soft, which means a slack, turmeric-yellow dough proved twice and fried fast at a high temperature so it puffs rather than crisps. The channa is deliberately loose and a little soupy, because the bara has to soak some of it up without falling apart.

  • Twenty seconds a side. Bara should be soft, not crisp.
  • Fry the curry paste until the oil separates before the chickpeas go in.
  • Keep the channa loose. It has to soak into the bara.

item.title: Beer Can Chicken
item.description: Beer can chicken: a whole chicken with a smoky brown-sugar rub, stood on a half-empty beer can and grilled over indirect heat until crisp.
item.content:encoded:
The beer steams inside the cavity, but the real work is done by the upright stance and the indirect heat. Standing the bird lets the fat run off the skin instead of pooling, and it raises the legs, which need longer than the breast, closer to the heat. Keeping the grill at a steady 175°C and pulling the chicken when the thigh reaches 74°C matters more than any timing, because grills and weather vary widely.

  • Pull it at 74°C in the thigh. Times vary with the grill and the weather.
  • Keep the bird over the cool side so the skin does not scorch.
  • No grill? Stand it on a baking tray in a 190°C oven for about 90 minutes.

item.title: Nashville Hot Chicken
item.description: Nashville hot chicken: buttermilk-brined, double-dredged and fried crisp, then brushed with a fiery cayenne paste and served on white bread with pickles.
item.content:encoded:
The heat is a paste, not a coating: cayenne whisked into some of the hot frying oil and brushed over the chicken the moment it comes out, so it clings and glows red without burning. Double dredging, with a dip in the brine between, builds the craggy crust that can carry it. The brine keeps the meat juicy through a crust that thick, and the pickles and white bread are not a garnish; they are what you eat between bites to survive it.

  • Whisk the paste into oil that is hot but not smoking, so the spices bloom without scorching.
  • Double dredge and press hard. The craggy coat is what holds the paste.
  • Keep the frying oil at 175°C. Cold oil makes greasy chicken.

item.title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice
item.description: One-pot chicken and rice: seared thighs and paprika-thyme rice cooked together in stock until tender, finished with peas, lemon and parsley.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken is seared first for two reasons: the skin renders the fat the rice is cooked in, and the browned bits on the base dissolve into the stock and season every grain. The thighs sit on top of the rice rather than in it, so the rice steams while the skin stays above the liquid. Keeping the lid on and the heat low is what stops the base scorching before the top is done.

  • Do not lift the lid while the rice simmers. The steam is what cooks it.
  • Sear the skin until properly golden, since it will not crisp again under the lid.
  • Keep the heat low. High heat scorches the base before the rice is tender.

item.title: Callaloo
item.description: Callaloo — Trinidadian dasheen leaves cooked with okra and coconut milk into a thick green purée.
item.content:encoded:
Okra is not a vegetable in this dish so much as a thickener — its mucilage is what gives callaloo its particular smooth, slightly viscous body. The leaves have to be cooked far past the point where they look done, until they lose all structure, which is the difference between callaloo and creamed greens.

  • Cook it well past the point where the leaves look done.
  • Okra is the thickener. Do not leave it out.
  • Scotch bonnet whole and out before it bursts, unless you want real heat.

item.title: Sweet and Sour Chicken
item.description: Sweet and sour chicken: crisp cornflour-coated chicken in a glossy sweet-tart sauce with pineapple and peppers. Better than the takeaway.
item.content:encoded:
The two things that go wrong are a soggy coating and a sauce that tastes only of sugar. Cornflour with a little plain flour gives a coating that stays crisp for the half-minute it takes to toss, and the sauce goes on off the heat at the very last moment, so the chicken is glazed rather than soaked. The vinegar matters as much as the sugar: at nearly equal weights the sauce is bright rather than cloying, and the pineapple juice rounds it out.

  • Toss with the sauce at the last moment. The coating stays crisp for about a minute.
  • Fry at 180°C. Cooler oil makes a heavy, greasy coating.
  • Cut the peppers into big chunks so they stay crunchy against the soft pineapple.

item.title: Mongolian Beef
item.description: Mongolian beef: thin flank steak coated in cornflour, seared quickly and glazed in a sweet, savoury garlic-ginger soy sauce with spring onions.
item.content:encoded:
Slicing the steak across the grain, and very thin, is what makes flank tender, and a cornflour coating protects it in the hot oil and gives the sauce something to cling to. The sauce is mostly soy sauce and brown sugar, cooked briefly with garlic and ginger until it thickens, and the beef goes back in only at the end. Two minutes in the sauce is enough; any longer and the coating goes soft and the meat tough.

  • Freeze the steak for 20 minutes first and it slices thinner and cleaner.
  • Cook the beef in two batches so it browns instead of stewing.
  • Return it to the sauce for no more than two minutes.

item.title: Moin Moin
item.description: Moin moin — Nigerian steamed bean pudding of peeled black-eyed beans, peppers and onion.
item.content:encoded:
The beans must be peeled — soaked and rubbed until the skins float off — because the skins make the finished pudding grainy and grey rather than smooth and orange. The batter needs to be thinner than seems right, closer to double cream, since it sets firm as the bean starch cooks.

  • Peel the beans properly. Skins make it grey and grainy.
  • Batter like double cream. Too thick and it sets solid and dry.
  • Beat air in for three minutes before steaming.

item.title: Egg Rolls
item.description: Egg rolls filled with seasoned pork, cabbage and carrot, wrapped in egg roll wrappers and deep-fried until blistered, golden and crisp.
item.content:encoded:
The filling has to be dry. The pork is cooked until its liquid has gone and the cabbage is cooked until the pan is dry, because any moisture turns to steam inside the wrapper and splits it or leaves it soggy. Egg roll wrappers are thicker than spring roll ones, which is why they blister into a crisp, bubbly shell rather than a shattering thin one. Rolling them tight and sealing the last corner with flour paste keeps the oil out.

  • Cool the filling completely before rolling, or steam splits the wrappers.
  • Roll tight and seal the last corner with the paste so oil cannot get in.
  • Keep the oil at 180°C and fry in small batches so the temperature stays up.

item.title: Crab Rangoon
item.description: Crab rangoon: crisp fried wontons filled with cream cheese, crab and spring onion, with sweet chilli sauce for dipping.
item.content:encoded:
Cream cheese is the reason it works: it stays soft and molten inside the crisp skin while the crab supplies sweetness, and a little garlic powder and Worcestershire sauce stand in for the seasoning takeaways rely on. Squeezing every drop of water out of the crab keeps the filling from weeping into the wrapper, and folding the wonton into a sealed pouch, with water on the seams, stops it bursting in the oil.

  • Dry the crab thoroughly. A wet filling splits the wrappers.
  • Press out the air and seal every seam or the oil gets in.
  • Fry at 175°C. Hotter burns the wrapper before the cheese melts.

item.title: Cajun Shrimp
item.description: Cajun shrimp: large shrimp coated in a smoky homemade Cajun spice blend and seared in garlic butter with lemon. On the table in eighteen minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Shrimp cook in two or three minutes, which is exactly why they are so easy to ruin: as soon as they curl from a C into an O they are overdone. The seasoning has to be fierce because there is no time to build flavour in the pan, so the blend leans on smoked paprika and cayenne with garlic and onion powder, oregano and thyme. Finishing with the butter off the heat turns the spices into a sauce instead of scorching them.

  • Dry the shrimp. Wet shrimp steam and turn rubbery.
  • Pull them the moment they form a loose C. A tight O means overcooked.
  • Add the second spoon of butter off the heat so the sauce stays creamy.

item.title: Nigerian Pepper Soup
item.description: Nigerian pepper soup — a thin, fiery broth of West African spices with goat, fish or chicken.
item.content:encoded:
Pepper soup spice is a specific blend — ehuru, uda, uziza and grains of paradise — and its aroma is volatile, so half goes in early for depth and half at the end for perfume. The broth is deliberately thin: it is a soup to drink, and thickening it changes what the dish is for.

  • Half the spice early, half at the end. The aroma does not survive a long simmer.
  • Keep it thin. Pepper soup is drunk, not spooned through.
  • Fish goes in last and is never stirred.

item.title: Coconut Shrimp
item.description: Coconut shrimp: large shrimp in a crisp panko and coconut crust, fried until golden and served with a sweet chilli or pineapple dipping sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Coconut burns faster than breadcrumbs because of its sugar and fat, which is why the coating is mostly panko with the coconut as the accent, and why the oil should stay at 175°C. The three-stage coating of flour, then egg, then crumbs gives each layer something to grip; leaving out the flour is the usual reason a coating slides off in the oil. Shrimp this size need only two minutes a side, so the coating and the shrimp finish together.

  • Do not skip the flour. It is what makes the crumb stick.
  • Keep the oil at 175°C, since coconut scorches above that.
  • Fry small batches so the oil stays hot and the shrimp do not steam.

item.title: One-Pot Chili Mac
item.description: One-pot chili mac: ground beef, beans, tomatoes and chili spices with macaroni cooked in the sauce and finished with melted cheddar.
item.content:encoded:
The macaroni cooks straight in the chili, so its starch thickens the sauce and it takes its flavour from the broth instead of from water poured away. The trick is the ratio: enough stock that the pasta is covered while it simmers and no more, so the sauce is thick by the time the pasta is done. The cheddar goes in off the heat, so it melts smooth instead of splitting into oil.

  • Stir often once the pasta goes in. Macaroni catches on the base.
  • Add the cheese off the heat so it melts smooth.
  • If it looks dry before the pasta is tender, add a splash of stock.

item.title: Waakye
item.description: Waakye — Ghanaian rice and beans coloured with sorghum leaves, served with shito and sides.
item.content:encoded:
The colour and the faint earthy flavour come from dried sorghum leaves, and a pinch of bicarbonate of soda in the water is what releases the pigment — without it the leaves give very little. The beans are part-cooked before the rice goes in so both finish at the same time.

  • The bicarbonate of soda is what draws the colour out of the leaves.
  • Part-cook the beans first so they finish with the rice.
  • Lid stays on for the full 25 minutes and the 10-minute rest.

item.title: Sheet Pan Chicken and Vegetables
item.description: Sheet pan chicken and vegetables: bone-in thighs, potatoes, carrots and broccoli roasted on one tray with lemon, garlic and herbs.
item.content:encoded:
Different vegetables need different times, so they are cut to different sizes and added in stages: potatoes and carrots go in with the chicken, and the broccoli joins for the last fifteen minutes so it browns instead of turning to mush. A hot oven crisps the skin while the potatoes cook in the rendered chicken fat, which is what makes the tray taste better than its parts. Use a large rimmed tray, since crowding steams everything.

  • Preheat the tray so the vegetables sizzle when they land.
  • Add the broccoli late or it burns before the potatoes are done.
  • Do not overcrowd. Use two trays if needed, or the vegetables steam.

item.title: Air Fryer Chicken Thighs
item.description: Air fryer chicken thighs: bone-in, skin-on thighs with a paprika and garlic rub, cooked to crisp skin and juicy meat in about 35 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Thighs are forgiving because they carry fat and connective tissue, but they are better cooked past the safe 74°C: at 80°C the collagen has melted and the meat is tender, where at 74°C it can still be tight near the bone. Starting them skin side down renders the fat under the skin in the dry heat, and flipping them for the last stretch crisps the skin against the moving air. Patting them dry and using only a little oil is what keeps the skin crisp instead of rubbery.

  • Dry the skin thoroughly. Damp skin steams and never crisps.
  • Take them to 80°C. Dark meat is tenderer past the minimum safe temperature.
  • Do not crowd the basket. The hot air has to reach the skin.

item.title: Air Fryer Salmon
item.description: Air fryer salmon: skin-on fillets with a lemon, garlic and paprika rub, cooked at 200°C for 8 to 10 minutes until just flaking. Crisp skin, moist centre.
item.content:encoded:
Salmon takes eight to ten minutes in the air fryer, and the gap between just done and dry is about two minutes wide, so a thermometer beats a timer. The moving air dries the surface quickly, which crisps the skin without leathering the flesh underneath, but it also means a thin tail finishes before a thick centre. Choosing centre-cut fillets of even thickness, or tucking the thin end under, is the fix.

  • Do not flip it. The skin crisps against the basket.
  • Take it out at 57°C for moist medium salmon. It keeps cooking as it rests.
  • Tuck a thin tail end under so it does not dry before the thick end is done.

item.title: Kelewele
item.description: Kelewele — Ghanaian spiced fried plantain with ginger, chilli, cloves and anise.
item.content:encoded:
The plantain must be properly ripe — black-skinned, not yellow — because its sugar is what caramelises in the oil into the almost-burnt edges the dish is about. Marinating in a wet spice paste rather than a dry rub means the seasoning sticks through the frying instead of falling to the bottom of the pot.

  • Black-skinned plantain only. Yellow ones will not caramelise.
  • A wet paste, not a dry rub. It stays on in the oil.
  • Take them darker than feels safe. That is where the flavour is.

item.title: Air Fryer Bacon
item.description: Air fryer bacon: streaky rashers cooked at 180°C in 8 to 12 minutes, crisp and evenly browned with no splatter and no turning.
item.content:encoded:
Bacon in a pan spends its time sitting in its own fat. In the air fryer the fat drips through the basket while hot air crisps the surface, so the rashers cook drier and more evenly and do not curl into waves. The one thing to watch is the drawer: fat that collects in a hot drawer can smoke, so a splash of water in the bottom keeps it quiet. Thin bacon takes 8 minutes and thick-cut 12, and the last minute is when it turns from good to burnt.

  • A splash of water in the drawer keeps the fat from smoking.
  • Check at 7 minutes. Bacon goes from crisp to burnt in a minute.
  • Empty the drawer between batches so old fat does not smoke.

item.title: Air Fryer Brussels Sprouts
item.description: Air fryer Brussels sprouts: halved sprouts cooked at 200°C until crisp and charred at the edges, then tossed in a balsamic and maple glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Brussels sprouts turn bitter and sulphurous when boiled and sweet and nutty when browned, and the air fryer browns them faster than an oven because the loose outer leaves crisp like chips while the cores soften. Halving them and starting them cut side down gives a flat, caramelised face, and shaking the basket halfway lets the leaves that fall loose crisp too. The glaze goes on after cooking, because the sugar in it would burn at this temperature.

  • Halve them to the same size so they cook at the same rate.
  • Shake the basket halfway so the loose leaves crisp instead of scorching.
  • Add the glaze after cooking. The sugar burns in the fryer.

item.title: Nyama Choma
item.description: Nyama choma — Kenyan goat or beef grilled slowly over coals and served with kachumbari and ugali.
item.content:encoded:
Nyama choma is grilled low and slow rather than seared, over coals that have burned down, so the connective tissue in cheaper cuts has time to soften while the outside dries into a crust. Salt is genuinely the only seasoning in the traditional version — everything else happens on the plate with kachumbari.

  • Coals burned down, not flaming. This is an hour of cooking, not fifteen minutes.
  • Salt only. The kachumbari does the rest.
  • Chop it on the board at the table — that is part of the meal.

item.title: Air Fryer Sweet Potato Fries
item.description: Air fryer sweet potato fries: sticks tossed in cornflour and a little oil and cooked at 190°C until crisp at the edges and soft inside.
item.content:encoded:
Sweet potato is full of sugar and water, so it tends to steam and burn at the same time and never crisp. Cornflour fixes the first problem: it absorbs surface moisture and sets into a thin shell. The second is fixed by cutting even 1 cm sticks and cooking at 190°C rather than hotter, so the sugars brown without blackening, and by shaking the basket every five minutes so the pieces do not fuse. Soggy fries are almost always crowded fries.

  • Cornflour is the crisping agent. Do not leave it out.
  • Cut the sticks evenly, or thin ones burn while thick ones stay soft.
  • Cook in two batches rather than crowding the basket.

item.title: Air Fryer Chicken Tenders
item.description: Air fryer chicken tenders: strips of chicken in a seasoned panko crust, cooked at 190°C until golden and crunchy with no deep frying.
item.content:encoded:
A crumb coating only crisps in an air fryer if it is oiled: the dry heat toasts panko, but without fat the crumbs stay pale and dusty, and a generous mist of oil on both sides fixes it. The coating is built in three stages so it clings, flour to grip the egg and egg to grip the panko, and the panko is pressed on rather than sprinkled, because loose crumbs blow around the basket in a fan-driven oven.

  • Spray the crumbs with oil. Without it they stay pale.
  • Press the panko on. Loose crumbs blow around the basket.
  • Keep the strips from touching so the coating crisps on all sides.

item.title: Air Fryer Shrimp
item.description: Air fryer shrimp: large shrimp seasoned with paprika, garlic and lemon and cooked at 200°C in 6 to 8 minutes until pink and just cooked through.
item.content:encoded:
Shrimp are done the moment they turn opaque and curl, and in a fan-driven fryer that happens in about six minutes, so they are the fastest thing in the basket and the easiest to overcook. Tossing them in oil before the spices lets the seasoning stick and protects the surface from drying, and one shake halfway means the shrimp at the edges do not overcook while the ones in the middle catch up. Large shrimp, roughly 16 to 20 to 450 g, hold up best.

  • Dry the shrimp. Wet shrimp steam instead of taking colour.
  • Take them out at the loose C. A tight curl means overcooked.
  • Frozen shrimp work well, thawed and patted dry.

item.title: Ugali and Sukuma Wiki
item.description: Ugali and sukuma wiki — stiff maize meal with collard greens fried with onion and tomato.
item.content:encoded:
Ugali is cooked far past the point where it looks done — pressed and turned against the side of the pot for a full ten minutes — because that is what develops the smooth, firm texture you can tear and dip with. Sukuma is cooked briefly and stays green; long-cooked greens go grey and lose the point of the dish.

  • Turn and press the ugali for ten minutes. Undercooked, it tastes raw and grainy.
  • Greens for eight minutes only. They should stay green.
  • A heavy pan and a strong wooden spoon. This takes real effort.

item.title: Air Fryer French Fries
item.description: Air fryer French fries from russet potatoes: soaked to remove starch, dried well and cooked at 190°C until crisp outside and fluffy within.
item.content:encoded:
Fries are crisp when the surface is dry and fluffy when the starch inside gelatinises, and soaking the cut potatoes washes off the surface starch that would glue them together and brown too fast. Drying them completely before the oil goes on is the step people skip and the one that matters most, because any water left on the surface has to steam off before browning can start. Russets, being floury, give the fluffiest centre.

  • Dry the potatoes completely. Damp fries steam instead of crisping.
  • Salt after cooking, while hot. Salt before draws water out.
  • Shake the basket every 8 minutes so the sticks brown evenly.

item.title: Air Fryer Broccoli
item.description: Air fryer broccoli: florets tossed in oil, garlic and chilli flakes and cooked at 190°C for 6 to 8 minutes until the tips char and crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Broccoli florets are mostly surface: the tiny buds char and crisp in the fast air, which is the flavour most people mean by roasted broccoli, while the stems steam tender in the same eight minutes. It works best when the florets are dry and cut to about the same size, and when the basket is not overloaded, because the buds need airflow to crisp. A squeeze of lemon at the end matters, since charred brassica benefits from acid.

  • Dry the florets after washing, or they steam and stay pale.
  • Cut them to about the same size so the small ones do not burn.
  • Finish with lemon. Acid lifts the charred flavour.

item.title: Bunny Chow
item.description: Bunny chow — a hollowed quarter loaf filled with Durban mutton curry, with the bread to dip.
item.content:encoded:
Durban curry is defined by its chilli-forward masala and the fact that it is thickened by potato rather than by a paste, so it is loose enough to soak into the bread but not so thin it runs straight through. The loaf must be a dense white bread with a strong crust, which is the only thing holding the whole construction together.

  • Fry the masala until the oil separates. It is the base of a Durban curry.
  • Potato is the thickener, added late so it holds some shape.
  • Unsliced white bread with a firm crust. Anything softer collapses.

item.title: Air Fryer Hard Boiled Eggs
item.description: Air fryer hard boiled eggs: whole eggs cooked at 150°C with no water, then chilled in ice water. Times for jammy, medium and fully set yolks.
item.content:encoded:
The eggs are cooked by dry heat, not water, but they follow the same rules: the white sets at about 80°C and the yolk at about 70 to 75°C, so a steady 150°C brings the whole egg up gradually and the timing is forgiving. The ice bath does two jobs. It stops the cooking so the yolk does not go grey-green at the edge, and it shrinks the egg slightly from its shell so it peels cleanly. Eggs a week or two old peel better than very fresh ones.

  • Use eggs straight from the fridge so the timing is consistent.
  • The ice bath is not optional. It stops the cooking and helps the peel.
  • Every air fryer is different. Test one egg first and adjust by a minute.

item.title: Breakfast Sandwich
item.description: Breakfast sandwich on a toasted English muffin, with a soft-set egg, melted cheese and crisp bacon. Fifteen minutes and one pan.
item.content:encoded:
The sandwich is a set of timings more than a recipe. The bacon goes in first because it takes longest and leaves the fat the eggs are cooked in, the muffins are toasted while the egg sets so everything is hot at once, and the cheese goes on the egg in the pan rather than on the bread so that it melts while the yolk is still soft. Piercing the yolk with a fork keeps it from bursting or running out of the muffin.

  • Prick the yolk so it sets softly instead of bursting.
  • Put the cheese on the egg in the pan, so it melts before the sandwich is built.
  • Toast the muffins while the egg cooks so everything comes together hot.

item.title: Sausage, Egg and Cheese Biscuit
item.description: Sausage, egg and cheese biscuit: flaky buttermilk biscuits filled with a sage-spiced sausage patty, a fried egg and melted cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Biscuit dough is worked as little as possible: cold butter is left in pea-sized pieces and the dough is folded rather than kneaded, so the butter steams in the oven and pushes the layers apart. The sausage is seasoned with sage and black pepper because those two are where most of the flavour of breakfast sausage comes from, and cooking the patties hard in a hot pan gives the sandwich a browned crust to set against the soft biscuit.

  • Keep the butter cold. Warm butter melts into the flour and the biscuits will not rise.
  • Cut straight down with the cutter. Twisting seals the edges and stops the rise.
  • Make the patties thinner in the middle, since they puff as they cook.

item.title: Malva Pudding
item.description: Malva pudding — South African apricot jam sponge soaked in a hot cream and butter sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce goes over the sponge while both are hot, which is the only way it gets absorbed rather than pooling underneath — a cooled cake sheds it. A tablespoon of vinegar in the batter reacts with the bicarbonate of soda for lift and, more usefully, keeps the very sweet sponge from being cloying.

  • Hot sauce onto hot sponge, straight out of the oven.
  • Prick it all over first so the sauce has a way in.
  • It will look like too much sauce. It is not.

item.title: Crustless Quiche
item.description: Crustless quiche with spinach, mushrooms and Gruyère in a creamy egg custard baked until just set. No pastry, gluten-free, easy to slice.
item.content:encoded:
Without a crust it is simply a baked custard, and custard has one rule: it sets at around 80°C, and going beyond that turns it rubbery and makes it weep. That is why it comes out of the oven while the centre still trembles slightly, and why some cream goes in with the milk, since it forgives a degree or two of overbaking. The spinach has to be squeezed dry, because whatever water it holds ends up in a puddle at the bottom of the dish.

  • Squeeze the spinach dry. Any water left pools at the bottom.
  • Take it out while the very centre still wobbles. It sets as it rests.
  • Cook the mushrooms until their liquid has gone, or the custard turns watery.

item.title: Baked Oatmeal
item.description: Baked oatmeal with bananas, blueberries, cinnamon and walnuts: oats baked in milk and egg until golden and sliceable. Ideal for meal prep.
item.content:encoded:
Baking changes what oatmeal is. The oats swell in the milk and egg and set as a custard would, so the result slices into squares that can be eaten with a fork or in the hand, rather than spooned from a pan. Baking powder gives it a little lift so it is tender instead of dense, and the melted butter goes into the batter rather than on top, so it tenderises the whole thing rather than only browning the surface.

  • Use rolled oats, not instant. Instant oats turn to paste.
  • Tap the dish after pouring so the milk reaches the bottom.
  • It firms as it cools, so squares hold together best after 15 minutes.

item.title: Lamingtons
item.description: Lamingtons — squares of butter sponge dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut.
item.content:encoded:
The sponge has to be a day old and preferably chilled, because fresh cake falls apart the moment it meets the thin icing. The icing itself is deliberately runny — closer to a glaze than a frosting — so it soaks a millimetre into the crumb rather than sitting on the surface in a shell.

  • Day-old, chilled sponge. Fresh cake disintegrates in the icing.
  • Thin icing, not thick. It should run off the fork.
  • Two forks and a rack. It is a messy job however you do it.

item.title: French Toast Casserole
item.description: French toast casserole: cubed brioche soaked in a cinnamon-vanilla custard and baked under a pecan streusel. Assemble ahead and serve with maple syrup.
item.content:encoded:
It is a bread pudding with a breakfast attitude, so the bread decides everything. Brioche or challah is rich enough to hold the custard without collapsing, and drying the cubes for a while in the air means they drink the custard instead of dissolving in it. The streusel goes on top because a bare bread surface dries out in the oven, and the crisp, buttery pecan crust against the soft custard beneath is the point of the dish.

  • Use rich, slightly stale bread. Soft sandwich bread turns to mush.
  • Press the cubes under the custard so none dry out or burn.
  • Cover with foil if the streusel is browning before the middle sets.

item.title: Home Fries
item.description: Diner-style home fries: diced potatoes parboiled, then crisped in a hot skillet with onion, pepper and smoked paprika until golden.
item.content:encoded:
Raw diced potatoes brown before they cook through, and boiled ones fall apart in the pan, so parboiling them for five minutes is the compromise that works: the outsides are already soft and slightly roughed up, which is what gives them a crisp crust, while the middles finish in the skillet. Steam-drying after draining matters as much as the boiling, since surface water is what stops browning. Leaving them alone for the first eight minutes builds the crust.

  • Steam-dry the parboiled potatoes. Wet ones will not brown.
  • Leave them alone for the first 8 minutes so a crust forms.
  • Add the onion and pepper late, or they burn before the potatoes are done.

item.title: Crêpes
item.description: Classic French crêpes: a thin, lacy batter of eggs, milk, flour and melted butter, rested then cooked in a hot pan. Fill sweet or savoury.
item.content:encoded:
The batter has to be thin, about the consistency of single cream, and it has to rest. Thirty minutes lets the flour hydrate fully and the gluten relax, so the crêpes are tender rather than rubbery and do not tear when flipped. The first crêpe is always a bad one, because the pan is not yet at temperature and has too much or too little butter; it is a test, not a failure. Swirl the pan the instant the batter goes in, since it sets in seconds.

  • Rest the batter. It makes crêpes tender and less likely to tear.
  • The first crêpe is a test of the pan. Do not judge the batter by it.
  • Add a splash of milk if the batter thickens as it rests.

item.title: Pavlova
item.description: Pavlova — crisp-shelled meringue with a marshmallow centre, topped with cream and fresh fruit.
item.content:encoded:
Cornflour and vinegar are what create the marshmallow interior: the acid stabilises the foam and the starch keeps the centre from drying out into plain meringue. Cooling the pavlova in the switched-off oven with the door shut is the single best defence against the cracking that comes from a sudden temperature drop.

  • Sugar in slowly, a spoonful at a time. Rushing gives a weeping meringue.
  • Rub a little between your fingers — no grit means it is ready.
  • Cool in the closed oven. Cracks come from sudden cooling.

item.title: Chicken and Rice Soup
item.description: Chicken and rice soup with bone-in thighs poached in a herby broth, carrots, celery and long-grain rice, finished with lemon and dill.
item.content:encoded:
Poaching the chicken in the soup does two jobs at once. It cooks the meat gently, so it stays tender, and the bones flavour the broth so a carton of stock tastes homemade. The rice goes in late and cooks only until tender, since rice keeps swelling in hot liquid and will turn the soup to porridge if it goes in early. Lemon at the end is the difference between a soup that tastes flat and one that tastes bright.

  • Add the rice late. It keeps swelling and turns the soup to porridge.
  • Finish with lemon. It brightens a broth that tastes flat.
  • Use thighs, not breasts. They stay tender and give the broth body.

item.title: Cream of Mushroom Soup
item.description: Cream of mushroom soup made from scratch: mushrooms browned hard, simmered with thyme and stock, then blended half-smooth with cream.
item.content:encoded:
Mushrooms are mostly water and taste of very little until it has gone, so they are browned in a hot pan, in batches, until they have released their liquid and started to colour. That is where the flavour is. A little flour gives the soup its velvet body without needing more than a splash of cream, and blending only half of it leaves pieces that make it a soup instead of a purée. Thyme and a squeeze of lemon lift the earthiness.

  • Brown the mushrooms in batches. Crowding steams them and they stay grey.
  • Blend only half, so there are still pieces to bite.
  • Do not boil once the cream is in, or it can split.

item.title: Anzac Biscuits
item.description: Anzac biscuits — oat and coconut biscuits bound with golden syrup and bicarbonate of soda.
item.content:encoded:
The bicarbonate of soda is dissolved in boiling water and stirred into the melted butter and syrup, where it reacts immediately and aerates the mixture — added dry with the flour it does far less. There are no eggs, which is why the originals kept for the length of a sea voyage and why the texture depends entirely on baking time.

  • Dissolve the bicarbonate of soda in boiling water first. It has to foam.
  • Twelve minutes chewy, sixteen crisp. Pick your side.
  • Leave them on the tray for five minutes or they will fall apart.

item.title: Taco Soup
item.description: Taco soup with ground beef, black and kidney beans, corn and tomatoes in a chili-cumin broth, topped with cheese, avocado and crushed chips.
item.content:encoded:
It is a taco filling loosened into a broth, so the seasoning is the whole game: chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, garlic and oregano, cooked into the beef first so they bloom in the fat instead of tasting dusty. The two kinds of bean give different textures, one holding its shape and one breaking down slightly to thicken the broth. Everything at the end, the cheese, avocado, lime and crushed chips, is what turns a pot of beef and beans into tacos in a bowl.

  • Cook the spices in the beef for a minute so they bloom and lose the raw taste.
  • Crush the chips over the top at the table so they stay crisp.
  • A squeeze of lime at the end brightens the whole pot.

item.title: Ham and Bean Soup
item.description: Ham and bean soup: navy beans soaked overnight and simmered with a smoked ham hock, carrots and celery until the broth turns creamy.
item.content:encoded:
The beans and the hock do each other a favour: the hock gives up smoke, salt and gelatin that turns the broth silky, and the beans, cooked gently in it, release starch that thickens it into something creamy without a spoonful of cream. Soaking overnight makes the cooking time predictable and the beans more evenly tender. Salt goes in only at the end, because the ham is already salty and a broth that reduces gets saltier still.

  • Salt at the end. The ham is salty and the broth concentrates as it simmers.
  • Mash some beans against the pot to thicken it, with no flour or cream.
  • A spoonful of cider vinegar at the end wakes up the smoke and fat.

item.title: Cabbage Soup
item.description: Cabbage soup with carrots, celery, peppers and tomatoes simmered in vegetable stock with paprika and thyme. Light, filling and about 100 calories.
item.content:encoded:
Cabbage tastes sweet and mellow when it is cooked slowly and sulphurous when it is not, so the trick is to let it simmer long enough to soften completely and to start the soup by softening the other vegetables first, which builds a base for the cabbage to cook in. Smoked paprika supplies the depth that meat would, and a splash of vinegar at the end lifts a pot that otherwise tastes sweet and flat.

  • Simmer until the cabbage is properly soft. Half-cooked cabbage tastes sulphurous.
  • Smoked paprika gives a savoury depth without any meat.
  • Add the vinegar at the end so it stays bright.

item.title: Kalua Pork
item.description: Kalua pork — Hawaiian salted pork shoulder wrapped in banana leaf and slow cooked until it shreds.
item.content:encoded:
Kalua pork traditionally cooks in an imu, an underground oven, and the whole flavour is smoke, salt and pork with nothing else — which means the salt has to be coarse and generous, and any extra seasoning takes it away from what it should be. Banana leaf keeps the meat moist and adds a faint grassy note that foil alone cannot.

  • Salt, smoke, pork. Adding anything else makes it a different dish.
  • Wrap tightly. All the moisture has to stay in the parcel.
  • Toss the shredded meat through the juices, every drop of them.

item.title: Macaroni Salad
item.description: Classic macaroni salad: elbow pasta in a creamy, tangy mayonnaise dressing with celery, pepper and red onion, chilled until the flavours meld.
item.content:encoded:
Pasta absorbs dressing as it sits, which is why a macaroni salad that looks right when mixed is dry two hours later. The answer is to dress it while the pasta is only just cooled and to make the dressing looser than seems right; a splash of the vinegar and a little milk keep it creamy through the chill. Cooking the macaroni a couple of minutes past al dente helps too, because firm pasta stays hard and chalky once it is cold.

  • Overcook the pasta slightly. Firm macaroni turns chalky when cold.
  • Make the dressing looser than looks right. The pasta soaks it up.
  • Stir in a splash of milk before serving if it has tightened up.

item.title: Pasta Salad
item.description: Italian pasta salad: rotini tossed in a red wine vinaigrette with cherry tomatoes, cucumber, olives, peppers and mozzarella. Serve cold.
item.content:encoded:
A pasta salad is served cold, and cold mutes seasoning, so the dressing has to taste too sharp on its own: a two-to-one ratio of oil to vinegar with mustard to emulsify it, garlic and oregano. Dressing the pasta while it is still slightly warm lets it absorb the vinaigrette instead of just wearing it. The vegetables and cheese go in once the pasta has cooled, so the tomatoes keep their shape and the mozzarella does not melt into the oil.

  • Dress the pasta while it is warm. It soaks up the vinaigrette.
  • Make the dressing sharper than you would for a green salad. Cold dulls flavour.
  • Add the tomatoes and cheese once the pasta has cooled.

item.title: Loco Moco
item.description: Loco moco — rice topped with a hamburger patty, brown gravy and a fried egg.
item.content:encoded:
The gravy is built in the pan the patties cooked in, so all the browned fond ends up in it — made separately it tastes like packet gravy on a burger. The egg has to be fried in hot fat with a runny yolk, because the yolk running into the gravy and rice is the point of the assembly.

  • Build the gravy in the patty pan. That fond is the flavour.
  • Runny yolks, always. They finish the dish at the table.
  • Dimple the patties so they stay flat under the egg.

item.title: Broccoli Salad
item.description: Broccoli salad: raw florets with crisp bacon, red onion, cheddar, cranberries and sunflower seeds in a sweet, tangy creamy dressing.
item.content:encoded:
The broccoli is raw, so the size of the pieces decides the eating: cut the florets small enough to fit on a fork with the other ingredients, and the stems peeled and diced small or left out. The dressing does the seasoning and also gently softens the florets as they sit, which is why the salad is better after half an hour in the fridge than immediately. Sugar and vinegar in the dressing balance the bitterness of raw broccoli and the salt of the bacon.

  • Cut the florets small so every forkful holds a bit of everything.
  • Add the bacon and seeds at the last moment, or they go soft in the dressing.
  • It improves after 30 minutes chilled as the dressing softens the broccoli.

item.title: Twice-Baked Potatoes
item.description: Twice-baked potatoes: crisp-skinned russets scooped and mashed with butter, soured cream, cheddar and bacon, then refilled and baked until golden.
item.content:encoded:
The first bake is for the potato and the second is for the skin. A russet baked directly on the rack for an hour has a dry, fluffy middle that mashes light and a skin that is crisp enough to stand up to being refilled, which is why boiling the potatoes or microwaving them will not do. The filling is mashed while the potatoes are hot, since cold flesh does not absorb the butter and dairy, and it is over-filled and mounded so the tops brown in the second bake.

  • Bake on the rack for a crisp skin that holds the filling.
  • Mash the flesh while it is hot so it takes up the butter.
  • Leave a thin wall of potato in each skin so it does not tear.

item.title: Fried Okra
item.description: Southern fried okra: sliced okra dipped in buttermilk and coated in seasoned cornmeal, fried until crisp, golden and never slimy.
item.content:encoded:
Okra has a reputation for slime, which comes from mucilage released when the pods are cut and heated wet. Coating the slices in cornmeal and frying them hot and fast seals the surface before it can leak, so the inside steams tender while the outside turns crisp. Cornmeal alone, rather than flour, gives the coarse, sandy crust that is traditional in the South and it is naturally gluten-free. Frying in small batches keeps the oil hot enough to do it quickly.

  • Keep the oil at 180°C. Cool oil lets the okra go soft and greasy.
  • Dry, fresh okra is less slimy than wet or frozen okra.
  • Fry in small batches so the temperature does not drop.

item.title: Breakfast Hash
item.description: Breakfast hash — crisp fried potatoes with peppers and onions, finished with eggs under the grill.
item.content:encoded:
Par-boiling the potatoes and then drying them gives a floury surface that crisps in the pan, which raw diced potato never does in the time available. Leaving the pan alone for five minutes at a time is the other half — the crust forms in contact with hot metal, and stirring resets the clock every time.

  • Par-boil and steam dry. Raw potato will not crisp in the time you have.
  • Leave the pan alone for five minutes at a stretch. Stirring stops the crust.
  • Grill the eggs rather than covering the pan, so the tops set but the yolks do not.

item.title: Hush Puppies
item.description: Hush puppies: cornmeal and buttermilk batter with onion, dropped into hot oil until puffed, golden and crisp. Serve with fried fish or barbecue.
item.content:encoded:
The batter is thick enough to hold on a spoon, which is why it puffs into a ball rather than spreading into a pancake, and the baking powder makes it fry light and hollow inside. Fine cornmeal gives a tender crumb, while coarse cornmeal makes gritty ones. The oil temperature is critical: too cool and they soak up fat and stay heavy, too hot and the outside browns before the middle cooks. A steady 175°C gives them about three minutes to puff and colour through.

  • Keep the oil at 175°C and check between batches.
  • Grate the onion so it melts into the batter and flavours every bite.
  • Do not overmix. A few lumps make a lighter hush puppy.

item.title: Collard Greens
item.description: Southern collard greens simmered with smoked ham hock, onion, garlic and cider vinegar until silky, with a savoury pot liquor for cornbread.
item.content:encoded:
Collards are tough, and the answer is time and a gentle simmer in something savoury: the ham hock supplies smoke, salt and gelatin, and after an hour the leaves are silky rather than chewy. The broth left in the pot, the pot liquor, is prized in the South and is full of flavour and nutrients that leach from the greens, so it is served with them. A splash of cider vinegar and a pinch of sugar at the end balance the smoke and the bitterness.

  • Wash the leaves well. Collards hold grit in their veins.
  • Cook them until silky. Undercooked collards are tough and bitter.
  • Serve the pot liquor with cornbread. It is half the point.

item.title: Ribollita
item.description: Ribollita — Tuscan bean and cavolo nero soup thickened with stale bread and reboiled the next day.
item.content:encoded:
The name means "reboiled", and it is not romanticism: the soup is made one day, left overnight for the bread to dissolve completely into it, and reheated the next, which is when it becomes a single thick mass rather than soup with bread in it. Puréeing a third of the beans gives body without cream or stock.

  • Make it a day ahead. Reboiled is the recipe, not a suggestion.
  • Twenty minutes on the soffritto. Everything else depends on it.
  • Finish with far more raw olive oil than seems polite.

item.title: Cherry Pie
item.description: Cherry pie with a tart cherry filling thickened with cornflour, under a flaky all-butter double crust. Cool fully so the filling sets.
item.content:encoded:
A fruit pie fails in two places: a filling that runs and a base that stays pale and damp. The cornflour tossed through the cherries is what sets the filling, but only if the pie bubbles thickly through the vents, which is the signal that it has come to the boil and the starch has done its work. The bottom crust gets its colour from starting on a preheated tray at high heat, and the pie must cool for three hours, because a warm cherry pie is soup.

  • The filling is done when it bubbles thickly through the vents. That is how you know the cornflour has cooked.
  • Start the pie on a hot tray so the bottom crust browns.
  • Wait for it to cool. A warm cherry pie runs across the plate.

item.title: Blueberry Pie
item.description: Blueberry pie under a lattice crust: a third of the berries are cooked to a jammy base so the filling sets firm. Cool fully before slicing.
item.content:encoded:
Blueberries are the difficult pie fruit: they hold their shape, so the filling can stay loose and watery however much thickener you add. The fix is to cook a third of them with the cornflour and sugar on the hob first, mashing them slightly, until it is a thick, glossy jam, and then to fold in the rest raw, so the pie has both a set base and whole berries. A lattice top, rather than a solid lid, lets the steam out and the excess juice evaporate.

  • Cook a third of the berries first. It is what sets the filling.
  • Use frozen berries straight from the freezer so they do not bleed into the crust.
  • Cover the edge with foil if it darkens before the middle bubbles.

item.title: Whoopie Pies
item.description: Whoopie pies: domed, tender chocolate cake rounds sandwiched with a fluffy marshmallow buttercream. Soft, moist and made in one bowl.
item.content:encoded:
A whoopie pie is a cake baked as a cookie, so the batter is soft and thick rather than a dough, and it domes as it bakes. Buttermilk and bicarbonate give it lift and a tender crumb, and the cocoa is bloomed by the hot melted butter for a deeper flavour. The filling has to be fluffy and stable enough to sit between two soft rounds without squeezing out, which is what the marshmallow cream is for.

  • Cool the cakes completely before filling or the buttercream melts.
  • Use a cookie scoop for even sizes, so the halves match.
  • Chill the filled pies for 15 minutes for cleaner bites.

item.title: Roasted Vegetable Buddha Bowl
item.description: Roasted vegetable buddha bowl — roast vegetables, grains and chickpeas with a tahini dressing.
item.content:encoded:
A bowl like this fails when everything is the same texture, so the components are cooked separately and deliberately differently: vegetables roasted hard, chickpeas crisped, grains dressed while warm, greens raw. Whisking iced water into tahini makes it seize and then loosen into a pale, creamy dressing, which is the only reliable way to get the consistency right.

  • Iced water into the tahini. It seizes first, then loosens — keep going.
  • Dress the grains warm so they take the acid.
  • Sections, not a mix. The contrast is the whole appeal.

item.title: Chocolate Crinkle Cookies
item.description: Chocolate crinkle cookies: fudgy, brownie-like cookies rolled in icing sugar that crack into a snowy crinkle pattern as they bake.
item.content:encoded:
The crinkles are a chemistry trick. The dough is wet, oil-based and chilled solid, and it is rolled in granulated sugar and then a thick coat of icing sugar. In the oven the cookie puffs and spreads, and the outer coat, which has dried and set, cannot stretch with it, so it splits and lets the dark dough show through the white. Oil rather than butter keeps them fudgy, and the chill is what makes a wet dough rollable.

  • Roll in icing sugar twice if the coat looks thin. A thick coat gives the best cracks.
