  • Take them out while the centres are soft. They firm as they cool.
  • Chill the dough until it is properly firm, or it is too sticky to roll.

item.title: Banana Muffins
item.description: Banana muffins: tall, moist and domed, made with very ripe bananas, yogurt and cinnamon, and started at a high heat for a bakery rise.
item.content:encoded:
Bakery muffins have tall domed tops because the oven starts very hot: five minutes at 200°C makes the batter rise fast before the crust sets, and dropping to 180°C then bakes the middle through without burning the top. Overripe bananas, speckled brown or black, are sweeter and give more moisture, and the yogurt keeps the crumb tender. Stir the batter until just combined, since muffins mixed like a cake turn tough and tunnelled.

  • Use bananas with black speckles. Yellow ones give a bland muffin.
  • Start hot for the dome, then drop the temperature.
  • Stop mixing while the batter is still lumpy.

item.title: Affogato
item.description: Affogato — vanilla gelato with a shot of hot espresso poured over it at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The whole dish is a temperature contrast that lasts about ninety seconds, so the glass is chilled, the ice cream is hard-frozen and the espresso is pulled at the last moment. A single shot to one scoop is the ratio that keeps it a dessert rather than a coffee with cream in it.

  • Chill the glasses. It buys another thirty seconds of contrast.
  • One shot per scoop. More and it becomes a coffee float.
  • Pour the espresso the moment it is made, at the table.

item.title: Apple Cider Donuts
item.description: Baked apple cider donuts: cake doughnuts made with reduced apple cider, brushed with butter and rolled in cinnamon sugar while still warm.
item.content:encoded:
The cider is reduced from a cupful to about a quarter of that, which concentrates the apple flavour into a syrup that survives the bake; put in as it comes, the cider is too dilute to taste. The donuts are baked in a doughnut tin rather than fried, so the batter is closer to a muffin than a dough and stays tender. The cinnamon sugar sticks only to a surface that is still warm and buttered, so they are coated as soon as they are cool enough to handle.

  • Reduce the cider properly. Fresh cider tastes of nothing once baked.
  • Coat them while warm. The butter is the glue for the sugar.
  • Pipe the batter, since spooning gives uneven rings.

item.title: Peanut Brittle
item.description: Old-fashioned peanut brittle: roasted peanuts in amber sugar and corn syrup, lightened with bicarbonate of soda and stretched thin until it snaps.
item.content:encoded:
Brittle is sugar taken to the hard-crack stage, 150°C, at which the syrup will set glassy and snap. Corn syrup stops the sugar recrystallising into grains. The bicarbonate is added at the very end because it reacts with the acids in the caramelised sugar and releases carbon dioxide, filling the brittle with tiny bubbles that make it light and tender rather than a tooth-breaking slab. Everything must be ready before the syrup is on the heat, because the last stage takes seconds.

  • Have everything measured before you start. The last stage takes seconds.
  • Take it to 150°C. Below that it is chewy and sticks to the teeth.
  • Hot sugar burns badly. Keep children and pets out of the kitchen.

item.title: Dinner Rolls
item.description: Soft dinner rolls from a rich milk-and-egg dough, shaped into balls, risen twice and brushed with melted butter straight from the oven.
item.content:encoded:
The milk, egg and butter in the dough make the crumb tender and the crust thin and soft rather than crisp, which is the difference between a dinner roll and a bread roll. The dough is deliberately soft and slightly sticky and is kneaded until it stretches into a thin, translucent window, because it is the gluten that lets the rolls rise tall instead of spreading. Shaping them to touch in the tin means they rise upwards and bake into a soft, pull-apart sheet.

  • Knead until the dough passes the window test. That is what gives height.
  • Keep the dough slightly sticky. Too much flour makes dry rolls.
  • Brush with butter the second they leave the oven.

item.title: Berry Smoothie Bowl
item.description: Berry smoothie bowl — frozen fruit blended thick enough to spoon, topped with fruit, seeds and granola.
item.content:encoded:
The difference between a smoothie and a smoothie bowl is liquid, and specifically how little of it: the fruit must be frozen solid and the liquid added a tablespoon at a time, using the tamper rather than more milk to keep the blades moving. Any more and it becomes a drink and the toppings sink.

  • Frozen fruit and almost no liquid. Add milk by the tablespoon.
  • Use the tamper, not more milk, to keep the blades turning.
  • Chill the bowls and eat it straight away.

item.title: Poutine
item.description: Authentic Quebec poutine: double-fried chips topped with squeaky cheese curds and hot peppery brown gravy poured over so the curds soften but do not melt.
item.content:encoded:
There are three components and each has one rule. The chips must stay crisp under gravy, which means frying twice: once at a low temperature to cook them through and again hot to crisp them. The gravy must be hot and thin enough to run, since a thick gravy sits on top instead of soaking down. And the curds must be fresh, at room temperature and squeaky, so the heat of the gravy softens them without melting them into a pool; cold curds stay hard and melted ones lose their squeak.

  • Fry twice. A single fry gives limp chips that collapse under gravy.
  • Keep the curds at room temperature so the gravy softens them without melting them.
  • The gravy should be piping hot and thin enough to pour, not thick enough to sit on top.

item.title: Butter Tarts
item.description: Canadian butter tarts: flaky all-butter pastry filled with a gooey, sticky butter, brown sugar and maple filling, baked until bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
The filling is the whole argument: runny or set, raisins or none. What makes it gooey is a high ratio of sugar and butter to egg, baked only until the egg sets at the edge while the middle is still wobbly, so it firms as it cools but stays sticky. A little vinegar cuts the sweetness and helps it set. The pastry has to be cold and thin so it crisps under a wet filling, and the filling is stirred, not whisked, because air makes it puff and crack.

  • Stir the filling. Whisking in air makes it puff up and crack.
  • Take them out while the middle still wobbles. It sets as it cools.
  • Run a knife around each tart while it is warm, or the sugar glues it to the tin.

item.title: Cold Brew Coffee
item.description: Cold brew coffee — coarse coffee steeped in cold water for 18 hours to a smooth, low acid concentrate.
item.content:encoded:
Cold water never extracts the bitter and sour compounds that hot water pulls out in seconds, which is why cold brew tastes smooth and sweet without being weaker — the trade is time, roughly eighteen hours for what hot water does in four minutes. Grinding coarse is essential: fine grounds over-extract even cold and clog every filter you own.

  • Coarse grind. Fine grounds turn cold brew bitter and cloudy.
  • Do not stir during the steep.
  • Filter twice, and be patient with the second pass.

item.title: Nanaimo Bars
item.description: Classic no-bake Nanaimo bars: a chocolate, coconut and walnut crumb base, a vanilla custard buttercream layer and a glossy dark chocolate top.
item.content:encoded:
Each layer does a different job. The base is crumbs, coconut and nuts bound with egg that has been cooked gently to a thick custard, so it is chewy and holds together. The middle is a soft butter icing coloured and flavoured with custard powder, which sets to a creamy, fudgy layer. The top is a thin coat of dark chocolate that snaps. The method is really just patience: each layer has to be firm before the next goes on, and the chocolate cooled so it does not melt through the middle.

  • Chill each layer until firm before adding the next, or they smear.
  • Let the chocolate cool for a few minutes so it does not melt the custard layer.
  • Cut with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry so the chocolate does not crack.

item.title: Tourtière
item.description: Tourtière, the Quebec meat pie: spiced pork and beef with cinnamon and clove, bound with potato and baked in all-butter pastry until deep golden.
item.content:encoded:
The spice is what makes it tourtière rather than an ordinary meat pie: cinnamon, clove and allspice in a pork filling, which smells like Christmas to anyone from Québec. The grated potato is not a filler but a binder, since it dissolves as the filling simmers and thickens the stock so the pie holds together when sliced. The filling has to be cooked almost dry and cooled completely before it goes in the pastry, because hot, wet filling melts the butter and steams the base crust to paste.

  • Cook the filling almost dry. Wet filling steams the bottom crust.
  • Cool the filling completely before it goes into the pastry.
  • Grated potato is the binder. Do not leave it out.

item.title: Maple Glazed Salmon
item.description: Maple glazed salmon: skin-on fillets brushed twice with a maple, Dijon and garlic glaze and baked until lacquered. Ready in 22 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Maple and salmon are a Canadian pairing that works because the sweetness balances the fish oil and the mustard in the glaze cuts through both. The glaze goes on in two stages: the first coat bakes in and seasons the fish, and the second, brushed on part-way, stays sticky and glossy instead of burning off. A brief grill at the end caramelises the maple sugars, but they go from amber to bitter in seconds, so watch it.

  • Glaze in two stages. The first seasons the fish and the second stays glossy.
  • Take it out at 57°C. Salmon is best just done.
  • Watch it under the grill. Maple sugar burns in seconds.

item.title: Chicken Milanese
item.description: Chicken Milanese — chicken breast beaten thin, breaded and fried in butter until deep gold and crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Pounding to an even 5 mm means the cutlet cooks through in the three minutes the crust needs to brown — any thicker and you choose between a pale crust and dry meat. Clarified butter takes the heat without the milk solids burning, which whole butter would do in a shallow fry.

  • Even thickness beats thinness. A cutlet thin at one end and thick at the other cooks two different ways.
  • Rest after breading. Fifteen minutes is the difference between a crust that stays on and one that peels.
  • A rack, not kitchen paper — paper traps steam and softens the underside immediately.

item.title: Roasted Root Vegetables
item.description: Roasted root vegetables: carrots, parsnips, swede and sweet potato roasted on a hot tray until caramelised, then glazed with maple and thyme.
item.content:encoded:
Root vegetables are full of sugar and starch, which is why they caramelise so well and why they burn if they are crowded or the oven is too cool. A very hot tray sears the cut faces, and spreading them out means they roast in dry heat instead of steaming in each other's moisture. The maple goes on late for the same reason the sugar in any glaze does: added at the start it would burn long before the vegetables were tender.

  • Preheat the trays. Vegetables that hit hot metal brown rather than steam.
  • Add the maple late or it burns before the vegetables are tender.
  • Cut everything to the same size so it finishes together.

item.title: Prawn Cocktail
item.description: Classic prawn cocktail: cold prawns in a tangy Marie Rose sauce of mayonnaise, ketchup, horseradish and lemon, served on crisp lettuce in a glass.
item.content:encoded:
A prawn cocktail is only as good as its sauce and its cold. The prawns must be dry and chilled, the lettuce crisp, and the Marie Rose properly balanced: mayonnaise for body, ketchup for sweetness, horseradish and lemon to cut through both and cayenne for a little warmth. Everything that goes wrong with it, the watery pink pool at the bottom of the glass, the limp lettuce, comes from wet ingredients, so the prawns are patted dry and the lettuce is dressed at the last moment.

  • Dry the prawns thoroughly. Wet prawns thin the sauce into a pink puddle.
  • Shred the lettuce finely and add the prawns just before serving so it stays crisp.
  • Taste the sauce on its own. It should be sharper than you think, since cold food mutes flavour.

item.title: Pasta Puttanesca
item.description: Pasta puttanesca — tomatoes, anchovies, olives, capers and chilli, made in the time the pasta boils.
item.content:encoded:
The anchovies are melted into warm oil rather than added to a hot pan, so they dissolve completely instead of frying — done properly the sauce tastes savoury and deep rather than of fish. No salt is added at any stage: anchovies, olives and capers between them bring more than enough.

  • Start the anchovies in cold oil. Dropped into a hot pan they seize and stay in lumps.
  • No Parmesan. Cheese on a puttanesca is a genuine offence in Naples and it does not need it.
  • Do not salt the sauce until you have tasted it at the end.

item.title: Beef and Barley Soup
item.description: Beef and barley soup: seared chuck, carrots, celery and mushrooms simmered with pearl barley in a rich broth until the beef is spoon-tender.
item.content:encoded:
Two things go into the pot for different lengths of time. Beef chuck needs an hour of gentle simmering to break down its collagen into gelatin, which is what makes the broth rich and the meat tender, while pearl barley needs only about 35 minutes and turns to mush if it goes in with the beef. So the barley waits, and its starch thickens the soup at the end. Browning the beef properly, in batches, is the flavour base; a crowded pan steams and gives a grey, thin broth.

  • Brown the beef in batches. A crowded pan steams and the broth comes out thin.
  • Add the barley late. It turns to mush if it simmers for two hours.
  • The soup thickens overnight, so thin it with stock or water when reheating.

item.title: Damper
item.description: Damper, the Australian bush bread: a quick round loaf of self-raising flour, butter and milk, cross-cut and baked golden. Serve warm with golden syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Damper is the bread of the stockman who had flour, salt and a fire, and its virtue is speed: self-raising flour does the work yeast would do, so there is no rising, and the dough is worked only until it comes together, since kneading makes a tough, dense loaf. The cross cut in the top lets the heat reach the middle and gives a place to tear it. It is a loaf to be eaten within the hour, warm, with butter and golden syrup or beside a stew.

  • Handle the dough as little as possible. Kneading toughens a raised-by-powder bread.
  • Cut the cross deep so the middle bakes through.
  • Eat it within the hour. It goes stale quickly.

item.title: Crispy Skin Barramundi
item.description: Crispy skin barramundi: fillets seared skin side down until crackling, then finished with a nutty lemon, caper and parsley brown butter.
item.content:encoded:
Barramundi has thick, oily skin that turns to crackling if it is treated right and rubber if it is not. That means bone-dry skin, a hot pan with a thin film of oil, and pressing the fillet flat for the first half-minute so it cannot curl away from the surface. Then it is left alone: the skin releases from the pan when it is ready, and forcing it earlier tears it. Most of the cooking, about four fifths, happens on the skin side.

  • Bone-dry skin is everything. Pat it until the paper towel comes away dry.
  • Press the fillet flat for the first 30 seconds or the skin curls and stays pale.
  • Spoon the sauce beside the fish, so the skin stays crisp.

item.title: Pots de Crème
item.description: Pots de crème au chocolat — dark chocolate baked custards, set in a bain-marie and served chilled.
item.content:encoded:
Custard sets by coagulating egg protein, which happens around 80°C and curdles above 85°C — the bain-marie holds the pots below that ceiling so they set smooth rather than grainy. Pouring the hot cream onto the chocolate rather than melting them together avoids seizing.

  • Strain the custard. It takes ten seconds and is the difference between silky and slightly grainy.
  • They should wobble when they come out. A firm pot in the oven is an overcooked pot on the plate.
  • Use chocolate you would eat on its own — there are only three other ingredients.

item.title: Lamb Cutlets
item.description: Barbecued lamb cutlets marinated in rosemary, garlic and lemon, cooked hot and fast to medium-rare with the fat cap crisped. Serve with mint sauce.
item.content:encoded:
A cutlet is a lamb chop cut from the rack, small, tender and quick, and the job is to brown the outside hard while leaving the middle pink. That takes a very hot surface and about three minutes a side, which is why the marinade is scraped off before cooking: oil and garlic burn on a hot grill and taste bitter. Standing the cutlet on its fat edge for the last half minute renders and crisps the fat, which is the best part of it.

  • Scrape the marinade off before the grill. Garlic and herbs burn and turn bitter.
  • Cook to about 54°C. Cutlets this small overcook in a minute.
  • Render the fat cap by standing the cutlets on their edge at the end.

item.title: Grilled Prawn Salad
item.description: Grilled prawn salad: king prawns barbecued in two minutes a side, on cos lettuce with mango, avocado, tomato and a lime and chilli dressing.
item.content:encoded:
The prawns need only a hot grill and two minutes a side, so the salad is where the effort goes: sweet mango and creamy avocado against crisp cos and a sharp lime and chilli dressing. The prawns are marinated in the zest only, not the juice, because acid turns shellfish mushy in minutes, and the dressing goes on at the last moment so the lettuce keeps its crunch. Whole prawns with the tails on stay juicier and look better.

  • Marinate with the zest, not the juice. Acid turns prawns mushy.
  • Skewer the prawns so they turn in one go and cannot fall through the grate.
  • Dress the salad at the last moment so the lettuce stays crisp.

item.title: Salade de Chèvre Chaud
item.description: Salade de chèvre chaud — grilled goat cheese toasts on dressed leaves with walnuts and honey.
item.content:encoded:
A log-shaped goat cheese with a rind holds its shape under the grill where a soft, rindless cheese collapses through the toast. Dressing the leaves before the toasts land keeps them crisp — hot cheese on undressed leaves steams them flat.

  • Use a rinded log. Rindless goat cheese slides off the toast and through the grill rack.
  • Dress the leaves first, then add the toasts. The other way round gives you a warm, wilted salad.
  • Stand and watch it. Three minutes is right and five is a puddle.

item.title: Creamy Tuscan Pasta
item.description: Creamy Tuscan pasta: penne in a garlic and sun-dried tomato cream sauce with wilted spinach and Parmesan. Vegetarian, ready in thirty minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is built in three ideas. The oil the sun-dried tomatoes are packed in is the cooking fat, so their flavour goes into everything. Stock goes in with the cream, thinning it enough to reduce properly without splitting and giving it more savour than cream alone. And the pasta finishes in the sauce with a splash of its own starchy water, which is what makes a cream sauce cling to penne instead of sliding off it. Spinach goes in last so it wilts and keeps its colour.

  • Use the oil from the jar. It carries the tomato flavour.
  • Finish the pasta in the sauce with a splash of its water so the sauce clings.
  • Simmer, never boil hard, once the cream is in.

item.title: Southland Cheese Rolls
item.description: Southland cheese rolls: white bread rolled around a thick mature cheddar, onion and evaporated milk filling, buttered and grilled until golden.
item.content:encoded:
The filling is a cheese paste rather than a slice of cheese: mature cheddar melted with evaporated milk and grated onion, which is thick enough to spread, stays put when it is rolled, and does not run out when it is grilled. Flattening the bread first is what lets it roll without cracking, and the butter on the outside is what browns it into the crisp, golden cylinder the roll is famous for. It is a snack from the bottom of the South Island, and nobody there uses a sharp knife on the recipe.

  • Flatten the bread first. It rolls tight without cracking.
  • Use a mature cheddar. A mild one gives a bland filling.
  • Butter the outsides generously. That is what turns them golden and crisp.

item.title: Cheese and Bacon Rolls
item.description: Cheese and bacon rolls: soft yeast dough rolled with crisp bacon, mature cheddar and spring onion, sliced into spirals and baked until golden.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is a soft, enriched white dough, not a crusty one, so the finished roll is tender and slightly sweet against the salty bacon and sharp cheese. The bacon is cooked crisp and cooled first, because raw bacon would release fat and water into the spiral and leave it greasy and damp, and cooled so it does not melt the cheese before the oven does. Rolling the log tightly and slicing it with a serrated knife, sawing gently, keeps the spirals round.

  • Cool the bacon before scattering, so it does not melt the cheese.
  • Roll the log as tightly as you can so the spirals hold together.
  • Slice with a serrated knife, sawing gently, so the rolls stay round.

item.title: Pork Shogayaki
item.description: Pork shogayaki — thin pork loin in a ginger, soy and mirin glaze, with shredded cabbage. Ready in 25 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Grated ginger is added twice — some in the marinade for penetration, the rest at the end for aroma, since gingerol degrades quickly over heat and a single early addition tastes flat. Dusting the pork in a little flour gives the glaze something to cling to instead of pooling in the pan.

  • Score the fat edge. Unscored pork loin curls into a cup and cooks unevenly.
  • Half the ginger goes in at the end. That late hit is where the aroma comes from.
  • The iced cabbage is not garnish — the cold crunch against the hot glaze is the point of the plate.

item.title: Afghan Biscuits
item.description: Afghan biscuits: crunchy chocolate cornflake biscuits from New Zealand, baked until firm, iced with chocolate and topped with a walnut half.
item.content:encoded:
The cornflakes are the point. They are folded into the dough at the very end, crushed only enough that they stay in chunks, and they give the biscuit its crunch and its rough, craggy surface. The dough itself is a short, buttery chocolate one, so it must not be overworked, and the chocolate icing with its walnut half is not decoration: it is what makes it an Afghan rather than a chocolate cornflake cookie. Nobody is quite sure where the name comes from.

  • Fold the cornflakes in last and keep some chunks. They are the crunch.
  • Ice the biscuits only when completely cold, or the icing slides off.
  • Do not overmix the dough. It should be short, not stretchy.

item.title: Hokey Pokey Ice Cream
item.description: Hokey pokey ice cream: creamy no-churn vanilla ice cream with crunchy pieces of homemade honeycomb toffee. Whipped cream, condensed milk, no machine.
item.content:encoded:
Hokey pokey is honeycomb toffee: sugar and golden syrup boiled to amber, then foamed with bicarbonate so the cooling toffee sets full of bubbles, light and shattery instead of solid. The ice cream is the easy part, whipped cream folded into condensed milk, which freezes soft enough to scoop without a churn or custard. The toffee is folded in only at the end and in shards, since fine dust dissolves into the cream and disappears, and the pieces have to be added cold and dry.

  • Have the bicarbonate measured before you start. The foam happens in seconds.
  • Keep the crushed toffee dry. It goes sticky in humid air and dissolves into the cream.
  • Hot sugar burns badly. Keep the pan and the tray away from children.

item.title: Buta no Kakuni
item.description: Buta no kakuni — Japanese braised pork belly, simmered until a chopstick passes through, with egg and mustard.
item.content:encoded:
The belly is boiled in plain water with rice or leek tops first, then discarded — that pre-boil removes both scum and a great deal of fat, which is why kakuni tastes rich rather than greasy despite the cut. Cooling in the braising liquid overnight lets the seasoning penetrate and makes the surface fat easy to lift off.

  • The hour-long pre-boil is what makes this rich instead of greasy. Do not skip it.
  • Overnight in the liquid, then skim. Both the flavour and the texture depend on that rest.
  • A chopstick, not a knife, is the doneness test — it should meet nothing at all.

item.title: Kumara Soup
item.description: Kumara soup: New Zealand orange sweet potato simmered with ginger, cumin and chilli, blended velvety with coconut milk and finished with lime.
item.content:encoded:
Kumara is sweeter and denser than the pale sweet potatoes elsewhere, so it needs something to push against: fresh ginger and toasted cumin and coriander for warmth, a little chilli for heat, and lime at the end for acid. The soup is thickened by the kumara itself, blended until smooth, and the coconut milk goes in afterwards so it stays creamy and does not split under a hard boil. It is one of the few soups that is better with no cream in it.

  • Simmer until the kumara is very soft. Firm pieces leave the soup gritty.
  • Add the coconut milk after blending, and do not boil it.
  • Finish with lime. It stops the sweetness feeling heavy.

item.title: Roasted Kumara Salad
item.description: Roasted kumara salad with smoked paprika, rocket, feta, red onion and toasted pumpkin seeds in a wholegrain mustard and lemon dressing. Serve warm.
item.content:encoded:
Kumara roasts better than almost any vegetable because its sugars caramelise before the flesh dries out, so the edges go dark and sticky while the middle stays soft and creamy. It is dressed while it is still warm, since warm vegetables absorb dressing where cold ones just wear it. The salad is built on contrasts: sweet against the salt and tang of feta, soft against the crunch of pumpkin seeds, and the peppery bite of rocket to cut through all of it.

  • Preheat the tray so the kumara sears rather than steams.
  • Dress it while it is warm. It soaks the dressing up.
  • Add the rocket at the last moment so it does not wilt.

item.title: Whitebait Fritters
item.description: Whitebait fritters: tiny whitebait bound only with beaten egg and fried in foaming butter until golden. Serve on white bread with lemon.
item.content:encoded:
The whitebait are the point and the batter is barely there: nothing more than beaten egg, so each fritter is a lace of set egg holding a cluster of tiny fish. Beating the eggs until frothy gives it a light, puffed texture, and cooking at a moderate heat in foaming butter sets the egg before the fish overcook. Whitebait are translucent and turn white and opaque as they cook, which tells you when a fritter is done. Dry them well, or the fritters are watery and fall apart.

  • Beat the eggs until frothy. It is what makes the fritters light.
  • Cook at medium heat. Hot butter burns before the egg sets.
  • Dry the whitebait well or the mixture is watery and will not hold.

item.title: Shui Zhu Fish
item.description: Shui zhu fish — Sichuan poached fish in chilli broth, finished with smoking oil poured over at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The fish is velveted in egg white and cornflour and poached for barely two minutes, so it stays silky in a dish that looks aggressive. The smoking oil poured over the aromatics at the end blooms them instantly — done in the pan instead, the chillies would burn long before the dish reached the table.

  • The oil must be smoking. Anything cooler and the chillies steam rather than bloom.
  • Slide the fish in one slice at a time and leave it alone — stirring breaks it apart.
  • Most of the chillies are there for aroma, not to be eaten. Push them aside as you go.

item.title: Seafood Chowder
item.description: New Zealand seafood chowder: firm white fish, mussels and prawns in a thick, creamy bacon, potato and celery base. Serve with crusty bread.
item.content:encoded:
A chowder is built in layers: a base of bacon, onion and celery, a roux, a liquid of fish stock and milk thickened by the starch of the potato, and the seafood last, each piece for only as long as it needs. Firm white fish holds its shape in chunks, while prawns and mussels need two or three minutes, and the cream goes in at the very end because a long simmer breaks it. The bacon and the fish stock give the base a depth that milk alone would not.

  • Add the seafood last and cook it briefly. Overcooked shellfish turns rubbery.
  • Let the potatoes just begin to break down. Their starch thickens the chowder.
  • Do not let it boil once the cream is in.

item.title: Kumara and Coconut Curry
item.description: Kumara and coconut curry: orange sweet potato and chickpeas simmered in coconut milk with red curry paste, spinach and lime. Vegan.
item.content:encoded:
Kumara suits curry because it is sweet and holds its shape, so it stands up to a long simmer in coconut milk without dissolving and its sweetness balances the salt and heat of the paste. The paste is fried in oil first with the onion, garlic and ginger, which is the step that turns it from a raw, harsh smell into a deep, fragrant one. Mashing a few of the cooked pieces against the side of the pan thickens the sauce, and the lime at the end is not optional.

  • Fry the curry paste until it darkens. Raw paste tastes harsh.
  • Mash a few pieces of kumara to thicken the sauce, with no flour.
  • Check the curry paste is vegan. Some contain shrimp paste.

item.title: Lo Bak Go
item.description: Lo bak go — steamed daikon and rice flour cake with dried shrimp and lap cheong, pan-fried crisp in slices.
item.content:encoded:
The daikon is cooked down first and its liquid kept, because that liquid is what hydrates the rice flour — using water instead loses most of the flavour. The cake must chill overnight before slicing: warm, it is too soft to cut and falls apart in the pan.

  • Keep the daikon cooking liquid. It carries the flavour and hydrates the flour.
  • Overnight in the fridge, without exception. A warm cake cannot be sliced.
  • Fry it properly — the contrast between crisp exterior and soft interior is the whole pleasure.

item.title: Bacon and Egg Pie
item.description: New Zealand bacon and egg pie: whole eggs baked into a crisp shortcrust base with bacon, onion, peas and cheese, under a golden puff pastry lid.
item.content:encoded:
It is a picnic pie, eaten warm or cold, so every part of it has to be dry. The base is baked blind so it stays crisp under the eggs, the bacon and onion are cooked and drained so they do not release water, and the pie rests for fifteen minutes so the eggs set and the slice holds its shape. Whole eggs cracked into the filling bake into firm yolks that show in the middle of each slice. Shortcrust below and puff above is the classic Kiwi construction.

  • Blind bake the base. It is what keeps the bottom crisp under the eggs.
  • Drain the bacon and onion so they do not release water into the pie.
  • Rest the pie. Cut hot, the eggs run and the slice collapses.

item.title: Pan-Seared Salmon
item.description: Pan-seared salmon: skin-on fillets cooked mostly on the skin side in a hot pan until crisp, then turned briefly and finished with lemon and dill.
item.content:encoded:
Salmon is cooked in a pan almost entirely from the skin side, so the heat has to travel up through the fillet, which browns and crisps the skin and cooks the flesh gently from the bottom. When the flesh has turned opaque about three quarters of the way up, the fish is nearly done and needs only a minute on the other side, and the middle stays translucent and moist. Pulling it at 54°C to 57°C, rather than the 63°C some guides give, is the difference between silky and dry.

  • Let the skin release by itself. If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.
  • Pull it at 54°C to 57°C for silky, medium salmon.
  • A white protein that seeps out is a sign of high heat. Lower the burner slightly next time.

item.title: Smothered Pork Chops
item.description: Southern smothered pork chops: floured bone-in chops browned, then simmered in a rich onion gravy until tender. One skillet, served over rice or mash.
item.content:encoded:
A pork chop dries out because it is lean and fast; smothering solves it by finishing the chop in gravy at a gentle simmer, where it stays moist and slowly tenderises instead of toughening. The chops are floured so they brown well and so the flour that comes off in the pan becomes the base of the gravy. The onions get a full ten minutes to go deep golden, because that is where most of the sweetness in the sauce comes from.

  • Give the onions the full ten minutes. Their sweetness is the gravy.
  • Simmer gently. A hard boil toughens the chops.
  • Use bone-in chops. The bone keeps them moist during the long simmer.

item.title: Bhindi Masala
item.description: Bhindi masala — okra fried dry with onion and spices, kept crisp rather than slimy. A 40-minute dry curry.
item.content:encoded:
Okra releases mucilage when cut wet, so it is washed and dried completely hours ahead and never covered while cooking — trapped steam is what makes it slimy. Adding acid only at the very end matters too: acid early in the cook draws the mucilage out.

  • Dry the okra hours ahead. This is the single most important step.
  • Never cover the pan, at any stage. Trapped steam is what causes slime.
  • Amchur goes in at the end. Acid early in the cook makes the problem worse.

item.title: Pork Tenderloin
item.description: Roast pork tenderloin: seared in a skillet, brushed with a Dijon, garlic and herb coating, roasted to 63°C and rested for a juicy, rosy slice.
item.content:encoded:
Tenderloin is the leanest cut of pork, with almost no fat to protect it, so it is right at only one moment and dry after that. That moment is 63°C in the middle, after which it climbs a couple of degrees as it rests. Searing first builds the crust that a short roast alone would not, and the mustard and herb coating both seasons it and bastes it in the oven. Trimming off the tough silver skin matters because it shrinks with heat and makes the meat curl.

  • Take it out at 63°C. Past 70°C it is dry and chalky.
  • Trim the silver skin. It shrinks in the heat and makes the meat curl.
  • Rest for the full 10 minutes so the juices stay in the slices.

item.title: Seared Scallops
item.description: Pan-seared scallops: bone-dry sea scallops seared in a very hot pan for a deep golden crust, then basted with garlic butter and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Scallops are mostly water, and the whole job is to get that water out of the way so the surface can brown before the middle overcooks. They must be bone dry, the pan very hot, and they must have room, since a crowded pan floods with liquid and they steam grey. What you want is a deep gold crust on one side, formed in two minutes without being touched, and a translucent, barely set middle. The butter goes in only after the crust is made, since it would burn at that heat.

  • Dry the scallops until the paper towel comes away dry. Wet scallops steam.
  • Do not move them for the first 2 minutes. That is how the crust forms.
  • Add the butter after searing. In the hot oil it would burn.

item.title: Shahi Paneer
item.description: Shahi paneer — paneer in a pale cashew and cream gravy with cardamom and rose. Mild Mughlai cooking.
item.content:encoded:
The gravy is built on blanched cashews and melon seeds rather than tomato, which is why it stays pale — the onions are boiled rather than browned for the same reason. Sieving the blended paste is what gives the glassy restaurant texture that no amount of blending alone achieves.

  • Boil the onions, do not brown them. Colour in the base means it is no longer shahi paneer.
  • Sieve the paste. It takes two minutes and transforms the texture.
  • Rose water is powerful — a teaspoon perfumes, a tablespoon ruins.

item.title: Turkey Burgers
item.description: Juicy turkey burgers with grated onion, breadcrumbs, smoked paprika and Worcestershire, pan-cooked to 74°C and served on toasted buns.
item.content:encoded:
Turkey mince is lean and mild, so left alone it makes a dry, bland burger. The fixes are about moisture and seasoning: grated onion and a little breadcrumb hold water in the patty, Worcestershire sauce and smoked paprika add the meaty depth turkey lacks, and a dimple pressed into the centre stops the patty puffing into a dome. Turkey has to reach 74°C and cannot be served pink, which is why the moisture has to be built in instead of left to the doneness.

  • Do not overmix. Handled too much, the patties turn dense and bouncy.
  • The dimple stops the burger puffing up in the middle.
  • Cook to 74°C and no further. A thermometer is worth using.

item.title: Baked Cod
item.description: Baked cod with a lemon and parsley breadcrumb crust: fillets brushed with Dijon, topped with buttery panko and ready in about 25 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Cod is lean and flaky, and it goes from moist to chalky in about two minutes, so the coating has two jobs: the panko browns and gives crunch, and the film of mustard and butter underneath insulates the top of the fillet so it cooks gently. Mixing the crumbs with melted butter before they go on is what lets them brown in a bake this short. Cod is done when it turns opaque and flakes at 60°C; the residual heat takes it a few degrees higher on the plate.

  • Coat the crumbs in melted butter. Dry crumbs stay pale in a short bake.
  • Pat the fish dry so the crumb sticks and the tray does not steam.
  • Take it out at 60°C. Cod turns chalky quickly.

item.title: Honey Mustard Chicken
item.description: Baked honey mustard chicken: boneless thighs glazed with Dijon, wholegrain mustard, honey and garlic, basted twice for a sticky, lacquered finish.
item.content:encoded:
Honey mustard is a balance: the honey supplies sweetness and caramelises in the oven, the Dijon supplies tang and body, and the wholegrain mustard adds texture and a mild heat. It is used in two stages because sugar burns: a first coat before baking seasons the meat, and a second brushed on partway keeps a glossy layer that has not had time to scorch. Thighs suit it better than breasts, staying moist through the long bake and holding the glaze.

  • Glaze in two stages. Honey burns if it is on for the whole bake.
  • Use thighs. They stay juicy and hold the glaze.
  • Spoon the tray juices over the top before serving. They are the best part.

item.title: Beef Barbacoa
item.description: Beef barbacoa — chuck braised for hours with dried chillies, cloves and bay until it shreds.
item.content:encoded:
Toasting the dried chillies before soaking wakes the oils in their skins, which is where their fruit and smoke live; soaking them straight from the packet gives a flat, tannic sauce. Chuck and cheek both carry enough collagen that four hours turns them silky rather than dry.

  • Toast the chillies briefly — 30 seconds a side. Burnt chilli makes the whole pot bitter.
  • Cheek is the better cut if your butcher has it: more collagen, more silk.
  • Cook it the day before. Barbacoa is better on day two, every time.

item.title: Cajun Chicken Pasta
item.description: Cajun chicken pasta: blackened, spice-crusted chicken and peppers in a creamy Parmesan sauce tossed with penne and finished with spring onions.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken is seasoned heavily and seared hard, which builds a dark, spicy crust that is the flavour of the whole dish; that crust and the browned bits it leaves in the pan are what the sauce is built on. The cream is loosened with stock and cut with Parmesan so it stays tangy rather than heavy, and the pasta is finished in the sauce with its own starchy water so everything clings. The peppers go in after the chicken, so they soften without going to mush.

  • Sear the chicken hard. The dark crust is the flavour of the sauce.
  • Cook the chicken in two batches so it browns instead of steaming.
  • Use the pasta water to loosen the sauce rather than more cream.

item.title: Sheet Pan Sausage and Peppers
item.description: Sheet pan sausage and peppers: Italian sausages roasted with bell peppers, red onion and garlic on a hot tray until browned, with a splash of balsamic.
item.content:encoded:
Sausages need a hot oven to brown and render their fat, and the peppers and onions need the same, since they are cooked in that fat and take on the sausage seasoning. The vegetables are cut large enough that they roast rather than turn to mush, turned once, and given a splash of balsamic at the end that brings out their sweetness. The whole trick is a large, hot tray with room on it: a crowded one makes steam, and steam gives grey sausages and wet peppers.

  • Use a big tray and do not crowd it. Steam makes grey sausages.
  • Leave the garlic in its skins so it turns sweet and soft instead of burning.
  • Finish with balsamic. It brings out the sweetness of the peppers.

item.title: Tinga Tostadas
item.description: Tinga tostadas — crisp tortillas topped with smoky chipotle chicken, beans, crema and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Tinga is defined by the ratio of chipotle to tomato: enough chipotle to smoke the sauce, enough tomato to keep it from being just heat. A smear of refried beans on the tostada before the chicken is structural — it glues the toppings down so the first bite does not shed everything onto the plate.

  • Beans first, always. They are the glue that holds a tostada together.
  • Build them at the table. A dressed tostada goes soft in about four minutes.
  • Chipotles in adobo vary in heat. Start with two and add the third after tasting.

item.title: Garlic Butter Chicken Bites
item.description: Garlic butter chicken bites: cubes of chicken breast dusted with spices and cornflour, seared golden and tossed in melted garlic butter with lemon.
item.content:encoded:
A thin dusting of cornflour is what gives cubes of chicken breast a savoury, lightly crisp crust in a few minutes and holds in the juices, while the spices on it season every piece. The garlic butter is made in the pan, after the chicken, so that it picks up the browned bits, and it is added at the end with the heat low so the garlic softens and perfumes the butter without scorching. The chicken is seared in two batches, because a crowded pan steams and the bites turn pale and rubbery.

  • Cut the cubes the same size so they finish together.
  • Cook in two batches. Crowding steams the chicken.
  • Keep the heat low for the garlic. It burns in seconds and turns bitter.

item.title: Flank Steak
item.description: Grilled flank steak: marinated in soy, garlic, lime and cumin, cooked hot and fast to medium-rare, then sliced thin against the grain.
item.content:encoded:
Flank is a lean, flat, coarse-grained cut with a strong beefy flavour and a lot of tough muscle fibre, so it needs two things: a marinade whose salt and acid start to tenderise it, and a fast, very hot cook that leaves the middle rare, since a well-done flank is leather. The other half of tenderness is in the cutting. The fibres run in long, obvious lines, and slicing across them, thinly and at a slight angle, turns them into short, easy bites.

  • Cook it hot and fast, no further than medium-rare. Well-done flank is tough.
  • Slice across the grain. It is the difference between chewy and tender.
  • Pat the steak dry before it goes on the grill so it browns.

item.title: Slow Cooker Pulled Chicken
item.description: Slow cooker pulled chicken: breasts cooked with a smoky paprika rub until they shred easily, then tossed in barbecue sauce for buns or tacos.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken breast pulls apart when it is cooked slowly until the muscle fibres separate, and the trick is to stop at that point rather than long after, when it turns to dry threads. A small amount of liquid in the pot is enough, since the chicken gives up its own juices, and the shredded meat is then returned to a little of that liquid before the sauce goes in, so it reabsorbs moisture instead of drying on the board. A spice rub, not just sauce, seasons it through.

  • Shred it once it is tender, not long after. Overcooked chicken turns to dry threads.
  • Return some of the cooking liquid to the shredded meat so it stays juicy.
  • Add the barbecue sauce at the end. It scorches on the base of the pot.

item.title: Buttermilk Biscuits
item.description: Buttermilk biscuits — tall, flaky Southern biscuits made with cold butter and a folded dough.
item.content:encoded:
Layers come from sheets of cold butter trapped between sheets of dough: in the oven the butter steams, pushing the layers apart. Folding the dough over itself three or four times builds those sheets, and a straight-down cut with a sharp cutter keeps the edges free to rise rather than sealing them shut.

  • Cold butter, cold buttermilk, warm oven. Any warm butter and you get scones, not biscuits.
  • Never twist the cutter. Twisting seals the edge and the biscuit rises lopsided.
  • Sides touching on the tray gives you height; spaced apart gives you spread.

item.title: Hard Boiled Eggs
item.description: Hard boiled eggs done right: lowered into boiling water, timed for soft, jammy or fully set yolks, then cooled in ice water so they peel cleanly.
item.content:encoded:
Egg white sets at around 80°C and yolk at 65 to 70°C, so the difference between a runny yolk and a chalky one is a matter of minutes, which is why the eggs go into water that is already boiling: it starts the clock at a known moment. The ice bath matters for two reasons. It stops the cooking, and so prevents the grey-green ring around an overcooked yolk, and it shrinks the egg away from the shell a little so it peels cleanly. Eggs that are a week or two old peel more easily than very fresh ones.

  • Put the eggs into water that is already boiling so the timing is accurate.
  • Do not skip the ice bath. It stops the cooking and helps the peel.
  • Use eggs a week or two old. Very fresh ones cling to the shell.

item.title: Chicken Jalfrezi
item.description: Chicken jalfrezi: tender chicken in a thick onion and tomato masala, topped with charred, crunchy peppers, onion and fresh green chillies.
item.content:encoded:
A jalfrezi is a stir-fry as much as a curry. The sauce is a plain, sharp onion and tomato masala, cooked thick enough to coat, and the vegetables are fried separately and added at the end so the peppers and onion keep their bite and their char instead of dissolving into it. That contrast, a rich soft sauce against crunchy, fiery pieces, is the dish. Fresh green chillies give a bright, immediate heat, unlike the deep, dried-chilli heat of a madras.

  • Cook the peppers and onion separately. In the sauce they turn soft and lose the point of the dish.
  • Take the onions to deep golden. That colour is the base of the sauce.
  • Slit the green chillies and leave the seeds in for more heat.

item.title: Chicken and Waffles
item.description: Chicken and waffles — buttermilk-brined fried chicken on yeasted waffles with hot sauce and maple syrup.
item.content:encoded:
A yeasted waffle batter, rested overnight, sets up crisper and tastes savoury enough to stand next to fried chicken — a baking-powder batter goes soggy under the syrup within a minute. The buttermilk brine does two jobs: its acid tenderises and its salt seasons past the surface.

  • 165C, not hotter. Thighs on the bone need time, and a hot pan burns the crust first.
  • Rest the coated chicken 15 minutes before frying so the crust bonds.
  • Yeasted waffle batter overnight. It is a different food from the quick version.

item.title: Chicken Madras
item.description: Chicken madras: a hot, tangy, deep-red curry of chicken in a tomato and tamarind sauce, with toasted mustard seeds and madras curry powder.
item.content:encoded:
Madras is the hot one on the British menu, and its heat is only part of it: the sauce is sour as well, with tamarind or lemon supplying the tang that a korma or a tikka masala lacks. The curry powder is fried in the oil with mustard seeds first, which releases the oils in the spices and takes off the raw, dusty edge. A madras should be dark red, thin enough to pour but never soupy, and hot enough to make you sweat without covering the spices.

  • Toast the curry powder in the oil. Raw curry powder tastes dusty.
  • Taste for sourness at the end. Add tamarind a little at a time.
  • Use dried chillies for the depth of heat and fresh ones for freshness.

item.title: Chicken Balti
item.description: Chicken balti: the Birmingham curry cooked fast and hot in a deep pan with plenty of ginger, garlic, dried fenugreek leaves and fresh coriander.
item.content:encoded:
A balti is defined by speed and the vessel. It is cooked at a high heat in a thin, deep pan, so the sauce is fresh and sharp rather than long-simmered, and the spices stay bright. The flavour comes from three things: lots of fresh ginger and garlic, a large handful of coriander, and dried fenugreek leaves crushed in at the end, which give the characteristic bitter, maple-like scent. It is served in the pan it is cooked in, and eaten by tearing naan and scooping.

  • Keep the heat high. A balti is fast and fresh, not slow-simmered.
  • Crush the dried fenugreek leaves between your palms as you add them.
  • Serve in the pan and eat with torn naan.

item.title: Chicken Dhansak
item.description: Chicken dhansak: chicken simmered in a red lentil curry that is hot, sweet and sour at once, with pineapple and lemon. A Parsi dish, British style.
item.content:encoded:
Dhansak is the one curry on the menu that is thickened by lentils rather than by onion or cream. Red lentils cook down to a purée that gives the sauce its body and a slight sweetness, and the dish balances three flavours against each other, heat from chilli, sweetness from pineapple or jaggery and sourness from lemon or tamarind. The lentils go into the pot separately and are added later, so the chicken cooks in a spiced tomato sauce first and is not overcooked while the lentils soften.

  • Cook the lentils until they collapse. That is the thickener.
  • Balance the three flavours at the end with lemon, salt and a pinch of sugar.
  • Add the pineapple late, or it disappears into the sauce.

item.title: Maryland Crab Cakes
item.description: Maryland crab cakes — jumbo lump crab with minimal binder, Old Bay, and a hot grill.
item.content:encoded:
The measure of a crab cake is how little is in it besides crab, which means the binder has to be a barely-set custard rather than breadcrumb bulk. Chilling the shaped cakes for an hour lets that binder firm up so they hold together under the grill without being packed tight.

  • Fold, do not mix. Every extra turn breaks the lumps you paid for.
  • Tall mounds, not flat discs. Flat means dry.
  • Chill an hour before cooking or they slump on the tray.

item.title: Chicken Bhuna
item.description: Chicken bhuna: chicken in a thick, intense masala made by cooking onions and tomatoes down until the oil separates, with almost no added liquid.
item.content:encoded:
Bhuna is a technique before it is a curry: the word means to fry the spices and the masala until the water has gone and the oil separates out at the edges, then to keep adding small splashes of water and frying again. The result is a sauce with no free liquid, intensely concentrated and clinging to the chicken. It takes patience rather than skill: the onions must be cooked down for twenty minutes, the tomatoes must be reduced until they are jammy, and the chicken cooks in what is left.

  • Cook the onions down for the full 20 minutes. They are the sauce.
  • Add water only a spoonful at a time. Bhuna is meant to be dry.
  • You know the masala is ready when the oil separates and pools at the edges.

item.title: Chicken Pathia
item.description: Chicken pathia: a hot, sweet and sour Parsi-style curry of chicken in a thick tomato sauce, sharpened with lemon and tamarind and balanced with sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Pathia sits between a madras and a sweet and sour: it is as hot as the first, but it has a pronounced sweetness and a sharp acidity from lemon and tamarind, and a thick sauce rather than a thin one. The trick is the balance, which is why the tomato purée goes in early to cook down and sweeten, and the sugar and the sour elements are adjusted at the end by taste. It is a dish for people who like curry with a bite of acid.

  • Cook the purée until it darkens. Raw purée is sharp and metallic.
  • Adjust sugar and lemon at the end. The balance is the point.
  • Add water gradually. Pathia should be thick.

item.title: Bread and Butter Pudding
item.description: Bread and butter pudding — buttered bread and raisins baked in vanilla custard until crisp on top.
item.content:encoded:
The soak is the recipe: thirty minutes lets the custard get into the crumb so the pudding sets as one thing rather than as bread sitting in scrambled egg. Leaving the top layer proud of the custard is what gives you the crisp, almost caramelised peaks that make the dish worth eating.

  • Day-old bread, not fresh. Fresh bread turns to paste.
  • The 30-minute soak is the difference between pudding and bread in custard.
  • Leave the top points dry so they crisp instead of steaming.

item.title: Saag Aloo
item.description: Saag aloo: cubed potatoes and spinach fried with cumin seeds, garlic, ginger, turmeric and chilli into a dry, vibrant vegan curry. Ready in 40 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The potatoes are parboiled first so they are just tender, which lets them brown in the pan instead of stewing, and the spinach goes in at the end so it wilts in the heat of the potatoes and keeps its colour. It is a dry curry, so the seasoning has to be in the fat: cumin seeds crackled in the oil, then onion, garlic, ginger and ground spices fried before the vegetables go in. The lemon at the end is not garnish, it is what lifts the spinach.

  • Parboil the potatoes so they brown instead of stewing.
  • Add the spinach last so it keeps its colour.
  • Finish with lemon. It lifts the whole dish.

item.title: Bombay Potatoes
item.description: Bombay potatoes: tender waxy potatoes tossed in toasted mustard and cumin seeds, turmeric, chilli and tomato, coated in a dry golden masala.
item.content:encoded:
The potatoes are boiled until tender and the spices are cooked separately in the pan, so that the potatoes can be added to a hot, fragrant base and tossed just long enough to take on colour. Mustard seeds are the sign of a good one: they pop in the hot oil and release a nutty, sharp flavour, and the turmeric turns the whole pan golden. A tomato breaks down to a light coating instead of a sauce, and the dish is dry, which is what separates it from a potato curry.

  • Pop the mustard seeds in hot oil. They give the dish its nutty depth.
  • Boil the potatoes until just tender. Overcooked ones break up in the pan.
  • Toss gently so the potatoes stay whole and take on the golden colour.

item.title: Onion Bhajis
item.description: Onion bhajis: thinly sliced onion in a spiced gram flour batter with cumin, nigella and chilli, fried until crisp, lacy and golden. Vegan and gluten-free.
item.content:encoded:
The batter is barely a batter: just enough gram flour and water to glue slices of onion together, with salt drawn into the onion first so that it releases its own liquid and the mixture needs almost no added water. That is what keeps the bhaji crisp rather than doughy, since the thin coating fries into a lattice around loose strands of onion. Fried at a steady 175°C they are cooked through and crisp in about five minutes, and no hotter.

  • Salt the onions first. They release water, so you need little in the batter.
  • Keep the batter thick and sticky. A wet batter fries into a doughy ball.
  • Fry at 175°C. Hotter browns the outside before the onions cook.

item.title: Scotch Eggs
item.description: Scotch eggs — soft-boiled eggs wrapped in sausage meat, breadcrumbed and fried with the yolk still soft.
item.content:encoded:
Everything depends on the egg being cooked to six minutes and then chilled hard: any longer and the yolk sets, any warmer and the shell will not come off cleanly. The sausage layer is thin and even, so the meat cooks through in the same four minutes it takes the crumb to brown, which is the whole trick.

  • Six and a half minutes, then straight into ice. This is the only timing that matters.
  • Double crumb them. A single coat cracks and lets the fat in.
  • Even meat thickness all the way round, or you get raw patches.

item.title: Peshwari Naan
item.description: Peshwari naan: soft yeasted flatbread stuffed with a sweet filling of coconut, ground almonds and sultanas, cooked in a hot pan until blistered.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is a yogurt-and-milk dough, soft and slightly sticky, because that is what makes the naan puff and stay tender. The sweet filling of coconut, almonds and sultanas sits inside it, and the trick is sealing it completely and rolling gently so it does not break through. Cooked on a very hot, dry pan or a stone, the naan blisters and chars in patches, and brushing it with ghee straight after keeps it soft.

  • Seal the filling well and roll gently. Pressing hard splits the dough.
  • Use a very hot dry pan. A cooler one dries the naan instead of blistering it.
  • Brush with ghee straight away. It keeps the naan soft.

item.title: Chip Shop Curry Sauce
item.description: Chip shop curry sauce: the mild, sweet, golden British takeaway sauce made with onion, apple, curry powder and a little sugar. Vegan.
item.content:encoded:
This is not an Indian curry and is not meant to be. It is a British invention, a smooth, sweet, mild sauce built on a roux, curry powder, sweetness from apple and sugar and a savoury depth from stock, whose job is to make chips taste better. The onion is cooked very soft and blended, so the sauce is glossy rather than gritty, and the curry powder is fried in the fat first to bring out the flavour. Sugar and a splash of vinegar at the end finish the sweet-and-savoury balance.

  • Cook the onion and apple until very soft. They give the sweetness and body.
  • Fry the curry powder for a minute so it loses its raw taste.
  • Blend it smooth. A chippy sauce is glossy and silky.

item.title: Roast Lamb Shoulder
item.description: Slow-roast lamb shoulder: bone-in shoulder studded with garlic and rosemary, roasted low under foil until it falls apart, then crisped at the end.
item.content:encoded:
Shoulder is a hard-working muscle laced with connective tissue, which is why it is cheap and why it repays a long cook: at 160°C over three or four hours the collagen melts into gelatin and the meat goes from tough to something you can pull apart with a spoon. Covering it for the first three hours steams it and keeps it moist, and uncovering it for the last half hour at a higher heat browns and crisps the fat. Garlic and rosemary pushed into slits season it from inside, and the onions beneath it become the base of the gravy.

  • Seal the tin tightly with foil. The trapped steam is what makes it tender.
  • Do not rush it. If it resists a fork, it needs longer.
  • Uncover for the last half hour to brown and crisp the fat.

item.title: Roast Duck
item.description: Roast duck with crisp skin: a whole duck dried in the fridge, pricked, salted and roasted low so the fat renders, then finished hot for shatter-crisp skin.
item.content:encoded:
A duck has as much fat as meat, sitting under the skin, and the whole job is to get rid of it and leave the skin dry and crisp. So the bird is left uncovered in the fridge to dry the skin, pricked all over so the fat can escape, salted, and roasted low for two hours while that fat renders out into the tin and is poured off twice. Only at the end does the heat go up to crisp the skin. Cooked like a chicken, a duck comes out flabby and greasy.

  • Dry the skin uncovered in the fridge. It is the biggest single help for crispness.
  • Prick the skin, not the meat, so the fat can drain.
  • Keep the rendered fat. It makes the best roast potatoes.

item.title: Roast Turkey Crown
item.description: Roast turkey crown: a bone-in breast under sage and herb butter and streaky bacon, roasted until juicy. Easier and quicker than a whole bird.
item.content:encoded:
A whole turkey is a compromise, because its breast is cooked through long before its legs, so the breast is dry by the time the thighs are done. A crown, the breast alone on the bone, has no such problem: one meat, one time, one temperature. Butter under the skin bastes it from within, bacon over the top protects the exposed breast and adds savoury flavour, and pulling it at 70°C, with a rest that carries it to a safe 74°C, is what keeps it juicy.

  • Use a thermometer. Turkey breast is done in the narrowest of margins.
  • Rest it for the full 30 minutes. The carry-over heat finishes the cooking.
  • Butter under the skin, not just on top. It bastes the meat from within.

item.title: Gammon, Egg and Chips
item.description: Gammon, egg and chips: pan-fried gammon steaks with fried eggs and caramelised pineapple rings, served with crisp homemade oven chips and peas.
item.content:encoded:
It is a plate of contrasts, all cooked in one sequence: the chips go in the oven first because they take longest, the gammon is fried while they finish, and the eggs and pineapple share the same pan so they pick up its flavour. Gammon is cured and salty, and needs only a fast fry, so it stays tender; a long cook makes it tough and saltier still. Snipping the fat rind at intervals stops the steak curling up in the pan and lets it lie flat and brown evenly.

  • Snip the fat rind so the steak stays flat in the pan.
  • Do not overcook gammon. It is cured and turns tough and salty.
  • Preheat the tray. Chips that hit hot metal crisp instead of steaming.

item.title: Scampi and Chips
item.description: Scampi and chips: prawns in a crisp golden crumb coat, fried and served with thick chips and a homemade tartare sauce. The pub favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Real scampi are langoustine tails, and because they are hard to find fresh, most home cooks use large raw king prawns, which take the same coat. The three-stage breading, flour, egg, crumbs, is repeated for the crispest result: a second dip in egg and crumbs gives a thicker crust that seals the delicate flesh so it steams inside the coating instead of drying out. The tartare sauce is not a garnish. Its capers and gherkin acidity are what cut through the fried richness.

  • Double-crumb the scampi for a thick coat that seals in the moisture.
  • Fry the scampi for no more than 3 minutes, or they go rubbery.
  • Make the tartare sauce sharp. It cuts through the fried richness.

item.title: Cheese and Onion Pie
item.description: Cheese and onion pie: soft onion, potato and crumbly Lancashire or mature cheddar in a creamy filling, baked in golden shortcrust pastry.
item.content:encoded:
It is a very simple pie whose success depends on cooking the onions properly: slowly in butter until they are soft and sweet and have given up their water, so the filling is rich rather than sharp and does not steam the pastry. The diced potato gives it body, and a little cream and egg bind the cheese into a filling that sets and slices rather than running. Lancashire cheese is traditional because it is crumbly and melts creamily; a mature cheddar with a spoonful of mustard does nearly as well.

  • Cook the onions slowly until sweet. Raw or half-cooked onions turn the filling watery.
  • Cool the filling before it goes into the pastry so the butter does not melt.
  • Serve it warm or cold. It slices best after resting.

item.title: Pie and Mash
item.description: London pie and mash: a minced beef pie in crisp shortcrust and puff, with buttery mash and the bright green parsley liquor poured over.
item.content:encoded:
It is three simple things done properly. The pie is a savoury minced beef filling, cooked down until it is thick and dark and then cooled, because a hot or runny filling steams the pastry into a soggy base. The mash is smooth and buttery, and it is the vehicle for the liquor, the parsley sauce that makes it London: green, thin, made with a stock and a lot of parsley and poured over the lot. In the pie shops the liquor is made with the water eels were cooked in; a chicken or fish stock works as a home version.

  • Cool the filling completely. Hot filling steams the pastry.
  • Blend the liquor to a bright green. It is the signature of the dish.
  • Use floury potatoes for the mash. They mash light and take butter.

item.title: Liver and Onions
item.description: Liver and onions: thin lamb's liver fried fast so it stays tender, with slowly caramelised onions, crisp bacon and a rich onion gravy. Serve with mash.
item.content:encoded:
Liver is unforgiving: it is done in two minutes and ruined in three, going from tender and rosy to grey and grainy. That is why it is sliced thin, dusted in flour to brown quickly, fried in a hot pan for a minute or so a side, and taken out and left alone while the sauce is made. Soaking it in milk beforehand softens the stronger flavour. The onions are the counterpoint, cooked slowly until sweet and jammy, so every mouthful has the mineral richness of the liver against their sweetness.

  • Fry the liver hot and fast. More than two minutes a side and it turns grainy.
  • Cook the onions slowly. The sweetness is what balances the liver.
  • Slice it evenly, about 1 cm, so every piece cooks at the same rate.

item.title: Sausage Casserole
item.description: Sausage casserole: browned pork sausages simmered with carrots, mushrooms and butter beans in a rich tomato and onion gravy. Serve with mash.
item.content:encoded:
Sausages do not need long, but the gravy does, so the sausages are browned first to build flavour in the pan and then finish cooking in the sauce, where they release their seasoning into it. Tomato purée cooked for a couple of minutes gives depth, Worcestershire sauce adds savour, and the beans, added late, thicken the gravy as they break down. It is a dish that gets better the longer it sits, which makes it a good one to cook a day early.

  • Brown the sausages hard. It builds the flavour of the whole pot.
  • Add the beans late so they thicken the gravy without disintegrating.
  • It is better the next day, so make it ahead.

item.title: Hunter's Chicken
item.description: Hunter's chicken: bacon-wrapped chicken breasts baked in smoky barbecue sauce under melted cheddar. A pub classic, ready in 45 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The bacon does the work that skin would: wrapped tightly around the breast it bastes the meat in its own fat, keeps it juicy through the bake and adds smoky savour, and the barbecue sauce brushed on top caramelises into a glaze. The cheese goes on for the last few minutes only, so it melts and browns without going rubbery. Baked chicken breast is done at 74°C and dries out beyond it, which is why the bacon wrap and the thermometer matter.

  • Wrap the bacon tightly and tuck the ends under so it holds.
  • Add the cheese at the end. Baked for the whole time it goes rubbery.
  • Use a thermometer. Chicken breast dries out fast beyond 74°C.

item.title: Corned Beef Pie
item.description: Corned beef pie: chunks of corned beef, onion and diced potato in a thick savoury gravy, baked between golden shortcrust pastry.
item.content:encoded:
It is a pie made from the cupboard: tinned corned beef needs no cooking, only warming through, so the whole trick is in the filling. Onion and potato are cooked first until soft, and the gravy is made thick, thick enough to hold the chunks together when the pie is cut, since corned beef breaks into flakes and a thin gravy would leave the slice a heap. Keep the beef in chunks. Stirred to a paste it loses everything that makes the pie what it is.

  • Keep the corned beef in chunks. Mashed, it loses its texture.
  • Make the gravy very thick so the slice holds together.
  • Cool the filling for a few minutes so it does not melt the pastry.

item.title: Sausage Plait
item.description: Sausage plait: seasoned sausage meat with onion and sage wrapped in puff pastry, cut and plaited, glazed and baked until golden.
item.content:encoded:
A plait looks harder than it is: it is a sheet of puff pastry with a log of filling down the middle and diagonal strips cut down the sides, folded over one another. The filling is sausage meat seasoned with sage and softened onion, which gives moisture and keeps the meat loose. What matters most is temperature: cold pastry stays crisp and puffs, so the plait is shaped and chilled briefly before baking, and it goes into a very hot oven so the pastry sets before the fat in it melts away.

  • Cool the onions first. Hot filling melts the pastry.
  • Chill the plait before baking so the layers puff.
  • Slice it with a serrated knife and it stays neat.

item.title: Carrot and Coriander Soup
item.description: Carrot and coriander soup: sweet carrots and onion simmered with ground coriander and blended velvety with fresh coriander. Vegan and cream-free.
item.content:encoded:
Carrots are sweet and coriander is not, and the soup is the argument between them. Ground coriander seed is cooked in the oil with the onion so its warm, citrusy note runs through the whole base, and the fresh leaf goes in at the end, blended in, for the green, herby edge that would be lost if it cooked. The carrots give body and colour and nothing else is needed: blending for a couple of minutes, longer than seems necessary, is what makes it velvety without cream.

  • Simmer until the carrots are very soft. Firm ones leave the soup grainy.
  • Blend longer than seems needed. It is what makes it silky without cream.
  • Stir in the fresh coriander at the end. Cooking dulls its flavour.

item.title: Parsnip Soup
item.description: Parsnip soup: parsnips roasted until sweet and caramelised, then simmered with onion and mild curry spice and blended into a creamy, warming soup.
item.content:encoded:
Parsnips are sweeter than any other root, and roasting them first is what turns that sweetness into something deeper: the edges caramelise, the flavour goes nutty and toasty, and the soup made from them tastes like more than boiled parsnip. A little mild curry powder is the traditional companion, since its warm spices sit well with the sweetness without making it a curry. A potato in the pot gives the soup body and a smooth texture, so it needs little or no cream.

  • Roast the parsnips first. It is the difference between sweet and deep.
  • Cut out any woody core from large parsnips before roasting.
  • Blend well. A silky texture is the whole appeal.

item.title: Stilton and Broccoli Soup
item.description: Stilton and broccoli soup: broccoli and potato simmered and blended smooth, finished with crumbled Stilton for a sharp, savoury, creamy blue cheese soup.
item.content:encoded:
Stilton is the flavour and it goes in at the end, off the heat, so that it melts into the soup without going stringy or grainy and keeps its sharpness; cooked for long, blue cheese turns bitter. The broccoli is cooked only until tender, since overcooked broccoli goes grey and sulphurous, and a potato gives body without flour. Salt goes in last because Stilton is salty and it is impossible to judge the seasoning until the cheese has melted.

  • Take the soup off the heat before adding the cheese. Boiled blue cheese turns bitter.
  • Cook the broccoli only until tender. Grey broccoli tastes sulphurous.
  • Salt at the end. Stilton is very salty.

item.title: Pea and Mint Soup
item.description: Pea and mint soup: frozen peas, onion and potato simmered briefly with vegetable stock and blended with fresh mint into a bright green vegan soup.
item.content:encoded:
The colour is the thing to protect, and it comes from cooking the peas for as little time as possible: a few minutes in hot stock and then straight to the blender, so the chlorophyll stays green rather than turning to olive. The mint is added to the blender rather than to the pot for the same reason, since heat kills its fresh flavour. Frozen peas are frozen within hours of picking and are usually sweeter than fresh peas from the market, so they are the right choice here.

  • Do not overcook the peas. A few minutes is enough to keep the colour bright.
  • Add the mint to the blender, not the pot. Heat dulls it.
  • Serve hot or cold. It is good either way.

item.title: Lentil and Bacon Soup
item.description: Lentil and bacon soup: a thick, smoky, hearty soup of green lentils, carrots, celery and crisp bacon, with thyme and a splash of vinegar to lift it.
item.content:encoded:
The bacon is the flavour foundation: rendered slowly, it leaves its fat and its smoke in the pan for the vegetables to cook in, and a few crisp pieces are kept back for the top. Green or brown lentils hold their shape through a long simmer, while red ones dissolve, so they are used here for a soup with body and bite; blending only a portion thickens it without turning it to purée. A splash of vinegar at the end is what lifts a soup that is otherwise all earth and smoke.

  • Use green or brown lentils. Red lentils dissolve to mush.
  • Blend only a third for body and keep the rest chunky.
  • Finish with vinegar. It lifts the smoke and earth.

item.title: Cock-a-Leekie Soup
item.description: Cock-a-leekie soup: Scotland's chicken and leek broth, made with bone-in thighs, pearl barley and prunes, with the leeks added in two stages.
item.content:encoded:
The leeks go in twice: half at the start, to dissolve into the broth and flavour it, and half near the end, cut in rings, so that a soup with leeks in it still has leeks that taste like leeks. The prunes are the peculiar part of the recipe and the oldest, a sweet-sour note against the savoury chicken that is best described as a seasoning rather than a fruit. Cooking on the bone gives a broth that sets to a light jelly when cold, which is the sign of a good one.

  • Add the leeks in two halves. The first flavours the broth and the second stays green.
  • Do not skip the prunes. They are the traditional sweet-sour note.
  • Skim the broth early for a clear soup.

item.title: Chip Butty
item.description: Chip butty: thick, golden oven chips piled into soft buttered white bread and finished with ketchup or brown sauce. Simple, hot and filling.
item.content:encoded:
A chip butty is defined by the contrast between the crisp, hot chips and the soft, cold, buttered bread, which is why the bread is fresh and thick-sliced and buttered generously, and why the chips go in hot, straight from the oven, so the butter melts into them. Fat chips are better than thin ones, because their fluffy insides steam into the bread and their crisp edges hold their crunch. Ketchup is the sauce in the south and brown sauce in the north, and both are right.

  • Butter the bread thickly. It melts into the hot chips.
  • Use thick-cut chips. They stay fluffy inside against the soft bread.
  • Eat it straight away. The contrast disappears in minutes.

item.title: Bacon Sandwich
item.description: Bacon sandwich, or bacon butty: back bacon cooked until crisp at the edges, in thick, soft, buttered white bread with brown sauce or ketchup.
item.content:encoded:
The argument about the bacon butty is crisp against soft. Bacon cooked hard in a pan or under a grill has crisp edges, but the fat and the middle need to stay tender enough to bite through cleanly, which is why medium heat and patience beat a hot pan. The bread is thick-sliced, soft white, buttered edge to edge, since it has to soak up the bacon fat and juice as well as hold together. The sauce is a matter of party allegiance, brown or red.

  • Cook the bacon at a medium heat. High heat curls it and burns the fat.
  • Butter to the edges. Every bite needs it.
  • Use soft white bread. Anything crusty fights back.

item.title: Fish Finger Sandwich
item.description: Fish finger sandwich: cod strips in a crisp panko crumb, fried until golden and served in soft buttered bread with tartare sauce and crisp lettuce.
item.content:encoded:
A fish finger sandwich is one of the small triumphs of the British kitchen, and it turns on contrast: crisp panko crumb against soft bread, and the sharp, creamy tartare sauce against the bland, sweet fish. Making the fish fingers from scratch is barely more work than opening a box and gives a thicker, better crumb on real cod. The strips are cut thick, so the fish stays moist while the crumb browns, and they are fried in a shallow pool of oil that comes halfway up the fish so the crumb crisps on all sides.

  • Cut the fingers thick. Thin ones dry out before the crumb browns.
  • Press the panko on firmly so it stays on in the pan.
  • Make the tartare sharp. It cuts through the fried crumb.

item.title: Baked Beans on Toast
item.description: Baked beans on toast: haricot beans in a quick, sweet and smoky homemade tomato sauce, spooned over thick buttered toast. Ready in fifteen minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The tinned beans are the shortcut and the sauce is the improvement: a few minutes of simmering with tomato purée, a little sugar, smoked paprika, mustard and vinegar makes a sauce that is sweeter, smokier and thicker than the one in the tin, and takes about as long as the toast. The beans are simmered only until the sauce clings, because cooked longer they burst. The toast has to be thick, properly toasted and buttered to the edges, since it is what carries the beans.

  • Simmer only until the sauce clings. Longer and the beans burst.
  • Butter the toast while it is hot so it melts in.
  • A little sugar and vinegar balance the tomato. Taste and adjust.

item.title: Egg and Soldiers
item.description: Egg and soldiers: a soft-boiled egg with a runny yolk in an egg cup, served with fingers of hot buttered toast for dipping. Ready in eight minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The whole dish is the timing. Six minutes in boiling water sets the white all the way through and leaves the yolk runny, which is what you dip into, and each minute either way makes a real difference: five and the white is still slippery, seven and the yolk has begun to set. The toast is cut into soldiers, narrow fingers just the width of the yolk opening, and buttered while it is hot so it melts in. Salt goes on the egg, not in the water.

  • Time it. Five, six or seven minutes give three quite different eggs.
  • Take the tops off as soon as the eggs are out, or the yolk keeps cooking.
  • Butter the toast while it is hot so it melts into the bread.

item.title: Porridge
item.description: How to make porridge: rolled oats stirred into milk and water with a pinch of salt for 8 minutes until thick, creamy and never lumpy.
item.content:encoded:
Porridge is oats, liquid and salt, and the difference between a good bowl and a gluey one comes down to salt and stirring. Salt does for oats what it does for bread, drawing out the nuttiness, which is why the Scots have always insisted on it.
