Regular stirring releases the starch from the oats gradually so the porridge thickens evenly and creamy rather than sticking to the pan in lumps, and two minutes off the heat lets it thicken a final time. Half milk and half water gives richness without heaviness.

  • Add the salt. Porridge without it is flat.
  • Stir often so it thickens evenly and does not catch.
  • Loosen with a splash of milk if it firms up as it sits.

item.title: Drop Scones
item.description: Drop scones, or Scotch pancakes: small, thick, fluffy griddle pancakes from a simple self-raising batter, served warm with butter, jam or syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Drop scones are thicker and smaller than a crêpe and slightly less airy than an American pancake, and the batter is stiff enough that it holds its shape when dropped from a spoon. Self-raising flour does the lifting, and a moderate griddle heat cooks them through without burning the outside. The signal to turn them is bubbles rising through the surface and popping, which means the underside has set; turn too soon and they tear, too late and they dry out.

  • Wait for bubbles to burst on the surface before flipping.
  • Keep the heat moderate. Too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks.
  • Wrap them in a tea towel to keep them soft and warm.

item.title: Rhubarb Crumble
item.description: Rhubarb crumble: tart pink rhubarb with orange and ginger under a crisp, sandy oat crumble topping. Best served hot with custard.
item.content:encoded:
Rhubarb is nearly all water and very sour, so it needs sugar and a way of keeping its juice from drowning the crumble. Tossing the raw pieces with sugar and leaving them for a quarter of an hour draws the liquid out, which is drained off and only partly returned, so the topping sits on fruit rather than in soup. The crumble is rubbed in butter and flour with a handful of oats for crunch and no liquid at all, which is what keeps the crumbs sandy and crisp instead of pasty. Ginger and orange are rhubarb's natural companions.

  • Drain the rhubarb after sugaring. Too much liquid makes a soggy topping.
  • Do not press the crumble down. Loose crumbs bake crisp.
  • Serve it with custard. It is what the sourness is for.

item.title: Gooseberry Fool
item.description: Gooseberry fool: stewed, sweetened gooseberries crushed and folded through softly whipped double cream for a tart, creamy early-summer pudding.
item.content:encoded:
A fool is the simplest pudding there is, fruit purée and cream, and it works because gooseberries are so sour that the cream and sugar have something to work against. The fruit is stewed with just enough water to soften, crushed, sweetened while hot and cooled completely, since folding it into cream while warm turns the cream to liquid. The cream is whipped only to soft peaks, so that it folds without being knocked flat and the fool stays airy and loose rather than stiff. Elderflower cordial is the classic addition.

  • Cool the fruit completely. Warm purée turns the cream to soup.
  • Whip the cream only to soft peaks so it folds without going stiff.
  • Sweeten to taste. Gooseberries vary a lot in sourness.

item.title: Blackberry and Apple Pie
item.description: Blackberry and apple pie: tart Bramley apples and juicy blackberries in a sweet shortcrust case, baked until the purple juices bubble through.
item.content:encoded:
Bramley apples break down to a soft, tart purée as they cook, and the blackberries keep their shape and their deep colour, and together they make a filling that is both saucy and textured. The apples are sliced thin so they cook through in the time it takes the pastry to brown, and the cornflour with the sugar thickens the blackberry juice, which would otherwise soak the base. The pastry is a sweet shortcrust, which stays crisp and tender under a wet filling better than a plain one.

  • Use Bramleys. They collapse into a sauce around the whole blackberries.
  • Start on a hot tray so the base cooks through and stays crisp.
  • Cover the edge with foil if it browns too fast.

item.title: Apple Charlotte
item.description: Apple charlotte: a mould lined with buttered bread and filled with a thick cinnamon apple purée, baked golden and turned out. A classic hot pudding.
item.content:encoded:
The filling and the case have opposite jobs. The apples have to be cooked down until they are almost dry, a thick, stiff purée, because any water they hold will soak through the bread and the charlotte will slump when it is turned out. The bread, dipped in melted butter, fries in the oven into a crisp golden shell that holds the purée in. The success of the pudding is in the lining: gaps between the slices let the filling leak, so the bread is cut to fit and overlaps slightly.

  • Cook the apples until nearly dry. Wet filling makes the charlotte collapse.
  • Overlap the bread so there are no gaps for the filling to leak through.
  • Rest before turning out so the case firms and holds.

item.title: Apple Turnovers
item.description: Apple turnovers: flaky puff pastry folded over a spiced, lightly cooked apple filling, glazed and baked until puffed and golden. Ready in 45 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The apples are cooked first, briefly, in butter and sugar until they have softened and given up their juice and then cooled, because raw apple would still be crunchy when the pastry was done, and a hot or wet filling would melt the butter layers in the pastry and stop it puffing. Puff pastry rises because its layers of butter turn to steam, so it must be cold going in and baked hot, and the edges are pressed and sealed with a fork so the steam goes up rather than out. Scoring the top lets the filling breathe.

  • Cool the filling completely so it does not melt the pastry butter.
  • Seal the edges well or the filling leaks.
  • Keep the pastry cold and bake it hot for the best puff.

item.title: Eve's Pudding
item.description: Eve's pudding: tart Bramley apples baked under a light, golden butter sponge. A classic British nursery pudding, best served hot with custard.
item.content:encoded:
It is an apple pudding with a sponge lid, and the trick is to keep the two textures distinct: the apples are cooked just enough to soften and sweeten so that they finish under the sponge in the oven, and the sponge is a light, creamed mixture that is spread carefully over the top so it bakes into a golden crust. Bramley apples are the choice because they are tart and collapse into a soft sauce, which the sweet sponge needs.

  • Cook the apples until only just soft. They finish in the oven.
  • Spread the sponge right to the edges to seal in the apple.
  • Serve it hot. It is a pudding for a cold night.

item.title: Steamed Syrup Sponge
item.description: Steamed syrup sponge pudding: a light lemon butter sponge steamed for 90 minutes over golden syrup, then turned out so the syrup runs down the sides.
item.content:encoded:
Steaming cooks the sponge in moist heat, and nothing else gives that texture: soft, damp and light, with no crust. The pudding sits in a basin with the golden syrup at the bottom, which turns to a hot, runny sauce as the sponge cooks above it and runs down the sides when the pudding is turned out. It needs a tight lid of pleated foil and paper to keep the water out and to leave room for the sponge to rise, and the pan must never boil dry, so it is topped up with boiling water.

  • Pleat the paper and foil so the pudding has room to rise.
  • Keep the water at a gentle simmer and top up with boiling water. Never let it boil dry.
  • Turn it out at once so the syrup runs down the sides.

item.title: Semolina Pudding
item.description: Semolina pudding: a creamy milk pudding of semolina, vanilla and sugar stirred over the heat for ten minutes, finished with jam and a grating of nutmeg.
item.content:encoded:
Semolina pudding is the simplest of the milk puddings and easy to get wrong: stirred into cold milk it clumps and stirred into boiling milk it sets in lumps. The fix is to rain the semolina into warm milk in a thin stream, whisking all the time, and keep stirring for the ten minutes it takes the grains to swell and thicken the milk. The vanilla and a little butter give it the flavour that makes it a pudding rather than porridge, and a spoonful of jam on top gives the sweet and the sour that it needs.

  • Rain the semolina in slowly while whisking. Dumped in, it lumps.
  • Stir constantly while it cooks. It catches on the base.
  • The jam is not a garnish. It is the sweet-sour balance.

item.title: Manchester Tart
item.description: Manchester tart: a crisp sweet pastry case with raspberry jam, thick vanilla custard, sliced banana and a dusting of coconut. A classic British tart.
item.content:encoded:
The tart has four layers, each doing something different: a crisp pastry base that holds the rest, a layer of raspberry jam whose sharpness cuts through the custard, a thick vanilla custard, and a scattering of coconut. The custard is cooked on the hob, thickened with cornflour, and poured into a baked case, so it needs no oven time and stays smooth and pale. Baking the pastry blind and painting it with egg wash first is what stops the jam and custard turning the base to paste, and a wait of two hours in the fridge sets the custard so it cuts cleanly.

  • Whisk the custard constantly as it thickens. It catches and curdles if left.
  • Blind bake the case until golden so it stays crisp under the custard.
  • Chill for the full 2 hours so it slices cleanly.

item.title: Yorkshire Curd Tart
item.description: Yorkshire curd tart: a crisp shortcrust case filled with soft curd cheese, currants, lemon zest and allspice and baked until just set and golden.
item.content:encoded:
A curd tart is a baked custard whose body comes from curd cheese rather than cream: a soft, lightly sour, crumbly cheese that gives the filling a texture somewhere between cheesecake and set egg. Currants, lemon zest and allspice are the traditional flavours, and the tart is baked only until the middle has a slight wobble, since overbaking turns curd cheese grainy and makes it weep. If curd cheese is hard to find, full-fat cream cheese and a little ricotta make a good stand-in.

  • Take it out while the centre still wobbles. It sets as it cools.
  • Blind bake the case so the filling does not make it soggy.
  • Plump the currants in hot tea for a richer flavour.

item.title: Knickerbocker Glory
item.description: Knickerbocker glory: tall glasses layered with raspberry jelly, peaches, raspberries, vanilla ice cream and whipped cream, finished with a glacé cherry.
item.content:encoded:
It is a dessert built by layers, and the point is the contrast between them: the cold, wobbling jelly, the soft fruit, the dense ice cream and the light cream, each in its own stripe down the glass. The jelly has to be properly set and then broken up with a fork so it sits in ruby chunks rather than a solid block, and the layers are built so the ice cream sits in the middle, insulated by cream from the warmth of the glass and the hands. It is the ancestor of every layered sundae.

  • Make sure the jelly is fully set before you break it up.
  • Build the layers just before serving. The ice cream melts quickly.
  • Use tall, narrow glasses so the layers show.

item.title: Homemade Custard
item.description: Homemade custard: silky pouring custard made from egg yolks, milk, cream and vanilla, cooked gently until it coats a spoon. Serve with any pudding.
item.content:encoded:
Custard is egg yolks that have been coaxed into thickening the milk, and the whole skill is in not letting them cook any harder than they need to. They set at about 80°C and scramble at 85°C, so the sauce is stirred constantly over gentle heat until it coats the back of a spoon, and taken off the moment it does. A teaspoon of cornflour is an insurance policy that makes it far harder to curdle, and straining it at the end catches any bits. If it does curdle, a quick whisk or blend can rescue it.

  • Keep the heat low and never let it boil. It scrambles above 85°C.
  • Stir constantly and scrape the base of the pan.
  • If it curdles, whisk or blend it straight away and it can often be saved.

item.title: Dorset Apple Cake
item.description: Dorset apple cake: a rustic, moist rubbed-in cake full of chunks of tart apple and cinnamon, with a crunchy demerara top. Eat warm with clotted cream.
item.content:encoded:
A Dorset apple cake is made like a scone rather than a sponge: butter is rubbed into flour, then sugar, egg and a little milk are stirred in, which gives a crumbly, moist, slightly rustic cake that suits chunks of fruit. The apples are diced small enough to soften completely in the bake and folded in whole, not mashed, so every slice has pockets of soft, tart apple. The demerara on top bakes to a crunchy crust. It is eaten warm from the oven with clotted cream, or cold with butter.

  • Use Bramleys. They break down partly and give a tart, soft filling.
  • Dice the apples small so they cook through.
  • Cover the top with foil if it browns before the middle is done.

item.title: Madeira Cake
item.description: Madeira cake: a firm, moist, fine-crumbed butter cake with lemon zest and ground almonds, baked until golden. A classic for tea or for decorating.
item.content:encoded:
Madeira cake is a pound cake with a little added flour and a small amount of milk, and the result is close-grained, moist and firm enough to slice thin and to carry icing or marzipan, which is why it is the base for so many celebration cakes. Creaming the butter and sugar for a full four minutes puts air in, and eggs added one at a time with a spoonful of flour stop the mixture curdling. The lemon zest gives it its flavour, while the ground almonds keep it moist for days.

  • Cream the butter and sugar for the full four minutes. It is where the lightness comes from.
  • Add a spoonful of flour with each egg so it does not curdle.
  • Use it as the base for a lemon icing or a marzipan-covered celebration cake.

item.title: Coffee and Walnut Cake
item.description: Coffee and walnut cake: two light coffee sponges with chopped walnuts, sandwiched with coffee buttercream and finished with walnut halves.
item.content:encoded:
The coffee has to be strong enough to taste, and instant coffee is the traditional and best choice here because it dissolves in a spoonful of hot water into a concentrate that flavours the batter and the icing without adding liquid. An all-in-one method, with the butter soft and everything beaten together, makes a light, tender sponge in one bowl, and the walnuts are chopped fairly fine so they distribute through the crumb rather than sinking. The buttercream is beaten well to lighten it, and slightly bitter walnut balances the sweetness.

  • Use instant coffee dissolved in a little water. It gives the flavour with no extra liquid.
  • Cool the sponges completely before icing or the buttercream melts.
  • Chop the walnuts fairly fine so they do not sink.

item.title: Christmas Cake
item.description: Traditional Christmas cake: a rich, dark, brandy-soaked fruit cake baked slowly at a low heat and fed for weeks. Make ahead for marzipan and icing.
item.content:encoded:
A Christmas cake is made in advance because it is better for waiting. The fruit is soaked overnight in brandy so it goes into the cake plump and moist and does not steal moisture from the batter, the cake is baked very slowly at a low temperature so it cooks through without the outside burning, and the tin is lined and wrapped in several layers of paper for the same reason. Afterwards it is fed with a spoonful of brandy every week, which keeps it moist and matures the flavour, so that it is at its best when it is cut.

  • Soak the fruit overnight. It keeps the cake moist and the fruit plump.
  • Feed with a spoonful of brandy a week for a month before decorating.
  • Line and wrap the tin thickly. It protects the edges in the long bake.

item.title: Battenberg Cake
item.description: Battenberg cake: pink and yellow almond sponge cut into strips, stacked in a checkerboard with apricot jam and wrapped in marzipan.
item.content:encoded:
Battenberg is a puzzle in geometry more than a recipe, and it works because the sponge is made in one batter that is divided, half coloured pink, and baked in a single tin split down the middle with a foil divider, so both halves cook at exactly the same rate and height. That is what makes the strips match. The cake is trimmed and cut into four identical strips, glued with warm apricot jam and wrapped in marzipan rolled out to the exact length so the seam sits neatly underneath. Accurate measuring is the entire skill.

  • Use a foil divider so both halves bake to the same height.
  • Measure and trim precisely. The neat checkerboard depends on it.
  • Warm the jam and use it sparingly, so it glues but does not slide.

item.title: Malt Loaf
item.description: Malt loaf: a dark, sticky, moist loaf of sultanas soaked in strong tea with malt extract and black treacle. Slice thickly and spread with butter.
item.content:encoded:
There is no butter and no egg in a malt loaf, and that is what makes it dense, moist and slightly chewy: all of its moisture and richness comes from fruit soaked in hot tea and from malt extract and treacle, which are sticky and full of sugar and keep the crumb damp for days. The fruit is soaked before it goes in so it is plump and does not draw water from the batter. It improves with age: after a day or two wrapped, the crumb becomes even stickier and the malt flavour deepens.

  • Soak the fruit in the tea. It keeps the loaf moist for days.
  • Wrap it and leave it a day. The flavour and stickiness improve.
  • Slice thick and spread with plenty of butter.

item.title: Lardy Cake
item.description: Lardy cake: a sticky, spiced Wiltshire yeast bake folded with lard, sugar and dried fruit, baked golden and turned out while hot so the syrup soaks in.
item.content:encoded:
The lard, sugar and fruit are folded into the dough in layers, in the way puff pastry is made, so that as the cake bakes the fat melts and the sugar caramelises between the layers into a syrup. The cake is turned upside down straight from the oven so that this syrup runs down through the crumb and soaks it, which is what makes it sticky and glossy and distinguishes it from a plain fruit bread. Lard gives a distinctively rich, savoury-sweet flavour, though butter works too.

  • Turn it out while it is hot. Otherwise the syrup sets in the tin.
  • Fold and roll gently so the fat stays in layers.
  • Use lard for the authentic flavour, or butter for a lighter one.

item.title: Sally Lunn
item.description: Sally Lunn: the large, light, golden Bath teatime bun from a rich milk, butter and egg dough, glazed and served split with butter or clotted cream.
item.content:encoded:
A Sally Lunn sits between a bread and a cake: its dough is enriched with milk, butter and eggs, so the crumb is soft and rich and yet light and airy like a brioche without the butter of one. It is a wet dough that needs kneading to develop the gluten, and it rises twice, once in the bowl and once in the tin, which is what gives the bun its height and its fine texture. The sugar glaze applied as it comes from the oven gives it the glossy golden top for which it is known.

  • Knead it well. The soft dough needs gluten to rise tall.
  • Prove it to the top of the tin before baking.
  • Glaze it straight from the oven for a glossy top.

item.title: Cornish Saffron Buns
item.description: Cornish saffron buns: soft, golden yellow yeast buns scented with saffron and full of currants and candied peel, brushed with a sugar glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Saffron gives the buns their colour, a deep golden yellow, and a honeyed, slightly medicinal flavour that is unlike anything else in British baking. It needs time to give up its colour, so the threads are steeped in warm milk for half an hour before they go into the dough, and even a pinch is enough. The buns are enriched with butter and egg, and are studded with currants and peel, and the result is a soft, springy, faintly perfumed bun that is eaten spread with butter.

  • Steep the saffron in the warm milk for the full 30 minutes. It releases its colour slowly.
  • A pinch is enough. Too much tastes medicinal.
  • Glaze the buns while hot for a glossy, sticky finish.

item.title: Fat Rascals
item.description: Fat rascals: Yorkshire teatime fruit scone-cakes with currants and peel, decorated with glacé cherry eyes and almond teeth, baked golden and crumbly.
item.content:encoded:
A fat rascal is somewhere between a rock cake and a scone: a rich, crumbly dough with a great deal of fruit, stiff enough to hold its shape as a dome. It is made like a scone, by rubbing butter into flour so it stays short, and the egg and a very little milk bind it into a dough that is stiff, not sticky, which is what keeps it from spreading in the oven. The face, cherry eyes, almond teeth and a peel nose, is the traditional decoration and is pressed in before baking.

  • Keep the dough stiff. A soft one spreads and loses its face.
  • Rub the butter in until it looks like breadcrumbs for a crumbly texture.
  • Press the cherries and almonds in firmly so they stay on.

item.title: Custard Slice
item.description: Custard slice: crisp layers of puff pastry sandwiching a thick vanilla custard, topped with a glossy white icing feathered with chocolate.
item.content:encoded:
The custard has to be very thick, thicker than any pouring custard, because it must hold its shape when the slice is cut and not squash out. That means a proper pastry-cream method with cornflour to bind it and egg yolks for richness, cooked until it bubbles so the starch is fully set. The pastry is baked between two trays, weighted, so it rises evenly and stays flat and crisp instead of puffing into a dome, and the whole slice is chilled until set so it slices cleanly without crushing.

  • Cook the custard until it bubbles. That is what makes it stiff enough to slice.
  • Bake the pastry between trays so it stays flat.
  • Cut with a serrated knife using a gentle sawing action.

item.title: Jam Tarts
item.description: Jam tarts: small, crisp shortcrust pastry cases filled with a spoonful of raspberry or strawberry jam and baked until the edges are golden.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry is a simple shortcrust with a little sugar, and the two things that matter are keeping it cold and filling the cases only two-thirds full: jam boils up as it bakes and, overfilled, it spills over the edge and glues the tart into the tin. A good set jam works better than a runny one, and a thin layer of pastry, cut thin, gives a crisp shell. The tarts must cool before they are eaten, since the jam inside is hotter than a hot cup of tea and retains its heat.

  • Fill the cases only two-thirds full. Jam boils over and glues the tarts in.
  • Use a well-set jam. A runny one bubbles over.
  • Let them cool before eating. The jam is dangerously hot.

item.title: Chocolate Biscuit Cake
item.description: No-bake chocolate biscuit cake: broken biscuits, cherries and nuts bound in melted dark chocolate, butter and golden syrup, chilled and sliced.
item.content:encoded:
It is a fridge cake, held together entirely by set chocolate, and the balance is between chocolate and biscuit: too little chocolate and it crumbles when cut, too much and it is a block of fudge with a few biscuits in it. The biscuits are broken into irregular chunks of different sizes so that there are gaps for the chocolate to fill, and the mixture is cooled slightly before the biscuits go in, so that it coats them without dissolving them. Golden syrup gives the chocolate a glossy, fudgy chew that stays soft enough to cut.

  • Break the biscuits into different sizes. Big chunks for texture, small ones to fill the gaps.
  • Cool the chocolate slightly so it does not melt the biscuits.
  • Press it firmly into the tin so it slices cleanly.

item.title: Cheese Scones
item.description: Cheese scones: tall, golden, tender scones sharp with mature cheddar and a little mustard powder and cayenne, best eaten warm with butter.
item.content:encoded:
A scone rises because of cold butter and a hot oven, and cheese asks only for more of the same. The butter is rubbed in cold so it steams and lifts the dough, the dough is handled as little as possible and patted out thick, at least 3 cm, and the scones are cut straight down without twisting so that the edges are not sealed and can rise. The mustard powder and pinch of cayenne do not make the scones taste of either; they sharpen the flavour of the cheese, which is why every good recipe has them.

  • Press the cutter straight down. Twisting seals the edges and stops the rise.
  • Handle the dough as little as possible. Overworked dough is tough.
  • Use a mature cheddar. Mild cheese gives a bland scone.

item.title: Digestive Biscuits
item.description: Homemade digestive biscuits: crumbly, lightly sweet wholemeal and oatmeal biscuits made with butter, rolled thin and baked until golden.
item.content:encoded:
A digestive is a short biscuit, meaning it is crumbly and tender rather than hard, and that comes from rubbing cold butter into the flour so that it coats the grains and stops the gluten developing. Wholemeal flour and fine oatmeal give the characteristic coarse, nutty, faintly sweet texture, and only a little milk is used to bring the dough together, because a wet dough turns tough. Rolling it thin, 3 mm, and pricking it with a fork makes a crisp biscuit that snaps rather than bends.

  • Roll the dough thin. Thick digestives are soft rather than snappy.
  • Add the milk gradually. A wet dough makes hard biscuits.
  • They crisp up as they cool, so do not bake them until they feel hard.

item.title: Custard Creams
item.description: Homemade custard creams: crisp vanilla biscuits made with custard powder, sandwiched with a soft vanilla buttercream filling.
item.content:encoded:
The custard powder is what gives the biscuit its name and its flavour: it is mostly cornflour and vanilla flavouring and colour, and in a biscuit dough it makes a crumb that is fine, short and crisp, and pale yellow. The dough is chilled before it is rolled so that it is firm and does not spread, which is what keeps the edges sharp, and the biscuits are baked only until the very edges take colour, so they stay pale. The filling is a plain vanilla buttercream, beaten until light and fluffy.

  • Chill the dough so the biscuits keep their shape.
  • Bake only until the edges colour. Pale biscuits taste better.
  • Cool the biscuits completely before filling.

item.title: Bourbon Biscuits
item.description: Homemade bourbon biscuits: crisp, dark chocolate biscuits with a hint of golden syrup, sandwiched with a smooth chocolate buttercream.
item.content:encoded:
A bourbon has no bourbon in it. The name is a mystery, but the biscuit is a dark, crisp chocolate shortbread with a sugared surface, sandwiched with chocolate cream. Golden syrup and cocoa give it colour and a slightly caramelised flavour, and the dough is rolled thin and chilled so it stays sharp-edged. The filling is chocolate buttercream, and because the biscuit is crisp and sweet it needs the cream to be only slightly sweet, so the cocoa is doubled and the sugar reduced.

  • Chill the dough and roll it thin for sharp, crisp biscuits.
  • Prick the surface in neat rows for the classic look.
  • Cool the biscuits completely before filling.

item.title: Jammie Dodgers
item.description: Homemade Jammie Dodgers: buttery vanilla shortbread biscuits sandwiched with raspberry jam and a heart-shaped window cut from the top.
item.content:encoded:
The biscuit is a buttery shortbread dough, rich in butter and light on liquid, and the texture depends on handling it as little as possible: overworked, the butter melts into the flour and the biscuits turn tough and spread. The dough is rolled between paper, chilled and cut, because warm dough sticks, and the small heart cut into half of the rounds is what shows the jam. A thin layer of jam is right, since a thick one squeezes out and burns onto the tray.

  • Roll the dough between paper so it does not stick, and chill if it softens.
  • Use only a thin layer of jam. It squeezes out under the top biscuit.
  • Fill the biscuits only when cold or the jam runs.

item.title: Ginger Nut Biscuits
item.description: Ginger nut biscuits: hard, crisp, spicy ginger biscuits made with golden syrup and bicarbonate, with a cracked top. Perfect for dunking.
item.content:encoded:
A gingernut is a hard biscuit by design, made to survive a dunk in tea without collapsing, and the hardness comes from baking it until it is thoroughly dry and from the golden syrup and sugar, which caramelise and set as the biscuit cools. The bicarbonate, meeting the acid in the golden syrup, makes it spread and crack on the surface as it bakes, giving the crackled top. Ginger is the flavour, and a generous amount of it is needed for it to taste after baking, so it is ground ginger and not just a hint.

  • Leave plenty of space between them. They spread a lot.
  • They harden as they cool, so do not overbake in the hope of crispness.
  • Use a generous amount of ginger so it survives the bake.

item.title: Viennese Whirls
item.description: Viennese whirls: piped, buttery, tender biscuits made with cornflour, sandwiched with vanilla buttercream and raspberry jam.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is unlike other biscuit doughs: it is a very soft, whipped butter mixture that is piped, not rolled, and its melting texture comes from the cornflour that replaces some of the flour and from beating the butter and sugar until very light. That soft dough is hard to pipe if it is cold and spreads if it is warm, so the butter is soft but not greasy and the piping bag is filled in small amounts. A large star nozzle gives the ridges that make it crisp at the edges and tender in the middle.

  • Beat the butter well. The lightness of the biscuit depends on it.
  • Use a large star nozzle. A small one is very hard to pipe.
  • Keep the dough at room temperature. Cold dough will not pipe.

item.title: Garibaldi Biscuits
item.description: Garibaldi biscuits: a thin, crisp biscuit dough rolled around a layer of currants, cut into rectangles and baked until golden. The squashed fly biscuit.
item.content:encoded:
A Garibaldi is two thin sheets of biscuit dough with a layer of currants pressed between them, which is why the currants show as dark, flattened flecks under a paper-thin top, and why the biscuit acquired a rude nickname. The dough is a plain, lightly sweet one, rolled very thin so the whole biscuit is crisp, and the currants are pressed in with a rolling pin so they are embedded rather than loose. The biscuit is cut into rectangles before baking, and scored, so it snaps along the lines.

  • Roll thin. Thick Garibaldis are cakey rather than crisp.
  • Press the layers together firmly so the currants stay in.
  • Score the biscuits before baking so they snap cleanly.

item.title: Oatcakes
item.description: Scottish oatcakes: crisp, nutty, rustic oat biscuits made from oatmeal, oil and hot water, rolled thin and baked. Vegan, perfect with cheese.
item.content:encoded:
There is nothing in an oatcake but oatmeal, a little fat, salt and enough hot water to hold it together, and the character is all in the oatmeal: medium-ground gives the best texture, coarse enough to stay nutty and crisp and fine enough to bind. Hot water softens the meal and makes the dough workable, but it stiffens quickly as it cools, so the dough is rolled at once, while it is warm, and cut quickly. Oatcakes are baked slowly until they are dry and crisp, since underdone ones are limp.

  • Roll the dough while it is still warm. It cracks as it cools.
  • Use medium oatmeal. Fine gives a pasty oatcake and coarse will not bind.
  • Bake until dry. Undercooked oatcakes are limp.

item.title: Cheese Straws
item.description: Cheese straws: crisp, flaky twists of mature cheddar and Parmesan pastry with mustard and a pinch of cayenne, baked until golden. Ideal for parties.
item.content:encoded:
A cheese straw is a shortcrust with a great deal of cheese in it, and the two things that matter are the cheese itself and the cold. Mature cheddar and a little Parmesan give a sharp flavour that survives baking, and mustard powder and cayenne heighten it without adding heat. The pastry is chilled before it is cut so the butter stays firm and the straws bake flaky and hold their twist, and they are baked until golden, since underbaked cheese straws are limp and greasy.

  • Use a mature cheddar. A mild one disappears in the bake.
  • Chill the pastry so the straws hold their twist.
  • Bake until deep golden for crisp, not greasy, straws.

item.title: Rocky Road
item.description: No-bake rocky road: chunks of biscuit, mini marshmallows and glacé cherries bound in melted milk and dark chocolate and chilled until firm.
item.content:encoded:
Rocky road is named for the lumpy, rocky look of the finished slab, which is exactly what you want: big irregular chunks of biscuit, marshmallow and fruit with the chocolate acting as mortar, not a smooth block with bits in. That means the chocolate should be cooled a little before the marshmallows go in, or they melt into it, and that the ratio has to be right: enough chocolate to coat and bind and not so much that the pieces are drowned. Mixing dark and milk chocolate balances the sweetness of the marshmallow.

  • Cool the chocolate a little before the marshmallows go in or they melt.
  • Leave the chunks big and the top rough. That is the point.
  • Cut it with a hot knife so the chocolate does not shatter.

item.title: Coconut Ice
item.description: No-cook coconut ice: pink and white layers of sweet, chewy coconut fudge made from desiccated coconut, icing sugar and condensed milk. Sets in the fridge.
item.content:encoded:
This is a sweet that needs no cooking, and the only skill is in the proportions and the pressing. Icing sugar, coconut and condensed milk make a firm, malleable paste, and its texture depends on the ratio: too much milk and it will not set, too little and it is dry and crumbly. Pressing each layer down firmly into the tin, and firmer still when the second layer goes on, is what makes the finished slab hold together and cut cleanly into blocks rather than crumbling.

  • Press each layer down very firmly so the slab holds together.
  • Add the colouring a drop at a time. It takes very little.
  • If the mixture is too wet, add a spoonful of coconut.

item.title: Toffee Apples
item.description: Toffee apples: crisp apples on sticks dipped in a glossy, hard toffee of sugar, golden syrup and vinegar boiled to the crack stage. Perfect for Bonfire Night.
item.content:encoded:
The toffee has to reach 150°C, the hard-crack stage, or it will not set hard and will stay sticky and drip off the apple. A splash of vinegar stops the sugar recrystallising into grains. The apples must be dry and, if they are waxed, scrubbed with hot water first, since toffee will not stick to wax or to damp skin, and they should be cold, since a cold apple sets the toffee at once and gives a thin, even coat. The final dip is fast, because the toffee begins to set the moment it leaves the heat.

  • Boil to 150°C. Below that the toffee stays sticky.
  • Dry the apples completely, and scrub off any wax.
  • Hot sugar burns badly. Take great care and keep children well away.

item.title: Scottish Tablet
item.description: Scottish tablet: the crumbly, grainy, intensely sweet sugar, butter and condensed milk confection, boiled to soft ball and beaten until it sets.
item.content:encoded:
Tablet is sugar deliberately encouraged to crystallise, which is exactly the opposite of what a caramel or a toffee wants, and it is the graininess that distinguishes it from fudge, which is smooth. The mixture is boiled to the soft-ball stage, 116°C, then beaten while it cools, and the beating triggers the crystals to form, so it thickens and turns matte and opaque and must be poured at once, before it sets in the pan. The result is hard, crumbly and melts on the tongue.

  • Stir constantly while it boils. The condensed milk catches on the base.
  • Beat until it turns matte and grainy. That is the sign it is ready to pour.
  • Pour quickly. It sets in seconds once it has grained.

item.title: Treacle Toffee
item.description: Treacle toffee: the dark, hard, bittersweet Bonfire Night sweet of black treacle, golden syrup, sugar and butter, boiled to crack stage and broken up.
item.content:encoded:
Treacle toffee is a hard-crack toffee, taken to 150°C so that it sets hard enough to snap, and it is treacle that makes it what it is: dark, slightly bitter, and almost burnt-tasting against the sweetness of the sugar and syrup. Because black treacle is so dark, the colour is a poor guide to when it is done, and a sugar thermometer, or the drop-in-cold-water test, matters more. Vinegar is added to stop the sugar recrystallising, and the toffee is poured into a shallow tray so it sets thin enough to break into shards.

  • Use a thermometer. The dark colour hides how far it has gone.
  • Use a large pan. The mixture bubbles up to double its size.
  • Wrap the pieces in waxed paper to stop them sticking together.

item.title: Irish Soda Farls
item.description: Irish soda farls: soda bread dough patted into a round, cut into four and cooked on a dry griddle until golden. Fast, no yeast, ideal with a fry-up.
item.content:encoded:
A farl is soda bread without the oven: the same buttermilk-and-bicarbonate dough, patted flat rather than shaped into a loaf, cut into four quarters, the word farl meaning a fourth part, and cooked on a dry griddle so that it puffs, browns and cooks through in minutes. The acid in the buttermilk and the alkali in the bicarbonate react as soon as they meet, so the dough must be mixed and cooked quickly, before the fizz has gone. Handle it lightly, because kneading toughens it.

  • Work quickly. The rise begins when the buttermilk meets the bicarbonate.
  • Do not knead. It makes the farls tough.
  • Use a dry griddle at medium heat so they cook through without burning.

item.title: Guinness Cake
item.description: Guinness cake: a dark, moist chocolate stout cake made with a can of Guinness, topped with a thick cream cheese frosting like the head on a pint.
item.content:encoded:
Stout and chocolate belong together because both are bitter and roasted, and the Guinness gives the cake a deep, malty richness rather than a taste of beer. It is melted into the butter and cocoa, so the cocoa dissolves and its flavour blooms, and the bicarbonate reacts with the acidity of the stout and the soured cream to make the cake rise and stay tender and moist. The cake is baked in a tin and cooled completely before it is topped with cream cheese frosting, and the white frosting is meant to look like the head on a pint.

  • Do not worry that the batter is thin. It bakes into a moist, tender cake.
  • Cool the cake completely before the topping goes on.
  • Use full-fat cream cheese. Low-fat is too soft to hold its shape.

item.title: Selkirk Bannock
item.description: Selkirk bannock: a large, round, rich Scottish Borders fruit loaf of buttery yeast dough and sultanas, baked golden and glazed. Slice and butter.
item.content:encoded:
A Selkirk bannock is a rich yeast bread, a kind of Scottish tea loaf, and the richness is in the butter and sugar and the sultanas, which are kneaded in at the end when the gluten is developed so they do not tear it. Like all enriched doughs it rises slowly and takes two risings to develop its structure and its light crumb, and the sugar glaze applied as it comes hot from the oven gives it a glossy, slightly sticky crust. Queen Victoria is said to have liked it, and the story is used to sell it to this day.

  • Knead the sultanas in at the end so they do not tear the dough.
  • Prove it until puffy before baking. Underproved loaves are dense.
  • Glaze it hot for the traditional sticky, glossy crust.

item.title: Black Bun
item.description: Black bun: the dark, dense, spiced Scottish Hogmanay fruit cake soaked in whisky and baked in a buttery pastry case. Best made weeks ahead.
item.content:encoded:
It is a fruit cake wrapped in pastry, and the pastry is what makes it a black bun and not just a Christmas cake: the cake inside is a very dark, dense, heavily spiced mixture, with more fruit than batter, that would dry out and burn in a naked bake, while the pastry case protects it through the long, slow baking and adds a buttery crust. It is baked at a low heat for two and a half hours so it cooks through, and, like other fruit cakes, it needs weeks to mature, which is why it is made before Christmas for Hogmanay.

  • Pack the filling in firmly so it slices cleanly.
  • Cover the top with foil if the pastry browns before the fruit cooks.
  • Make it a few weeks ahead. It matures and improves.

item.title: Forfar Bridie
item.description: Forfar bridie: a folded, crimped pastry semicircle filled with chopped steak, onion and beef suet, baked until golden. The Angus pasty, with no potato.
item.content:encoded:
A Forfar bridie is like a Cornish pasty with the vegetables taken out: the filling is steak, onion and a little suet, and nothing else, so the meat must be good, chopped rather than minced, and cut small so it cooks through in the short bake. The suet is what keeps it moist, melting into the meat and making a little gravy inside the pastry, and the pastry is a rough puff or a sturdy shortcrust, folded into a semicircle and crimped along the curved edge with a small vent.

  • Dice the steak small so it cooks through in the short bake.
  • The suet keeps it moist. Do not leave it out.
  • Crimp the edge firmly so the juices stay inside.

item.title: Scotch Pie
item.description: Scotch pie: a small hand-raised hot-water-crust pie of peppery, mace-scented lamb with a hollow top for gravy or beans. The Scottish bakery classic.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry is a hot water crust, made by melting fat into boiling water and stirring it into flour, which makes a dough that is pliable when warm and sets rigid when cool, so that it can be moulded round a jar into a free-standing case. That is why a Scotch pie has straight, sturdy sides and a top that sits slightly below the rim, a hollow to be filled with gravy, beans or mash. The filling is minced lamb or mutton seasoned heavily with black pepper and mace and cooked only in the pie itself.

  • Work the dough while it is warm. It sets hard as it cools.
  • Season the meat heavily. It is only lightly cooked in the pie.
  • Press the lid slightly below the rim to make the hollow for gravy.

item.title: Clootie Dumpling
item.description: Clootie dumpling: a rich, spiced Scottish fruit pudding boiled in a floured cloth for three hours, then dried in the oven for a dark, chewy skin.
item.content:encoded:
A clootie is a cloth, and the pudding is boiled in one, which is what gives it its skin: the cloth is scalded and floured so that a paste of flour forms on the surface, and after boiling the dumpling is dried in a low oven until that skin turns dark, dry and slightly chewy. It is a rich, dark, spiced fruit mixture, held together by suet and sweetened with treacle and syrup, and it is served hot with custard and cold, fried, at breakfast the next day. The cloth must be large enough to allow for expansion.

  • Flour the cloth generously. The flour makes the skin.
  • Tie loosely. The pudding swells as it cooks.
  • Keep the water at a gentle boil and top it up with boiling water, never cold.

item.title: Lorne Sausage
item.description: Lorne sausage: seasoned beef and pork pressed into a tin, chilled firm and cut into square slices, then fried. The Scottish square sausage for a morning roll.
item.content:encoded:
A Lorne sausage is sausage meat in slab form: the mixture is a fine, well-seasoned blend of beef and pork bound with breadcrumbs, packed into a tin and chilled until solid, then sliced into squares that fit a bread roll. It must be packed firmly to remove air and chilled until stiff, or it will not slice, and it is fried, not baked, so that the surface browns in the fat and the inside stays juicy. The seasoning is simple, salt, pepper, nutmeg and coriander, so the meat itself carries the flavour.

  • Pack the mixture firmly so there are no air pockets.
  • Chill until stiff. A soft block will not slice.
  • Fry over a medium heat so it browns and cooks through.

item.title: Ulster Fry
item.description: The Ulster fry: sausages, bacon, fried eggs, black pudding, mushrooms and tomatoes served with fried soda farls. The Northern Irish full breakfast.
item.content:encoded:
The Ulster fry is a full fry-up with its own bread: soda farls, and potato bread or pancakes, fried in the fat of the pan alongside everything else. The order matters, because everything has to come to the plate hot at once. The sausages, which take longest, go on first, the black pudding and bacon after them, and the farls, eggs and tomatoes last, cooked in the fat that has rendered from the rest. There is no baked beans on an Ulster fry, and cooking everything in one pan is what gives it its flavour.

  • Start the sausages first. They take longest.
  • Fry the soda farls in the pan fat, for the flavour.
  • Warm the plates so everything stays hot.

item.title: Mint Sauce
item.description: Homemade mint sauce: finely chopped fresh mint softened in a little hot water and sugar and sharpened with vinegar. The classic sauce for roast lamb.
item.content:encoded:
Mint sauce is three things in balance: mint for freshness, vinegar for sharpness and sugar to take the edge off both, and the trick is to soften the mint first. The chopped leaves are steeped in a little hot water and sugar, which draws out the flavour and stops the vinegar turning them brown and hard, and the vinegar is added afterwards so that the sauce stays green. It is left to stand so the flavours meld, and it keeps a fresher, cleaner taste than any jar.

  • Chop the mint with a little sugar. It stops the leaves clumping and bruising.
  • Soften the mint in hot water first. Vinegar alone leaves it tough and dull.
  • Make it a little before serving so the flavours meld.

item.title: Apple Sauce
item.description: Homemade Bramley apple sauce: tart cooking apples simmered with a little sugar and lemon until they collapse into a fluffy, tangy sauce for roast pork.
item.content:encoded:
Bramley apples are the right apple for apple sauce because they are so acidic and so low in water-holding structure that they collapse to a pulp in minutes, giving a light, fluffy purée rather than the solid chunks of an eating apple. They need only a splash of water to start them steaming, and a little sugar is needed only to take the edge off the acid, not to make the sauce sweet, since it is a sauce that has to cut through the fat of roast pork. Lemon juice keeps the colour bright.

  • Use Bramleys. Eating apples do not collapse into a fluffy sauce.
  • Go easy on the sugar. It is meant to be tart against pork.
  • Cook with a lid on so the apples steam in their own juice.

item.title: Horseradish Sauce
item.description: Homemade horseradish sauce: fresh horseradish grated into lightly whipped cream with vinegar, English mustard and a little sugar. Fiery, for roast beef.
item.content:encoded:
Fresh horseradish has a heat that is quite unlike chilli, sharp and nasal rather than burning, and it comes from an enzyme reaction that starts only when the root is cut or grated and is at its strongest for a few minutes afterwards. The vinegar is added straight away to stop it, fixing the heat at the level you want, and the cream softens and rounds it. Grate it in a well-ventilated room, or with the windows open, because the fumes are as fierce as the sauce.

  • Add the vinegar immediately after grating. It stops the heat building.
  • Grate it with the window open. The fumes are strong.
  • Whip the cream only to soft peaks. Stiff cream turns the sauce heavy.

item.title: Brandy Butter
item.description: Brandy butter: unsalted butter beaten with icing sugar and brandy until pale and fluffy, then chilled. The traditional partner for Christmas pudding.
item.content:encoded:
It is a sauce that is not a sauce: cold, firm butter that melts on the hot pudding into a rich, boozy pool. To get that, the butter has to be beaten with the sugar until it is pale and fluffy, which lightens it and makes it spreadable and creamy rather than greasy, and the brandy is added a spoonful at a time, since too much too fast makes it curdle and split. The mixture is chilled to firm it, and is kept in the fridge until the moment it is served.

  • Beat the butter until pale. It is what makes it light.
  • Add the brandy a spoonful at a time so it does not split.
  • Chill it firm, then serve it cold on hot pudding.

item.title: Marmalade
item.description: Seville orange marmalade: bitter oranges and lemon simmered until the peel is soft, then boiled with sugar to a glossy, clear amber set. Makes four jars.
item.content:encoded:
Marmalade sets because of pectin, and the oranges are full of it, mostly in the pith and the pips, which is why the pips and pith are tied in a muslin bag and cooked with the fruit, and then removed: the pectin goes into the liquid, and the bitterness stays behind. The peel is simmered in plenty of water until it is completely tender before the sugar goes in, since sugar hardens peel. It is only then that the pan is boiled hard to setting point, 105°C, which is what gives a set that is firm but not rubbery.

  • Simmer the peel until it is completely soft. It will not soften once the sugar is in.
  • Use the wrinkle test on a cold saucer, or a thermometer at 105°C.
  • Seville oranges are in season only in January and February. Buy extra and freeze them.

item.title: Lemon Curd
item.description: Homemade lemon curd: fresh lemon juice and zest, sugar, butter and eggs cooked gently into a tart, glossy, silky spread for toast, scones and tarts.
item.content:encoded:
Lemon curd is a custard thickened with eggs and set with butter, and the only skill is gentle heat. The eggs begin to thicken at about 75°C and curdle above 85°C, so the mixture is cooked over barely simmering water, stirred constantly, until it coats the back of a spoon, and taken off the heat at once. Straining it through a sieve at the end catches any specks of cooked egg and the zest, which leaves it perfectly smooth. Whole lemons, rather than bottled juice, are essential to the taste.

  • Keep the heat gentle. Above 85°C the eggs scramble.
  • Stir constantly and scrape the sides of the bowl.
  • Strain it. It takes a minute and makes the curd perfectly smooth.

item.title: Pilau Rice
item.description: Pilau rice: fluffy basmati rice cooked with browned onion, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and cumin until fragrant and every grain is separate.
item.content:encoded:
The rice is only as good as its preparation: basmati is rinsed until the water runs clear to remove surface starch, which is what makes the grains separate rather than sticky, then soaked for half an hour so it swells evenly and cooks without breaking. The whole spices are fried in the oil first to release their fragrance into it, and the onion is browned so that it colours and flavours the rice. Then the rice is cooked covered, at a very low heat, with just enough water, and left undisturbed, so it steams rather than boils.

  • Rinse until the water runs clear. It is what stops the rice being sticky.
  • Do not lift the lid while it cooks. The steam is what cooks it.
  • Fluff with a fork, not a spoon, so the grains stay whole.

item.title: Pickled Eggs
item.description: Pickled eggs: hard-boiled eggs steeped in spiced malt vinegar with peppercorns and chilli for a week. The classic chip shop and pub snack.
item.content:encoded:
The eggs are hard-boiled, then peeled and packed in a jar and covered with hot, spiced vinegar, which begins to work immediately but takes about a week to reach the middle: the white takes on the colour and the sharpness first and the yolk turns slowly firm and tangy. Malt vinegar is the traditional choice, giving the amber colour, and the spices, peppercorns, mustard seeds and chilli, are what give it its pub flavour. They must be kept refrigerated, and eaten within three months.

  • Use eggs a week or two old. They peel much more easily.
  • Keep the eggs completely covered by the liquid.
  • Wait the week. The flavour reaches the middle only slowly.

item.title: Cup of Tea
item.description: How to make a proper cup of tea: freshly boiled water, a warmed mug, a teabag brewed four minutes, then milk and, if you like, sugar. Simple and exact.
item.content:encoded:
A cup of tea is simple, and every step has a reason. Freshly boiled water matters because tea needs water at 100°C to extract its flavour and re-boiled water has lost oxygen and tastes flat. The mug is warmed so the water does not cool. Tea is left for three to four minutes, because it is the tannins that give tea its strength and its bitterness, and they are extracted more slowly than the flavour. And milk goes in after, so that the strength can be judged by colour, and the milk itself does not scald.

  • Use freshly drawn water each time. Water that has been boiled before tastes flat.
  • Brew for three minutes for a mild cup and four for a strong one.
  • Add the milk last so you can judge the colour.

item.title: Elderflower Cordial
item.description: Homemade elderflower cordial: creamy elderflower heads and sliced lemon steeped in sugar syrup for a day, then strained. Dilute for a fragrant summer drink.
item.content:encoded:
The elderflowers must be picked on a dry, sunny morning when the blossoms are freshly open and full of pollen, since the flavour is in the pollen and the scent fades within hours of picking. They are steeped rather than boiled, because heat destroys the delicate flowery perfume, so the sugar syrup is poured over them hot and left to cool and infuse. Citric acid preserves the cordial and brightens it, and the lemon slices add sharpness that keeps it from being merely sweet.

  • Pick the flowers on a dry, sunny morning, when they are full of pollen.
  • Do not wash them. It rinses off the pollen and the scent.
  • Dilute to taste, about 1 part cordial to 5 parts water.

item.title: Lemon Barley Water
item.description: Lemon barley water: pearl barley simmered with lemon zest, then sweetened and sharpened with lemon juice and chilled. The traditional Wimbledon drink.
item.content:encoded:
The barley gives the drink its body and its slightly cloudy, silky texture: as it simmers, the pearl barley releases starch into the water, which is what makes the drink smooth and faintly thick rather than thin and watery like lemon squash. The lemon zest goes in during the simmer and the juice only at the end, so that its freshness is not cooked away. It has been the drink of English summers since the nineteenth century and the barley itself is an old restorative for the sick.

  • Use strips of zest with no white pith. The pith is bitter.
  • Add the lemon juice after cooking. Heat dulls it.
  • Serve very cold, with plenty of ice.

item.title: Shandy
item.description: How to make a shandy: cold lager and cold lemonade poured half and half over ice, the light, refreshing pub-garden drink for a hot day.
item.content:encoded:
A shandy is a beer cocktail with a long, honourable history and just one rule: everything cold. Cold lager and cold lemonade keep the fizz, and pouring the lager first, at an angle, and topping with the lemonade last, means the drink mixes itself without the head foaming over. The traditional ratio is half and half, though many prefer more lager, and a cloudy, traditional cloudy lemonade gives a more natural flavour than a clear, sugary one. In Britain lemonade means the clear, sweet fizzy drink, not the still, freshly squeezed kind, and it is the fizz that makes a shandy. It is also the simplest way to stretch a drink on a hot day: a shandy has roughly half the alcohol of a pint of lager, which is why it has always been the choice of the driver, the cricketer and anyone hoping for a second round.

  • Have everything cold. A warm shandy is flat.
  • Pour the lager first, at an angle, then the lemonade.
  • Vary the ratio to taste. Some prefer two parts lager to one lemonade.

item.title: Hot Buttered Rum
item.description: Hot buttered rum: dark rum, brown sugar, a spoonful of spiced butter and hot water stirred in a mug with a cinnamon stick. A winter warmer in minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The butter is the surprise: a spoonful of butter mashed with brown sugar and spices melts into the hot water and rum and gives the drink a richness and a silky texture that nothing else does, a little like a hot toddy that has been given a dessert. The spiced butter can be made in advance and kept in the freezer, which turns the drink into a matter of stirring, and the rum should be a good dark one, since its molasses and caramel notes are what the spices are meant to play against.

  • Make the spiced butter in batches and freeze it in balls.
  • Use a good dark rum. Its molasses notes carry the spice.
  • Do not boil the rum. It drives off the alcohol.

item.title: Pimm's Cup
item.description: Pimm's Cup: a jug of Pimm's No. 1 topped with lemonade and loaded with ice, cucumber, mint, strawberries and orange. The classic English summer drink.
item.content:encoded:
A Pimm's cup is a drink built by ratio and by fruit: one part Pimm's to three parts cold lemonade, which lets the herby, bittersweet liqueur come through without drowning in sugar, and a generous jug of fruit, cucumber, strawberries, orange and mint, whose juices flavour it as it stands. The whole thing is made in a jug over plenty of ice, not in the glass, and topped with the lemonade at the last moment so that it stays fizzy. Borage and cucumber are traditional, the latter because it is refreshingly cool. British lemonade, the clear fizzy kind, is the right mixer, though ginger ale gives a spicier drink, and the fruit is not decoration: it is left to stand in the jug for a few minutes so the strawberries and orange give up a little of their juice, which is what turns the jug from a mixed drink into something that tastes of summer.

  • Top up with lemonade only when serving, or it goes flat.
  • Use plenty of ice. A warm Pimm's is dreadful.
  • Keep the proportions at one part Pimm's to three parts lemonade.

item.title: Gin and Tonic
item.description: How to make a proper gin and tonic: a big measure of gin over plenty of ice, topped with cold tonic in a one-to-three ratio and finished with a lime wedge.
item.content:encoded:
A gin and tonic is a drink with almost nothing in it, and so every detail shows. The glass is filled with ice first, plenty of large cubes, because the more ice the slower it melts and the less it dilutes the drink, and the tonic is chilled and freshly opened so the fizz is sharp. The ratio of one part gin to three parts tonic keeps the botanical flavour of the gin without letting the quinine bitterness take over, and the garnish is chosen to suit the gin: lime for a classic dry one.

  • Fill the glass with ice. More ice means less dilution.
  • Use a fresh, very cold bottle of tonic. Flat tonic ruins the drink.
  • Stir once, gently. More knocks the fizz out.

item.title: Montreal Smoked Meat Sandwich
item.description: Homemade Montreal smoked meat: brisket cured five days, crusted with black pepper and coriander, smoked, finished tender and piled on rye with mustard.
item.content:encoded:
Montreal smoked meat is brisket cured in salt and spice, crusted with cracked pepper and coriander, smoked, and then cooked until it will pull apart with a fork. Nearly all of its flavour comes from the five days in the brine, before any heat is used: the cure carries salt and spice to the centre of the meat and turns it pink. The crust builds a dark bark in the smoker, and finishing the meat wrapped with a little water turns its collagen into gelatine, which is what makes the slices soft and juicy rather than dry. The sandwich is the one Montreal's Jewish delicatessens are known for: thick slices, cut by hand against the grain, on rye with plain yellow mustard.

  • Weigh the curing salt and use pink curing salt no. 1, not pink Himalayan salt. It makes a five-day cure safe and turns the meat pink.
  • Slice against the grain. Brisket cut along the grain is stringy however well it is cooked.
  • No smoker? Skip the smoking, add 1 teaspoon of smoked paprika to the crust and cook the wrapped brisket at 150°C for 5 hours. It will be less smoky but as tender.

item.title: Peameal Bacon Sandwich
item.description: Homemade peameal bacon sandwich: pork loin brined four days, rolled in cornmeal, sliced thick, fried golden and piled on a Kaiser roll with mustard.
item.content:encoded:
Peameal bacon is not the bacon of an English breakfast. It is a lean, boneless pork loin, brined until it is pink and seasoned through, and rolled in cornmeal, which fries to a fine golden crust. The name comes from the ground dried yellow peas it was once rolled in. The loin is so lean that the salt-and-sugar cure is what keeps it juicy in a hot pan, and the four days in the brine are the only real work in the recipe. In Toronto it is sliced thick, fried, and served on a soft Kaiser roll with nothing but mustard, which is the version here.

  • Pat the loin very dry after rinsing. Cornmeal will not stick to a wet surface.
  • Slice it thick, 1 cm. Thin slices of lean pork dry out before they brown.
  • Weigh the curing salt and use pink curing salt no. 1, not pink Himalayan salt. It turns the pork pink and makes the cure safe. For a loin thicker than 8 cm, cure it for a day longer.

item.title: Beavertails
item.description: Homemade beavertails: a whole-wheat yeast dough stretched flat, fried until blistered and golden, and coated in cinnamon sugar with a squeeze of lemon.
item.content:encoded:
A beavertail is a flat, stretched pastry the shape of a beaver's tail, and the name is the only joke in it: the dough is a whole-wheat yeast dough, pulled thin and fried until the surface blisters into ridges, then sugared while it is hot. The ridges matter, because they hold the cinnamon sugar and the lemon juice while the thin middle stays soft. The dough should be soft and slightly sticky so that it stretches without tearing, and the oil must stay at 180°C, so the pastry puffs before it can soak up fat. They are eaten hot, outdoors, in winter; skaters on Ottawa's Rideau Canal are famous for it.

  • Keep the oil at 180°C. Cooler oil soaks into the dough; hotter oil browns the outside before the middle cooks.
  • Stretch the dough with your hands as well as the rolling pin. It should be thin in the middle and thicker at the edges.
  • Sugar them the moment they leave the pan. The topping will not stick to a cold tail.

item.title: Date Squares
item.description: Homemade date squares: a buttery brown sugar oat crumble layered around a thick cooked date filling and baked until golden, then cut into 16 squares.
item.content:encoded:
Date squares, which some bakeries sell as matrimonial cake, are two layers of the same buttery oat crumble with a cooked date filling between them, and everything in them comes out of the pantry. The filling has to be cooked until the dates collapse into a thick paste, because dates that are only warmed leave a wet layer that soaks into the base and makes the squares fall apart when cut. The base is sweetened with brown sugar and lifted very slightly with bicarbonate of soda, and it is pressed down firmly, so it holds together. The last step is patience: the squares slice cleanly only once they are cold.

  • Cook the dates until they are a thick paste. A loose filling makes a soggy base.
  • Press the bottom layer down hard with the back of a spoon or a flat-bottomed glass.
  • Chill the squares 30 minutes before cutting if they crumble. Butter firms up as it cools.

item.title: Pouding Chômeur
item.description: Pouding chômeur: a plain cake batter baked under a hot maple and cream sauce, so the cake rises and the sauce sinks to a caramel pool. A Québec classic.
item.content:encoded:
Pouding chômeur, which means unemployed man's pudding, is said to date from the Depression of the 1930s, when it was made from the cheapest things in the kitchen: flour, sugar, milk and a syrup. A stiff cake batter is spread in a dish and hot maple sauce is poured over it. As it bakes the batter rises up through the sauce and the sauce sinks below, so every portion has a light cake on top and a pool of caramel underneath. The two things that make it work are a stiff batter, one that would not pour, and a sauce poured on while it is still hot. Serve it warm.

  • Keep the batter stiff. A pourable batter mixes with the sauce and the pudding turns to a sweet mush.
  • The sauce must be hot when it goes on, so that it stays underneath as the cake rises.
  • Put a tray under the dish. The sauce bubbles up as it bakes and can spill over the edge.

item.title: Sugar Pie
item.description: Tarte au sucre, the Québec sugar pie: a flaky shell filled with brown sugar, maple syrup and cream, baked until set and sliced cold in small pieces.
item.content:encoded:
Tarte au sucre is the pie of Québec's sugar shacks and country kitchens: a pastry shell filled with little more than sugar, cream and a spoonful of flour, baked until set. There is no fruit and no nuts. The flavour is brown sugar and cream, in most versions with some maple syrup, deepened by the heat into something close to caramel. The flour thickens the filling and the egg turns it from a syrup into a soft, sliceable custard. It has to cool completely to set, and it is meant to be very sweet, so cut small slices and serve them with unsweetened whipped cream or strong coffee.

  • Whisk the filling again just before pouring. The flour settles quickly.
  • A slight wobble in the middle is right. It firms up completely as the pie cools.
  • Use dark brown sugar and a dark or amber maple syrup for a deeper flavour.

item.title: Toutons
item.description: Newfoundland toutons: rounds of yeast bread dough fried in a pan until puffed and golden, then split and eaten hot with a spoonful of molasses.
item.content:encoded:
Toutons, from Newfoundland, are pieces of bread dough fried in a pan until they puff and turn golden, and they were made from whatever dough was left when the bread was done. They are a breakfast, eaten hot, split open and poured over with molasses, or with butter and a slice of crisp salt pork or bacon. The dough is left to rise before frying and the pieces are flattened to about 1 cm, thin enough to cook through without burning and thick enough to puff into a soft, chewy round with a crisp, fried surface.

  • Fry over medium, not high, heat. High heat browns the outside before the dough has cooked through.
  • Keep the discs 1 cm thick. Thicker ones stay raw in the middle and thinner ones turn into crackers.
  • Add a little more oil between batches. The dough absorbs it quickly.

item.title: Halifax Donair
item.description: Halifax donair: a kneaded, spiced beef loaf sliced and seared, piled in a pita with tomato and onion, and finished with the sweet condensed-milk garlic sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The Halifax donair is a city speciality: spiced beef, sliced thin and crisped, in a pita with tomato, raw onion and a pale, sweet, garlicky sauce made from condensed milk. It was named the city's official food in 2015. Unlike a Greek gyro or Turkish döner, the meat is beef, and the flavour is heavier on garlic and pepper. Kneading the meat to a paste is what makes it dense enough to slice thin, as it would be on a cone, and the vinegar stirred into the condensed milk thickens the sauce within a minute. The sauce is the point: use a lot of it, and eat the donair over its foil.

  • Knead the meat until it looks like a paste. Loosely mixed mince makes a loaf that falls apart when sliced.
  • Slice thin, then sear. The crisp edges are what a donair shop gets from the griddle.
  • The sauce thickens as it stands. If it sets too firm, loosen it with a spoonful of water.

item.title: Bumbleberry Pie
item.description: Homemade bumbleberry pie: a double-crust pie of rhubarb, apple, strawberries, blueberries and raspberries, baked until the juices bubble through the top.
item.content:encoded:
Bumbleberry is not a berry. It is a name for a pie of mixed fruit, usually rhubarb and apple with whichever berries are ripe, and it is a Canadian summer habit, especially in the West. The mixture is balanced on purpose: rhubarb and apple keep their shape and bring sharpness, and the soft berries bring colour and sweetness. Cornflour thickens the juice so it stays in the pie, and the pie must cool for three hours, because a pie cut hot runs. The pastry is a plain all-butter one, rolled to 3 mm, and the pie goes in a hot oven first to set the base.

  • Cut the rhubarb small, about 1 cm. Large pieces stay hard while the berries collapse.
  • The hot tray gives a crisp base. It also catches any juice that bubbles over.
  • Frozen berries work if you do not thaw them first. Toss them in the cornflour while still frozen.

item.title: Cedar Plank Salmon
item.description: Cedar plank salmon: a whole fillet glazed with brown sugar, Dijon, lemon and dill, grilled on a soaked cedar plank until it flakes with a sweet smoky flavour.
item.content:encoded:
Cooking salmon on a board of cedar is an old method of the Pacific Northwest coast, where salmon was roasted on split cedar beside the fire. The plank does two jobs. It keeps the fish away from the flame, so the flesh cooks gently in the heat and smoke that rise around it, and as the wood smokes it gives the salmon a sweet, resinous flavour that nothing in a pan can. The plank must be soaked for an hour first, or it burns instead of smoking, and it must be untreated cedar sold for cooking. The glaze here is brown sugar, mustard and lemon, which caramelises lightly and stays out of the salmon's way.

  • Use an untreated plank made for cooking. Wood from a lumber yard can be treated with chemicals.
  • Do not skip the soak. A dry plank catches fire; a soaked one smokes.
  • Take the salmon off at 52°C in the thickest part. It carries on cooking on the hot plank.

item.title: Cretons
item.description: Homemade cretons: a Québec pork spread of minced pork simmered with onion, milk and warm spices, mashed and chilled until set, for spreading on toast.
item.content:encoded:
Cretons is the pork spread that Québec eats at breakfast on toast: minced pork simmered with onion, milk and warm spices, then mashed and chilled until it sets. It is a cousin of French rillettes, but softer and lighter, held together by milk and a little breadcrumb rather than a large amount of fat, and it is flavoured with the cinnamon, cloves and allspice of the tourtière. It is cheap, it takes one pan, and it keeps for a week in the fridge. The pork is simmered slowly, and stirred often, so that it breaks down into a soft, fine texture, and it must be chilled for several hours to set.

  • Stir often as it simmers. The mixture catches on the base of the pan as the milk thickens.
  • Mash it while warm. Cold cretons cannot be worked into a smooth paste.
  • Season it once it is cold. Chilled food tastes less salty than warm food, so add a little more salt than seems right.

item.title: Ukrainian Cabbage Rolls
item.description: Ukrainian cabbage rolls, or holubtsi: tender cabbage leaves wrapped around a beef and rice filling and baked slowly in a tomato sauce. A prairie favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Cabbage rolls, holubtsi in Ukrainian, came to the Canadian prairies with the Ukrainian settlers who arrived from the 1890s, and they are still on the table at weddings, church suppers and Christmas. Blanching softens the leaves so they roll without tearing. The rolls are packed seam down in a tomato sauce that is sharpened with vinegar and rounded with a little brown sugar, and they bake slowly, for over an hour, until the cabbage is silky and the rice inside has swelled. They are better the next day, and they freeze well.

  • Do not overfill the leaves. The rice swells as it cooks and will split an overstuffed roll.
  • Shave down the thick rib of each leaf so it rolls without tearing.
  • Line the dish with spare cabbage leaves. They stop the rolls from catching on the bottom.

item.title: Flapper Pie
item.description: Flapper pie: a graham cracker crust filled with a set vanilla custard and topped with a golden meringue. A Prairie church-supper classic, served cold.
item.content:encoded:
Flapper pie is a pie of the Prairies, a graham cracker crust filled with vanilla custard and topped with meringue, and it turns up on church-supper and potluck tables in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The custard is thickened with cornflour and egg yolks, and it is cooked until it bubbles, so it sets firm enough to slice. The whites of the eggs go to the meringue, which is spread onto the custard while it is still hot and sealed to the edge of the crust, so it does not shrink or weep as it bakes. It is served cold, from the fridge.

  • Whisk constantly as the custard thickens. It catches and lumps at the base of the pan.
  • Spread the meringue on the hot custard. Cold custard makes the meringue slide and weep.
  • Use a clean, dry bowl for the egg whites. A trace of fat stops them forming peaks.

item.title: Wild Rice Soup
item.description: Creamy chicken and wild rice soup: carrot, celery and thyme simmered with nutty wild rice and chicken breast, thickened lightly and finished with cream.
item.content:encoded:
Wild rice is not rice. It is the seed of a tall grass that grows in the shallow lakes of Ontario, Manitoba and the American Upper Midwest, and the Anishinaabe have harvested it there for centuries. It cooks for about 45 minutes and, when it is ready, the grains split open and turn chewy and nutty, which is why it suits a soup so well: it holds its texture however long the soup simmers. The soup itself is simple. The vegetables are softened in butter, flour thickens the stock lightly, and cream goes in at the end. The chicken is cooked whole in the soup and shredded, so nothing is lost.

  • Rinse the wild rice first. It can carry dust from harvest.
  • Add the stock a little at a time. The flour lumps if it goes in all at once.
  • Keep the soup below a boil once the cream goes in, or it can split.

item.title: Bannock
item.description: Bannock: a quick bread of flour, shortening and baking powder, pan fried in cast iron until golden outside and soft inside. Eat it with jam, honey or butter.
item.content:encoded:
Bannock is a quick bread that Indigenous cooks across Canada have made for generations from flour, fat, baking powder and water. The name is Scottish, the flour came with the fur trade, and the bread has since become a staple of northern kitchens and campfires. It is cooked in a cast-iron pan over a low fire, in the oven, or wrapped on a stick over coals. The dough is mixed just until it holds together, so it stays tender, and pressed thick, about 2 cm, and it is fried slowly, so the middle cooks through before the outside burns. It is ready in half an hour, and is best eaten warm.

  • Keep the heat medium-low. High heat browns the outside before the thick dough is cooked.
  • Handle the dough as little as you can. Overworked bannock is tough.
  • Tap a wedge. It should sound hollow and feel light when it is done.

item.title: Bloody Caesar
item.description: Bloody Caesar: vodka, Clamato juice, Worcestershire and hot sauce over ice in a celery-salt-rimmed glass, garnished with a celery stick. A Canadian classic.
item.content:encoded:
The Caesar was invented in Calgary in 1969 by Walter Chell, who was asked to create a drink for the opening of a new Italian restaurant and made one that tasted like spaghetti alle vongole: tomato and clam. It is a Bloody Mary with Clamato, tomato juice seasoned with clam broth, in place of plain tomato juice, and the clam broth gives it a salty, savoury depth that the older drink does not have. The rim of celery salt is not decoration. It is the first flavour to reach the mouth and it changes the drink. Chill everything before making it and use a lot of ice, so the drink does not dilute.

  • Chill the Clamato and the glass beforehand. A warm drink melts the ice and turns thin.
  • Add the hot sauce in dashes and taste. The Clamato is already salty and mildly spiced.
  • For a drink without alcohol, leave out the vodka and add a splash of lime juice.

item.title: Hawaiian Pizza
item.description: Homemade Hawaiian pizza: a chewy yeast crust with tomato sauce, mozzarella, ham and pineapple. It was invented in Chatham, Ontario, in 1962. Serves four.
item.content:encoded:
Hawaiian pizza is Canadian. It was made in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek-born restaurateur in Chatham, Ontario, who put tinned pineapple on a pizza to see what would happen. The idea works because it balances: sweet, acidic pineapple against salty ham and rich cheese. It works only if the pineapple is well drained, because wet fruit turns the centre of the pizza soggy, and if the oven is as hot as it will go, so the crust cooks before the toppings release their moisture. The dough takes an hour to rise, and the whole pizza takes 12 minutes to bake.

  • Drain the pineapple, then pat it dry. Wet pineapple makes a soggy centre.
  • Use low-moisture mozzarella, not the fresh kind in brine. It melts and browns without releasing water.
  • Preheat the trays. A hot base cooks the crust before the toppings can wet it.

item.title: Ginger Beef
item.description: Calgary ginger beef: thin strips of steak fried crisp in a cornflour coating and tossed in a sticky, sweet, gingery chilli sauce. Serve it with rice.
item.content:encoded:
Ginger beef is a Chinese-Canadian invention of Calgary in the 1970s, crisp fried strips of beef in a sticky, sweet, gingery sauce, and it is now on almost every Chinese-Canadian restaurant menu in the West. It is closer to a sweet-and-sour dish than to anything in China, and it works by contrast: a thin cornflour coating fries to a shell that stays crisp for a minute or two once the sauce goes on, and the sauce is sharp with vinegar and hot with ginger and chilli, so the sweetness does not cloy. The trick is to toss the beef in the sauce at the last moment and eat it straight away.

  • Partly freeze the steak first. It slices thinly and evenly when firm.
  • Fry in batches. A crowded pan drops the oil temperature and the coating turns soggy.
  • Add the beef to the sauce at the last moment. It stays crisp for only a few minutes.

item.title: Maple Glazed Carrots
item.description: Maple glazed carrots: carrot coins simmered in butter until tender, then reduced with maple syrup and thyme to a shiny glaze. A fast side dish.
item.content:encoded:
The method is the same as for any glazed vegetable: cook the carrots in a covered pan with butter and a little water, so they steam tender, then uncover the pan and let the liquid boil down with the sweetener until it turns to a glaze. Maple syrup is the sweetener, and it gives caramel with a faint woodiness that brown sugar lacks. The carrots go in a single layer in a wide pan, so the glaze coats them evenly, and a squeeze of lemon at the end keeps the dish from tasting flat and sweet.
