It is the easiest vegetable at the Christmas or Thanksgiving table, and it takes 25 minutes from start to finish.

  • Use a wide pan so the carrots sit in one layer and glaze evenly.
  • Cut the carrots the same thickness so they cook at the same speed.
  • Take them off the heat as soon as the syrup has thickened. It burns quickly once the water has gone.

item.title: Maple Taffy
item.description: Maple taffy, tire d'érable: maple syrup boiled to 112°C, poured in ribbons over snow or crushed ice and rolled onto a stick into a soft, chewy toffee.
item.content:encoded:
Maple taffy, tire d'érable, is what visitors to a Québec or Ontario sugar shack do with maple syrup in early spring: boil it, pour it in ribbons over clean snow, and roll it onto a stick as it sets into a soft, chewy toffee. It has one ingredient. The syrup must reach 112°C, hot enough to set on cold snow and not so hot that it goes brittle, so a thermometer helps. In the sugar shack it is eaten with dill pickles and plain doughnuts, sour and plain things that cut the sweetness and let you eat more of it.

  • Use a thermometer and take the syrup off at 112°C. At 110°C it stays runny; at 118°C it sets hard and cracks.
  • Use a big pot. Boiling maple syrup rises like milk and will spill over a small one.
  • The ice must be very cold and firmly packed. Warm ice melts the syrup instead of setting it.

item.title: Vegemite Toast
item.description: Vegemite toast the Australian way: thick-cut toast buttered while hot, then scraped with the thinnest layer of Vegemite and cut into fingers.
item.content:encoded:
Vegemite, a dark, salty spread made from brewer's yeast, was first made in Melbourne in 1922, and the way Australians eat it has not changed much since: on hot buttered toast, scraped very thin. The order matters. Butter goes on first, while the toast is hot, and it melts into the bread, and the Vegemite goes on last in a layer you can almost see through. Butter is the reason it does not taste harsh: the fat softens the salt and the savoury flavour of the yeast, so the combination tastes rounded and rich. Spread it on thick, straight from the jar, and it tastes only of salt. Add a slice of cheese or mashed avocado if you like.

  • Butter first, Vegemite second. The butter is what stops it tasting harshly salty.
  • Scrape it thin. A little goes a very long way, and it should not be so thick that you cannot see the butter.
  • Use thick-cut bread, so the toast stays crisp under the butter.

item.title: Fairy Bread
item.description: Fairy bread, the Australian children's party classic: soft white bread buttered to the edges, covered in hundreds and thousands and cut into triangles.
item.content:encoded:
Fairy bread is white sandwich bread, spread with butter and covered in hundreds and thousands, the tiny, hard, coloured sugar balls that are called sprinkles or nonpareils in other countries. It is served at children's birthday parties across Australia and New Zealand, cut into triangles, and it has a place there as fixed as the cake. The two details that make it work are that the butter goes on right to the edge, because the sprinkles stick only where the butter is, and that the bread is soft and fresh, because stale bread will not hold the sprinkles. It has no other requirement, and it takes ten minutes.

  • Soften the butter until it spreads without tearing the bread. Cold butter tears soft bread.
  • Butter right to the crust. The sprinkles stick only where there is butter.
  • Make them no more than an hour before serving. The colours start to bleed into the butter after that.

item.title: Cheesymite Scrolls
item.description: Cheesymite scrolls: soft yeast dough spread with Vegemite butter, rolled with grated cheddar and baked into golden spirals. Makes twelve scrolls.
item.content:encoded:
A cheesymite scroll is a soft yeast bun rolled up with a thin layer of Vegemite and plenty of grated cheese, and it is a fixture of Australian bakery counters and school lunchboxes. The dough is a soft, slightly enriched dough that stays tender when baked, and the Vegemite is beaten into butter first so it spreads in an even, thin layer rather than in dark streaks. Cheddar bakes to a brown, crisp lace where it drips, and that is the best part. The dough takes an hour to rise, but the scrolls themselves need only twenty minutes to puff before they go in the oven.

  • Beat the Vegemite into the butter first. Neat Vegemite spreads in streaks and can taste harsh.
  • Roll the dough up tightly. Loose scrolls unwind in the oven.
  • Cut the roll with a length of thread or dental floss. A knife squashes the spirals.

item.title: Sausage Sizzle
item.description: Sausage sizzle: thick sausages browned and served on a slice of white bread with soft fried onions and tomato sauce. The Australian barbecue classic.
item.content:encoded:
The sausage sizzle is a barbecued sausage served on a slice of white bread, with fried onions and tomato sauce, and it is eaten at school fairs, at fundraisers outside hardware stores and, on election day, at polling stations, where it is called the democracy sausage. The sausage is cooked whole over a moderate heat until it is brown and cooked through, and the bread is not a bun but a plain slice, folded around the sausage to catch the onions and the sauce. The onions do the work: they are cooked slowly in oil until soft and sweet, which takes 15 minutes, and they are what turns a plain sausage in bread into something you queue for.

  • Cook the sausages over moderate heat. High heat splits the skins and leaves the middles raw.
  • Keep turning them so they brown evenly.
  • Cook the onions until they are properly soft. Raw-tasting onions ruin the sandwich.

item.title: Steak Sandwich
item.description: Australian steak sandwich: thin seared sirloin with caramelised onion, tomato, rocket and melted cheese, piled into toasted Turkish bread with mustard mayo.
item.content:encoded:
An Australian steak sandwich is a whole steak, not thin slices, in a toasted roll with sweet caramelised onion, tomato, rocket and cheese, and it is on nearly every pub menu. The steak is cut thin, about 1.5 cm, and cooked hot and fast so it stays tender, and it must rest before it is sliced, or the juice runs out onto the bread. Onions cooked slowly in butter with a little sugar and balsamic become soft and dark and take about 20 minutes, and that is where most of the flavour comes from. The bread is toasted so that it does not go soggy, and the mustard mayonnaise adds sharpness.

  • Cut steaks thin, about 1.5 cm. Thick steaks are hard to bite through in a sandwich.
  • Rest the meat before slicing, or the juices will soak the bread.
  • Toast the rolls. It gives a crisp barrier between the bread and the juices.

item.title: Aussie Burger
item.description: Aussie burger with the lot: a beef patty topped with bacon, a fried egg, cheese, beetroot and grilled pineapple, in a toasted bun with tomato sauce.
item.content:encoded:
An Australian burger with the lot is a beef patty with a good deal more than lettuce and tomato on it: a slice of bacon, a fried egg, cheese, sliced beetroot and a ring of grilled pineapple, all in a soft bun with tomato sauce. The beetroot and pineapple are the surprise to anyone who has not had one, and they make sense once you taste it, because both add sweetness and acid to a salty, rich stack. The patty is seasoned only with salt and pepper and pressed thin so it cooks quickly, and the egg is fried with its yolk left runny, because the yolk is the sauce.

  • Press a dent in the middle of each patty. It stops the centre from puffing up in the pan.
  • Drain the beetroot well. Wet beetroot makes the bun soggy and stains it purple.
  • Cook the egg last, so the yolk is still runny when the burger is put together.

item.title: Tuna Mornay
item.description: Tuna mornay: pasta, tinned tuna and peas in a creamy cheddar sauce, topped with breadcrumbs and cheese and baked until bubbling. A tin-cupboard classic.
item.content:encoded:
Mornay is the French name for a béchamel enriched with cheese, and tuna mornay is the Australian way of using it: tinned tuna and pasta in a cheese sauce with peas, topped with breadcrumbs and baked until golden. It is a dish of the tin cupboard, and it is best when it is treated as a proper white sauce and not a shortcut. Butter and flour are cooked together first, then the milk goes in slowly, so the sauce is smooth, and the cheese goes in off the heat, so it melts into the sauce and does not turn oily. The tuna is stirred in at the end, gently, so it stays in chunks.

  • Undercook the pasta by 2 minutes. It finishes cooking in the sauce in the oven.
  • Add the milk slowly at first. Lumps form when it goes in all at once.
  • Stir in the tuna gently. Over-stirring turns it to paste.

item.title: Zucchini Slice
item.description: Zucchini slice: grated zucchini, bacon, onion and cheese set in an egg and flour batter and baked in a tin, then cut into squares. Good hot or cold.
item.content:encoded:
A zucchini slice is a baked savoury cake of grated zucchini, bacon, onion and cheese, held together with eggs and a small amount of flour, and it is the dish Australians bring to a lunch when they have been given too many zucchini. It is not quite a quiche, because there is no pastry, and not quite a frittata, because there is flour. The most important step is to squeeze the grated zucchini hard in a clean cloth, since it is nearly all water, and any that is left makes a slice that is wet in the middle. Baked, it sets firm enough to cut into squares, and it is as good cold as hot.

  • Squeeze the zucchini hard. It is 95% water and will make the slice wet.
  • Fry the bacon first if you like a crisp texture. Raw bacon gives a softer bite.
  • Do not over-mix the batter. It makes the slice rubbery.

item.title: Bacon and Egg Roll
item.description: Bacon and egg roll: crisp bacon and a soft-yolked fried egg in a buttered crusty roll with tomato or barbecue sauce. The Australian corner-shop breakfast.
item.content:encoded:
The bacon and egg roll is Australia's breakfast sandwich: crisp bacon and a fried egg in a soft, crusty white roll, with tomato sauce or barbecue sauce, and it is sold at every corner shop and café from early morning. It is the classic hangover food. The details are what matter. Bacon is fried until it is crisp at the edges and chewy in the middle, the egg is cooked with the yolk soft so that it runs into the bread, and the roll is buttered, not toasted. Barbecue sauce is the traditional choice in some states and tomato sauce in others, and both are correct.

  • Fry the bacon slowly so the fat renders and the edges crisp. High heat burns it before it cooks.
  • Keep the yolk soft. It runs into the bread and acts as a sauce.
  • Use a fresh, soft roll with a thin crust. A hard crust squeezes the egg out.

item.title: Rissoles
item.description: Australian rissoles: beef mince mixed with grated onion, breadcrumbs and Worcestershire sauce, pan-fried until brown and served with gravy and mash.
item.content:encoded:
A rissole in Australia is a flat patty of beef mince, mixed with grated onion, breadcrumbs, egg and Worcestershire sauce, and pan-fried until brown. It is the Sunday night dinner of countless childhoods, and it is served with mashed potato, peas and gravy made from the pan. The breadcrumbs and egg keep the patty tender and hold it together, and grated onion, rather than chopped, melts into the meat and gives it juice as well as flavour. A dusting of flour on the outside makes a crust and gives the gravy, which is made in the same pan, its body.

  • Grate the onion rather than chopping it. It disappears into the meat and keeps the patties juicy.
  • Do not overwork the mixture. Compressed mince gives dense patties.
  • Cook over medium heat. High heat burns the flour coating before the middles are done.

item.title: Pumpkin Scones
item.description: Australian pumpkin scones: soft, golden scones made with mashed cooked pumpkin, baked close together so they rise tall, and eaten warm with butter.
item.content:encoded:
Pumpkin scones are a Queensland tradition, made famous by Flo Bjelke-Petersen, the wife of Queensland's long-serving premier, who served them to visitors, and they are a plain scone with mashed pumpkin worked into the butter and sugar. The pumpkin makes them moist, tender and slightly sweet, and it gives the crumb a pale gold colour. They are baked close together on the tray, so they rise up instead of out. The pumpkin must be cool, and it must be well drained, since a wet pumpkin gives a dough that is too sticky to shape. Eat them warm with butter and jam.

  • Drain the pumpkin well and let it cool. Wet or warm pumpkin makes a sticky dough.
  • Cut straight down without twisting the cutter. Twisting seals the edges and stops the scones rising.
  • Bake them touching. Their sides support each other and they rise higher.

item.title: Potato Scallops
item.description: Potato scallops: thick potato slices part-boiled, dipped in a light fizzy batter and fried until crisp and golden. The Australian chip-shop favourite.
item.content:encoded:
A potato scallop is a thick slice of potato, dipped in batter and deep-fried, and it is sold in Australian fish-and-chip shops under different names: scallops in New South Wales and Queensland, potato cakes in Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia. It is one of the few things that has to be fried twice to be right, in a way: the slices are part-boiled first so that they are soft in the middle, and they must be dried thoroughly after that, or the batter will not stick. The batter is made with cold soda water, whose bubbles keep it light and crisp.

  • Dry the boiled slices well. A wet surface makes the batter slide off in the oil.
  • Use very cold soda water and mix just before frying. The bubbles make the batter light.
  • Do not crowd the pan. Too many at once drops the oil temperature and the batter turns greasy.

item.title: Dim Sim
item.description: Australian dim sims: pork and cabbage dumplings in a thick round wrapper, steamed until tender and served with soy and chilli sauce. Pan-fry for a crisp base.
item.content:encoded:
The dim sim of Australian fish-and-chip shops is a Chinese-Australian version of siu mai: larger, packed with cabbage as well as pork, in a thicker wrapper, and usually steamed and then fried. It came from Melbourne in the 1940s and it is now a takeaway staple in every state. Cabbage gives the filling its juiciness and lightens the pork. It must be salted and squeezed dry first, or the wet filling tears the wrappers, and the filling must be mixed until it is sticky, so it holds together when bitten. Round dumpling wrappers, sold as gow gee wrappers, save an hour of dough-making.

  • Squeeze the salted cabbage very dry. Wet filling tears the wrappers.
  • Stir the filling in one direction until sticky. It gives a firm, springy texture.
  • Do not overfill. Wrappers split when packed too full.

item.title: Mince on Toast
item.description: Savoury mince on toast: beef mince simmered with onion, carrot, peas, tomato paste and Worcestershire sauce, then piled on thick buttered toast.
item.content:encoded:
Savoury mince on toast is a family dinner that Australians and New Zealanders grew up on: beef mince cooked with onion and carrot, seasoned with tomato paste and Worcestershire sauce, thickened lightly, and spooned over buttered toast. It is the meal of a hungry night with little in the cupboard. The mince is browned properly first, so it has a roasted flavour and does not stew, and a spoonful of flour stirred through it gives the sauce body so it sits on the toast and does not run off. Frozen peas go in at the end, for colour and sweetness, and grated cheese on top melts into the mince.

  • Brown the mince well before adding liquid. Grey, boiled mince has little flavour.
  • Keep the sauce thick. Thin sauce soaks the toast and turns it to paste.
  • Grate the carrot. It cooks quickly and disappears into the sauce.

item.title: Lemonade Scones
item.description: Lemonade scones: self-raising flour, cream and fizzy lemonade make light, tall scones with no butter to rub in. Serve warm with jam and whipped cream.
item.content:encoded:
Lemonade scones have three ingredients and no butter to rub in: self-raising flour, cream and lemonade. The lemonade in question is the clear fizzy soft drink sold as lemonade in Australia and Britain (lemon-lime soda, such as Sprite or 7-Up in North America), and it does two jobs: its bubbles give lift on top of the raising agent in the flour, and its sugar sweetens the scone lightly. The cream provides the fat that butter would. The dough is soft and sticky, and it is patted rather than rolled, then cut with a straight-down press. It goes together in ten minutes and is out of the oven 15 minutes later.

  • Use the lemonade straight from a newly opened bottle. Flat lemonade gives a flatter scone.
  • Handle the dough as little as possible. Kneading makes the scones tough.
  • Use plenty of flour on the bench and the cutter. The dough is very soft.

item.title: Chicken Salt
item.description: Homemade chicken salt: fine salt blended with paprika, garlic, onion, celery salt and chicken stock powder. The Australian seasoning for hot chips.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken salt is the seasoning that Australian takeaways shake over hot chips, and there is no chicken in it, at least not much: it is fine salt with paprika, garlic and onion powder, celery salt, turmeric for colour and a little chicken stock powder, which gives it its savoury, meaty depth. The blend should be fine, so it clings to the surface of a hot chip, and it should be made in a small amount and kept in a jar, since the spices lose their smell after a few months. It is also good on roast potatoes, popcorn, roast chicken skin, fried eggs and potato scallops.

  • Grind the mixture fine. Coarse salt bounces off chips instead of sticking to them.
  • Salt chips the moment they come out of the fryer, while the surface is still hot and slightly oily.
  • Taste a pinch on a chip and adjust. Chicken stock powder varies a lot in saltiness.

item.title: Cream Buns
item.description: Australian cream buns: soft yeast buns baked golden, iced with a simple glaze, then split and filled with strawberry jam and whipped cream.
item.content:encoded:
The Australian cream bun is a soft, slightly sweet yeast bun, iced on top, split and filled with jam and whipped cream, and it has been in bakery windows for over a century. The dough is enriched with milk, egg and butter, so the crumb is soft and tender and it stays that way for a day. The buns are shaped into smooth, tight balls, which keeps them round as they rise and bake, and they must be cooled completely before they are split, since warm buns melt the cream. The icing is plain: icing sugar and a few drops of milk or water, coloured pink if you want to be traditional.

  • Cool the buns completely before splitting them. Warm buns melt the cream.
  • Shape tight, smooth balls. Loosely shaped buns bake into uneven lumps.
  • Fill just before serving. The cream softens the bun within a few hours.

item.title: Pie Floater
item.description: Pie floater: a hot meat pie floating in a bowl of thick green pea soup, topped with tomato sauce. The South Australian pie-cart classic, made at home.
item.content:encoded:
A pie floater is South Australia's own dish: a hot meat pie, upside down, floating in a bowl of thick green pea soup, topped with tomato sauce, and traditionally sold from pie carts in Adelaide. The pie and the soup are two things that work better together than either does alone. The soup is rich and sweet, and the flaky pastry soaks it up and softens while the meat stays hot and savoury. The soup is made from green split peas, which need no soaking and break down in about an hour, with a piece of smoked bacon for flavour, and it should be thick enough to hold up a pie.

  • Make the soup thick, so it holds the pie up. Add water at the end if it is too thick.
  • Serve the pies straight from the oven so that they are steaming when they meet the soup.
  • Blend only part of the soup. Some whole peas give the bowl a texture.

item.title: Tim Tam Cheesecake
item.description: No-bake Tim Tam cheesecake: a chocolate biscuit crust, a whipped cream cheese and dark chocolate filling with chopped biscuit, chilled until firm.
item.content:encoded:
A Tim Tam is an Australian chocolate biscuit: two malted biscuits sandwiched with chocolate cream and coated in chocolate. Crushed with butter, it makes a firm, dark crust with no baking, because the chocolate in the biscuit does the work of a binder. More biscuit, chopped, goes into the filling for texture. The filling is cream cheese, whipped cream and melted dark chocolate, folded together gently so that the cream stays airy, and it is the chocolate that sets it: as the cold chocolate firms up in the fridge it holds the cheesecake together without gelatine, provided it has at least 6 hours. Decorate with halved biscuits just before serving.

  • Cool the chocolate before mixing it in. Hot chocolate melts the cream cheese and makes a runny filling.
  • Stop whipping the cream at soft peaks. Stiff cream is hard to fold in and makes a grainy filling.
  • Cut with a hot, dry knife, wiping it between slices, for clean edges.

item.title: Jam Drops
item.description: Jam drops: soft, buttery biscuits made with a little custard powder, with a well of raspberry jam pressed into each one before baking. Makes 24.
item.content:encoded:
A jam drop is a small, soft, buttery biscuit with a well of jam pressed into it before it goes in the oven, and it is a fixture of Australian biscuit tins, school fêtes and CWA tea tables. Custard powder in the dough is the old trick: it is mostly cornflour with vanilla flavouring, and it gives the crumb a fine, tender, slightly sandy texture and a pale gold colour. The jam goes in before baking, so it sets to a glossy, chewy dot instead of staying runny, and it should be a thick, set jam, since a thin one boils over the sides of the well as it bakes. They take under an hour from start to tin.

  • Use a thick, set jam. Runny jam bubbles over the edge and burns on the tray.
  • Do not overfill the wells. Half a teaspoon is enough, and it spreads as it bakes.
  • Take the biscuits out while they are still pale. They firm up as they cool.

item.title: Golden Syrup Dumplings
item.description: Golden syrup dumplings: soft dumplings simmered under a lid in a sauce of golden syrup, brown sugar and butter, served hot with cream or ice cream.
item.content:encoded:
Golden syrup dumplings are the pudding of a cold night when the oven is not on: a soft dough dropped by the spoonful into a pan of simmering golden syrup, brown sugar and butter, and cooked under a lid until they puff and the sauce turns into caramel. Everything happens in one pan. The dumplings steam on top of the sauce, and their bottoms soak it up, so each has a tender crumb with a syrupy underside. The rule is not to lift the lid, because the steam is what cooks them through, and to keep the heat low, so that the syrup does not catch and burn.

  • Keep the sauce at a gentle simmer. A hard boil breaks the dumplings up and can burn the sugar.
  • Do not lift the lid. Steam is what cooks the tops.
  • Use a wide pan so all the dumplings sit on the sauce with room to swell.

item.title: Peach Melba
item.description: Peach Melba: peaches poached in vanilla syrup, served over vanilla ice cream with a sieved raspberry sauce and toasted almonds. Made for Nellie Melba.
item.content:encoded:
Peach Melba was made by the chef Auguste Escoffier in the 1890s for the Australian soprano Nellie Melba, first as peaches on ice cream and later with raspberry sauce added. It has lasted because it is balanced: peaches are perfumed and sweet, ice cream is cold and creamy, and raspberry sauce is sharp, so no part of it is cloying. The peaches are poached in a light vanilla syrup only until they are tender, which takes minutes, and peeled first, because their skins go leathery in hot syrup. The sauce is raw raspberries pressed through a sieve with sugar and lemon juice, and it needs no cooking at all.

  • Use peaches that are ripe but still firm. Soft ones fall apart in the syrup.
  • Cool the peaches in the syrup. They keep absorbing flavour, and they will not go brown.
  • Sieve the sauce. The seeds are the only thing wrong with fresh raspberries.

item.title: Hedgehog Slice
item.description: Hedgehog slice: crushed biscuits, coconut and walnuts bound with butter, sugar, cocoa and egg, pressed into a tin, topped with chocolate and chilled.
item.content:encoded:
Hedgehog slice is a chocolate slice of coarsely crushed sweet biscuits, coconut and walnuts, bound with a cooked mixture of butter, sugar, cocoa and egg, and it is called after the pieces of biscuit that stick out of it like spines. It is a dish of the Australian and New Zealand biscuit tin, and it needs no oven. The binder is cooked briefly on the stove to thicken the egg, which makes it firmer than a slice held together with butter alone. The biscuits should be crushed unevenly, so there are chunks as well as crumbs, and the slice should be chilled for at least two hours before it is cut.

  • Crush the biscuits unevenly. Some crumbs and some chunks give the hedgehog texture.
  • Stir the egg constantly over low heat. It scrambles if the heat is too high.
  • Warm the knife under hot water to cut the chocolate top without cracking it.

item.title: Neenish Tarts
item.description: Neenish tarts: small sweet pastry shells filled with jam and vanilla buttercream and iced half chocolate, half white. A classic Australian tea-shop tart.
item.content:encoded:
Neenish tarts are little sweet pastry cases with a thin layer of jam, a filling of soft vanilla cream, and a top iced in two halves, chocolate and white, and they have been a fixture of Australian and New Zealand tea shops and church-hall trays for a hundred years. The pastry is a sweet, short one made with icing sugar, which gives a fine, crumbly texture and stays crisp under the filling. The filling is a buttercream, beaten until it is pale and light. The icing is stiff, so it stays where it is put and makes a clean line down the middle, and it needs about twenty minutes to set.

  • Cool the pastry cases completely before filling them. Warm cases melt the buttercream.
  • Keep the icing thick. It should hold its shape on the tart without running over the edge.
  • Ice the white half first, then wipe the knife before the chocolate half so the colours stay clean.

item.title: Lemon Slice
item.description: No-bake lemon slice: crushed biscuits, coconut, condensed milk and butter with lots of lemon zest, pressed into a tin, iced with lemon icing and chilled.
item.content:encoded:
Lemon slice is an Australian no-bake: crushed sweet biscuits, coconut, condensed milk and melted butter pressed into a tin, with lemon zest in the base and a lemon icing on top. Condensed milk is the binder, and it is what makes the slice dense, chewy and sweet rather than crumbly. The lemon comes twice, as zest in the base, which perfumes it, and as juice in the icing, which cuts through all that sweetness. The slice needs two hours in the fridge to set firm enough to cut cleanly. It is served in small squares.

  • Crush the biscuits finely. Big pieces make a crumbly slice that will not hold together.
  • Use plenty of lemon zest. It is the only lemon in the base.
  • Cut with a hot, dry knife, wiping it between cuts.

item.title: Lemon Delicious Pudding
item.description: Lemon delicious pudding: a light lemon sponge that bakes above its own tangy lemon custard, made in one dish with a water bath. An Australian classic.
item.content:encoded:
Lemon delicious is an Australian pudding that divides itself as it bakes: a light lemon sponge on top and a thin, tangy lemon custard underneath. The batter is a curdled-looking mixture of butter, sugar, egg yolks, flour, lemon juice and milk, and the egg whites are whisked separately and folded in. The whisked whites are what make the sponge: they hold air, and the air floats up to form a light cake on top, while the heavier liquid sinks to form the sauce. The dish is set in a bath of hot water in the oven, so that the custard cooks gently and does not curdle.

  • Whisk the whites to soft peaks, no further. Stiff whites are hard to fold in without deflating them.
  • Use a clean, dry bowl for the whites. Any grease stops them whipping.
  • Do not skip the water bath. It cooks the custard gently and stops it splitting.

item.title: Self-Saucing Chocolate Pudding
item.description: Self-saucing chocolate pudding: a chocolate batter sprinkled with brown sugar and cocoa, covered with boiling water and baked into a sponge over its sauce.
item.content:encoded:
A self-saucing pudding is a dessert that makes its own sauce, and the method is surprising the first time: the batter goes in the dish, a mixture of brown sugar and cocoa is sprinkled on top, and boiling water is poured over the whole thing. It looks wrong. In the oven the batter rises through the water and the sugar and cocoa dissolve into it and sink, and so the cake that comes out has a soft chocolate sponge on top of a thin, glossy chocolate sauce. It is made in one bowl and one dish. Do not stir once the water has gone on, and serve it hot, straight from the oven, with cream.

  • Pour the water over the back of a spoon so it does not dig holes in the batter.
  • Do not stir after adding the water. The layers are what make the sauce.
  • Serve it straight away. The sauce thickens and soaks into the cake as it cools.

item.title: Honey Joys
item.description: Honey joys: cornflakes tossed in a melted butter, sugar and honey syrup, spooned into paper cases and baked until crisp and golden. Makes twelve.
item.content:encoded:
Honey joys are cornflakes coated in a syrup of melted butter, sugar and honey and baked in paper cases, and they are on every Australian children's party plate next to fairy bread and chocolate crackles. The syrup is boiled for a minute, which sets it: it coats the flakes thinly, and as it bakes it turns to a crisp, glassy coating that holds each little cluster together. The flakes should be turned carefully, not stirred hard, or they break to dust. The whole batch is made in about 25 minutes, and the joys set completely as they cool in the tin.

  • Turn the flakes gently. Stirring hard breaks them to crumbs.
  • Boil the syrup for a full minute. It sets to a crisp coating as it cools.
  • Do not press the mixture down. Loose clusters bake crisper.

item.title: Chocolate Crackles
item.description: Chocolate crackles: puffed rice cereal, cocoa, icing sugar and coconut bound with melted coconut oil, spooned into paper cases and chilled until set.
item.content:encoded:
Chocolate crackles are puffed rice cereal, cocoa, icing sugar and coconut held together with melted coconut oil, set in paper cases, and they are the other half of the Australian children's party plate. In Australia they are made with Copha, a solid vegetable shortening made from coconut oil, which sets hard at room temperature, and refined coconut oil does the same job. It has to be a solid fat that is melted, because oil that stays liquid makes a puddle at the bottom of the case. The mixture takes a few minutes to put together, has no eggs, no dairy and no oven, and sets in the fridge in half an hour.

  • Use a solid fat that sets hard. A liquid oil will not set the crackles.
  • Sift the icing sugar and cocoa. Lumps do not dissolve in the fat.
  • Stir gently so the puffed rice does not crush.

item.title: Macadamia Nut Cookies
item.description: Macadamia nut cookies: chewy brown sugar cookies with roasted macadamias and white chocolate chunks, golden at the edges and soft in the middle. Makes 20.
item.content:encoded:
The macadamia is Australia's own nut, native to the rainforests of Queensland and New South Wales, and its buttery flavour and crisp, creamy texture make it the best of all nuts for a cookie. It is high in fat, so it stays crisp in the dough where a walnut goes soft, and it is not bitter. Here it is chopped coarsely and roasted first, which brings out its flavour, and paired with white chocolate, which is sweet and creamy in the same way. The dough is made with more brown sugar than white, which gives a chewy centre, and the cookies are baked until only the edges are golden.

  • Take the cookies out when the centres still look soft. They firm up as they cool.
  • Chop the nuts coarsely. Fine chopping makes them disappear into the dough.
  • Chop the white chocolate into chunks. Chips hold their shape and taste less rich.

item.title: Coconut Slice
item.description: Australian coconut slice: a buttery shortbread base, a layer of raspberry jam, a chewy baked coconut topping and a pink icing. Cut into 16 squares.
item.content:encoded:
Coconut slice is a tray bake in three layers, a buttery shortbread base, a thin layer of raspberry jam and a topping of coconut, egg and sugar that bakes to a chewy, golden-brown crust. The base is baked first, so that it stays crisp under the jam and the topping. The topping must be spread carefully and pressed so that it covers the jam to the edge, because jam left showing burns. The slice is iced pink once it has cooled, which is the tradition, and the icing is best made thick so that it sets firm and can be cut without smearing.

  • Press the topping right to the edges of the tin. Exposed jam burns.
  • Ice only when the slice is cold. Warm slice melts the icing into a puddle.
  • Cut with a hot, dry knife for clean squares.

item.title: Boiled Fruit Cake
item.description: Boiled fruit cake: dried fruit boiled with butter, sugar and spice, then mixed with eggs and flour and baked into a dark, moist cake. No creaming or soaking.
item.content:encoded:
A boiled fruit cake is the pantry cake of Australian and New Zealand kitchens: dried fruit boiled with butter, sugar, spice and water, cooled, then mixed with eggs and flour and baked. The boiling does the work that other fruit cakes need days for. It plumps and softens the fruit, dissolves the sugar and melts the butter, so there is no creaming to do, no soaking and no need to leave the fruit overnight. Bicarbonate of soda stirred in after boiling makes the mixture foam and reacts with the acid in the fruit, giving a cake that is dark, moist and tender. It keeps for a fortnight.

  • Cool the fruit completely before adding the eggs. Hot fruit scrambles them.
  • Double-line the tin. A slow bake will burn the outside of a single-lined cake.
  • Cover the top with foil if it browns too much before the middle is cooked.

item.title: Cinnamon Teacake
item.description: Australian cinnamon teacake: a light, plain butter cake, brushed with melted butter and coated in cinnamon sugar while still hot, and eaten warm with tea.
item.content:encoded:
A cinnamon teacake is a plain, light butter cake that owes everything to its topping: as soon as it comes out of the oven it is brushed with melted butter, which soaks in, and covered with cinnamon sugar, which sticks to the butter and forms a sweet, spiced crust. It was a staple of Australian tearooms and country kitchens, made when someone dropped in, and the batter comes together in fifteen minutes from a handful of ingredients. The cake itself is quiet on purpose, a vanilla butter cake with a soft crumb, so the cinnamon crust is the point. It is best warm.

  • Brush the butter on while the cake is hot. It soaks in and holds the sugar on.
  • Do not overmix once the flour goes in. Overmixing makes a tough, dry cake.
  • Beat the butter and sugar until pale. It is the only thing that makes the cake light.

item.title: Chocolate Ripple Cake
item.description: Chocolate ripple cake: crisp chocolate biscuits sandwiched with whipped cream into a log, covered in cream and chilled overnight until it slices like cake.
item.content:encoded:
The chocolate ripple cake is an Australian party dessert with two ingredients and one trick: crisp chocolate biscuits are sandwiched with whipped cream into a log, and the log is left in the fridge overnight. In that time the moisture from the cream is absorbed by the biscuits, which soften into something between a cake and a mousse, so the finished dessert slices cleanly, with stripes of biscuit and cream through every slice. The dessert is entirely no-bake. The cream must be whipped firm enough to hold the biscuits upright and sweetened only lightly, since the biscuits are sweet already.

  • Whip the cream firm. Soft cream does not hold the log together, and it slides.
  • Leave it overnight. Less than 8 hours, and the biscuits are still crisp.
  • Cut on the diagonal for the classic striped slice.

item.title: Melting Moments
item.description: Melting moments: tender, crumbly butter and cornflour biscuits sandwiched in pairs with a passionfruit buttercream. Makes twelve sandwiched biscuits.
item.content:encoded:
Melting moments are butter biscuits so short that they dissolve on the tongue, and the name is exact. Cornflour replaces part of the plain flour in the dough, which lowers the gluten and makes the crumb fine, sandy and tender, and the high proportion of butter makes them rich. They are made in Britain, Australia and New Zealand alike, and in Australia they are often filled with passionfruit buttercream, whose sharp, fragrant tang balances all that butter. The dough is soft, and it is piped or dropped and pressed with a fork, and the biscuits are baked at a low temperature, just until set, since they must stay pale.

  • Beat the butter until very pale. Air is what makes the biscuit light.
  • Strain the passionfruit if you do not want the seeds. Some people like them.
  • Handle the baked biscuits carefully. They are very fragile until they have cooled.

item.title: Lolly Cake
item.description: Lolly cake: crushed malt biscuits, condensed milk and butter mixed with chopped pink and white marshmallows, rolled in coconut logs, chilled and sliced.
item.content:encoded:
Lolly cake is a New Zealand no-bake: crushed malt biscuits bound with condensed milk and melted butter, mixed with chopped pink and white marshmallow sweets, which are called lollies in New Zealand, shaped into logs, rolled in coconut and chilled. It is on every school-fair and birthday-party table. The sweets soften slightly in the mixture and leave soft, chewy pockets of pink and white through a dense, sweet, biscuity cake. Malt biscuits give it a toasty, malted flavour, and digestive biscuits are a fair substitute. The mixture is sticky, so wet hands, or a sheet of baking paper, make it easier to shape.

  • Crush the biscuits finely. Big chunks make the logs crumble when sliced.
  • Cut the marshmallows with wet scissors so they do not stick.
  • Slice with a sharp, wet knife and wipe it between cuts.

item.title: Louise Cake
item.description: Louise cake: a soft butter shortcake base, a layer of raspberry jam and a coconut meringue topping, baked golden and cut into squares. A New Zealand classic.
item.content:encoded:
Louise cake is a New Zealand tray bake in three layers: a soft, buttery shortcake base, a thin layer of raspberry jam, and a topping of coconut folded into whisked meringue, baked until the top is crisp and golden and the underside is chewy. It has been on tearoom counters and cake-stall tables for generations. The meringue is what sets it apart from other jam-and-coconut slices. The whites must be whisked to stiff peaks before the sugar goes in a spoonful at a time, and the coconut is folded in gently so that the mixture stays airy. The base is baked first so that it does not go soggy under the jam.

  • Whisk the whites to stiff peaks before adding sugar. The sugar goes in a spoonful at a time.
  • Bake the base first. It stays crisp under the jam and the meringue.
  • Cut with a hot, wet knife, wiping it between cuts, so the meringue does not shatter.

item.title: Ginger Crunch
item.description: Ginger crunch: a crisp, spicy ginger shortbread base with a thick golden syrup and ginger icing poured on while hot and cut into squares while warm.
item.content:encoded:
Ginger crunch is a New Zealand slice made of a crisp ginger shortbread base and a thick, fudgy ginger icing, and it is a fixture of cake stalls and café counters. The base is baked until it is crisp and golden. The icing is a warm mixture of butter, golden syrup, icing sugar and ground ginger, poured over the base while both are hot, so it sets into a smooth, slightly chewy layer that bonds to the biscuit. The timing matters: cut it into squares while it is still warm. Once the icing is cold and set, it shatters when cut.

  • Pour the icing on while the base is hot. It bonds and sets smooth.
  • Cut into squares while warm. Cold icing cracks.
  • Press the base down firmly. A loose base crumbles when cut.

item.title: Boil-Up
item.description: Boil-up: a Māori one-pot meal of pork bones simmered until tender, then potatoes, kūmara, doughboy dumplings and greens cooked in the broth.
item.content:encoded:
A boil-up is a Māori and Pacific family meal of pork bones simmered until the meat falls off, then potatoes, kūmara, dumplings called doughboys and greens cooked in the same pot, and it is served in big bowls with the broth. It is the food of the family gathering, cheap and filling, and it is cooked in one pot. The long simmer, an hour, is what makes the broth, and the vegetables go in later so they do not turn to mush. The traditional green is puha (sow thistle) or watercress, with cabbage or silverbeet as a substitute. The doughboys are dropped on top of the broth and steam under a lid.

  • Skim the foam in the first 10 minutes. It keeps the broth clear.
  • Add the potatoes and kūmara late. A long simmer turns them to mush.
  • Do not lift the lid while the doughboys cook. The steam makes them light.

item.title: Mussel Fritters
item.description: New Zealand mussel fritters: chopped steamed green-lipped mussels in a light egg batter with spring onion, fried until golden and served with lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Green-lipped mussels are New Zealand's signature shellfish, and mussel fritters are the way they are eaten at the beach: steamed mussels, chopped, in a light egg batter with spring onion, and fried until crisp outside and tender inside. A good fritter is more mussel than batter, so the batter is thin, and the mussels are folded in at the last minute. Steaming opens fresh mussels in about 4 minutes in a covered pan with a splash of water, and the meat is then chopped coarsely; frozen or vacuum-packed cooked mussel meat is a good shortcut. Serve them hot with lemon or sweet chilli sauce.

  • Pat the chopped mussels dry. Wet mussels thin the batter.
  • Keep the batter thick. It should drop from a spoon, not pour.
  • Fry over medium-high heat so the outside crisps before the middle overcooks.

item.title: Feijoa Cake
item.description: Feijoa cake: a moist butter cake with chopped fragrant feijoa folded through it and a crunchy cinnamon-sugar top. The New Zealand way with a feijoa glut.
item.content:encoded:
Feijoas, also called pineapple guavas, fall from garden trees all over New Zealand between March and June, and a cake is the classic way to use a glut of them. The flesh, scooped out of the skin with a spoon, has a perfumed flavour of pineapple, guava and mint, and it stays soft and juicy through baking, so it makes a moist cake. The skin is bitter and is not used. The batter is a simple butter cake, and the fruit is folded in last, so that it is spread through the crumb, and the cinnamon sugar on top bakes to a crisp crust. If feijoas are not available, ripe pears or apples with a little lemon zest will do.

  • Use ripe feijoas that give slightly under your thumb. Hard ones are sour and gritty.
  • Fold the fruit in gently. Overmixing makes a tough cake.
  • Do not use the skin. It is bitter and tough.

item.title: Kūmara Gnocchi
item.description: Kūmara gnocchi: soft dumplings made from baked New Zealand sweet potato, a little flour and parmesan, tossed in browned sage butter.
item.content:encoded:
Kūmara is the sweet potato that Māori brought to New Zealand, and it makes a gnocchi that is lighter and sweeter than the potato kind. The kūmara is baked whole, not boiled, so it dries out instead of taking on water. Extra water is the enemy of gnocchi, because it means more flour, and more flour means heavy dumplings. The flesh is mashed while it is hot, mixed with an egg yolk, parmesan and just enough flour to make a soft, slightly sticky dough, and handled as little as possible. The gnocchi are ready when they float, and they need only a butter sauce, browned with sage, to be complete.

  • Bake the kūmara. Boiled kūmara is wet and needs so much flour that the gnocchi turn heavy.
  • Add flour gradually and stop when the dough is just workable. It will be softer than potato dough.
  • Cook one test gnocchi first. If it falls apart, mix in a spoonful more flour.

item.title: Corn Fritters
item.description: Corn fritters: sweetcorn, spring onion and herbs in a thick egg batter, fried until golden and crisp and served with sour cream and sweet chilli sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Corn fritters are the brunch dish of the New Zealand and Australian café: sweetcorn in a thick batter with spring onion and herbs, fried until golden, and stacked with sour cream, sweet chilli sauce, and sometimes bacon or avocado. The batter is thick, and there is only enough of it to hold the corn together, so each fritter is mostly corn, sweet and juicy inside a crisp shell. It is made in a bowl and one frying pan in about half an hour. Tinned, frozen or fresh kernels all work, provided they are drained and dried, as excess water gives a pale, soggy fritter that falls apart in the pan.

  • Drain and dry the corn well. Water makes the batter thin and the fritters pale.
  • Keep the batter thick. It should sit on a spoon.
  • Fry over medium heat so the middle cooks before the outside burns.

item.title: Belgian Biscuits
item.description: Belgian biscuits: two soft, spiced biscuits sandwiched with raspberry jam, iced pink and topped with a glacé cherry. A New Zealand bakery favourite.
item.content:encoded:
A Belgian biscuit is two soft, spiced biscuits sandwiched with raspberry jam, iced with pink icing and topped with half a glacé cherry, and it is a staple of New Zealand and Australian bakeries. It is said to have been called a German biscuit until the First World War, and the name changed. The biscuit is a spiced butter dough, flavoured with cinnamon, ginger and mixed spice and sweetened with a spoonful of golden syrup, and it is rolled about 5 mm thick, so that it is soft rather than crisp. The icing is coloured naturally with raspberry jam, and the whole biscuit is eaten with a cup of tea.

  • Roll the dough to 5 mm. Thin biscuits are crisp, and Belgian biscuits should be soft.
  • Cool the biscuits completely before filling. Warm biscuits melt the jam into a mess.
  • Keep the icing thick. Thin icing runs down the sides.

item.title: Date Loaf
item.description: Date loaf: dates softened in boiling water with bicarbonate of soda, then baked with brown sugar and walnuts into a dark, moist loaf to slice and butter.
item.content:encoded:
A date loaf is a fixture of New Zealand and Australian cake tins: a dark, sticky, moist loaf of dates and walnuts that is sliced and buttered. It has no creaming and no mixer. Boiling water is poured over the chopped dates with bicarbonate of soda, which softens the fruit so it can be broken into a paste and lifts the loaf, and the mixture is left to stand before the egg and the flour are stirred in. The dates supply both the sweetness and the moisture, so the loaf stays moist for days, and it improves after a day in the tin.

  • Mash the dates against the side of the bowl after soaking. They should break down into a paste.
  • Do not overmix once the flour goes in. It makes the loaf tough.
  • Cover with foil if the top browns too fast before the centre is cooked.

item.title: Cincinnati Chili
item.description: Cincinnati chili: a thin, cinnamon and cocoa-spiced beef sauce ladled over spaghetti and topped with a mountain of finely grated cheddar, three-way style.
item.content:encoded:
Cincinnati chili is not chili in the Texan sense. It is a thin, finely textured meat sauce, spiced with cinnamon, allspice, cloves and a little cocoa, and it is served over spaghetti, which is why it is closer to a Greek pasta sauce than to a bowl of red. The ordering is a code: a three-way is spaghetti, chili and cheese; four-way adds onions or beans; five-way adds both. The beef is not browned. It is broken up in cold water and simmered, which gives the sauce its fine, smooth texture, and the long, slow simmer, an hour and a half, lets the spices mellow. The cheese is grated so finely that it melts into the sauce.

  • Break the beef up in cold water. Browning it first gives a coarse, grainy texture that is not right for this sauce.
  • Grate the cheese finely, on the smallest holes of a box grater. It should fall like snow over the chili.
  • The chili is better the next day. Make it ahead, chill it, and skim off the solid fat.

item.title: Chicago Deep Dish Pizza
item.description: Chicago deep dish pizza: a buttery cornmeal crust pressed up the sides of a deep pan, layered with mozzarella, sausage and chunky tomato, and baked hot.
item.content:encoded:
A Chicago deep dish is a pie, not a pizza in the Neapolitan sense: a thick, biscuity crust pressed up the sides of a deep pan, filled with a layer of sliced mozzarella, a layer of sausage, and a topping of chunky tomatoes, with the cheese on the bottom and the sauce on top, which is the reverse of the ordinary order. The order is functional. Under a long bake, the cheese would burn if it were on top, so the tomatoes shield it. The dough has some cornmeal and a good deal of oil or butter, which gives it a crisp, fried bottom and a sandy, golden crumb. The pizza is baked for 35 minutes and rests for 10 before it is cut.

  • Use low-moisture mozzarella, sliced and not grated. It melts in one layer and does not release water.
  • Drain the tomatoes well. Wet sauce turns a deep dish into a soup.
  • Butter the tin generously. It fries the crust and makes it easy to lift out.

item.title: Detroit Style Pizza
item.description: Detroit style pizza: a thick, airy rectangular pizza baked in an oiled pan, with cheese to the edges for a crisp caramelised crust and sauce stripes on top.
item.content:encoded:
A Detroit pizza is a thick, rectangular, focaccia-like pizza baked in a well-oiled steel pan, and what sets it apart is the cheese, which is pushed right to the edges of the pan, where it fries against the hot metal into a lacy, dark, crisp crust. The dough is wet, about 75% water, which gives an open, airy crumb, and the oil in the pan fries the base. Traditionally the cheese is Wisconsin brick cheese, which is fatty and melts without going oily; a mixture of low-moisture mozzarella and Monterey Jack is a good substitute. The sauce goes on in stripes after the cheese, so the cheese can brown.

  • Use a dark metal pan. It browns the base and edges better than glass or a light aluminium one.
  • Push the cheese all the way to the edges. That is what makes the crisp crust.
  • Put the sauce on late. It keeps the cheese from browning when it is baked on top.

item.title: Chicago Hot Dog
item.description: Chicago hot dog: an all-beef frank in a steamed poppy seed bun with mustard, green relish, onion, tomato, pickle, sport peppers and celery salt. No ketchup.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago hot dog is an all-beef frankfurter in a steamed poppy seed bun, dressed with yellow mustard, bright green sweet pickle relish, chopped white onion, two tomato wedges, a dill pickle spear, two pickled sport peppers and a dash of celery salt. It is described as dragged through the garden, and there is no ketchup. The elements are not interchangeable. The mustard is yellow, the relish is neon green, the tomatoes are wedges and not slices, and the order matters, because the wet ingredients go on first and the dry last. The hot dog is simmered, not grilled, and the bun is steamed until soft.

  • Do not add ketchup. In Chicago it is regarded as a mistake.
  • Simmer the frankfurters gently and do not boil them, or the skins split.
  • Warm the buns. A cold bun turns the whole thing stiff.

item.title: Juicy Lucy
item.description: Juicy Lucy: a Minneapolis burger with a slice of cheese sealed inside the beef patty, so that it melts into a molten centre. Let it rest before biting in.
item.content:encoded:
A Juicy Lucy is a burger with the cheese on the inside: two thin patties are sealed around a slice of cheese, so that it melts into a molten centre as the burger cooks. It comes from Minneapolis, where two bars still argue over who invented it. The seal is the whole technique. If the edges of the patties are not pinched shut, the cheese escapes into the pan, and if the meat is too lean the patty cracks. The cheese inside is at lava temperature when the burger comes off the heat, so it is rested for a few minutes and bitten into carefully.

  • Seal the edges completely. A gap lets the cheese leak into the pan.
  • Use mince with at least 15 to 20% fat. Lean beef cracks when it is pinched.
  • Rest the burger for 3 minutes. The molten cheese inside is hot enough to burn.

item.title: Hot Brown
item.description: Kentucky Hot Brown: an open-faced turkey sandwich on toast, covered in a creamy parmesan Mornay sauce, topped with bacon and tomato and grilled.
item.content:encoded:
The Hot Brown was made in 1926 at the Brown Hotel in Louisville, Kentucky, as an answer to the ham-and-eggs supper that guests were tired of, and it is an open-faced sandwich of toast, sliced roast turkey and bacon, covered with a creamy cheese sauce and grilled until the top blisters. The sauce is a Mornay, a béchamel with cheese, and it must be thick enough to sit on the turkey and not run off. The tomatoes go on top of the sauce, so they warm through and slightly soften, and the bacon goes on last, so it stays crisp. It is eaten with a knife and fork.

  • Whisk the milk in a little at a time so the sauce is smooth.
  • Make the sauce thick. Thin sauce runs off the turkey and turns the toast soggy.
  • Add the bacon after grilling. Under the grill it goes chewy.

item.title: Frito Pie
item.description: Frito pie: corn chips piled in a bowl, covered with hot beef and bean chili and topped with cheddar and raw onion. A Texas and New Mexico classic.
item.content:encoded:
Frito pie is a bowl of corn chips covered in chili, and it comes from Texas and New Mexico, where it is sold at football games and county fairs, often in the bag of chips itself, split open along the side. The reason it works is texture. The chips soften slightly under the hot chili, so that some are crunchy and some are tender, while the cheese melts and the raw onion adds a sharp crunch. The chili should be a thick one, with little liquid, or the chips will turn to paste. It is made in one pot in about an hour and it is better with cheap, thick corn chips than with delicate ones.

  • Make the chili thick. Loose chili turns the chips to mush.
  • Assemble at the table, one bowl at a time. Chips left under chili go soft.
  • Use thick, sturdy corn chips. Thin tortilla chips collapse.

item.title: Egg Foo Young
item.description: Egg foo young: fluffy Chinese-American omelette patties with shrimp, bean sprouts and spring onion, served over rice with a glossy savoury brown gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Egg foo young is a Chinese-American dish, a fluffy omelette patty of eggs, bean sprouts, spring onion and shrimp or pork, fried until golden and served under a savoury brown gravy, and it is a fixture of takeaway menus. It is made from very little. The eggs are beaten only lightly, so the patties stay tender, and the bean sprouts stay crisp because they are not cooked before frying. The patties are cooked in a good amount of hot oil, which makes the edges lacy and crisp, while the gravy is made in a minute with stock, soy sauce, oyster sauce and cornflour, and it is spooned over just before serving so the patties are not soggy.

  • Beat the eggs lightly. Overbeaten eggs make dense, rubbery patties.
  • Do not pre-cook the bean sprouts. They stay crisp inside the patty.
  • Spoon the gravy on at the table, just before eating. It keeps the patties crisp.

item.title: Muffuletta
item.description: Muffuletta: a round sesame loaf layered with salami, ham, mortadella and provolone and soaked with a tangy olive salad, pressed and cut into wedges.
item.content:encoded:
The muffuletta is a New Orleans sandwich, made in the early 20th century at an Italian grocery in the French Quarter: a big round sesame loaf split and filled with Italian cured meats and cheese, and covered with olive salad. It is the salad that defines it. Chopped olives, pickled vegetables, capers, garlic and oregano are marinated in olive oil and red wine vinegar, and the oil soaks into the bread from the inside, so the sandwich improves as it stands. It is wrapped and pressed for an hour before it is cut into wedges, which lets the oil and the vinegar work through the bread and the meats.

  • Pull out some of the soft crumb from the loaf. It gives more room for the filling.
  • Do not skimp on the oil in the olive salad. It flavours and moistens the bread.
  • Serve at room temperature, not cold. Cold provolone and cold meat taste of little.

item.title: Red Beans and Rice
item.description: New Orleans red beans and rice: kidney beans simmered for hours with smoked sausage, ham hock and the trinity until creamy, and served over white rice.
item.content:encoded:
Red beans and rice is a Monday dish in New Orleans, a habit that dates from the days when Monday was wash day and a pot of beans could be left on the stove all day. The beans are simmered with the trinity, onion, green pepper and celery, with smoked sausage and a ham hock for flavour, until they collapse into their own creamy gravy, which takes two hours or more. Some of the beans are mashed against the pot at the end to thicken it. The beans are soaked overnight and, for safety, boiled hard for ten minutes before the long simmer, since raw kidney beans contain a toxin that only a rolling boil destroys.

  • Boil the soaked beans hard for 10 minutes before simmering. Raw or under-boiled kidney beans are toxic.
  • Mash some of the beans at the end. They thicken the gravy without any flour.
  • Salt late. Salt added early can keep the bean skins tough.

item.title: Shrimp Boil
item.description: Shrimp boil: shell-on shrimp, smoked sausage, corn and baby potatoes cooked in one pot of Old Bay water, then spread on a table with melted butter and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
A shrimp boil is a Lowcountry feast, in South Carolina and Georgia sometimes called Frogmore stew, in which shrimp, smoked sausage, corn and potatoes are cooked in a single pot of spiced water and tipped out over a table covered with newspaper. It is made in stages. Everything goes into the pot at a different time, according to how long it takes to cook: potatoes first, sausage next, then corn, and finally the shrimp, which need only 3 minutes and turn rubbery if they are left in longer. The water is seasoned with Old Bay, lemon, garlic and onion, and those flavours are carried into the corn and the potatoes. It is served with melted butter, lemon and cocktail sauce.

  • Add the ingredients in stages. Each one has a different cooking time.
  • Leave the shells on the shrimp. They protect the meat and flavour the water.
  • Take the shrimp out after 3 minutes. Overcooked shrimp are rubbery.

item.title: Hoppin' John
item.description: Hoppin' John: black-eyed peas and rice simmered together with smoked bacon, onion, pepper and celery. The Southern one-pot dish eaten on New Year's Day.
item.content:encoded:
Hoppin' John is a dish of black-eyed peas and rice cooked with smoked pork, and it is eaten across the American South on New Year's Day, when it is said to bring good luck for the year, the peas standing for coins. It is at its best as a one-pot dish, with the rice cooked in the peas' own liquid, so that it takes up their flavour. The peas do not need soaking, and take about 35 minutes to soften; the rice goes in afterwards and cooks for 18 minutes in the same pot. Smoked bacon supplies fat and flavour, and a dash of hot sauce or vinegar at the table brightens the whole pot.

  • Rinse the peas and pick out any stones. They do not need soaking.
  • Do not stir once the rice is in. Stirring makes it sticky.
  • Finish with hot sauce or a splash of vinegar. It brightens the whole pot.

item.title: Steamed Clams
item.description: Steamed clams, New England style: fresh clams purged of sand, steamed open in a covered pot and served with melted butter, lemon and a cup of broth.
item.content:encoded:
Steamed clams, called steamers in New England, are eaten by the bucketful at summer shacks, dipped in melted butter and rinsed in a cup of the cooking broth to remove any sand. They are among the simplest of shellfish dishes: the clams are scrubbed, left in salted water to spit out their sand, and steamed in a covered pot with a little water until the shells open, which takes only 6 to 8 minutes. Salted water makes them think they are back in the sea, so they filter it and clean themselves. Any clam that is open before cooking and does not close when tapped is discarded, as is any that stays shut after cooking.

  • Lift the clams out of the water. Pouring it out sends the sand back over them.
  • Discard any clam that stays shut. It was not alive.
  • Do not overcook. Clams that steam for too long turn rubbery.

item.title: Succotash
item.description: Succotash: sweetcorn, lima beans, onion and red pepper cooked in butter, with thyme and a splash of cream. A colourful Southern side dish for any meal.
item.content:encoded:
Succotash is a dish of corn and beans, from the Narragansett word msickquatash, and it was eaten by Native American cooks in New England long before it reached the Southern table, where it became a summer side dish, made with lima beans, corn and whatever else was in the garden. Corn and beans complement each other, since the beans supply protein that corn lacks. Here they are cooked in butter with onion and red pepper for sweetness and colour, with a little thyme, and finished with cream. It is quick, since the frozen vegetables need only 10 minutes, and it works as a side with roast chicken, ham, fish or barbecue.

  • Use frozen lima beans. Tinned ones are soft and dull.
  • Do not overcook the corn. It should keep a little bite.
  • Leave out the cream for a lighter, fully dairy-free version, using olive oil instead of butter.

item.title: Corn Pudding
item.description: Southern corn pudding: whole and puréed sweetcorn baked in a custard of eggs, milk and cream until set and golden. A creamy holiday side dish.
item.content:encoded:
Corn pudding is a baked dish of sweetcorn in a custard, something between a soufflé and a savoury pudding, and it is a Southern side dish for Thanksgiving, Christmas and church suppers. Half the corn is puréed with the milk and cream, which gives the pudding a creamy body and a strong sweetcorn flavour, and half is left whole for texture. A little flour thickens the custard so that it sets firmly without going rubbery. It is baked until the middle is just set, with a slight wobble, and is left for 10 minutes to firm, and it is served hot from the dish with a spoon.

  • Purée only half of the corn. The whole kernels give texture.
  • Take it out when the middle just wobbles. It keeps setting as it stands.
  • Use a shallow dish so the custard cooks evenly.

item.title: Spoonbread
item.description: Southern spoonbread: a light, puffed, soufflé-like cornmeal pudding made with milk, buttermilk and whisked egg whites, baked and eaten with a spoon.
item.content:encoded:
Spoonbread is a Southern dish that is somewhere between a cornbread, a soufflé and a bowl of grits: cornmeal cooked to a thick porridge with milk, lightened with beaten egg whites, and baked until it puffs and turns golden on top and stays soft and custardy underneath. It is served with a spoon, as the name says, straight from the dish. The cornmeal must be cooked on the stove first, until it thickens, so that it is fully softened before it goes in the oven, and the whites are folded in gently, since the air in them is what makes the spoonbread rise. It falls after a few minutes out of the oven, so get it to the table at once.

  • Cook the cornmeal until thick. Raw cornmeal makes a gritty spoonbread.
  • Fold in the whites gently. Beating them in loses the air.
  • Serve immediately. It sinks within a few minutes of coming out of the oven.

item.title: Pimento Cheese
item.description: Southern pimento cheese: sharp cheddar, cream cheese, mayonnaise and diced pimentos, mixed into a thick, tangy spread for crackers, celery and sandwiches.
item.content:encoded:
Pimento cheese is the spread of the American South, sometimes called the pâté of the South: sharp cheddar, mayonnaise and diced pimentos, with cream cheese in many versions. It is eaten on white bread, with crackers, in a grilled cheese, on a burger or with celery, and it is served at the Masters golf tournament and in every church-hall lunch in the region. Grate the cheese from a block. Pre-shredded cheese is coated with starch, which makes the spread dry and grainy, and a coarse grate gives it the right chunky, creamy texture. The spread is best after chilling for half an hour, so that the flavours blend.

  • Grate your own cheese. Pre-shredded cheese is coated with starch and makes a dry spread.
  • Drain the pimentos well. Wet pimentos thin the spread.
  • Use a sharp, aged cheddar. Mild cheese gives a bland spread.

item.title: Toasted Ravioli
item.description: Toasted ravioli: meat or cheese ravioli breaded in seasoned crumbs and parmesan, fried until crisp and golden and served with warm marinara for dipping.
item.content:encoded:
Toasted ravioli is the appetiser of St. Louis, Missouri: ravioli that is breaded and deep-fried, not baked, in spite of the name, and served with marinara for dipping. It is said to have been created by accident in a restaurant on The Hill, the city's Italian quarter, when a cook dropped a ravioli in the breadcrumbs. The ravioli are boiled for 2 minutes, only enough to soften the pasta, so that they finish cooking in the fryer, and then dried carefully, because wet pasta does not hold the coating. The breadcrumbs are seasoned with parmesan and Italian herbs, and the double dip in egg and crumbs makes a shell that stays crisp.

  • Dry the boiled ravioli well. Wet pasta will not hold the coating.
  • Use one hand for the dry ingredients and one for the wet ones, to keep your fingers from clogging.
  • Fry at 180°C. Cooler oil makes greasy ravioli.

item.title: Oysters Rockefeller
item.description: Oysters Rockefeller: oysters on the half shell under a buttery topping of spinach, herbs and breadcrumbs, baked on rock salt until golden. A New Orleans dish.
item.content:encoded:
Oysters Rockefeller was created in 1899 at Antoine's in New Orleans, and named for John D. Rockefeller because the sauce was as rich as he was. It remains a dish of raw oysters baked briefly under a topping of green herbs, spinach, butter and breadcrumbs, and the original recipe is a secret. The oysters cook in the oven in about 8 minutes, just long enough for their edges to curl, and any longer makes them tough. The topping is cooked first, so it is fully wilted and dry, and squeezed of moisture, since wet greens would water down the oysters. Rock salt holds the shells level, so that none of the juice is lost, and keeps them hot at the table.

  • Squeeze the spinach dry. Wet greens water down the oysters.
  • Do not over-bake. Oysters toughen quickly, and 8 minutes is enough.
  • Nestle the shells in rock salt so they stay level and hold in their juices.

item.title: Fried Pickles
item.description: Fried pickles: dill pickle chips dipped in buttermilk and egg, coated in seasoned cornmeal and flour, and fried until crisp. Serve with a creamy dip.
item.content:encoded:
Fried pickles are a Southern bar snack: dill pickle chips in a crisp coating of cornmeal and flour, fried until golden, and dipped in a cool, creamy sauce. They are a contrast, the hot, crunchy coating against the cold, sour pickle inside. The pickles must be dried very well, first, since moisture makes the coating slip off, and the coating has both flour and cornmeal, the flour to stick and the cornmeal to crisp. Because the pickles are salty, the coating is barely salted. The dip, sour cream with mayonnaise, dill, garlic and lemon, is there to cool them down.

  • Dry the pickles thoroughly. Wet pickles lose their coating in the oil.
  • Do not salt the coating. The pickles are salty enough.
  • Fry in small batches so the oil stays hot and the coating crisps.

item.title: Stuffed Mushrooms
item.description: Stuffed mushrooms: mushroom caps filled with a garlicky mixture of cream cheese, parmesan, breadcrumbs and parsley, and baked until golden and tender.
item.content:encoded:
Stuffed mushrooms are an appetiser to make for a party: mushroom caps filled with a mixture of cream cheese, parmesan, garlic and herbs, and baked until the filling is golden and the mushrooms are tender. The stems are chopped and cooked with garlic first, until they are dry, and stirred into the filling, so nothing is wasted and the mushroom flavour is doubled. Cooking the stems until the moisture has gone is the key step, because they are mostly water, and water makes a soggy filling. Breadcrumbs soak up any extra liquid the mushrooms release as they cook. They can be filled ahead and baked when guests arrive.

  • Cook the stems until the pan is dry. Wet stems make a watery filling.
  • Do not wash the mushrooms. Wipe them, or they take on water and turn soggy.
  • Fill them up to a day ahead and keep them in the fridge. Bake when the guests arrive.

item.title: Jalapeño Poppers
item.description: Baked jalapeño poppers: halved jalapeños filled with cream cheese and cheddar and topped with crunchy panko and parmesan, baked until golden and bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
Jalapeño poppers are peppers stuffed with cheese, and the fun of them is in the balance: hot green pepper, cool cream cheese, savoury cheddar and a crisp, buttery crust. Almost all of the heat is in the white ribs and seeds of the pepper, and not in the flesh, so scraping them out with a teaspoon controls how spicy the popper is. They are baked here, not fried, at 200°C, which cooks them in about 25 minutes with far less mess and gives a golden panko and parmesan crust. Wear gloves when handling the peppers, or wash your hands well, and do not touch your eyes afterwards.

  • Scrape out the seeds and ribs to reduce the heat. Leave some in for a hotter popper.
  • Wear gloves. The capsaicin stays on your fingers for hours.
  • Cool for 5 minutes before eating. The filling is scalding.

item.title: Beignets
item.description: New Orleans beignets: squares of soft yeast dough fried until puffed and golden, then buried in powdered sugar. Eat them hot with a cup of coffee.
item.content:encoded:
A beignet, in New Orleans, is a square of soft yeast dough, fried until it puffs into a hollow pillow and buried in powdered sugar, and it is eaten hot, with a cup of chicory coffee, at the cafés of the French Quarter. It is a French pastry that arrived with the city's Creole cooks. The dough is a soft, enriched one, and it is rolled thin, about 6 mm, since the beignet puffs to several times its thickness in the oil, and it is fried at 180°C, so that it browns evenly and cooks through. The sugar is dusted on thickly, and it is impossible to eat one without making a mess.

  • Roll the dough thin, about 6 mm. The beignets puff up to several times that in the oil.
  • Keep the oil at 180°C. Cooler oil makes greasy beignets, and hotter oil browns them before they cook through.
  • Dust with sugar at the last minute, when they are still hot and the sugar clings.

item.title: Indian Pudding
item.description: New England Indian pudding: cornmeal cooked in milk with molasses, ginger and cinnamon and baked slowly until dark, creamy and spoonable. Serve warm.
item.content:encoded:
Indian pudding is one of the oldest desserts of New England: cornmeal, milk and molasses baked slowly until it turns dark and creamy, and the name is a colonial one, given because the settlers used the Native American cornmeal for what was, in England, a wheat-flour pudding. It is thickened on the stove first, so that the cornmeal is soft, and then baked for two hours at a low temperature, which turns the milk and molasses to a deep caramel colour and flavour. The trick of the recipe is the cold milk poured on top just before baking, which is not stirred in but forms a creamy layer as the pudding cooks. It is served warm, with vanilla ice cream.

  • Whisk the cornmeal in gradually. It lumps if it goes in all at once.
  • Pour the cold milk over the top and do not stir. It makes the creamy layer.
  • Use plain molasses, not blackstrap. Blackstrap is bitter.

item.title: Apple Brown Betty
item.description: Apple brown betty: layers of spiced apple slices and buttered breadcrumbs baked until golden on top and soft inside. An old American pudding, served warm.
item.content:encoded:
Apple brown betty is an old American pudding, a colonial way to use stale bread: sliced apples, sugar and spice, layered with buttered breadcrumbs and baked, so the crumbs soak up the apple juice and turn soft in the middle while the top layer bakes crisp and golden. It is not a crumble, as its crumbs are layered through the fruit and not sprinkled on top, and it is not a pudding of the sponge kind, as there is no batter. The dish is covered for the first half of baking, so the apples steam soft, and uncovered for the second, so the top browns. Tart apples, such as Bramley or Granny Smith, hold their shape.

  • Use tart apples such as Bramley or Granny Smith. Sweet apples turn to mush.
  • Keep the crumbs buttery. Dry crumbs stay pale and sandy.
  • Cover for the first 30 minutes. It steams the apples soft before the top browns.

item.title: Shoofly Pie
item.description: Shoofly pie: a Pennsylvania Dutch pie with a gooey dark molasses filling under a buttery brown sugar crumb topping. Serve it with strong coffee.
item.content:encoded:
Shoofly pie is a Pennsylvania Dutch pie, made from molasses, and it is said to be called that because the sweet, sticky filling drew flies that had to be shooed away from the cooling pie. It has two layers: a soft, dark molasses filling and a topping of buttery brown sugar crumbs, and the crumbs sink slightly into the filling as it bakes. This is the wet-bottom version, with a gooey, almost custardy layer under the crumbs, and it is the one most people prefer. The filling is thinned with hot water and set with a little bicarbonate of soda, which makes it foam and rise, then settle, as it cools. The pie is very sweet and is best with strong black coffee.

  • Use plain unsulphured molasses, not blackstrap. Blackstrap makes the pie bitter.
  • Pour the filling in before you scatter the crumbs, and scatter them gently so they do not sink.
  • Let the pie cool. The filling sets as it cools and is too runny to slice hot.

item.title: Sweet Potato Pie
item.description: Southern sweet potato pie: a smooth, spiced custard of roasted sweet potato, brown sugar and evaporated milk in a blind-baked shell. A holiday favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Sweet potato pie is a Southern holiday dessert, and it belongs to the African American table, where it has been a Thanksgiving and Christmas pie for generations. It is more like a custard than a pumpkin pie, smoother and sweeter and more delicately spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg and ginger. The sweet potatoes are roasted whole, not boiled, so their flavour concentrates and they do not take on water, and the flesh is beaten smooth. The shell is blind-baked before the filling goes in, so that its base is crisp, and the pie is baked until it is just set. It is cooled for at least 3 hours before slicing.

  • Roast the sweet potatoes, do not boil them. Boiled sweet potato is watery and makes a loose filling.
  • Beat the flesh until smooth, or push it through a sieve, to remove the stringy fibres.
  • Blind-bake the shell. Without it, the base is pale and soft.

item.title: Chess Pie
item.description: Southern chess pie: butter, sugar, eggs and a little cornmeal and vinegar, baked in a flaky shell until golden with a crackled top. A very sweet classic.
item.content:encoded:
Chess pie is a Southern pie with a filling of just butter, sugar, eggs and a spoonful of cornmeal, baked until the top is golden and crackled and the inside is a firm, smooth, sweet custard. Nobody is sure about the name. One story says it came from "just pie", spoken with a Southern accent, another that the pies were kept in a pie chest. A spoonful of vinegar is the traditional and essential ingredient, because it cuts the sweetness, and a little cornmeal gives the filling body and a slight grain. The filling is not cooked first and is poured raw into an unbaked shell.

  • Do not skip the vinegar. It is the only thing that keeps the pie from tasting flat and sugary.
  • Cool the melted butter before whisking it into the eggs, or it will scramble them.
  • Serve small slices. The pie is very rich.

item.title: Hummingbird Cake
item.description: Hummingbird cake: a moist Southern layer cake of banana, crushed pineapple and pecans, sandwiched and covered with a thick cream cheese frosting.
item.content:encoded:
Hummingbird cake is the Southern layer cake of banana, pineapple and pecans, made famous when Southern Living magazine printed a recipe for it in 1978, and it is a cake that tastes better than it should. It is very moist, because it is made with oil and not butter, and with mashed banana and crushed pineapple, juice included. It is spiced lightly with cinnamon, and the pecans are chopped and stirred in. The batter is stirred by hand, in two bowls, and no mixer is needed. The cream cheese frosting is thick, tangy and sweet, and it keeps the layers from being cloying. The cake keeps well and is better on the second day.

  • Stir the batter only until combined. Overmixing makes the cake tough.
  • Cool the layers completely before frosting them. Warm cake melts the frosting.
  • Chill the frosting for 15 minutes if it is soft. It spreads better when it is firm.

item.title: Banana Split
item.description: Banana split: a banana halved lengthwise, three scoops of ice cream, warm chocolate sauce, strawberries, pineapple, whipped cream, nuts and a cherry on top.
item.content:encoded:
The banana split is an American soda-fountain sundae, a banana cut in half lengthwise, laid in a long dish with three scoops of ice cream between the halves, and covered with sauces, whipped cream, nuts and a cherry. It is said to have been invented in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, in 1904 by a pharmacist, David Strickler, and it became a lasting American treat. The classic has vanilla, chocolate and strawberry ice cream, and three toppings, chocolate, strawberry and pineapple.
