The chocolate sauce here is a simple ganache, warm and glossy, and it takes 5 minutes. Use a firm ripe banana, since a soft one collapses when split.

  • Use firm ripe bananas with a little green left. Very ripe ones fall apart when split.
  • Warm the chocolate sauce. It sets when it meets the ice cream and makes a fudgy shell.
  • Assemble at the last minute. The ice cream melts quickly.

item.title: Root Beer Float
item.description: Root beer float: three scoops of vanilla ice cream in a chilled tall glass, topped with cold root beer that fizzes into a creamy foam. Serve with a straw.
item.content:encoded:
A root beer float is a scoop or two of vanilla ice cream in a tall glass, topped with cold root beer, and it is a soda-fountain classic said to have been invented in Colorado in the 1890s. The interest is in the reaction. The bubbles of the root beer nucleate on the surface of the ice cream, so the drink foams, and the ice cream and the root beer combine to form a creamy foam that tastes of vanilla and sassafras-like spice. The root beer is poured slowly down the side of the glass, so that the foam does not overflow, and the glass is chilled beforehand so that the ice cream melts slowly. A float is drunk and eaten at the same time.

  • Chill the glass and the root beer. Warm ingredients make an overflowing foam and a thin drink.
  • Pour the root beer slowly, in stages, down the side of the glass.
  • Use a good vanilla ice cream. A plain one is the whole flavour of the float.

item.title: Bananas Foster
item.description: Bananas Foster: bananas cooked in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, flamed with rum and spooned over vanilla ice cream. A New Orleans dessert in 18 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Bananas Foster was invented in 1951 at Brennan's restaurant in New Orleans, named for a friend of the owner, and it has been set alight at the table ever since. It is a very simple dish, bananas cooked briefly in a sauce of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, then flamed with rum and spooned over vanilla ice cream, and the flame is more than theatre: it burns off the harshness of the alcohol and caramelises the sugar in the sauce. The bananas should be firm, just ripe, so that they hold their shape. The dish takes 8 minutes to cook, and it must be served at once, while the sauce is hot and the ice cream is cold.

  • Use firm, just-ripe bananas. Soft ones turn to mush in the pan.
  • Take the pan off the heat before adding the rum, and never pour it straight from the bottle into a hot pan.
  • Keep your hair and sleeves away from the pan, and stand back when the rum lights.

item.title: Mint Julep
item.description: Mint julep: bourbon, sugar and gently pressed fresh mint over a dome of crushed ice in a frosted cup. The classic drink of the Kentucky Derby.
item.content:encoded:
The mint julep is a Southern drink of bourbon, sugar, mint and crushed ice, and it is the drink of the Kentucky Derby, where over 100,000 are served each year. The mint is pressed gently against the sugar, not shredded, since bruising it releases its oils and fragrance without bitterness, and the drink is built in a metal cup that frosts on the outside as the ice chills it. Crushed ice is the essential part: it dilutes the bourbon at just the right rate and packs into a dome. The sprig of mint on top is the point of the garnish. It sits by your nose as you drink, and the smell of it is half of the flavour.

  • Press the mint gently. Shredded leaves make the drink bitter and grassy.
  • Use crushed ice, made by wrapping ice cubes in a tea towel and hitting them with a rolling pin.
  • Hold the cup by the rim or base so your hand does not warm the frost.

item.title: Gooey Butter Cake
item.description: St. Louis gooey butter cake: a thin, buttery cake base under a rich, gooey layer of cream cheese, eggs and sugar, dusted with icing sugar. Cut into squares.
item.content:encoded:
Gooey butter cake is a St. Louis speciality, a coffee cake with a thin, dense, buttery base and a topping so rich and soft that it stays gooey in the middle even when cooked. It is said to have come about by accident in the 1930s, when a baker got the proportions wrong and the cake did not rise, and it was sold anyway. The base is a simple dough of flour, butter and egg pressed into the tin, and the topping is beaten from cream cheese, eggs, butter and icing sugar, and poured on. It is baked until the edges are golden and the centre still wobbles, and it firms as it cools, though it never sets solid. It is very sweet, and it is cut into small squares.

  • Bake until the centre still wobbles. It sets as it cools and stays gooey.
  • Beat the cream cheese until it is completely smooth before adding the sugar. Lumps do not disappear.
  • Cut with a hot knife, and wipe it between squares.

item.title: Pralines
item.description: New Orleans pralines: soft, creamy pecan candies made by boiling sugar, cream and butter to 115°C, beating until thick and dropping in spoonfuls to set.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans praline is a creamy, sugary, pecan-studded candy, sold in the shops of the French Quarter, and it is a descendant of the French praline, which was made from almonds and hard caramel. In Louisiana, pecans replaced the almonds, and cream and butter were added, which changed the candy from a brittle to a soft, crumbly, fudge-like disc that dissolves on the tongue. The sugar syrup is boiled to 115°C, the soft-ball stage, and then beaten off the heat, which makes tiny sugar crystals form and gives the praline its creamy, slightly grainy texture. The candy sets quickly, so it is dropped onto paper in spoonfuls as soon as it thickens.

  • Use a thermometer and take the pan off at 115°C. Lower gives soft, sticky pralines and higher gives hard ones.
  • Beat until the mixture loses its shine. That is the point at which the sugar crystallises.
  • Work quickly once it thickens. It sets in a minute or two.

item.title: Pollo a la Brasa
item.description: Pollo a la brasa: a chicken marinated in soy, garlic, cumin and paprika, roasted until the skin is crisp and served with a bright green ají sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Pollo a la brasa is the Peruvian roast chicken that is sold from rotisserie shops all over Lima, and what makes it different from other roast chickens is the marinade. It is built from soy sauce, garlic, cumin, paprika, lime and vinegar, a combination that shows the Chinese influence on Peruvian cooking, and it is rubbed under the skin as well as over it, so the flesh is seasoned right through. The salt and acid in the marinade also draw moisture to the skin, so it dries in the fridge and crisps in the oven. The green sauce that goes with it, ají verde, is made from fresh chilli, coriander and mayonnaise, and it is served in a pool beside the chicken and used for the fries.

  • Get the marinade under the skin. It is the only way to season the breast.
  • Leave the chicken uncovered in the fridge for the last hour. The skin dries and crisps in the oven.
  • Seed the jalapeños for a mild sauce and leave the seeds in for a hot one.

item.title: Tallarines Verdes
item.description: Tallarines verdes: spaghetti tossed in a creamy Peruvian pesto of basil, spinach, garlic, queso fresco and evaporated milk. A Peruvian home classic.
item.content:encoded:
Tallarines verdes, green noodles, is Peru's version of spaghetti with pesto, brought to the country by Italian immigrants in the 19th century and made over with local ingredients. Where Genoese pesto is oil, pine nuts and cheese, the Peruvian version is basil and spinach blended with evaporated milk, garlic, and a soft white cheese such as queso fresco, so it is creamy, mild and deep green. The spinach is what keeps the colour bright, and is cooked for less than a minute. The sauce is stirred into the hot pasta off the heat, since boiling it turns it a muddy brown, and it is traditionally served with a thin fried steak or a breaded chicken cutlet.

  • Blanch the spinach for no more than 30 seconds. Longer turns it grey.
  • Toss the sauce with the pasta off the heat. Boiling it turns the green to brown.
  • Use queso fresco, or feta with a little milk. It gives the sauce its mild, creamy flavour.

item.title: Chicha Morada
item.description: Chicha morada: Peru's deep purple drink of purple corn simmered with pineapple, apple, cinnamon and cloves, sweetened, finished with lime and served cold.
item.content:encoded:
Chicha morada is the purple drink of Peru, made by boiling dried purple corn, a variety native to the Andes, with pineapple, apple, cinnamon and cloves, and served cold, with lime, over ice. The kernels and the cobs both go in the pot, and it is the cobs that give the drink its colour, a deep, clear magenta-purple from the anthocyanin pigments in the corn, which are the same family as those in blueberries. It is not fermented, in spite of the name, which it shares with an Andean corn beer, and it is drunk with lunch as an everyday drink. The pineapple peel and core go in as well as the fruit, since they carry a lot of flavour. Sugar is added after straining, so it can be adjusted to taste.

  • Use the cobs as well as the kernels. Most of the colour is in the cob.
  • Add the sugar and lime after straining. It keeps the flavour balanced and the colour bright.
  • If you cannot find purple corn, blueberries and a little hibiscus tea make a different but colourful drink.

item.title: Tacu Tacu
item.description: Tacu tacu: Peruvian rice and beans fried with onion, garlic and ají amarillo into a golden, crisp-crusted cake, topped with a fried egg and salsa criolla.
item.content:encoded:
Tacu tacu is a Peruvian dish of rice and beans, fried together into a cake with a crisp, golden crust and a soft, savoury middle, and it was born of leftovers: yesterday's rice and yesterday's beans, mashed with onion, garlic and chilli. It is a legacy of the Afro-Peruvian kitchen, and the name is usually taken to mean a mix. The crust is what matters, so the cake is fried in a good amount of oil in a heavy pan, and left undisturbed until it releases. Cold, day-old rice is best, since warm rice turns to mush. The classic finish is a fried egg with a runny yolk, and a salsa criolla of red onion, lime and chilli.

  • Use cold, day-old rice. Warm rice is too wet and the cakes fall apart.
  • Leave the cakes alone while they fry. Moving them breaks the crust before it forms.
  • Mash about half of the beans. They act as glue for the cake.

item.title: Picanha
item.description: Picanha: the Brazilian rump cap with its fat cap left on, coarsely salted, grilled to medium-rare and sliced thin, with a tomato and onion vinagrete.
item.content:encoded:
Picanha is the cut of beef that Brazilians love best, the rump cap, a triangular piece of muscle with a thick layer of fat on one side, and it is the centrepiece of the churrasco, the Brazilian barbecue. The fat is what makes it: as the meat cooks the fat melts and bastes it, and what is left turns crisp and golden. It is seasoned with nothing but coarse salt, and is cooked hot and quickly to medium-rare, then sliced thin against the grain. It is served with vinagrete, a fresh salsa of tomato, onion and pepper in vinegar and oil, whose sharpness cuts the richness of the meat, and with farofa.

  • Do not trim the fat cap. It bastes the meat and crisps into the best part.
  • Salt with coarse salt only. Fine salt dissolves into the surface and makes it too salty.
  • Slice against the grain, thin. Along the grain the meat is chewy.

item.title: Farofa
item.description: Farofa: toasted cassava flour fried in butter with bacon, onion, garlic and egg until golden, crisp and sandy. The Brazilian side for barbecue and beans.
item.content:encoded:
Farofa is toasted cassava flour, fried in fat with whatever is nearby, and it sits on every Brazilian table beside rice, beans and grilled meat. It is a texture more than a flavour: dry, sandy and lightly crisp, it soaks up juices from the meat and the bean broth, and gives the plate something to crunch against. The cassava flour, farinha de mandioca torrada, is already toasted, and the cooking in butter only flavours it and dries it a little more. The garnish is chosen to suit the meal, bacon and egg in this version, called farofa de ovos, and it is added in stages, since the flour goes in last and is stirred until golden.

  • Use toasted cassava flour, sold as farinha de mandioca torrada. Raw cassava flour is different and does not work here.
  • Add the flour gradually. It soaks up the fat and needs stirring to stay loose.
  • Add the salt at the end. Bacon is salty and the amount varies.

item.title: Bolo de Cenoura
item.description: Bolo de cenoura: Brazil's bright orange carrot cake, blended in a blender for a moist crumb and covered in a glossy hot chocolate glaze. Serves 12.
item.content:encoded:
Bolo de cenoura is the carrot cake of Brazil, and it has nothing in common with the American cake of that name apart from the carrots: no spice, no nuts, no cream cheese, but a light, moist, bright orange sponge, covered in a chocolate glaze that is poured on while it is hot and sets into a thin, fudgy shell. The carrots are blended raw with the eggs and oil until they are a smooth, orange purée, so there are no shreds in the crumb, and the cake is tender and even. The glaze is a simple mixture of butter, cocoa, sugar and milk, boiled for three minutes, and it must be poured over the cake while both are warm.

  • Blend the carrots until there are no shreds. The crumb should be smooth.
  • Pour the glaze over the cake while it is warm, and while the glaze is hot. It sets in a thin, glossy layer.
  • Do not overmix once the flour is in. Fold until it just comes together.

item.title: Quindim
item.description: Quindim: small, glossy Brazilian custards of egg yolks, sugar, butter and coconut, baked in a water bath and turned out with a layer of coconut on top.
item.content:encoded:
Quindim is a Brazilian dessert of egg yolks, sugar and coconut, a golden, glossy little custard that is famous for its colour, an intense yellow that comes from twelve egg yolks and nothing else. It descends from the egg-yolk sweets of Portuguese convent kitchens, and Brazil added the coconut. It is baked in a water bath, which cooks it gently, and it separates as it bakes into two layers, a firm, chewy coconut layer that ends up on top when it is turned out, and a smooth, shiny custard underneath. The moulds are greased and dusted with sugar so the quindim releases cleanly, and the mixture is stirred, not whisked, so no bubbles form.

  • Stir the yolks, do not whisk. Foam makes the surface pitted instead of glossy.
  • Bake in a water bath so the custard cooks gently and stays smooth.
  • Cool them completely before turning out. Warm quindim is too soft to unmould.

item.title: Choripán
item.description: Choripán: a grilled fresh pork chorizo split in a crusty roll and loaded with a garlicky parsley and oregano chimichurri. The Argentine barbecue sandwich.
item.content:encoded:
The choripán is the Argentine barbecue sandwich, a whole grilled chorizo in a crusty roll with chimichurri, and it is eaten while the rest of the asado is still cooking, at football grounds and at street stalls across the country. The chorizo is the fresh, uncured kind, made of pork and fat, and it is grilled slowly, so it stays juicy inside. It is then split, or butterflied, and finished on the grill, so that the cut side browns. The chimichurri is the whole point. It is a sharp, garlicky mix of parsley, oregano, vinegar and oil, and it needs at least 30 minutes to soften the garlic and blend the flavours. Spoon it on generously, since the bread will soak it up.

  • Use fresh chorizo, not the cured Spanish kind. It has to be cooked through.
  • Cook over moderate heat so the sausage is cooked in the middle before the skin burns.
  • Make the chimichurri ahead. It improves for a day.

item.title: Medialunas
item.description: Medialunas: sweet, flaky Argentine crescent rolls made from a butter-layered yeast dough and brushed with sugar syrup while hot. Best with strong coffee.
item.content:encoded:
A medialuna, which means half moon, is the Argentine croissant: smaller, sweeter and softer than the French one, brushed with a sugar syrup as soon as it leaves the oven, and eaten with coffee, at breakfast or in the afternoon, in every café in the country. The dough is a sweet, enriched yeast dough, and it is layered with butter in two folds, not the dozens of turns of a French croissant, so it is easier and gives a tender, flaky crumb, not a shattering one. The rests are important: the chill between the folds stops the butter melting into the dough, and the final rise makes the crescents puffy. The syrup gives the shine and keeps them soft.

  • Chill the dough between folds. If it is warm, the butter melts into it and the layers are lost.
  • Brush the syrup on while the medialunas are still hot. It soaks in and gives the shine.
  • Do not skimp on the final rise. It is what makes them light.

item.title: Arepa de Choclo
item.description: Arepa de choclo: a thick Colombian sweet corn pancake of blended fresh sweetcorn and cornmeal, griddled in butter until golden and folded round melted cheese.
item.content:encoded:
The arepa de choclo is a Colombian arepa made with fresh sweet corn rather than corn flour, and it is more like a thick, tender pancake than the dense, round arepa of Venezuela and the rest of Colombia. The kernels are blended to a coarse purée and mixed with a little cornmeal, sugar and butter, which gives a sweet, soft batter with plenty of texture, and it is cooked on a buttered griddle until it forms a golden crust. It is sold from street carts and bakeries across the Andes, folded around a slice of salty white cheese that melts into it. The sweet corn, the butter and the salty cheese are a natural balance.

  • Leave some texture in the corn. A perfectly smooth purée makes a gummy arepa.
  • Cook over medium, not high, heat. High heat browns the outside before the middle sets.
  • Use a salty, melting cheese. The sweetness of the corn needs it.

item.title: Sancocho de Gallina
item.description: Sancocho de gallina: a big Colombian soup of chicken simmered with green plantain, yuca, potatoes and corn on the cob, finished with coriander and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Sancocho is the soup of the Colombian weekend, the meal of family gatherings and river-bank picnics, and it is cooked in one big pot with chicken, or a hen, green plantain, yuca and potatoes, with corn on the cob, in a broth flavoured with garlic, spring onion, cumin and coriander. It is a soup of starches, and each is added at a different time so that it cooks without falling apart: the plantain and yuca, which take longest, go in first, and the potato and corn go in later. The plantain and the yuca dissolve slightly into the broth and thicken it. It is served in deep bowls with rice, avocado and hot sauce on the side.

  • Add the vegetables in stages. The plantain and yuca take much longer than the potato.
  • Skim the foam early. It keeps the broth clear.
  • Green plantains hold their shape. Ripe ones dissolve.

item.title: Empanadas de Pino
item.description: Empanadas de pino: large Chilean baked empanadas filled with spiced beef and lots of onion, a slice of egg, an olive and raisins. The national snack of Chile.
item.content:encoded:
The empanada de pino is the national empanada of Chile, a large half-moon pastry filled with a mixture called pino, which is beef and a great deal of onion, cooked slowly with cumin and paprika, and then studded with a slice of hard-boiled egg, an olive and a few raisins. The onions are the secret. There is as much onion as meat, and they are cooked until they are soft and sweet, which makes the filling moist and rich. The sweet raisin and salty olive are what mark it as Chilean. The pastry is soft and buttery, more like a bread than a shortcrust, and it is baked, not fried, until it is golden. The filling must be cool before it goes in the dough.

  • Cook the onions until they are sweet and soft. Undercooked onion makes a sharp filling.
  • Cool the filling before you fill. Warm pino melts the dough and makes it hard to seal.
  • Do not overfill. The pastry splits in the oven if the filling is too full.

item.title: Picadillo
item.description: Cuban picadillo: minced beef simmered with tomato, olives, raisins and capers until thick and glossy, sweet, salty and tangy. Serve over white rice.
item.content:encoded:
Picadillo is the Cuban home-cooking classic of minced beef, cooked with onion, pepper and garlic and simmered with tomato, and it is defined by three ingredients that do not usually appear together: green olives, raisins and capers. Between them they make the dish sweet, salty and tangy at once, and it is a legacy of Spanish cooking, where the same mixture of sweet and salt is found in old meat dishes. The beef is browned well first, so the flavour is deep, and then simmered until the sauce is thick and clings to the meat. It is served over white rice, often with black beans, fried plantains, or a fried egg on top.

  • Brown the beef properly, on a high heat. Grey, steamed beef gives a flat picadillo.
  • Add the olives and raisins late so they keep their shape and bite.
  • It should be thick, not soupy. Simmer it a little longer if it is loose.

item.title: Moros y Cristianos
item.description: Moros y cristianos: Cuban black beans and white rice cooked together in one pot with bacon, onion, pepper, garlic and cumin. The classic Cuban side dish.
item.content:encoded:
Moros y cristianos, Moors and Christians, is the Cuban dish of black beans and white rice cooked together in the same pot, and it is named for the two peoples of medieval Spain, the dark Moors and the pale Christians. Unlike rice served next to beans, the rice here cooks in the bean liquid, so every grain is grey-black and flavoured by them, speckled with the whole beans. It starts with a sofrito of bacon, onion, green pepper and garlic, with cumin and oregano, and a splash of vinegar at the end sharpens the whole pot. The lid stays on for 20 minutes without lifting, so that the rice steams properly, and it is left to stand for 10 minutes before it is fluffed.

  • Do not lift the lid while the rice cooks. The steam is what cooks it.
  • Use the bean liquid from the tins. It colours and flavours the rice.
  • Cook over the lowest heat. High heat burns the bottom before the top is done.

item.title: Pernil
item.description: Pernil: a Puerto Rican pork shoulder marinated in garlic, oregano and citrus, roasted slowly until it pulls apart and finished hot for crackling skin.
item.content:encoded:
Pernil is the Puerto Rican roast pork shoulder, the centrepiece of Christmas and of every big family celebration on the island, and it is defined by two things: a garlic-and-oregano marinade called adobo, and the crackling, the crisp, golden skin called cuerito, which people fight over. The marinade is pushed into holes cut all over the meat, so the seasoning goes deep, and the pork is left overnight in the fridge. It roasts covered at a low temperature for hours, until the meat is tender enough to pull with a fork, and the foil comes off for a final blast of heat that crisps the skin. The sour orange used on the island is replaced here by orange and lime juice.

  • Push the adobo deep into the meat. Rubbing it on the surface flavours only the crust.
  • Roast covered for the first four hours, so the meat steams tender in its own juice.
  • Dry the skin with paper towels before the final blast. Damp skin will not crackle.

item.title: Mofongo
item.description: Mofongo: fried green plantains mashed with garlic, olive oil and crisp pork crackling, shaped into domes and served with warm broth. A Puerto Rican classic.
item.content:encoded:
Mofongo is a Puerto Rican dish of fried green plantains, mashed while hot with garlic, olive oil and pork crackling, and shaped into a ball or dome, and it is a descendant of the West African fufu that came to the Caribbean with enslaved cooks. It is a dish of contrast. The plantain is starchy, not sweet, and the garlic and olive oil give it a rich, pungent flavour, while the crackling adds salt and crunch. The plantain chunks are fried only until they are pale and tender, and never brown, because a browned plantain is hard to mash and makes a dry mofongo. It is served with a cup of warm broth, which is spooned over to moisten it, and is often filled with shrimp or chicken.

  • Use green plantains, not yellow. Ripe ones are sweet and sticky, not starchy.
  • Mash the plantain while it is hot. Cold plantain will not come together.
  • Add the broth a spoonful at a time. Too much makes it soggy.

item.title: Arroz con Gandules
item.description: Arroz con gandules: Puerto Rico's national dish of rice and pigeon peas, cooked with sofrito, ham and olives in one pot, with a crisp bottom layer.
item.content:encoded:
Arroz con gandules, rice with pigeon peas, is Puerto Rico's national dish, served at Christmas and every family gathering, and it is built on sofrito, the blend of green pepper, onion, garlic and coriander that is the base of most Puerto Rican cooking. The sofrito is fried with diced ham, tomato paste and spices, the rice is toasted in it, and then everything cooks together in stock, with pigeon peas and green olives. The rice takes its colour from annatto, a yellow-orange seed, and its flavour from the fried base. The best part is the pegao, the layer of crisp golden rice that forms on the bottom of the pot and is scraped out and shared. The pot must not be stirred while it cooks.

  • Stir only once, after the liquid has boiled down. Stirring later makes the rice sticky.
  • Cook the sofrito until the liquid has gone. Wet sofrito makes soggy rice.
  • Scrape the pegao from the bottom of the pot and serve it. It is the best part.

item.title: Tostones
item.description: Tostones: green plantain slices fried, smashed flat and fried again until crisp and golden, salted and served with a garlic and lime mojo for dipping.
item.content:encoded:
Tostones are green plantains that are fried twice: the first time to cook them through and soften them, and the second, after being smashed flat, to crisp them into golden, salted discs. They are a staple of Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Cuba and much of the Caribbean and Latin America, where they are served as a snack, an appetiser or a side dish with rice and beans, and they are eaten hot, since a cold tostone goes hard. The plantains must be green and firm, so they are starchy and not sweet, and the first fry is gentle. The garlic mojo is the dip: raw garlic, lime and olive oil, and it is what makes them addictive.

  • Use green plantains. Yellow ones with black spots make sweet, soft maduros instead.
  • Smash them while they are still warm. Cold plantain cracks.
  • Fry twice, at two temperatures. The first fry cooks them and the second crisps them.

item.title: Coquito
item.description: Coquito: the Puerto Rican Christmas drink of coconut milk, cream of coconut, condensed and evaporated milk, rum and cinnamon, blended and chilled.
item.content:encoded:
Coquito is the Christmas drink of Puerto Rico, a chilled, creamy blend of coconut, milk and rum, and it is often called the Puerto Rican coconut eggnog, although the classic version has no eggs. It is sweetened with condensed milk and cream of coconut, enriched with evaporated milk and coconut milk, and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg and vanilla, and it is made in a blender in ten minutes. It needs at least four hours in the fridge, so that the flavours can blend and it can turn cold and thick. Coquito is poured into small glasses, since it is very rich, and is made in large batches and given away in bottles, each family having its own recipe.

  • Shake the coquito before you pour it. The coconut fat settles at the top when it is cold.
  • Use cream of coconut, the sweet syrupy kind, not coconut cream. It is what gives coquito its body.
  • Taste it before chilling. It is sweeter than most people expect, and the rum can be adjusted.

item.title: Jamaican Oxtail Stew
item.description: Jamaican oxtail stew: oxtail seasoned with allspice, thyme and scotch bonnet, browned and braised for hours with butter beans in a rich, glossy dark gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Oxtail stew is one of the great dishes of Jamaica, a dark, glossy braise of oxtail and butter beans, seasoned with allspice, thyme, spring onion and scotch bonnet, and eaten with rice and peas. Oxtail is a cut of bone and connective tissue, and it needs a long, gentle cook, which turns the collagen into gelatine and gives the gravy its body and stickiness. The meat is seasoned for at least four hours, browned in caramelised sugar, which gives the stew its deep colour, and then simmered for three hours until it is falling from the bone. The scotch bonnet goes in whole, so it gives fragrance and only a little heat, and the butter beans, added near the end, thicken the stew.

  • Season the oxtail ahead. Four hours or overnight makes a big difference.
  • Brown it well in the caramelised sugar. That is where the dark colour comes from.
  • Leave the scotch bonnet whole and do not pierce it, or the stew will be very hot.

item.title: Escovitch Fish
item.description: Jamaican escovitch fish: whole snapper fried until crisp and covered with a hot vinegar pickle of onion, carrot, pepper and scotch bonnet. Good hot or cold.
item.content:encoded:
Escovitch fish is a Jamaican dish of whole fried fish, usually red snapper, covered with a hot pickle of onion, carrot, pepper and scotch bonnet in vinegar, and it descends from the Spanish escabeche, a way of preserving fried fish in vinegar. The Jamaican version is spiced with allspice and thyme and eaten fresh, and the fish is served on Sundays, at Easter, and by the roadside at beach shacks with bammy or festival. The fish is fried until the skin is crisp, and the pickle is poured over it while both are hot, so that the vinegar sinks into the flesh without turning the crust soggy. It can be eaten hot, but is just as good served at room temperature the next day.

  • Dry the fish thoroughly. Wet fish steams and the skin does not crisp.
  • Pour the pickle over while it is hot. It seeps into the fish without wetting the crust.
  • Slice the scotch bonnet finely and seed it for a fragrant, not fiery, pickle.

item.title: Chiles en Nogada
item.description: Chiles en nogada: roasted poblanos stuffed with a spiced fruit and meat picadillo, under a cool walnut cream sauce with pomegranate seeds and parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Chiles en nogada is a showpiece of Mexican cooking, a roasted poblano chile stuffed with a picadillo of minced pork and beef, apple, pear, raisins and almonds, and covered in a cool, white walnut sauce, the nogada, with pomegranate seeds and parsley on top, so that it wears the green, white and red of the Mexican flag. It comes from Puebla, and is served there in late summer and early autumn, when walnuts and pomegranates are in season. The dish balances sweet, savoury and rich: the fruit in the filling is sweet, the chile is smoky, the walnut sauce is creamy and mild. The chiles are charred and sweated in a covered bowl so that their skins slide off, and the filling is made ahead.

  • Steam the charred chiles in a covered bowl. The skins slide off easily afterwards.
  • Cook the filling until it is almost dry. A wet filling makes the chile burst.
  • Serve the sauce cool, on warm chiles. It is not meant to be hot.

item.title: Pan de Muerto
item.description: Pan de muerto: a soft, buttery Mexican sweet bread scented with orange and aniseed, shaped with bone-like strips on top, brushed with butter and sugared.
item.content:encoded:
Pan de muerto, the bread of the dead, is the sweet bread that Mexican families bake for the Day of the Dead, on 1 and 2 November, and lay on the altars for those who have died. Each loaf is a round, for the cycle of life and death, with strips of dough laid across the top to represent bones, and a small ball in the centre for the skull. The dough is enriched with butter and eggs and scented with orange zest and aniseed, so it is soft, rich and fragrant, and the loaves are brushed with melted butter and rolled in sugar as soon as they come out of the oven. It is a bread to eat with hot chocolate, on the day itself.

  • Add the butter gradually and knead until the dough is silky. It makes the crumb soft.
  • Use orange blossom water sparingly. A little perfumes the whole loaf.
  • Brush with butter and roll in sugar while the bread is warm, so the sugar sticks.

item.title: Akara
item.description: Akara: Nigerian black-eyed pea fritters of skinned, blended beans whipped with onion and chilli and deep-fried until golden, crisp outside and fluffy inside.
item.content:encoded:
Akara is the Nigerian bean fritter, made from black-eyed peas that have been soaked, skinned, blended with onion and chilli and whipped until light, and then dropped into hot oil to form golden balls that are crisp outside and fluffy inside. It is sold at dawn from roadside stalls in Nigeria and across West Africa, and is also eaten in Brazil as acarajé, where the recipe travelled with enslaved cooks. Two steps decide whether it works. The skins must be rubbed off, since they make the akara heavy and gritty, and the paste must be whipped for several minutes, since the air incorporated is what makes it puff. It is eaten hot, with pap (a maize porridge), bread or a pepper sauce.

  • Rub off as many of the skins as you can. They make the fritters heavy and dark.
  • Beat the paste until it is pale and light. The trapped air is what makes akara fluffy.
  • Keep the batter thick. If it is thin the fritters spread and soak up oil.

item.title: Efo Riro
item.description: Efo riro: a rich Nigerian spinach stew built on a fried red pepper and scotch bonnet base with palm oil, beef, smoked fish and crayfish. Serve with rice.
item.content:encoded:
Efo riro is a Yoruba stew of leafy greens, and the name means stirred greens. It is one of the most popular dishes in Nigeria, cooked at weddings and on Sundays. The greens, spinach here, are stirred into a thick base of red pepper, scotch bonnet and onion that has been blended and cooked down in palm oil until the water has evaporated and the sauce has darkened, and this cooking of the pepper base is the most important step. The stew is enriched with beef, smoked fish and ground dried crayfish, which give it a deep, savoury flavour, and it is cooked without a lid, so that the spinach does not release too much water. It is eaten with pounded yam, eba or rice.

  • Cook the pepper purée until it is dry and dark. A watery base makes a watery stew.
  • Cook the stew without a lid once the spinach goes in, or it will turn to soup.
  • Squeeze frozen spinach dry before adding it.

item.title: Chin Chin
item.description: Chin chin: crunchy, lightly sweet Nigerian fried dough cubes flavoured with nutmeg, cut small and fried until golden. A West African party snack.
item.content:encoded:
Chin chin is a Nigerian snack of small pieces of dough, fried until they are crisp and golden, and it is on the table at every party, wedding and Christmas gathering, as well as being sold in packets across West Africa. It is a stiff dough of flour, sugar, butter, egg and milk, spiced with nutmeg, and it is rolled thin and cut into small squares, since the size decides the crunch. Thin, small pieces fry through completely and stay crisp for weeks, and thick pieces are hard and doughy in the middle. The dough must be stiff, so there is only just enough milk to bring it together, and the oil should be moderately hot, about 170°C, so that the chin chin cooks through before it browns.

  • Keep the dough stiff. Soft dough makes greasy chin chin that goes soft.
  • Cut the pieces small and even. They then fry at the same speed.
  • Fry at a moderate 170°C. Hotter oil browns the outside while the middle stays raw.

item.title: Nigerian Meat Pie
item.description: Nigerian meat pie: golden, flaky hand pies filled with curry-spiced minced beef, diced potato and carrot in a thick gravy. A West African bakery favourite.
item.content:encoded:
The Nigerian meat pie is a hand-sized pie of flaky, buttery pastry with a filling of minced beef, diced potato and carrot, seasoned with curry powder and thyme, and it is sold from every bakery, at parties, and in school lunchboxes. It came from British baking, and the Nigerian version has taken on its own flavour. The vegetables are diced very small so that the filling is even, and it is thickened with a flour paste until it is dry enough to stay inside the pastry. The dough is a rubbed-in one with plenty of butter, and cold, so it bakes into layers. The filling must be completely cool before the pies are filled, or the pastry melts.

  • Dice the potato and carrot very small. Big pieces make the filling lumpy and split the pastry.
  • Cool the filling completely. Warm filling makes the pastry greasy and hard to seal.
  • Keep the butter cold. It makes the layers flaky.

item.title: Red Red
item.description: Red red: a Ghanaian stew of black-eyed peas in a palm oil, tomato and ginger sauce, served with sweet fried ripe plantain. Named for its two red ingredients.
item.content:encoded:
Red red is a Ghanaian dish of black-eyed peas in a red sauce, and the name refers to the two red things that give it its colour, the palm oil and the tomato, and to the ripe plantains that are fried until red-gold and eaten alongside. It is served at street stalls throughout the country and is one of the most loved vegetarian dishes of West Africa. The peas are simmered until soft, and the sauce is made by frying onion, ginger and tomato in palm oil, and then the two are combined and simmered, so that the peas take up the flavour. The plantain is fried until caramelised, and the sweetness of it against the spicy, earthy beans is the point of the dish.

  • Use very ripe plantains, with black skins. They caramelise and are sweet.
  • Leave the scotch bonnet whole for flavour without much heat.
  • Palm oil gives the dish its colour and flavour, but vegetable oil with a little paprika works.

item.title: Shito
item.description: Shito: Ghana's dark, fiery black pepper sauce of onion, tomato, chilli, ginger and dried shrimp, cooked slowly in oil until deeply savoury. Keeps for weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Shito is Ghana's essential condiment, a dark, oily sauce of onion, tomato, ginger, chilli and dried shrimp that is fried slowly in oil until the ingredients have dissolved into a thick, glossy, deeply savoury paste, and it is spooned onto rice, kenkey, fried plantain, fried fish, eggs and bread. Shito is the Ga word for pepper, and the sauce is black in colour from the long frying. The oil is what keeps it, since the sauce is sealed under a layer of it, and a good shito keeps for weeks. The cooking is slow and needs stirring, since it burns easily, and it is finished when the oil has separated from the paste and it has darkened to the colour of chocolate.

  • Cook it on low heat and stir often. The paste catches on the bottom and burns.
  • Use plenty of oil and keep the shito under it. The oil keeps air off it, but the jar still belongs in the fridge.
  • Use a clean, dry spoon each time. Water or crumbs make it spoil.

item.title: Beef Tibs
item.description: Beef tibs: cubes of beef seared hot in spiced butter with onion, garlic, ginger, green chilli and berbere until browned. Serve with injera.
item.content:encoded:
Tibs is one of the most common dishes in an Ethiopian restaurant, cubes of beef sautéed in a hot pan with onion and spices, and eaten with injera, the sour flatbread. It is a fast dish, unlike the slow stews, or wats, that are the core of the cuisine, and it can be cooked in 20 minutes. It relies on three things. The beef is seared hard in batches, so it browns and does not steam, the fat is niter kibbeh, a butter cooked with spices, or ghee as a substitute, and the seasoning is berbere, the deep red spice blend of chilli, fenugreek, coriander and others. Rosemary is a common addition, and green chillies are sliced in for freshness.

  • Cook the beef in two batches. A crowded pan steams it.
  • Do not cook it too long. Tibs is best a little pink in the middle.
  • No niter kibbeh? Use ghee with a pinch each of cardamom and turmeric.

item.title: Sosaties
item.description: Sosaties: Cape Malay lamb kebabs marinated in a curry, apricot jam and vinegar sauce, threaded with dried apricots and onion and grilled over a fire.
item.content:encoded:
Sosaties are the kebabs of the Cape Malay community of South Africa, cubes of lamb marinated in a sweet and sour curry sauce, threaded onto skewers with dried apricots and onions, and grilled over the coals at a braai, the South African barbecue. The marinade is what makes them: onions softened with curry powder, coriander and turmeric, sharpened with vinegar and sweetened with apricot jam, which gives the lamb a sticky, caramelised crust. The dish reflects the food brought to the Cape by Malay and Indonesian slaves and settlers in the 17th century, with its pairing of spice and fruit. The lamb needs eight hours in the marinade, and the leftover marinade is boiled into a sauce.

  • Marinate the lamb for at least 8 hours. The sauce needs time to soften the meat.
  • Cut the lamb into even cubes so that it cooks at the same rate.
  • Boil the leftover marinade before using it as a sauce. It has been in contact with raw meat.

item.title: Koeksisters
item.description: Koeksisters: plaited strips of dough deep-fried until golden and plunged into ice-cold, spiced sugar syrup, so they are crisp outside and syrupy inside.
item.content:encoded:
The koeksister is the sweet of the Afrikaner kitchen, a plait of dough that is fried and then dropped into a syrup, and it is one of the best-known South African sweets. It is at its best when eaten the same day, crisp on the outside and running with syrup inside. The whole recipe depends on temperature. The syrup must be ice cold, so that when the hot koeksister goes in the dough absorbs it quickly, without going soggy, and the koeksister must be hot from the fryer, so that its surface is sealed and crisp. The syrup is boiled first with cinnamon and ginger and then chilled for at least four hours, and it is kept on ice while the dough is being fried.

  • Keep the syrup ice cold. Warm syrup makes the koeksisters soggy instead of crisp.
  • Put the hot koeksisters in the syrup straight from the oil. The temperature difference is what makes them crisp.
  • Pinch the ends of the plait firmly so it does not unravel in the oil.

item.title: Bastilla
item.description: Bastilla: a Moroccan pie of saffron and ginger chicken, soft egg and cinnamon almonds in crisp buttered filo, dusted with icing sugar. A feast dish.
item.content:encoded:
Bastilla, also spelled pastilla, is the great pie of Morocco, made for weddings and feasts, and it is famous for its contradiction: a pie of savoury, saffron-and-ginger chicken and soft egg, layered with almonds cooked with sugar and cinnamon, in crisp pastry that is dusted with icing sugar and cinnamon. It is sweet and savoury at once, a mixture of Andalusian and Berber cooking. It is built in stages: the chicken is braised until it falls apart, the sauce is boiled down and thickened with egg, the almonds are fried and sweetened, and the pastry, a thin, crisp warqa in Morocco and filo elsewhere, is brushed with butter and layered. It is baked until golden and crisp and served hot.

  • Boil the sauce down until it is thick before adding the egg. Too much liquid makes the pastry soggy.
  • Cool the filling before you assemble the pie. A hot filling makes the filo limp.
  • Butter every sheet of filo, and keep the unused sheets under a damp cloth.

item.title: Baghrir
item.description: Baghrir: Moroccan semolina and yeast pancakes cooked on one side only, so they are covered in tiny holes that soak up warm honey and butter. Serves four.
item.content:encoded:
Baghrir is the Moroccan pancake with a thousand holes, a soft, spongy, semolina pancake that is cooked on one side only, so that the top surface is covered in tiny bubbles that burst and leave small, open holes, which is why the pancake is so good at absorbing warm honey and butter. It is a breakfast and tea-time pancake, sold at street stalls and made at home, and it is eaten warm. The batter is thin, and it is blended for a couple of minutes so that it is smooth and frothy, and then left to stand for half an hour, so that the yeast and baking powder can start working. It is cooked over medium heat, without flipping, until the surface is dry.

  • Cook one side only. The holes form on the side that is not touched by the pan.
  • Do not grease the pan. A dry pan gives the best holes.
  • Lay the finished pancakes side by side, not stacked. Stacking makes them soggy.

item.title: Thieboudienne
item.description: Thieboudienne: the national dish of Senegal, fish stuffed with parsley, garlic and chilli, stewed in tomato sauce with vegetables and served on red rice.
item.content:encoded:
Thieboudienne, pronounced cheb-oo-jen, is the national dish of Senegal, a one-pot feast of fish and rice that is usually cooked for a family meal and served on one big platter, from which everyone eats. It is a dish of many parts: fish steaks stuffed with a paste of parsley, garlic and chilli called rof, a tomato sauce simmered with cassava, carrot, cabbage, aubergine and sweet potato, and rice that is cooked in the sauce, so that it turns red and takes on all the flavours. It is said to have been created in the city of Saint-Louis in the 19th century. Everything is cooked in stages in the same pot, and the fish and vegetables are lifted out when they are done, and the rice is cooked in what is left.

  • Stuff the fish deeply. The parsley paste seasons it from the inside.
  • Lift the fish out as soon as it is cooked. It falls apart if it stays in the sauce.
  • Cook the rice in the flavoured sauce, not in water. That is what makes it thieboudienne.

item.title: Poulet Yassa
item.description: Poulet yassa: Senegalese chicken marinated in lemon juice, mustard and lots of onions, browned, and simmered until the onions melt into a sharp, sweet sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Poulet yassa is one of the great dishes of West Africa, a Senegalese dish of chicken cooked in a sauce of onions, lemon and mustard, and it comes from the Casamance region in the south. It is remarkable for its mountain of onions, about the weight of the chicken, which are marinated with lemon juice and mustard, and cooked slowly until they collapse into a thick, sweet and sour sauce. The chicken is marinated for at least four hours, so that the lemon and mustard flavour the meat, and is then browned under a hot grill before it goes into the pot, so it has some colour and flavour of its own. Scotch bonnet gives heat, and green olives are often added. It is served over white rice.

  • Use a lot of onion. They cook down to a fraction and are the sauce.
  • Brown the chicken before simmering it. It gives the dish a deeper flavour.
  • Leave the scotch bonnet whole and take it out before serving.

item.title: Mafé
item.description: Mafé: a rich West African stew of beef, sweet potato, carrot and cabbage in a thick peanut and tomato sauce, simmered until tender. Serve over rice.
item.content:encoded:
Mafé, also written maafe or mafe, is the peanut stew of West Africa, and it is eaten across Senegal, Mali, The Gambia and Guinea, made with beef, lamb or chicken and whatever vegetables are in the market. Peanuts, native to South America, arrived in Africa in the 16th century and became one of its staple crops, and here they thicken the sauce and give it a deep, nutty flavour. The peanut butter must be plain and unsweetened, and it is whisked into some warm stock before it is added, so that it does not lump. The stew is cooked slowly, so that the meat is tender, and the vegetables are added in stages, so that they hold their shape. It is served over rice or with couscous.

  • Use plain peanut butter with no sugar or salt. Sweetened peanut butter makes the stew sweet.
  • Whisk the peanut butter into warm stock before adding it. It goes in without lumps.
  • Stir now and then. The peanut sauce catches on the bottom of the pot.

item.title: Githeri
item.description: Githeri: the everyday Kenyan stew of maize and beans simmered with tomato, onion, potato and carrot, and flavoured with curry powder and coriander.
item.content:encoded:
Githeri is one of the staple dishes of Kenya, a stew of maize and beans that comes from the Kikuyu people of the central highlands, and it is eaten daily in homes, schools and workplaces across the country. In its simplest form it is only the two ingredients boiled together, and it is often made in a very large pot, since it feeds a crowd cheaply. Maize and beans together are a complete protein, which is why they have been eaten together for thousands of years. In this version they are simmered with tomato, onion, potato and carrot, and given flavour with a little curry powder and turmeric. It is made with tinned beans and corn, so it is ready in about an hour.

  • Mash a few of the beans against the side of the pot. It thickens the stew.
  • Cook the tomatoes down into a sauce before adding the liquid.
  • Use dried beans and maize if you have them. Soak overnight and simmer for 1 to 2 hours first.

item.title: Zereshk Polo ba Morgh
item.description: Zereshk polo ba morgh: Persian saffron chicken with steamed basmati rice, crowned with sweet-sour barberries fried in butter and slivered pistachios.
item.content:encoded:
Zereshk polo ba morgh is one of the most loved dishes in Persian cooking, served at weddings and family celebrations: saffron chicken alongside steamed rice that is scattered with zereshk, dried barberries, which are small, ruby-red and sharply tart. The barberries are fried for a minute in butter with sugar, which softens their sourness into something sweet and sharp, and they are the jewels of the dish. The rice is Persian steamed rice: it is parboiled in salted water, drained, and steamed with a tea towel wrapped round the lid, which absorbs the condensation and keeps the grains dry and separate, and it forms a golden crust on the bottom, called tahdig. The chicken is stewed with onion and saffron until it is tender.

  • Rinse the barberries briefly and cook them for no more than 2 minutes. They burn and turn bitter.
  • Wrap the lid in a tea towel. It absorbs steam so the rice stays fluffy.
  • Do not stir the rice once it is steaming. The crust forms undisturbed.

item.title: Khoresh Gheimeh
item.description: Khoresh gheimeh: a Persian stew of lamb, yellow split peas, tomato and dried limes with saffron and cinnamon, topped with crisp fried potato sticks.
item.content:encoded:
Khoresh gheimeh is a Persian stew of lamb and yellow split peas, served at family gatherings, at religious ceremonies and at funerals, and it is a dish with a distinctive flavour: earthy, tangy and lightly sweet, from dried limes, saffron and cinnamon, in a sauce of tomato and onion. The dried limes, limoo amani, are what make it Persian. They are simmered whole, so that they release a sour, slightly bitter, fermented flavour into the stew, and they should be pierced so that the liquid gets in. The split peas are not soaked, but are simmered until tender, so that they thicken the sauce, and the stew is served over rice, topped with thin, crisp French-fry-style potatoes.

  • Pierce the dried limes. They then release their flavour into the stew.
  • Take out the limes if the stew becomes too sour. They can turn bitter if left too long.
  • Fry the potatoes just before serving. They go soft if they wait.

item.title: Persian Love Cake
item.description: Persian love cake: a moist ground almond cake scented with cardamom, orange, saffron and rose water, with a rose glaze, pistachios and dried rose petals.
item.content:encoded:
Persian love cake is a modern classic, a moist, fragrant cake of ground almonds, scented with cardamom, orange zest, saffron and rose water, and it is named after the story that it was baked to win someone's heart. It is not a traditional Iranian cake, but a dessert that was built from Persian flavours, and it has become popular across the world. Ground almonds give it a dense, moist, slightly chewy crumb, and a little flour and yoghurt keep it light. The flavours should be balanced so none of them dominates: the rose water is added a tablespoon at a time, since too much makes the cake taste of soap. It is finished with a thin glaze, pistachios and rose petals.

  • Add the rose water a tablespoon at a time and taste. Too much tastes of soap.
  • Use ground almonds, not almond flour that has been heavily blanched. The skins add flavour and moisture.
  • Cover with foil if the top browns too fast. The cake is dense and takes a while.

item.title: Faloodeh
item.description: Faloodeh: a Persian frozen dessert of thin rice noodles in a rose-scented sugar syrup, scraped into icy shards and served with a squeeze of lime.
item.content:encoded:
Faloodeh is one of the oldest frozen desserts in the world, said to date from about 400 BC in Shiraz, in Iran, a granita of thin starch noodles in a rose-scented sugar syrup. The noodles are what make it unusual: they freeze into the ice and give it a chewy, slippery texture against the crisp ice crystals, and rose water gives it its perfume. It is served with a squeeze of lime juice or a spoonful of sour cherry syrup, to cut the sweetness, and it is eaten in the summer, from stalls that sell little else. It is made without a machine. The mixture is frozen in a shallow dish and scraped with a fork at intervals to break up the ice into fine flakes.

  • Scrape the ice with a fork at regular intervals. It gives fine flakes rather than a solid block.
  • Rinse the noodles well. Starch on their surface makes the syrup cloudy.
  • Serve with lime. It cuts the sweetness and sharpens the flavour.

item.title: Satsivi
item.description: Satsivi: poached chicken in a rich Georgian walnut sauce spiced with coriander, fenugreek, cinnamon and garlic, served cold with pomegranate seeds.
item.content:encoded:
Satsivi is a Georgian dish of cold chicken in a thick, spiced walnut sauce, and it is the dish of the Georgian New Year table, prepared days ahead, which improves the flavour. The sauce is made from a great many walnuts, ground with garlic and spices such as coriander seed, fenugreek, cinnamon and cayenne, and thinned with the chicken cooking broth and a little vinegar to the consistency of double cream. It is heated gently, and never boiled, or it separates, and it is poured over the chicken and left to cool. The flavour is deep, nutty and warm, and slightly sharp from the vinegar. It is served at room temperature, scattered with pomegranate seeds and coriander, with bread, but not with rice.

  • Grind the walnuts until they release their oil. It gives the sauce its body.
  • Heat the sauce gently and do not let it boil. It splits.
  • Make it a day ahead. The flavours improve as it stands.

item.title: Badrijani Nigvzit
item.description: Badrijani nigvzit: fried aubergine slices spread with a spiced garlic and walnut paste, rolled up and finished with pomegranate seeds. A Georgian appetiser.
item.content:encoded:
Badrijani nigvzit, aubergine with walnuts, is one of the most popular starters of the Georgian table, and it is on the menu of every Georgian restaurant. It is made from slices of aubergine that are fried until they are soft and golden, spread with a paste of ground walnuts, garlic, vinegar and spices, and rolled up, so that each roll is a bite of creamy, nutty, garlicky filling in a soft, silky wrapper. It is served cold, topped with pomegranate seeds, whose tartness cuts the richness. The aubergine slices are salted first, to draw out their bitter juice, and dried well, because wet slices soak up oil, and the filling must be thick enough to hold in the roll.

  • Salt and dry the slices. Wet aubergine soaks up oil and the rolls turn greasy.
  • Keep the filling thick. A loose paste slides out of the rolls.
  • Cool the fried slices before rolling them, so the filling does not melt.

item.title: Simit
item.description: Simit: chewy Turkish bread rings dipped in grape molasses and rolled in sesame seeds, then baked until deep golden. The street bread of Istanbul.
item.content:encoded:
Simit is the bread of the streets of Istanbul, a thin ring of chewy, sesame-crusted bread, sold from carts on every corner, and eaten for breakfast with tea, with white cheese or spread with jam. The dough is a simple lean one, but the finish is what makes it: each ring is dipped in a thin solution of grape molasses, called pekmez, and rolled in sesame seeds, and the molasses gives it its deep golden colour and slightly sweet, caramel flavour as it bakes. The seeds are pressed on generously, so that the whole ring is covered. It is baked in a very hot oven, which gives a crisp, thin crust and a chewy inside. It is best warm from the oven, on the day it is made.

  • Coat the rings completely in sesame seeds. They give the crust its crunch and flavour.
  • Use a very hot oven. A cool one gives a pale, soft simit.
  • Date syrup or thin honey can replace the pekmez if you cannot find it.

item.title: Çılbır
item.description: Çılbır: Turkish poached eggs on cool garlic yoghurt, drizzled with sizzling red chilli and mint butter. A classic breakfast, served with crusty bread.
item.content:encoded:
Çılbır, pronounced chul-bur, is the Turkish dish of poached eggs on garlicky yoghurt with chilli butter, and it is one of the oldest recorded dishes in Turkish cooking, said to have been served in the kitchens of the Ottoman court. It is a dish of contrasts. The yoghurt is cool and sharp with garlic, the eggs are warm and soft, and the butter, melted and stirred with Aleppo pepper and dried mint just before serving, is hot, and it sizzles as it hits the yoghurt. The yoghurt should be at room temperature, since cold yoghurt cools the eggs, and the eggs must be fresh, so that the whites hold together in the water. It takes 20 minutes, and it needs crusty bread for the mopping.

  • Use very fresh eggs. Older eggs spread into wispy ribbons in the water.
  • Use room-temperature yoghurt. Cold yoghurt chills the eggs.
  • Heat the butter just to foaming. If it browns and burns, the spices turn bitter.

item.title: Kabuli Pulao
item.description: Kabuli pulao: Afghanistan's national dish of tender lamb and fragrant basmati rice cooked in lamb broth, topped with caramelised carrots, raisins and nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Kabuli pulao is the national dish of Afghanistan and it is served at every celebration: fragrant rice, coloured golden brown by the lamb broth in which it is cooked, with pieces of tender lamb, and a topping of sweet strips of carrot, plump raisins and nuts. It is a dish of contrasts. The rice is savoury and lightly spiced with cumin, cardamom and cinnamon, and the carrots, which are fried and then caramelised with sugar, and the raisins, are sweet, and the combination has made it famous. The rice is cooked in the broth from the lamb, and it goes into the pot at the point when the broth has reduced, so that there is just enough liquid, and it is then steamed under a tight lid.

  • Measure the broth. Too much makes soggy rice and too little leaves it hard.
  • Cover the pot with foil under the lid. It keeps in the steam.
  • Fry the carrots gently and caramelise them slowly. Fast heat burns the sugar.

item.title: Bolani
item.description: Bolani: thin, crisp Afghan flatbreads stuffed with a spiced potato and spring onion filling and pan-fried until golden. Eat them with chutney.
item.content:encoded:
Bolani is an Afghan stuffed flatbread, a thin round of dough folded around a savoury filling and fried until it is crisp and golden, and it is sold on the streets of Kabul and eaten at home for lunch or as an appetiser. The most common filling is potato, spiced with cumin, coriander and chilli, and lightened with spring onions and fresh coriander, and there are also fillings of pumpkin, leek and lentils. The dough is a simple flour and water dough with a little oil, and it is rested for an hour, so that it relaxes and can be rolled very thin, which is the secret of a crisp bolani. It is folded into a half moon, pressed to seal and fried in a little oil in a hot pan.

  • Roll the dough very thin. Thick bolani are doughy and not crisp.
  • Let the potato filling cool before you spread it, or it makes the dough soft.
  • Drain the potatoes well. Wet filling makes it hard to fold and seal.

item.title: Borani Banjan
item.description: Borani banjan: Afghan fried aubergine slices simmered in a spiced tomato sauce and covered with garlic and mint yoghurt. Serve with flatbread.
item.content:encoded:
Borani banjan is an Afghan dish of fried aubergine in a tomato sauce, covered with garlicky yoghurt, and it is served as a starter or a side dish, with flatbread, at meals and feasts. The layers are what make it. The aubergine is silky and rich from being fried, the tomato sauce is warm and lightly spiced with coriander and turmeric, and the yoghurt, flavoured with garlic and dried mint, is cool and sharp on top, so each mouthful has three temperatures and textures. The aubergine slices are salted for half an hour first, which draws out the moisture and bitterness, and reduces the amount of oil they absorb. It is served warm or at room temperature.

  • Salt the aubergine and rinse it. It removes bitterness and cuts the amount of oil it drinks.
  • Let the aubergine cool a little before adding the yoghurt. Hot aubergine makes the yoghurt split.
  • Serve warm or at room temperature, not cold.

item.title: Kathi Roll
item.description: Kathi roll: Kolkata street food of spiced grilled chicken, lemony onions and green chutney rolled in a paratha lined with a layer of cooked egg.
item.content:encoded:
The kathi roll is the street food of Kolkata: a paratha, lined with a thin layer of egg, wrapped around spiced kebab, sliced onions and green chutney, and served in a twist of paper so it can be eaten on the move. It is said to have been invented in the early 20th century at Nizam's in Kolkata, where kebabs were wrapped in paratha for customers who did not want to wait for a table. The bread is what makes it: a flaky, layered paratha, rolled thin and cooked on a hot griddle. Spiced chicken, marinated in yoghurt, ginger and garam masala, is fried until browned, and the onions are tossed with lemon juice and chaat masala, which lifts the whole roll. The egg goes on the pan first, and the paratha is pressed on top.

  • Roll the parathas very thin. Thick ones make a heavy, doughy roll.
  • Marinate the chicken for at least an hour. It makes it tender and flavourful.
  • Cook the paratha only part-way at first. It is finished on the egg.

item.title: Dum Aloo
item.description: Dum aloo: baby potatoes fried until golden and slow-cooked in a rich, red, spiced yoghurt and tomato gravy scented with fennel and ginger. Serve with naan.
item.content:encoded:
Dum aloo is a dish of small potatoes cooked in a rich, spiced gravy, and it is a favourite of Kashmir and Punjab, served at weddings and festivals and in restaurants throughout India. Dum means steam-cooking in a sealed pot, and the potatoes finish cooking that way, so they absorb the gravy. The potatoes are boiled, peeled and pricked all over with a fork, so that the sauce goes right in, and fried until they are golden and crisp on the outside. The gravy is a mixture of fried onion, tomato and yoghurt, flavoured with fennel, ginger and Kashmiri chilli, which gives it a deep red colour without much heat. The yoghurt is whisked and added slowly over low heat, so that it does not split.

  • Prick the potatoes all over. The gravy then goes right in to the middle.
  • Add the yoghurt slowly over low heat, whisking. Hot heat makes it curdle.
  • Cook the tomato base until the oil separates. It is the sign that the raw taste is gone.

item.title: Sarson da Saag with Makki di Roti
item.description: Sarson da saag with makki di roti: slow-cooked Punjabi mustard greens with ginger and garlic, served with maize flatbreads and a spoonful of white butter.
item.content:encoded:
Sarson da saag with makki di roti is the great winter dish of Punjab, made when the mustard fields are green, and eaten with white butter and a lump of jaggery, on cold days. The saag is a dish of mustard greens, with spinach added to soften the bitterness, cooked slowly until they collapse, thickened with a spoonful of maize flour, and roughly mashed, and finished with a tadka of fried onion, garlic and ginger in ghee. The flatbread that goes with it, makki di roti, is made with maize flour and warm water, which has no gluten and no stretch, so it is pressed by hand, gently, and it is cooked on a hot griddle. It is a dish of the field and the farmhouse, and it needs patience.

  • Cook the greens until they are completely soft. Undercooked mustard greens are bitter.
  • Grease your palms and the plastic. Maize dough has no gluten and sticks and cracks.
  • Use warm, not hot, water for the roti dough. It makes it easier to shape.

item.title: Dal Baati Churma
item.description: Dal baati churma: the Rajasthani feast of baked wheat balls soaked in ghee, a spiced five-lentil dal and a sweet churma of crushed baati, jaggery and nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Dal baati churma is the signature meal of Rajasthan, a three-part feast of baked wheat dumplings, a dal made from five lentils and a sweet crumb of crushed dumplings, and every part is served swimming in ghee. The baati are said to have been made first by desert warriors on the march, who buried balls of dough in the hot sand or under dung fire, and they turn out hard and crusty outside and crumbly within, and are broken open and drenched with ghee. The panchmel dal is a mix of five lentils, each of which adds its own texture, tempered at the end with cumin, mustard seeds and chilli in hot ghee. The churma is made by crushing baatis and mixing them with jaggery, ghee and nuts, and it is a dessert.

  • Make the dough stiff. A soft dough makes flat, soggy baati.
  • Turn the baatis halfway through. They then brown evenly.
  • Crush the churma while the baati are still warm. It mixes with the ghee easily.

item.title: Kadhi Pakora
item.description: Kadhi pakora: crisp gram flour onion fritters in a tangy, smooth Punjabi curry of yoghurt and gram flour, finished with a sizzling spiced ghee tadka.
item.content:encoded:
Kadhi pakora is a comfort dish of Punjab, a tangy, pale yellow curry of yoghurt thickened with gram flour, with soft, spongy onion fritters, or pakoras, floating in it, and it is served over plain rice. It is the food of Sunday lunches and of the days when someone in the family is feeling under the weather. The kadhi is a delicate thing. It must be stirred constantly as it comes to the boil, since yoghurt splits when heated unevenly, and it is simmered gently for half an hour, until the raw taste of the gram flour has gone and it is smooth and thick. Yoghurt that has turned a little sour gives the best flavour. The fritters are soaked in it, and the tadka of spiced ghee goes on the top just before serving.

  • Stir constantly until it boils. Yoghurt curdles if it is heated unevenly.
  • Simmer for the full 30 minutes. Raw gram flour tastes harsh.
  • Beat the pakora batter until it is light. It makes fluffy, not dense, fritters.

item.title: Lemon Rice
item.description: South Indian lemon rice: cooked rice tossed with a tempering of mustard seeds, lentils, peanuts and curry leaves, turmeric and plenty of tangy lemon juice.
item.content:encoded:
Lemon rice, called chitranna in Karnataka and elumichai sadam in Tamil Nadu, is a South Indian rice dish, and it is made in millions of homes as a lunchbox dish, and offered at temples. It takes leftover cooked rice and makes something bright of it, with turmeric for colour, lemon juice for tang, and a tempering, or tadka, of mustard seeds, split lentils, peanuts and curry leaves, fried in hot oil until they crackle. The lentils and peanuts add crunch, and the curry leaves add a distinctive fragrance. The rice must be cold and dry, since freshly cooked rice is sticky and clumps. The lemon juice goes in at the end, off the heat, because heat makes it bitter and dulls its flavour.

  • Use cold, day-old rice. Warm rice clumps and turns mushy.
  • Add the lemon juice off the heat. Heat dulls its flavour.
  • Fry the dals until they are golden. They give the rice its crunch.

item.title: Mishti Doi
item.description: Mishti doi: the Bengali sweet yoghurt, made from reduced milk sweetened with caramelised sugar, set overnight in small pots until thick and creamy.
item.content:encoded:
Mishti doi is the sweet yoghurt of Bengal, and it is served at weddings and festivals, and sold in small clay pots throughout Kolkata. It is made from milk that is boiled down until it is thick and rich, sweetened with sugar, some of which is caramelised first so that the yoghurt has a golden-brown colour and a slight caramel flavour, and set with a spoonful of live yoghurt overnight in a warm place. The clay pots do more than look nice. They are porous, so they absorb some of the whey and give the yoghurt a firmer, creamier set. It takes patience, since the yoghurt needs 8 to 10 hours to set at a warm temperature, and it is served chilled.

  • Reduce the milk properly. Thin milk makes a loose, watery set.
  • Make sure the milk is only lukewarm when you add the yoghurt. Too hot kills the cultures.
  • Leave the pots undisturbed while they set. Moving them breaks the set.

item.title: Halwa Puri
item.description: Halwa puri: the Pakistani weekend breakfast of puffed fried bread with a golden cardamom semolina halwa and a spiced chickpea curry. Serves eight.
item.content:encoded:
Halwa puri is the great weekend breakfast of Pakistan, eaten in Lahore and Karachi on Sunday mornings, and it is a combination of three dishes on one plate: puri, a small, puffed, deep-fried bread; a sweet semolina halwa, cooked in ghee with sugar and cardamom until it is golden and glossy; and a spicy chickpea curry, called chana or aloo cholay. The mixture of sweet and savoury is the point: a bite of hot, crisp puri torn and dipped in the curry, and another spooned through the halwa. The halwa is made by roasting the semolina in ghee until it smells nutty, and adding hot syrup. The puri dough is stiff and rested, so that it puffs when it hits the hot oil.

  • Make the puri dough stiff and rest it. A soft dough will not puff.
  • Roast the semolina until it smells nutty. Underroasted semolina tastes raw.
  • Add the hot syrup carefully. It spits when it hits the hot semolina.

item.title: Shorshe Ilish
item.description: Shorshe ilish: Bengali fish steaks simmered in a pungent paste of ground mustard seeds, green chillies and mustard oil. Made with hilsa or another oily fish.
item.content:encoded:
Shorshe ilish is the most famous dish of Bengal, both in Bangladesh and in West Bengal: hilsa, a rich, oily, silver river fish, cooked in a sharp paste of ground mustard seeds, green chillies, turmeric and mustard oil. The mustard is the whole thing. It is ground fresh, with green chilli and salt, and it gives a pungent heat that rises through the nose, like wasabi or horseradish, and which is balanced by the rich, oily fish. Two tricks control it: soaking the seeds and grinding them with a little salt, and never boiling the paste for long, since it turns bitter. Hilsa is full of small bones, and mackerel, salmon or herring steaks are a good substitute.

  • Grind the mustard seeds with the chillies and salt. It tames the bitterness.
  • Do not boil the mustard paste hard or for long. It turns bitter.
  • Warn everyone about the bones. Hilsa is full of fine ones.

item.title: Chotpoti
item.description: Chotpoti: the Bangladeshi street snack of spiced chickpeas and potato in a tamarind gravy, topped with egg, onion, green chilli, coriander and crisp wafers.
item.content:encoded:
Chotpoti is a Bangladeshi street snack, sold in bowls made of paper from carts in Dhaka and Chittagong, and it is a dish of contrasts: warm, spicy, tangy chickpeas and potato in a tamarind-spiked gravy, and toppings of raw onion, green chilli, coriander, chopped boiled egg and crushed crisps for crunch. It is related to the chaat of India and the chana of Pakistan, but it has a character of its own, with its tang of tamarind and a dose of chaat masala. The chickpeas are simmered until soft, and some are mashed, to thicken the gravy without any flour, and everything is served at once, while the base is hot and the toppings are cold and crisp.

  • Mash a few of the chickpeas. It thickens the gravy without flour.
  • Add the crisp wafers at the last moment. They go soft in the gravy.
  • Adjust the tamarind to taste. It should be tangy, not sour.

item.title: Bhapa Pitha
item.description: Bhapa pitha: Bangladeshi steamed rice-flour cakes with a filling of fresh coconut and date palm jaggery, a winter sweet of Bengal, eaten warm.
item.content:encoded:
Bhapa pitha is a steamed rice cake of Bengal, made in the winter when new rice and date palm jaggery, called khejur gur, come into season, and it is a sweet that is made in the house for festivals and for guests, such as at Poush Sankranti. The cakes are made from a soft dough of rice flour and hot water, shaped into little cups filled with a mixture of grated coconut and jaggery, sealed, and steamed until the outside is translucent and the inside is soft and sticky. They are eaten warm. The dough needs to be made with very hot water, since it cooks the starch, and it is kneaded while warm, when it is easy to shape. The flavour of the date jaggery, which is smoky and caramel-like, is the key.

  • Use very hot water for the dough. It cooks the flour and makes the dough pliable.
  • Knead while the dough is warm. Cold rice dough cracks.
  • Keep the dough covered while you work. It dries and cracks quickly.

item.title: Dal Bhat
item.description: Dal bhat: the Nepali daily meal of steamed rice, a thin spiced lentil soup, a cauliflower and potato curry and a fiery tomato pickle, served together.
item.content:encoded:
Dal bhat is the daily meal of Nepal. It is eaten twice a day, by nearly everyone, from Kathmandu to the high Himalayas, and the Nepali saying goes that dal bhat power, 24 hour. It is a set of dishes, not one, and each has a role. Bhat is plain steamed rice, and it is the base. Dal is a thin, savoury lentil soup, poured over the rice, and it is tempered with garlic and cumin fried in hot oil. Tarkari is a vegetable curry, here potato and cauliflower, cooked with cumin, turmeric and ginger, and achar is a sharp, fresh pickle, usually of tomato, that is served in a small spoonful to lift the rest. It is eaten with the right hand, mixed on the plate, and seconds are always offered.

  • Pour the tempered oil into the dal while it is still sizzling. It is what gives dal its fragrance.
  • Keep the dal thin. It should be a soup to pour, not a thick stew.
  • Char the tomatoes until blackened in places. It gives the achar a smoky depth.

item.title: Sel Roti
item.description: Sel roti: ring-shaped Nepali doughnuts of rice flour, banana, milk and cardamom, fried until crisp outside and soft within. Made at festival times.
item.content:encoded:
Sel roti is a Nepali ring-shaped bread, and it is a festival food, made in vast quantities for Tihar and Dashain, given to guests and neighbours, and eaten for breakfast. It is a batter of rice flour, sugar, ghee, milk and ripe banana, spiced with cardamom, that is poured through a funnel or the hole in a cup, in a ring, into hot oil, and fried until crisp outside and soft and slightly chewy within. The rice flour makes it naturally gluten-free, and gives it a texture unlike wheat doughnuts. The banana sweetens the batter and makes it tender. The batter is rested for an hour, so that it thickens to the right consistency, thick enough to hold the ring shape, and thin enough to pour.

  • Get the batter consistency right. Too thin and it spreads, too thick and it will not pour.
  • Fry at 180°C. Cooler oil makes them greasy, and hotter oil burns the outside.
  • Use very ripe bananas, with black-flecked skins. They are sweeter and easier to mash.

item.title: Thukpa
item.description: Thukpa: a warming Himalayan noodle soup of chicken, cabbage, carrot and spinach in a ginger, garlic and cumin broth, finished with lime and coriander.
item.content:encoded:
Thukpa is the noodle soup of the Himalayas, and it comes from Tibet and is eaten across Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan and Ladakh. It is a soup of cold mountain days, made with a rich broth, hand-pulled or dried noodles, meat and whatever vegetables are at hand, and it is served in a big bowl, very hot. The flavours are simple and warming: ginger, garlic, cumin and chilli in the base, soy sauce for savour, a fistful of fresh coriander and a squeeze of lime at the end. The noodles are cooked separately, so they do not cloud the broth or go soft, and the vegetables are added to the broth for only a few minutes, so that they keep their colour and crunch.

  • Cook the noodles separately. They soak up the broth and turn it starchy.
  • Add the vegetables late so they keep their crunch.
  • Serve with chilli sauce on the side. Each person can add as much as they like.

item.title: Watalappan
item.description: Watalappan: a silky Sri Lankan coconut custard of jaggery, eggs and coconut milk, spiced with cardamom and nutmeg and topped with cashews. Served chilled.
item.content:encoded:
Watalappan, also written wattalapam, is a Sri Lankan dessert of coconut milk, jaggery, eggs and spices, and it was brought to the island by the Malay community and is served at Eid and at weddings. It is a steamed custard, and jaggery, the dark, unrefined palm sugar, is what makes it distinctive, with a deep, smoky, caramel flavour that white sugar cannot give. Cardamom, nutmeg and sometimes cloves scent the custard, and chopped cashews are scattered on the top. It is cooked gently in a water bath, so that the eggs set to a smooth custard and not to a scrambled mass, and the eggs are beaten only lightly, so no bubbles form, and strained. It is chilled for two hours before serving.

  • Beat the eggs lightly. Foam gives a bubbly, rough custard.
  • Strain the mixture. It removes the egg strands and gives a silky finish.
  • Take it out while it still wobbles. It sets as it cools.

item.title: Mie Goreng
item.description: Mie goreng: Indonesian fried noodles with sweet soy sauce, garlic and chilli, chicken, prawns and greens, and crisp fried shallots. Ready in 30 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Mie goreng is fried noodles, and in Indonesia it is sold from carts and small roadside stalls, cooked to order in a wok over a fierce flame. The noodles came with Chinese settlers, but the flavour is Indonesian: shallots, garlic and chilli fried first, then kecap manis, the thick, sweet soy sauce that gives the dish its dark, glossy coat. Chicken and prawns are the usual protein, with an egg scrambled in, greens such as pak choi or choy sum, and bean sprouts for crunch.
