It is finished with fried shallots, and there is nearly always cucumber or pickled vegetables on the side to cut the sweetness. The whole thing cooks in a few minutes, so the secret is having everything chopped and ready before you begin.

  • Cook the noodles just short of tender. They finish in the wok, and overcooked ones break into mush.
  • Use a very hot wok and cook in one batch. A crowded, cool pan steams the noodles instead of frying them.
  • If you cannot find kecap manis, simmer 3 tablespoons of soy sauce with 2 tablespoons of brown sugar for 2 minutes and use that.

item.title: Bakso
item.description: Bakso: Indonesian beef meatballs, made springy with tapioca starch and ice, served in a clear beef broth with noodles, fried shallots and sambal.
item.content:encoded:
Bakso is the meatball soup of Indonesia, sold from carts and stalls in every town, and the meatballs are unlike European ones: firm, smooth and springy, so they bounce when you bite them. The bounce comes from beating raw beef with ice, garlic and tapioca starch until it turns into a sticky paste, then shaping it and poaching it in water, not frying it. The ice keeps the meat cold while it is processed, which is what makes the paste smooth. The name is thought to come from a Hokkien word for minced meat, and the dish is generally traced to Chinese settlers, though in Indonesia it is made with beef. It is served in a clear broth made from beef bones, with noodles, tofu, egg and fried shallots, and each person adds sambal and sweet soy sauce at the table.

  • Keep everything cold. Very cold mince and ice give the tight, springy texture. Warm meat makes soft, crumbly meatballs.
  • Poach the meatballs in water that is barely simmering. A hard boil makes them split and turn rubbery.
  • Test a spoonful of the mixture before shaping the rest. It is the only way to check the seasoning of a raw meatball.

item.title: Opor Ayam
item.description: Opor ayam: Javanese chicken simmered until tender in a mild, pale coconut sauce with lemongrass, galangal and candlenuts, and served with rice.
item.content:encoded:
Opor ayam is a dish from Central Java, and it is made in enormous quantity at Lebaran, the days that follow the end of Ramadan, when it is served with compressed rice cakes and a bowl of sambal. It is chicken cooked in coconut milk, and unlike most Indonesian curries it is mild and pale, with no chilli in the sauce. The flavour comes from a paste of shallots, garlic, candlenuts, toasted coriander, cumin and white pepper, and from whole lemongrass, galangal, bay leaves and lime leaves that scent the sauce as it simmers. The candlenuts thicken it and give it a soft, rich body. Cook it over a low heat, because coconut milk that boils hard can separate, and give it time: it is better after it has sat.

  • Simmer gently. A hard boil can make the coconut milk split into oil and curds.
  • Fry the paste until it smells cooked and the oil begins to show at the edge. Raw paste tastes harsh.
  • It tastes better after a rest. Make it a few hours ahead, or the day before, and warm it slowly.

item.title: Teh Tarik
item.description: Teh tarik: strong black tea with condensed milk, poured back and forth from a height until frothy and smooth. Malaysia's favourite drink, ready in 10 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Teh tarik means pulled tea, and it is the drink of the mamak stalls of Malaysia, the open-fronted restaurants that stay open late into the night. It is made from very strong black tea, sweetened with condensed milk and softened with a little evaporated milk. The pulling is the point of the name: the tea is poured from one vessel to another, from a height, again and again, in a long, thin stream. This cools it to a drinkable heat, mixes the milk right through and makes the tea light and frothy. It takes practice to do it without splashing, and watching a stall-holder do it fast is part of the pleasure. At home, two jugs and a sink are enough. The result is sweet, creamy, and much lighter than you would expect.

  • Make the tea stronger than you think you need. The milk softens it a great deal.
  • Start with a low pour and raise it as you get the feel for it. The stream should be steady, not a splash.
  • For a less sweet cup, use 3 tablespoons of condensed milk and 3 of evaporated milk.

item.title: Assam Laksa
item.description: Assam laksa: Penang rice noodles in a sour, spicy mackerel and tamarind broth, topped with pineapple, cucumber, mint and a drizzle of sweet prawn paste.
item.content:encoded:
Assam laksa is the laksa of Penang, and it is nothing like the creamy, coconut-rich curry laksa. It is sour, sharp and hot, with a thin broth made from mackerel and flavoured with tamarind, which is what assam means. The fish is simmered with lemongrass and Vietnamese mint, the flesh is flaked off the bones, and the bones go back into the pot to make the broth deeper. A paste of dried chillies, shallots, galangal and shrimp paste is fried and added. It is served over thick, round rice noodles and topped with raw pineapple, cucumber, red onion, chilli and mint, and a swirl of petis udang, a dark, sweet, thick prawn paste. The cool, fresh toppings against the hot, sour broth are what make it.

  • Check every bit of the flaked fish for small bones before you return it to the pot. Mackerel has many.
  • Add the tamarind a little at a time. Brands vary a lot in sourness, so taste as you go.
  • The raw toppings matter. Do not skip the pineapple and mint, which cool the hot broth.

item.title: Bak Kut Teh
item.description: Bak kut teh: Singapore pork rib soup, simmered slowly with whole garlic and white pepper into a clear, warming broth. Serve with rice and chilli in soy sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Bak kut teh means meat bone tea, and there is no tea in the soup: the name comes from the strong Chinese tea that is served alongside to cut through the richness of the pork. The soup is said to have started as a nourishing meal for Chinese labourers in the port towns of Malaysia and Singapore. The Singapore version is the clear, peppery one, in the Teochew style: pork ribs are simmered for a long time with whole cloves of garlic and a great deal of white pepper, and only a little soy sauce, so that the broth stays pale. The Malaysian versions are darker and are flavoured with star anise, cinnamon and herbs. It is eaten with rice, a plate of greens, and chillies in dark soy sauce for dipping the meat. Blanching the ribs first is what keeps the broth clear.

  • Do not skip the blanching. It removes the scum and blood that would make the broth cloudy.
  • Crush the peppercorns lightly, not to a powder. Whole cracked corns give a steady heat and keep the broth clear.
  • The soup is better the next day. Chill it, skim off the fat and reheat.

item.title: Tinola
item.description: Tinola: Filipino chicken soup with plenty of ginger, green papaya and chilli leaves, simmered in a light, clear broth. Simple, warming and full of flavour.
item.content:encoded:
Tinola is one of the most common dishes in Filipino homes, a light soup of chicken cooked in a broth with a lot of ginger. It has no cream and no heavy spices. The ginger is sliced into thin matchsticks and cooked in oil with onion and garlic until fragrant, then the chicken is browned and seasoned with fish sauce, called patis, before the water goes in. Green papaya, which is firm and mild, is added late so that it softens but keeps its shape. The leaves that go in last are chilli leaves, or malunggay, which is moringa, and baby spinach is a good substitute where they cannot be found. It is eaten with white rice, and the broth is sipped from the bowl. It is the kind of dish that is made when someone is unwell or tired.

  • Cut the ginger into fine matchsticks. It is a main ingredient, not a flavouring, and thick pieces are too fiery.
  • Add the papaya late. Cooked too long it turns to mush and clouds the broth.
  • Use bone-in chicken with the skin on. It gives the broth its body and flavour.

item.title: Kaldereta
item.description: Kaldereta: Filipino beef stew braised in a rich tomato and liver-spread sauce with potatoes, carrots, peppers and olives. A festive dish, best with rice.
item.content:encoded:
Kaldereta is a Filipino stew, and its name comes from the Spanish word for a cooking pot. It is a fiesta dish, made in the provinces with goat, and in many homes with beef, which is easier to find. The sauce is built on tomato and thickened and enriched with liver spread, a pâté that melts into the sauce and gives it a deep, savoury, slightly sweet body. There is heat from small chillies, and colour and sweetness from red and green peppers, and it is filled out with potatoes, carrots and olives. Some cooks finish it with grated cheese. The meat is browned well first and then simmered for a long time over low heat, so that the tough beef chuck becomes soft. It is served with plenty of rice.

  • Brown the beef in batches. Crowding the pot makes it steam and turn grey rather than brown.
  • Add the liver spread after the beef is nearly tender. It thickens the sauce and can catch on the bottom of the pot if it goes in too early.
  • Cut the vegetables large. They cook for a long time, and small pieces fall apart.

item.title: Bistek Tagalog
item.description: Bistek Tagalog: Filipino beef steak. Thin beef slices marinated in soy sauce and citrus, quickly browned and topped with soft onion rings.
item.content:encoded:
Bistek is the Filipino version of beef steak, from the Spanish word bistec, and the name Tagalog points to the region around Manila where it is a home staple. It is nothing like a thick grilled steak: the beef is sliced thin, marinated in soy sauce and calamansi, a small Philippine citrus, and cooked quickly in a hot pan. The marinade then goes into the pan with a little water to make a sauce, which is salty, sharp and slightly sweet, and soft rings of onion are laid on top. It is served with white rice, which soaks up the sauce. The beef stays tender because the slices are thin and cook in a couple of minutes, and because the acid in the marinade softens it. Lemon and orange juice together make a good stand-in for calamansi.

  • Slice the beef against the grain and thin. It is the main reason the meat stays tender.
  • Pat the beef dry before frying. Wet meat steams and does not brown.
  • Do not marinate for more than an hour. The acid starts to make the thin slices mushy.

item.title: Gai Yang
item.description: Gai yang: Thai grilled chicken marinated in coriander root, garlic, white pepper and fish sauce, cooked until crisp, with a sharp, hot dipping sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Gai yang means grilled chicken, and it comes from Isan, the north-east of Thailand, and from the street stalls of Bangkok, where flattened chickens are cooked over charcoal until the skin is dark, crisp and slightly sweet. The marinade is what separates it from a plain roast: coriander roots, garlic and white pepper are pounded into a paste, then mixed with fish sauce, oyster sauce and palm sugar, and the sugar gives the skin its deep colour. It is eaten with sticky rice and a papaya salad, and with a dipping sauce, nam jim jaew, which is sharp with lime and fish sauce and hot with chilli flakes and toasted rice powder. At home, roasting the chicken flat and finishing it under a hot grill gives crisp skin without a fire, and a barbecue makes it even better.

  • Spatchcock the chicken so that it lies flat. It cooks evenly and the skin crisps all over.
  • Use the coriander roots if you can find them. They have a deeper, earthier flavour than the leaves.
  • Wipe off any thick clumps of marinade before grilling. They scorch before the skin is crisp.

item.title: Bò Lúc Lắc
item.description: Bò lúc lắc: Vietnamese shaking beef. Garlic and oyster sauce beef cubes seared in a hot wok and served on a watercress salad with a lime and pepper dip.
item.content:encoded:
Bò lúc lắc means shaking beef, named for the way the cook shakes the wok to toss the cubes of beef as they sear. It comes from the south of Vietnam and is a restaurant dish and a party dish, and the use of steak cubes and butter is often put down to French influence. The beef is marinated with garlic, oyster sauce, soy sauce and a little sugar, then cooked in a very hot pan in small batches, so that the outside browns quickly while the middle stays pink and juicy. It is served on a bed of watercress, tomato and red onion, dressed lightly with vinegar, which the hot beef wilts. The dip of lime juice, salt and black pepper, muối tiêu chanh, is what makes it: it is sharp and salty, and the beef needs it. Serve with rice.

  • Cook the beef in two batches. If the pan is crowded the cubes steam and turn grey.
  • Let the pan get very hot before the beef goes in. It should sizzle loudly on contact.
  • Cut the cubes the same size, about 2.5 cm, so that they all cook to the same doneness.

item.title: Mohinga
item.description: Mohinga: Burmese rice noodles in a golden fish and lemongrass broth thickened with chickpea flour, topped with boiled egg, coriander and crisp onions.
item.content:encoded:
Mohinga is often called the national dish of Myanmar. It is eaten for breakfast, at street stalls and at home, ladled over thin rice noodles, and it is a thick, golden, savoury fish soup. Catfish is traditional, and any firm white fish will work. The fish is cooked in water with lemongrass and turmeric, and flaked. A paste of onion, garlic and ginger is fried until golden, and the broth is thickened with chickpea flour and toasted rice, which gives it a body and a slightly nutty taste. Tradition adds the pith of the banana stem, and this version leaves it out because it is hard to find. It is served with a halved boiled egg, coriander, fried onions and lime, with fish sauce and chilli flakes at the table for each person to adjust the bowl.

  • Whisk the toasted flour into cold water before it goes into the pot. Added dry it forms lumps.
  • Stir the broth often as it thickens. The flour settles and can catch on the bottom.
  • Fry the paste until it is properly golden. Pale paste leaves the soup tasting raw.

item.title: Laphet Thoke
item.description: Laphet thoke: Burmese tea leaf salad of fermented tea leaves, cabbage, tomato and lime, with crunchy peanuts, sesame seeds, fried beans and garlic chips.
item.content:encoded:
Laphet thoke is the tea leaf salad of Myanmar, and it is a dish of hospitality: it is served at the end of a meal, at meetings and at gatherings, traditionally in a round lacquer box with a compartment in the middle for the tea leaves and others around it for the crunchy things. The tea leaves are fermented, which makes them savoury, sour and slightly bitter, and they are softened with oil, lime and chilli. Around them go fried garlic, roasted peanuts, toasted sesame, and crisp fried beans or split peas, and shredded cabbage and tomato turn it into a salad. The contrast of soft, sour leaves and hard, salty crunch is the whole point. Fermented tea leaves are sold in jars in Burmese and some Asian grocers and online, and there is no proper substitute for them.

  • Add the crunchy things at the last moment. Left to sit in the dressing they go soft.
  • Taste the tea leaves from the jar first. Brands vary in saltiness, so adjust the soy sauce to match.
  • Dried shrimp are a traditional addition. A spoonful of them makes a fuller salad if you eat fish, though it is then no longer vegan.

item.title: Ohn No Khao Swè
item.description: Ohn no khao swè: Burmese chicken and coconut noodle soup, thickened with chickpea flour and served with egg noodles, boiled egg, shallots and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Ohn no khao swè is a Burmese noodle soup of chicken in coconut milk. Ohn no means coconut and khao swè means noodles, and it is a whole meal in one bowl. It is generally thought to be related to the khao soi of northern Thailand, and the two share the idea of noodles in a spiced coconut broth with a set of toppings, though the Burmese broth is milder and is thickened with chickpea flour instead of a red curry paste. The onions are cooked until soft and golden, with garlic and ginger, turmeric and paprika, and the chicken is simmered in stock. The coconut milk and the chickpea flour go in later to make the broth rich and thick. It is served over egg noodles, and each person adds their own egg, sliced shallot, coriander, lime and chilli.

  • Mix the chickpea flour with cold water to a smooth slurry before it goes into the pot. Dry flour makes lumps.
  • Stir the soup while it simmers. Chickpea flour settles and can catch on the bottom.
  • Serve the toppings separately, so each person can choose. The crunch of raw shallot against the rich broth is the point.

item.title: Fish Amok
item.description: Fish amok: the national dish of Cambodia. White fish steamed in a soft, mousse-like coconut curry with lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime. Serve with rice.
item.content:encoded:
Fish amok, or amok trey, is the best-known dish of Cambodia. It is not a curry in the sense of a stew: pieces of fish are mixed with a paste called kroeung, made from lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, kaffir lime and garlic, and with coconut milk and egg, and the mixture is steamed until it sets to a soft, quivering, mousse-like texture. In Cambodia it is cooked in a cup of folded banana leaf on a bed of leaves, and finished with a spoonful of thick coconut cream, a few shreds of lime leaf and a little red chilli. It is fragrant and creamy rather than hot. The cooking is gentle, which keeps the fish moist. At home, ramekins work well, with spinach at the bottom of each, and steamed rice on the side.

  • Keep the water at a gentle simmer. A rolling boil makes the custard bubbly and tough.
  • Choose firm fish. Delicate fillets break down and turn the amok watery.
  • Do not overfill the ramekins. The mixture puffs a little as it steams.

item.title: Kuy Teav
item.description: Kuy teav: Cambodian pork noodle soup with a clear, sweet broth of pork bones, charred onion and daikon, rice noodles, minced pork, prawns and fried garlic.
item.content:encoded:
Kuy teav is the breakfast noodle soup of Cambodia, sold from stalls at dawn and eaten in the markets of Phnom Penh, and it shows the influence of the Chinese families who brought rice noodle soup to Cambodia. The broth is the heart of it: pork bones are boiled first to remove scum, then simmered for a couple of hours with a charred onion, ginger and daikon, and a little rock sugar, until it is clear, light and naturally sweet. It is served over rice noodles with minced pork, slices of pork and prawns poached in the hot broth, and topped with bean sprouts, herbs, spring onions and fried garlic. At the table each person adds lime juice, chillies, hoisin sauce and chilli sauce. The toppings can vary, but the broth stays the same.

  • Do not skip boiling and rinsing the bones. It is the reason the broth comes out clear and clean.
  • Simmer gently. A hard boil clouds the broth and makes it greasy.
  • Slice the pork very thin so that it cooks in seconds in the hot broth.

item.title: Nom Banh Chok
item.description: Nom banh chok: Khmer rice noodles with a fragrant lemongrass and turmeric fish gravy, piled with crisp raw vegetables and herbs. A Cambodian breakfast.
item.content:encoded:
Nom banh chok, often called Khmer noodles, is a Cambodian breakfast, and it is also a dish for weddings and for the Khmer New Year. The noodles are fresh rice noodles, traditionally pressed straight from a mould into boiling water, and the gravy is made from fish that is poached, flaked and pounded with kroeung, the fragrant paste of lemongrass, turmeric, galangal and kaffir lime leaf. It is thickened lightly with rice flour and softened with coconut milk. The noodles are put in a bowl, the gravy is poured over them, and then comes a large heap of raw and blanched vegetables and herbs: cucumber, green beans, bean sprouts, mint, basil and, in Cambodia, banana blossom. Lime and fresh chillies finish it. It is fresh, mild and fragrant, a very different thing from a heavy curry.

  • Flake the fish carefully and check for bones. The gravy is smooth and small bones are unpleasant.
  • Make the gravy thick. It should coat the noodles, not pool in the bowl.
  • Pile the vegetables high. They give the crunch and freshness that balance the warm gravy.

item.title: Jeyuk Bokkeum
item.description: Jeyuk bokkeum: Korean spicy pork stir-fry. Thin pork slices in a gochujang, chilli and garlic marinade, cooked hot and fast and served with rice and lettuce.
item.content:encoded:
Jeyuk bokkeum is spicy stir-fried pork, one of the most common dishes in Korean homes and restaurants. Jeyuk means pork and bokkeum means stir-fried, and it is also called dweji bulgogi, meaning pork bulgogi. The pork is sliced thin and mixed with a red marinade of gochujang, Korean chilli flakes, soy sauce, garlic, ginger, sugar and honey, and it is then cooked in a very hot pan with sliced onion until the edges of the meat are dark and slightly sticky. The sugar is not only for sweetness: it is what caramelises and gives the meat its glaze. It is eaten with steamed rice, and with lettuce or perilla leaves, so that each bite can be wrapped with a little rice and kimchi. Shoulder is lean and chewy, and belly is richer.

  • Slice the pork thin. If the butcher will not, freeze it for 30 minutes first, which makes it firm enough to slice by hand.
  • Cook over high heat and do not crowd the pan. If the pork steams it turns grey and the sauce goes watery.
  • The marinade burns easily because of the sugar. Keep the meat moving once it starts to caramelise.

item.title: Yukgaejang
item.description: Yukgaejang: fiery Korean beef soup of shredded brisket, bean sprouts, spring onions and glass noodles, seasoned with chilli and garlic and finished with egg.
item.content:encoded:
Yukgaejang is a red, spicy Korean beef soup, thick with shredded meat and a great deal of spring onion. Beef brisket is simmered until it is tender enough to pull apart by hand, and the shreds are mixed with a seasoning of chilli flakes, garlic, soy sauce and sesame oil and returned to the broth, which turns it a deep red. Bean sprouts, sweet potato noodles and beaten egg go in near the end. Traditionally it also contains bracken fern, which is hard to find outside Korea, and the spring onions and sprouts here do the job of adding sweetness and bulk. Koreans eat hot soups like this in the heat of summer as well as in winter, on the idea that heat is answered with heat. It is served with rice, and it keeps well and improves after a night in the fridge.

  • Shred the beef along the grain. It gives long, tender strands, not crumbs.
  • Add the egg in a thin stream and stir only once, so that it forms ribbons and does not cloud the broth.
  • Use plenty of spring onion. It sweetens the soup and balances the heat.

item.title: Oden
item.description: Oden: Japanese winter one-pot of daikon, eggs, fish cakes, konnyaku and tofu, simmered slowly in a light dashi broth and served with hot mustard.
item.content:encoded:
Oden is a Japanese winter dish, sold at convenience-store counters, from street stalls and in izakaya, and made at home in a big pot. A number of ingredients are simmered gently in a light dashi broth flavoured with soy sauce, and are picked out one at a time and eaten with a dab of hot Japanese mustard. The daikon is the centrepiece: it turns translucent and sweet as it soaks up the broth. Boiled eggs, potatoes, konnyaku, tofu and fish cakes go in as well, and the fish cakes give the broth much of its savoury depth. Chikuwa, satsuma-age, hanpen and fish balls are all used, and they are sold in Japanese and other Asian grocers. The dish is easy and slow, and it improves when it is left to sit off the heat.

  • Bevel the edges of the daikon rounds with a knife. It stops them breaking up in the pot.
  • Keep the broth at a bare simmer. A rolling boil makes the fish cakes tough and the broth cloudy.
  • Reheat oden slowly and add fresh fish cakes at the end. The flavour is at its best on the second day.

item.title: Chicken Nanban
item.description: Chicken nanban: fried chicken dipped in a sweet and sour soy and vinegar sauce, then topped with a thick, creamy egg tartar sauce. A Miyazaki classic.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken nanban is a speciality of Miyazaki prefecture in Kyushu, said to have been created there in the 1950s, and it has spread through Japan. Nanban means southern barbarian, an old word for the Europeans who arrived by sea in the south, and it is used for dishes with a vinegar marinade. The chicken is coated in flour and beaten egg and fried, so that it has a soft, eggy crust, and while it is still hot it is dipped in nanban sauce, a mix of soy sauce, rice vinegar and sugar. That gives it a sweet and sour edge. It is finished with a thick tartar sauce of chopped boiled egg, mayonnaise, pickles and onion. It is served with shredded cabbage and rice, and the contrast of hot crisp chicken, tangy sauce and creamy tartar is the whole idea.

  • Dip the chicken in the sauce while it is hot. It absorbs the sauce, and cold chicken only gets wet.
  • Do not soak it for long. Half a minute is enough, or the crust goes soft.
  • Keep the oil at 170°C. Hotter oil browns the egg coating before the chicken is cooked.

item.title: Taiwanese Oyster Omelette
item.description: Taiwanese oyster omelette: small oysters in a chewy starch batter with egg and greens, topped with a sweet and tangy red sauce. Ready in 20 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The oyster omelette is one of the best-loved snacks of the night markets of Taiwan, and in Hokkien it goes by a name that sounds like o-a-tsian. It is not a French omelette: small oysters are cooked in a pan, a batter of sweet potato starch and water is poured over, and the starch sets to a translucent, chewy, slightly sticky layer. Greens and beaten egg go on top, and the whole thing is cooked until the egg is set and the bottom is crisp. It is served with a sweet, tangy sauce, red and glossy, made from ketchup and sweet chilli sauce. The mix of textures, soft oysters, chewy starch and set egg, is the reason people queue for it. Use the smallest oysters you can find.

  • Stir the starch batter every time before you pour it. It sinks to the bottom of the bowl in seconds.
  • Use a non-stick pan, and let it get properly hot, so that the batter sets and does not stick.
  • Oysters are cooked through in this dish, but buy them fresh and keep them cold until you cook them.

item.title: Rosół
item.description: Rosół: Polish chicken soup, a clear golden broth simmered slowly with chicken, root vegetables and allspice, served with thin egg noodles and fresh parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Rosół is the Polish chicken soup, and in many homes it is the Sunday soup, made in a large pot and served before the main course. A whole chicken is set in cold water and brought slowly to a simmer, and root vegetables go in: carrot, parsnip, celeriac and leek, with an onion that has been charred to give the broth its golden colour, and whole allspice, peppercorns and bay. It is simmered very gently for a couple of hours, never allowed to boil hard, which would cloud it. The broth is strained until it is clear, and served over fine egg noodles with slices of carrot, pieces of the chicken and fresh parsley. The clarity and depth of the broth are the whole point, and they come from patience, not from ingredients.

  • Start with cold water and heat slowly. It draws the flavour out of the chicken and keeps the broth clear.
  • Do not let the soup boil. A hard boil stirs up the fat and scum and makes the broth cloudy.
  • Cook the noodles separately. Cooked in the broth they cloud it and soak it up.

item.title: Kapuśniak
item.description: Kapuśniak: Polish sauerkraut soup with smoked pork ribs, sausage, potatoes and carrots. Sour, smoky and hearty, and even better the next day.
item.content:encoded:
Kapuśniak is a Polish cabbage soup, and this version is made with sauerkraut, which gives it a clean, sour edge. It is a homely pot of soup, made in winter with smoked pork, potatoes and carrots, and it is thick enough to serve as the whole meal, with slices of rye bread. The smoked ribs give the broth its depth, the sausage adds more, and the sauerkraut is cooked down with onion and tomato until it turns soft and mellow. Some cooks make it with fresh cabbage, and it is then a milder soup. Both versions improve when they are left to sit, so it is a good soup to make a day ahead. Both the sauerkraut and the smoked meat are salty, so taste before you add any salt.

  • Squeeze the sauerkraut and taste a strand. If it is very sour, rinse it briefly under cold water first.
  • Go carefully with the salt. The sauerkraut and smoked meat are already salty.
  • It is better the next day. Chill it and reheat gently, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

item.title: Rakott Krumpli
item.description: Rakott krumpli: Hungarian layered potato bake of sliced potatoes, hard-boiled eggs, smoked sausage and sour cream, baked until golden and bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
Rakott krumpli means layered potatoes, and it is one of the most common everyday dishes in Hungarian homes, a cheap, filling supper that is easy to feed a family from. Boiled potatoes are sliced and layered in a dish with hard-boiled eggs, slices of paprika-red smoked sausage, called kolbász, and sour cream, and the top is covered in more sour cream and baked until it is golden. The sour cream keeps everything moist and gives a slight tang, and the eggs and sausage make it a meal on its own. Some families add bacon or a layer of onion. It is usually eaten with pickled vegetables, called savanyúság, and a spoonful of these cuts through the richness of the dish.

  • Use waxy potatoes. Floury ones fall apart when sliced and layered.
  • Slice the potatoes and eggs to an even thickness so that the layers cook and cut cleanly.
  • Do not skip the rest before cutting. It lets the sauce settle so that the portions hold together.

item.title: Bacalhau com Natas
item.description: Bacalhau com natas: flaked salt cod, golden potatoes and soft onions baked under a creamy béchamel until bubbling. A comforting Portuguese classic.
item.content:encoded:
Bacalhau com natas means salt cod with cream, and it is one of the best-loved of the very many ways the Portuguese cook dried salt cod, which is said to number one for every day of the year. Flaked cod is mixed with golden fried potatoes and soft, slowly cooked onions, covered with a thick, creamy white sauce, and baked until the top is golden and bubbling. It is a comforting, family dish, served for Sunday lunch and at celebrations, and it is simple to make once the cod has been soaked. The soaking is the one part that needs planning: dried cod is very salty and needs a full day in several changes of cold water before it can be cooked. Choose thick loin pieces, which flake into large, tender pieces.

  • Taste a flake of the soaked cod before cooking. If it is still very salty, soak it for a few hours more.
  • Drain and dry the fried potatoes well. Wet potatoes make the bake watery.
  • Leave the salt out of the sauce until you have tasted it with the cod. It may not need any.

item.title: Ajvar
item.description: Ajvar: Balkan roasted red pepper and aubergine relish, cooked slowly with oil, garlic and vinegar until dark and thick. Spread on bread or serve with meat.
item.content:encoded:
Ajvar is the red pepper relish of the Balkans, and in Serbia and its neighbours it is a household ritual, made in autumn when the peppers are ripe and cheap. Families roast great quantities of peppers on stoves and in ovens, peel and grind them, and cook them slowly for hours, with sunflower oil, stirring constantly, to make jars for the winter. The relish is smoky, sweet and deep red-brown, and it is spread on bread, eaten with white cheese, and served alongside grilled meats such as ćevapi. Roasted aubergine is often added, which makes it smoother and milder, and this version uses it. Roasting the peppers until they are blackened is what gives ajvar its smoky flavour, and the long, slow frying in oil is what makes it thick, dark and rich.

  • Roast until the skins are properly black. Pale skins give a bland relish without the smoky taste.
  • Drain the roasted peppers well. Extra water means a longer time on the stove.
  • Stir often near the end. The thick mixture catches on the bottom of the pan and burns easily.

item.title: Štrukli
item.description: Štrukli: Croatian baked cheese pastry. Stretched dough rolled around a fresh cheese and egg filling, baked in sour cream until golden and bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
Štrukli is a Croatian dish from Zagorje, the hilly region north of Zagreb, and it is a rolled pastry filled with fresh cheese. The dough is stretched paper-thin, in the way of strudel, over floured cloth or the backs of the hands. It is then covered with a filling of fresh cheese, egg and sour cream and rolled up, and cut into pieces. Štrukli is cooked in one of two ways, either boiled or baked, and this recipe bakes it, standing the pieces in a dish and pouring a sauce of sour cream, milk and egg over them, so the top goes golden and crisp and the pastry beneath stays soft. It is eaten as a main dish with a salad, or as a rich side dish. Stretching the dough takes patience, and the first attempt may tear, but the tears do not matter once it is rolled.

  • Drain the cottage cheese in a sieve until it stops dripping. Wet cheese makes the filling run out of the roll.
  • Stretch the dough from the centre outward with the backs of your hands, not the fingertips, which tear it.
  • Do not worry about holes. They close up when the dough is rolled around the filling.

item.title: Prebranac
item.description: Prebranac: Serbian baked beans. Large white beans slow-cooked with plenty of onion, paprika and bay until creamy inside and crisp on top. Vegan and filling.
item.content:encoded:
Prebranac is the baked bean dish of Serbia, and it is eaten across the Balkans. It is a staple of family tables and, because it contains no meat, of the fasting days observed before Easter and Christmas. The beans are first boiled until they are tender, then mixed with a large quantity of onion that has been cooked slowly in oil until sweet and soft, with sweet paprika and bay leaf, and baked in an earthenware dish until the top is dark and crisp and the inside is creamy. The onions are what make it: there is nearly as much onion as there are cooked beans, by weight, and it melts into a sauce. It is eaten warm or at room temperature, with bread and a tomato and onion salad or pickled peppers.

  • Cook the onions slowly. Browned, they turn bitter, and only sweet, soft onions give the sauce its body.
  • Add the paprika at the very end of the onion cooking, off a high heat. It burns in seconds and turns bitter.
  • Keep the beans whole. Stir gently, because broken beans turn the dish to mush.

item.title: Kjötsúpa
item.description: Kjötsúpa: Icelandic lamb soup of lamb on the bone, swede, potatoes, carrots and rice, simmered slowly into a hearty broth. Iceland's comfort food.
item.content:encoded:
Kjötsúpa means meat soup, and it is the classic soup of Iceland: lamb cooked on the bone in a large pot with the root vegetables that grow in a cold climate, swede, potatoes and carrots, and a little rice. It is served at home, in restaurants and at gatherings, and it is the kind of soup that is made in quantity and eaten over several days. The flavours are simple and rely on the lamb: there is no spice beyond salt, pepper and a little thyme, and the broth is light and clear, with the fat skimmed. The lamb is lifted out at the end, pulled from the bones and returned to the pot, and each bowl gets a share of the meat, the vegetables and the broth. It is a soup for a cold, dark day.

  • Start with cold water and bring it up slowly. It draws the flavour out of the bones and helps the scum come to the top.
  • Skim the fat as it simmers. Lamb shoulder is fatty, and skimming keeps the broth clean.
  • Cut the vegetables in large chunks so that they hold their shape after cooking.

item.title: Plokkfiskur
item.description: Plokkfiskur: Icelandic fish stew of flaked white fish and potatoes in a creamy onion sauce, served with dark rye bread and butter. Warm, soft and simple.
item.content:encoded:
Plokkfiskur is a thick, comforting fish stew from Iceland, made from cooked white fish, boiled potatoes and onion in a creamy white sauce. The name means picked fish, and the fish is flaked into pieces and folded into the sauce and not blended, so it stays in soft, tender chunks. It is a home dish, and it is said to have grown from a way of using leftover cooked fish and potatoes, though it is a good enough dish to make from scratch. It is eaten with rúgbrauð, the dark, dense, slightly sweet Icelandic rye bread, and with butter, which is the classic accompaniment. Haddock or cod both work. The seasoning is mild, with nutmeg and white pepper, and the effect is soft and warming.

  • Use the poaching milk for the sauce. It carries the flavour of the fish.
  • Fold gently. Some of the potato will break down and thicken the stew, but you want soft chunks and not a mash.
  • Taste for salt at the end. Fish and milk are mild, and the stew needs proper seasoning.

item.title: Kleinur
item.description: Kleinur: Icelandic twisted doughnuts, a soft, cardamom-scented dough cut into diamonds, knotted and deep-fried until golden. Best with a hot cup of coffee.
item.content:encoded:
Kleinur are the twisted doughnuts of Iceland, and they belong to coffee time: they are made for family visits, bake sales and Christmas, and kept in a tin. The dough is soft and slightly cakey, flavoured with cardamom and a little vanilla, and is raised with baking powder, not yeast. It is rolled out, cut into diamonds, and each piece has a slit cut in the middle and one end pulled through to make a twist, which opens up as it fries. The kleinur are fried in oil until deep golden, and they are eaten plain, without a glaze, though some people dust them with sugar. They are close cousins of the klejner of Denmark and the klenäter of Sweden. They are best on the day they are made, while the outside is still crisp.

  • Use a thermometer and keep the oil at 175°C. If it is cooler the dough soaks up oil, and if it is hotter the outside browns before the middle is cooked.
  • Lower the pieces in gently and never leave hot oil unattended. Fry a few at a time so that the temperature does not drop.
  • Do not roll the dough thinner than 5 mm. Thin pieces turn hard and crisp instead of soft.

item.title: Cepelinai
item.description: Cepelinai: Lithuania's national dish. Large potato dumplings stuffed with seasoned pork, simmered and served with a sour cream and crisp bacon sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Cepelinai are the national dish of Lithuania, large oval potato dumplings that are named after the Zeppelin airships, because of their shape. The dumpling is made of grated raw potato mixed with cooked mashed potato, and the raw potato provides the starch that holds it together. Inside is a filling of seasoned minced pork, though curd cheese and mushrooms are also traditional. The dumplings are simmered gently in salted water until they float, and served with a sauce of crisp bacon and onion stirred into sour cream. They are heavy and filling, and two per person is a full meal. The hard part is making sure they do not fall apart, so the dough must be squeezed dry, and the water must never boil hard.

  • Squeeze the grated potato as dry as you can. Wet dough makes dumplings that break up in the water.
  • Keep the cooking water at a gentle simmer. A hard boil tears the dumplings apart.
  • Cook one dumpling as a test. If it falls apart, mix a spoonful of potato starch into the dough.

item.title: Šaltibarščiai
item.description: Šaltibarščiai: Lithuanian cold beetroot soup of kefir, cucumber, radish and dill, served with hot boiled potatoes and halved eggs. Bright pink and refreshing.
item.content:encoded:
Šaltibarščiai is the cold beetroot soup of Lithuania, and the name means cold borscht. It is a summer dish, made with cooked beetroot, cucumber, radishes, spring onions and dill in kefir or buttermilk, and it turns a startling bright pink as soon as the beetroot is stirred in. It is eaten cold, but the tradition is to serve it with hot boiled potatoes, and the contrast of the hot potato and the cold, tangy soup is part of the charm. Halved boiled eggs go on top. The soup is at its best after a couple of hours in the fridge, when the flavours have blended and it is properly cold. It is refreshing, tart and mild, and it is a very different thing from the hot, meaty borscht.

  • Grate the beetroot on the coarse side of the grater. Fine grating turns the soup to a pulp.
  • Chill the soup thoroughly. It tastes flat at room temperature and is at its best very cold.
  • Serve the potatoes piping hot. The contrast is the point of the dish.

item.title: Kugelis
item.description: Kugelis: Lithuanian baked potato pudding of grated potato, bacon, onion and egg, baked until dark and crisp on top and soft inside. Serve with sour cream.
item.content:encoded:
Kugelis is a Lithuanian potato pudding, and it is one of the country's best-loved home dishes, made in winter and for family gatherings. Raw potatoes are grated finely and mixed with fried bacon and onion, eggs and milk, poured into a dish and baked for well over an hour, until the top is dark brown and crisp and the middle is soft, dense and almost creamy. The bacon adds salt and a smoky flavour, and the potato does the rest. It is cut into squares and eaten warm with sour cream, and some cooks serve it with a sauce of more bacon and onion. The word is related to kugel, the Jewish baked pudding, and the two are cousins, although this one is made from potato and bacon. It is heavy, filling food.

  • Work fast once the potatoes are grated. Mix them with the egg and milk straight away, to stop them turning grey.
  • Press out only some of the liquid. The starch in it helps the pudding hold together.
  • Bake until the top is properly dark. The crisp crust is the best part.

item.title: Alfredo Sauce
item.description: Alfredo sauce: butter, garlic, cream and freshly grated Parmesan whisked into a silky sauce that coats fettuccine. Ready in 20 minutes, with no flour.
item.content:encoded:
Alfredo sauce began in Rome as very little: fettuccine tossed with butter and Parmigiano-Reggiano, a dish credited to the restaurateur Alfredo di Lelio in the early twentieth century. The version with cream is an American development, and it is the one most people mean when they search for the sauce. It is only cream, butter, garlic and cheese, and it works because of two things. The cream is reduced a little, so it has body before the cheese goes in, and the cheese is added off the heat, so that it melts into the cream and does not seize into strings. Freshly grated Parmesan matters more than anything else on the list. This makes about 400 ml of sauce, enough to coat 400 g of dried pasta, and it is as good on chicken, broccoli or gnocchi as it is on fettuccine.

  • Grate the Parmesan yourself on the fine side of the grater. Pre-grated cheese is coated to stop it clumping, and it stops it melting smoothly too.
  • Take the pan off the heat before the cheese goes in. Cheese added to boiling cream clumps and turns grainy.
  • Loosen the sauce with pasta water and not more cream. The starch in the water helps the sauce cling to the pasta instead of pooling on the plate.

item.title: Marinara Sauce
item.description: Marinara sauce: whole tinned tomatoes, garlic, olive oil and basil simmered into a bright, sweet sauce for pasta, pizza and parmigiana. Vegan and simple.
item.content:encoded:
Marinara is the simplest of the tomato sauces, and it has no meat in it. In Italy alla marinara means sailor style and describes a quick sauce of tomato, garlic, oregano and olive oil, the kind a fishing crew could make on a boat with a tin of tomatoes and a clove of garlic. In America the name has come to mean an all-purpose red sauce for pasta, pizza and baked dishes, usually with basil, and that is the sauce here. It cooks in half an hour and it should taste of the tomatoes, so the tomatoes are the part to spend money on: whole peeled tinned ones, crushed by hand. The garlic is cooked gently in the oil and never browned. This makes about 750 ml, enough for 500 g of pasta, a large tray of stuffed shells or two pizzas.

  • Cook the garlic gently in the oil. Browned garlic turns bitter, and nothing added afterwards corrects it.
  • Crush whole tomatoes by hand. Tinned chopped tomatoes are treated with calcium chloride and stay firm however long they cook.
  • Simmer uncovered so that the sauce reduces. A lid keeps the water in and gives a thin sauce.

item.title: Buffalo Wing Sauce
item.description: Buffalo wing sauce: cayenne hot sauce whisked into melted butter with vinegar and garlic. Toss it with wings, cauliflower or chicken, or use it as a dip.
item.content:encoded:
Buffalo sauce is two ingredients and a few seasonings: a vinegary cayenne hot sauce and butter. It is said to have come from the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, New York, in the 1960s, where chicken wings were fried and tossed in it, and it has since spread from the wings to cauliflower, chicken sandwiches, pizza and dips. The ratio decides the heat. More butter makes it milder and richer, and less makes it sharper and thinner. The butter also makes the sauce cling to fried food and gives it its orange colour. It has to be warm when it is whisked, so that the butter and the hot sauce form a smooth emulsion, and it should never boil. This makes about 200 ml, enough to coat 1 kg of wings, and it keeps for a fortnight in the fridge.

  • Whisk the sauce while it is warm and do not boil it. Boiling breaks the butter away from the hot sauce and leaves an oily layer.
  • Toss the wings while they are still hot. Hot food takes up the sauce, and cold food leaves it in the bowl.
  • Stir or shake the sauce before using it again. The butter sets in the fridge and separates as it warms.

item.title: Chimichurri
item.description: Chimichurri: finely chopped parsley, garlic, oregano and chilli in red wine vinegar and olive oil, the fresh green sauce of the Argentine barbecue.
item.content:encoded:
Chimichurri is the sauce that goes with everything at an Argentine asado, spooned over grilled steak, sausages and provolone, and it is one of the simplest sauces there is: parsley, garlic, oregano, chilli, vinegar and olive oil. The name has several explanations, none of them confirmed. The parsley is chopped by hand and finely, because a food processor turns it to a paste and bruises it, and the garlic is crushed with the salt to a smooth paste so that no one bites into a raw lump. The sauce needs half an hour to stand, which softens the garlic and lets the vinegar and oil bring the herbs together, and it is better after a few hours. There is a red version, chimichurri rojo, which adds red pepper and paprika.

  • Chop the parsley by hand. A food processor bruises it and turns the sauce into a dark, wet paste.
  • Dry the leaves thoroughly after washing. Water dilutes the vinegar and makes the sauce look dull.
  • For chimichurri rojo, add 1 tablespoon of sweet paprika and 2 tablespoons of finely chopped red pepper from a jar.

item.title: Turkey Gravy
item.description: Turkey gravy: a smooth roux of turkey fat and flour whisked with hot stock and the roasting-tin juices. Rich, lump-free gravy for the holiday table.
item.content:encoded:
The gravy is the last thing made for a roast turkey and the most stressful, because everything else is ready and waiting. It is simpler than it looks. Fat from the roasting tin is cooked with flour into a roux, which is whisked with hot stock and the dark, salty juices left in the tin, and simmered until it coats a spoon. The browned bits stuck to the tin are where the flavour is, so the tin is put on the hob and scraped. The stock goes in hot and a ladle at a time, which is what keeps the gravy smooth. The drippings are salty, and the gravy reduces as it simmers, so it is seasoned at the end and never at the start. This makes about 800 ml, enough for eight people.

  • Add the stock hot and a ladle at a time. Cold stock poured onto a roux is what makes lumps.
  • Season at the end. The juices are salty and the gravy reduces, so salt added early makes it too salty.
  • No drippings? Roast 1 kg of turkey wings with an onion at 200°C for an hour, cover with water and simmer for an hour, and use that stock and the wing fat.

item.title: Pan-Seared Ribeye Steak
item.description: Pan-seared ribeye steak: dry-brined, seared in a hot cast iron pan and basted with garlic and thyme butter for a dark crust and a juicy, pink middle.
item.content:encoded:
Ribeye is the steak that is worth cooking well. It is cut from the rib, and it has more fat running through it than sirloin or fillet, with a cap of tender fat around the outside, which is why it is so juicy and so flavourful. Cooking it well is a matter of four things: a thick steak, salt applied early, a very hot pan, and a rest. Salting the steak and leaving it uncovered in the fridge dries the surface, and a dry surface browns fast instead of steaming. Cast iron holds the heat when the cold steak hits it. The butter, garlic and thyme go in at the end and are spooned over the steak as it finishes, so they perfume the meat without burning. A steak this thick takes about 8 minutes in the pan, and it needs 8 more to rest.

  • Salt the steak at least 45 minutes ahead and leave it uncovered in the fridge. The salt draws out moisture, the surface dries, and the steak browns instead of steaming.
  • Take the steak off the heat 3 to 5 degrees below the temperature you want. It keeps cooking while it rests.
  • Turn the extractor fan on and open a window. A pan hot enough to sear a steak smokes.

item.title: Chicken Casserole
item.description: Chicken casserole: tender chicken, rice, mushrooms and broccoli in a from-scratch cheddar sauce, topped with buttery crumbs and baked until golden.
item.content:encoded:
In Britain a chicken casserole is a stew, chicken simmered in a pot with vegetables and stock. In America it is a baked dish, a whole meal in one tin, and this is the American one. Chicken, rice, mushrooms and broccoli go into a dish with a cheddar sauce and are baked under a crust of buttered crumbs. Traditionally the sauce comes from a can of condensed soup, and this one is made from butter, flour, milk and stock, which takes 6 minutes more and tastes of cheese and chicken and not of the tin. The rice is boiled for 8 minutes first, so that it finishes cooking in the sauce and does not stay hard. It is a dish to make ahead, since it can be assembled a day before and baked when it is needed.

  • Boil the rice for a few minutes first. Raw rice in a baked casserole is often still hard when the chicken is done.
  • Cut the broccoli into small florets. Large pieces stay raw in the middle while the sauce bakes.
  • If the rice is still firm after the covered bake, stir in 100 ml of hot stock, cover again and bake for 10 minutes more.

item.title: Crispy Chicken Tenders
item.description: Crispy chicken tenders: strips of chicken brined in buttermilk, coated in seasoned flour and shallow-fried until golden, craggy and juicy inside.
item.content:encoded:
A good chicken tender is a strip of breast that is juicy in the middle and covered in a crust that is properly crisp and full of craggy bits, and it is nothing like the uniform, pale nuggets from a freezer. Two things do it. The buttermilk brine seasons the chicken all the way through and its acidity tenderises the meat, which is why lean breast stays moist. And the flour is worked with a little of the buttermilk before the chicken goes in, which leaves small clumps that fry into the crunchy bits. The tenders are shallow-fried in a moderate amount of oil, at 175°C, in batches, and drained on a rack, not on paper towels, so that the underside stays crisp. The same method makes nuggets: cut the chicken into 3 cm pieces and fry for 2 to 3 minutes.

  • Rub a few spoonfuls of buttermilk into the flour. It makes the small clumps that fry into the crunchy, craggy bits.
  • Keep the oil at 175°C. If it is cooler the coating soaks up oil, and if it is hotter the crust darkens before the middle is cooked.
  • Drain the tenders on a wire rack. On paper towels the underside steams and loses its crispness.

item.title: Pan-Seared Pork Chops
item.description: Pan-seared pork chops: thick bone-in chops brined briefly, seared in a hot pan and basted with garlic and thyme butter until golden, juicy and just cooked.
item.content:encoded:
Pork chops have a reputation for being dry, and the reason is that they are overcooked and under-seasoned. Modern pork is lean, and a chop cooked past 63°C turns tough and pale. Three habits fix it. A short brine of salt and sugar in water, 30 minutes for chops of this thickness, seasons the meat through and helps it hold on to its juice. The chop is cooked in a very hot pan, so that it browns before the centre overheats. And the thermometer decides when it is done, not the clock: 63°C in the thickest part, then a 5-minute rest, in which it climbs a few degrees more. A little pink in the middle at that temperature is normal and safe. Butter, garlic and thyme go in at the end and are spooned over the chops for the last minute or two.

  • Brine for no longer than 30 minutes. Chops left in salty water for hours turn spongy and taste cured.
  • Dry the chops thoroughly after brining. A wet surface steams, and the chop goes grey instead of golden.
  • Take them off the heat at 63°C. The chop climbs a few degrees while it rests, and every degree beyond that dries it out.

item.title: Bacon-Wrapped Pork Tenderloin
item.description: Bacon-wrapped pork tenderloin: pork rubbed with brown sugar and paprika, wrapped in streaky bacon and roasted until the bacon is crisp and the pork is juicy.
item.content:encoded:
Pork tenderloin is lean and cooks quickly, which is why it is easy to dry out, and bacon is the answer to both problems: it bastes the meat with its own fat as it roasts and gives a crisp, salty, smoky crust that the tenderloin does not have by itself. The trick is that the two cook at different speeds, and the bacon needs more heat than the pork does. So the wrapped tenderloins are seared in a pan on the seam to set the bacon, roasted in a hot oven until the pork reaches 63°C, and put under the grill for a few minutes to crisp the top. A rub of brown sugar, paprika and garlic caramelises against the bacon. Use thin, streaky bacon, since thick rashers do not crisp before the pork is done.

  • Use thin, streaky bacon. Thick bacon is still soft and pale when the pork is done, and thin bacon crisps.
  • Sear the tenderloins on the bacon seam first. It sets the bacon so that it does not unroll in the oven.
  • Rest the pork for 10 minutes before slicing. Cut too soon, the juices run out onto the board.

item.title: Seared Ahi Tuna
item.description: Seared ahi tuna: sesame-crusted steaks seared for a minute a side, rare in the middle and sliced with a soy, ginger and rice vinegar dipping sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Seared ahi is a restaurant dish that is easier at home than it looks. A thick tuna steak is coated in sesame seeds, laid in a smoking-hot pan for about a minute on each side and sliced. The outside is browned and nutty and the middle is raw, cool and ruby red, which is how tuna is best eaten: past medium it turns dry and tastes like tinned. It only works with the right fish. Buy tuna sold as sushi or sashimi grade, cut thick, at least 2.5 cm, from a fishmonger you trust, since a raw centre depends on the freshness of the fish. The pan has to be very hot before the fish goes in, and the steaks need to be dry. Pregnant women, the elderly and anyone with a weakened immune system should not eat fish that is raw in the middle.

  • Buy tuna sold for eating raw, and cook it the day you buy it. Tuna that is raw in the middle needs to be very fresh.
  • Get the pan hotter than you think. A pan that is not smoking steams the tuna, turns it grey and cooks it right through.
  • Slice with the sharpest, thinnest knife you have, in one pull. Sawing tears the soft flesh.

item.title: Grilled Shrimp Skewers
item.description: Grilled shrimp skewers: large shrimp marinated in garlic, lemon, smoked paprika and olive oil, then grilled for a few minutes until pink and lightly charred.
item.content:encoded:
Shrimp are the fastest thing you can put on a grill, and the fastest thing to ruin. They go from translucent to pink in about two minutes a side, and they are overcooked the moment they curl tight into an O. A loose C is the sign that they are done. The marinade is simple and does not take long. Olive oil keeps the shrimp from drying on the grill, garlic and lemon give it brightness, and smoked paprika and a little chilli give it the smoky, slightly spicy edge that makes a grilled shrimp taste of the grill. Fifteen minutes is enough, since the lemon juice starts to cook the shrimp if it is left much longer, and they turn mealy. Threading two skewers through each row of shrimp, side by side, stops them spinning when you turn them.

  • Watch the shape. A loose C means the shrimp are cooked, and a tight O means that they are overdone and rubbery.
  • Marinate for no more than 30 minutes. The lemon juice starts to cook the shrimp and makes the texture mushy.
  • Heat the grate fully and oil it well before the skewers go on. Shrimp stick to a cold or dry grate and tear when they are turned.

item.title: Apple Fritters
item.description: Apple fritters: diced apple and cinnamon in a thick batter, fried until crisp and craggy, then dipped in a sweet vanilla glaze. A doughnut-shop classic.
item.content:encoded:
An apple fritter is a doughnut with the discipline taken out. There is no cutter and no ring, only a thick, lumpy batter full of diced apple, dropped into hot oil, where it spreads into an irregular shape with lots of craggy edges that fry crisp. Those edges and the glaze on top are what people come for. This is the quick, baking-powder kind, made without yeast, so it is ready to fry in 15 minutes and the whole batch is glazed in under an hour. Firm apples matter: a tart, crisp apple such as a Granny Smith holds its shape and its tang against the sugar, and a soft apple collapses to purée. The apples are cut small, about 1 cm, so that they cook through in the two and a half minutes the fritters need. The glaze goes on while they are still warm and sets to a thin crackle.

  • Use a firm, tart apple such as Granny Smith. Soft apples turn to purée in the batter and the fritters go soggy.
  • Keep the oil at 175°C. If it is too cool the fritters soak up oil, and if it is too hot they brown before the apple is cooked.
  • Dip the fritters in the glaze while they are warm, not hot. A hot fritter melts the glaze and it runs off instead of setting.

item.title: Bagel and Lox
item.description: Bagel and lox: a toasted bagel with cream cheese, cured salmon, red onion, capers, tomato and dill. The New York deli breakfast, ready in 13 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Bagel and lox is a breakfast of the Jewish delicatessens of New York, and it depends on the quality of a few things and on the order in which they go on. Lox is salmon cured in salt, not smoked, and it is silky, salty and mild; the smoked salmon that most shops sell as lox is a cousin of it, and works well too. The bagel is toasted, so that it is crisp on the outside and chewy in the middle. Plain cream cheese goes on first, in a generous layer, to make a base and hold the salmon in place. Then come the salmon, thin slices of red onion, capers, tomato and cucumber if you like, and dill and black pepper on top, with a squeeze of lemon. It is eaten open-faced or closed, and it is the better for being made just before you eat it.

  • Soften the cream cheese first. Cold cream cheese tears the bagel as you spread it.
  • Slice the onion paper thin and soak it in cold water for 5 minutes if it is strong.
  • Assemble just before eating. The salmon and vegetables soften the toasted bagel within a few minutes.

item.title: Chicken Tetrazzini
item.description: Chicken tetrazzini: spaghetti, chicken, mushrooms and peas in a creamy Parmesan sauce, topped with crisp breadcrumbs and baked until golden and bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken tetrazzini is named, it is said, after the Italian opera singer Luisa Tetrazzini, who was a star in San Francisco in the early twentieth century, and it is an American dish, not an Italian one. It is a way of using cooked chicken, and in many homes it is what happens to a roast chicken or a Thanksgiving turkey on the day after. Spaghetti, chicken, mushrooms and peas are bound in a cream sauce made with Parmesan, put into a dish under a layer of Parmesan and crumbs, and baked. The sauce is a plain white sauce, made with butter, flour, stock and milk, and it needs to be a little looser than you want it, since the pasta soaks it up in the oven. The spaghetti is boiled for two minutes less than the packet says, so that it finishes cooking in the dish.

  • Boil the spaghetti for 2 minutes less than the packet says. It keeps cooking in the oven and would be soft if it were fully cooked first.
  • Make the sauce looser than you think it should be. The pasta absorbs a lot of it while it bakes.
  • A splash of dry sherry or white wine, added to the mushrooms and cooked away, is the traditional flavour if you want it.

item.title: Manicotti
item.description: Manicotti: pasta tubes filled with ricotta, spinach and Parmesan, then baked in marinara under melted mozzarella until bubbling. An Italian-American classic.
item.content:encoded:
Manicotti means little muffs, and the name is used in America for large tubes of pasta, stuffed with cheese and baked in tomato sauce. It is an Italian-American dish, related to the cannelloni of Italy but made with dried pasta tubes, ricotta and mozzarella. There are two problems with it, and both are easy to solve. The tubes tear if they are boiled to softness, so they go into the water for only 6 minutes, less than the packet says, and finish cooking in the oven. And they are hard to fill with a spoon. The way to fill them is to put the mixture in a piping bag, or a large freezer bag with a corner cut off, and squeeze it into the tube from one end. The spinach makes the filling lighter and adds colour, and it has to be squeezed dry.

  • Undercook the tubes. They finish in the oven, and a tube boiled soft tears when you fill it.
  • Squeeze the spinach as dry as you can. Any water left in it comes out in the oven and thins the sauce.
  • Pipe the filling in. It is quicker than spooning, and the tubes do not split.

item.title: Queso Dip
item.description: Queso dip: a smooth, pourable Tex-Mex cheese dip of Monterey Jack, cheddar, evaporated milk and green chiles that stays creamy without processed cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Queso, or chile con queso, is the Tex-Mex cheese dip that sits in the middle of the table with a bowl of tortilla chips, and most restaurant versions are made with processed cheese, which melts smooth and does not set hard as it cools. Real cheese melts into strings and goes grainy when it cools, and it needs help. The help here is evaporated milk, which has proteins that stabilise the cheese, and a spoonful of cornflour, which stops the cheese from separating. Monterey Jack melts smoothly and mildly, and a little mature cheddar gives it flavour. The dip is made in a saucepan in a few minutes and can sit over a low heat, or in a slow cooker, for an hour or two. The cheese has to be grated by hand from a block, since pre-grated cheese is coated in starch that keeps it from melting.

  • Grate the cheese from a block. Pre-grated cheese is coated with starch and does not melt as smoothly.
  • Keep the heat low once the cheese goes in. Hot cheese sauce turns grainy and oily.
  • If the dip thickens on standing, stir in a splash of milk over low heat.

item.title: Chicken Enchilada Soup
item.description: Chicken enchilada soup: shredded chicken, black beans and corn in a smoky red enchilada broth thickened with masa, finished with lime and topped with cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken enchilada soup takes the flavours of a plate of enchiladas, the red chilli sauce, the cumin, the cheese, the chicken and the corn tortilla, and turns them into a bowl of soup. The base is a broth of stock, tomatoes and enchilada sauce, spiced with chilli powder, cumin and smoked paprika. The chicken is poached in the soup itself, so it is tender and flavours the broth, and then it is shredded and returned. A spoonful of masa harina, the corn flour used for tortillas, stirs into the soup and thickens it and gives it the flavour of corn tortillas, which nothing else does. Lime juice and fresh coriander go in at the end. The toppings are half of it: melted cheese, avocado, sour cream and crisp tortilla strips.

  • Poach the chicken in the soup. It flavours the broth and shreds easily once cooked.
  • Mix the masa harina with cold water before it goes in. Added dry, it makes lumps.
  • Add the lime juice and coriander at the end. Their fresh flavour fades if they cook.

item.title: Stuffed Peppers with Beef and Rice
item.description: Stuffed peppers with beef and rice: sweet bell peppers filled with seasoned beef, tomato and rice, baked in tomato sauce and finished with melted cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Stuffed peppers are the American kind of the dish: bell peppers filled with ground beef, rice and tomato, baked in a dish with sauce, and topped with cheese. They are different from the Greek and Middle Eastern ones, which are filled with rice and herbs and no meat, but the idea is the same, a vegetable that serves as its own container. Three things make them good. The peppers are blanched for a few minutes first, so that they are soft by the time the filling is cooked, and not still raw and crunchy. The filling is cooked before it goes in and only heated through in the oven, so there is no risk of raw meat in the middle. And they are baked standing in a little tomato sauce, which keeps the tops from drying out and makes a sauce to eat them with.

  • Boil the peppers first. Raw peppers baked with the filling stay firm and crunchy, and the filling overcooks while they soften.
  • Drain the tomatoes. Wet filling makes the peppers watery and the cheese slide off.
  • Choose peppers that stand on their own. A thin slice off the base helps a wobbly one.

item.title: Sourdough Pancakes
item.description: Sourdough pancakes: fluffy, lightly tangy pancakes made with sourdough discard and a pinch of bicarbonate. A good use for the starter you would throw away.
item.content:encoded:
Anyone who keeps a sourdough starter throws a good deal of it away, and pancakes are the best use for it. The starter brings a mild tang, like buttermilk, and a little flavour of fermented flour, and it makes the pancakes tender. It also makes the batter acidic, which is where bicarbonate of soda comes in. The acid and the bicarbonate react when they meet and give off carbon dioxide, and that is what makes the pancakes light and fluffy. So the bicarbonate goes in last, and the pancakes go on the griddle at once, before the bubbles have escaped. The starter does not have to be active, and discard that has sat in the fridge for a week works as well. The pancakes are not sour. They taste of pancakes, with a faint tang that is nice with maple syrup.

  • Add the bicarbonate last and cook straight away. Once it meets the acid in the starter it starts to fizz, and the lift is gone within minutes.
  • Cook on medium heat. The pancakes are thick, and high heat browns them before the middles are cooked.
  • If the batter is too thick to pour, stir in a splash of milk. Starters vary in thickness.

item.title: Ricotta Pancakes
item.description: Ricotta pancakes: thick, creamy, tender pancakes made with ricotta, lemon zest and whisked egg whites, served with berries and honey. Ready in 25 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Ricotta pancakes are thick, soft and creamy in the middle, with a texture somewhere between a pancake and a soufflé, and they hardly need any flour. The ricotta gives them body and a little tang, and it keeps the crumb moist, and the whisked egg whites, folded in at the end, are what make them rise and stay light. There is only enough flour to hold it together, so the batter is delicate, and the pancakes are cooked over medium-low heat, in a pan that is not too hot, so that the middle sets before the outside darkens. Lemon zest lifts the flavour and keeps the richness in check. They are usually made small and thick, a scoop at a time, and served in a stack with berries and honey.

  • Fold the whites in gently. Stirring knocks out the air, and the pancakes turn flat and dense.
  • Cook over medium-low heat. The pancakes are thick and delicate, and high heat browns the outside before the inside is set.
  • Drain the ricotta in a sieve for 15 minutes if it is watery. Wet ricotta makes the batter loose.

item.title: Hash Brown Bake
item.description: Hash brown bake: a crisp base of grated potato topped with bacon, onion, cheddar and a savoury egg custard, baked until golden and set. Serves a crowd.
item.content:encoded:
A hash brown bake is a breakfast dish for a crowd, made in a single dish. The crust is grated potato pressed into the tin and baked until the edges crisp, the filling is bacon, cheese and onion, and the top is a savoury egg custard that sets around it all. The potatoes have to be squeezed as dry as you can get them, because any water that stays in them makes the base soggy and pale. The crust goes into the oven on its own for 25 minutes before anything is added to it, which sets it and gives it a chance to brown. There is no flour and no bread, so it is gluten-free as written. It cuts into squares and reheats well, so it is a good dish to make the day before a busy morning and warm on the day.

  • Squeeze the grated potato until no more water comes out. Wet potato makes a soft, pale base.
  • Bake the base alone first. It sets the crust so that the egg does not soak into it.
  • Cut into squares after the rest. A hot bake is soft and does not hold its shape.

item.title: Brussels Sprouts with Bacon
item.description: Brussels sprouts with bacon: halved sprouts roasted in bacon fat until caramelised and crisp, then tossed with crisp bacon pieces, garlic and lemon juice.
item.content:encoded:
Most people who dislike Brussels sprouts have only had them boiled, and boiled sprouts are the problem: a sprout that is cooked in water for too long releases sulphur compounds and turns grey, soft and bitter. Roasted, cut side down at a high temperature, they are a different vegetable. The cut faces caramelise to a deep brown, the outer leaves turn crisp and nutty, and the middle goes soft and sweet. Bacon is the natural partner, since its smoky saltiness balances the bitterness, and it cooks the sprouts in its own fat. Here the bacon is cooked separately until crisp, and some of the fat is used to coat the sprouts before they go into the oven, so that both are at their best. A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts it all.

  • Put the tray in the oven to heat first. A hot tray browns the cut faces at once, and a cold one steams them.
  • Lay the sprouts cut side down and do not crowd the tray. Sprouts packed together steam and turn soft.
  • Add the garlic late. It burns and turns bitter if it roasts for the full time.

item.title: Cornbread Dressing
item.description: Cornbread dressing: crumbled cornbread, onion, celery and sage soaked in stock and baked until crisp on top and moist inside. The Southern holiday side dish.
item.content:encoded:
In the American South the side dish that goes with the turkey is called dressing, not stuffing, and it is made with cornbread and not white bread. It is baked in a dish, not in the bird, so it can be made ahead and its top gets crisp. The base is plain, unsweetened cornbread, baked a day early, and crumbled, and it soaks up stock and turns to something between a savoury pudding and a bread stuffing, with a crisp crust. Onion, celery and sage are cooked in butter, and eggs bind everything. The most important step is the stock: the mixture should be very wet before it goes into the oven, wetter than looks right, since the cornbread drinks it and the oven dries it. It should look like a thick porridge, and it bakes to a moist, sliceable dressing.

  • Make the mixture wetter than looks right. The cornbread absorbs a lot of stock, and the oven dries the top.
  • Bake the cornbread a day ahead, or dry it in a low oven. Fresh cornbread turns to paste when it is soaked.
  • For a crisper top, bake uncovered for the whole time. If it browns too fast, cover it loosely with foil.

item.title: Parker House Rolls
item.description: Parker House rolls: soft, buttery, folded dinner rolls baked packed together in a tin and brushed with butter and flaky salt. The Boston hotel classic.
item.content:encoded:
Parker House rolls are named after a Boston hotel, the Parker House, where they are said to have been made from the nineteenth century, and they are the soft, buttery, slightly sweet dinner rolls of the American holiday table. They are recognisable by their shape. A round of dough is creased just off centre with the back of a knife and folded over, so that the bigger half sits over the smaller one, and the rolls are packed side by side in a tin, where they rise into each other and bake as a sheet of soft, pull-apart rolls. The dough is enriched with milk, egg and a good deal of butter, and each roll is brushed with melted butter before it is folded, which is why the layers come apart so easily. They are finished with more butter and a little flaky salt.

  • Brush every round with butter before folding. It keeps the folded halves from sticking and lets the rolls pull apart.
  • Roll the dough to 1 cm and no thinner. Thin dough makes flat rolls that dry out.
  • Pack the rolls close together. They rise against each other and stay soft.

item.title: Saskatoon Berry Pie
item.description: Saskatoon berry pie: a flaky double-crust pie filled with dark saskatoon berries, sugar and lemon, with a hint of almond. The Prairie summer pie.
item.content:encoded:
The saskatoon is a small, dark purple berry that grows wild across the Canadian Prairies, on shrubs that flower in spring and fruit in July, and saskatoon pie is the dish that everyone who lives there has an opinion about. The berries look like blueberries and taste like a blueberry crossed with an almond, sweet and a little nutty, with crunchy tiny seeds that add to the flavour. They are related to apples and pears. The filling here is very simple: berries, sugar, cornflour, lemon and a drop of almond extract. Saskatoons are sold fresh and frozen in Western Canada and are hard to find elsewhere, and blueberries make a good pie with the same method. The pastry is all-butter and kept cold, so it bakes flaky, and the pie must cool completely before it is cut, or the filling runs.

  • Keep the butter cold and work quickly. Butter that melts into the flour makes a tough, greasy crust.
  • Cook the pie until the filling bubbles thickly through the slits. A pie that is pulled out too early has a runny filling.
  • If you use blueberries, add a handful of chopped apple for pectin, and a little more almond extract to match the saskatoon flavour.

item.title: Bullet Soup
item.description: Bullet soup: a Métis soup of small floured beef meatballs, potatoes, carrots and macaroni in a broth thickened by the flour. Served with bannock.
item.content:encoded:
Bullet soup is a Métis dish of the Canadian Prairies, and the name has nothing to do with guns. It comes from the French word boulettes, which means little meatballs, and the meatballs in this soup are small and round, about the size of a large marble. The meat is mixed with grated onion, salt and pepper, rolled into balls and dredged in flour, then put into the pot with cold water and brought to the boil. The flour on the meatballs comes off into the broth and thickens it into a light, silky gravy, which is the character of the soup. Vegetables and pasta go in as it simmers. It is a soup made in large pots for families and gatherings, and it is often made for New Year. It is eaten with bannock, to dip into the broth.

  • Start the meatballs in cold liquid and bring it up slowly. The flour comes off gradually and thickens the broth, and the meatballs hold together.
  • Keep the meatballs small, about 2.5 cm. Larger ones need longer, and the vegetables overcook.
  • Add the pasta near the end. It keeps swelling in the broth and soaks it up, so the soup is thickest on the day it is made.

item.title: Three Sisters Stew
item.description: Three sisters stew: squash, sweetcorn and beans, the three crops grown together by Indigenous peoples of North America, simmered with tomato and sage. Vegan.
item.content:encoded:
The three sisters are corn, beans and squash, and they are grown together by many Indigenous peoples of North America, including the Haudenosaunee. The corn stalk gives the bean vine something to climb, the beans put nitrogen back into the soil, and the broad leaves of the squash shade the ground and keep the weeds down. They also make a balanced meal, since corn and beans together give a complete protein. The three are cooked together in many forms across many nations, as soups, stews and baked dishes, and there is no single recipe. This one is a general stew, in the way it is often cooked now, with onion, tomato and sage, and it is vegan. The squash is cut into large pieces so that it holds its shape, and a few pieces are mashed against the side of the pot to thicken the broth.

  • Cut the squash into 2 cm cubes. Smaller pieces fall apart in the stew and thicken it too much.
  • Mash a few pieces of squash into the broth. It thickens the stew without flour.
  • Use dried beans if you prefer them. Soak them, cook them until tender first, and use their cooking water in place of some of the stock.

item.title: Maritime Blueberry Grunt
item.description: Maritime blueberry grunt: blueberries stewed in a covered pan with soft biscuit dumplings steamed on top. A Nova Scotia dessert, served hot with cream.
item.content:encoded:
A grunt is an old Maritime pudding, made on the stove and not in the oven, and it belongs to Nova Scotia and its neighbours, where wild blueberries grow. Blueberries are stewed with sugar in a wide pan until they are juicy, and biscuit-style dumplings are dropped on top, the pan is covered and the dumplings steam for 15 minutes. The name is said to come from the sound the berries make as they bubble. The dumplings are light on the top, where they steam, and dense and purple underneath, where the berry juice soaks in. The lid must stay on. Lifting it lets out the steam, and the dumplings go heavy. Grunts are eaten hot, with a spoonful of cream or a scoop of vanilla ice cream, and they are best on the day they are made.

  • Do not lift the lid while the dumplings steam. Lifting it lets out the steam, and the dumplings turn heavy and wet.
