  • Keep the berries at a gentle simmer. If they boil hard the dumplings sink and the juice catches on the pan.
  • Use a pan wide enough to hold the dumplings side by side. They puff up and stick together if they are crowded.

item.title: Garlic Fingers
item.description: Garlic fingers: pizza dough brushed with garlic butter, topped with mozzarella and baked until bubbling, then cut into strips. An Atlantic Canadian favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Garlic fingers are the side dish of the pizzerias of Atlantic Canada, and they are made from the same dough as the pizzas, stretched out flat, brushed with garlic butter, covered in mozzarella and baked. The result is cut across into fingers. They are not garlic bread, which is a length of baguette, and they are not a pizza either, since there is no sauce. They are chewy, buttery, cheesy and garlicky, and they are eaten hot, dipped in a sauce, most often donair sauce, the sweet and garlicky sauce of the Halifax donair. They are also good with marinara. The dough is a basic pizza dough that rises for an hour. The oven has to be very hot, and the pan or stone hot as well, so that the base crisps as the cheese melts.

  • Preheat the tray with the oven. A hot tray crisps the base while the cheese melts, and a cold one leaves it pale and soft.
  • Stretch the dough thin, about 5 mm. Thicker dough is bready in the middle and has less crust.
  • Cut the fingers as soon as they come out of the oven. When they cool, the cheese sets and the strips pull apart in strings.

item.title: Newfoundland Snowballs
item.description: Newfoundland snowballs: soft, chewy chocolate fudge balls of oats and coconut, made on the stove with no baking and rolled in shredded coconut.
item.content:encoded:
Newfoundland snowballs are a kitchen sweet of the province, and they are found on Christmas plates and at church sales. They are not made with snow, although they do look like it, rolled in white coconut. They are a soft, chewy chocolate fudge held together with oats and coconut. A syrup of sugar, butter and milk is boiled for a few minutes, poured over a dry mixture of oats, cocoa and coconut, and chilled until it can be rolled. Everything depends on the boil. Too short a boil gives balls that will not hold their shape, and too long a boil makes them hard and crumbly. Five minutes at a steady boil gets it right, and it should be timed from the moment it comes to a full bubble. They keep in the fridge for a week and freeze well.

  • Time the boil from the moment the syrup reaches a full rolling boil. Too short and the balls fall apart, and too long and they are dry.
  • Chill the mixture properly before rolling. Warm mixture is too soft and sticks to your hands.
  • Wet your hands with cold water for rolling. The mixture will not stick to them.

item.title: Cod Cakes
item.description: Cod cakes: flaked cod, mashed potato, onion and summer savory shaped into patties and pan-fried until golden and crisp. A Newfoundland classic.
item.content:encoded:
Cod cakes, or fish cakes, are a staple of Newfoundland cooking, from the time when cod was the province's main catch, and they are the way that a small piece of fish and a pot of potatoes feed a family. Traditionally they are made with salt cod, soaked, cooked with the potatoes and mashed, and this version uses fresh cod, which is easier to find. The fish and potato are mixed in about equal parts, with onion and summer savory, the herb that most Newfoundland cooks use, and thyme is a good substitute. They are shaped into thick cakes, dusted with flour and fried in a little oil until crisp on the outside and soft within. They are served with pickled beets, mustard pickles or tartar sauce, and often with scrunchions, fried salt pork, on top.

  • Dry the mashed potato well. Wet mash makes soft cakes that fall apart in the pan.
  • Chill the shaped cakes before frying. Cold cakes keep their shape and turn crisp.
  • Use salt cod if you have it. Soak it for 24 hours in several changes of water, boil it with the potatoes, and leave the added salt out.

item.title: Puffed Wheat Squares
item.description: Puffed wheat squares: puffed wheat bound with a boiled brown sugar, syrup, butter and cocoa mixture, pressed into a tin and cut into chewy chocolate squares.
item.content:encoded:
Puffed wheat squares, or puffed wheat cake, are a Prairie treat that turns up at potlucks, school bake sales and funeral lunches, and they are made from puffed wheat cereal, a boiled brown sugar and syrup mixture, and cocoa. They are not made with marshmallow, like the rice cereal treats. The binder here is a caramel, made by boiling brown sugar, syrup and butter for two minutes, and it sets to a chewy, sticky, chocolatey square that is much crunchier than a marshmallow one, because puffed wheat is so light and dry. The boil is short and gentle. Boil for longer and the squares set hard as toffee. They need only an hour in the fridge and can be made by a child with an adult at the stove.

  • Boil for only 2 minutes. A longer boil makes the syrup set hard, and the squares turn into toffee.
  • Work fast once the syrup is on the cereal. It sets as it cools and is hard to mix.
  • Press the mixture down firmly. Loose squares crumble when they are cut.

item.title: Schmoo Torte
item.description: Schmoo torte: a Winnipeg dessert of light pecan sponge layered with whipped cream and toasted pecans, then drizzled with homemade butterscotch sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Schmoo torte is a dessert from Winnipeg, in Manitoba, and it is a special-occasion cake in Canada's Prairie provinces, served at weddings, at bar and bat mitzvahs and at family celebrations. The story goes that it was invented by a mother for her son's bar mitzvah. It is a light sponge cake made with toasted pecans, cut into three layers and filled with whipped cream, with more pecans between the layers and a butterscotch sauce poured over it. The sponge is aerated with whisked egg whites, so it is light, and there is very little flour in it. The torte is at its best after a couple of hours in the fridge, when the cream has soaked into the sponge and everything has settled, and it is cut with a serrated knife.

  • Fold the whisked whites in gently. The sponge has almost no flour, and it relies on the air in the whites for its lift.
  • Cut the cooled sponge with a serrated knife, using a gentle sawing motion. A warm sponge crumbles.
  • Chill the assembled torte for at least 2 hours. The cream soaks into the sponge and the layers slice cleanly.

item.title: Maple Walnut Cake
item.description: Maple walnut cake: two soft layers of maple syrup cake with toasted walnuts, filled and covered in maple buttercream and topped with walnut halves.
item.content:encoded:
Maple and walnut is one of the oldest flavour pairings in the maple-producing regions of Canada and the northeastern United States, and it is used in ice cream, fudge, pies and cakes. The maple syrup in this cake does more than sweeten it. It keeps the crumb moist, because it is a liquid sugar, and it gives a deep, caramel flavour that white sugar cannot. The walnuts are toasted first, which brings out their oils and takes away their bitterness. The buttercream is made with maple syrup as well and is beaten until it is light and pale. Use dark maple syrup labelled robust taste in Canada, or Dark Color, Robust Flavor in the United States, and not the pale kind, whose flavour disappears in baking. The cake is made in two 20 cm tins and needs to cool completely before it is filled.

  • Use dark maple syrup. Pale syrup loses its flavour when it is baked.
  • Toast the walnuts first. It brings out their flavour and takes away the bitterness of the skins.
  • Cool the layers completely before filling. Warm cake melts the buttercream and slides.

item.title: Maple Fudge
item.description: Maple fudge: pure maple syrup and cream boiled to soft-ball, cooled and beaten until thick, then set in a tin and cut into smooth, creamy squares.
item.content:encoded:
Maple fudge is a sugar-shack sweet, made in Québec, Ontario and the Maritimes from the syrup itself, and it is one of the few fudges that contains no chocolate and no white sugar. Pure maple syrup and cream are boiled together to 112°C, the soft-ball stage, then cooled without stirring and beaten until they turn from glossy to thick and dull. The cooling and beating decide whether the fudge is smooth or grainy. Beaten while it is hot, the sugar forms large crystals and the fudge is gritty, and cooled to about 43°C first, it forms tiny ones and sets creamy. Use a deep pan, because maple syrup foams up as it boils, and a candy thermometer. It makes about 36 small pieces and keeps for a week.

  • Use a deep, heavy pan of at least 3 litres. Maple syrup and cream foam up a long way as they boil.
  • Cool the fudge to 43°C before beating. Beaten hot, it forms large sugar crystals and turns gritty.
  • Beat until it loses its gloss. If you stop while it is still shiny, it will not set.

item.title: Maple Glazed Donuts
item.description: Maple glazed donuts: soft, light yeast donuts fried until golden and dipped in a shiny glaze of maple syrup and icing sugar. A Canadian favourite.
item.content:encoded:
A maple glazed donut is a yeast donut, soft, light and slightly chewy, covered in a thin, shiny glaze that tastes of maple, and in Canada it is a doughnut-shop staple, next to honey crullers and Boston creams. The dough is enriched with milk, egg and butter, and scented with a little nutmeg, and it is proved twice, once as a mass and once after it is cut into rings, so that the donuts are puffy before they reach the oil. They fry in about 3 minutes in all, at 175°C, until the pale band round the middle shows they have risen properly. The glaze is made from icing sugar and maple syrup and is dipped while the donuts are still warm, so it goes on thin and sets to a shiny coat. Use dark maple syrup for a proper flavour.

  • Keep the oil at 175°C. If it is too cool the donuts soak up oil, and if it is too hot they brown outside and stay raw inside.
  • Let the cut donuts puff up before frying. Dense donuts that have not risen fry heavy and greasy.
  • Dip the donuts while they are warm, not hot. A hot donut melts the glaze and it runs off.

item.title: Pâté Chinois
item.description: Pâté chinois: layers of seasoned beef, sweetcorn and creamy mashed potato baked until golden. The Québec comfort dish, a cousin of shepherd's pie.
item.content:encoded:
Pâté chinois is the everyday casserole of Québec, and it has three layers: seasoned ground beef, a layer of corn, and mashed potatoes on top, baked until the edges are golden. It looks like a shepherd's pie, but the corn layer, which is usually creamed corn and whole kernels together, makes it a different dish, sweeter and softer. It is eaten with ketchup or with pickled beets. The name means Chinese pie, and where it comes from is not clear. One popular story ties it to the Chinese workers who built the railways in Canada, and another to the Chinese cooks of Maine, but no one has proved either. It is a dish for a weeknight, cheap and filling, and it reheats very well. The beef should be browned properly, and the potatoes mashed smooth, with butter.

  • Mash the potatoes until they are smooth and fairly stiff. Loose mash sinks into the corn.
  • Brown the beef properly and drain off any extra fat. Wet beef makes a soupy pâté.
  • Rough up the top of the potato with a fork. The ridges brown and crisp in the oven.

item.title: Salmon Chowder
item.description: Salmon chowder: a creamy chowder of salmon, potatoes, sweetcorn and bacon, seasoned with thyme and finished with fresh dill and lemon. A West Coast favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Salmon chowder is a dish of the Pacific coast of Canada and the northwestern United States, where salmon is the fish that everyone has in the freezer, and it is made in the same way as any chowder: bacon, onion, potatoes, milk and stock, and the fish added last. The point of adding it last is that salmon is delicate. It cooks in a few minutes in the hot chowder, and boiled for longer it turns dry and chalky. So the chunks go in for the final 6 minutes, and the pot is taken off the heat as soon as they turn opaque. Sweetcorn gives the chowder sweetness, and thyme, dill and lemon keep it from being heavy. A little of the potato is mashed against the pot to thicken it, so that no flour is needed beyond a spoonful.

  • Add the salmon last and cook it only until it turns opaque. Longer, and it turns dry and chalky.
  • Keep the chowder at a gentle simmer once the milk is in. A hard boil can curdle it.
  • Skin the salmon and check for pin bones with your fingertips before cutting it up.

item.title: Butter Tart Bars
item.description: Butter tart bars: a buttery shortbread base with the gooey brown sugar and egg filling of a Canadian butter tart, baked in a tin and cut into squares.
item.content:encoded:
A butter tart is a small pastry case filled with a sweet, runny filling of butter, brown sugar, syrup and egg, and it is one of Canada's best-known sweets. It is also fiddly. The pastry has to be rolled, cut and pressed into a tin, and the filling can boil over in the oven. Butter tart bars take the same filling and put it on a shortbread base in a single tin, which is baked, cooled and cut into squares, so that all of the filling is there and none of the fiddling. The base is pressed into the tin and baked first, so that it stays crisp under the filling. The filling is baked until it is just set, with a slight wobble in the middle, and it sets fully as it cools. Raisins and pecans are optional, and as in Canada, they are a matter of strong opinion.

  • Press the base firmly and bake it before the filling goes on. It keeps the base crisp under the wet filling.
  • Take the bars out while the centre still wobbles a little. They set as they cool, and overbaked ones are stiff and dry.
  • Cool the bars completely before cutting. A warm filling is runny and squeezes out of the sides.

item.title: Chicken and Chorizo Pasta
item.description: Chicken and chorizo pasta: chicken and Spanish chorizo in a smoky tomato and cream sauce with peppers and spinach, tossed through penne. A weeknight dinner.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken and chorizo is a pairing that Spanish cooks have been using for generations, and in Britain it has become a weeknight standard. The chorizo does most of the work. It is fried first in its own fat, and the fat turns red and smoky with paprika, and everything after it is cooked in that fat, so that the chicken, the peppers and the tomato sauce all taste of it. Use the hard, cured kind of chorizo, sold in a ring or a length, and not the soft, raw one. A little cream at the end softens the smoke and makes the sauce cling to the pasta, and spinach goes in for the last minute to wilt. The pasta is cooked separately in salted water and finished in the sauce with a splash of its cooking water, which is what makes it glossy.

  • Use cooking chorizo, the hard, cured kind. It renders its oil and holds its shape, and the soft raw kind breaks up.
  • Cook the chicken and vegetables in the chorizo oil. It gives the whole dish its red colour and smoky taste.
  • Add a splash of pasta water at the end. Its starch loosens the sauce and makes it glossy and clinging.

item.title: Cheese and Onion Quiche
item.description: Cheese and onion quiche: soft, sweet onions and mature cheddar in a set egg custard in a crisp shortcrust case. A picnic and salad-table classic.
item.content:encoded:
A cheese and onion quiche is the vegetarian quiche of British cooking, and it is served at picnics, buffets and Sunday lunches, cold or warm, with salad and potatoes. It has none of the bacon of a quiche Lorraine. The flavour comes from two things, onions cooked slowly in butter until they are soft, sweet and golden, and a good, sharp cheddar. The onions take 15 minutes and cannot be rushed, because onions that are only softened taste raw and sharp, and the moisture they release makes the custard watery. The pastry case is blind-baked first, so that it stays crisp under the filling. The custard is made of eggs, cream and milk, in about the proportion of one egg to 100 ml of liquid, which sets to a soft, silky filling that is just firm enough to slice.

  • Cook the onions slowly until they are golden. Onions that are only softened stay sharp, and the water in them leaks into the custard.
  • Blind-bake the case and let the onions cool a little before filling. A hot filling in a cold case turns the base soggy.
  • Take the quiche out when the middle still wobbles slightly. It sets as it rests, and overbaked custard turns rubbery.

item.title: Tim Tam Cake
item.description: Tim Tam cake: a moist chocolate cake with crushed Tim Tam biscuits baked in, sandwiched with ganache, covered in it and topped with whole biscuits.
item.content:encoded:
The Tim Tam is one of Australia's best-known chocolate biscuits, two chocolate malted biscuits with a chocolate cream between them, coated in more chocolate, and the Tim Tam cake is what the Australians do when there is a packet in the cupboard and a birthday to celebrate. The biscuits go in three places. Some are crushed into the batter, where they soften as the cake bakes and leave pockets of chocolate; some are set between the layers; and the rest are stuck upright round the edge or on the top. The cake itself is a simple, moist, oil-based chocolate cake, mixed in one bowl, with hot water to bring out the cocoa. The ganache is only chocolate and cream, warmed and left to thicken to a spreading consistency. Any chocolate-coated malted biscuit will work if you cannot find Tim Tams.

  • Whisk the hot water in last. It blooms the cocoa, and it makes a thin batter that gives a very moist crumb.
  • Let the ganache cool until it thickens. Warm ganache runs off the cake, and cold ganache is too stiff to spread.
  • Assemble the cake on the day. The biscuits soften against the ganache within a day.

item.title: Honeycomb
item.description: Honeycomb: sugar and golden syrup boiled to hard-crack, then foamed with bicarbonate of soda into a light, crunchy, golden candy. Also cinder toffee.
item.content:encoded:
Honeycomb is sugar that has been turned into foam. Sugar and golden syrup are boiled to 150°C, the hard-crack stage, and taken off the heat, and bicarbonate of soda is whisked in. It reacts with the acid in the hot sugar and gives off carbon dioxide, so that the mixture puffs up to several times its volume, and it sets in that state, full of tiny bubbles, into a light, brittle, crunchy candy that dissolves on the tongue. It has other names: cinder toffee in Britain, sponge toffee, and hokey pokey in New Zealand, and it is the centre of a chocolate bar, and the crunch in hokey pokey ice cream. It is very simple, and very hot. Molten sugar at 150°C causes severe burns, so use a large, deep pan, and keep children well back. The candy takes in moisture from the air quickly, so keep it airtight.

  • Use a large, deep pan. The mixture rises to several times its volume when the bicarbonate goes in.
  • Do not stir after the sugar has dissolved, and do not spread the foam in the tin. Both knock out the bubbles.
  • Store it airtight the same day. Honeycomb takes moisture from the air and turns sticky within hours.

item.title: Blueberry Bread Loaf
item.description: Blueberry bread loaf: a tender, moist loaf studded with blueberries and scented with lemon, baked with a crisp sugar crust on top. Easy and keeps well.
item.content:encoded:
A blueberry loaf is a quick bread, made with baking powder and not yeast, and it sits between a muffin and a cake: it is moist and tender like a muffin, with a fine crumb, and it slices. The batter is stirred together in a couple of bowls in ten minutes, and it can be baked in a loaf tin and eaten warm for breakfast or wrapped for a packed lunch. Lemon zest lifts the flavour of the berries. A few practices decide how it turns out. The berries are tossed in a spoonful of flour so that they stay suspended in the batter and do not sink. Frozen berries go in straight from the freezer, and are not thawed, since thawed berries bleed purple through the batter. And the sugar on top bakes into a light, crisp crust that contrasts with the soft crumb.

  • Toss the berries in flour before folding them in. The flour coating holds them up in the batter and stops them sinking to the bottom.
  • Add frozen berries straight from the freezer. Thawed ones bleed and turn the batter grey-purple.
  • Stir the batter only until it comes together. Overmixing develops the gluten and makes a tough, tunnelled loaf.

item.title: Raspberry and White Chocolate Muffins
item.description: Raspberry and white chocolate muffins: tall, tender bakery-style muffins with tart raspberries and chunks of white chocolate. Easy and made in one bowl.
item.content:encoded:
Raspberry and white chocolate is a pairing that is a fixture of Australian cafes: the tartness of the raspberries cuts through the sweetness of the white chocolate, and neither is heavy. These are made the way a bakery makes them, tall, with a domed top and a tender crumb. The dry and wet ingredients are mixed separately and stirred together only until they meet, since overmixed muffin batter is tough and tunnelled. The oven starts hot, at 200°C, for the first 5 minutes, which makes the batter spring up quickly into a high dome, and is then turned down so that the middles cook through before the tops darken. Frozen raspberries go in straight from the freezer, and stay whole. Chunks of white chocolate are best chopped from a bar, since chips are made to hold their shape and do not melt into pockets.

  • Mix the batter until it only just comes together. A lumpy batter gives tender muffins, and a smooth one gives tough ones.
  • Start the oven hot and turn it down after 5 minutes. The blast of heat makes the domed bakery-style top.
  • Do not thaw frozen raspberries. Thawed ones break up, bleed into the batter and make the muffins wet.

item.title: Honey Soy Baked Chicken
item.description: Honey soy baked chicken: thighs and drumsticks marinated in honey, soy sauce, garlic and ginger, then baked on one tray until sticky, dark and glossy.
item.content:encoded:
Honey soy chicken is a staple of Australian home cooking, and it is popular for a reason: the marinade is four things from the cupboard, it needs no attention, and the result is sweet, salty, sticky and dark. Honey and soy sauce are the base, garlic and ginger give it depth, and a splash of rice vinegar stops it being cloying. The honey caramelises on the skin in the oven, and the soy gives the glaze its dark colour. The chicken should be bone-in, on the skin, and the pieces are laid on a single layer on a tray, so that the skin is exposed to the heat. It is basted with the marinade once during baking, which builds the glaze. The dish bakes in 45 minutes, and it gives a little sauce in the tray, to be poured over rice.

  • Lay the chicken skin side up in one layer, with space between the pieces. Crowded chicken steams, and the skin does not colour.
  • Baste once halfway through. It builds the glaze, and a chicken that is basted too often has soggy skin.
  • Watch the last 10 minutes. The honey burns quickly, and the glaze turns from dark and glossy to bitter.

item.title: Honey Soy Chicken Stir-Fry
item.description: Honey soy chicken stir-fry: chicken strips with peppers, broccoli and snow peas in a glossy honey and soy sauce, cooked in a hot pan. Ready in 27 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
A stir-fry is a dish of speed, and its whole method is a matter of having everything ready and cooking each part at high heat for a short time. The chicken is sliced thin and tossed in cornflour, which gives it a light coating that keeps it tender and helps the sauce cling. It is cooked first, taken out, and the vegetables go in, hardest first, so that each ends up crisp and none is overcooked. The sauce is honey and soy sauce, with garlic, ginger, rice vinegar and a little cornflour to thicken it, and it goes in at the end and thickens in seconds. Everything is returned to the pan just long enough to heat through. It is best made in a wok or a very large frying pan, and in two batches if the pan is small, so that the food fries and does not steam.

  • Have everything cut and measured before the pan goes on. A stir-fry cooks in minutes, and there is no time to chop.
  • Cook the chicken in a single layer and in batches if you need to. If the pan is crowded the chicken steams and turns grey.
  • Add the vegetables in order of hardness. Carrot and broccoli need longer than pepper and snow peas.

item.title: San Choy Bow
item.description: San choy bow: savoury pork mince stir-fried with water chestnuts, mushrooms and hoisin, spooned into crisp lettuce cups and topped with crunchy noodles.
item.content:encoded:
San choy bow is a Cantonese dish that is well known in Australia, where it has been on the menu of Chinese restaurants for decades. The name means lettuce wrap in Cantonese, and it is a hot, savoury filling of minced pork, mushrooms and water chestnuts, wrapped in a cool, crisp lettuce leaf that is used as a cup. The filling is stir-fried until it is dry and well browned, and it is flavoured with hoisin, oyster sauce and soy sauce, garlic and ginger. The water chestnuts stay crunchy, and that crunch, the crisp lettuce and the crisp noodles on top are what set it apart from a pile of savoury mince. Iceberg lettuce is the traditional cup, since its leaves are crisp and hold their shape, and butter lettuce is a good substitute. It is eaten with the hands.

  • Cook the pork until it is dry and browned. Wet mince turns the lettuce cups soggy.
  • Dice the water chestnuts, mushrooms and carrot finely and evenly. They then cook at the same rate and sit neatly in the cups.
  • Fill the cups at the table. The hot filling wilts the lettuce if it sits.

item.title: One-Pot Lasagna
item.description: One-pot lasagna: broken lasagne sheets cooked right in a beef and tomato sauce in one skillet, finished with ricotta and melted mozzarella. No layering.
item.content:encoded:
A traditional lasagne takes hours: a meat sauce, a white sauce, a lot of layering and an hour in the oven. One-pot lasagna keeps what people like about it, the meat sauce, the pasta and the ricotta and mozzarella melted on top, and does it in one pan in about 35 minutes. The lasagne sheets are broken into pieces and cooked directly in the sauce, so the pasta takes up the flavour of the sauce and its starch thickens it, and there is no boiling and draining. The pan is covered while the pasta cooks and stirred every few minutes, to stop the pieces sticking. The ricotta goes on in spoonfuls at the end and the mozzarella melts over it under a lid. It is best in a deep, wide pan with a lid, and it needs more liquid than you might expect.

  • Stir every few minutes as the pasta cooks. The pieces settle and stick to the bottom of the pan.
  • Break the sheets into pieces about 5 cm across. Larger pieces overlap and cook unevenly.
  • Add a splash of hot stock if the pasta is still firm and the pan is dry. Different brands need different amounts of liquid.

item.title: Honey Soy Chicken Wings
item.description: Honey soy chicken wings: wings baked on a rack until crisp without frying, then tossed in a sticky honey, soy, garlic and ginger glaze with sesame seeds.
item.content:encoded:
The difficulty with baked wings is the skin, which has a lot of fat and water, and which turns leathery and pale in an oven when it should be crisp. The answer is baking powder, not the bicarbonate of soda but the kind with an acid in it. Tossed with salt and a little baking powder, the skin dries out and raises tiny blisters as the wings bake, and the surface crisps up much like a fried one. They are baked on a rack, so that hot air reaches all round, and turned once. The glaze goes on last, and it is not baked on: honey, soy sauce, garlic, ginger and rice vinegar are simmered for a few minutes until they thicken to a syrup, and the hot wings are tossed in it. Baked on, the honey would burn before the skin was crisp.

  • Use baking powder and not bicarbonate of soda, and check that it is aluminium-free. The wrong one leaves a metallic taste.
  • Dry the wings thoroughly and leave space between them on the rack. Wet, crowded wings steam and stay pale.
  • Glaze the wings after baking. Baked on, the honey burns before the skin is crisp.

item.title: Grilled Moreton Bay Bugs
item.description: Grilled Moreton Bay bugs: slipper lobsters split, brushed with garlic and lemon butter and grilled until just opaque. Lobster tails or langoustines also work.
item.content:encoded:
Moreton Bay bugs are a flat-headed lobster of the warm waters of northern Australia, and they are named after Moreton Bay, near Brisbane, where they were caught. They are also called slipper lobsters, and they have no claws. The meat is in the tail, and it is sweet and firm, somewhere between a lobster and a large prawn. They are usually cooked on the barbecue, and the simplest way is the best: split them lengthwise, brush the flesh with garlic butter and grill them, flesh side down first, for a few minutes each side, until they turn opaque. They take very little time and toughen if overcooked. Bugs are sold whole and raw, or already cooked, and they need to be raw here. Where they are not sold, raw lobster tails, split the same way, or large langoustines can be used.

  • Cook the bugs from raw. Ones that have already been cooked go rubbery when they are grilled again.
  • Grill them flesh side down first. It gives the flesh a little colour and seals in the juices.
  • Watch them closely. They go from opaque to tough in a minute or two.

item.title: Banana Cake with Chocolate Icing
item.description: Banana cake with chocolate icing: a moist, tender cake made with very ripe bananas and cinnamon, covered in a glossy chocolate icing. A cake-stall favourite.
item.content:encoded:
A banana cake is not a banana bread. It is lighter, with a finer, softer crumb, and it is iced, which turns it from a loaf that is eaten for breakfast into a cake for afternoon tea, a birthday or a school fete. The bananas do the work. They should be very ripe, with black skins, because as they ripen the starch turns to sugar and they become sweeter, softer and more fragrant, and they blend into the batter as a moist, smooth mash. The cake is made by creaming butter and sugar, in the traditional way, and the flour is added alternately with the milk and mashed banana so that the batter stays light. The chocolate icing goes on when the cake is completely cold. It is a plain, glossy icing made from icing sugar, cocoa, butter and milk.

  • Use bananas with black-spotted skins. Under-ripe bananas are starchy and make a bland, drier cake.
  • Fold the flour in gently, only until you cannot see any dry flour. Overmixing makes the cake tough.
  • Ice the cake only when it is completely cold. On a warm cake the icing melts and slides off.

item.title: Hāngī
item.description: Hāngī cooked in the oven: pork, kūmara, potato, pumpkin and cabbage steamed tender under foil and a wet cloth. A kitchen version of the earth-oven meal.
item.content:encoded:
A hāngī is the Māori way of cooking a feast in the ground. A pit is dug and lined with stones heated in a wood fire, baskets of meat and vegetables go on the hot stones, wet cloths and then earth are laid over the top, and everything cooks slowly in its own steam for several hours. The earth, the stones and the wood give it a flavour that a kitchen cannot fully copy, and it is best eaten at a real one, where it is cooked for a gathering. This oven version copies the part that a kitchen can, the long, moist cooking that leaves the pork falling apart and the vegetables soft and sweet. The pork sits in a deep tin under cabbage leaves, a wet tea towel and a tight seal of foil traps the steam, and the vegetables go in halfway through so that they end up tender but whole. Pork, kūmara, potato, pumpkin and cabbage are the classic foods, and chicken, lamb and a bread stuffing are often cooked alongside.

  • Seal the tin as tightly as you can. The steam does the cooking, and a tin that leaks dries the pork out.
  • Add the vegetables halfway through. In for the full three hours they fall apart in the juices, and this way they come out soft but still whole.
  • Use shoulder rather than loin. The fat and connective tissue in shoulder turn tender and juicy over three hours, and lean loin dries out.

item.title: Pāua Fritters
item.description: Pāua fritters: pounded, minced pāua (abalone) in a thick egg batter with onion and parsley, fried until golden. Serve with lemon and buttered white bread.
item.content:encoded:
Pāua is the New Zealand abalone, a sea snail with a large, muscular foot that is very tough as it comes off the rock. Its flesh is firm, sweet and mildly briny, and in New Zealand it is most often minced and fried into fritters, served with lemon, white bread and butter. Its toughness is the whole difficulty, and every step of the method is there to deal with it. The meat is pounded thin between sheets of plastic wrap until it goes limp, then minced in short pulses so that it stays in small pieces, and it is fried for only 2 to 3 minutes a side, because pāua that is cooked for longer turns tough again. The batter is thick, only just enough to bind the pieces. Pāua is sold cleaned by New Zealand fishmongers, and abalone from other coasts is handled in the same way.

  • Pound the pāua thin before mincing it. Skipping this step leaves the fritters rubbery, however finely the meat is chopped.
  • Mince in short pulses. A processor left running turns the meat into a paste and the fritters go dense.
  • Fry for 2 to 3 minutes a side and no longer. Pāua that is cooked for longer turns tough again.

item.title: Smoked Eel Pâté
item.description: Smoked eel pâté: hot-smoked eel blended with cream cheese, sour cream, lemon and horseradish into a rich, smoky spread. No cooking, and it keeps for days.
item.content:encoded:
Freshwater eel, tuna in Māori, has been eaten in New Zealand for centuries, and smoked eel is sold in delis and fishmongers across the country. Hot-smoked eel is oily, rich and firm, with a sweet smoky flavour, and it flakes much like smoked mackerel. That makes it very good in a pâté, because its own fat carries the flavour and all it needs is something soft to bind it, something sharp to cut through the richness, and something green. Cream cheese and a little sour cream give a smooth body, lemon and horseradish keep it from tasting heavy, and chives add freshness. There is no cooking, only flaking and blending, and the pâté is ready to eat in half an hour. Serve it thickly spread on crackers or dark rye bread with slices of cucumber, which are cool and crisp against the rich fish. Smoked mackerel or smoked trout can be used in the same way.

  • Check the fish for bones as you flake it. Smoked eel fillets have few, but a small one is unpleasant to find in a smooth spread.
  • Pulse rather than run the processor. A short blend leaves some texture, and a long one turns the pâté to a paste.
  • Season at the end. Smoked eel and horseradish are both salty and sharp, and it is easier to add more than to take it away.

item.title: Garlic Butter Crayfish
item.description: Garlic butter crayfish: rock lobster tails boiled in salted water until bright red, split and finished with hot garlic butter, lemon and parsley. Serves four.
item.content:encoded:
In New Zealand the crayfish is the rock lobster, a spiny lobster with no claws, called kōura in Māori. The town of Kaikōura on the South Island's east coast takes its name from it, kai meaning food and kōura crayfish. All the meat is in the tail, sweet, firm and delicate, and the best treatment for it is the simplest one: cook it briefly in well-salted water, split it and pour hot butter over the top. The boiling is the part to get right. Tails of this size cook in 8 to 10 minutes, and a minute too long tightens the meat. The butter is made while they cook. It is melted with plenty of garlic and a little chilli, softened over low heat and never browned, and the lemon juice and parsley go in at the end. Cold-water lobster tails cook in the same way, and large prawns need only 3 minutes.

  • Time the tails and taste one. A minute too long and crayfish goes firm and dry, and the meat should be only just opaque.
  • Salt the water well. It seasons the meat all the way through, and unsalted water leaves it bland.
  • Keep the garlic pale. Garlic that browns in the butter turns bitter and hides the sweetness of the meat.

item.title: Slow-Cooked Lamb Shanks in Red Wine
item.description: Slow-cooked lamb shanks in red wine: browned shanks braised in wine, stock, tomato and rosemary until the meat falls from the bone. Serve on mash.
item.content:encoded:
A lamb shank is the lower part of the leg. It is one of the toughest cuts and one of the cheapest, and it is one of the best, because it is packed with connective tissue and built around a marrow bone. Cooked quickly it is chewy. Cooked for hours in liquid at a low temperature, the connective tissue turns to gelatin and the meat becomes tender enough to slide off the bone, while the gelatin makes the sauce glossy and a little sticky. New Zealand is known for its lamb, and the shank is one of the ways it comes to a winter table, on mashed potato or kūmara with something green. The method is a plain braise. Brown the shanks hard, because that is where the flavour starts, soften onion, carrot and celery in the same pot, stir in tomato paste, then boil red wine down to take its raw edge off. Stock, rosemary, thyme and a spoonful of redcurrant jelly for gloss and a touch of sweetness go in next, and the last 30 minutes are uncovered so the sauce thickens.

  • Brown the shanks properly. The dark crust is where most of the sauce's flavour comes from, so do not crowd the pot.
  • Keep the oven at 160°C. A harder boil shrinks the meat and toughens it before the connective tissue has had time to melt.
  • Cook it the day before if you can. The shanks are better reheated in their sauce, and the fat sets on the cold sauce so it is easy to lift off.

item.title: Crispy Pork Belly with Kūmara Mash
item.description: Crispy pork belly with kūmara mash: salted, dried and slow-roasted belly with blistered crackling, on buttery mash with a sharp apple and cabbage slaw.
item.content:encoded:
Pork belly is a slab of meat and fat, and the skin on top is what makes it worth cooking. Turning that skin into crackling takes two things, dryness and heat in two stages. The skin is scored, rubbed with coarse salt and left uncovered in the fridge for 4 hours, so that the salt draws moisture out and the cold air dries the surface. The belly then roasts for 2 hours at a low temperature, which melts the fat and makes the meat tender, and finishes for 20 minutes at 240°C, when the dry skin puffs, blisters and crackles. The spices go on the meat side only, since oil on the skin softens it. Kūmara, New Zealand's orange sweet potato, is mashed with butter and milk, and its sweetness is what the rich, salty pork wants. A slaw of green apple and cabbage in vinegar and mustard cuts through the fat.

  • Dry the skin. It has to be dry to crackle, so leave the salted pork uncovered in the fridge and pat the skin dry again before it goes in the oven.
  • Keep oil and spices off the skin. Oil on the skin softens it, and it will not blister.
  • Slice with a serrated knife, skin side up, using a sawing motion. Pressing straight down with a plain blade shatters the crackling.

item.title: Venison Stew
item.description: Venison stew: cubes of venison braised for hours with bacon, carrots, parsnips, red wine, juniper and redcurrant jelly into a dark, rich winter stew.
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand farms red deer in large numbers, and hunters take wild deer in the high country, so venison is a familiar winter meat there. It is very lean, and that decides how it has to be cooked. A steak from the leg can be cooked fast and pink, but the shoulder and the shin are full of connective tissue and need hours in liquid to turn tender, and because the meat has almost no fat of its own, the stew has to supply some. Bacon does it here, and browning the venison hard in batches gives the depth of flavour that the lean meat lacks. Red wine, tomato paste, redcurrant jelly, juniper and thyme make a sauce that suits game, sharp, a little sweet and resinous. The parsnips are added for the last 45 minutes so that they stay in pieces. The stew is cooked low in the oven, at a temperature at which the liquid barely trembles, because lean meat toughens in a hard boil.

  • Brown the venison in batches. It is very lean, and browning it hard gives the stew the flavour the meat lacks. A crowded pot steams rather than browns.
  • Keep the oven low. Lean meat toughens if the stew boils, so the surface of the liquid should barely tremble.
  • Add the parsnips late. They cook in 45 minutes, and much longer turns them to mush.

item.title: Creamed Mushrooms on Toast
item.description: Creamed mushrooms on toast: mushrooms browned in butter, then simmered in cream with mustard, thyme and lemon and piled on thick toast. An easy breakfast.
item.content:encoded:
Creamed mushrooms on toast is a breakfast that is on the menu of nearly every New Zealand café, and it is easy to see why. Mushrooms are cooked until deeply golden, then bound with a small amount of cream, sharpened with mustard and lemon and finished with thyme and parsley, and heaped on toast that is thick enough to hold the sauce. The method has one rule. Mushrooms are mostly water, so they must be cooked in a hot pan, in batches, until that water has boiled away and they brown. Mushrooms crowded into a cold pan stew in their own liquid and turn grey and rubbery, and no amount of cream fixes that. Only then do the onion, garlic and a spoonful of flour go in, and the cream and stock, which simmer for just a few minutes into a glossy sauce that coats the mushrooms and does not swamp them. A poached egg on top makes it a bigger meal.

  • Cook the mushrooms in batches in a hot pan. A crowded pan steams them, and they turn grey and rubbery instead of golden.
  • Do not salt the mushrooms until the end. Salt draws the water out early, and they stew instead of browning.
  • Toast the bread thick and crisp. Thin, soft toast collapses under the sauce.

item.title: Potato Top Pie
item.description: Potato top pie: a crisp shortcrust case of beef mince in thick gravy, capped with mashed potato and melted cheese instead of a pastry lid. A family pie.
item.content:encoded:
The potato top pie is a fixture of New Zealand bakeries and dairies, a pie that has beef mince in gravy under a soft cap of mashed potato and cheese instead of a pastry lid. The mash browns and crisps at the edges while the filling stays juicy underneath, and it is a useful way to use leftover mashed potato. This one is made as a single family pie in a 23 cm dish. Three things keep it from turning wet. The filling is cooked down until it is thick enough for a spoon to leave a trail, and cooled a little, because thin, hot filling bubbles up through the potato and soaks the pastry. The case is blind-baked, so that the base stays crisp. And the potatoes are a floury variety and are steamed dry after draining, since wet mash slumps and will not brown. Grated cheese on top gives it a crust that goes golden and crisp.

  • Cook the filling down until it is thick and let it cool a little. Thin, hot filling bubbles up through the mash and soaks the pastry.
  • Steam the potatoes dry in the colander after draining. Wet mash slumps on top of the filling and will not brown.
  • Rough up the surface of the mash with a fork before adding the cheese. The ridges catch the heat and turn golden and crisp.

item.title: Mince and Cheese Pie
item.description: Mince and cheese pie: six individual pies of beef mince and melted tasty cheddar in thick gravy, in a shortcrust base under a flaky puff pastry lid.
item.content:encoded:
The mince and cheese pie is one of the best known pies in New Zealand. It is sold hot from the pie warmer in bakeries and dairies, eaten in the hand, and it has a very particular construction: a shortcrust base for strength, a flaky puff lid for lightness, and a filling of beef mince in a thick, savoury gravy with cheese melted through it. The filling is what makes the pie. It has to be thick enough not to run when the pie is broken open, so the gravy is thickened with cornflour and simmered until it is like a paste, and it has to be cool before the cheese goes in and before it goes into the pastry, or the cheese melts out and the pastry starts to cook before it reaches the oven. The pies are baked on a hot tray, so that the base is crisp underneath, and they are glazed with egg for a deep gold.

  • Make the filling thick and let it cool before adding the cheese. Warm filling melts the cheese out of the mince and softens the pastry before it bakes.
  • Bake the pies on a preheated tray. Heat from below cooks the base through and keeps it crisp instead of pale and soft.
  • Seal the lids well with egg and press the edges together. A pie that opens at the seam leaks its filling onto the tray.

item.title: Lamb and Rosemary Pie
item.description: Lamb and rosemary pie: lamb shoulder cooked slowly in a rosemary gravy, baked in a shortcrust base under a golden puff pastry lid. A deep family pie.
item.content:encoded:
Lamb and rosemary is one of the great pairings, and in New Zealand, a major lamb producer, it is a common filling for a pie. The meat is shoulder, cut into small chunks and cooked slowly in a gravy until it is tender enough to break under a fork. Shoulder is the right cut, because it has the fat and connective tissue that make a rich gravy and keep the meat moist, and lean leg would dry out. The rosemary goes into the pan with the garlic and tomato paste so that its oils are released in the fat, and a spoonful of redcurrant jelly takes the edge off the gravy in the way that mint jelly does at a roast. The filling is made ahead and cooled, which is a real advantage, because the pie is then only a matter of assembling and baking, and a cold filling keeps the pastry crisp.

  • Use shoulder rather than leg. Its fat and connective tissue give a rich gravy and meat that stays moist, where leg turns dry and stringy.
  • Make the gravy thick and cool the filling. A thin or hot filling steams the pastry from inside and leaves the base pale and soft.
  • Bake on a preheated tray. Heat from below sets the base and keeps it crisp under the filling.

item.title: Cheese and Marmite Pinwheels
item.description: Cheese and Marmite pinwheels: puff pastry rolled up with Marmite and tasty cheddar, sliced and baked until flaky, cheesy and golden. A party snack.
item.content:encoded:
Marmite is a dark, savoury spread made from yeast extract that New Zealanders eat on toast and crackers, and with cheese it is a favourite snack in New Zealand. Cheese and Marmite go together because the cheese's fat and creaminess soften the spread's concentrated saltiness and give it a place to go. Here they are rolled inside puff pastry, and the roll is chilled until firm, so that it slices cleanly into pinwheels. In the oven the pastry puffs into crisp layers, the cheese melts into the swirl and the Marmite darkens into a savoury spiral. The whole thing takes 20 minutes to put together, and it uses ready-rolled pastry, which is why it turns up at parties, school events and after-work drinks. Spread the Marmite thinly, since it is strong, and use a sharp tasty cheddar, so that the cheese is not lost. Any yeast extract spread works, and a stronger one needs a lighter hand.

  • Spread the Marmite thinly. It is strong, and a thick layer takes over the cheese and makes the pinwheels too salty.
  • Chill the rolled logs before slicing. Cold pastry cuts cleanly with a sharp knife, and warm pastry squashes and smears.
  • Space the pinwheels well apart. They puff and spread as the pastry layers rise, and crowded ones join up.

item.title: Savoury Corn Muffins
item.description: Savoury corn muffins: tall, moist muffins packed with corn, tasty cheddar, spring onion and smoked paprika. Mixed in one bowl, and easy to make.
item.content:encoded:
Savoury muffins sit next to the sweet ones in New Zealand cafés, and corn and cheese is one of the classics. They are lunchbox food, eaten warm from the oven or cold, split and buttered. What keeps these moist is creamed corn. It is thick and sweet, it carries its own moisture and starch into the batter, and it gives a soft, tender crumb that stays that way for days, while the whole kernels give the muffins their texture and a pop of sweetness. Tasty cheddar and spring onion make them savoury, and smoked paprika adds a faint smokiness without heat. The method is the standard muffin method and its one rule: mix the wet and the dry ingredients only until they are combined. A few streaks of flour are fine, and overmixed batter develops gluten and bakes into tough, tunnelled muffins.

  • Fold the batter only until it comes together. Overmixing develops gluten and gives tough muffins with tunnels in them.
  • Drain the kernels well. Extra water from the tin thins the batter and gives a gummy crumb.
  • Fill the holes right to the top. The batter is thick, and a full hole gives the domed tops and the golden cheese crust.

item.title: Rēwena Parāoa
item.description: Rēwena parāoa: Māori potato bread raised with a fermented potato starter, the bug, instead of yeast. Soft, moist, faintly sweet and sour, with a golden crust.
item.content:encoded:
Rēwena parāoa is a Māori bread raised with a fermented potato starter, called a bug or rēwena, instead of commercial yeast. Boiled potato is mashed with flour, sugar and water and left in a warm place, and the wild yeasts and bacteria in the flour and the potato ferment it over a day or two, until it is bubbling and smells sweet and sour, rather like a sourdough starter. The bug is then mixed into flour to make the dough. It gives the bread a soft, moist crumb, a mild sourness and a faint sweetness. The bug can be kept going indefinitely by feeding it. Two rules matter. The potato water must not be salted, since salt slows the fermentation, and the bug must be kept warm, because a cold kitchen slows it down and leaves the bread heavy. Rēwena is eaten warm with butter and jam, and it is also served alongside a boil-up.

  • Do not salt the potato water. Salt slows the fermentation, and the bug will be sluggish.
  • Keep the bug warm, around 25°C. In a cool kitchen it can take an extra day, and it is ready when it foams and smells sweet and sour.
  • Keep the leftover bug going. Feed it with a spoonful of flour, a pinch of sugar and a little lukewarm water, and it will be ready to raise the next loaf.

item.title: Tan Square
item.description: Tan square: buttery shortbread base, a soft chewy caramel of condensed milk, butter and golden syrup, and a crumble of the same dough on top.
item.content:encoded:
Tan square, also called tan slice, is one of the simplest and most loved slices in New Zealand baking, because it needs only two mixtures. A soft shortbread dough is beaten together in one bowl, and three quarters of it is pressed into a tin as the base, while the last quarter is set aside to crumble over the top. Between the two layers goes a caramel made in a saucepan from sweetened condensed milk, butter and golden syrup, warmed just until smooth. In the oven the caramel sets to a soft chew, the base bakes to a crumbly shortbread and the crumbs on top go golden and crisp. The layers hold together only when the slice is cold, so it has to cool completely in the tin before it is cut, and then it slices into neat squares with a chewy centre.

  • Press the base down firmly and evenly, right into the corners. A loose base crumbles when the slice is cut.
  • Let the caramel cool for a few minutes before pouring it over. It should be thick, and not hot and runny, or it soaks into the base.
  • Leave the slice to cool completely in the tin. The caramel firms up as it cools, and a warm slice slides apart when cut.

item.title: Peppermint Slice
item.description: Peppermint slice: a no-bake chocolate, coconut and biscuit base, a pale green peppermint icing layer and a glossy dark chocolate topping. Cut into squares.
item.content:encoded:
The peppermint slice is a favourite of New Zealand tearooms and bake sales, and it is a slice that never goes near the oven. It has three layers. The base is crushed biscuits, desiccated coconut and cocoa held together with melted butter and sweetened condensed milk, which sets firm and slices cleanly. The middle layer is a peppermint icing of icing sugar, butter and a little milk, coloured a pale green if you like, which gives the slice its cool, sweet centre. The top layer is dark chocolate, melted with a spoonful of coconut oil so that it sets glossy and does not shatter when the slice is cut. Each layer has to be cold before the next goes on, or the layers blur together, and the whole slice is best after a cold night in the fridge.

  • Press the base down firmly with the back of a spoon. A loose base crumbles when the slice is cut.
  • Add the peppermint essence by the half teaspoon and taste. Brands differ in strength, and too much makes the slice taste medicinal.
  • Cool the melted chocolate for a few minutes before pouring, and cut with a hot, dry knife. Hot chocolate melts into the icing, and a cold knife cracks the topping.

item.title: Squiggle Slice
item.description: Squiggle slice: a no-bake biscuit base with custard icing, crunchy honeycomb and a chocolate topping, finished with a yellow chocolate squiggle. Cut in bars.
item.content:encoded:
The Squiggle is a New Zealand biscuit made by Griffin's, a crisp biscuit topped with a custard-yellow icing and pieces of honeycomb, coated in chocolate and finished with a yellow squiggle piped across the top. This slice takes those layers and stacks them in a tin. A crushed-biscuit base is bound with melted butter, a soft icing flavoured with custard powder goes on top, then crunchy honeycomb, then a layer of milk and dark chocolate, and the yellow squiggles go on last. Custard powder is what gives the icing its pale yellow colour and its vanilla-custard flavour. Everything is made without baking, but every layer must be cold before the next goes on, and the slice needs 2 hours in the fridge for the chocolate to set. Cut it into small bars, since the slice is very sweet.

  • Beat the icing until it is pale and fluffy. Under-beaten icing is heavy, and it slides when the slice is cut.
  • Cool the chocolate for a few minutes before pouring. Hot chocolate melts the honeycomb and softens the icing beneath.
  • Cut with a hot, dry knife, wiping it between cuts. The chocolate topping cracks under a cold blade.

item.title: Peanut Brownies
item.description: Peanut brownies: fudgy dark chocolate brownies with roasted peanuts in the batter and a swirl of peanut butter on top. A crackly crust and a soft centre.
item.content:encoded:
A brownie should be dense and fudgy inside with a thin, shiny, crackled crust, and the crust depends on one step, whisking the sugar and eggs for 3 minutes until they are thick and pale. The dissolved sugar rises to the surface as the brownies bake and sets into a paper-thin sheet. There is little flour in the batter, only enough to hold it together, and the rest of the body comes from melted butter and dark chocolate. Peanuts go in twice. Chopped roasted peanuts are folded through the batter and scattered on top for crunch, and a swirl of peanut butter is dragged through the surface in ribbons that stay soft and salty against the bitter chocolate. The one way to spoil brownies is to overbake them: they should come out while a skewer still shows moist crumbs, and they finish setting as they cool.

  • Whisk the eggs and sugar until thick and pale. This makes the thin, shiny, crackled crust.
  • Take the brownies out while a skewer still shows moist crumbs. They keep cooking in the hot tin, and an overbaked brownie is dry and cakey.
  • Wait until they are cold to cut them. Warm brownies are too soft and smear the knife.

item.title: Condensed Milk Biscuits
item.description: Condensed milk biscuits: buttery, crisp-edged biscuits sweetened with condensed milk, rolled into balls and pressed flat with a fork. Made without eggs.
item.content:encoded:
Condensed milk biscuits are a New Zealand childhood bake, and they are among the easiest biscuits there are. There is no egg. Sweetened condensed milk does much of the work of both the sugar and the binder, which gives a dough that is soft, rolls into balls without chilling for long and bakes into a biscuit that is crisp at the edges and tender in the middle. The condensed milk browns as it bakes, and the milk solids in it give a caramel flavour that plain sugar does not. Pressing each ball with a fork flattens it to an even thickness, so that all of them bake at the same rate, and the pattern is the traditional finish. Stirring in chocolate chips gives a chocolate chip version, and the dough also takes desiccated coconut or oats.

  • Pull the biscuits out while the tops are still pale. They firm up as they cool, and overbaked ones are hard rather than crisp.
  • Flour the fork between biscuits. The dough is buttery, and the fork sticks to it.
  • Weigh the dough balls at 20 g if you can. Biscuits of the same size bake in the same time.

item.title: Boston Bun
item.description: Boston bun: soft, spiced sultana buns with a little mashed potato for tenderness, covered in a thick layer of pink icing and desiccated coconut.
item.content:encoded:
A Boston bun is a large, soft, spiced fruit bun covered with a thick layer of pink icing and desiccated coconut, and it is a fixture of New Zealand and Australian bakeries. The origin of the name is unknown. The classic dough contains mashed potato, which holds moisture and keeps the crumb soft and tender for days, and it is spiced with mixed spice and studded with sultanas. The bun is a yeast dough, made in stages: the yeast is proved in warm milk, the dough is kneaded until it is smooth and elastic and the sultanas are worked in at the end, and it rises twice. The icing should go on when the buns are completely cold, since on a warm bun it melts and slides off, and the coconut is pressed on while it is still wet. Boston buns are eaten sliced and buttered with a cup of tea.

  • Let the buns cool completely before icing them. On a warm bun the icing melts and slides off.
  • Use cold, plain mashed potato with no butter or milk. It adds moisture and softness without making the dough greasy.
  • Add the sultanas after the dough has been kneaded. Kneading them in from the start tears the gluten and stains the dough.

item.title: Date Scones
item.description: Date scones: tall, soft scones with chopped dates and a little cinnamon, rubbed in by hand and baked hot. Best split and buttered while still warm.
item.content:encoded:
The date scone is one of the great New Zealand scones, and it is eaten warm and buttered at morning tea and in cafés. Chopped dates go into the dough with a little cinnamon, and as the scones bake they soften and turn jammy, sweetening the crumb around them. The rules of a good scone are the same as ever. The butter is rubbed into the flour until the mixture looks like fine crumbs, which coats the flour and keeps the scones tender. The milk goes in all at once and is mixed with a round-bladed knife only until the dough holds together, since more mixing develops gluten and makes tough scones. The dough is patted out and never rolled, cut with a sharp knife straight down without twisting, and set close together on the tray so that they rise and support each other. The oven is very hot. Wrapping the scones in a tea towel as they come out keeps them soft.

  • Mix as little as you can. The dough should be soft and a little sticky, and more mixing makes tough scones.
  • Cut straight down without twisting. A twisting cutter seals the edges and stops the scones from rising evenly.
  • Set the scones touching on the tray. Their neighbours hold them upright, and they rise taller.

item.title: Chilaquiles Rojos
item.description: Chilaquiles rojos: crisp tortilla wedges tossed in a guajillo and tomato salsa, topped with fried eggs, crema, queso fresco and onion. Ready in 50 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Chilaquiles are a Mexican breakfast built from stale tortillas: corn tortilla wedges are fried until crisp, folded through a hot salsa for a moment so that the edges soften and the middles keep a bite, and finished with eggs, cream, cheese and onion. The rojos are the red version. Where the green kind is sharp and bright with tomatillos, this one is deeper and a little sweet, made with dried guajillo and ancho chillies and ripe tomatoes, and the chillies are toasted and soaked before they are blended. The salsa is then fried in a little oil, which cooks out its raw taste and darkens the colour. The chips go in last, and the plate goes to the table at once, because chilaquiles are the best in the first few minutes and turn to a soft mash if they stand. Shredded chicken is a common addition, and the eggs can be scrambled or left runny.

  • Use tortillas that are a day or two old. They are drier, they fry crisp and they take up less oil than fresh ones.
  • Simmer the salsa until it coats a spoon before the chips go in. A thin salsa turns the wedges to mush in seconds.
  • Fold the chips in for 30 seconds and serve. The dish is at its best while the centres of the wedges are still crisp.

item.title: Chicken Flautas
item.description: Chicken flautas: corn tortillas rolled around shredded chicken, green chillies and Monterey Jack, fried until crisp and served with crema and salsa verde.
item.content:encoded:
Flautas take their name from the Spanish for flutes, and the shape is the point: two corn tortillas are overlapped to make a long strip, filled, and rolled into a thin cylinder that fries into a crisp, golden tube. They are close to taquitos, which are shorter and often made with a single tortilla, and the two names are used loosely. The filling is finely shredded chicken, and it has to be seasoned well and kept fairly dry. A wet filling steams the tortilla from the inside and splits the roll, so the chicken is stirred with only a little crema and lime juice, and the cheese is folded in once it has cooled. The tortillas must be warm and pliable, or they crack as they are rolled. They fry in shallow oil in a few minutes, and they go on the plate with shredded lettuce, crema, crumbled queso fresco and salsa verde.

  • Warm the tortillas before rolling. Cold corn tortillas crack, and the filling spills into the oil.
  • Keep the filling dry. Moisture steams the tortilla from the inside and makes the flautas split as they fry.
  • Roll tightly and fry seam side down first. The seam seals in the hot oil, and the roll does not open.

item.title: Caldo de Res
item.description: Caldo de res: Mexican beef soup of bone-in shank simmered until tender, with corn, carrots, potatoes, chayote and cabbage. Served with lime and coriander.
item.content:encoded:
Caldo de res is the beef soup of the Mexican family table, a large pot of bone-in beef and big pieces of vegetables that is put on for a Sunday or for someone who is ill. The cut matters. Beef shank has a lot of connective tissue and a marrow bone, and two hours of gentle simmering turns the tissue to gelatin, which gives the broth its body and leaves the meat soft enough to pull from the bone. The beef goes into cold water with an onion, garlic, bay and peppercorns and comes slowly to a boil so that the scum can be skimmed, and the vegetables go in later, in order of how long they take: carrots and potatoes first, corn and chayote next and cabbage last, so that each is tender and none is mush. Everything is served in deep bowls with lime, chopped onion and coriander, with rice and warm tortillas on the side.

  • Start the beef in cold water and skim it. Scum that stays in the pot clouds the broth.
  • Keep the simmer gentle. A hard boil makes the broth cloudy and the meat stringy.
  • Add the vegetables in stages. Cabbage and chayote cook in minutes, and left in for the full time they fall apart.

item.title: Beef Fajitas
item.description: Beef fajitas: skirt steak marinated in lime, cumin and chilli, seared and sliced across the grain over charred peppers and onions, with warm flour tortillas.
item.content:encoded:
Fajita comes from the Spanish faja, a belt or girdle, and it was first the name of the cut, the long, thin skirt steak that ranch hands on the Texas and Mexico border were given from the beef. Skirt is very beefy and very tough, and it only works cooked fast over high heat and sliced thin across the grain. A short marinade of lime juice, oil, garlic and spices seasons it and softens the surface, but it is not left for hours, because the lime juice turns the outside of thin meat mushy. The steak is seared in a smoking cast iron pan for 2 to 3 minutes a side, rested for as long as it took to cook, and only then sliced, and the peppers and onions cook in the same pan so that they take up the browned bits. Everything comes to the table together with warm tortillas, soured cream and guacamole for each person to build.

  • Marinate for no longer than a few hours. Lime juice starts to break down the surface of thin steak, and the texture turns mushy.
  • Get the pan smoking hot before the steak goes in. A cool pan steams it, and it turns grey and tough.
  • Slice across the grain, in thin strips, after the rest. Slicing along the grain leaves skirt steak chewy however well it is cooked.

item.title: Chimichangas
item.description: Chimichangas: large flour tortillas rolled around spiced beef, refried beans, rice and cheese, then fried until blistered and crisp. Serve with soured cream.
item.content:encoded:
A chimichanga is a burrito that has been fried, and it is a dish of the Sonoran and Arizona border. The best known story is that Monica Flin, who ran the El Charro cafe in Tucson, dropped a burrito into the fryer by accident and turned a curse into the name, but the story is disputed and other Arizona kitchens have claimed the dish. What is not in doubt is the texture: a crisp, blistered shell with a soft filling inside, which is why the filling has to be thick and fairly dry. This one is spiced beef, cooked down with passata, mixed with refried beans and rice and left to cool a little before the cheese goes in. The tortillas are warmed so that they fold without cracking, the parcels are sealed with beaten egg and fried seam side down first, and the whole batch can be baked instead of fried if you would rather not use the oil.

  • Cook the filling until there is no liquid in the pan. A wet filling steams the tortilla and splits it in the oil.
  • Fry seam side down first. The heat seals the fold before it can open.
  • To bake instead, brush the parcels with oil and bake at 220°C for 18 minutes, turning once. They are less blistered and a little paler.

item.title: Pork Chile Verde
item.description: Pork chile verde: pork shoulder braised until tender in a sauce of grilled tomatillos, poblano and jalapeño chillies. Serve with tortillas, rice and beans.
item.content:encoded:
Chile verde is a stew of pork in a green sauce, cooked in northern Mexico and across the American Southwest, where the chilli is often the Hatch or Anaheim. This version uses tomatillos, poblanos and jalapeños, all grilled first until they blister, because the char adds a smoky depth to the sharp, lemony tomatillos and takes away their rawness. The poblanos are steamed in a covered bowl so that their skins slip off. Pork shoulder is the cut to use, since it has enough fat and connective tissue to stay moist through two and a half hours of cooking, and it is browned in batches before it goes into the sauce. The stew starts covered and finishes uncovered, so that the sauce thickens until it clings to the meat. Lime juice and coriander go in at the end, and the stew is served with warm tortillas, rice and beans.

  • Grill the vegetables until they blister and blacken in places. The char is what gives the sauce its smoky depth.
  • Brown the pork in batches. A crowded pot steams the meat, and the stew loses the flavour of the crust.
  • Finish the stew uncovered. The sauce should coat the pork, and a thin sauce tastes of tomatillo and little else.

item.title: Pozole Verde
item.description: Pozole verde: pork and hominy in a green broth of tomatillos, poblano chillies, coriander and toasted pumpkin seeds, served with radish, cabbage and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Pozole is the Mexican stew of pork and hominy, and it comes in three colours: white, red and green. The green is usually linked to the state of Guerrero, and what sets it apart is a sauce of tomatillos, fresh chillies and herbs thickened with toasted pumpkin seeds, which give it a nutty richness and a slightly gritty body that the red version does not have. The pork is simmered first with onion, garlic and bay, so that it is tender and the broth has flavour. The green sauce is blended smooth and then fried in a little oil, which is the step that cooks out the raw taste of the tomatillos and turns the colour from bright to olive green. It then simmers with the hominy and the pork for 25 minutes. The garnishes are half of the dish: shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, avocado, chopped onion, lime and tostadas, each in its own dish, so that everyone builds their own bowl.

  • Fry the sauce before it goes into the pot. This cooks out the raw flavour of the tomatillos and gives the pozole its deeper colour.
  • Toast the pumpkin seeds until they pop and no further. Seeds that scorch turn the whole pot bitter.
  • Serve the garnishes separately. The cold, crisp cabbage, radish and lime are what balance the rich broth.

item.title: Arroz con Pollo
item.description: Arroz con pollo: chicken thighs and rice cooked in one pot with a sofrito of onion, pepper, garlic and tomato, with peas, olives and red pepper strips.
item.content:encoded:
Arroz con pollo means rice with chicken, and it is cooked, in versions of its own, across Spain and Latin America, from Cuba and Puerto Rico to Colombia and Peru. What they share is one pot: chicken is browned, a sofrito of onion, green pepper, garlic and tomato is cooked in the fat, the rice is stirred in raw so that it takes up the flavour, and the whole thing simmers under a lid until the rice has swallowed the stock. The colour comes from turmeric here, though annatto or saffron are used in other kitchens. Bone-in thighs are the cut to use, because they stay juicy through 20 minutes of cooking under the lid and give the rice their own flavour. The lid must stay on. Lifting it lets the steam out and leaves the top layer of rice hard. Peas, olives and strips of roasted red pepper go on at the end.

  • Brown the chicken hard and leave the fat in the pan. The sofrito and the rice take their colour and flavour from it.
  • Do not lift the lid while the rice cooks. The steam is what cooks the grains, and the top layer stays hard if it escapes.
  • Leave the pan covered off the heat for 10 minutes. The rice finishes in its own steam and does not stick.

item.title: Mississippi Pot Roast
item.description: Mississippi pot roast: a chuck roast slow-cooked with butter, pepperoncini and a ranch and gravy seasoning until it shreds. Serve over mashed potatoes.
item.content:encoded:
Mississippi pot roast is credited to Robin Chapman of Ripley, Mississippi, and it spread across the internet as a recipe with an unlikely list of ingredients: a chuck roast, a packet of ranch seasoning, a packet of gravy mix, a stick of butter and a handful of pepperoncini, left in the slow cooker for a day. It works because each of them does something. The butter melts into the juices and makes them rich, the pepperoncini and a little of their brine add a mild heat and a vinegary tang that cuts through the fat, and the two seasonings give the meat a herby, savoury, gravy-like flavour. Chuck is the right cut, because it is marbled and full of connective tissue that turns to gelatin over 8 hours and leaves the roast shreddable and the juices glossy. No water or stock is added, since the roast gives off its own liquid. The seasoning mixes are written out here, so the recipe needs no packets.

  • Do not add water or stock. The roast gives off plenty of its own liquid, and extra dilutes the juices.
  • Sear the roast first if you have 10 minutes. The browning adds a roasted flavour that the slow cooker cannot give.
  • Use the low setting. High gets there sooner and leaves the meat drier and more stringy, and the connective tissue needs the long, gentle cook.

item.title: Cheeseburger Macaroni
item.description: Cheeseburger macaroni: beef, elbow macaroni and a ketchup, mustard and cheddar sauce cooked in one skillet. A homemade version of Hamburger Helper.
item.content:encoded:
Hamburger Helper is the boxed dinner in which ground beef and pasta are cooked in a skillet with a powdered sauce, and this is a homemade dinner in that mould, with the flavour of a cheeseburger: beef, onion, ketchup, mustard, Worcestershire sauce and cheddar. It is made in a single pan. The macaroni cooks directly in a mixture of stock and milk, and the starch it releases thickens the sauce as it goes, so there is no draining and nothing to wash except the pan. The cheese goes in at the end, off the heat, so that it melts into a smooth sauce and does not turn grainy. Sharp cheddar, grated from a block, gives more flavour than mild, and pickles and chives on top finish it. It takes about 40 minutes, and leftovers reheat well with a splash of milk.

  • Stir often while the pasta cooks. The starch settles, and the macaroni sticks to the base of the pan if it is left.
  • Add the cheese off the heat. Cheese stirred into a boiling sauce turns grainy and oily.
  • Grate the cheddar from a block. Pre-grated cheese is coated in starch and does not melt as smoothly.

item.title: Crispy Baked Chicken Thighs
item.description: Crispy baked chicken thighs: bone-in thighs dry-brined with salt and baking powder and roasted on a rack in a hot oven until the skin shatters.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken thighs are forgiving. Dark meat has more fat and connective tissue than breast, so it stays juicy even when it is cooked well past done, and it is more tender at 80°C than at 74°C. The skin is the problem, because it is mostly fat and water and turns rubbery in an ordinary oven. Three things fix it. The thighs are salted and left uncovered in the fridge, which dries the surface, and a little aluminium-free baking powder in the salt raises the pH of the skin so that it browns and blisters. They roast on a rack, so that hot air reaches the underside and the fat drips away instead of soaking the skin. And the oven is hot, at 220°C. There is no marinade and no sauce, only the crisp skin and the juice, with lemon and parsley at the end, and the rack and the tray do the rest.

  • Use aluminium-free baking powder, and no more than 1 teaspoon. Too much leaves a bitter, chemical taste on the skin.
  • Roast on a rack. Thighs sitting in their own fat steam on the underside, and the skin there stays pale and soft.
  • Take them to 80°C or more. Dark meat at 74°C is safe but still tough near the bone, and it turns tender once the connective tissue has melted.

item.title: Braised Beef Short Ribs
item.description: Braised beef short ribs: bone-in ribs seared and braised for three hours in red wine and stock until tender, with the sauce reduced to a glossy glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Short ribs come from the lower part of the rib cage, a short length of bone under a thick layer of meat, and they are fatty, tough and packed with collagen, which is exactly why they braise so well. Three hours in liquid at a low heat turns the collagen to gelatin, so that the meat is tender enough to fall off the bone, and the fat melts into the braising liquid and is skimmed off at the end. The ribs are cut in the English style, thick pieces on a single bone, and not across the bones in the thin flanken cut used for Korean galbi. The method is a standard braise, and every step counts. The ribs are seared until dark, because the browning is the flavour of the sauce. The wine is boiled down by half to take away its sharpness. And the liquid is strained, skimmed and reduced at the end, then finished off the heat with a spoonful of balsamic vinegar and cold butter for gloss.

  • Sear the ribs until they are dark brown. The crust is where most of the flavour of the sauce comes from.
  • Skim the fat from the strained liquid before you reduce it. Short ribs give off a lot, and it makes the sauce greasy.
  • Braise at 150°C. A harder boil tightens the meat before the collagen has melted, and it turns out dry.

item.title: Roast Beef Tenderloin
item.description: Roast beef tenderloin: a trimmed, tied fillet seared and roasted to a rosy medium-rare under a garlic and herb crust, with a sharp horseradish cream.
item.content:encoded:
The tenderloin is the most tender cut of beef, because the muscle does almost no work, and it is also the leanest and the mildest, which is why it is easy to overcook and needs a strong crust and a sharp sauce. Everything in the method follows from that. The roast is trimmed and tied into an even cylinder, with the thin tail folded under, so that it cooks at the same rate along its length. It is salted well and left at room temperature for 45 minutes, and then seared all over for the crust. The garlic, mustard and herbs go on after the sear, so that they do not burn in the pan. A thermometer is what decides when it is done, not the clock: 50°C in the centre for medium-rare, and it rises another 4 or 5 degrees as it rests. The horseradish cream is stirred together while it rests, and it is the sharpness the rich, mild meat wants.

  • Use a thermometer. A tenderloin goes from rosy to grey in a few minutes, and the clock cannot tell you which.
  • Fold the thin tail under and tie it. A tapered end cooks faster than the rest and is grey before the middle is ready.
  • Rest the beef for the full 15 minutes. Sliced sooner, it loses its juices onto the board.

item.title: Honey Garlic Glazed Salmon
item.description: Honey garlic glazed salmon: skin-on fillets seared in a skillet and finished in a sticky glaze of honey, garlic, soy sauce and lemon. Ready in 22 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
A glaze has to reduce to a syrup to coat the fish, and the easiest place to do it is the pan the salmon was seared in. The fillets are cooked most of the way on their skin, which crisps as the fat renders, and the honey, garlic, soy sauce and lemon go in for the last two minutes, where they bubble into a syrup that is spooned over the fish. Honey scorches quickly, so the heat is lowered before the glaze goes in, and it is spooned over the salmon and not boiled dry. The soy sauce brings savoury depth, the garlic a sharp, sweet backbone and the lemon a balance to the sugar.
