The fillets should be patted dry, laid into a hot pan skin side down and pressed with a spatula for 10 seconds so that they do not curl, and left alone until the skin releases.

  • Dry the skin and press the fillet down for the first 10 seconds. Moisture makes the skin stick, and the fillet curls away from the pan.
  • Lower the heat before the glaze goes in. Honey scorches quickly, and burnt honey tastes bitter.
  • Take the salmon off while the middle is still a little translucent. It keeps cooking as it rests.

item.title: Pan-Seared Tilapia
item.description: Pan-seared tilapia: thin fillets dusted with paprika, seared golden for two to three minutes a side and finished with a lemon, garlic and caper butter.
item.content:encoded:
Tilapia is a mild white fish with thin fillets, and that decides how it is cooked: fast, in a hot pan, with a light coating. A thin fillet has no time to build a crust, and without a coating it steams and sticks to the pan. A dusting of flour with paprika and garlic powder browns quickly and protects the delicate flesh, and the fillets need only 2 to 3 minutes on the first side and 2 on the second. They should be turned once, and only when they release from the pan. Tilapia has a gentle flavour, and this is why the sauce matters. The butter, garlic, lemon and capers are made in the same pan in about a minute, and their sharpness is what the fish wants. Frozen fillets are fine if they are thawed completely and patted very dry, since any water on the surface will stop them browning.

  • Pat the fillets dry, and dust them only lightly. Damp fish steams, and a thick coating turns pasty.
  • Leave the fillets alone until they release. A fillet that sticks is not ready to turn, and it tears.
  • Thaw frozen fillets in the fridge overnight, or in a bag in cold water for 30 minutes, and dry them well.

item.title: Shrimp Stir-Fry
item.description: Shrimp stir-fry: shrimp seared hot and fast, then tossed with broccoli, snap peas, red pepper and carrot in a glossy garlic, ginger and soy sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Shrimp are the fastest thing that goes into a wok, and the whole method is a matter of timing. They cook in about 2 minutes, so they are seared first and taken out, where they cannot overcook while the vegetables cook, and they go back in at the very end with the sauce. A light coating of cornflour keeps them tender and helps the sauce cling. The vegetables go in in order of how long they take, carrot and broccoli first and the pepper and snap peas after, so that each is crisp-tender and none is limp. The sauce is stirred together beforehand, because there is no time to measure once the pan is hot. The pan has to be very hot and not crowded. In a small pan, or if the shrimp are large and many, they should be cooked in two batches so that they sear and do not steam.

  • Pat the shrimp dry before the cornflour goes on. Wet shrimp steam in the pan and turn pale and rubbery.
  • Get the pan very hot before the shrimp go in, and work in two batches if it is small.
  • Stir the sauce again just before it goes in. The cornflour settles, and the sauce will not thicken if it stays at the bottom of the bowl.

item.title: Indian Chicken Curry
item.description: Indian chicken curry: chicken thighs simmered in a sauce of browned onions, tomatoes, ginger, garlic and spices, finished with garam masala and coriander.
item.content:encoded:
Every Indian household has its own chicken curry, and many of them start the same way: onions cooked slowly until they are golden brown, ginger and garlic, ground spices cooked briefly in the oil, tomatoes cooked down until the oil separates at the edges, and then the chicken and a little water. The onions are the base of the flavour, and they need a full 12 minutes over a steady heat. The spices go in after them and are cooked for only 30 seconds, since ground spices burn quickly and turn bitter. The tomatoes are cooked until they collapse into a paste and the oil shows at the edges of the pan, which is the sign that the raw taste has gone. This is a curry with a light, spiced gravy, not a creamy one like butter chicken, and it is meant to be eaten with rice or chapatis. The garam masala goes in at the end, because its aroma does not survive long cooking.

  • Brown the onions until they are deep golden. Pale onions leave the curry tasting raw and sharp.
  • Cook the tomatoes until the oil separates. It is the sign that their raw acidity has cooked away.
  • Use thighs and not breast. They stay tender through 20 minutes of simmering, and breast turns dry.

item.title: Hashbrown Casserole
item.description: Hashbrown casserole: shredded potatoes baked in a soured cream and cheddar sauce under a crisp buttered cornflake topping. The classic potluck side dish.
item.content:encoded:
Hashbrown casserole is a dish of American potlucks and church suppers, and in Utah, where it is tied to the Latter-day Saints, it is known as funeral potatoes, because it is a dish that is made in quantity and taken to gatherings after funerals. The classic recipe uses frozen shredded potatoes, canned cream of chicken soup, soured cream, cheese and a topping of crushed cornflakes. Here the canned soup is replaced by a quick white sauce of butter, onion, flour and stock, which takes about 8 minutes and tastes of onion and cheese and not of the tin. The potatoes have to be thawed and squeezed dry in a tea towel, because water in the potatoes is what makes a casserole loose and watery. The soured cream goes in off the heat, so that it does not curdle, and the topping goes on just before the dish goes into the oven, so that the cornflakes stay crisp.

  • Thaw the hash browns completely and squeeze them dry. Wet potatoes make a loose, watery casserole.
  • Stir in the soured cream off the heat. Boiled, it splits and turns grainy.
  • Add the cornflake topping just before baking. Cornflakes left on top of a wet casserole go soft.

item.title: Garlic Mashed Potatoes
item.description: Garlic mashed potatoes: Yukon Gold potatoes boiled with garlic cloves until soft, then mashed with warm milk, butter and soured cream. Mellow and creamy.
item.content:encoded:
The way to flavour mashed potatoes with garlic all the way through, without the burn of raw garlic, is to cook the garlic with the potatoes. Eight peeled cloves boiled in the same pot for 20 minutes lose their sharpness, turn soft and sweet and break down into the mash, so that every forkful tastes of garlic and none of it bites. Yukon Gold potatoes are a good choice for this. They have a medium starch content and a buttery flavour, so they mash into a creamy, slightly dense purée without needing a ricer, and they do not go gluey as easily as very floury potatoes. The milk and butter are warmed before they go in, because cold dairy chills the potatoes and stiffens them, and the soured cream at the end adds a little tang. The mash is worked by hand, only until it is smooth. A mixer or a processor bursts the starch grains and turns it to glue.

  • Cook the garlic with the potatoes. It turns soft and sweet, and it spreads through the mash evenly.
  • Warm the milk and butter. Cold dairy chills the potatoes and makes the mash stiff and starchy.
  • Mash by hand and stop as soon as it is smooth. A mixer or a processor bursts the starch and turns the mash to glue.

item.title: Sweet Potato Fries
item.description: Sweet potato fries: sticks soaked, dried and tossed in cornflour and smoked paprika, then baked on a hot tray until crisp at the edges, with a lime dip.
item.content:encoded:
Sweet potatoes make difficult fries. They have more sugar and less starch than white potatoes, so they brown quickly at the edges while the middle stays soft, and they never crisp the way a russet chip does. Four steps help. The sticks are cut evenly, about 1 cm thick, so that they cook at the same rate. They are soaked in cold water for 20 minutes to draw out some of the surface starch and sugar, and then dried completely, because any water left on them will steam in the oven. A tablespoon or two of cornflour forms a thin coating that crisps, and the fries are roasted at 230°C in a single layer on trays that have been heating in the oven, so that they start to brown the moment they land. Even so, baked sweet potato fries are crisp at the edges and soft inside, which is different from deep-fried ones, and they are good in their own way, with a dip.

  • Dry the sticks completely. Any water left on them steams in the oven, and they turn soft.
  • Preheat the trays and do not crowd them. Sticks laid on a hot tray in one layer brown, and crowded ones steam.
  • Cut the sticks the same thickness. Thin ones burn before thick ones are cooked through.

item.title: Fruit Salad
item.description: Fruit salad: strawberries, blueberries, grapes, pineapple, kiwi and orange tossed in a honey, lime and mint dressing. A fresh, bright salad in 20 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
A fruit salad is only as good as its fruit and the way it is cut. This one mixes soft berries, firm grapes, juicy pineapple and citrus, so that every spoonful has a different texture and colour, and everything is cut to about the size of a grape so that no piece dominates. The dressing is what turns a bowl of cut fruit into a salad. Lime juice brightens the flavour and slows browning, honey dissolves into the juices and rounds off the acidity, and mint gives a cool, fresh note. The fruit that is firm and holds its shape goes in first and is dressed, and the delicate berries are folded in last, so that they do not bruise or bleed. Half an hour in the fridge lets the flavours mingle. Left for much longer than two hours, the fruit softens and releases its juice and the salad turns watery.

  • Add the strawberries and blueberries last, and fold instead of stirring. Soft berries bruise and bleed into the rest.
  • Serve within 2 hours of making it. After that the fruit softens and releases its juice, and the salad turns watery.
  • Cut the fruit into similar bite-sized pieces. Every spoonful should have a little of everything.

item.title: Double Chocolate Muffins
item.description: Double chocolate muffins: cocoa muffins packed with chocolate chips, made with buttermilk, oil and hot coffee for a moist, deep chocolate crumb.
item.content:encoded:
A double chocolate muffin has chocolate twice, as cocoa in the batter and as chips through it, and it is a different muffin from a vanilla one with chips added. The cocoa needs some help. Cocoa powder stirred into hot liquid blooms, releasing more of its flavour, and here the liquid is hot strong coffee, which deepens the chocolate without making the muffins taste of coffee. Hot water works as well. The muffins are made with oil and not butter, which keeps the crumb moist for days, and with buttermilk, whose acid reacts with the bicarbonate of soda to give lift and softens the crumb. The dry and wet mixtures are combined with as few strokes as possible, since overmixed muffin batter develops gluten and bakes into tough, tunnelled muffins. The cases are filled almost to the top, and the batter domes as it bakes.

  • Stir until only just combined. Overmixed batter makes tough muffins with tunnels in them.
  • Use the hot coffee or water. It blooms the cocoa and gives a deeper chocolate flavour.
  • Fill the cases almost to the top. The batter rises into a dome, and it needs the room.

item.title: Fruit Smoothie
item.description: Fruit smoothie: frozen strawberries and mango, banana, yoghurt and orange juice blended thick and cold. Sweet without added sugar, ready in five minutes.
item.content:encoded:
A smoothie is a matter of proportions, and the ones that go wrong are watery, icy or too thin to hold a straw. Frozen fruit is what fixes that. It gives the smoothie thickness and cold without the dilution of ice, so most of the fruit in this one is frozen: strawberries for colour and tartness, and mango for sweetness and a smooth body. A ripe banana adds sweetness and creaminess, and yoghurt gives body and a little tang. Orange juice supplies the liquid that gets the blades turning, and it adds sweetness of its own, which is why no sugar is needed. The order matters. The liquid and the soft ingredients go into the jug first and the frozen fruit goes on top, so that the blades reach the liquid at once and the jug does not jam. Blend until there are no chunks, and add juice a spoonful at a time if it is too thick to move.

  • Put the liquid in first. The blades pull the frozen fruit down into it, and the jug does not jam.
  • Use frozen fruit and not ice. Ice waters the smoothie down as it melts.
  • Use a ripe banana with brown spots. An underripe one is starchy and leaves the smoothie chalky.

item.title: Green Smoothie
item.description: Green smoothie: baby spinach, banana, frozen pineapple, cucumber, ginger and lime blended with coconut water. Bright green, and it tastes of fruit.
item.content:encoded:
A green smoothie that tastes good has one rule, which is that the fruit has to be in charge. Spinach is very mild, and 60 g of it in a smoothie for two is barely noticeable behind a ripe banana and sweet pineapple, so it adds colour and nutrients and almost no flavour. Ginger and lime juice add brightness and a little heat, cucumber adds cool freshness and volume, and coconut water is the liquid, with a light sweetness of its own. Water works if you prefer. The greens are blended with the liquid first, for 30 seconds, which breaks them down completely and leaves no flecks of leaf, and the rest goes in afterwards. Kale can replace the spinach, though it is stronger and its stalks should be removed. The colour dulls to a brownish green as the smoothie stands, so it is best drunk soon after it is made.

  • Blend the spinach with the liquid first. It breaks the leaves down completely and leaves no flecks.
  • Use a ripe banana and frozen pineapple. They provide the sweetness and the cold that hide the greens.
  • Drink it soon after blending. The colour turns from bright to dull green after about an hour.

item.title: Protein Shake
item.description: Protein shake: Greek yoghurt, milk, banana, oats, peanut butter and cocoa blended thick, with about 35 g of protein and no protein powder needed.
item.content:encoded:
Most protein shakes are powder and water, and they taste of chalk. This one gets its protein from ordinary food. Fat-free Greek yoghurt has about 10 g of protein in every 100 g, milk adds another 8 g in a glass, and the oats and peanut butter add several more, which together come to about 35 g in a single glass with no powder at all. At about 570 kcal it is a small meal in a glass and not a light snack. The banana sweetens and thickens it, the cocoa gives it a chocolate flavour, and the oats add fibre and slow the way the drink is digested, so it keeps you full for longer. They need a full minute in the blender to break down completely, or the shake is gritty. If you use protein powder, one scoop of whey or pea protein can go in alongside the yoghurt for a shake with more than 50 g of protein, and it needs a splash more milk to keep it pourable.

  • Blend for a full minute. The oats need time to break down, and a short blend leaves the shake gritty.
  • Use fat-free Greek yoghurt for the most protein for the calories. The full-fat kind is creamier, with a little less protein.
  • For more protein, add a scoop of whey or pea protein powder and a splash more milk.

item.title: Iced Tea
item.description: Iced tea: black tea brewed strong for five minutes, sweetened while hot, diluted with cold water and poured over ice with lemon. Clear, bright and not bitter.
item.content:encoded:
Iced tea is a drink of the American South, and printed recipes for it go back well before the St. Louis World's Fair of 1904, which helped to make it popular across the country. Its method rests on brewing the tea strong for a short time and then diluting it with cold water, which is better than brewing it weak. Steeping black tea for 5 minutes gives it flavour and colour without the tannins that turn bitter if it is left much longer, and the tea bags are lifted out and not squeezed for the same reason. The sugar goes in while the tea is hot so that it dissolves completely, and the cold water cools the tea and gets it to the right strength at once. A small pinch of bicarbonate of soda, a Southern habit, softens the tannins further. If the tea is chilled fast, it can turn cloudy, and a little boiling water stirred in clears it.

  • Steep for 5 minutes and no longer. Longer steeping pulls out the bitter tannins.
  • Do not squeeze the tea bags. Squeezing forces out the most bitter compounds.
  • If the tea turns cloudy in the fridge, stir in a splash of boiling water. It clears at once.

item.title: Whiskey Sour
item.description: Whiskey sour: bourbon, fresh lemon juice and sugar syrup shaken hard until cold and served over ice, with an optional egg white for a silky, foamy top.
item.content:encoded:
The whiskey sour is one of the oldest cocktails, and a recipe for it was printed in Jerry Thomas's bartending guide of 1862. It is the plainest kind of drink, a spirit, lemon and sugar, and its whole character comes from the balance between them. The proportions here are 2 parts bourbon to 1 part lemon juice and two-thirds of a part of syrup, which is sharp enough to be a sour and not so sharp that the whiskey disappears. The lemon has to be squeezed fresh, because bottled juice is flat and slightly bitter. The egg white came into the drink later and is what makes it a Boston sour, and it gives it a silky texture and a thick foam. To make the foam, everything is shaken once without ice, which lets the white whip, and then again with ice to chill it. Without the egg, it is simply shaken with ice.

  • Use fresh lemon juice. Bottled juice is flat, and a sour is nothing but lemon and sugar.
  • Shake once without ice if you use egg white. Without ice the white whips properly, and the drink gets its foam.
  • Taste and adjust. Add a teaspoon more syrup if your lemons are very sharp.

item.title: Moscow Mule
item.description: Moscow mule: vodka, fresh lime juice and spicy ginger beer built over ice in a copper mug and garnished with lime and mint. Cold, sharp and fizzy.
item.content:encoded:
The Moscow mule is a highball, a long drink built directly in the glass, and it dates from 1941, when a vodka company and a maker of ginger beer in the United States are said to have put their products together in one drink. Its name is a joke, since it has nothing to do with Moscow, and the copper mug it is served in is the drink's trademark and is usually credited to the same promotion. The mug is not only for show. Copper conducts cold quickly, and a mug filled with ice frosts on the outside and keeps the drink very cold. The recipe is three ingredients. The vodka gives the drink its body, the lime juice its sharpness, and the ginger beer its fizz and spice, and the last of these decides how good the drink is. Ginger beer should have a real bite of ginger. Ginger ale, which is sweet and mild, makes a different drink. If you use a copper mug, choose one lined with stainless steel or nickel, since lime juice and ginger beer are acidic and can pull copper from an unlined mug.

  • Use a ginger beer with a real ginger bite and not ginger ale. Ginger ale is sweet and mild, and the drink loses its heat.
  • Chill everything, including the mug, the vodka and the ginger beer. The ice then melts slowly, and the drink stays fizzy.
  • Stir once and gently. Stirring hard drives out the fizz.

item.title: Cosmopolitan
item.description: Cosmopolitan: vodka, orange liqueur, cranberry juice and fresh lime juice shaken until ice cold and strained into a chilled glass, with an orange twist.
item.content:encoded:
The cosmopolitan has several claimed inventors and its origin is disputed, and the version most bartenders make today, with citron vodka, orange liqueur, lime and a little cranberry, is usually credited to Toby Cecchini, who made it at the Odeon in New York in the late 1980s. It is a sour, in the same family as the margarita and the daiquiri, and it works for the same reason: a spirit, an orange liqueur and citrus, in balance. The cranberry juice does not sweeten the drink. It is there for its colour and its tartness, and only 30 ml is used, which turns the drink pale pink and leaves it dry and crisp. More cranberry makes it sweet and heavy. The lime juice has to be freshly squeezed. The drink is shaken hard with plenty of ice, which chills it and dilutes it to the right strength, and it is strained into a glass that has been chilled with ice water while it is made.

  • Use fresh lime juice. Bottled juice turns the drink flat and dull.
  • Measure the cranberry juice. Too much makes the drink sweet and pink instead of dry and crisp.
  • Chill the glass. A warm glass warms the drink within a minute.

item.title: Daiquiri
item.description: Daiquiri: white rum, fresh lime juice and sugar syrup shaken hard and strained into a chilled glass. Just three ingredients, clean, sharp and balanced.
item.content:encoded:
The daiquiri is named after the Daiquirí area of Cuba, near Santiago, where there was an iron mine, and the drink is said to have been invented around 1900 by an American mining engineer, Jennings Cox, who mixed rum, lime and sugar for his guests. It is the classic rum sour, and everything about it is proportion: 60 ml of rum, 25 ml of lime juice and 15 ml of sugar syrup, a dry, sharp balance with the sweetness kept in the background. There is nothing to hide behind, so each ingredient counts. The lime juice has to be squeezed to order, the syrup is a plain mixture of equal parts sugar and water, and the rum should be a decent white rum. The drink is shaken hard for 15 seconds, which chills it and adds the right dilution, and it is strained into a glass that has been chilled. This is the shaken drink, not the frozen strawberry version, which is a different drink.

  • Squeeze the lime juice to order. It loses its bright aroma within the hour, and the drink tastes flat.
  • Taste and adjust the balance. Add a teaspoon more syrup if your limes are very sharp, or a little more lime if they are mild.
  • Shake hard for the full 15 seconds. The dilution from the ice is part of the recipe.

item.title: Manhattan
item.description: Manhattan: rye whiskey, sweet vermouth and Angostura bitters stirred with ice until cold and silky, strained into a chilled glass with a cocktail cherry.
item.content:encoded:
The Manhattan is one of the great classics of the American bar, and the story that it was invented in 1874 at the Manhattan Club in New York for a party is repeated in cocktail books, though historians doubt it. What is certain is what is in it: rye whiskey, sweet vermouth and bitters, in a ratio of 2 to 1. It is a drink made only of spirit and fortified wine, and for that reason it is stirred and not shaken. Shaking would aerate it and make it cloudy, and stirring for 30 seconds over ice chills it and adds the small amount of water that softens the alcohol and blends the flavours. Rye gives a spicy, dry edge, and bourbon a rounder and sweeter drink. Sweet vermouth is wine, and once opened it should be kept in the fridge and used within a month or two, since stale vermouth tastes flat and sour and spoils the drink.

  • Stir and do not shake. Shaking clouds a drink that is only spirit and wine, and thins its texture.
  • Keep the vermouth in the fridge once it is open. It goes flat and sour within a month or two.
  • Use rye for a drier, spicier drink and bourbon for a rounder, sweeter one.

item.title: Martini
item.description: Martini: gin and dry vermouth stirred with ice until bracingly cold and strained into a chilled glass, finished with a lemon twist or a green olive.
item.content:encoded:
The martini is the most argued-over cocktail there is, and even its origin is disputed. A drink called the Martinez, made with sweet vermouth and Old Tom gin, appeared in print in the 1880s, and the dry gin version known today was established by the early twentieth century. Over the years the amount of vermouth has shrunk, from roughly equal parts at first to 3 or 4 to 1 by the 1930s and much drier since, and this recipe uses 6 to 1, which is dry but still tastes of vermouth. It is only two ingredients, so it must be very cold and very fresh. The gin and glass should be chilled, the drink is stirred, not shaken, and vermouth that has been open for months is a common reason a martini tastes wrong. A lemon twist gives a bright, citrus edge and an olive a savoury, salty one, and a splash of olive brine makes it a dirty martini.

  • Stir and chill the glass. A martini is only gin and vermouth, and it has to be very cold.
  • Use fresh vermouth and keep it in the fridge once opened. Stale vermouth tastes of sherry and vinegar and ruins the drink.
  • Change the ratio to suit you: 3 to 1 for a wetter martini, 8 to 1 for a drier one, and a spoonful of olive brine for a dirty one.

item.title: Burnt Ends
item.description: Burnt ends: a brisket point rubbed and roasted low until tender, then cubed and cooked again in butter, honey and barbecue sauce until sticky and dark.
item.content:encoded:
Burnt ends began in Kansas City barbecue restaurants as the trimmings pitmasters cut from the end of a brisket, the dark, fat-streaked point, and gave away or ate themselves. They became the thing people queued for, and they work because they are cooked twice. The first cook is a slow roast, which melts the tough collagen in the point into gelatine so the meat turns tender and rich, and the rub builds a dark bark on the outside. The second cook is the one that gives the name its meaning. The meat is cubed, so every piece has bark on several sides, tossed in butter, honey and barbecue sauce, and returned to the oven until the glaze reduces to a sticky lacquer that clings to the cubes. The point is used rather than the flat because it carries far more fat, and fat is what stops cubes of beef drying out during a second cook.

  • Cook to feel and not to the clock. A brisket is ready when a probe slides in like it is going into soft butter, which is usually near 93°C, but varies from one piece of meat to the next.
  • Cut the cubes after the rest and not before. Cutting straight from the oven lets the juices run out onto the board.
  • If you cannot find a brisket point, use a 1.8 kg beef chuck roast instead and cook it the same way. It is called poor man's burnt ends and it is tender and rich.

item.title: Country-Style Ribs
item.description: Country-style ribs: meaty pork shoulder ribs rubbed with spices, braised in the oven until tender and glazed with barbecue sauce until sticky and dark.
item.content:encoded:
Country-style ribs are not ribs in the way spare ribs are. They come from the blade end of the pork shoulder, next to the rib cage, and they are thick, meaty and full of fat and connective tissue, more like a pork chop cut from a roast than a rack of bones. That decides how to cook them. A quick grill leaves them tough and chewy, but two and a half hours in a covered dish turns the connective tissue into gelatine and the meat into something you can cut with a fork. The rub goes on first for flavour that goes all the way through, a splash of apple juice in the dish gives steam and a little sweetness, and the tightly covered foil keeps the ribs moist. The barbecue sauce goes on only at the end, because sugar burns over a long cook, and a short blast in a hot oven turns it into the sticky glaze.

  • Keep the foil tight. If steam escapes, the ribs dry out on top and need longer, and the tender result is what the covered cook is for.
  • Add the sauce at the end, not the beginning. Barbecue sauce is full of sugar and it scorches and turns bitter over hours in the oven.
  • Save the liquid from the dish. Skim the fat, boil it down for 5 minutes and spoon it over the ribs as a light sauce.

item.title: Filet Mignon
item.description: Filet mignon: thick tenderloin steaks seared hard in cast iron, basted with butter, thyme and garlic and finished in the oven to a rosy medium-rare.
item.content:encoded:
Filet mignon is cut from the tenderloin, a muscle that does almost no work, which is why it is the softest cut on the animal and also the mildest. Everything about cooking it follows from that. Because it is lean and tender, it needs flavour brought to it, in the form of a hard, dark crust from a very hot pan and a spoonful of thyme and garlic butter at the end. Because it is thick, a steak of 4 cm cannot cook through in the pan without the outside going grey, so it is seared on the hob and finished in the oven, which cooks the middle gently while the crust stays as it is. And because it is lean it has no margin for error, so a thermometer matters more here than for any other steak. Pulled at 52°C it rests up to a rosy medium-rare, and a few degrees more turns it firm and dry.

  • Use a thermometer. Pull the steak at 52°C for medium-rare, 57°C for medium. It rises 3 to 5 degrees as it rests, so waiting for the final temperature overshoots.
  • Dry the steak thoroughly. Surface moisture steams in the pan and stops the crust forming.
  • Rest before cutting. The juices settle back into the meat in 5 minutes and stay in the steak instead of pooling on the plate.

item.title: Galbi Jjim
item.description: Galbi jjim: Korean beef short ribs soaked, parboiled and braised in a sweet soy sauce with pear, garlic and ginger until tender, with carrots and daikon.
item.content:encoded:
Galbi jjim is the braised counterpart to grilled galbi, and it is the short rib dish Korean families make for holidays and birthdays. Two steps that look fussy are what separate it from an ordinary braise. The ribs are soaked in cold water for an hour, which draws out blood, and then boiled briefly and rinsed, which removes the scum that would otherwise cloud the sauce and give a stale taste. What follows is a sweet, savoury braising liquid: soy sauce for salt and depth, brown sugar and mirin for sweetness, and grated Korean pear, whose enzymes tenderise the meat and whose sweetness rounds the sauce. Garlic, ginger and sesame oil supply the aroma. The carrots, daikon and shiitake go in for the last half hour so they keep their shape, soaking up the sauce, and the pot is simmered uncovered at the end so it reduces to a glossy glaze.

  • Do not skip the soak and the parboil. They are what make the sauce clear and clean tasting, and they cost you more time than effort.
  • Add the vegetables late. If they go in with the ribs, the carrots and daikon fall apart before the meat is done.
  • Chill the pot overnight if you can. The fat sets on top and lifts off in a sheet, leaving a sauce that is rich but not greasy.

item.title: King Ranch Chicken Casserole
item.description: King Ranch chicken casserole: shredded chicken, corn tortillas, peppers and green chiles in a creamy sauce, baked under cheddar until bubbling. Feeds eight.
item.content:encoded:
King Ranch chicken is a Texas potluck staple, named for the ranch and not for any royalty, and it is built from what a Texas pantry holds: tortillas, chicken, a can of tomatoes with green chiles, cheese and a creamy sauce. The classic version uses tinned condensed soup, and it works, but this one makes the sauce from scratch with butter, flour, stock and sour cream, which takes five minutes more and tastes cleaner. The tortillas are the point where a casserole like this can go wrong. Layered raw they turn to paste, so they are torn and dipped into the sauce, or briefly heated first, and used as a layer that soaks up the liquid and gives the dish body, a bit like lasagne. The result slices into squares and is even better the next day.

  • Drain the tomatoes. Extra liquid makes the tortillas swell into a wet, heavy layer instead of holding together.
  • Tear the tortillas rather than cutting neat strips. Ragged pieces overlap and soak up sauce more evenly.
  • Rest the dish for 10 minutes. It sets enough to cut into clean squares that keep their layers.

item.title: Maque Choux
item.description: Maque choux: fresh sweetcorn cooked with bacon, onion, pepper and tomato in its own milky juices, then finished with a little cream and cayenne.
item.content:encoded:
Maque choux, pronounced mock shoo, is a Cajun way of cooking corn that comes from south Louisiana, where the Cajun and Native American cooking of the bayou meet. Fresh corn is cut from the cob and simmered with the trinity of onion, bell pepper and celery, and the part that makes it distinct is the corn milk. When you scrape the back of a knife down a stripped cob, it releases a starchy, sweet liquid that thickens the dish and gives it a creaminess that cream alone does not have, so the recipe keeps that step. Bacon adds smoke and salt, tomato adds a little acidity to balance the sweetness of the corn, and a splash of cream and some cayenne round it off. It is a side dish in the South, but with a piece of grilled fish or sausage it is dinner.

  • Do not skip scraping the cobs. The starchy corn milk is what thickens the dish, and it is the difference between maque choux and corn in a pan.
  • Use fresh corn in season. Frozen kernels work, about 700 g, but you lose the milk and the dish is thinner.
  • Stir often. The starch in the corn catches on the base of the pan.

item.title: Porcupine Meatballs
item.description: Porcupine meatballs: beef meatballs mixed with raw rice and simmered in tomato sauce until the rice swells and sticks out like quills. One pan, easy.
item.content:encoded:
Porcupine meatballs are a mid-century American home-cooking classic, a dish that was designed to stretch a pound of ground beef across a family and still put a full meal on the table, and it works better than it has any right to. The rice goes in raw. As the meatballs simmer in the tomato sauce, the grains cook slowly inside them, absorbing the fat and juice from the beef, and swell until some poke through the surface like quills, which is where the name comes from. Because the rice takes up moisture from inside the meatball as it cooks, the meatballs stay soft and light rather than dense, which is the opposite of what you would expect from adding a dry ingredient. The sauce needs enough liquid for the rice to finish, so it is made a little loose and simmered under a lid, and it thickens as the rice releases some of its starch into it.

  • Use raw long-grain rice. Cooked rice makes soft, pasty meatballs, and instant rice turns to mush before the beef is done.
  • Keep the balls loosely packed. Pressing them hard makes them dense, and the rice needs room to swell.
  • Cook them covered and check the rice at the end. If the sauce has cooked away before the rice is soft, add a splash of stock and keep going.

item.title: Shrimp Creole
item.description: Shrimp Creole: shrimp simmered briefly in a spicy tomato sauce of onion, celery, green pepper, thyme and cayenne, served over white rice.
item.content:encoded:
Shrimp Creole comes from New Orleans, where the tomato entered the city's cooking through its Spanish and French Creole kitchens, and it is the tomato-based cousin of the brown roux dishes of Cajun country. The sauce is a study in patience with cheap ingredients. Onion, celery and green pepper, the Louisiana trinity, are cooked slowly until soft and sweet, then tomatoes are simmered with bay, thyme, cayenne and a little Worcestershire sauce until they reduce to a thick, deep red sauce that could stand on its own. That is the part that takes the time, and it can be made a day ahead. The shrimp go in only at the end, for about four minutes, because they turn from tender and sweet to rubbery in the time it takes to answer a phone. Served over plain white rice, which soaks up the sauce, it is one of the great fast-finishing dinners.

  • Cook the sauce before the shrimp go in. It can be made a day ahead and improves overnight, and the shrimp then need only 4 minutes.
  • Pull the pan off the heat as soon as the shrimp are pink and curled loosely. A tight curl means they are overcooked.
  • Taste for heat at the end. Cayenne varies, and the sauce can take more or less depending on how much you like.

item.title: Steak au Poivre
item.description: Steak au poivre: steaks pressed with cracked black peppercorns and pan-seared, with a brandy, stock and cream sauce made in the same pan.
item.content:encoded:
Steak au poivre is the bistro classic that shows how much can be done with one pan and a few ingredients. The pepper is cracked, not ground, so the pieces are big enough to form a crust and to give texture and bursts of heat and citrus-like aroma against the beef, and pressing it into the steak before it goes in the pan means the pepper toasts and mellows in the fat rather than sitting harsh on top. The sauce is made in the same pan without washing it, so the browned bits left by the steaks, the fond, go into it and give it its depth. Brandy is added off the heat so it does not catch, then reduced with stock, and cream rounds it into something that coats the steak and softens the pepper. A spoon of Dijon adds sharpness. It takes twenty minutes and tastes like a restaurant.

  • Crack the peppercorns coarsely. Ground pepper burns and turns bitter in a hot pan, whereas cracked pieces toast and form a crust.
  • Keep the brandy away from a direct flame. Take the pan off the heat before you add it, in case it ignites, and keep a lid close.
  • Do not wash the pan before the sauce. The brown bits that stick to it are concentrated beef flavour.

item.title: Stuffed Pork Chops
item.description: Stuffed pork chops: thick bone-in chops filled with a sage, apple and celery bread stuffing, seared in a pan and finished in the oven until juicy.
item.content:encoded:
Pork chops have a reputation for being dry, and stuffing them is the way to fix that as much as to make them look impressive. The stuffing in the pocket adds moisture and fat, and it insulates the middle of the chop, which slows its cooking and forgives a minute or two over. The details still matter. The chops must be thick, at least 4 cm, or there is nothing to cut a pocket into, and bone-in chops stay juicier than boneless ones. The stuffing is cooked before it goes in, so it is already seasoned and safe to eat, and it is cooled slightly so it does not start to steam the meat from the inside. A quick sear in a hot pan gives the crust, and the oven finishes them gently to 63°C, the temperature at which pork is done and still pink and juicy in the centre. Sage and apple are the classic partners for pork, and here they make the stuffing.

  • Buy chops at least 4 cm thick. A thin chop cannot hold a pocket, and it overcooks before the stuffing is hot.
  • Do not overfill. Stuffing swells as it heats, and a bulging pocket splits open in the oven.
  • Use a thermometer and pull the chops at 63°C. Pork cooked much beyond that dries out, and 63°C is the temperature the pork is officially safe at with a 3-minute rest.

item.title: Bacon and Cabbage
item.description: Bacon and cabbage: a cured pork joint simmered until tender, with cabbage and potatoes cooked in the same pot and served in thick slices with mustard.
item.content:encoded:
Long before corned beef and cabbage became the Irish-American dinner for St Patrick's Day, bacon and cabbage was the everyday and Sunday dinner in Ireland, where a joint of cured pork was the affordable meat and the boiling pot was the cooking method. Irish bacon is not the streaky rasher of a breakfast plate. It is a joint of cured pork loin or collar, mild and pink, and it cooks in one pot with everything else. The bacon simmers gently, never boils hard, so the meat stays tender and slices cleanly, and the salty, savoury cooking water is put to use twice, first for the cabbage and then for the potatoes, which take their flavour from it. Nothing is browned and there is no sauce beyond a spoonful of English or Dijon mustard, because the point of the dish is the flavour of the pork and the sweetness of good cabbage.

  • Keep the water at a bare simmer. Hard boiling toughens the meat and it shrinks and turns stringy.
  • If the joint is very heavily cured, soak it in cold water before cooking. Ask the butcher; most modern joints are mild and need no soaking.
  • Use the cooking liquid. Taste it first and, if it is not too salty, keep some for cooking the cabbage and for the plate.

item.title: Clapshot
item.description: Clapshot: an Orkney mash of potatoes and swede with butter and chives. Sweeter and more golden than plain mashed potato, and the partner to haggis.
item.content:encoded:
Clapshot is from Orkney, where the swede is called a neep (in Scotland a neep is a swede and not a turnip), and it is the northern cousin of the mashed potato and swede that goes with haggis on Burns Night. Mixing the two vegetables together before mashing, and not serving them separately as in haggis, neeps and tatties, gives a sweeter, more golden dish where the swede's earthy sweetness stops the potato tasting bland. The proportion is half and half, and each vegetable needs treating on its own terms. Swede holds more water than potato and takes longer to cook, so it goes in the pan first, and then the potatoes are added, so that both are ready together. The mash is drained thoroughly, dried out in the hot pan, and beaten with plenty of butter and chives, because watery vegetables give a watery mash.

  • Start the swede first. It takes about 10 minutes longer than potato, and cooked together from cold the potato falls apart before the swede softens.
  • Steam the vegetables dry in the hot pan after draining. Any water left in them thins the mash and dilutes the butter.
  • Use a masher, not a food processor. Blending the potato overworks the starch and turns it gluey.

item.title: Meat and Potato Pie
item.description: Meat and potato pie: chunks of beef and potato in thick onion gravy under a golden shortcrust lid, the Lancashire pie for a cold day. Serves eight.
item.content:encoded:
The meat and potato pie is the pie of Lancashire and Wigan in particular, where it is sold hot from bakeries and eaten in a bread roll at the football, and it is a different thing from a steak pie. The filling is plain and hearty, cubes of beef and potato in a thick, salty gravy with a lot of onion, and nothing else is added. The potato does two jobs: it makes the pie filling and stretches the meat, and its starch thickens the gravy from inside, so a spoonful of the pie holds together instead of running. Adding it near the end of the stewing is the important step, because potato added at the start dissolves into the sauce, whereas potato added for the last 15 minutes stays in chunks that are soft but whole. The filling is cooled before it goes into the pastry, so the base does not go soggy under a hot filling.

  • Add the potatoes late. In for the whole cook they melt into the gravy, and you lose the chunks that make the pie.
  • Cool the filling before it goes into the pastry. A hot filling melts the fat in the base, which then bakes soggy and pale.
  • Make the gravy thick. It thins a little in the oven, and a runny filling floods the dish when you cut into it.

item.title: Salmon Fishcakes
item.description: Salmon fishcakes: flaked poached salmon in mashed potato with spring onion, lemon and capers, coated in breadcrumbs and fried until crisp and golden.
item.content:encoded:
A good fishcake is mostly fish and only enough potato to hold it, and the mistakes with them come from too much potato and too much moisture. Both are avoidable. The potatoes are boiled whole in their skins if you have the time, or in large chunks, drained hard and left to steam dry in the pan, so they mash fluffy and not wet. Salmon is poached gently for a few minutes only, so it stays moist and flakes into big pieces that are folded through by hand and not mashed. The cakes then need to be chilled for half an hour, which lets the starch set so they hold their shape in the pan. Coating them in flour, egg and breadcrumbs gives the crust that contrasts with the soft middle. Lemon zest, capers, spring onion and parsley keep the salmon's richness from feeling heavy.

  • Steam the potatoes dry. Wet mash means wet cakes that will not hold together, and dry mash is what lets the fish stay the main flavour.
  • Flake the salmon by hand and fold it in gently. Beating it in reduces it to a paste and the fishcakes lose their texture.
  • Chill the cakes before coating. Cold, firm cakes keep their shape in the pan and do not break as you turn them.

item.title: Arctic Char
item.description: Arctic char: skin-on fillets pan-seared until the skin is crisp and the flesh just flakes, finished with lemon, garlic butter and fresh dill.
item.content:encoded:
Arctic char is a cold-water fish of the salmon family that lives in the northern lakes and coastal rivers of Canada, and in the far north it is a staple, often eaten smoked or dried. Farmed char is now sold across Canada and the United States, and it is a good fish for cooking at home. It sits between salmon and trout: the flesh is pink, fine-flaked and delicate, milder and less oily than salmon, and the skin is thin and crisps beautifully in a hot pan. That is how it is best cooked, mostly skin-side down, so the skin protects the flesh from the heat and the fat under it renders. The fillets are dried well and pressed down for the first few seconds so the skin does not curl. A splash of butter, garlic, lemon and dill at the end is all it needs, because the fish has its own gentle sweetness.

  • Dry the skin thoroughly. Moisture stops it crisping, and it is the difference between crackling skin and a limp one.
  • Cook mostly on the skin side. The skin shields the flesh, so the fish cooks gently from below and stays moist.
  • Check with a thermometer if you like. 52 to 55°C gives a silky centre, and 63°C / 145°F is the official safe temperature and will be firmer.

item.title: Jiggs Dinner
item.description: Jiggs dinner: the Newfoundland Sunday boiled dinner of salt beef with cabbage, carrots, turnip and potatoes, served with a mash of yellow split peas.
item.content:encoded:
Jiggs dinner is the boiled dinner of Newfoundland, eaten on Sundays and holidays and served at the table with a great deal of pride, and it takes its name from Bringing Up Father, an American comic strip of the early twentieth century whose hero, Jiggs, was always eating corned beef and cabbage. In Newfoundland the salt beef is more heavily cured than what is sold elsewhere, and the meal is built around it. Everything goes into one large pot at different times so that it all finishes together: the beef first, for the longest, then the turnip and carrots, then the potatoes, and the cabbage at the end so it stays green. The pease pudding, a smooth mash of yellow split peas, is the essential side and is cooked in a separate pan here. The cooking liquid is the gravy, tasting of beef and vegetables, and the leftover beef makes a very good cold hash the next day.

  • Add the vegetables in stages. The swede and carrots need 30 minutes, the potatoes 20, and the cabbage 15, and if they all go in together the cabbage turns to mush.
  • If you use a very salty salt beef, soak it overnight in cold water, changing the water twice. Ordinary corned beef only needs rinsing.
  • Slice the beef across the grain. Along it, the meat comes off in stringy strips.

item.title: Rappie Pie
item.description: Rappie pie: Acadian grated potato pulp squeezed dry and scalded with boiling chicken stock, layered with chicken and baked until dark and crisp on top.
item.content:encoded:
Rappie pie, from the French râpé, meaning grated, is the signature dish of the Acadian communities of Nova Scotia, and it is unlike any other potato dish. Potatoes are grated to a fine pulp, then wrung out in a cloth until the starchy liquid is gone. What remains is a dry, fibrous pulp that is then scalded with boiling chicken stock, and the effect is dramatic: the pulp swells, turns translucent and sets into a soft, sticky, gelatinous mass. It is layered with pieces of chicken and baked for hours until the top forms a dark, crisp crust and the inside is savoury and soft. Made this way it is more like a dense potato custard than a pie. It is served with butter melted into the middle, or in some homes with molasses, and it is a food that people from Nova Scotia miss when they are away from home.

  • Squeeze the pulp as dry as you can. Left wet it will not absorb the stock and the pie sets loose and pale.
  • Have the stock at a full boil when it goes on. The heat is what cooks the starch and turns the pulp translucent.
  • Be patient with the bake. The long, slow cook is what browns the top to a dark, crisp crust and sets the inside.

item.title: Doner Kebab
item.description: Doner kebab at home: spiced lamb and beef mince kneaded, baked as a loaf, sliced thin and fried crisp, served in flatbread with salad and garlic sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The doner kebab on a vertical spit is the invention of Turkish cooks in nineteenth-century Bursa, and the meat sold in kebab shops around the world is a compressed, seasoned mince or stack of layers, shaved as it roasts. At home you can get remarkably close to that texture without a spit. The trick is in the kneading. The mince is worked with salt, spices and grated onion for several minutes, until it turns sticky and pulls into strands, because that is what gives the meat the tight, springy, sliceable texture of doner and stops it crumbling like meatloaf. The mixture is packed hard into a tin with no air gaps, baked, rested and then cut with a sharp knife into slices as thin as paper, which is what allows the edges to crisp when they hit a hot pan. The final frying is what gives the char you look for.

  • Knead until sticky. It is the step that turns mince into doner, so if the mixture is still crumbly, keep going for another minute or two.
  • Squeeze the onion dry before adding it. Excess water makes the loaf loose and stops it slicing thin.
  • Slice while the loaf is still just warm. A cold loaf is firmer, but very thin slices are easier with a sharp knife and a steady hand.

item.title: Yaki Udon
item.description: Yaki udon: thick udon noodles stir-fried with pork belly, cabbage, carrot and shiitake in a soy, oyster and mirin sauce, topped with bonito flakes.
item.content:encoded:
Yaki udon is the stir-fried noodle dish of Japanese home cooking, the udon cousin of yakisoba, and it is a favourite of the izakaya and of the weeknight table because it takes one pan and about twelve minutes. Udon is thick and chewy, with a satisfying bite that survives frying, and that makes it very different from the thin egg noodles in a Chinese chow mein. The important step is loosening the block of noodles before they go in the pan, so they separate and coat evenly in sauce. The sauce is a balance of soy, oyster sauce and mirin for savoury depth and gentle sweetness, with a little sugar, and it is added to a very hot pan so it caramelises on the noodles rather than stewing them. Pork belly gives richness, cabbage gives sweetness and shiitake give a deep flavour, and a shower of bonito flakes that dance in the steam finishes it.

  • Loosen the noodles before they go in. Fresh udon comes in a tight block, and if it goes in whole the sauce coats only the outside.
  • Pour the sauce in around the edge of a hot pan. It sizzles and caramelises on contact, instead of pooling and stewing the noodles.
  • Keep the heat high and the tossing constant. Udon is soft and sticks easily, and a hot, busy pan stops it breaking.

item.title: Chicken Burrito Bowl
item.description: Chicken burrito bowl: chipotle and lime chicken thighs over rice with black beans, corn salsa, guacamole and lettuce. A burrito in a bowl.
item.content:encoded:
A burrito bowl is everything you would put in a burrito, arranged in a bowl in separate portions, so each spoonful can be built to taste. The strength of the format is the contrast, hot chicken and rice against cold, crisp lettuce and fresh salsa, and the recipe is built to keep the components distinct. The chicken uses thighs, which stay juicy through a hot pan or grill, marinated for a short time in lime juice, chipotle, cumin and garlic so they take on flavour and a smoky, gently spicy edge. The rice is cooked plain, then stirred with lime and coriander leaves so it is fragrant but does not fight the rest. Black beans are warmed with cumin, and a quick corn salsa and a mashed avocado bring freshness and creaminess. Everything except the chicken can be made in advance, which makes the bowl a very good option for meal prep.

  • Keep the components separate in the bowl. Each one is best against the others, and mixed together they lose their contrast.
  • Do not marinate for hours. The acid in lime juice turns chicken firm and chalky if it sits too long, and 20 minutes is plenty.
  • Squeeze lime over the avocado. It keeps the guacamole green, and it brightens everything in the bowl.

item.title: Chickpea Salad
item.description: Chickpea salad: tinned chickpeas tossed with cucumber, tomato, red onion, olives and herbs in a lemon and olive oil dressing. Ready in 15 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Chickpea salad is one of those recipes that hits the mark for a working lunch: it uses a tin from the cupboard and a few vegetables, needs no cooking, is filling and improves as it sits. The chickpeas are the point. They are firm and mild, with a nutty flavour that takes up dressing well, and they give the salad the protein and fibre that make it a meal, not a side. The dressing does the heavy lifting, and lemon juice and olive oil in a two to one ratio, with garlic, oregano and a spoonful of Dijon to make it cling, is bright and sharp enough to lift the starchy chickpeas. The vegetables are chosen for crunch and contrast, cool cucumber, sweet tomato and sharp red onion, and salty olives make it Mediterranean. Rinsing and draining the chickpeas well, and drying them lightly, stops the dressing from turning watery.

  • Dress the chickpeas first. They soak up the dressing while you chop, which gives a better flavour than dressing them at the end.
  • Drain and dry the chickpeas well. Water clinging to them thins the dressing and makes the salad soggy.
  • Add the tomatoes and cucumber just before serving if you are making it ahead. They release water and dilute the dressing if left for hours.

item.title: Crunchwrap
item.description: Crunchwrap: a big flour tortilla layered with taco beef, cheese, a crisp tostada, sour cream, lettuce and tomato, folded into a parcel and toasted in a pan.
item.content:encoded:
The crunchwrap is a fast-food invention that turned out to be a very good idea for home cooks, because it is essentially a tostada, a taco and a quesadilla in one hand-held parcel. The genius is the structure. A crisp tostada goes in the middle, between the warm, saucy beef and the cool lettuce and tomato, so there is a crunch inside a soft wrap. The big tortilla is folded in pleats over the top, and toasted seam side down, so the fold is sealed shut with heat and the outside becomes crisp and golden. Getting it right is about layering and order. The cheese sauce or grated cheese goes on the tortilla first so it melts into the beef and glues the layers together, the tostada goes on the beef, and the wet ingredients, sour cream, lettuce and tomato, go on top of the tostada where they cannot soften it. Fold it tightly and it holds.

  • Cook them seam side down first. The heat seals the pleats, and if you start on the smooth side they unfold.
  • Put the wet fillings on top of the tostada. Lettuce, tomato and sour cream on the crisp shell keep it crunchy for longer.
  • Do not overfill. A pile that is more than 3 cm high will not fold shut, and it is better to cook two smaller ones.

item.title: Italian Sub
item.description: Italian sub: crusty rolls layered with salami, ham, capicola and provolone, then lettuce, tomato, onion and pepperoncini, dressed with oil and vinegar.
item.content:encoded:
The Italian sub is a New Jersey and Philadelphia classic that belongs to the Italian-American delicatessens of the early twentieth century, where cold cuts and cheese from home were piled onto local bread. It is a sandwich with a system. There are three cured meats, usually salami, ham and capicola, for different flavours, salty, mild and peppery, and one cheese, provolone, which is sharp and melts on the tongue. There is a dressing rather than mayonnaise: olive oil and red wine vinegar with oregano and garlic, shaken and sprinkled directly on the meat and bread, where it soaks in and seasons every bite. The crisp shredded lettuce, tomato, thin red onion and pickled pepperoncini make it sharp and fresh against the fat. The bread has to be a proper roll with a crackly crust and a soft middle, and the assembled sandwich is wrapped and left for ten minutes so the dressing soaks in.

  • Fold the meat instead of laying it flat. Loose ruffles give volume and a softer bite than flat layers.
  • Put the tomatoes and lettuce on top of the meats, and not against the bread. That keeps the roll dry and crisp.
  • Wrap and rest the sandwich before you eat it. The dressing soaks into the bread and meat, and the flavours come together.

item.title: One-Pot Pasta
item.description: One-pot pasta: spaghetti, cherry tomatoes, onion, garlic and basil simmered together in one pot with water, so the starchy liquid becomes the sauce.
item.content:encoded:
One-pot pasta breaks the usual rule of boiling pasta in lots of water and draining it, and it works because of what usually goes down the sink. When pasta cooks, it releases starch, and in a large pot of water that starch is discarded. In this method there is only just enough water to cook the pasta, so the starch stays in the pot and thickens the liquid into a glossy sauce that clings to the strands, without cream or a separate sauce. The other ingredients cook in the same liquid, so they flavour it: cherry tomatoes burst and add their juice and sweetness, onion and garlic dissolve into the background, and the oregano and olive oil bring it together. The only skill is in the liquid. The pot is stirred often, so nothing sticks, and the water should be almost gone when the pasta is just tender, leaving a saucy, not soupy, finish.

  • Stir often. There is little liquid and a lot of starch, and the pasta sticks to the base of the pot if it is left alone.
  • Watch the water at the end. If the pasta is still firm and the pot is dry, add a splash more; if it is tender and soupy, cook for another minute uncovered.
  • Use a wide pot with a heavy base. A wide surface lets the pasta lie in the liquid instead of standing out of it.

item.title: Roasted Chickpeas
item.description: Roasted chickpeas: tinned chickpeas dried well, tossed in olive oil and smoked paprika and roasted in a hot oven until crisp. A crunchy, high-fibre snack.
item.content:encoded:
Roasted chickpeas are the rare healthy snack that people actually want to eat, because they are crunchy, salty and easy to eat by the handful, and they take five minutes of effort. There is one rule, and it decides everything: they have to be dry. A chickpea straight from the tin is coated in water, and if it goes into the oven wet it steams, turning soft and chewy instead of crisp. So the chickpeas are drained, rinsed, and then rolled in a clean towel until they are properly dry, and the papery skins that come loose are picked out, since skins that stay on can char. Oil is added in a thin coating only, just enough for the spices to cling, and the salt and spices go on at the end of cooking, when the surface is dry and takes the seasoning. A hot oven and a long roast drive off the moisture from inside.

  • Dry the chickpeas well. Any water left on them steams in the oven and stops them crisping, so it is worth the minute with a towel.
  • Season after roasting. Spices added at the start can burn, whereas salt and spice tossed onto hot chickpeas cling to the oil.
  • Leave them to cool before you judge. Roasted chickpeas crisp as they cool, and they seem soft while hot.

item.title: Taco Salad
item.description: Taco salad: seasoned ground beef over crisp romaine with black beans, corn, tomato, cheddar, avocado and tortilla chips, in a creamy salsa dressing.
item.content:encoded:
Taco salad is a taco turned inside out, with the fillings piled over lettuce instead of tucked into a shell, and it exists because the flavours of a taco are good enough to carry a salad. The beef is the anchor and it is cooked with a full spice mix and a splash of water so it is moist and savoury, then cooled slightly before it goes on the lettuce, so that the leaves stay crisp instead of wilting. The rest is built for texture: crisp romaine, sweet corn, creamy beans and avocado, juicy tomato and sharp cheddar. The tortilla chips are crushed in at the last moment, so they keep their crunch, and the dressing of sour cream, salsa and lime is deliberately thick so that it clings and works as both a dressing and a sauce. It is a good lunch for a crowd because everything can be prepared ahead and put together at the table.

  • Cool the beef for a few minutes before it goes on the lettuce. Hot meat wilts the leaves in seconds.
  • Add the tortilla chips last, at the table. They soften quickly in the dressing, and it is the crunch that makes it a taco salad.
  • Keep the dressing thick. A thin dressing pools at the bottom of the bowl, whereas a thick one clings to the lettuce and the beans.

item.title: Turkey Chili
item.description: Turkey chili: ground turkey simmered with kidney and black beans, peppers, tomatoes, chilli powder, cumin and smoked paprika into a thick, lighter chilli.
item.content:encoded:
Turkey chili is a lighter version of a beef chili, and the challenge is that ground turkey is lean and mild, so it needs building up. Three things do that. First, the meat is browned properly in a little oil, until it has colour and a few crisp edges, because grey, steamed turkey has almost no flavour. Second, the spices, chilli powder, cumin, oregano and smoked paprika, are cooked in the pan for a minute before the liquid goes in, which wakes up the oils in them and takes away the raw taste. Third, smoked paprika supplies the smoky depth that lean turkey lacks, and a long, slow simmer of 40 minutes lets the flavours meld while the beans break down a little and thicken the pot. Two kinds of bean, kidney and black, give a good contrast of texture. The result is a chilli that is high in protein and fibre and tastes hearty.

  • Brown the turkey until it is coloured and no longer pale. It has little fat to brown in, so it needs a good stretch of time in the pan.
  • Cook the spices in the pan before adding liquid. A minute in the hot oil takes away their raw, dusty taste.
  • Use dark-meat turkey mince if you can find it. It has more fat and flavour and keeps the chilli from tasting dry.

item.title: Wedge Salad
item.description: Wedge salad: a crisp iceberg lettuce wedge topped with blue cheese dressing, crumbled bacon, cherry tomatoes and chives. The classic steakhouse salad.
item.content:encoded:
The wedge salad is one of the simplest salads and one of the most satisfying, and it belongs to the American steakhouse, where it has been served since the middle of the twentieth century. It has no cleverness beyond contrast, and the contrasts are the point: the cold, crisp, watery iceberg against a thick, cool, tangy dressing, salty smoky bacon, sweet tomato and sharp chives. Iceberg is the right lettuce here, the only one with the crunch and water content to hold a heavy dressing without wilting, and cutting it into wedges instead of tearing it gives a structure of layered leaves that catch the dressing between them. The dressing is made thick, so that it clings to the wedge instead of sliding off it. The bacon is cooked crisp so it stays crunchy against the wet lettuce, and everything is added at the last minute.

  • Chill the iceberg well before you cut it. Cold, crisp lettuce is what makes the salad work, and a cool wedge stays crunchy under a heavy dressing.
  • Keep the dressing thick. It should sit on the lettuce like a sauce, not run off it.
  • Dress at the table. Iceberg is a robust lettuce, but a wedge left dressed for 30 minutes starts to weep and lose its snap.

item.title: Chicken and Sweetcorn Soup
item.description: Chicken and sweetcorn soup: diced chicken and creamed sweetcorn in ginger stock, thickened lightly and finished with ribbons of egg and spring onion.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken and sweetcorn soup is a fixture of the Chinese takeaway menu in Britain and Australia, and it is closer to a Cantonese-style thickened soup than to a Western chowder. The base is a good chicken stock scented with ginger, into which finely diced chicken breast cooks for a few minutes and stays tender. Creamed sweetcorn goes in for sweetness and body, so the soup is silky and gently sweet, with whole kernels giving bursts of texture. A slurry of cornflour and water thickens it lightly, and the timing of that matters: too much and it is gluey, too little and it is thin. The egg is the trick that gives the soup its ribbons. Beaten egg is poured in a thin stream into the simmering soup while it is stirred gently in one direction, so that it sets into fine, silky threads instead of lumps. A few drops of sesame oil and white pepper give the takeaway flavour.

  • Pour the egg in a thin stream into a moving, barely simmering soup. Dumped in all at once it sets into rubbery scrambled lumps.
  • Add the cornflour slurry gradually and stop when the soup coats a spoon. It thickens more as it cools.
  • Cut the chicken very small. Tiny pieces cook quickly and stay tender, which is what keeps the soup smooth.

item.title: Prawn Mayo Sandwich
item.description: Prawn mayo sandwich: cold cooked prawns folded through mayonnaise with lemon and cayenne, piled onto buttered soft bread with crisp lettuce.
item.content:encoded:
The prawn mayonnaise sandwich is a fixture of the British packed lunch, a supermarket meal-deal staple and a service-station standard, and it is far better made at home for a simple reason: the prawns. Shop sandwiches use small prawns in a lot of thin dressing, whereas at home you can use good prawns, mixed with just enough mayonnaise to bind them and no more. The details are small. Prawns are dried thoroughly before they are dressed, because water from them thins the mayonnaise and makes soggy bread. The dressing is mayonnaise with a little lemon juice for sharpness, black pepper and a pinch of cayenne, and it is deliberately not a Marie Rose, which would add ketchup and turn it into a prawn cocktail. The bread is buttered edge to edge, which forms a barrier between the filling and the crumb, and a leaf of crisp lettuce goes in for crunch.

  • Dry the prawns properly. Any water on them thins the mayonnaise and soaks the bread, so pat them with paper before mixing.
  • Butter the bread to the edge. It seals the crumb against the filling and keeps the sandwich from going soggy.
  • Use just enough mayonnaise to bind the prawns. They should glisten, not swim.

item.title: White Sauce
item.description: White sauce: butter, flour and milk cooked into a smooth, glossy sauce, the base for cauliflower cheese, lasagne, fish pie and parsley sauce.
item.content:encoded:
White sauce, or béchamel, is a foundation sauce and it is worth learning properly, because the same three ingredients make many dishes: cheese sauce for cauliflower cheese and macaroni, parsley sauce for gammon and fish, the filling of a lasagne, the binding for a fish pie. It is made of a roux, equal weights of butter and flour cooked together, and milk, and it works because of what happens to the flour. Cooked in butter for a minute or two, the starch grains are coated in fat and lose their raw taste, and when milk is added gradually they swell and thicken the liquid without clumping. The lumps that people fear come from adding the milk too quickly or cold, when the flour seizes into balls. Warm milk, added a little at a time with constant whisking, gives a smooth sauce every time, and a grating of nutmeg is the traditional seasoning.

  • Warm the milk first. Cold milk added to hot roux clumps, and warm milk goes in smoothly.
  • Add the milk in stages, whisking between additions. The first splash makes a thick paste, and it is then easy to loosen.
  • If you do get lumps, whisk hard off the heat, or pour the sauce through a sieve. Simmer it after that for the full 5 minutes to cook out the flour.

item.title: Indian Tacos
item.description: Indian tacos: puffy fry bread topped with seasoned beef and beans, lettuce, tomato, cheese and sour cream. Also called Navajo or frybread tacos.
item.content:encoded:
Indian tacos, also called Navajo tacos, frybread tacos and, increasingly in Canada, Indigenous tacos, are a fair food and a family food across Indigenous communities in Canada and the United States. Their base is fry bread, a simple dough of flour, baking powder, salt and warm liquid that is stretched into rounds and fried in hot oil until it puffs into a golden, blistered disc, crisp on the edge and soft and chewy in the middle. Fry bread has a hard history, since it came out of the government rations given to Indigenous nations forced from their lands, flour, lard and sugar, and it is remembered as a food of survival and endurance as well as celebration. Piled with seasoned beef, beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheese and sour cream, it becomes a whole meal. The dough is rested for half an hour so that it relaxes and stretches easily, and the oil must be hot enough to puff it quickly.

  • Do not knead the dough hard. A short knead keeps the fry bread tender, and heavy kneading makes it tough.
  • Keep the oil at 180°C. Too cool and the bread soaks up oil and turns greasy, and too hot and it browns before it puffs.
  • Fry one at a time and keep the pan safe. Use a deep, wide pan with the oil no more than half-way up the sides, and never leave it unattended.

item.title: Sautéed Fiddleheads
item.description: Sautéed fiddleheads: fresh fiddleheads cleaned, boiled 15 minutes, then finished in butter with garlic and lemon. A spring vegetable of eastern Canada.
item.content:encoded:
Fiddleheads are the tightly curled fronds of the ostrich fern, harvested for a few weeks each spring in the woods and river valleys of New Brunswick, Quebec and Nova Scotia, and they are one of the great seasonal foods of eastern Canada. They taste like a cross between asparagus and green beans, with a slightly nutty, grassy note, and a crunch that survives cooking. They must be cooked properly, and this is not a matter of taste but of safety. Raw or undercooked fiddleheads have been linked to outbreaks of foodborne illness, so Health Canada advises cleaning them thoroughly, then boiling them for at least 15 minutes, or steaming them for 10 to 12 minutes, and throwing away the cooking water. Only once boiled are they finished in the pan. Butter, garlic and a little lemon are all they need, and their season is short, so people eat them as often as they can while they last.

  • Boil them for the full 15 minutes and discard the water. This is Health Canada advice and it applies even if you plan to sauté them afterwards.
  • Wash them thoroughly. Each frond has papery brown scales tucked into its curl, and several rinses remove them.
  • Use ostrich fern fiddleheads, the kind sold for eating in Canada. Other ferns, bracken in particular, are not recommended, so buy from a supplier you trust.

item.title: Thai Beef Salad
item.description: Thai beef salad: seared steak sliced thin over lettuce, cucumber, tomato, red onion, mint and coriander, in a lime, fish sauce and chilli dressing.
item.content:encoded:
Thai beef salad, yam nua, is the dish that made many Australians and Britons fall for Thai food, a salad where seared steak is the centre, and its flavour is a balance of four tastes that Thai cooking aims for in almost every dish: sour, salty, sweet and hot. The dressing does all four with lime juice, fish sauce, palm sugar and fresh chilli, and its power comes from being made and tasted before it goes on: a teaspoon more sugar or lime is the difference. The steak is seared hard on the outside and left rare to medium-rare in the middle, then rested and sliced thin against the grain, so it stays tender, and its juices are tipped into the dressing. The salad is crunchy and cool, with cucumber, tomato, red onion and lettuce, and herbs, mint and coriander, give it a fresh, perfumed lift. Roasted peanuts finish it.

  • Taste the dressing before it goes on. Limes, fish sauces and chillies vary a lot, and balancing the four flavours is the skill of the dish.
  • Slice the steak thinly against the grain. It makes lean sirloin tender, and the thin slices take up the dressing.
  • Do not dress the salad until the last minute. Lime juice wilts lettuce and herbs within a few minutes.

item.title: Blueberry Scones
item.description: Blueberry scones: tall, buttery scones with cold butter in the flour, blueberries folded through and a cream and coarse sugar glaze. Crisp and tender.
item.content:encoded:
A good scone is tall, flaky and tender, and it has more in common with a biscuit or a pie crust than with a cake. The secret is cold fat. Butter rubbed or grated into the flour stays in small pieces, and in the heat of the oven those pieces melt and release steam, which lifts the dough into layers and gives the crumb its flakiness, so everything is kept as cold as possible, including the cream and the egg. The second rule is to handle the dough as little as possible. Overmixing develops gluten, which makes scones tough, so the wet ingredients go in with a fork until the dough just holds together. Blueberries are the third variable. Frozen ones are used straight from the freezer, tossed in a little flour so they do not bleed purple through the dough, and they go in whole and are folded gently. The wedges are chilled before baking, which keeps the butter cold and stops the scones spreading.

  • Keep everything cold. Warm butter melts into the flour and gives dense, greasy scones, whereas cold butter gives layers.
  • Stop mixing as soon as the dough holds together. It should look rough and a bit shaggy, and overworking it toughens the scones.
  • Use frozen blueberries straight from the freezer if you like. They hold their shape better than fresh and are less likely to burst and stain the dough.

item.title: Breakfast Sausage
item.description: Homemade breakfast sausage: ground pork mixed with sage, thyme, black pepper, cayenne and maple syrup, shaped into patties and fried until browned.
item.content:encoded:
American breakfast sausage is a patty of ground pork seasoned mainly with sage, and the reason to make it yourself is how easy it is and how much better it is than most that you can buy. There is nothing to stuff and no casing to buy, only a bowl, ground pork and a jar of spices. The key is the fat. Pork with about 20 percent fat gives patties that are juicy and hold together, and leaner meat, such as pork loin mince, turns dry and crumbly, so the packet should be checked. Sage supplies the characteristic flavour, thyme and black pepper support it, a pinch of cayenne gives background warmth and a touch of maple syrup adds the slightly sweet, savoury note that goes so well with pancakes and syrup. The mixture is handled lightly and chilled briefly, so the spices spread and the patties keep their shape in the pan.

  • Use pork with 20 percent fat. Lean mince gives dry patties, and the fat is what makes them juicy.
  • Do not overwork the mixture. Mixing only until combined keeps the patties tender, whereas kneading makes them rubbery.
  • Press a small dimple into the centre of each patty. They puff as they cook, and the dimple keeps them flat.

item.title: Ciabatta
item.description: Ciabatta: a very wet dough stretched and folded over a few hours, shaped into flat slippers and baked hot with steam for a crisp crust and open crumb.
item.content:encoded:
Ciabatta means slipper in Italian, for the flat, elongated shape of the loaf, and it is a young bread: it was invented in 1982 in the Veneto by a baker, Arnaldo Cavallari, who wanted an Italian answer to the French baguette. Its defining character is a very wet dough, with water at 80 percent of the weight of the flour, which is why it makes a large, irregular, glossy-walled crumb and a thin crust. It also makes the dough impossible to knead in the ordinary way, because it is a sticky, slack mass. The method is to replace kneading with time: a series of stretch and folds every half hour, with wet hands so the dough does not stick, which builds strength in the dough gradually, and long rests between them in which the yeast makes gas and the gluten aligns. The loaves are shaped as little as possible, so as not to knock out the gas, and are baked in a very hot oven with steam.

  • Keep your hands wet. The dough is meant to be sticky, and wet hands stop it from sticking to you.
  • Be gentle at the shaping stage. The bubbles you have built are the crumb, and squashing the dough closes them.
  • Bake with steam. It keeps the crust soft while the loaf expands, and then it sets thin and crisp.

item.title: English Muffins
item.description: English muffins: soft yeasted milk dough cooked slowly on a griddle until golden on both sides, then split and toasted to hold pools of melted butter.
item.content:encoded:
English muffins are a British invention that became an American breakfast icon, and they are made on a griddle, not baked in an oven. That matters, because it gives the flat top and bottom, the pale sides and the tender, slightly chewy crumb. The dough is a soft enriched dough of milk, butter and a little sugar, wetter than a bread dough, and the wetness is what gives the muffins their open, holey interior, the nooks and crannies that catch melted butter and jam. The rounds are cut and dusted with cornmeal, which stops them sticking and gives the characteristic gritty, golden surface, and they are cooked on a low heat, so that the centre has time to cook through before the outside browns. If they colour too fast, they can be finished in the oven. The traditional way to eat one is to split it with a fork, not cut it with a knife, because the tearing keeps the craggy surface that toasts best.

  • Cook them over a low heat. A hot griddle browns the outside before the middle has cooked, leaving a doughy centre.
  • Split them with a fork and not a knife. The torn surface toasts to a crisp, and it makes more nooks for the butter.
  • Keep the dough soft and slightly sticky. It is the moisture that gives them their open, holey crumb.

item.title: Homemade Pop-Tarts
item.description: Homemade Pop-Tarts: flaky butter pastry rectangles filled with strawberry jam, sealed with a fork, baked golden and topped with a thin sugar icing.
item.content:encoded:
Homemade toaster pastries take a few hours and reward the effort with a pastry that is flaky and buttery, far from the dry, sweet cardboard of the packet. The pastry is a simple pie dough, cold butter cut into flour and bound with an egg and ice water, and its flakiness comes the usual way: cold butter melts in the oven, releasing steam that pushes the layers apart. The dough has to be chilled for an hour before rolling, so that the gluten relaxes and the butter is firm.
