The filling is jam, thickened with a little cornflour so that it stays in the pastry and does not run out in the oven, and it is spread thinly, since overfilling is the main cause of leaks. The rectangles are sealed with a fork, and pricked so steam can escape. When they are cool they are iced and can be eaten as they are, or warmed briefly in the toaster.

  • Keep the dough cold. If it warms up and turns greasy while rolling, put it back in the fridge for 15 minutes.
  • Do not overfill. Jam expands in the oven and will burst through a thin seal, so a tablespoon per tart is enough.
  • Wait until the tarts are fully cool before icing. A warm pastry melts the icing off in a sticky puddle.

item.title: Johnnycakes
item.description: Johnnycakes: thin cornmeal pancakes made by scalding fine cornmeal with boiling water and frying in butter until the edges are crisp and lacy.
item.content:encoded:
Johnnycakes are one of the oldest American foods, a flat cornmeal cake that Native peoples of New England made long before Europeans arrived, and that colonists learned from them. Rhode Island still fiercely defends its own version, made with a particular white flint corn ground fine, and it is very different from cornbread. The batter is made by scalding the cornmeal with boiling water, which softens the grains, cooks some of the starch and makes a batter that fries into a thin, crisp-edged cake with a creamy centre and the sweet, toasty flavour of corn. Milk loosens it for a thin, pancake-like cake. Fried in butter, the edges turn crisp and lacy while the middle stays tender. They are served hot with butter and maple syrup for breakfast, or with butter and salt as a side for chowder and beans, and they are naturally gluten-free.

  • Scald the cornmeal with boiling water, not warm. The heat is what softens the grains and turns the batter creamy.
  • Stir the batter before each batch. The cornmeal settles fast and a batter that has separated makes thin, gritty cakes.
  • Cook them on medium heat. Too hot, and the cake browns before the middle is set, and too cool, and it is pale and greasy.

item.title: Malasadas
item.description: Malasadas: soft, eggy yeast doughnuts without a hole, fried until golden and rolled in sugar. The Portuguese sweet loved in Hawaii.
item.content:encoded:
Malasadas are a Portuguese sweet that came to Hawaii with immigrants from Madeira and the Azores, who arrived to work on the sugar plantations in the nineteenth century, and Hawaii now has a devotion to them that rivals the Portuguese one. They are made on Shrove Tuesday, Malasada Day in Hawaii, to use up the eggs and butter before Lent. They are a simple sweet, a rich, eggy yeast dough that is rolled, left to rise, fried and coated in sugar, but their texture is what makes them special: a thin crisp shell around a light, airy, slightly chewy centre. Evaporated milk gives the dough its distinctive richness and gentle caramel note, and the eggs give the crumb its softness and colour. The pieces are proved on small squares of baking paper, so that they can be lowered into the oil without deflating.

  • Use a thermometer for the oil. At 175°C the malasadas cook through and brown together, but too hot and they burn outside and stay raw inside.
  • Prove the dough on squares of baking paper. You can lower the paper and dough together into the oil, which keeps the puffy dough from being squashed.
  • Sugar them while still warm. The sugar sticks to the surface as it cools and turns into a crust.

item.title: Pecan Sandies
item.description: Pecan sandies: crumbly butter cookies studded with toasted chopped pecans and rolled in icing sugar while still warm. Shortbread with nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Pecan sandies are a shortbread-style cookie with chopped pecans, named for their sandy, crumbly, melting texture. They are made with a very high ratio of butter to flour and very little sugar, and with no egg, and that is what produces the texture: without egg there is no structure to bind the dough, and without much sugar and liquid there is little gluten, so the cookie bakes into something short, tender and fragile. The pecans are toasted first, for a deeper, more buttery flavour that stands up to the butter. The dough is chilled before it is shaped, so that the butter firms up and the cookies keep their round shape in the oven, instead of spreading into thin, greasy discs. Once baked, the cookies are cooled just for a few minutes and rolled in icing sugar while still warm, which makes it stick to them and give the powdery snow coating.

  • Toast the pecans first. It takes 6 minutes in the oven and gives the cookies a richer, more nutty flavour.
  • Chill the dough before shaping. Butter-rich dough that starts warm spreads thin in the oven.
  • Roll them in the sugar twice, first when warm and again when cold. The first coat melts into the surface, and the second stays powdery.

item.title: Pumpkin Muffins
item.description: Pumpkin muffins: moist, spiced muffins made with pumpkin purée, oil and brown sugar, with cinnamon, ginger and nutmeg, and pumpkin seeds on top.
item.content:encoded:
Pumpkin muffins are an autumn bake that depends on getting the balance of moisture and spice right. Pumpkin purée is very wet and very mild, so it provides moisture and colour but almost no flavour of its own, which is why these muffins are full of spice: cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg and cloves make the taste that people call pumpkin. Oil is used rather than butter, because it gives a moister, softer muffin that stays that way for days, whereas butter gives more flavour but a drier crumb once cold. Brown sugar adds a caramel note that suits the spice. The method is the standard muffin method, and its one rule is not to overmix: the wet ingredients are stirred into the dry just until the flour disappears, because too much stirring develops gluten and makes tough, tunnelled muffins with peaked, rubbery tops. A hot oven at the start gives the muffins their domes.

  • Stir until just combined. Overmixing makes muffins tough and peaked, and a few streaks of flour disappear in the oven.
  • Start the oven hot and turn it down. The first 5 minutes at 200°C give the muffins a quick rise and a domed top.
  • Use tinned pumpkin purée, not pie filling. Pie filling has sugar and spices already added and will throw the balance off.

item.title: Thumbprint Cookies
item.description: Thumbprint cookies: buttery, tender cookies rolled in chopped nuts, pressed with a thumb and filled with raspberry jam before baking. A festive favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Thumbprint cookies are a butter cookie with a well in the middle, and the well is the whole idea: a small jewel of jam that bakes into a glossy, sticky centre, surrounded by a crumbly, tender cookie. The dough is a simple one, butter, sugar, flour and egg yolks, and using yolks only and no whites is what makes the cookie so tender and rich, since there is no egg white to make it firm or cakey. It is chilled for half an hour, so the butter firms up and the cookies keep their thickness while they bake. The rolling in egg white and chopped nuts is the extra step that turns a plain cookie into a bakery cookie, and it gives a crisp, toasty exterior that contrasts with the soft middle. The well is pressed in before baking, and pressed again halfway if the dough puffs it closed. Use a thick jam, since runny jam will bubble out.

  • Use a thick jam or preserve. A loose jam bubbles over the edge and burns, and a set one stays in its well.
  • Press the wells again after the first bake. The dough puffs in the oven and closes the well, and a second press restores it.
  • Fill the wells only part-way. Jam expands when hot, and a full well overflows.

item.title: Eggs Royale
item.description: Eggs Royale: toasted English muffins topped with smoked salmon, poached eggs and warm hollandaise sauce. Eggs Benedict with smoked salmon instead of ham.
item.content:encoded:
Eggs Royale is eggs Benedict with smoked salmon in place of ham, and it is a brunch dish of the hotel and the good cafe, where it is served with the same hollandaise and poached eggs as the original. The dish rewards attention to three elements. The poached egg needs to be fresh, with a firm white that clings to the yolk, and it is cooked in gently simmering, not boiling, water with a splash of vinegar, so the white sets quickly around the yolk. The hollandaise is an emulsion of egg yolk and warm melted butter, and it is easiest made in a blender, where hot butter is streamed into whizzing yolks and lemon juice. The heat from the butter cooks the yolks just enough to thicken them. And the muffin is toasted crisp, which stops it going soft under the egg. Smoked salmon goes on the muffin cold, and its silky saltiness against the rich sauce is what makes it Royale.

  • Use the freshest eggs you can. Old eggs have a thin white that spreads into wisps in the water.
  • Keep the water at a bare simmer. A rolling boil tears the whites apart, and a bare simmer sets them neatly.
  • Pour the butter in slowly. Adding it all at once splits the sauce, and if it does, whisk in a teaspoon of hot water to bring it back.

item.title: Rock Cakes
item.description: Rock cakes: craggy, crisp-edged little fruit cakes made by rubbing butter into flour, stirring in dried fruit and spice and baking in rough heaps.
item.content:encoded:
Rock cakes take their name from their look, and it is a fair one: a rough, craggy heap of golden dough, studded with fruit, that looks as if it has been picked up from a hillside. They are a British teatime and school-baking staple, and they are one of the simplest cakes to make, since they use the rubbing-in method, in which butter is rubbed into flour with the fingertips, and the dough is bound with just an egg and a splash of milk. The dough must be stiff, which is unusual for a cake. It should be so firm that it holds a rough heap on the spoon, and if it is too wet the cakes spread into flat cookies instead of holding a rocky shape. The dried fruit is generous and the spice is mixed spice, the warm, sweet blend of cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves. The outside bakes crisp and the inside stays soft and crumbly, best eaten warm with butter.

  • Keep the mixture stiff. Wet dough spreads into flat, chewy cookies, and a stiff one keeps its rocky shape.
  • Pile the heaps with forks and not a spoon. The forks leave the craggy surface, and it crisps in the oven.
  • Eat them the same day. Rock cakes are at their best warm from the oven, and they turn hard and dry after a day.

item.title: Swiss Roll
item.description: Swiss roll: a thin, whisked sponge baked in minutes, rolled while hot, then unrolled, spread with raspberry jam and rolled again into a neat spiral.
item.content:encoded:
A Swiss roll is a sponge that has to bend without breaking, and it is made possible by two things: a whisked sponge with no fat in it, and rolling it while it is still hot. A fatless sponge relies on eggs whisked with sugar until they are thick, pale and mousse-like, and this traps a great deal of air, which expands in the oven so the sponge rises without any raising agent. The result is light, supple and thin. It bakes in about ten minutes in a shallow tin, and the moment it comes out it is turned onto sugared paper and rolled up with the paper inside, which sets the sponge into a curve while it is warm and pliable. When it has cooled it unrolls without cracking, is spread with jam and is rolled up again, and the memory of the first roll makes the second easy. The main hazard is overbaking, which dries the sponge and makes it crack.

  • Whisk the eggs until they hold a trail. That trapped air is the only raising agent, so the mixture must be thick and mousse-like.
  • Fold the flour in gently. Stirring knocks out the air, and the sponge bakes flat and dense.
  • Roll it while it is hot. A cold sponge cracks, and a hot one takes the curve and holds it.

item.title: Maple Oatmeal Cookies
item.description: Maple oatmeal cookies: chewy oatmeal cookies made with real maple syrup and brown sugar, with pecans folded in and a thin maple glaze over the top.
item.content:encoded:
Maple syrup is Canada's signature sweetener, and in a cookie it does more than add sweetness. It brings a caramel, woody, faintly buttery flavour that brown sugar alone cannot, so a maple oatmeal cookie tastes distinct from an ordinary one, and rolled oats give it the chew and the nutty, toasty background that maple loves. The recipe uses the two sugars for different jobs: brown sugar keeps the cookies soft and moist, while a few tablespoons of syrup add the flavour, and because syrup is liquid the dough is a touch softer and the cookies spread a little more. Real maple syrup matters here. Pancake syrup is corn syrup with flavouring, and its taste vanishes in the oven. The glaze, icing sugar stirred with more maple syrup, is drizzled over the cooled cookies and gives a second hit of maple. Grade A dark or amber syrup has the strongest flavour, and is the best choice for baking.

  • Use real maple syrup. Pancake syrup has little flavour and loses it in the oven, and the maple taste is the whole point.
  • Take the cookies out while the centres are soft. They firm up as they cool, and a cookie baked until it is hard in the oven is crisp and dry the next day.
  • Use rolled oats, not instant. Instant oats are cut fine and make a flat, pasty cookie, while rolled oats keep their chew.

item.title: Nalysnyky
item.description: Nalysnyky: thin Ukrainian crepes rolled around a sweet farmer's cheese filling with vanilla and lemon, then fried in butter until golden.
item.content:encoded:
Nalysnyky are the thin crepes of Ukrainian cooking, and they are a home dish that has travelled well: Ukrainian families in the Canadian prairies, in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have made them for generations, for breakfast, for Sunday brunch and for the meatless days of the Christmas Eve supper. The batter is a thin one, of flour, eggs and milk, and it is rested for half an hour so the flour hydrates and the crepes are tender and do not tear when they are rolled. The filling is a sweetened farmer's cheese, a dry, crumbly fresh curd cheese known in Ukrainian as tvorog, mixed with egg yolk, sugar, vanilla and lemon zest. Rolled into little parcels, the crepes are fried in butter until the outside is golden and crisp, which is what makes nalysnyky different from a simple filled crepe. They come to the table with sour cream, jam or fruit.

  • Drain the cheese if it is wet. Extra moisture leaks through the crepe as it fries and makes the parcel soggy.
  • Rest the batter. It lets the flour swell and settle, and the crepes come out tender, with no torn edges.
  • Do not cook the first side too long. The crepe gets another turn in the pan when it is fried, and a pale one browns better in butter.

item.title: Pyrizhky
item.description: Pyrizhky: soft, golden yeast buns filled with mashed potato, fried onion and cheese, brushed with egg and baked. A favourite Ukrainian bakery bun.
item.content:encoded:
Pyrizhky are small, filled buns, the Ukrainian relatives of the Russian pirozhki and the Polish pierogi, and they are one of the most popular baked goods among the Ukrainian communities of the Canadian prairies, where they are sold at church suppers and family gatherings. The dough is a soft, enriched yeast dough, made with milk, an egg and butter, which gives a tender crumb and a golden, glossy crust when it is brushed with egg. The filling is the classic one, mashed potato with fried onion and a little cheese, a combination of comfort that appears in all the Ukrainian dumpling and bun traditions. The onions are cooked slowly until golden, because they are what give the potato its sweetness and depth. The filling must be cool and not too moist when it goes into the dough, or the steam it produces tears the seams open in the oven. The buns are sealed with a firm pinch and set seam side down.

  • Cool the filling before it goes in. A hot filling steams and softens the dough, and it tears the seams in the oven.
  • Seal the buns firmly. Pinch the edges together twice, and set them seam side down so they do not open.
  • Cook the onion until it is properly golden. It is the source of sweetness in the filling, and raw or pale onion tastes sharp.

item.title: Apple Tea Cake
item.description: Apple tea cake: a soft, buttery cake topped with overlapping slices of apple and cinnamon sugar and baked until golden. Served warm with cream.
item.content:encoded:
An apple tea cake is a Sunday-afternoon cake in Australian homes, the sort that is made from a tin of flour and a bowl of apples and eaten warm with a cup of tea. The batter is a simple butter cake, creamed butter and sugar with eggs, self-raising flour and milk, and it is soft and moist rather than rich, because it is meant to be a base for the apple. The apples go on top, not inside, and it is a better arrangement than it sounds. Thin slices sink a little into the batter as it bakes and soften in the heat, releasing juice that is absorbed by the crumb around them, while the tops brown and caramelise under the sprinkle of cinnamon sugar. Granny Smith apples are the usual choice, since they are tart and keep their shape. The cake is finished with a brush of warmed apricot jam for a shine.

  • Slice the apples thin and arrange them close. They shrink as they bake, and gaps leave bare batter on top.
  • Beat the butter and sugar well. Three minutes of creaming gives the cake its soft, light crumb.
  • Serve it warm. The apples are juiciest and the cinnamon sugar crunchiest in the first hour.

item.title: Blackberry Cobbler
item.description: Blackberry cobbler: juicy blackberries baked under a rough, golden buttermilk biscuit topping until the fruit bubbles into a jammy sauce. Serve warm.
item.content:encoded:
A cobbler is a fruit dessert with a biscuit or batter topping laid in rough lumps over the fruit, so that the crust looks like cobblestones, and the blackberry version is one of the great Southern summer desserts, made when the brambles along every fence are heavy with fruit. It has two parts, and each needs to be right. The fruit needs a little sugar to bring out its flavour and cornflour to thicken its juices, or the filling stays as thin as soup, and a squeeze of lemon and its zest sharpen the sweetness. The topping is a buttermilk biscuit dough, a cousin of scone dough, with cold butter cut into the flour for a flaky, tender crust, and it is dropped in spoonfuls with gaps between them, so steam can escape and the fruit can bubble up through. It goes on top of the fruit and not underneath, which means the underside steams and the top browns, and the contrast is what makes it. Frozen berries work well, straight from the freezer.

  • Leave gaps in the topping. Steam and fruit juice need somewhere to escape, and a solid crust turns doughy underneath.
  • Use cold butter and mix the dough as little as you can. Like a scone, it is at its best when it is rough and shaggy.
  • Stand the dish on a baking tray. Blackberry juice is sticky and bubbles over the edge, and the tray saves the oven floor.

item.title: Caramel Corn
item.description: Caramel corn: popcorn coated in a butter, brown sugar and corn syrup caramel, then baked low and slow until every piece is dry, crisp and shiny.
item.content:encoded:
Caramel corn is what makes a bag of popcorn into a confection, and the difference between a good batch and a sticky, chewy one is in the baking. The caramel is a mixture of butter, brown sugar and corn syrup boiled for a few minutes and finished with a little bicarbonate of soda, which makes the hot caramel foam and turns it light and porous, so that it cracks crisply and does not glue teeth together. The syrup matters too, since corn syrup prevents the sugar from crystallising and gives a smooth coating. But the caramel is only half the recipe. Once it is poured over the popcorn and mixed, the popcorn goes into a low oven for about 45 minutes, and is stirred every 15, which dries the coating out completely, turning it from a sticky glaze into a brittle shell. Cooled on baking paper, it breaks into crunchy clusters, and stored airtight, it keeps for a week.

  • Do not skip the baking. It is what dries the caramel into a crisp coating, and without it the popcorn stays sticky and chewy.
  • Add the bicarbonate of soda off the heat. It makes the caramel foam and turns it porous, so it snaps cleanly.
  • Pick out unpopped kernels before coating. They are the only thing that breaks a tooth.

item.title: Flag Cake
item.description: Flag cake: a vanilla sheet cake covered in cream cheese frosting and decorated with strawberry stripes and a square of blueberries. Feeds a crowd.
item.content:encoded:
The flag cake is the dessert of the Fourth of July and Memorial Day, and its appeal is that it looks like a lot of work and is one of the easiest big cakes to make. A sheet cake, baked in a rectangular tin, gives a large flat canvas that is easy to decorate and easy to cut into 15 squares, and it is the right shape for a flag. The cake is a soft vanilla butter cake that is sturdy enough to hold a covering of frosting and fruit without collapsing, and it has to be completely cold before it is frosted, or the frosting melts. Cream cheese frosting is tangy and balances the sweet cake, and it is thick enough to hold the berries. The decoration is fruit, not sprinkles: a square of blueberries in one corner for the stars and rows of halved strawberries for the red stripes, with the frosting showing through as the white stripes. It is best made on the day it is served.

  • Cool the cake completely before frosting. Warm sponge melts the frosting and it slides off.
  • Hull and dry the strawberries. Wet fruit bleeds into the frosting and streaks it pink.
  • Decorate the cake close to serving time. The berries release juice after a few hours in the fridge.

item.title: Strawberry Rhubarb Pie
item.description: Strawberry rhubarb pie: sweet strawberries and tart rhubarb thickened with cornflour in a flaky butter crust, baked until bubbling and cooled so it slices.
item.content:encoded:
Strawberry rhubarb pie is the pie of late spring, when the first rhubarb stalks and the first strawberries overlap, and it works because each fruit fixes the other. Rhubarb is very tart and stringy, and strawberries are sweet, soft and mild, so together they make a filling that is balanced, sharp against sweet, with a lovely red colour. The trouble with the pairing is water. Both fruits are very wet, and they release a lot of juice as they bake, so unless it is thickened and the crust is well baked, the filling will run all over the plate and the base will be soggy. Cornflour tossed with the sugar before it goes on the fruit thickens the juice as it heats. The other secret is to bake the pie until the filling is bubbling thickly in the centre, not just at the edges, since only then has the cornflour gone off, and to cool it for at least three hours, when it sets into a filling that can be sliced.

  • Bake until the filling bubbles in the middle. That is the sign the cornflour has thickened, and a pie taken out earlier stays runny.
  • Wait for the pie to cool. A warm rhubarb pie is a delicious puddle, and it needs 3 hours to set into slices.
  • Bake it on a hot tray on the lowest shelf. It gives the base a burst of heat, and it catches any juice that boils over.

item.title: Bakewell Pudding
item.description: Bakewell pudding: a puff pastry case spread with raspberry jam and filled with a rich egg, butter and almond custard baked until just set.
item.content:encoded:
The Bakewell pudding is the original dessert of Bakewell in Derbyshire, and it is not the same thing as a Bakewell tart, though they are often confused. The story of its origin is that a cook at the White Horse Inn, around 1820, misunderstood the instructions for a jam tart and poured an egg and almond mixture over the jam, instead of mixing it into the pastry, and the accident became a local speciality. The result is a very different dessert from the tart: a base of flaky puff pastry, a layer of jam, and above it a rich, buttery, egg-yolk-heavy almond custard that bakes into a soft, set filling, more like a baked custard than a sponge. There is no flour in the filling and no icing on top. The custard is set by the egg yolks and it must be baked gently and taken out while it still has a slight wobble in the centre, because overbaking curdles it. It is eaten warm, with cream or custard.

  • Take it out with a slight wobble. The custard carries on setting as it cools, and overbaking makes it curdle and turn grainy.
  • Bake it on a hot tray. The heat under the tin cooks the base of the pastry, and puff pastry without it can turn out pale and soft.
  • Let the melted butter cool slightly before whisking it with the sugar and eggs. Hot butter can scramble the yolks.

item.title: Fifteens
item.description: Fifteens: a Northern Irish no-bake sweet of crushed digestive biscuits, marshmallows and glacé cherries bound with condensed milk and rolled in coconut.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteens are a Northern Irish sweet, a no-bake slice that is a staple of church halls, coffee mornings and Christmas boxes, and their name is their recipe: fifteen digestive biscuits, fifteen marshmallows and fifteen glacé cherries, held together with condensed milk. It is a sweet you can measure by counting, which is why it is a first recipe for children in Ulster, and it is hard to get wrong. The biscuits are crushed, not ground, so there are still small crumbs and larger pieces that give a crunch, and the marshmallows and cherries are cut into pieces so that when the roll is sliced each slice shows a mosaic of white and red. The condensed milk is added a little at a time, because the amount needed depends on how finely the biscuits were crushed, and the mixture should be sticky enough to hold together and stiff enough to be shaped into a log. The coconut coating gives a snowy outside.

  • Add the condensed milk gradually. Too much makes a mixture that will not hold its shape, and too little leaves a dry crumb that falls apart.
  • Dust the scissors with coconut as you cut the marshmallows. They are sticky, and coconut on the blades stops them clogging.
  • Chill the roll until it is firm. A cold, hard roll slices cleanly, and a soft one squashes.

item.title: Maple Glazed Ham
item.description: Maple glazed ham: a fully cooked smoked ham heated slowly, then brushed with maple syrup, Dijon and cloves and baked hot until it is glossy and lacquered.
item.content:encoded:
A baked ham is the centrepiece of the Christmas and Easter table across Canada, and maple syrup is the Canadian glaze, from the sugar shacks of Quebec and Ontario. Most hams sold for baking have already been cured, smoked and fully cooked, so the job at home is only to warm one through gently without drying it out, and to build a glaze on the outside. The ham is heated slowly, covered, at a low temperature, until the centre reaches 60°C, and the glaze goes on only in the last half hour at a higher heat. That order matters. Maple syrup is mostly sugar and it burns over a long bake, so it goes on late, in several coats, each of which caramelises to build up a deep, glossy lacquer. Dijon mustard and a little cider vinegar cut the sweetness and give the glaze sharpness, and cloves supply the classic ham spice. Scoring the surface in diamonds lets the glaze run into the meat and gives the outside its crackled look.

  • Buy a fully cooked ham and only heat it. The temperature to aim for is 60°C, and going much higher dries it out.
  • Add the glaze late. Maple syrup is mostly sugar and it burns, so a glaze that goes on for the whole bake ends up bitter and black.
  • Use pure maple syrup. Maple-flavoured pancake syrup is thin and mostly corn syrup, and it has no depth.

item.title: Jelly Slice
item.description: Jelly slice: a biscuit and coconut base topped with a creamy raspberry jelly and condensed milk layer, set in the fridge and cut into pink squares.
item.content:encoded:
Jelly slice is an Australian party and cake-stall classic, the pink or green square that vanishes first from the plate, and it is made from a handful of pantry ingredients. The recipe has two layers. The base is crushed plain biscuits and melted butter, with a little coconut, pressed into a tin and chilled, and it stays soft enough to cut but firm enough to hold the topping. The top is jelly crystals dissolved in hot water, cooled until lukewarm and stirred into sweetened condensed milk, and this is where the recipe is clever: the condensed milk turns the clear jelly into a creamy, pastel, mousse-like layer with a soft wobble and a sweet, fruity flavour. The jelly must be cooled before the milk goes in, or the milk curdles, and the slice needs several hours in the fridge to set. It is cut into small squares, since it is very sweet, and it is a favourite at children's birthday parties.

  • Let the jelly cool before it meets the milk. Hot jelly curdles condensed milk, and lukewarm jelly blends into a smooth, creamy layer.
  • Press the biscuit base down firmly. A loose base crumbles when you cut, and a packed one holds together.
  • Cut with a hot knife. Wipe it between cuts for clean edges.

item.title: Cheese Ball
item.description: Cheese ball: cream cheese and sharp cheddar mixed with spring onion, garlic and Worcestershire, shaped into a ball, chilled and rolled in chopped pecans.
item.content:encoded:
The cheese ball is an American party staple from the 1950s and 1960s, when it appeared on buffet tables at every holiday party and cocktail hour, and it has lasted because it is easy to make and easy to eat. It is a spread that has been turned into a centrepiece. Cream cheese gives the base its smooth, tangy body, and grated sharp cheddar gives it flavour and a little texture, while spring onion, garlic and a spoonful of Worcestershire sauce supply the savoury, slightly sharp notes that keep it from tasting flat. The mixture needs to be chilled before it can be shaped, because at room temperature it is too soft to hold a form, and it needs to be chilled again once it is rolled in chopped pecans, so that it firms up and can be cut into with a knife. It is made a day ahead, which lets the flavours meld, and it is put out with crackers, pretzels and vegetable sticks.

  • Soften the cream cheese properly. Cold cream cheese leaves lumps, and it does not blend with the cheddar.
  • Grate the cheddar finely from a block. Pre-shredded cheese has a coating that makes the mixture dry and grainy.
  • Make it a day ahead. The garlic and onion soften and the flavours join up overnight, and the ball is easier to shape.

item.title: French 75
item.description: French 75: gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup shaken with ice, strained into a flute and topped with cold sparkling wine. Sharp, dry, fizzy and strong.
item.content:encoded:
The French 75 is a cocktail from the First World War, named after the French 75 mm field gun, the quick-firing artillery piece that was the pride of the French army, and the drink is said to have the same kick: it tastes light and lemony, but it is strong. The best-known account places its invention at Harry MacElhone's New York Bar in Paris around 1915, and it appeared in print in the 1930s in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book. It is a simple structure and a good one, gin with lemon juice and sugar in the form of a Tom Collins, with the soda swapped for sparkling wine. The gin gives it botanical bite, the lemon gives sharpness and the syrup rounds the edge, and the bubbles lift the whole thing. Champagne is the classic choice, but a dry sparkling wine such as prosecco or cava is a very good substitute, and it does not need to be expensive. Everything except the wine is shaken hard with ice, so that it is really cold, and the wine is added at the end, gently, so that it keeps its fizz.

  • Use fresh lemon juice and not a bottle. Bottled juice tastes flat, and the drink depends on the fresh, sharp lemon.
  • Chill the glass and the wine. A cold glass keeps the drink fizzy for longer, and warm sparkling wine goes flat quickly.
  • Pour the wine last and slowly. Adding it to the shaker will froth it over, and pouring quickly loses the bubbles.

item.title: Kettle Corn
item.description: Kettle corn: popcorn popped in a pot with a little sugar and oil so each piece gets a thin, crisp, sweet coating, then tossed with salt. Ready in 13 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Kettle corn is the popcorn of country fairs, where it is made in a big iron kettle over a fire and stirred with a paddle, and it is one of the few fair foods that is genuinely easy to make at home, in one pot. What sets it apart from ordinary popcorn is that the sugar goes in with the kernels, so it melts in the hot oil as the corn pops and coats each piece in a thin, sweet, crunchy shell, and the salt goes on at the end for the sweet and salty contrast. It is a quick recipe but a fussy one, because the sugar can burn. The pot must be shaken constantly, so the sugar does not sit on the bottom and scorch, and the popcorn must come off the heat the moment the popping slows, since the few seconds after the last pops are when the sugar turns from golden to black. It is tipped out of the pot at once, since the hot base carries on cooking it, and stirred so the pieces do not fuse into a lump.

  • Shake the pot without stopping. The sugar burns in seconds if it sits still against the metal.
  • Take it off the heat when the pops are 2 or 3 seconds apart. Waiting for the last kernels burns the sugar, and a few unpopped ones are the price.
  • Tip it out of the pot at once. The pot stays hot and carries on cooking the popcorn, and the sugar can scorch.

item.title: Mocha
item.description: Mocha: strong espresso mixed with hot milk melted with real dark chocolate and cocoa, and topped with whipped cream. The coffee for chocolate lovers.
item.content:encoded:
A mocha is a cafe latte with chocolate, and the name is older than the drink: Mocha is the Yemeni port from which coffee was shipped to Europe for centuries, and its beans were prized for a natural chocolate flavour, so a chocolate coffee took its name. The modern mocha, a shot of espresso with steamed milk and chocolate, became a coffeehouse standard in the 1980s and 1990s. Most cafe mochas rely on a sweet chocolate syrup, and the home version is better made with real chocolate, because it gives a deeper, less sugary flavour. Dark chocolate and cocoa are heated with milk and whisked until smooth, which makes a rich hot chocolate that is then joined with the coffee. The trick is balance. The coffee must be strong enough to be tasted through the milk and chocolate, and the chocolate must be bitter enough to make the drink not too sweet. Whipped cream and a dusting of cocoa are the finish.

  • Use real dark chocolate as well as cocoa. The chocolate gives body and the cocoa gives depth, and syrups and mixes are mostly sugar.
  • Whisk the milk rather than boiling it. Boiled milk forms a skin and turns the chocolate grainy, and whisking makes a light froth.
  • Make the coffee strong. A weak brew vanishes under the milk and chocolate, and espresso or moka pot coffee holds its own.

item.title: Sazerac
item.description: Sazerac: rye whiskey stirred with sugar and Peychaud's bitters, strained into a glass rinsed with absinthe and finished with a lemon twist. From New Orleans.
item.content:encoded:
The Sazerac is the cocktail of New Orleans, and in 2008 the Louisiana legislature made it the official cocktail of the city. Its history is tied to the Sazerac Coffee House in the French Quarter and to Antoine Peychaud, the Creole apothecary whose bitters give the drink its taste, and it began as a cognac drink, the base changing to rye whiskey after phylloxera destroyed the French vineyards in the 1870s and made cognac scarce. What makes it distinct is the absinthe rinse. A little absinthe is swirled around a chilled glass to coat the inside and the excess is tipped out, so that the drink is poured into a glass that smells of anise but tastes only of rye, sugar and bitters. The bitters are Peychaud's, which are lighter and more floral than Angostura, with a note of cherry and anise, and they are essential. The drink is stirred, not shaken, over ice for a silky, cold, spirit-forward finish and served without ice, with a lemon peel twisted over the top.

  • Rinse and discard the absinthe. Too much overpowers the whiskey with aniseed, and the point is a scent rather than a flavour.
  • Use Peychaud's bitters. They are the signature of the drink, and Angostura alone makes a different, spicier cocktail.
  • Stir and do not shake. Shaking makes the drink cloudy and dilutes it, and this is a drink that should be clear, silky and strong.

item.title: Apple Chutney
item.description: Apple chutney: cooking apples, onions and sultanas simmered slowly with brown sugar, cider vinegar and warm spices into a thick, sweet, tangy chutney.
item.content:encoded:
Chutney came to Britain from India in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and the British made it their own, using the fruit and vegetables they had, and none is more typical than apple chutney, made in autumn when orchards produce more apples than anyone can eat. It is a preserve, which means its ingredients do two jobs: the vinegar and the sugar are seasoning and they are also what keep it. Cooking apples such as Bramley are the right choice, since they are tart and break down into a soft pulp that thickens the chutney, whereas eating apples hold their shape and taste bland. Onions add savouriness, sultanas give sweetness and body, and ginger, allspice and a little chilli give the warm spice. The secret to a good chutney is simmering it long enough, at least an hour, until the vinegar has cooked off and the mixture is thick and jammy, because a chutney that is potted too soon is thin and sharp. It improves with keeping, and is best after a few weeks in the jar.

  • Use cooking apples such as Bramley. They collapse into a pulp that thickens the chutney, and eating apples stay in lumps and taste flat.
  • Stir often in the last 20 minutes. As the chutney thickens it catches on the base of the pan, and a burnt taste spoils the whole batch.
  • Sterilise the jars and fill them while everything is hot. It keeps the chutney safe, and the hot jars will not crack when the hot chutney goes in.

item.title: Black Velvet
item.description: Black velvet: chilled sparkling wine topped with a layer of stout poured over the back of a spoon so the two stay apart. Dark, creamy and fizzy.
item.content:encoded:
The black velvet is a cocktail of two drinks that seem to have nothing in common, stout and sparkling wine, and it is one of the few beer cocktails to have lasted for well over a century. The story is that it was invented in 1861 at Brooks's Club in London, on the death of Prince Albert, when a steward, in the spirit of mourning, is said to have decided that even the champagne must be in black, and mixed it with stout. Whether or not the story is true, the combination works. The stout brings roasted, chocolatey, slightly bitter flavours, and a creamy head, while the sparkling wine brings acidity, dryness and lively bubbles, and the two balance each other so that the drink is smoother than either alone. The technique is the interesting part. Poured slowly over the back of a spoon onto the wine, the stout floats, forming two distinct layers, a black one on top of a pale gold one, and the drinker stirs them together or drinks through them. It is served in Ireland and Britain at Christmas and on St Patrick's Day.

  • Use a dry sparkling wine such as brut cava or prosecco. A sweet one turns the drink cloying, and the stout is already sweet and malty.
  • Pour slowly over the back of a spoon. Pouring in a stream mixes the two and the layers are lost, and it also makes the drink foam over.
  • Serve very cold. The drink depends on cold wine and cold stout, and both taste flat and heavy at room temperature.

item.title: Homemade Almond Milk
item.description: Homemade almond milk: raw almonds soaked overnight, blended with cold water and strained through a cloth into creamy, fresh almond milk with no additives.
item.content:encoded:
Making almond milk at home takes almost no skill and gives a drink that tastes of almonds, which is more than many of the cartons on the shelf do, since shop-bought almond milk can contain as little as 2 percent almonds, with the rest water and thickeners. Homemade almond milk is made with many times that, and the difference is the creamy, faintly sweet, nutty flavour. The method has three stages. The almonds are soaked for at least 8 hours, which softens them so that they blend to a fine paste and release more of their flavour, and which also makes them easier to digest. They are then blended with cold water at high speed for about a minute, until the water turns a milky white. Finally the mixture is strained through a nut milk bag or a clean muslin cloth, squeezing out the liquid, which leaves the pulp behind. The ratio of almonds to water sets the richness: one part almonds to six of water is a good everyday milk. It keeps for four days.

  • Rinse the soaked almonds before blending. The soaking water carries bitter compounds from the skins, and discarding it gives a sweeter milk.
  • Use cold water. Warm water speeds up spoilage, and it makes the milk taste a little flat.
  • Keep the pulp. It can be stirred into porridge, baked into cookies or dried in a low oven and ground into almond flour.

item.title: Marshmallow Hot Chocolate
item.description: Marshmallow hot chocolate: real chocolate and cocoa whisked into hot milk until thick and smooth, topped with marshmallows that melt into a sweet cap.
item.content:encoded:
A good hot chocolate is a rich, hot, thick drink of chocolate and milk, and it is a different thing from a mug of cocoa powder stirred into hot water. This one uses both real chocolate and cocoa, and the reason is that each does a different job. Melted chocolate carries cocoa butter, which gives the drink its body and a smooth, silky feel, and cocoa powder gives the deep chocolate flavour and a slight bitterness, and together they make a drink that is rich without being too sweet. The cocoa and sugar are whisked with a little of the milk first to make a paste, which stops the cocoa forming lumps, and the rest of the milk is added and heated gently, never boiled, since boiled milk forms a skin and can taste cooked. A pinch of salt sharpens the chocolate, and vanilla rounds it off. The marshmallows go on at the end, where they float and slowly melt into a sweet, sticky cap, and can be browned briefly under a hot grill.

  • Make a paste with the cocoa first. Cocoa powder is hard to wet and it floats in lumps if it goes straight into a large pan of milk.
  • Heat the milk gently and do not let it boil. Boiling scalds it, forms a skin and dulls the flavour.
  • Use chocolate you would eat. A dark chocolate of 60 percent gives a balanced drink, and milk chocolate makes it sweeter and more childlike.

item.title: Singapore Sling
item.description: Singapore sling: gin, cherry liqueur, orange liqueur and Bénédictine shaken with pineapple and lime juice and grenadine. A rosy tropical long drink.
item.content:encoded:
The Singapore sling is a drink of the Raffles Hotel, where it is said to have been created around 1915 by Ngiam Tong Boon, a bartender at the Long Bar, who wanted to give women a cocktail that looked like a glass of fruit juice, at a time when it was thought improper for them to drink in public. The pink drink he made hid a good deal of gin. The original recipe has been lost, and the version now sold at the Long Bar was reconstructed in the 1970s, but it has kept the structure: gin as the base, a mix of liqueurs, cherry brandy, orange liqueur and Bénédictine, for sweetness, fruit and a herbal depth, pineapple juice for tropical body and froth, lime juice for sharpness and a splash of grenadine for the pink blush. It is a long drink, so the mixture is shaken hard, which makes a foam on top from the pineapple juice, and it is served over ice in a tall glass. Its ingredients are many, but each is a splash, and the result is balanced, not sweet.

  • Shake hard and for long enough. The pineapple juice makes a foam on top, and a good shake makes it thick and creamy.
  • Use fresh pineapple juice if you can. Carton juice is sweeter and thinner and does not froth as well.
  • Measure the small liqueurs carefully. Each is only a splash, but the Bénédictine in particular is strong and can take over.

item.title: Oysters Kilpatrick
item.description: Oysters Kilpatrick: fresh oysters on the half shell topped with Worcestershire sauce and crisp bacon and grilled until the edges curl. An Australian classic.
item.content:encoded:
Oysters Kilpatrick is an Australian dish, generally said to have been created in Sydney in the early to middle years of the twentieth century and named for a Mr Kilpatrick, though the details are disputed, and it stays on the menu of seafood restaurants and pubs across the country. Its formula is simple and rests on contrast: the oyster is soft, briny and cool from the sea, and it is topped with the two things that make it savoury and crunchy, salty smoked bacon and Worcestershire sauce, and then grilled briefly, so that the oyster just warms through and its edges curl. The bacon must be cooked first, until it is crisp, because the short grilling time would not render it. Worcestershire sauce provides the tangy, savoury, slightly sweet note that has been the traditional partner of oysters since the nineteenth century, and a squeeze of lemon lifts them. The oyster should not be overcooked, or it turns rubbery, and it is done when the edges curl and the topping bubbles.

  • Cook the bacon first. The grilling is too short to crisp it, and raw bacon on an oyster is chewy.
  • Do not overcook the oysters. A minute too long and they turn tough and shrunken, and they should just curl at the edges.
  • Buy oysters from a supplier you trust, and keep them cold and alive until you open them. Discard any that are open and do not close when tapped.

item.title: New England Clambake
item.description: New England clambake: lobsters, clams and mussels steamed together over potatoes, sausage, corn and onions in one big pot. Served with butter and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
The clambake is the great summer feast of the New England coast, and its roots are older than the region's European settlement. Native peoples of the coast, including the Wampanoag and Narragansett, cooked shellfish in pits lined with hot stones and covered with seaweed, and the colonists adopted the method. A traditional bake takes a day, with a fire, stones, rockweed, and layers of shellfish, potatoes and corn steamed under wet canvas. The stovetop version here keeps the method and drops the pit: everything steams in a single large pot, with the food that needs longest at the bottom, and the shellfish on top so that their juices run down and flavour the rest. A smoked sausage, traditionally linguiça in the Portuguese communities of southern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, adds smoke. The point is the whole meal on one table, eaten with the hands, with melted butter for the lobster and the broth in the bottom of the pot as a drink.

  • Layer the pot in order of cooking time. The potatoes and sausage go at the bottom, the lobsters next, and the quick-cooking shellfish on top.
  • Buy shellfish that are alive and smell of the sea. Tap open ones, and discard any that stay open, and any that do not open after cooking.
  • Crack the lobster claws with a nutcracker before you serve. It saves people struggling at the table, and lets the butter reach the meat.

item.title: American Goulash
item.description: American goulash: ground beef, elbow macaroni, tomatoes, onion and paprika cooked together in one pot to a thick, savoury supper. A weeknight favourite.
item.content:encoded:
American goulash has little to do with the Hungarian stew that gave it its name. It is a plain, hearty supper of ground beef, elbow macaroni and tomatoes, cooked together in one pot, and it belongs to the tradition of thrifty American casseroles that can feed a family from a pound of mince and a packet of pasta. It goes by other names, including American chop suey in New England and slumgullion elsewhere, and every family has its own version: some add green pepper, some cheese, some a shake of Italian seasoning. What they share is the method, in which the dry pasta goes into the sauce to cook there, absorbing the tomato and the beef stock and releasing its starch, so that the whole dish thickens into something between a sauce and a stew. That is why it is so easy, since there is only one pot to wash, and why it is best served at once, before the macaroni swells. Paprika is the sole nod to its Hungarian namesake, and the Worcestershire sauce rounds out the savour.

  • Stir often once the macaroni goes in. The pasta releases starch and sticks to the base of the pan if it is left alone.
  • Add a splash of stock or water if it gets too thick. Macaroni carries on drinking the sauce as it stands, and it is better a little loose in the pan.
  • Use good tomatoes and let the paste brown. Cooked-out tomato paste gives depth, and a tinned tomato with no added sugar tastes fresher.

item.title: Shrimp Étouffée
item.description: Shrimp étouffée: shrimp smothered in a thick Louisiana sauce of butter roux, onion, celery, pepper and shrimp stock, served over rice. A Cajun classic.
item.content:encoded:
Étouffée is a French word for smothered, and it describes exactly what happens: shellfish, most often crawfish or shrimp, are cooked in a thick sauce that clings to them and to the rice underneath. The dish belongs to Cajun country in south Louisiana, and it is usually said to have come out of the crawfish town of Breaux Bridge. It sits between a gumbo and a Creole: thicker than a gumbo and served over rice rather than in a bowl of broth, and, in the classic Cajun version, without the tomatoes of a Creole sauce, though many cooks add a spoonful of paste for colour. Everything starts with a roux made from butter and flour and cooked to the colour of peanut butter, a stage that takes patience and constant stirring, followed by the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper. A quick stock made by simmering the shrimp shells is the step that lifts the dish, because it puts the flavour of the shrimp itself into the sauce. The shrimp go in at the very end, so they stay tender and sweet.

  • Stir the roux the whole time. It burns in seconds if it is left alone, and a burnt roux has to be thrown away and started again.
  • Make the stock from the shells. Ten minutes of simmering puts the flavour of the shrimp into the sauce and costs nothing.
  • Add the shrimp last and pull the pan off the heat as soon as they turn pink. Cooked for longer, they turn rubbery and tight.

item.title: Steak Diane
item.description: Steak Diane: pan-seared steaks in a quick sauce of shallots, mushrooms, brandy, Worcestershire sauce, mustard and cream. A restaurant classic in 25 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Steak Diane was one of the showpieces of the mid-century restaurant, cooked and flamed beside the table by a waiter who made a small theatre of the brandy. Its exact origin is disputed, with claims from New York and London hotels and from European restaurants, but it was a fixture of formal menus in the United States, Britain and Australia from the 1940s through the 1970s, and it has never gone away. The idea is simple and sound: a tender cut of beef is seared quickly and set aside to rest, and the sauce is built in the same pan from what the steak left behind. Shallots and mushrooms give sweetness and depth, brandy brings warmth, Worcestershire sauce and Dijon mustard bring savour and tang, and cream softens it into something rich and silky. Flambéing is optional and the drink does no harm if it is simply boiled for a minute, and the real test of the dish is timing, since the steak must be rested and the sauce made in the ten minutes it takes to cook.

  • Have the pan very hot before the steaks go in. The crust forms in the first minute, and a pan that is only warm steams the meat grey.
  • Rest the steaks while you make the sauce. The juices settle back into the meat, and they go into the sauce and not onto the board.
  • Take the pan off the heat before adding the brandy. It stops the spirit catching too fast, and it is a good deal safer, particularly if you do flame it.

item.title: Swiss Steak
item.description: Swiss steak: floured, pounded steaks browned and slowly braised in tomatoes, onions and green pepper until fork-tender. Serve over mashed potatoes or noodles.
item.content:encoded:
Swiss steak has nothing to do with Switzerland. The name is thought to come from swissing, a textile term for pressing or rolling cloth to smooth it, which cooks borrowed for the pounding of flour into a tough cut of beef with a mallet. That pounding is the point of the dish. It breaks up the fibres of an inexpensive steak, such as top round or chuck, and it works a coat of flour into the meat that thickens the braising liquid into a gravy. The steak is then browned, smothered with onions, peppers and tomatoes, covered, and cooked slowly until it is tender enough to cut with a fork. It was a fixture of American home cooking through the middle of the twentieth century, when it turned up in every community cookbook and on the school lunch menu, and it was made to feed a family from a modest piece of meat. It is at its best over mashed potatoes, which catch the sauce, and it reheats well, which makes it a good dish to cook on Sunday for the week.

  • Pound the flour in properly. It tenderises the meat and coats it so that the gravy thickens on its own, without a second step.
  • Brown the steaks until they are deep golden. The crust adds the flavour of the finished sauce, and a pale steak leaves it thin and bland.
  • Keep the pot tightly covered and cook at a low heat. Steam is what softens the meat, and a lid that leaks lets the sauce reduce before the steak is done.

item.title: Beef in Black Bean Sauce
item.description: Beef in black bean sauce: thin steak slices stir-fried with green pepper, onion, garlic and fermented black beans in a glossy sauce. Ready in 32 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Beef in black bean sauce is one of the classics of the Chinese takeaway in Britain, and of the Cantonese restaurant menu that it descends from. The black beans are not the black beans of Latin America. They are soya beans that have been fermented and salted, called douchi in Chinese, and they give a deep, salty, faintly winey savour that is entirely their own. They need a quick rinse to remove excess salt and are then chopped and fried with garlic and ginger in hot oil, which wakes the flavour and scents the whole pan. The other key to the dish is the treatment of the beef. It is cut very thin, against the grain, and tossed in a light coating of cornflour, soy sauce and rice wine, which locks in the juices and gives the beef a silky texture, a technique the Chinese call velveting. It is then seared in a smoking wok for only a minute or two, and returned to the pan at the end, so that it stays tender. The green pepper and onion give crunch and sweetness against the salty sauce.

  • Rinse the black beans briefly. They are very salty, and a quick rinse lets you control the seasoning of the sauce, but do not wash them for long or they lose their flavour.
  • Cook the beef in two batches in a very hot wok. A crowded pan drops in temperature and the beef stews and turns grey instead of searing.
  • Slice the beef against the grain while it is still cold. Semi-frozen meat, sliced thin, is easier to cut, and the short fibres are what make it tender.

item.title: Chicken Dopiaza
item.description: Chicken dopiaza: chicken in a spiced onion and tomato sauce, finished with chunks of fried onion and pepper that keep their bite. A curry-house classic.
item.content:encoded:
The name dopiaza means two onions, and the whole idea of the dish is that onions appear twice. The first lot is chopped finely and cooked slowly with whole spices until deep golden, so that it melts into the sauce and gives it sweetness and body. The second is cut into large pieces and fried quickly at a high heat, so that the edges brown and the middle stays crisp, and it is added at the end for texture and a fresh onion flavour. The dish is found across northern India and Pakistan and on the menu of nearly every British curry house, where it has become a mild-to-medium curry with plenty of sauce, and a chunk of green or red pepper is often included. It is a good curry to make at home because it has no cream and no unusual ingredients, only onions, tomatoes and spices from the cupboard, and because the trick of the two onions gives it a character that a simple onion base cannot match. It is better still the next day.

  • Take the first onions to a deep gold. They give the sauce its sweetness, and pale ones leave a raw, sharp taste.
  • Fry the second onions over high heat and add them last. They should keep a crunch, because that contrast is what the dish is named for.
  • Use thighs and not breast. They stay tender in a sauce, and breast turns dry and stringy.

item.title: Chicken with Cashew Nuts
item.description: Chicken with cashew nuts: sliced chicken stir-fried with toasted cashews, peppers and water chestnuts in a glossy oyster and soy sauce. Ready in 35 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken with cashew nuts is a favourite of the Chinese takeaway in Britain and America, and its ancestors are in Cantonese and Sichuan cooking, where stir-fries of diced chicken with nuts have a long history. The Chinese-American version, sometimes called cashew chicken, is milder and more saucy than its forebears, and the British takeaway version leans on oyster sauce. What makes it work is contrast: soft, tender chicken, crisp peppers and water chestnuts, and cashews that are toasted until golden so that they stay crunchy in the sauce. The chicken is coated in cornflour, soy and rice wine before it is cooked, a step that keeps the breast from drying out in the heat of a wok, and the sauce is mixed in advance so that it can be poured in all at once and thicken in seconds. The dish depends on speed and preparation, since stir-frying takes only a few minutes, so everything is cut, measured and to hand before the pan goes on the heat.

  • Toast the cashews yourself. They pick up a deeper flavour and stay crunchy in the sauce, whereas raw nuts turn soft and pale.
  • Cook the chicken in batches. Too much in the pan lowers the heat and the chicken stews and releases water instead of browning.
  • Mix the sauce before you start. A stir-fry moves too fast to measure ingredients in the middle of it.

item.title: Chicken Cacciatore
item.description: Chicken cacciatore: bone-in chicken thighs braised with peppers, mushrooms, tomatoes, olives and white wine until tender in a rich sauce. Serve with polenta.
item.content:encoded:
Cacciatore means hunter in Italian, and alla cacciatora describes meat cooked the way a hunter's household might have done it, with what could be gathered on the way home: onions and herbs, mushrooms, a splash of wine and tomatoes. The dish was originally made with rabbit or game birds, and it is now made all over Italy with chicken, with as many variations as there are regions. Cooks in Tuscany and the north favour red wine, in Rome and the south it is often white, and a few add anchovy, capers or rosemary. In the United States it has been an Italian-American staple for over a century, and the version that is now familiar, with green and red peppers and mushrooms, is the one that emerged there. What all the versions share is the method, and it is a good one. The chicken is browned first, then braised gently in the sauce, so the meat flavours the tomatoes and the tomatoes flavour the meat. Bone-in thighs are ideal because they stay juicy through the long simmer, and the sauce is finished uncovered so that it thickens into something that clings to polenta or pasta.

  • Brown the chicken skin side down and leave it alone. The skin renders and crisps, and the browned fat flavours the whole sauce.
  • Keep the skin above the sauce when it simmers. It stays golden and does not go soft and pale in the liquid.
  • Finish the sauce uncovered. A wet, thin sauce is the usual failing of the dish, and the last 10 minutes reduces it to a thick coating.

item.title: Scouse
item.description: Scouse: the Liverpool stew of beef, onions, carrots and potatoes cooked slowly until the potatoes break down and thicken it. Serve with pickled red cabbage.
item.content:encoded:
Scouse is the stew of Liverpool, so closely tied to the city that its people are known as Scousers. It is a relative of lobscouse, the salted-meat stew eaten by sailors across northern Europe, and it probably came into the port on the ships, where it was a cheap, filling dish for people who had little to spend. Its main features have not changed. It is made from beef or lamb, with onions, carrots and a large quantity of potatoes, cooked slowly in stock. The important detail is that some of the potatoes are cut small and cooked until they collapse, thickening the stew into a rich, starchy gravy, and the rest are left in chunks, so that there is something to bite. It has a meatless version, known as blind scouse, which was made when there was no meat to be had. Scouse is traditionally served with pickled red cabbage or beetroot, whose sharpness cuts through the richness, and with crusty bread to mop up the gravy. The stew improves on the second day, and it is a good dish for a cold evening.

  • Cut the potatoes in two sizes. The small pieces melt and thicken the stew, and the large ones stay as chunks.
  • Stir gently after the potatoes go in. They break up easily, and a stew that has to be stirred hard is too thick.
  • Serve it with pickled red cabbage, which is not an optional extra. The sharp vinegar is the traditional counterpoint to the rich, starchy stew.

item.title: Boiled Lobster
item.description: Boiled lobster: live lobsters cooked in a large pot of well-salted boiling water until bright red, then cracked and served with melted butter and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
In the Maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, boiled lobster is not a luxury but a local supper. Lobster is fished from the cold Atlantic waters, and it has been served at community lobster suppers in church halls and fire stations for generations, in a tradition that is as much part of summer there as a barbecue is elsewhere. The cooking is as simple as cooking gets. A large pot of water is salted heavily, in the Maritimes often with sea water, and brought to a rolling boil, the lobsters go in head first and are cooked until the shell turns bright red. The timing depends on the weight, and is the one thing that matters, since an overcooked lobster is tough and rubbery, whereas one cooked just right is sweet, tender and juicy. Melted butter and lemon are the only accompaniments, and a nutcracker is the other essential tool. Buying live lobsters from a fishmonger and cooking them on the same day gives the best flavour.

  • Salt the water heavily. It should taste like the sea, since the meat takes up the seasoning as it cooks.
  • Time the cooking from the moment the water returns to the boil. A 700 g lobster needs about 13 minutes, and a heavier one needs a minute or two more for every extra 100 g.
  • Do not overcook it. The meat sets in minutes, and after that it turns tough, so lift the lobster out as soon as it is red and do not let it sit in the hot water.

item.title: Honey Prawns
item.description: Honey prawns: crisp battered king prawns tossed in a sticky honey and lemon glaze with a little mayonnaise and sesame seeds. An Australian favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Honey prawns are a staple of the Chinese restaurant menu in Australia, ordered at banquets and takeaways from Sydney's Chinatown to suburban shopping strips, and the dish has the character of the Australian Chinese repertoire: generous, sweet and shamelessly popular. It has a cousin in the honey walnut prawns of Cantonese cooking. The prawns are coated in a light, crisp batter and fried until golden, then tossed at once in a glossy sauce of honey sharpened with lemon, with a spoonful of mayonnaise for body and richness, and scattered with toasted sesame seeds and spring onion. The contrast between the crunch of the batter and the sticky, sweet coating is the whole idea, so it must be eaten straight away, before the sauce softens the crust. A cornflour-heavy batter is the key to a coating that stays crisp, since cornflour has no gluten and fries to a delicate shell, and a hot, deep oil sets the batter before the prawns overcook. King prawns give the best result, as their size holds up to the batter and their flavour stands out.

  • Dust the prawns with cornflour before they go into the batter. It gives the batter something to hold on to, and it stops the coating sliding off in the oil.
  • Toss the prawns in the glaze at the last moment. A glazed prawn loses its crunch within minutes, so time the dish for the table.
  • Keep the oil at 180°C and fry in batches. Too cool and the batter turns greasy, and too many prawns at once drop the heat.

item.title: Seafood Risotto
item.description: Seafood risotto: creamy rice cooked in a mussel and fish stock with squid and prawns added near the end, and finished with lemon, parsley and butter.
item.content:encoded:
Risotto ai frutti di mare is the risotto of the Italian coast, and it is one of the dishes that Australians, with their access to fresh seafood and a long tradition of Italian cooking, have made their own, at home and in restaurants from Melbourne to Fremantle. The important idea is that the flavour of the sea is put into the rice itself. The mussels are steamed open in white wine, and the liquid they release goes into the stock, so that the risotto is cooked in a broth that already tastes of shellfish. The squid, which needs a little cooking to soften, goes in for the last few minutes, and the prawns, which need only a few, go in after that, so that neither is overcooked. It is traditionally finished without cheese, since the Italian view is that Parmesan overwhelms the delicate flavour of seafood, and instead a little butter, lemon zest and parsley give richness and freshness. The rice should be creamy and loose, with a little bite at the centre, and the risotto should be served at once.

  • Use the liquid from the mussels. It is full of salt and flavour, and it puts the sea into the rice more surely than shop-bought stock alone.
  • Add the squid and prawns late. Both toughen if they cook for long, and they finish cooking in the heat of the rice.
  • Skip the Parmesan. Its strong flavour hides the shellfish, and the butter and lemon give all the richness the dish needs.

item.title: Banana Ice Cream
item.description: Banana ice cream: frozen ripe bananas blended with a splash of milk and vanilla into a smooth, creamy soft serve. No churn, no cream and no added sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Banana ice cream, sometimes called nice cream, is one of the neatest tricks in the healthy kitchen. Ripe bananas are high in pectin and starch, and when they are frozen and then blended, they break down into a smooth, creamy, cold purée that has the texture of soft-serve ice cream. It contains no dairy, no cream, no eggs and no added sugar, because ripe bananas are sweet enough on their own. It became popular through the vegan and raw food movements in the 2000s, and it has stayed because it is genuinely quick and easy to do, and children like it. The result depends on two things. The first is that the bananas must be really ripe, with plenty of brown spots, since underripe ones taste starchy and bland. The second is patience with the blender: at first the frozen slices crumble into coarse pieces, then they clump into a ball, and then, with a few more minutes and a scrape or two of the sides, they turn smooth. A splash of milk helps the machine, and vanilla and a pinch of salt make it taste like ice cream and not like a frozen banana.

  • Use bananas with brown spots. They are sweeter and blend to a creamier texture, and green-tinged ones taste starchy.
  • Slice before freezing and spread the coins out on the tray. They freeze separately and do not weld into a block that is hard on the blender.
  • Stop when it is smooth. Overblending warms the mixture, and it turns soft and runny, so serve it straight away.

item.title: Beer Cheese Soup
item.description: Beer cheese soup: sharp cheddar melted into a base of onion, celery, carrot, lager and stock, seasoned with mustard and paprika. Served with croutons.
item.content:encoded:
Beer cheese soup is a dish of the American Midwest, and it is most closely tied to Wisconsin, where both beer and cheddar are local pride. It is one of the simplest ways of turning those two ingredients into a meal, and it has been a fixture of taverns and supper clubs there for generations. It is a cousin of beer cheese, the spread from Kentucky, in that both use the same partnership of sharp cheddar and lager, with mustard, Worcestershire sauce and a little heat. The soup is built on a roux: butter and flour are cooked with onion, celery and carrot, then thinned with beer and stock, and milk goes in last, so that the cheese can be melted in gently over a low heat. Two rules matter. The first is to grate the cheese yourself from a block, since packaged shreds contain starch that stops them melting smoothly and leaves the soup grainy. The second is never to let the soup boil after the cheese goes in, because high heat splits the cheese into strings and grease. A pale lager gives a clean, malty flavour, and a very hoppy beer can turn the soup bitter.

  • Grate the cheddar from a block. Pre-shredded cheese is coated in starch and makes a grainy soup.
  • Add the cheese over low heat and never let the soup boil. High heat splits the cheese into strings and oil.
  • Choose a mild lager or pale ale. A very hoppy beer turns bitter when it is reduced, and a light beer leaves the cheese flavour in front.

item.title: Chicken Gnocchi Soup
item.description: Chicken gnocchi soup: a creamy soup of shredded chicken, potato gnocchi, carrots, celery and spinach in a Parmesan-scented stock. Made in 40 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken gnocchi soup is an American invention with an Italian accent, one of the most requested soups from the chain restaurants of the 1990s and 2000s, and one of the most copied at home since. It is a very good idea. The gnocchi, soft little dumplings of potato, cook in minutes in the simmering soup and release a little starch that thickens it, so that a small amount of cream gives the broth a full, velvety body. The rest of the soup is straightforward: a base of onion, carrot and celery, a spoonful of flour to thicken, stock and milk, cooked chicken, and a handful of spinach at the end for colour. Shredded rotisserie chicken is the natural shortcut, because it is already seasoned and it makes the soup quick, and packaged shelf-stable gnocchi are the easiest option too, since they do not need to be boiled separately. The one care needed is timing. Gnocchi turn heavy and gummy if they are overcooked, so they go in last, are cooked until they float, and the soup is served at once.

  • Add the gnocchi last and serve straight away. They keep absorbing liquid, and a soup that stands turns thick and the gnocchi go soft.
  • Use rotisserie chicken if you can. It is already seasoned and tender, and it saves poaching a breast.
  • Add the cream off a full boil. A gentle heat keeps the soup smooth, and hard boiling can make the milk and cream split.

item.title: Garlic Noodles
item.description: Garlic noodles: spaghetti tossed in butter, plenty of garlic, oyster sauce and soy, finished with Parmesan and spring onions. Ready in 25 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Garlic noodles are a dish of the San Francisco Bay Area, where Vietnamese-American cooks in the 1970s and 1980s combined the flavours of Chinese and Vietnamese cooking with the ingredients that were to hand, butter, garlic and Parmesan among them, and the result is now cooked in homes across the United States. It is a dish whose success depends on a proportion that looks absurd on the page: a great deal of garlic, cooked gently in butter until it is fragrant and just golden, then combined with the savoury umami of oyster sauce and soy sauce, and a little sugar to round the edges. The noodles are tossed in the sauce with a few spoonfuls of their own cooking water, which emulsifies the butter into a glossy coating that clings to each strand. Parmesan adds a salty, savoury finish, and spring onions and sesame seeds give freshness and crunch. Spaghetti is the usual choice, because it is what most kitchens had, and egg noodles are a good alternative. It is a side dish at crab restaurants, and a full meal at home, with a fried egg on top.

  • Cook the garlic over low heat and stop when it is pale gold. Garlic that catches turns bitter, and there is a lot of it here.
  • Use the pasta water. Its starch turns the butter and sauce into a smooth, glossy coating that clings to the noodles.
  • Serve at once. Noodles tossed in a buttery sauce tighten as they cool, and are at their best straight from the pan.

item.title: Energy Balls
item.description: Energy balls: dates, oats, peanut butter, honey, chia seeds and chocolate chips blended and rolled into bite-sized balls. A no-bake snack for the lunchbox.
item.content:encoded:
Energy balls, also called energy bites or bliss balls, are the snack of the healthy-eating world of the past two decades, and they earned their place by being practical. They are made from ingredients that are calorie-dense and slow to digest, dates, oats, nuts or nut butter and seeds, blended and rolled into pieces that fit in the hand, and they need no baking. Dates are the base and the binder. Their sticky sweetness holds everything together and does away with the need for added sugar, while peanut butter and oats give protein, fibre and staying power, chia seeds add omega-3 fats, and a little honey and chocolate turn it from health food into a treat. They are useful as a snack before or after exercise, in a lunchbox, or on a walk, and the mixture is easy to vary: almond butter for peanut, cocoa for extra chocolate, dried cranberries for chocolate chips. The one thing to look for is the texture of the mixture: it should stay together when squeezed, and if it is dry, a spoonful of water or milk brings it back.

  • Use soft, fresh Medjool dates. Dry ones make a crumbly mix, and soaking them briefly puts it right.
  • Check the texture by squeezing. If the mixture will not hold, add a teaspoon of water at a time, and if it is sticky, add a spoonful of oats.
  • Wet your hands before rolling. The mixture is sticky, and damp hands keep it from clinging.

item.title: Italian Wedding Soup
item.description: Italian wedding soup: a clear chicken broth with tiny browned meatballs, small pasta, carrots and leafy greens, finished with Parmesan.
item.content:encoded:
Italian wedding soup has nothing to do with weddings. The name is a mistranslation of minestra maritata, married soup, which describes the marriage of flavours between the meat and the green vegetables in it, and the dish has its roots in southern Italy, where a broth of pork and bitter greens was eaten at celebrations. In the United States, Italian immigrants turned it into the soup that most people now know: a clear chicken broth with tiny meatballs, small pasta such as acini di pepe, carrots and a leafy green, finished with grated Parmesan. It is served at Italian-American restaurants and family tables everywhere, and it is loved because it is light yet satisfying. The meatballs are the heart of it and are made small, about the size of a cherry, so that a spoonful holds several. Baking them first browns them and keeps them from clouding the broth, and it is faster than frying. The greens, escarole for authenticity or baby spinach for ease, go in at the end so that they keep their colour.

  • Keep the meatballs small. Tiny ones cook fast, sit several to a spoonful, and are tender because they are not overworked.
  • Bake them and do not simmer them raw in the broth. They brown and hold their shape, and the broth stays clear.
  • Add the greens at the end. Escarole and spinach turn drab if they cook for long, and a few minutes is enough.

item.title: Waldorf Salad
item.description: Waldorf salad: crisp red apples, celery, grapes and walnuts folded into a creamy mayonnaise and yoghurt dressing and served on lettuce. Ready in 15 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The Waldorf salad was created in 1893 at the Waldorf Hotel in New York, by the maître d'hôtel Oscar Tschirky, known to his customers as Oscar of the Waldorf, and it first appeared at a charity ball. The original was not what many people expect. It was made of just apples, celery and mayonnaise, and the walnuts, which are now regarded as essential, were added in the years that followed. It became one of the best-known salads in the world, and it stayed on hotel and restaurant menus for a century, sometimes with grapes, sometimes with raisins, and often with a lot more mayonnaise than is good for it. The best version is a matter of balance. The apples should be crisp, sweet-tart and red, and are tossed in lemon juice at once so that they do not turn brown. The celery gives a clean, juicy crunch, grapes add sweetness, walnuts add richness and bite, and a dressing of mayonnaise lightened with yoghurt coats them without weighing them down. It is the sort of salad that is best made shortly before it is eaten, when the crunch is at its height.

  • Toss the apples in lemon juice as soon as they are cut. The acid keeps them from browning and adds a fresh edge to the salad.
  • Choose apples that are crisp and sweet-tart, such as Gala, Braeburn or Pink Lady. A soft, mealy apple turns the salad to mush.
  • Dress it shortly before serving. The walnuts soften and the apples release juice if it stands for more than an hour or so.

item.title: Salmon Burgers
item.description: Salmon burgers: chopped salmon mixed with lemon, dill, mustard and panko, shaped into patties, pan-fried and served in toasted buns with caper mayonnaise.
item.content:encoded:
A salmon burger is a good example of a dish that improves when made at home, since the ones sold frozen are usually dry and heavily bound with breadcrumbs, and it is easy to do it better. The secret is in the texture. Half of the salmon is chopped by hand into small pieces, so that there are chunks of fish you can see and bite, and half is pulsed to a coarse paste, which acts as the binder. Between them they need only a small amount of egg and panko to hold together, which means the patty tastes of salmon and not of breadcrumb. The flavourings are the classic partners of the fish: lemon zest and juice for freshness, dill, Dijon mustard for a little sharpness, and spring onion for bite.
