A quick chill before cooking helps the patties keep their shape in the pan, and the cooking must be brief, four or five minutes on each side, since salmon is best cooked just through and is dry if it goes too far. A caper mayonnaise on a toasted bun, with lettuce and tomato, completes a light lunch.

  • Chop half of the salmon by hand. The chunks give a burger you can taste and bite, and a paste alone is mushy.
  • Chill the patties before you cook them. Cold ones hold their shape in the pan, and warm ones fall apart.
  • Do not overcook them. Salmon is done when it is just opaque, and a patty cooked until firm through is dry.

item.title: Tortellini Soup
item.description: Tortellini soup: Italian sausage, carrots, tomatoes and cheese tortellini in a tomato broth with spinach wilted in at the end. Ready in 40 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Tortellini soup is an American home-cooking staple, and it has little in common with the delicate tortellini in brodo of Emilia, in which small stuffed pasta are served in a clear broth. It is a heartier, more casual dish, built on ingredients that are easy to find in a supermarket, and it appeared in family cookbooks and on food blogs because it makes a large pot of soup in about half an hour. Italian sausage provides the flavour foundation. It is browned first, and its fat and fennel seasoning flavour the whole soup. Carrots and onion add sweetness, a tin of tomatoes and chicken stock make the broth, and Italian seasoning ties them together. Fresh tortellini from the chill cabinet are the best choice, since they cook in a few minutes and stay tender, whereas dried tortellini need longer and become chewy. The spinach goes in at the very end and wilts in the heat of the broth. It is a soup that can be made with a spicy or a mild sausage, and it keeps well, though the pasta continues to swell in the pot.

  • Brown the sausage properly. It gives the broth a savoury depth, and pale, steamed sausage leaves the soup flat.
  • Use fresh tortellini from the chill cabinet. They cook in minutes and stay tender, whereas dried ones need longer and turn chewy.
  • Serve the soup straight away. The pasta keeps soaking up broth, and left in the pot it turns soft and swollen.

item.title: Vegetarian Chili
item.description: Vegetarian chili: a thick, smoky chili of three kinds of beans, peppers, carrots and sweetcorn simmered in spiced tomatoes. Hearty and completely meat-free.
item.content:encoded:
Chili is a dish of the American Southwest and Texas, and it began with beef, chillies and not much else. A meatless version might seem a compromise, but a good one does not taste like a compromise at all. A vegetarian chili works by building the same three layers of flavour that a meat chili has: a base of onion, peppers and carrot cooked until sweet, a bold blend of chilli powder, cumin, smoked paprika and oregano, toasted in the pan before the liquid goes in, and a long simmer that draws the ingredients together. Beans provide the body and the protein. Using three kinds, the meaty kidney bean, the creamy pinto and the firmer black bean, gives a variety of texture that a single bean cannot, and a little tomato paste and a spoonful of cocoa deepen the colour and the savour in the way that browned meat would. Sweetcorn added near the end brings a burst of sweetness against the heat. The chili tastes better the next day, and freezes well, and it is a good dish for feeding a mixed table.

  • Toast the spices in the pot before adding any liquid. A minute in hot oil takes away their raw, dusty taste and brings out their flavour.
  • Use three kinds of beans. They differ in texture, and the mixture gives a chili with more interest than a single bean.
  • Give it time. The simmer thickens the sauce and blends the flavours, and the chili tastes even better on the second day.

item.title: Currywurst
item.description: Currywurst: sliced fried sausage under a warm, spiced curry ketchup sauce and a dusting of curry powder. Berlin's street food, served with chips or a roll.
item.content:encoded:
Currywurst is the street food of Berlin, and it has a known birthday. It is credited to Herta Heuwer, who in 1949 ran a snack stand in the ruined city, and who, according to the story, obtained ketchup and curry powder from British soldiers and mixed them into a sauce to pour over grilled sausage. Whether or not every detail is right, the dish became a symbol of postwar Germany, and it is now eaten in enormous quantities, from stands and station kiosks and even in its own museum in Berlin. It is very simple: a sausage, traditionally a pork bratwurst, cut into rounds and served with a warm sauce of ketchup and curry powder, with more curry powder dusted over the top. The sauce is what matters, and it is better made at home than bought. It is built from onion, tomato paste and ketchup, with curry powder, paprika, Worcestershire sauce, sugar and vinegar, and simmered until it is thick, glossy and somewhere between sweet, sour and spicy. It is eaten with a bread roll for mopping up, or with chips, and with a toothpick or a small fork.

  • Choose a mild curry powder. Currywurst is sweet, tangy and gently spiced, and a strong Madras blend overpowers it.
  • Simmer the sauce until it is thick and glossy. A thin sauce runs off the sausage, and a good one clings.
  • Dust the curry powder on at the end. It is part of the dish, and gives the top a fresh, toasty aroma that the cooked sauce lacks.

item.title: Chiko Roll
item.description: Chiko Roll: a tube of crisp pastry filled with beef, cabbage, barley, carrot and celery, deep-fried until golden. The Australian football-ground snack.
item.content:encoded:
The Chiko Roll is one of Australia's great fast foods, invented in Bendigo, Victoria, by the boilermaker Frank McEncroe, who was inspired by the Chinese egg rolls he had seen in the United States and wanted a snack that could be eaten at football matches with one hand and no fork. He launched it in 1951 at the Wagga Show, and it was soon in country pubs, corner shops and fish and chip shops across the country. It is said that the name comes from the word chicken, though there is no chicken in it, and its filling is of beef, cabbage, barley, carrot, celery and onion, with a mild savoury seasoning. The pastry is much thicker and stronger than a spring roll wrapper, which is what allows it to be held and eaten on the move. A home version takes some effort, since the filling has to be cooked and cooled and the rolls wrapped tight, but the result is very good: a crisp, blistered shell around a soft, savoury filling. It is eaten with a squirt of tomato sauce, and is at its best hot, out of the fryer, wrapped in white paper.

  • Cool the filling completely before you roll. A warm filling steams the wrapper soft, and it tears as it is rolled.
  • Use two wrappers at once. A single spring roll wrapper is too thin, and the double layer gives the strong, crunchy shell that the Chiko Roll is known for.
  • Roll them tightly and seal the end well. A loose roll opens in the oil, and it is worth being careful, since hot oil is dangerous.

item.title: Monte Cristo
item.description: Monte Cristo: ham, turkey and Swiss cheese sandwiched in bread, dipped in egg batter, fried until golden and served with icing sugar and raspberry jam.
item.content:encoded:
The Monte Cristo is the American cousin of the French croque monsieur, a sandwich of ham and cheese that has been dipped in egg and fried, but it adds turkey and a dusting of icing sugar and jam on the side, so that it lands somewhere between lunch and pudding. It is thought to have appeared on American menus in the 1930s and 1940s, sometimes under the name French sandwich, and it was made famous in the 1960s by the Blue Bayou restaurant at Disneyland in California, where it has been served for decades. Its name refers to the Count of Monte Cristo, Dumas's hero. The combination of salty ham, mild turkey and melted Swiss cheese with a sweet, eggy crust and tart raspberry jam seems odd, but it works, in the same way as bacon with maple syrup does. It is made from soft white bread, which soaks up the egg and browns evenly, and it is cooked in butter over moderate heat, so that the outside turns golden while the cheese melts. It is a sandwich for a slow lunch and it is filling enough to be a whole meal.

  • Use soft white bread and dip it briefly. It soaks up the egg without collapsing, and a thick or stale slice would need longer.
  • Cook the sandwiches over medium-low heat. High heat browns the outside before the cheese melts, and gentle heat cooks them through.
  • Serve them straight away with the jam. The crust is crisp for only a few minutes, and the sweet, tart jam is the point of the dish.

item.title: Coney Dogs
item.description: Coney dogs: hot dogs in steamed buns topped with a fine, savoury beanless coney sauce, yellow mustard and chopped raw onion. The Detroit favourite.
item.content:encoded:
A coney dog is a hot dog in a soft, steamed bun, topped with a fine, loose beef sauce, yellow mustard and chopped raw onion, and it is the signature snack of Michigan, especially Detroit and Flint. The name comes from Coney Island in New York, and the dish was brought west by Greek and Macedonian immigrants who opened restaurants in the early twentieth century. Two Detroit rivals, American Coney Island and Lafayette Coney Island, share a wall and have argued about who is best for decades, and the coney dog has become a matter of local pride. The sauce is what makes the dish. It is not a chilli, and it has no beans, no chunks and no heavy sweetness. It is a finely textured, savoury, gently spiced sauce, made from beef mince that is broken up in cold liquid before it is heated, so that it stays in tiny particles instead of clumping, and cooked for an hour with onion, tomato paste, chilli powder, cumin and paprika. A natural-casing beef hot dog, a steamed bun, and the classic toppings are all the dish needs.

  • Break up the beef in cold liquid before it is heated. The proteins cannot set into lumps, and the sauce keeps the fine, loose texture.
  • Simmer the sauce uncovered for the whole time. It thickens and darkens as it reduces, and a sauce that is too wet slides off the dog.
  • Steam the buns. A soft, warm bun is part of the coney, and a toasted one is the wrong texture.

item.title: Chicken Chop Suey
item.description: Chicken chop suey: sliced chicken stir-fried with celery, carrot, mushrooms, mangetout and bean sprouts in a light oyster sauce. Ready in 27 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Chop suey is a dish of the Chinese diaspora in the United States, and it is as much an American creation as a Chinese one. Its name comes from the Cantonese tsap sui, meaning assorted bits, and it became popular in the late nineteenth century in the Chinese restaurants of San Francisco and New York, before spreading to Britain and Australia, where it was an early staple of the Chinese takeaway. A widely repeated story credits a chef to the Chinese statesman Li Hongzhang with inventing it in 1896, but this is a legend. Whatever its origin, it is a good dish, and a useful one. It is a stir-fry of sliced chicken and a mixture of crisp vegetables in a light, clear, savoury sauce, and it is traditionally made with celery, bean sprouts and mushrooms, which give it its characteristic juicy crunch. The chicken is tossed in cornflour before cooking, which keeps it tender, and the sauce is lightly thickened, so that it glosses everything without smothering it. It is served over rice, and it is the kind of dish where nothing is stronger than anything else.

  • Add the vegetables in order of how long they take. Carrot and celery need the longest, and bean sprouts only a moment, so they stay crisp.
  • Thicken the sauce lightly. It should coat the vegetables in a thin glaze and not cover them in a gluey coat.
  • Keep the heat high and the pan moving. Stir-frying is quick, and a hot wok keeps the vegetables crunchy instead of stewed.

item.title: Bran Muffins
item.description: Bran muffins: moist, dark muffins made with wheat bran, buttermilk, molasses and raisins. A high-fibre breakfast that tastes of brown sugar and cinnamon.
item.content:encoded:
The bran muffin is an American breakfast staple of the twentieth century, and it grew out of the health movements that promoted fibre long before the word became fashionable. Cereal companies printed recipes for it on their boxes from the 1930s, and by the 1970s and 1980s a bran muffin was as much a fixture of the coffee shop counter as a doughnut. Done badly it is dry, dense and dull, and that reputation has followed it. Done well, it is one of the best muffins there is: moist, dark, faintly sweet, with the toasty flavour of wheat and the rich bitterness of molasses. The way to avoid dryness is to soak the bran in buttermilk before mixing, so that it softens and takes up liquid instead of stealing it from the batter, and to use enough fat and sugar for tenderness. Molasses and brown sugar give colour and depth, cinnamon gives warmth, and raisins supply pockets of sweetness and moisture. The batter is stirred only until combined, as with any muffin, and a hot oven gives the domed tops.

  • Soak the bran in the buttermilk first. It softens the bran and stops it drawing moisture from the batter, which is the usual cause of dry bran muffins.
  • Stir only until combined. A few streaks of flour are fine, and overmixing makes the muffins tough.
  • Fill the cases well. Bran batter is dense and rises less than most, and a generous scoop gives a proper domed top.

item.title: Cinnamon Swirl Bread
item.description: Cinnamon swirl bread: a soft, enriched yeast loaf rolled up with butter, brown sugar and cinnamon so every slice shows a spiral. Wonderful toasted.
item.content:encoded:
Cinnamon swirl bread is a breakfast classic in America, and it belongs to the family of enriched sweet breads that European bakers took to the New World. It is a soft loaf, made with milk, egg and butter, with a thin spiral of cinnamon sugar running through the middle of each slice. It is best toasted, when the edges crisp and the sugar in the swirl melts, and it makes exceptional French toast. Making it at home is a good introduction to bread with a filling. The dough is a straightforward enriched one, and the only tricky part is the roll. The dough is rolled into a wide rectangle, buttered, sprinkled evenly with the sugar and cinnamon, and rolled up as tightly as possible, because a loose roll leaves gaps in the crumb and the loaf tears along the swirl as it rises. A rectangle the same width as the tin gives a log that fits it, and the final proof is done in the tin. Baked until deep golden, and cooled before slicing, it has a fine, even crumb and a swirl that holds together.

  • Roll the dough up as tightly as you can. A loose roll leaves air pockets and gaps in the swirl, and the loaf pulls apart when sliced.
  • Keep the filling off the last centimetre of dough. The sugar can leak out of the seam as it bakes, and a clean border seals better.
  • Cool the loaf before slicing. The crumb is still setting when it comes out, and a warm loaf squashes under the knife.

item.title: Funfetti Cake
item.description: Funfetti cake: a vanilla layer cake speckled with rainbow sprinkles, sandwiched and covered in vanilla buttercream. The birthday cake of American childhood.
item.content:encoded:
Funfetti is the American birthday cake: a vanilla sponge with rainbow sprinkles stirred through the batter, so that every slice is speckled with colour. It began as a boxed mix, launched by a cake mix company in the late 1980s, and it has stood for parties, school celebrations and children's birthdays ever since. It is easy to make from scratch, and it tastes much better than the box. The sponge is a standard butter cake, with butter and sugar creamed until pale and light, eggs and vanilla beaten in, and flour and milk added in turn, and the sprinkles folded in last. There is one point to know. The sprinkles must be jimmies, the long, cylindrical kind, and not nonpareils, the tiny round balls, because nonpareils dissolve and bleed into the batter and turn it a muddy grey, whereas jimmies hold their colour in the oven. Vanilla buttercream and a scattering of extra sprinkles finish it. It is a simple cake, and its appeal is in the fun of cutting into it and finding it full of confetti.

  • Use jimmies and not nonpareils. Nonpareils melt and bleed into the batter, and jimmies keep their colour through the bake.
  • Fold the sprinkles in at the very end. Stirring them for long breaks them down and streaks the batter with colour.
  • Cool the layers fully before frosting. Warm sponge melts the buttercream, and it slides off the cake.

item.title: Homemade Sandwich Bread
item.description: Homemade sandwich bread: a soft, tall white loaf made with milk and butter, with a fine crumb and thin golden crust. It slices well for sandwiches and toast.
item.content:encoded:
A sandwich loaf is the everyday bread of American kitchens, and making one at home is the best introduction to bread baking there is, since the dough is forgiving and the reward is very high. What distinguishes it from a crusty artisan loaf is the softness. It is an enriched dough, made with milk instead of water and with butter and a little sugar, which produce a tender, fine crumb and a thin, soft crust that suits a sandwich, where a chewy crust would fight the filling. The tin is what gives it its shape, a tall, even, rectangular loaf that slices into uniform pieces. The method is straightforward: mix, knead until the dough is smooth and elastic, let it rise until doubled, shape it into a tight roll so it has a good structure, and let it rise a second time in the tin until it crowns over the rim. Baked until the crust is golden and the base sounds hollow, brushed with melted butter for softness and cooled fully before cutting, it will keep for several days, which is longer than most shop-bought bread and much tastier.

  • Knead until the dough is smooth and stretches thin without tearing. That gluten development is what holds the tall, even shape.
  • Roll the dough up tightly before it goes in the tin. A tight roll gives a fine, even crumb, and a loose one leaves holes.
  • Let the loaf cool completely before slicing. The crumb is still steaming and setting, and a warm slice compresses into a gummy layer.

item.title: Pecan Sticky Buns
item.description: Pecan sticky buns: soft cinnamon-swirl buns baked on a bed of butter, brown sugar, maple caramel and pecans, then turned out so the topping runs down.
item.content:encoded:
A sticky bun is a cinnamon roll that is baked upside down on a layer of caramel and nuts, and then turned out so that the topping becomes a shining, sticky glaze. It is a speciality of Philadelphia and the Pennsylvania Dutch country, where it has been made since the nineteenth century, and pecans are the usual nut in the South. What sets it apart from a plain cinnamon roll is the caramel. Butter, brown sugar, maple syrup and a little cream are melted together and poured into the tin before the buns go in, and as they bake, the caramel bubbles up round the dough and sets, and the buns absorb some of it. When the tin is inverted the base becomes the top, and the pecans, which have toasted at the bottom of the tin, sit in a gleaming layer. The dough is a soft, enriched yeast dough, rolled with a cinnamon filling, cut into slices and left to rise again in the tin. The one important step is timing: the buns must be turned out while the caramel is still warm and liquid, or it sets solid to the tin.

  • Turn the buns out while the caramel is still warm. In a few minutes it sets hard, and the pecans stay stuck in the tin.
  • Roll the dough tightly and cut with a sharp knife or a length of thread. A blunt blade squashes the swirl, and the slices lose their shape.
  • Stand the tin on a baking tray. The caramel bubbles up at the edges and can drip onto the oven floor.

item.title: Scotcheroos
item.description: Scotcheroos: chewy peanut butter and crisped rice bars topped with a layer of melted chocolate and butterscotch. A Midwestern potluck classic.
item.content:encoded:
Scotcheroos are a bar from the American Midwest, most closely tied to Minnesota, Iowa and Wisconsin, where they turn up at church suppers, school fundraisers and Christmas cookie plates every year. They belong to the family of crispy cereal treats, but they are richer and more grown up than the marshmallow kind. The base is crisped rice cereal held together by a hot mixture of sugar, syrup and peanut butter, which sets to a firm, chewy bar, and the topping is a thin layer of chocolate and butterscotch, melted together and spread on top, which gives a glossy finish and a salty-sweet, caramelly flavour. The name is a play on butterscotch and perhaps on the word for a pushover, and it fits the way they vanish from a plate. They need no oven. The one point to watch is the sugar syrup, which should be brought only to the point at which it just starts to boil, because a longer boil produces a hard candy that breaks teeth. The base should be pressed firmly into the tin with a greased spatula so the bars cut cleanly.

  • Take the syrup off the heat as soon as it starts to boil. A longer boil sets to a hard candy, and the bars turn tough.
  • Press the base down hard. A firmly packed base cuts into neat squares, and a loose one crumbles.
  • Melt the chips gently. Overheated chocolate turns grainy, and butterscotch chips scorch easily.

item.title: Pineapple Upside-Down Cake
item.description: Pineapple upside-down cake: a butter sponge baked on caramelised brown sugar, pineapple rings and cherries, then turned over to show the glossy fruit.
item.content:encoded:
The pineapple upside-down cake is one of the great American cakes of the twentieth century, and its rise is linked to the canned pineapple industry. In 1925 the Hawaiian Pineapple Company held a recipe contest for dishes using its sliced pineapple, and it received thousands of entries for an upside-down cake, which had been made in cast-iron pans for generations before. It became a staple of the 1950s dessert table, and it has kept a following because it is as good as it looks. The trick is in the name. The fruit goes in the bottom of the tin, with a layer of melted butter and brown sugar, and the batter goes over the top. In the oven the butter and sugar turn to caramel that soaks up into the sponge, and when the cake is turned out, the pineapple rings and cherries are on top, gleaming in the caramel. The batter is a simple butter sponge with a little pineapple juice from the tin for flavour. The one hazard is turning it out: it should be done within a few minutes of leaving the oven, before the caramel sets and glues the fruit to the tin.

  • Turn the cake out while it is still warm. The caramel sets as it cools, and a cold cake sticks to the tin and tears the fruit off.
  • Pat the pineapple rings dry before they go in. Extra juice thins the caramel, and dry rings caramelise better.
  • Leave the tin on the cake for a minute after turning it out. It lets the last of the caramel drip down instead of staying behind.

item.title: Beer Bread
item.description: Beer bread: a quick bread with no yeast and no kneading, made from flour, sugar, salt and a bottle of lager and baked with melted butter poured over the top.
item.content:encoded:
Beer bread is the simplest loaf that can be made from scratch: self-raising flour, sugar, salt and a bottle of beer, stirred together in one bowl and baked. It became popular in American kitchens in the 1970s and 1980s as a quick bread that needed no yeast, no kneading and no rising time, and it has since become a standby for people who want fresh bread in an hour. The beer does two jobs. Its carbonation and the raising agents in the self-raising flour give the loaf its lift, and its malt and hops give it a distinctive toasty, slightly tangy flavour, with a hint of sweetness from the sugar. A lager gives a mild, neutral loaf, a pale ale a little more hop, and a dark stout or porter a richer, darker one. Melted butter poured over the top before and during the bake is what gives it its crisp, golden, buttery crust, which is the best part. The batter is thick and lumpy and should be stirred as little as possible, as with any quick bread, so that the crumb stays tender.

  • Stir only until the flour is wet. Overmixing makes a tough, dense loaf, and the lumps disappear in the oven.
  • Choose the beer for the flavour you want. A lager gives a mild loaf, a pale ale gives a hoppier one and a stout gives a dark, malty loaf.
  • Pour the butter in two stages. The first melts into the top, and the second gives the golden, crackling crust.

item.title: Aberdeen Butteries
item.description: Aberdeen butteries: flat, flaky, salty rolls made from a yeast dough layered with butter and lard. Also called rowies, they are Aberdeen's morning roll.
item.content:encoded:
The buttery, or rowie, is the roll of Aberdeen, and it is unlike any other bread in Britain. It is flat and round, golden and flaky, and very rich, made from a yeast dough that is layered with butter and lard in the way of a croissant, though the result is more rustic and much saltier. It is said to have been created in the nineteenth century for the fishermen of the North Sea, who needed a bread that was high in fat and would keep on a long trip, and it is still baked daily in Aberdeen and eaten warm, split and spread with butter or jam, or with a slice of cheese. The name rowie is a shortening of its Scots name, and it is sometimes described as a savoury croissant. The lamination is done in three stages, with the fat divided into portions, folded in and chilled between each, which is quicker and less exacting than a croissant, since there is only a modest amount of rolling. The flour should be strong, the salt generous, and the lard is part of the authenticity, giving a distinctive savoury flavour, though butter alone works. They are best eaten the day they are made, still warm.

  • Chill the dough between folds. The fat must stay firm to make layers, and it melts into the dough if it gets warm.
  • Do not roll too thin at the end. The butteries should be about 1.5 cm thick, so that they rise a little and stay soft in the middle.
  • Keep the salt in. It is what distinguishes a buttery from a sweet roll, and the flavour against butter and jam is the whole point.

item.title: Fondant Fancies
item.description: Fondant fancies: small squares of vanilla sponge filled with jam and buttercream, coated in pink, yellow and lilac fondant icing and piped with chocolate.
item.content:encoded:
Fondant fancies are the little iced cakes of the British teatime, small squares of sponge in pastel icing that are as much a part of the childhood party as sausage rolls and jelly. The commercial version, sold in boxes of pink, yellow and lilac, made the cake famous, but a home-made fancy is much better, and it is a project that rewards care. The sponge is a simple, fine-grained vanilla butter sponge baked in a square tin, split, and filled with apricot jam and vanilla buttercream, which makes each cake moist. It is chilled so that it can be cut cleanly into small squares, and each square is set on a wire rack and coated in a warm fondant icing, made by warming icing sugar with a little water until it pours, so that it flows over the top and down the sides in a smooth, shining shell. The icing needs some judgement: too thick and it clumps, too thin and it runs off, and it must be kept warm to stay fluid. A little piped chocolate on top is the traditional decoration.

  • Chill the sponge before cutting. A cold, firm cake cuts into sharp squares, and a soft one crumbles.
  • Keep the fondant just warm. If it is too hot it turns translucent and thin, and if it is too cool it sets in the bowl.
  • Ice over a tray. The drips can be scraped up, warmed and used again, so nothing is wasted.

item.title: Rough Puff Pastry
item.description: Rough puff pastry: a quick, flaky pastry made from flour, cold butter in chunks and iced water, rolled and folded four times. Puff pastry without the fuss.
item.content:encoded:
Rough puff is the cook's shortcut to puff pastry, and it is a valuable one, since it gives most of the rise and all of the flaky layers of the real thing in a fraction of the time. Full puff pastry requires a block of butter to be wrapped in dough and rolled and folded six times with long rests, a job for a professional kitchen. In rough puff, the butter is cut into chunks and mixed loosely with the flour, so that it stays in visible pieces, and the dough is then rolled and folded to flatten the pieces of butter into thin layers. When the pastry is baked, the water in the butter turns to steam and lifts the layers apart, and the pastry puffs. The keys to it are cold and restraint. The butter must be cold and the water iced, so that the fat stays solid, and the dough must be handled lightly, with no kneading, so that the gluten does not toughen it. Four folds are enough, with a rest between so that the dough relaxes. Rough puff is used for pies, sausage rolls, turnovers, tart cases and Eccles cakes, and it is at its best when it is made the day before.

  • Keep everything cold. Cold butter makes layers, and butter that softens smears into the dough and gives a heavy, greasy pastry.
  • Do not knead the dough. It should look shaggy, with pieces of butter showing, and those pieces are what makes it flaky.
  • Rest the dough between folds. It lets the gluten relax, so that it rolls out easily and does not shrink back.

item.title: Teisen Lap
item.description: Teisen lap: a moist, lightly spiced Welsh fruit cake baked in a square tin and cut into squares, eaten warm with butter and a cup of tea.
item.content:encoded:
Teisen lap is a traditional Welsh cake, and its name, which means a moist or sloppy cake, describes it well. It comes from the kitchens of south-west Wales, where it was baked on a griddle or in a tin and served at tea, at the harvest table and on market days, and it is a plain, comforting, everyday cake made from ingredients that every farmhouse had: flour, butter, sugar, dried fruit, an egg and milk. Unlike some rich fruit cakes, it is not heavily laden with fruit, and its charm is in its softness. The batter is a soft one, wetter than a rubbed-in scone mixture and firmer than a sponge, which gives the finished cake a tender, moist crumb that is easy to cut into squares. A spoonful of mixed spice and a scatter of sugar on top make it fragrant and slightly crunchy. It is eaten warm from the oven, spread with butter, or cold with a cup of tea, and it is best on the day it is made, though it keeps for a day or two. It is one of the simplest cakes in the Welsh repertoire, and one of the most likeable.

  • Make the batter soft. A stiff mixture gives a dry, scone-like cake, and a soft one gives the moist crumb the name promises.
  • Rub in the butter until fine. It coats the flour and gives the cake a tender crumb, and lumps of butter leave greasy holes.
  • Serve it warm. The cake is at its best in the first hour, with butter melting into the crumb.

item.title: Molasses Bread
item.description: Molasses bread: a dark, soft loaf of white and wholemeal flour sweetened with molasses and topped with oats. A Maritime bread for butter and baked beans.
item.content:encoded:
Molasses bread is a loaf of the Canadian Maritimes, where molasses has been part of the diet since the days when the ports of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland traded salt cod to the Caribbean in exchange for barrels of molasses and rum. It was cheaper than sugar, it kept, and it was in every kitchen, so it went into gingerbread, baked beans, cookies and bread. In a yeast loaf it gives a dark, tender crumb, a faintly bitter sweetness and a rich, toasty colour, and it makes the bread taste of something more than plain wheat. The dough is a simple one, made with a mix of white flour, for lightness, and wholemeal, for flavour and texture, with a little oil and no dairy or eggs. It is kneaded, given a first rise, shaped in the tin, and given a second, and it is finished with a brush of water and a sprinkle of rolled oats, which give it a rustic look and a nutty crust. It is eaten in thick slices with butter, alongside baked beans or fish chowder, or toasted at breakfast with jam.

  • Use unsulphured molasses. Blackstrap is much stronger and bitter, and makes a loaf that is harsh and heavy.
  • Expect a sticky dough. Wholemeal flour takes up water slowly, and the dough firms as it rests, so resist adding too much flour.
  • Let the loaf cool before you slice it. Molasses bread is moist and it compresses if it is cut warm.

item.title: Beaver Tails
item.description: Beaver Tails: flat, oval yeast pastries fried until golden and blistered, then tossed in cinnamon sugar and squeezed with lemon. Canada's market treat.
item.content:encoded:
The Beaver Tail is a fried pastry that is one of the best-loved treats in Canada, sold from stalls at winter markets and festivals, most famously on the frozen Rideau Canal in Ottawa, where skaters queue for one in the cold. It is a flat, oval piece of yeast dough, stretched out until it resembles a beaver's tail, fried in hot oil until golden and blistered, and topped while it is hot. The classic topping is cinnamon sugar with a squeeze of lemon, and there are now many others, from chocolate hazelnut spread to maple butter. The name and the brand were created in the late 1970s by a couple in Ontario, who had been making the pastry from a family recipe. The dough is a soft, lightly enriched one, made with a little wholemeal flour for a nutty flavour, and it is worked by hand, since stretching it rather than rolling gives it the uneven, blistered surface that traps the topping. The frying is quick, a minute or two on each side, and the pastry should be eaten at once, when it is hot, crisp on the outside and soft within, as it turns chewy as it cools.

  • Stretch the dough by hand and do not use a rolling pin. It gives the uneven, bubbly surface that a Beaver Tail is known for.
  • Keep the oil at 180°C. Too cool and the pastry soaks up oil and turns heavy, and too hot and it browns before the middle cooks.
  • Coat the tails while they are hot. The sugar sticks to the warm oil on the surface, and it will not cling once they have cooled.

item.title: Cherry Ripe Slice
item.description: Cherry ripe slice: a no-bake slice of coconut, glacé cherries and condensed milk pressed into a tin and topped with dark chocolate, like the Cherry Ripe bar.
item.content:encoded:
The Cherry Ripe is one of Australia's oldest chocolate bars, a stick of coconut and cherry filling wrapped in dark chocolate that has been sold since 1924, and its flavours have inspired a slice that appears at every school fete and afternoon tea. It is one of the simplest recipes in the Australian slice repertoire, made in one bowl without any baking, and it captures the bar's taste well. The base is desiccated coconut and sweetened condensed milk, which bind together and set into a firm, sticky, chewy layer, with quartered glacé cherries stirred through so that each square has jewels of red in it, and the chocolate topping is a thin layer of dark chocolate softened with a little coconut oil, so that it cuts without cracking. A cold set of a couple of hours does the rest. It is best made with good dark chocolate, which balances the sweetness of the base, and with glacé cherries that are bright and moist and not hard. The slice is rich, and it is meant to be cut small and eaten with tea.

  • Press the base down firmly. A tightly packed base holds together when cut, and a loose one falls apart.
  • Add the coconut oil to the chocolate. It keeps the topping soft enough to cut without cracking.
  • Dip the knife in hot water and wipe it between cuts. It gives clean, neat squares, without dragging the chocolate.

item.title: Orange and Almond Cake
item.description: Orange and almond cake: a flourless cake made from whole boiled oranges blended with eggs, sugar and ground almonds. Moist, fragrant and gluten-free.
item.content:encoded:
The orange and almond cake is a cake of remarkable economy. It contains no flour and no butter, and it is made from two whole oranges, which are boiled until soft and blended, skin and all, with eggs, sugar and ground almonds. The technique comes from the Sephardic Jewish cooks of the Mediterranean, who made cakes without flour for Passover, and it was brought to the English-speaking world by the writer Claudia Roden in the 1960s, since when it has become a classic in Australia, Britain and elsewhere. The whole fruit gives the cake its unique character. The peel, which is bitter when raw, softens and sweetens in the long simmer, and its oils flavour the whole cake, so that it has the depth of marmalade, and the ground almonds make a fine, moist, dense crumb that stays fresh for days. The cake is naturally gluten-free, and it improves on the second day, when the flavours have settled. It is best simply served, with a dusting of icing sugar and a spoonful of thick yoghurt or cream, and it can be made as a pudding with a syrup poured over the top.

  • Boil the oranges until they are completely soft. Under-cooked peel stays bitter, and it should collapse when pressed.
  • Purée the whole fruit, skin and pith included. The peel carries most of the flavour, and it turns sweet and mellow in the cooking.
  • Cover the cake with foil if it browns too fast. The batter is dense and wet, and it needs a long bake, and the top can darken before the centre sets.

item.title: Hobnobs
item.description: Hobnobs: crunchy, golden oat biscuits made with butter, brown sugar and golden syrup, optionally coated in dark chocolate. The tea-time biscuit, made at home.
item.content:encoded:
The Hobnob is the great British oat biscuit, first sold in 1985, and it has become the biscuit that people most readily reach for to dunk in tea. What distinguishes it from other oat biscuits is its texture: it is crisp at the edges, crumbly and slightly chewy in the middle, and dense with the toasted, nutty flavour of oats, without the sweetness of a flapjack or the softness of an American oatmeal cookie. That texture comes from a particular combination, a high proportion of oats to flour, butter and brown sugar for flavour and colour, and golden syrup for a caramelly depth and a crisp snap. A small amount of bicarbonate of soda, dissolved in a spoonful of milk and added to the hot butter, makes the dough foam slightly and gives an open, crunchy structure. The biscuits are shaped by hand, flattened into rounds, and baked at a moderate heat until golden. The plain ones are excellent, and the chocolate ones, made by spreading melted dark chocolate over the flat side and marking it with a fork, are better still.

  • Flatten the balls well. The dough does not spread much, and a thick biscuit stays soft in the middle instead of crisping.
  • Cool the biscuits completely before adding the chocolate. It sets glossy and smooth on a cold biscuit, and melts and smears on a warm one.
  • Use rolled oats and not porridge oats. They are thicker, and they give the crunch and the texture that the biscuit depends on.

item.title: Buckeyes
item.description: Buckeyes: balls of creamy peanut butter fudge dipped in dark chocolate, leaving a circle of peanut butter showing like the nut of the buckeye tree.
item.content:encoded:
A buckeye is a sweet from Ohio, and it is named for the nut of the buckeye tree, the state tree, which is a glossy, dark brown seed with a pale patch, a little like the eye of a deer. The candy imitates it exactly: a ball of smooth peanut butter fudge, dipped in melted chocolate so that a circle of the peanut butter is left showing at the top. Buckeyes are a fixture of Ohio at Christmas, and of the football season, since the Ohio State University teams are called the Buckeyes, and it is said that no Ohio household is without a tin of them in December. The recipe is easy and does not need any special equipment or cooking, only a bowl, a tray and a pan of chocolate. The peanut butter centre is a dough of peanut butter and butter with icing sugar, which is stiff enough to roll and sets firm in the fridge, and it should be chilled before dipping so that it does not melt into the chocolate. The chocolate coating is thinned with a little shortening or coconut oil, so that it is fluid and sets with a shine, and the dipping is done with a toothpick, which leaves a small hole that is smoothed over at the end.

  • Chill the balls until they are firm. A cold centre does not soften in the warm chocolate, and it stays round on the toothpick.
  • Add the shortening to the chocolate. It thins the coating so that it dips smoothly, and it sets with a gloss and snaps neatly.
  • Use ordinary creamy peanut butter. Natural peanut butter separates and leaves a greasy dough that will not roll.

item.title: Candied Yams
item.description: Candied yams: slices of sweet potato baked until tender in a syrup of butter, brown sugar, orange juice and cinnamon until glossy. A Thanksgiving staple.
item.content:encoded:
Candied yams are a dish of the American Thanksgiving table, and above all of the Southern one, where they are a fixture of Sunday dinners and holiday feasts. The yams in the name are not true yams, which are a starchy tropical tuber, but orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, called yams in the United States, a name that is thought to come from the West African yam, which enslaved cooks likened to the sweet potato. The dish is made by cooking slices of sweet potato in a syrup of butter, brown sugar and spice until they are tender and glazed, and it is much less sweet than it sounds, since the sweet potato itself has a mild, earthy flavour that balances the sugar. It should not be confused with the sweet potato casserole that is topped with marshmallows or pecans, which is mashed, and here the slices stay whole. A baking dish is best, covered with foil for the first half of the cooking so that the potatoes steam tender, and uncovered for the second, so that the syrup reduces to a glossy glaze. Orange juice gives freshness, and cinnamon, nutmeg and vanilla give warmth.

  • Cut the slices to the same thickness. Uneven slices cook at different rates, and thin ones turn to mush before thick ones are soft.
  • Bake with foil on first and off at the end. The steam softens them, and the uncovered stage reduces the syrup to a glaze.
  • Baste once or twice. The syrup that runs to the corners of the dish darkens and thickens, and spooning it back over gives an even shine.

item.title: Chocolate Truffles
item.description: Chocolate truffles: a soft ganache of dark chocolate, cream and butter, chilled, rolled into balls and coated in cocoa. A simple, luxurious sweet.
item.content:encoded:
The chocolate truffle takes its name from the fungus that it resembles, a rough, dark, round lump that is dusted with earth, and in the sweet shop the resemblance comes from the coat of cocoa powder. It is credited to a French confectioner, Louis Dufour of Chambéry, in the 1890s, and it is a strikingly simple sweet, being nothing more than a ganache, which is chocolate melted into hot cream, chilled until it is firm enough to shape, and rolled. It is that simplicity that makes the quality of the ingredients matter. A good dark chocolate, with a high cocoa content and a clean flavour, gives a truffle that tastes deep, complex and slightly bitter, and cream and a little butter make it silky. A spoonful of brandy or another spirit deepens the flavour, though it is optional. The ganache must be chilled until firm, and the rolling should be done quickly with cool hands, since the warmth of the fingers melts the chocolate, and rolling them in cocoa, chopped nuts or icing sugar stops them sticking. Each truffle should be soft and creamy in the centre, melting on the tongue.

  • Do not boil the cream. Steaming cream is hot enough to melt the chocolate, and boiling can make the ganache oily and grainy.
  • Roll with cool hands and work fast. The warmth of your palms melts the chocolate, so dust your hands with cocoa if it starts to stick.
  • Serve them at room temperature. Straight from the fridge they are hard and dull, and softer truffles have a much better flavour.

item.title: Hot Fudge Sauce
item.description: Hot fudge sauce: a thick, glossy chocolate sauce made from cocoa, brown sugar, cream, syrup, dark chocolate and butter, poured hot over ice cream.
item.content:encoded:
Hot fudge sauce is the thing that turns a scoop of ice cream into a sundae, and it is one of the great American dessert inventions of the early twentieth century, credited to a confectioner in Los Angeles or Chicago, depending on who is telling the story, who poured warm fudge over ice cream in the 1900s and 1910s. What makes it different from an ordinary chocolate sauce is its thickness and its chew. It is a sauce made by cooking cream, sugar and cocoa together until they have thickened, and then enriching them with dark chocolate and butter, so that it is dark, glossy and dense, and when it hits cold ice cream it thickens further into a soft, chewy layer that clings to the spoon. It is far easier to make than a shop-bought jar would suggest, and takes about ten minutes in a single saucepan with no thermometer. Both brown sugar and a little corn syrup or golden syrup are used: the brown sugar for a caramelly depth, and the syrup for smoothness, since it prevents the sugar from crystallising. A pinch of salt sharpens the chocolate. It keeps well in a jar in the fridge, and reheats in moments.

  • Whisk the cocoa with the sugar first. Cocoa is hard to wet and floats in lumps if it goes straight into liquid.
  • Simmer for the full 4 to 5 minutes. It thickens the sauce and cooks the raw taste out of the cocoa.
  • Stir in the chocolate off the heat. Overheated chocolate turns grainy, and the residual heat of the sauce is enough to melt it.

item.title: Peanut Butter Pie
item.description: Peanut butter pie: a chocolate biscuit crust filled with a light mousse of peanut butter, cream cheese and whipped cream, drizzled with chocolate. No baking.
item.content:encoded:
Peanut butter pie is a Southern classic, and it is at its best as a no-bake pie of a kind that appears at church suppers and summer cookouts from Georgia to Texas. The filling is a mousse, made by beating peanut butter with cream cheese and icing sugar, and then folding in whipped cream, which lightens it into a soft, airy, rich cream that is set by chilling. It tastes strongly of peanut butter and is sweet without being sickly, and the cream cheese adds a faint tang that stops it cloying. The crust is made from crushed chocolate sandwich biscuits bound with melted butter, since the chocolate and peanut butter pairing is one of the great American flavour combinations, and it needs no baking, only a chill in the fridge. Chopped peanuts and a drizzle of melted chocolate on top give a crunch and a finish. The pie must be chilled for many hours to set, and so it is a good dessert to make ahead. It is served in thin slices, because it is rich, and cuts most cleanly with a knife that has been dipped in hot water.

  • Soften the cream cheese properly. Cold cream cheese leaves lumps that do not beat out, and it spoils the smoothness of the filling.
  • Fold the cream in gently. Beating it in knocks out the air, and the filling turns dense instead of light and mousse-like.
  • Chill the pie for the full time. It sets slowly, and a pie cut too soon slumps on the plate.

item.title: Pork and Sauerkraut
item.description: Pork and sauerkraut: pork shoulder braised for nearly three hours on a bed of sauerkraut, apples, onion and caraway until tender. A New Year's Day dinner.
item.content:encoded:
Pork and sauerkraut is the traditional New Year's Day dinner in Pennsylvania Dutch country and much of the eastern United States, where it is eaten in the belief that it will bring good luck in the coming year. The reasoning is that pigs root forward when they forage, so pork is a symbol of progress, and the long strands of cabbage in the sauerkraut stand for a long life, and, being green, for money. It is a custom that came with German settlers in the eighteenth century, and it has outlasted many others. The dish is simple and it is a very good one. A joint of pork shoulder, which is fatty and full of flavour, is browned, set on a bed of sauerkraut with apples, onion, caraway and a little brown sugar, and left to cook slowly in a covered pot until it can be pulled apart with a fork. The sauerkraut softens and turns mellow, the apples and sugar soften its sourness, the caraway lends its earthy note, and the pork's juices run down through everything. It is served with mashed potatoes, which take up the juices, and it makes excellent leftovers.

  • Do not rinse the sauerkraut. Its sharp, fermented flavour is the point of the dish, and the apples and sugar soften it during cooking.
  • Use pork shoulder and not loin. The fat and connective tissue keep it moist and tender through the long cooking, and loin dries out.
  • Keep the pot covered. Steam keeps the pork moist and the sauerkraut soft, and a lid that is off dries out the top.

item.title: Tapioca Pudding
item.description: Tapioca pudding: small pearl tapioca simmered in milk until translucent, then thickened with egg and vanilla into a creamy pudding. A nursery classic.
item.content:encoded:
Tapioca pudding is the comfort dessert of many American childhoods, a cold, creamy pudding studded with soft, translucent pearls that is either loved or, for children who called it fish eyes or frog spawn, feared. Tapioca is a starch extracted from the root of the cassava plant, and the pearls were brought from South America and became a staple of the American pantry in the late nineteenth century, after the invention of the quick-cooking Minute Tapioca in 1894. The pudding is a simple one, made from small pearl tapioca, milk, sugar and eggs, and its charm is in its texture, which is soft and slightly chewy at once. The pearls need to be soaked first, for half an hour, so that they cook evenly, and then simmered in the milk, stirring often, until they turn from opaque white to clear. The egg yolks and a little sugar go in at the end and thicken it to a custard, and vanilla finishes it. It can be eaten warm, when it is loose and soft, or chilled, when it sets to a spoonable cream, and either way it is best with a little cinnamon or fresh fruit.

  • Soak the pearls first. It softens them so they cook evenly, and unsoaked pearls stay hard in the middle.
  • Stir often while it simmers. Tapioca settles and sticks to the base of the pan, and it can scorch.
  • Add the eggs off the boil. Boiling scrambles them, and the pudding turns grainy instead of smooth.

item.title: Blancmange
item.description: Blancmange: a smooth, delicate milk pudding thickened with cornflour, scented with lemon and vanilla, set in a mould and turned out. Served with jam or fruit.
item.content:encoded:
Blancmange is the white dish of medieval feasts, its French name meaning exactly that, and it began as a dish of shredded chicken or fish with rice and almonds, cooked in milk, for wealthy tables. Over the centuries it lost its meat and became sweet, and by the nineteenth century, when cornflour became available, it had turned into the pudding that Victorian and Edwardian kitchens made in fluted moulds and turned out for the family. The version that was served at British children's parties and school dinners in the twentieth century, often in bright pink from a powdered mix, was a poor relation of the real thing, which is made from nothing more than milk, cornflour and sugar, flavoured with vanilla and a strip of lemon peel. It is a pure, delicate dish and its pleasure is its texture: smooth, cool and just firm enough to keep its shape, with a gentle wobble. The essentials are to whisk the cornflour into cold milk first, so that there are no lumps, and to cook it while stirring until it has thickened and boiled for a moment, which removes the raw starch taste. The rest is chilling and turning out, and it is best served with sharp raspberry jam or fresh berries.

  • Whisk the cornflour into cold milk first. Added straight to hot milk it clumps, and the lumps do not smooth out.
  • Cook it until it has boiled for a minute. Cornflour needs to reach the boil to thicken, and undercooked starch tastes chalky.
  • Rinse the moulds with cold water before filling. It helps the blancmange release cleanly, and it keeps the surface smooth.

item.title: Chestnut Stuffing
item.description: Chestnut stuffing: pork sausage meat, cooked chestnuts, breadcrumbs, sage, thyme and lemon zest, baked until golden and crisp on top. A Christmas favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Chestnut stuffing is one of the classic stuffings of the British Christmas dinner, and it has been made in one form or another for centuries, since chestnuts were once a staple of the winter countryside and roasted on street corners in every town. It takes the standard sage and onion stuffing and enriches it with pork sausage meat and cooked chestnuts, which add sweetness, a soft, floury texture and a mellow, nutty flavour. The balance is what matters. The sausage meat gives fat and savour, the breadcrumbs make a light, open body, and the chestnuts are chopped roughly, so that they are noticed in the mouth and not lost, and the fresh sage, thyme, parsley and lemon zest give brightness. An egg binds the mixture, and a little stock keeps it moist. It can be cooked inside the bird, but is safer and crisper baked separately in a dish, where its top browns and crisps, or shaped into balls, which give more surface for the crust. It can be made a day or two ahead and baked on the day, and it is as good cold, in a turkey sandwich, as it is hot.

  • Chop the chestnuts roughly. Big pieces give texture and sweetness, while very fine ones vanish into the stuffing.
  • Use fresh breadcrumbs from day-old bread. They soak up the juices and stay light, and dried crumbs make the stuffing dense and dry.
  • Cool the cooked onion before mixing. A hot mixture can start to cook the egg and the sausage meat and makes the mixture greasy.

item.title: Gypsy Tart
item.description: Gypsy tart: a shortcrust tart filled with a light, foamy mixture of whipped evaporated milk and dark muscovado sugar. Intensely sweet, from Kent.
item.content:encoded:
Gypsy tart is a speciality of Kent, most closely associated with the Isle of Sheppey, and it is famous in a curious way, since for many British people it is remembered chiefly from school dinners of the 1950s to the 1980s. The story of its origin, which may or may not be true, is that a woman on the island took pity on hungry gypsy children who came to her door and made them a tart with what was in the cupboard, which was a tin of evaporated milk and some brown sugar. Whatever its truth, the recipe is that: a pastry case filled with a mixture of just two ingredients, evaporated milk that has been whipped to a froth and dark muscovado sugar. The whipping is the trick. The evaporated milk must be well chilled, and it whips with an electric whisk to a light, thick foam, which holds the sugar and bakes into a filling that is soft and airy on top and dense and fudgy underneath, tasting strongly of toffee. The tart is extremely sweet, and should be cut in thin slices, and it is often eaten with a little cream or a sharp fruit to cut the sugar.

  • Chill the evaporated milk thoroughly. Cold milk whips to a thick foam, and milk at room temperature stays thin and flat.
  • Add the sugar slowly with the whisk running. It dissolves as it goes, and a heap tipped in all at once sinks and stays gritty.
  • Watch the tart in the oven. The filling browns fast, and it should be golden with a slight wobble, since it sets as it cools.

item.title: Paska
item.description: Paska: a tall, rich, domed Easter bread flavoured with vanilla, lemon and raisins, decorated with a dough cross and iced. Blessed on Holy Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Paska is the Ukrainian Easter bread, a tall, golden, domed loaf that is the centrepiece of the Easter basket and the most important food of the Easter table. The word comes from the same root as Pascha, meaning Easter, and the bread is baked in the days before Easter, often on Holy Thursday or Saturday, when a household would set aside a whole day for the task. On Holy Saturday, it is placed in a basket with eggs, sausage, butter and cheese and carried to church to be blessed, and on Easter morning it is the first food eaten, after the fast of Lent. It is an enriched yeast bread, made with plenty of eggs and butter, and flavoured with vanilla and lemon zest, with raisins in some families, and it has a soft, fine, cake-like crumb and a thin, glossy crust. The height is part of its identity. It is baked in tall round tins, with a paper collar to hold the rising dough, so that it domes above the rim, and the top is decorated with a cross or a braid of dough, a symbol of the season. Ukrainian communities across Canada, especially on the prairies, have carried the tradition with them, and paska is baked in church halls and homes there every spring.

  • Use a paper collar. The tall dough rises past the rim of the tin, and the collar holds it upright so that the loaf domes and does not spread.
  • Cover the loaves with foil half-way through. The rich dough browns fast, and the foil lets the centre cook without scorching the top.
  • Let the dough rise fully at each stage. The eggs and butter make it heavy, and it needs time and warmth to lift.

item.title: Mango Cheesecake
item.description: Mango cheesecake: a no-bake cheesecake of cream cheese, mango purée and whipped cream on a buttery biscuit base, topped with fresh mango and passionfruit.
item.content:encoded:
Mangoes are one of the fruits of the Australian summer, and when they are in season, from November to March, they are eaten in every form, by the cheek, in salads, in smoothies and, on the Christmas table, in a mango cheesecake. It is a cake that suits the climate, since it needs no oven and is served cold, and it is a good way to use the fruit, whose sweet, perfumed flesh purées to a smooth, bright golden cream that gives the filling its flavour and its colour. The structure is that of a classic no-bake cheesecake: a base of crushed biscuits held with butter, and a filling of cream cheese beaten with sugar, into which the mango purée is stirred and whipped cream is folded, with gelatine to set it. Unlike kiwifruit, pineapple or papaya, mango does not contain an enzyme that breaks down gelatine, so the fresh purée can be used without cooking. The cheesecake needs several hours to set firmly enough to cut. Slices of fresh mango and the pulp of a passionfruit on top add a sharp, tropical contrast to the sweetness.

  • Use very ripe, fragrant mangoes. They give a sweet, deep flavour and a smooth purée, and underripe ones are sour and fibrous.
  • Cool the melted gelatine before you add it. Hot gelatine can split the cream cheese, and cold gelatine sets in strings.
  • Give the cheesecake the full time to set. It needs several hours before it holds a clean slice, and it is best made the day before.

item.title: Amaretto Sour
item.description: Amaretto sour: amaretto shaken with fresh lemon juice and a little sugar syrup until frothy, served over ice. Sweet almond, sharp lemon and a silky foam.
item.content:encoded:
The amaretto sour was a fixture of American bars in the 1970s, when amaretto, the sweet Italian almond liqueur, became fashionable and was mixed with bottled sour mix and served over ice in a short glass. That version had a reputation for being sickly, and the drink slipped out of favour, until a group of craft bartenders in the 2000s revisited it and found that it was a good drink with a bad recipe. The fix is simple and it is the reason the drink has come back. Fresh lemon juice replaces the sour mix, so the cocktail has real acidity and freshness, and egg white, or aquafaba for a vegan version, is shaken in to give the drink a silky texture and a cap of soft foam. Amaretto is very sweet, and it needs only a small amount of sugar syrup, or none at all, to balance a generous measure of lemon. The technique matters too: the drink is first shaken without ice, in a dry shake, to build the foam, and then with ice to chill it, and it is strained over fresh ice. A dash of bitters on the foam is a good finish.

  • Use fresh lemon juice. Bottled juice and sour mix taste flat and artificial, and the drink depends on the fresh, sharp acidity.
  • Shake once without ice and once with it. The dry shake makes a thick, stable foam, and the ice shake chills and dilutes the drink.
  • Adjust the syrup to taste. Amaretto brands vary in sweetness, and a drier one may need a little more sugar.

item.title: Cheeseburger Sliders
item.description: Cheeseburger sliders: seasoned beef and melted cheese layered on a slab of soft rolls, brushed with garlic butter and sesame seeds, and baked in one tray.
item.content:encoded:
Sliders are the party food of American life, small burgers on soft rolls that are eaten with the hands, and the tray-baked version has become the easiest way to make them for a crowd. The original slider was a small, steamed burger on a soft bun, made famous by the White Castle chain in the 1920s, and the name is thought to reflect how easily they slid down. The modern party slider is made without any flipping or frying of patties. Seasoned ground beef is browned and drained, laid on the bottom half of a slab of Hawaiian-style rolls, which are slightly sweet and very soft, topped with cheese, and covered with the top half of the rolls, then brushed with garlic butter and sprinkled with seeds before baking. They come out of the oven as a single golden tray, the cheese melted and the butter soaked into the bread, and can be cut apart with a knife into twelve individual sliders. The recipe scales easily, and the assembled tray can be prepared hours ahead and baked as guests arrive, which is why it is a favourite for game day.

  • Drain the beef well. Extra fat soaks into the soft rolls and makes them greasy, and it is worth pressing the meat in a sieve.
  • Cover with foil for the first stage. It melts the cheese and steams the bread soft, and uncovering at the end browns the top.
  • Keep the rolls in one slab. Cutting them in half as a block gives a neat sandwich that can be assembled quickly and separated after baking.

item.title: Fried Calamari
item.description: Fried calamari: squid rings soaked in milk, dusted in seasoned flour and semolina and fried briefly until crisp. Served with lemon and marinara.
item.content:encoded:
Fried calamari is a dish of the Italian coast that became an American restaurant classic, and it is probably the most-ordered seafood appetiser in the United States. In Italy, calamari fritti is simple and light, a handful of squid rings with a dusting of flour and a squeeze of lemon, eaten by the sea. The Italian-American version is a little more substantial, with a crisper coating and a bowl of warm marinara to dip it in. The most important factor in the result is the cooking time. Squid has two states, tender and rubbery, and the change from one to the other takes only a minute or so, so it must be fried quickly and lifted out as soon as the coating is golden, or it turns tough. A soak in milk for half an hour tenderises the squid and takes away any strong flavour, and a coating of flour with a little semolina gives a crisp and slightly sandy texture that stays crunchy. The oil must be hot, and the pieces must be fried in small batches so that the temperature stays high and the calamari does not stew.

  • Fry for no more than 2 minutes. Squid turns from tender to rubbery quickly, and the coating is golden by then.
  • Shake off the excess flour. A thick coat goes gummy in the oil, and a thin one crisps.
  • Fry in small batches. Too many pieces at once lower the temperature, and the coating soaks up oil instead of crisping.

item.title: Lemon Drop
item.description: Lemon drop: vodka, fresh lemon juice, orange liqueur and sugar syrup shaken with ice and strained into a sugar-rimmed glass. Sweet, sharp and easy to drink.
item.content:encoded:
The lemon drop is a cocktail that tastes like the sweet it is named after, a boiled lemon sweet, and it was created in the 1970s at Henry Africa's bar in San Francisco, where it is credited to the owner Norman Jay Hobday, who was known for his fern-filled, fruit-forward drinks and a bar that helped to invent the singles scene. It became a fixture of American cocktail menus in the 1990s, when the martini glass was fashionable and vodka was the spirit of choice, and it has stayed on many of them since. The structure is that of a sour: a spirit, lemon juice and sugar, with a splash of orange liqueur, which adds depth and a hint of orange to the lemon, and it is served in a chilled martini glass with a rim of sugar, which is the identifying feature of the drink. The sugar rim provides a first hit of sweetness that meets the sharp lemon on the tongue, and the balance is the point. It is at its best with fresh lemon juice, which gives brightness that a bottled version does not, and it should be shaken very cold, since a warm one is cloying. A citron vodka can double the lemon flavour.

  • Use fresh lemon juice. It gives the drink its clean, sharp edge, and bottled juice turns it flat and syrupy.
  • Shake the drink until the shaker is frosted. It should be very cold, since a warm lemon drop tastes sweet and heavy.
  • Sugar only half the rim if you prefer it less sweet. The rim is part of the drink, and a partial rim lets the drinker choose.

item.title: Lemon Pepper Wings
item.description: Lemon pepper wings: chicken wings oven-baked until crisp, then tossed in melted butter with lemon zest, lemon juice and plenty of black pepper. Atlanta style.
item.content:encoded:
Lemon pepper wings are the signature wing of Atlanta, where they have been a rival to the Buffalo wing since the 1970s and 1980s, and where the local speciality is the lemon pepper wet, wings tossed in lemon pepper seasoning and melted butter so that they are glossy and drenched. They are a different creature from the Buffalo wing. There is no hot sauce, no blue cheese and no celery, and the flavour is sharp, peppery, buttery and bright, rather than fiery. The best way to make them at home is in the oven, which is cleaner than deep-frying and gives a surprisingly crisp result if the wings are prepared properly. The method is to dry the wings very well, toss them in a little baking powder and salt, which raises the pH of the skin and helps it to blister and crisp, and bake them on a rack so that the hot air can circulate. When they come out, they are tossed while hot in butter mixed with lemon zest, lemon juice, black pepper and garlic. Lemon pepper seasoning is sold ready-made, but it is easy to make from fresh zest and freshly ground pepper, and it tastes brighter.

  • Dry the wings thoroughly and use baking powder. It is the difference between crisp skin and rubbery skin, and it works as well as frying.
  • Grind the pepper coarsely, just before use. Freshly cracked pepper has a sharp, floral heat that the pre-ground kind has lost.
  • Toss the wings in the butter while they are hot. The butter clings to hot skin, and it slides off the wings when they have cooled.

item.title: Orange Julius
item.description: Orange Julius: orange juice, milk, sugar, vanilla and ice blended until thick and frothy. The creamsicle-style shopping-mall drink, made in five minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The Orange Julius is a drink with a known origin. It was first sold in 1926 by Julius Freed, who opened an orange juice stand in Los Angeles and found that his customers wanted something less acidic, and who worked out a recipe in which the juice was blended with other ingredients, sweetened and whipped to a foam. The customers, so the story goes, said that it was so good that they wanted a Julius, and the name stuck. It became one of the standards of the American shopping-mall food court from the 1970s, sold in tall cups from a stand, and it has a flavour that many people describe as a creamsicle in a glass, sweet and tangy and creamy at once. The recipe is much simpler than the original. Orange juice, milk, a little sugar and vanilla are blended with a generous amount of ice until the ice is crushed and the drink is thick, cold and full of tiny bubbles, which take about a minute of blending. The milk softens the acidity, the vanilla gives the ice-cream note, and the froth is the point, so it should be blended until it is thick and drunk at once, before it separates.

  • Blend for the full minute. It crushes the ice fine and whips air into the drink, and that froth is what makes it an Orange Julius.
  • Use a good orange juice, ideally freshly squeezed or a chilled not-from-concentrate one. It is the main flavour, and the drink can only be as good as it.
  • Drink it straight away. It separates as it stands, and the foam collapses within minutes.

item.title: Seven Layer Dip
item.description: Seven layer dip: layers of spiced refried beans, guacamole, soured cream, salsa, cheddar, black olives and spring onions in a dish, served cold with chips.
item.content:encoded:
Seven layer dip is the great American party dip, a tall dish of Tex-Mex flavours arranged in stripes that has been at the centre of Super Bowl spreads, potlucks and barbecues since the 1970s. Its layers are the components of a taco, refried beans at the base, then guacamole, soured cream, salsa, grated cheese, black olives and sliced spring onions, and each scoop of a tortilla chip picks up a bit of all of them. The dish has no fixed rules, and some cooks add layers of shredded lettuce or diced tomato, and some use cream cheese, but the seven of the name are the classic ones. It is quick to make because nothing is cooked, and it is easy to get right if a few points are watched. The beans should be seasoned with chilli and cumin, since they are the base and are otherwise bland, and the guacamole should have plenty of lime juice, which keeps it green. The salsa should be drained, so that it does not run down through the layers, and each layer should be spread right to the edges of a clear glass dish, so that the stripes show. It is served cold, and is best made a little in advance.

  • Spread the soured cream to the edges of the dish. It seals the guacamole from the air and stops it browning.
  • Drain the salsa well. Extra liquid runs down through the layers and turns the dip watery.
  • Use a clear glass dish. The stripes are the whole appeal, and a clear dish shows every layer.

item.title: Sex on the Beach
item.description: Sex on the Beach: vodka and peach schnapps mixed with orange and cranberry juices over ice. A sweet, fruity, pink cocktail from the 1980s.
item.content:encoded:
Sex on the Beach is a cocktail of the 1980s, and it belongs to the era of the fruity, brightly coloured, easy-drinking long drink that swept spring-break bars in Florida and beyond. Its name was a piece of marketing as much as anything, and it is said to have been invented in Florida around 1987 as part of a promotion for peach schnapps, at a time when the American public was moving from the martini to something sweeter and easier. It has a simple structure. Vodka provides the alcohol, peach schnapps supplies a sweet, ripe fruit flavour, and orange and cranberry juices give the colour, a blush of pink over orange, and a balance of sweet and tart. The peach liqueur is the point, and without it, the drink is a Cape Codder with orange juice. It is a highball, which means it is built over ice in a tall glass and needs little skill, and it is a party drink, often made in jugs. The juices should be good ones, since they are most of the drink, and it is best served very cold and garnished with an orange slice and a cherry.

  • Use good juice. Orange and cranberry make up more than half of the drink, and a cheap sweetened cocktail juice makes it sickly.
  • Fill the glass with ice. A full glass keeps the drink colder for longer and dilutes it more slowly than a few cubes.
  • Pour the cranberry juice last and slowly, over the back of a spoon, for a sunset effect of red over orange.

item.title: Tom Collins
item.description: Tom Collins: gin, fresh lemon juice and sugar syrup shaken with ice, strained into a tall glass and topped with soda water. Long, cool and lemony.
item.content:encoded:
The Tom Collins is one of the oldest gin cocktails in the book, and its name has a curious story attached. In 1874 a hoax spread through New York, in which one man asked another whether he had met Tom Collins, who had been saying unpleasant things about him at a certain bar, and sent him off to find the man, and the joke became so popular that a drink was named in its honour. A drink of this kind, made with Old Tom gin, lemon juice, sugar and soda water, had been served for decades before that as the John Collins, and Jerry Thomas included the Tom Collins in his 1876 Bartender's Guide, the first edition to list it. It is a sour lengthened with soda, and it is the archetype of a long, cool summer drink. Its ingredients are a spirit, sharp citrus, sugar and bubbles, and the pleasure is in how well they balance. It works with a London dry gin, whose juniper and citrus notes stand out against the lemon, and with fresh lemon juice, and it should be built in a tall Collins glass with plenty of ice. It is a close relation of the gin fizz, from which it differs chiefly in being served over ice.

  • Use fresh lemon juice. The drink is mostly lemon and gin, and bottled juice makes it taste flat and metallic.
  • Add the soda last and stir only once. It keeps the bubbles, and stirring hard knocks out the fizz.
  • Use a tall glass full of ice. It keeps the drink cold and slows the dilution, and it looks right.

item.title: Branston-Style Pickle
item.description: Branston-style pickle: a dark, sweet and tangy pickle of diced swede, carrot, cauliflower, gherkin, apple and dates cooked in malt vinegar and dark sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Branston pickle is one of Britain's most loved condiments, a dark, chunky, sweet and sharp pickle that has been made since 1922, when the company Crosse and Blackwell began producing it in the Staffordshire village of Branston, and that has since become an essential part of the cheese sandwich and the ploughman's lunch. It is a pickle of finely diced vegetables, swede, carrot, cauliflower, onion and gherkin, with apple and dates for sweetness, cooked in malt vinegar with dark sugar and a blend of spices until the vegetables are tender and the liquid has reduced to a thick, glossy, syrupy sauce. Its flavour is the result of that combination of ingredients: the swede gives a mellow earthiness, the dates and sugar give a dark, treacly sweetness, the malt vinegar gives a rounded tang and the spices add warmth. The vegetables are cut very small so that the pickle is spoonable and spreadable, and it is cooked slowly, so that the flavours blend and the pieces become soft but do not lose their identity. It is best left for a few weeks in the jar to mature, and it goes with mature cheddar, pork pie, ham, cold turkey and sausage rolls.

  • Dice the vegetables very small and evenly. They cook at the same rate, and the pickle should be spreadable on a sandwich.
  • Stir often in the last 20 minutes. The sugar catches on the base as it thickens, and a burnt taste spoils the whole batch.
  • Leave the jars for at least 2 weeks before opening. The sharp vinegar mellows and the flavours join, and the pickle tastes rounder and darker.

item.title: Cucumber Raita
item.description: Cucumber raita: thick yoghurt stirred with grated cucumber, ground cumin, mint and a little garlic. The cooling side dish for curries, grills and biryani.
item.content:encoded:
A raita is the cooling dish of the Indian meal, a bowl of seasoned yoghurt that is served beside spicy food to soothe the palate, and cucumber raita is the best known, being on the table at almost every Indian restaurant in Britain and the world. The yoghurt is thick, cold and slightly tangy, and it stands in contrast to hot, richly spiced curries, kebabs and biryanis, where it calms the heat and adds freshness. The cucumber is grated and squeezed dry before it is stirred in, since it holds a great deal of water, and if it is added as it is, the raita goes thin and runny within minutes. A little ground cumin, which is roasted before grinding in the traditional Indian kitchen, gives a warm, earthy, nutty note, and a spoonful of chopped mint gives freshness, and the smallest amount of grated garlic adds bite without being noticeable. The raita is seasoned with salt, and finished with a sprinkle of chilli powder or paprika for colour. It is best served cold, and can be made an hour or so ahead, and it is a good deal more interesting than it looks.

  • Squeeze the grated cucumber dry. It is mostly water, and if it is added wet, the raita turns thin and pale.
  • Use thick whole-milk yoghurt. Low-fat yoghurt is watery and makes a raita that runs over the plate.
  • Add the salt at the end and taste. Yoghurt and cucumber vary, and the salt draws more water out of the cucumber as it stands.

item.title: Greek Frappé
item.description: Greek frappé: instant coffee, sugar and cold water shaken to a thick, creamy foam, poured over ice and topped up with water or milk. Greece's iced coffee.
item.content:encoded:
The frappé is the iced coffee of Greece, and it has a birth date and a place. It was invented in 1957 at the Thessaloniki International Fair, when a representative of Nestlé, Dimitris Vakondios, was demonstrating a chocolate drink for children that was made by shaking it with milk in a shaker, and, wanting a coffee during a break and unable to find hot water, made himself an instant coffee by shaking the granules with cold water and sugar in the shaker instead. The drink was such a success with those who tried it that it spread across the country, and it is now the drink of the Greek café, sipped slowly for hours at an outdoor table. It is made from instant coffee, which is essential, since ground coffee does not foam, sugar to taste and a little cold water, shaken or whisked until it forms a thick, tan, creamy foam that is unlike any other coffee drink. It is then poured over ice and topped up with cold water or milk, and drunk through a straw. It is ordered by sweetness in Greece: sketos with no sugar, metrios with a medium amount, and glykos with plenty.

  • Use instant coffee and not ground. It dissolves and traps air to make the frappé foam, and ground coffee will not.
  • Shake with only a little water. A small amount of liquid whips into a thick, stable foam, and too much stays thin.
  • Order the sweetness to taste. Two teaspoons of sugar gives a medium drink, one is lighter, and three or four is a sweet, dessert-like one.

item.title: Hot Crab Dip
item.description: Hot crab dip: lump crab meat folded into a creamy mix of cream cheese, soured cream, mayonnaise and cheddar, seasoned with Old Bay and baked until bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
