Hot crab dip is a dish of the Chesapeake Bay, and in Maryland, where the blue crab is a symbol of the state, it is served at nearly every party, football game and crab feast. It takes the crab that the region is known for, sweet, delicate lump meat, and turns it into something that can be scooped up with a cracker, in a mixture that has become a classic of American entertaining. The base is cream cheese, thinned with soured cream and mayonnaise into a smooth, tangy, rich dip, and it is flavoured with Old Bay seasoning, the celery-salt and paprika spice blend that is the taste of Maryland seafood, with Worcestershire sauce, lemon juice and spring onions. Cheddar and Parmesan melt through it and brown on top. The crab is folded in gently at the end, in whole lumps, so that there is real crab to find in each spoonful, and the dip is baked until it bubbles at the edges and browns on top. Good crab meat is the key. Fresh or pasteurised lump crab is best, tinned crab is the economy version, and a shop-bought imitation crab stick is a poor substitute. The dip is served hot, straight from the oven, with crackers, toasted baguette or celery.

  • Fold the crab in last and gently. Whole lumps are the point of the dish, and stirring hard breaks them down to a paste.
  • Pick over the crab for shell. Even good crab meat has hidden fragments, and a piece in a dip is unpleasant.
  • Serve it hot. It thickens and turns waxy as it cools, and a spoonful of warm dip is far better than a cold one.

item.title: Hurricane Cocktail
item.description: Hurricane cocktail: light and dark rum shaken with passion fruit and orange juice, lime and grenadine, and served over ice. The rum punch of New Orleans.
item.content:encoded:
The Hurricane is the drink of Bourbon Street, and it was created in the 1940s at Pat O'Brien's bar in New Orleans, where, according to the story, the bar owner had been left with a large stock of rum during the Second World War, when whisky was scarce, and had to sell it in order to obtain other spirits. He created a fruity, generous drink that he served in a glass shaped like a hurricane lamp, from which the drink took its name, and it has been the best-known drink in the French Quarter ever since. The original was made with passion fruit syrup, and it uses a good deal of rum, a light and a dark, which gives it its strength and the balance between the clean, grassy notes of the light rum and the caramel richness of the dark. The rest is fruit: passion fruit gives the tropical flavour that defines it, orange juice and lime juice provide the acidity, and grenadine gives it the dark red colour and a little sweetness. It is a strong drink dressed as a soft drink, and should be sipped with care, and it is served over plenty of ice, with an orange slice and a cherry, in a tall glass.

  • Use real passion fruit juice or pulp. It gives the drink its tropical flavour, and a sweetened juice cocktail turns it into a sugary punch.
  • Use both rums. The light rum keeps it crisp, and the dark rum gives depth, and the mix is what gives the drink its character.
  • Sip it slowly. It has two measures of rum and tastes like fruit juice, and it hits harder than it appears.

item.title: Beef Tips and Gravy
item.description: Beef tips and gravy: sirloin cubes browned hard, then simmered with mushrooms and onions in a rich brown gravy. Serve over mashed potatoes or noodles.
item.content:encoded:
Beef tips and gravy is American comfort food at its plainest: small pieces of beef in a brown gravy, ladled over something soft and starchy. It sits between a stew and a steak dinner. Unlike a stew it has few vegetables, and the gravy is the point, so the beef is dredged in seasoned flour before it is browned, and the flour that falls off in the pan thickens the liquid without a separate roux. The browned crust and the sticky fond on the base of the pot supply most of the flavour, and a spoonful of tomato paste and a splash of Worcestershire sauce add the depth that a plain stock lacks. The cut is the other decision. Sirloin tips are lean and become tender in about forty minutes, which is why this version can be made on a weeknight. Chuck is cheaper and richer, but it needs two hours at a bare simmer. In New England the words steak tips usually mean marinated beef that is grilled, so the stewed dish is sometimes named beef tips and gravy to keep the two apart. Serve it over mashed potatoes, which soak up the gravy better than anything else.

  • Dry the beef before dredging. Wet meat steams in the pan and never browns, and the brown crust is what flavours the gravy.
  • Brown the beef in batches. Crowding the pan drops the temperature and the meat turns grey instead of forming a crust.
  • Match the simmer to the cut. Sirloin is tender in 40 minutes, but if you use chuck it needs about 2 hours at a bare simmer before it gives way.

item.title: Bourbon Chicken
item.description: Bourbon chicken: golden chicken thigh pieces in a sticky glaze of soy, brown sugar, apple juice, garlic and ginger. The food-court favourite, at home.
item.content:encoded:
Bourbon chicken is the sweet, sticky, soy-dark chicken that American shopping malls made famous, handed out on cocktail sticks from a tray at the food-court counter. The name is usually explained as a nod to Bourbon Street in New Orleans, and although many home versions do add a splash of bourbon, the dish does not need it and the food-court original is often made without any whiskey at all. What defines it is the glaze: soy sauce for salt, brown sugar and apple juice for sweetness and a fruity edge, ketchup for body and colour, garlic and ginger for aroma, and a pinch of red pepper flakes to keep it from cloying. Chicken thighs are the right cut because they stay juicy while the sauce reduces and can be seared hard without drying out. The technique that makes it taste like the counter version is the coating. A spoonful of cornflour on the raw chicken gives a thin crust that grips the glaze, and a second cornflour slurry thickens the sauce to a lacquer in a minute. It goes on the table in about thirty-five minutes over plain white rice.

  • Cook the chicken in two batches. A crowded pan steams the meat, and you want colour on it before the sauce goes in.
  • Stir the cornflour mixture again just before you add it. The starch settles to the bottom of the cup within seconds.
  • Taste the sauce before thickening. If it is too salty add a splash of apple juice, and if it is too sweet add a little more vinegar.

item.title: Calzone
item.description: Calzone: pizza dough folded around ricotta, mozzarella, ham and basil and baked until golden and blistered. Serve with warm marinara for dipping.
item.content:encoded:
A calzone is a pizza folded over its filling, a stuffed half-moon of dough that comes from Naples, where the name is said to come from the Italian word for trouser leg. It began as street food, easy to hold and eat on the move, and it is still made in Naples both baked and fried. The version most people know from pizza restaurants, and from Italian-American kitchens in particular, is baked, and it is stuffed with a creamy white filling of ricotta and mozzarella with ham or salami, rather than the tomato sauce that goes on a pizza. The sauce stays outside, warm in a bowl for dipping, because tomato inside would turn the dough soggy. Success depends on moisture control. Ricotta is wet, so it should be drained; the filling should be seasoned but not loaded; and the edges have to be sealed and crimped so that it does not burst in the oven. The steam needs somewhere to go, which is why every calzone is slashed on top before baking. A very hot oven puffs the dough into a blistered, golden shell with a soft, chewy inside, and the dough here is a simple yeast dough that needs only an hour to rise.

  • Drain the ricotta. Wet cheese is the main cause of a soggy or burst calzone, and a sieve for as long as the dough takes to rise is all it needs.
  • Leave the border free of filling and seal it firmly. Any grease or filling on the edge stops it sticking, and the seam opens in the oven.
  • Do not skip the slits. Without a vent the steam inflates the calzone and tears it open along the seam.

item.title: Chicken à la King
item.description: Chicken à la king: tender chicken, mushrooms, red pepper and peas in a silky sherry cream sauce, served over toast, rice or in puff pastry cases.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken à la king is creamed chicken in its most formal dress: cooked chicken, mushrooms, sweet red pepper and peas in a velvety sauce of stock, milk, cream and dry sherry, traditionally ladled over toast, rice or puff pastry cases. It was a fixture of hotel dining rooms and ladies' luncheons in the United States in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and then of the home kitchen, where it was a favourite way of using up the remains of a roast bird. Where it came from is disputed. Several New York and Philadelphia hotels and restaurants have been credited with it over the years, and the King of the name is a customer, a hotelier or a chef depending on who is telling the story. What is not in doubt is the method. The vegetables are softened in butter, flour is cooked into a roux, and the liquid is whisked in gradually, so that the sauce is smooth. The sherry is added at the end, where its nutty edge lifts the cream. Diced red pepper stands in for the pimiento of the original, and a handful of frozen peas gives a colour that keeps the plate from being entirely beige.

  • Add the liquid slowly at first. Whisking in a small amount at a time makes a smooth sauce, whereas a big splash of cold liquid makes lumps.
  • Use cooked chicken thigh as well as breast if you have both. Thigh stays moist when reheated in the sauce, where breast can turn stringy.
  • Add the sherry after the sauce has thickened so it keeps its flavour. Cooked hard for a long time, it turns dull.

item.title: Chicken Divan
item.description: Chicken divan: sliced chicken and broccoli in a creamy Parmesan sauce with a golden breadcrumb crust. The classic American casserole, from scratch.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken divan is a casserole of chicken and broccoli under a creamy, cheesy sauce, browned in the oven, and it has a better pedigree than most casseroles. It was created in the 1930s at the Divan Parisienne restaurant in the Chatham Hotel in New York, where it was made with sliced chicken, broccoli and a Mornay or hollandaise sauce that was glazed until it coloured. It went from there into American cookbooks and then into the mid-century home kitchen, where the sauce became a can of cream of chicken soup stirred with mayonnaise and a pinch of curry powder. This version goes back to the sauce that the dish was named for. A butter and flour roux is thinned with stock and cream, and the sauce is enriched with Parmesan and sharpened with a spoonful of Dijon mustard, and a little curry powder is kept in as a nod to the way generations of American cooks made it. Blanching the broccoli for just three minutes keeps it green through baking, and the topping of breadcrumbs and cheddar gives the crunch a casserole needs. Use cooked chicken from a roast bird, or poach two breasts, and this is a good way to serve the leftovers.

  • Dry the blanched broccoli well. Water clinging to the florets thins the sauce in the dish and leaves a puddle at the bottom.
  • Blanch for 3 minutes and no longer. The broccoli finishes cooking in the oven, and any more than that and it turns khaki and soft.
  • Make the sauce slightly thicker than you think it needs to be. The vegetables release water as they bake and thin it out.

item.title: Chicken Pasta Bake
item.description: Chicken pasta bake: penne and chicken in a creamy tomato and pepper sauce, topped with mozzarella and cheddar and baked until bubbling and golden.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken pasta bake is a British weeknight staple, the dish that fills the oven dish on a Tuesday and empties it by Wednesday lunchtime. Pasta went from novelty to pantry basic in Britain in the second half of the twentieth century, and the pasta bake was the way the country adopted it: cooked pasta, a sauce, a blanket of cheese, and twenty minutes in the oven, with no need for the layering of a lasagne or the attention of a risotto. This one has three things that set it above the average. The chicken is browned in the pan first, so it carries some flavour of its own instead of just being cooked in the sauce. The sauce is made with passata, tomato purée and a spoonful of cream cheese, which melts in to give it a soft, creamy body without the heaviness of a white sauce. And the pasta is only part-cooked before it goes into the dish, so it keeps its bite and finishes cooking in the sauce as it bakes, absorbing flavour instead of turning to mush. Mozzarella brings the stretch, and a little mature cheddar on top brings the golden crust and a sharper taste.

  • Undercook the pasta by about 3 minutes. It carries on absorbing the sauce in the oven, and pasta cooked to the packet time turns soft and swollen.
  • Make the sauce a touch looser than you want it to end up. The pasta drinks it as it bakes, and a dry bake is the commonest fault.
  • Cook the chicken only until it is browned. It finishes cooking in the oven, and overcooking it now leaves it dry and chewy.

item.title: Cornish Game Hens
item.description: Roast Cornish game hens with herb butter under the skin, crisp golden skin and a lemon and white wine pan sauce. One small bird per person.
item.content:encoded:
Despite the name, a Cornish game hen is not game and is not always a hen. It is a young, small chicken, usually of a cross between the Cornish and White Plymouth Rock breeds, developed in the United States in the middle of the twentieth century and sold when it weighs about half a kilogram, so that one bird makes one portion. That is the appeal. A whole roast bird on each plate looks like a dinner-party dish, but it cooks in under an hour and needs little more than a herb butter and a hot oven. The size has two consequences for the cook. First, there is little fat to protect the breast, which is why the butter goes under the skin, directly on the meat, where it melts and bastes from within while the skin above crisps in the oven. Second, the birds cook quickly and go from perfect to dry in minutes, so a thermometer is worth having. The thigh should reach 74°C. After resting, the tin holds a small amount of buttery juices, and boiling these with white wine and stock for five minutes makes a pan sauce in the time it takes the hens to rest.

  • Dry the skin thoroughly, and if you have time, leave the hens uncovered in the fridge for an hour beforehand. The drier the skin, the crisper it roasts.
  • Check the thigh rather than the breast. The breast is done before the legs, so the thigh reading tells you the whole bird is safe.
  • Leave space around each bird in the tin. Crowded hens steam each other and the skin stays pale.

item.title: Crayfish Mornay
item.description: Crayfish mornay: sweet cooked crayfish tail in a creamy cheddar and Parmesan sauce, topped with crumbs and grilled until golden. A Kiwi seafood treat.
item.content:encoded:
In New Zealand the crayfish is what the rest of the world calls a spiny or rock lobster, and it is one of the country's most prized seafoods, with a sweet, firm, delicate flesh. Cooking it with a mornay sauce is a long-standing way of stretching it. A mornay is a béchamel enriched with cheese, and it is one of the classic sauces of French cookery; here it is made with a mix of sharp cheddar and Parmesan, a pinch of nutmeg and a hint of mustard, so that it tastes clearly of cheese without swamping the crayfish. The dish is built to be served in the empty shell, or in small ovenproof dishes, and then browned quickly under a hot grill. That is the important point about the method. The crayfish is already cooked, so it needs only to be warmed through, and the grill is there for the topping, not for cooking the shellfish. Ten minutes is enough, and any longer turns the tail meat rubbery. Buy cooked tails from a fishmonger, or cook and shell them yourself, and if crayfish is out of reach the same method works for lobster tails, langoustines or large prawns.

  • Do not overcook the crayfish. It is cooked already, so warm it in the sauce and grill briefly, or the meat goes tough.
  • Keep the sauce quite thick before adding the crayfish. The shellfish releases a little liquid under the grill, and a loose sauce turns watery.
  • Take the pan off the heat before adding the cheese. Cheese stirred into a boiling sauce can turn grainy and oily.

item.title: Creamed Corn
item.description: Creamed corn: sweetcorn simmered in butter, milk and cream until thick and silky, with a third blended for body. A creamy holiday and barbecue side.
item.content:encoded:
Creamed corn is one of the great American side dishes, a spoonable, sweet and savoury dish of kernels in a thick, milky sauce that turns up at Thanksgiving, Christmas and every Southern Sunday dinner. It has nothing to do with the canned cream-style corn that shares its name, which is corn puréed in a thickened liquid. The traditional method is far better. The kernels are cut from the cob and the cobs are scraped with the back of the knife to release the starchy, sweet liquid, known as corn milk, which thickens the dish naturally. This version keeps the idea but makes it work all year round, because frozen sweetcorn is picked and frozen at its peak and needs no scraping. A little butter and onion start the flavour, milk and cream make the sauce, and a spoonful of cornflour makes sure it thickens smoothly. The trick to the texture is to blend only about a third of the pan. That gives a silky, cohesive sauce and leaves the rest of the kernels whole, so each spoonful has both cream and bite. A pinch of sugar brings out the sweetness of the corn, and black pepper and thyme stop it from tasting one-dimensional.

  • Blend only part of it. Puréeing everything makes soup, whereas a third gives you a silky sauce with whole kernels for texture.
  • Taste the corn before adding the sugar. Fresh summer corn is very sweet and may need none, while frozen corn often needs the pinch.
  • Keep the simmer gentle. A hard boil can make the cream split and the corn tough.

item.title: Duck à l'Orange
item.description: Duck à l'orange: crisp-skinned duck breast in a glossy sauce of caramel, fresh orange juice, stock and vinegar. The French classic, made properly.
item.content:encoded:
Canard à l'orange is one of the dishes that defines the classic French repertoire, and one that has suffered more than most from bad copies. In its original form it was made with a sauce bigarade, built on the bitter Seville orange, and it was served in the restaurants that taught the rest of the world what French cooking was. When it spread to dinner parties in the 1960s and 1970s, it often arrived as a duck in sweet, syrupy marmalade, which is the reason it has a reputation for cloying. The way to get it right is to treat the sauce as a balance between sweet and sharp. A dry caramel is made from sugar and stopped with red wine vinegar, so that it is bittersweet instead of sugary, and fresh orange juice and stock are boiled down to a glossy, concentrated glaze. A little zest and a few segments at the end bring back the fresh orange aroma that cooking dulls. Duck breast is easy to work with. Started skin side down in a cold pan, the fat renders slowly and the skin turns crisp, and a short time in the oven finishes the meat pink. If you can find Seville oranges in January and February, use them, with a little extra sugar to balance their bitterness.

  • Start the duck in a cold pan. The fat melts out slowly and the skin crisps, whereas a hot pan seals the skin and leaves the fat underneath.
  • Watch the caramel closely. It goes from amber to bitter in seconds, and it is ready as soon as it turns the colour of a copper coin.
  • Save the duck fat that you pour off. It makes the best roast potatoes you will ever eat.

item.title: Fish and Brewis
item.description: Fish and brewis: salt cod and hard bread simmered until tender and topped with crisp fried salt pork scrunchions. A Newfoundland tradition.
item.content:encoded:
Fish and brewis is one of the best-loved traditional dishes of Newfoundland, and one that says a lot about the island's history. Brewis, which is pronounced to rhyme with "brews", is hard bread, also known as hardtack or sea biscuit, a dry, dense, long-keeping biscuit that fishing families and sailors relied on because it never spoiled. Salt cod was the other staple, the product that made the island's economy for centuries. Together they made a meal from what was in every store cupboard. Both are soaked overnight, which softens the bread and draws most of the salt from the fish, then simmered together until the cod flakes and the bread turns tender and slightly gelatinous. What makes it a dish and not a boiled dinner is the scrunchions: small cubes of salt pork fried slowly until they are golden, crisp and chewy, along with all the melted fat, which is spooned over the plate. Onions cooked in the fat are often added. It is served with boiled potatoes, and it remains a much-loved supper and a popular weekend breakfast, a plate that tastes of salt, fat and home.

  • Change the water on the cod at least twice while it soaks. Salt cod that has not been soaked properly is inedibly salty, and a nibble of a cooked piece will tell you whether it needs more soaking.
  • Keep the cod at a bare simmer. A rolling boil breaks the flesh into shreds and makes it tough.
  • Start the salt pork in a cold pan. This renders the fat slowly and leaves each cube crisp instead of burnt.

item.title: Fried Clams
item.description: Fried clams: plump clams dipped in evaporated milk, dredged in flour and cornmeal and deep-fried until crisp. The New England clam shack classic.
item.content:encoded:
Fried clams are the pride of the New England coast, sold in paper boats at clam shacks from Ipswich, Massachusetts, to the beaches of Maine, and served with tartare sauce, lemon and a heap of French fries. The classic version uses whole-belly soft-shell clams, often called steamers or Ipswich clams, whose sweet, briny bellies and firm necks stay tender when fried. The coating is what keeps them light. In the traditional method the clams are dipped in evaporated milk, which clings better than fresh milk and adds a faint caramel sweetness, and then dredged in a mixture of flour and fine cornmeal that fries to a thin, crisp, golden crust. The whole thing is over in a couple of minutes. Clams turn rubbery if they are fried for a moment too long, so the oil must be hot, at 190°C, and the batches small enough to keep the temperature up. Shucked clams are sold by the tub in fishmongers and supermarkets on the coast, and you can use them fresh or frozen and thawed. The homemade tartare sauce takes two minutes and is much better than the bought kind.

  • Use a thermometer and keep the oil at 190°C. Cooler oil makes the coating greasy, and clams need to go in and out fast.
  • Fry only a handful at a time. Crowding the pan lowers the temperature and makes the coating stick together.
  • Dredge the clams just before frying. If they sit in the flour, the coating goes gluey and does not crisp.

item.title: Herb-Crusted Rack of Lamb
item.description: Herb-crusted rack of lamb: seared racks coated in Dijon mustard and a crust of breadcrumbs, garlic and herbs, roasted pink. A dinner-party star.
item.content:encoded:
A rack of lamb is one of the most elegant cuts you can serve and one of the quickest to cook. It is the row of ribs from the lamb's back, sold with the bones trimmed clean, or Frenched, so that each cutlet has a neat handle, and roasted it becomes tender, sweet and pink, with a layer of fat on top that bastes it as it cooks. The classic British way to dress it is with a herb crust. The racks are first seared to brown the fat, then brushed with Dijon mustard, which is the glue that holds the coating on and adds a gentle sharpness, and pressed with breadcrumbs mixed with parsley, rosemary, thyme, garlic and lemon zest. Melted butter turns the crumbs golden in the oven. All of that happens in about twenty minutes, which is why a rack is one of the best dinner-party centrepieces for anyone who would rather be at the table than at the stove. The one skill is judging the doneness, and a probe thermometer takes the guesswork out of it. A single rack of eight cutlets is enough for two or three people, so two racks feed four generously.

  • Cool the seared racks briefly before you add the mustard and crust. On very hot meat, the butter in the crumbs melts and slides off.
  • Use a probe thermometer. The temperature rises about 4°C as the lamb rests, so take it out 4°C below your target.
  • Whole cuts of lamb are traditionally served pink, but if you prefer to follow official food-safety guidance, roast to 63°C and rest for a medium result.

item.title: Homemade Ravioli
item.description: Homemade ravioli: silky fresh egg pasta filled with ricotta, spinach and Parmesan, tossed in brown sage butter. A weekend project worth doing.
item.content:encoded:
Making ravioli by hand is a slow, satisfying job, and it is one of those things that is so much better than the bought kind that it is hard to go back. Fresh egg pasta has a tenderness and a flavour that dried pasta cannot match, and a filling of ricotta and spinach is soft, milky and lightly sweet, the classic Italian pairing for a reason. The dough is only flour and eggs, kneaded until smooth and left to relax for thirty minutes so that it rolls out thin without springing back. Rolled to the thickness of a coin or thinner, it is filled, sealed and cut into squares, and it cooks in three or four minutes. The most important detail is the filling. The spinach must be squeezed as dry as you can get it, and the ricotta drained, or the moisture will make the pasta soggy and burst the ravioli as they cook. Brown butter and sage is the simplest sauce and the best one for a delicate filling. A pasta machine makes rolling much easier, but a long rolling pin and some patience work just as well.

  • Squeeze the spinach in a clean tea towel. A wet filling makes the pasta soggy from the inside, and the ravioli can burst as they cook.
  • Press out the air pockets around each mound before you cut. Trapped air makes the ravioli balloon and split in the water.
  • Cook them in a gentle boil, not a rolling one. Vigorous water tears the edges of delicate pasta.

item.title: Kangaroo Steak
item.description: Kangaroo steak: lean fillet marinated with garlic and rosemary, seared pink and served with a red wine and berry pan sauce. An Australian classic.
item.content:encoded:
Kangaroo has been eaten in Australia for tens of thousands of years, and today it is on sale in supermarkets and butchers and on the menus of restaurants across the country. It is harvested from wild populations under government-managed quotas, and it is a very lean, dark, richly flavoured red meat with a taste somewhere between beef and venison and a fraction of the fat of either. That leanness is the thing to understand when you cook it. There is no marbling to protect the meat, so it dries out and toughens very quickly, and the golden rule is to cook it fast and hot and to stop while it is still rare to medium-rare. Two to three minutes a side in a smoking pan is enough for a fillet, followed by a proper rest. A short marinade in oil, garlic, rosemary and black pepper adds flavour and a little protection, and the pan sauce, made from red wine, stock and a spoonful of redcurrant or Davidson plum jam, gives the sweet, tart counterpoint that lean game meat likes. Slice it thinly across the grain, and serve it with sweet potato mash and greens.

  • Do not cook it beyond medium. Kangaroo has almost no fat, and once it passes medium it goes dry and tough.
  • Get the pan properly hot before the meat goes in. A quick, hard sear gives a crust while the centre stays pink.
  • Slice across the grain. Lean game meat has long, firm fibres, and cutting through them shortens them and makes each slice more tender.

item.title: Lamb Tagine
item.description: Lamb tagine: shoulder braised until tender with ginger, cinnamon, cumin and apricots in a thick, fragrant sauce, finished with toasted almonds.
item.content:encoded:
A tagine is both a Moroccan slow-cooked stew and the conical earthenware pot that gives it its name, and lamb with dried fruit is one of its best-known forms. The combination of savoury meat with sweet apricots or prunes is typical of the Moroccan kitchen, where warm spices, honey and dried fruit are used to balance the richness of lamb, and the resulting dish is neither sweet nor spicy in the hot sense, but deep, fragrant and rounded. The spices do the work. Ginger, cumin, coriander, turmeric, paprika and cinnamon are cooked in the oil with the onions, so that their flavours bloom before any liquid goes in, and a pinch of saffron adds colour and its unmistakable aroma. The lamb should be shoulder, which has the fat and connective tissue to stay moist through a long cook and to turn silky. It is braised at a low temperature, tightly covered, until it can be pulled apart, and the lid is taken off at the end so that the sauce reduces to a thick glaze. You do not need a traditional tagine pot, and a heavy casserole with a well-fitting lid does the same job. Serve it with couscous or flatbread to catch the sauce.

  • Use shoulder rather than leg. The fat and connective tissue melt during the long cook and keep the meat moist, whereas lean leg turns dry.
  • Cook the spices in the oil with the onions before adding liquid. Their flavour comes out into the fat, and raw spices stirred into stock taste dusty.
  • Take the lid off for the last half hour. Uncovered, the sauce reduces to a thick glaze instead of a thin stew.

item.title: Mixed Grill
item.description: Mixed grill: lamb chops, sausages, bacon, mushrooms and tomatoes cooked together under a hot grill and piled on the plate. The British pub classic.
item.content:encoded:
The mixed grill is one of the great British pub and carvery plates, a heap of different grilled meats with mushrooms, tomatoes and usually an egg, served with chips and peas. It comes from the tradition of the grill room in Victorian and Edwardian hotels and gentlemen's clubs, where a range of chops, kidneys and sausages were cooked to order over an open fire, and it has survived in pubs and steakhouses across the country. It is a good dinner to cook at home because the whole thing happens under one hot grill, and the skill is timing. The different items need different lengths of time. Sausages take the longest, so they go under first, followed by the lamb chops, mushrooms and tomatoes, and the bacon, which cooks in a few minutes, goes on last. Thick loin chops stay pink and juicy in the time it takes the sausages to brown. The mushrooms and tomatoes catch the meat juices as they drip, which is where much of the flavour comes from. Serve everything with a fried egg, chips, and English mustard and brown sauce on the side.

  • Start the sausages first. They need almost twice as long as the chops, and the order of cooking is what keeps everything hot on the plate together.
  • Use a foil-lined grill pan and leave the juices in it. The mushrooms and tomatoes soak up the meat juices as they cook, and that is where the flavour comes from.
  • Check that the sausages are cooked through by cutting one open. It should be hot and firm throughout, with no pink.

item.title: Pasta Primavera
item.description: Pasta primavera: linguine tossed with asparagus, peas, courgette and tomatoes in a light Parmesan cream sauce with lemon and basil.
item.content:encoded:
Pasta primavera means spring pasta, and it is one of the best-known Italian-American dishes, although it was born in New York and not in Italy. It is usually credited to Le Cirque, the Manhattan restaurant, where it appeared in the 1970s and became a sensation with diners who wanted something lighter than a meat sauce. The idea is a plate of pasta dressed with a mixture of just-cooked spring vegetables, such as asparagus, peas and courgettes, in a sauce so light that it is barely a sauce. The important thing is that the vegetables are cooked briefly, so that each one keeps its colour and its bite, and the way to do that with the least fuss is to add the harder ones, the asparagus and broccoli, to the pasta water for the last two minutes of cooking. The courgettes and tomatoes are softened in a pan with garlic and olive oil, and cream and Parmesan are stirred in with a splash of the starchy pasta water, which emulsifies everything into a glossy coating instead of a heavy cream sauce. Lemon zest and torn basil at the end give it a fresh, bright finish. Use any seasonal vegetables that are good at the market.

  • Save the pasta water. The starch in it binds the cream and cheese into a smooth sauce, and it is what stops the dish from being either dry or greasy.
  • Cut the vegetables to a similar size. They cook at the same rate that way, and every forkful has a bit of each.
  • Do not overcook the vegetables. They should be bright green and still slightly crisp, since they keep cooking in the hot sauce.

item.title: Pheasant Casserole
item.description: Pheasant casserole: jointed pheasant braised with smoked bacon, shallots, mushrooms and cider until tender, in a rich gravy. Country cooking.
item.content:encoded:
Pheasant is the quintessential British game bird, and a casserole is the most forgiving way to cook it. The shooting season runs from the first of October to the first of February, and for those months pheasants turn up in butchers and farm shops for a fraction of the price of most meat. They are also easy to get wrong. A pheasant is lean and has little fat under the skin, and roasted whole it can be dry, especially the breast. Braising in liquid gets round the problem, and the smoked bacon in this casserole adds the fat that the bird lacks. The legs and breasts are cooked differently, because the legs have tough sinews and need 45 minutes or longer to soften, while the breasts are done in about half an hour, so the legs go in first and the breasts join them later. Cider is the natural liquid, since it is sharp and slightly sweet, and its apple flavour suits game as well as it suits pork. Shallots, mushrooms and thyme complete a gravy that is deep and savoury, and a crisp apple stirred in at the end and a little cream soften the richness. Serve with mash to soak up the sauce.

  • Add the breasts halfway. They are done in about half the time of the legs, and left in from the start they turn dry and stringy.
  • Wild birds can contain shot. Run your fingers over the meat and chew carefully, and cut away any bruised flesh near a wound.
  • Ask the butcher to joint the birds. A pheasant is awkward to divide, and it takes a professional a minute.

item.title: Scalloped Potatoes and Ham
item.description: Scalloped potatoes and ham: thinly sliced potatoes and diced ham baked in a creamy cheddar sauce until tender and golden. A leftover-ham classic.
item.content:encoded:
Scalloped potatoes with ham is the American answer to what to do with the remains of the Easter or Christmas ham, and it is a better dinner than most of the meals that came before it. In American cooking, scalloped potatoes are potatoes sliced thinly and baked in a creamy white sauce, and when cheese is added they become au gratin, so this is a bit of both. The ham makes it a meal in a single dish, a salty, savoury counterpoint to the mild, creamy potato. The sauce is a proper béchamel, made with butter, flour and milk, flavoured with garlic, mustard and thyme, and melted cheddar. Making the sauce first, instead of pouring raw milk over the potatoes, is what stops the dish from curdling and gives it a smooth, thick consistency. The potatoes are sliced as thinly and evenly as you can manage, about the thickness of a coin, so that they all cook at the same time, and a mandoline makes this quick. The dish is baked covered for the first part, to steam the potatoes until they are tender, and uncovered for the last, to brown the top. It needs a rest before serving, since the sauce continues to thicken as it cools.

  • Slice the potatoes evenly, about the thickness of a coin. A mandoline does it in minutes, and uneven slices leave some hard and some collapsed.
  • Do not rinse the sliced potatoes. The surface starch is what helps thicken the sauce as it bakes.
  • Check the potatoes with a knife before you take the foil off. If the middle is still firm, give it another 10 minutes under cover.

item.title: Smothered Chicken
item.description: Smothered chicken: seasoned chicken thighs fried until golden, then simmered in a rich onion and pepper gravy. Southern soul food, best over rice.
item.content:encoded:
Smothered chicken is Southern soul food, a dish of fried chicken that is then cooked down in a thick onion gravy until the meat is almost falling from the bone. To smother means to cover and cook slowly in a sauce, and it is a technique found across the cooking of the American South, from Louisiana to the Carolinas, and it turns a tough or plain cut into something deeply savoury. Everything depends on three stages done properly. The chicken is seasoned generously and dredged in flour, then fried until it has a golden crust, which builds flavour and also provides the flour and fat for the gravy. The onions are cooked in the same fat, slowly, until they are a deep golden brown, and this is the step that must not be hurried, because their sweetness is what balances the seasoning. Then the gravy goes in, with stock, thyme and a dash of hot sauce, and the chicken goes back to simmer, covered, until it is tender and the gravy has thickened into something glossy. It is served over white rice, which drinks up the gravy, with greens and cornbread on the side. Bone-in thighs are the best cut for it, because they stay moist through the long simmer.

  • Take your time with the onions. Golden brown, not pale and not burnt, is the colour that gives the gravy its depth.
  • Only brown the chicken, do not cook it through. It finishes in the gravy, and fully cooked fried chicken turns dry during the simmer.
  • Keep the simmer low and the lid on. A hard boil toughens the meat and reduces the gravy too quickly.

item.title: Somerset Pork with Cider
item.description: Somerset pork with cider: seared chops simmered with onions, apples and wholegrain mustard in dry cider, finished with cream. A West Country classic.
item.content:encoded:
Somerset is cider country, and pork and cider is the county's best-known pairing, as natural there as beef and horseradish. The orchards that produce the cider apples also fed the pigs, and the sharp, slightly sweet acidity of the drink is exactly what cuts through the richness of pork. Made with chops, it is one of the quickest of the classic British cider dishes, and the sauce comes together in the pan while the meat is resting. The pork is seared first in butter and oil for a good crust. Onions and apples are softened in the same pan, and the cider is boiled hard to reduce it to about half, which concentrates the flavour and cooks off the raw alcohol, leaving something fruity and lightly tart. Stock, wholegrain mustard and thyme go in next, then the chops are simmered in the sauce until they are just cooked through, which keeps them juicy. At the end a splash of cream turns the pan juices into a silky, pale gold sauce, without any flour or thickener. Use a dry or medium dry cider, since a sweet one makes the sauce cloying. Serve with mashed potatoes or buttered new potatoes and a green vegetable.

  • Choose a dry or medium dry cider. A sweet one gives a sweet sauce, and the sharpness is what makes the dish.
  • Check the chops with a thermometer rather than cutting them. Pork is done at 63°C, and past that point it dries out fast.
  • Add the cream off a high heat. Cream boiled hard in an acidic sauce can curdle, so keep it at a gentle simmer.

item.title: Steak Kabobs
item.description: Steak kabobs: sirloin cubes marinated in garlic, soy and balsamic, skewered with peppers, onions and mushrooms, grilled charred and pink.
item.content:encoded:
Steak kabobs are the cookout centrepiece that every American backyard makes at some point in the summer: bite-size cubes of beef skewered with peppers, onions and mushrooms and cooked over a hot grill. The idea of cooking meat on a skewer is one of the oldest in the world, and it is the reason the dish has so many names, from shish kebab in Turkey to sosaties in South Africa. The American version is distinguished by its marinade, which is usually a sweet, savoury and tangy mixture of soy sauce, Worcestershire sauce, balsamic vinegar and garlic. The marinade does three things. The salt seasons the meat through to the middle, the acid tenderises the surface, and the sugar in the balsamic and honey helps the edges to caramelise and char on the grill. Sirloin is the best cut, because it is tender enough to cook quickly and has enough flavour to stand up to the marinade, and it should be cut into generous 3 cm cubes so that the outside can char while the centre stays pink. Threading the meat and the vegetables on separate skewers is a good habit, since each needs a different time to cook. Rest the kabobs for five minutes before serving.

  • Marinate for no more than 8 hours. The acid softens the surface of the beef, and a very long soak leaves it mushy.
  • Keep the beef and vegetables on separate skewers if you like your steak medium-rare. Mushrooms and peppers need longer than a cube of sirloin.
  • Leave a little space between the pieces on the skewer. Pieces packed tightly steam instead of char.

item.title: BBQ Sauce
item.description: Homemade BBQ sauce: ketchup, cider vinegar, brown sugar, treacle and smoked paprika simmered until thick and glossy. Better than a bottle.
item.content:encoded:
Barbecue sauce is an American institution with dozens of regional styles, from the thin, vinegary sauces of the Carolinas to the sweet, thick, tomato-based ones of Kansas City, and it is one of the simplest things to make from scratch. The all-purpose sauce here is in the Kansas City style, and it is built on a handful of store-cupboard ingredients. Ketchup gives it body and colour, and cider vinegar the tang that cuts through fatty meat. Brown sugar and a spoonful of treacle bring sweetness and a dark, molasses depth, and Worcestershire sauce and mustard add savoury complexity. Smoked paprika and a little garlic and onion powder provide the flavour of the grill without needing a smoker, and cayenne gives a gentle background heat. It only needs twenty minutes of simmering, which is what turns a sweet, thin mixture into something thick, glossy and well blended. The result is much better than most bottled sauces because you control the sweetness and the smoke, and it has no corn syrup or thickeners. Brush it on ribs and chicken in the last few minutes of grilling, when the sugars will caramelise, and use it at the table for dipping, in burgers and on pulled pork.

  • Simmer on low heat and stir often. The sugar in the sauce catches easily on the base of the pan, and it spits as it thickens.
  • Brush it on ribs and chicken only in the last 10 minutes of cooking. The sugar burns over a long time on the grill.
  • Adjust the balance to your taste at the end. Sweetness, tang and heat all shift a little as it reduces.

item.title: Black Bean Burgers
item.description: Black bean burgers: smoky, spiced black bean patties bound with oats and panko, seared until crisp outside. A hearty vegan burger that holds together.
item.content:encoded:
A good black bean burger is not a poor imitation of a beef burger, it is a different and very good thing in its own right: earthy, smoky and a little sweet, with a crisp crust and a soft, savoury middle. The difficulty with any bean burger is that it can fall apart, and the way to stop that is to control the moisture and get the binding right. Here, only about two thirds of the beans are mashed, which gives the mixture a sticky base, while the remainder are left whole for texture. Rolled oats, blitzed to a coarse flour, and panko breadcrumbs soak up the extra moisture, and a spoonful of ground flaxseed mixed with water sets to a gel that acts as an egg would, which keeps the burger vegan. Cumin, smoked paprika, chilli, tomato paste and soy sauce supply the depth that beans on their own lack, and a fresh handful of coriander lifts it at the end. Chilling the shaped patties for twenty minutes firms them up so they can be turned in the pan without breaking. Serve them in toasted buns with avocado, lettuce, tomato and pickles.

  • Leave part of the beans whole. Mashing them all makes a paste, and the whole beans give the burger its texture.
  • Do not skip the chill. It lets the oats absorb the moisture and firms the patties, which is what stops them breaking when you turn them.
  • Turn each patty only once, and only when the crust has formed. If it sticks, it is not ready to be moved.

item.title: Bone Broth
item.description: Bone broth: roasted beef bones simmered for twelve hours with vegetables, herbs and cider vinegar into a rich, gelatinous broth.
item.content:encoded:
Bone broth is stock that has been left to simmer for much longer than usual, often twelve hours or more, with the aim of drawing out everything the bones have to give: the gelatine from cartilage and connective tissue, the marrow, and a deep savoury flavour. A good one sets to a jelly when it is cold, which is the sign that it is rich in gelatine and the reason that it has a silky body that ordinary stock lacks. It has been marketed with a long list of health claims, and it is worth being clear that most are not well supported by evidence. What is certain is that it makes a flavourful, comforting drink and a superb base for soups, gravies, risottos and sauces. The method is simple and forgiving. The bones are roasted first, which caramelises them and gives the broth a deeper colour and taste, then simmered very gently, since a hard boil clouds the liquid and makes it taste greasy. A splash of cider vinegar helps to draw minerals from the bones, and onions, carrots, celery, garlic and herbs add sweetness. A mix of bones works best: knuckles and joints for gelatine, marrow bones for richness and oxtail for meaty flavour. It needs almost no attention once it is going, and the slow cooker does the job overnight.

  • Never let it boil. A hard boil clouds the broth and emulsifies the fat into it, giving a greasy taste, while a bare simmer keeps it clear.
  • Use a mix of bones, including something with joints. Knuckles and feet supply the gelatine that makes the broth set.
  • Add salt at the end, not the beginning. The broth reduces over the long simmer, and seasoning early can leave it too salty.

item.title: Cheeseburger Soup
item.description: Cheeseburger soup: browned ground beef, potatoes and vegetables in a thick, creamy cheddar soup, topped with pickles and bacon. A burger in a bowl.
item.content:encoded:
Cheeseburger soup is a Midwestern comfort dish that has become popular all over the United States, and it does exactly what the name says: it takes everything you like about a cheeseburger and puts it in a bowl. There is ground beef, browned with onion, mustard and Worcestershire sauce for that unmistakable burger flavour, potatoes, carrots and celery to make it a meal, and a creamy cheddar base thickened with a roux. The toppings do a lot of the work. Chopped dill pickles, diced tomato and crisp bacon on top bring back the tang, freshness and smoke of a burger with everything on it. The method is straightforward, but there are a couple of steps that matter. The beef should be browned properly and drained of excess fat, otherwise the soup will be greasy. A roux, which is butter and flour cooked together, thickens the soup smoothly, and the milk goes in warm. Most important, the cheese must go in over the lowest heat and only after the soup has stopped boiling, because a cheese sauce that boils splits into grease and grainy curds. Add it a handful at a time and stir until melted, and the result is smooth and glossy.

  • Drain the fat from the beef. Most of the grease ends up floating on the soup if you do not, and it can also stop the cheese from blending in.
  • Add the cheese off the heat. Cheese in a boiling soup separates into oil and curds, but off the heat it melts smoothly.
  • Use a mature cheddar and grate it yourself. Pre-grated cheese has an anti-caking coating that stops it melting smoothly.

item.title: Cilantro Lime Rice
item.description: Cilantro lime rice: fluffy long-grain rice finished with fresh lime juice, zest and a big handful of coriander. The burrito bowl side dish at home.
item.content:encoded:
Cilantro lime rice is the fragrant, lightly tangy rice that sits at the base of a burrito bowl, and it is one of the easiest ways to turn plain rice into something that people notice. Cilantro is the American name for fresh coriander leaves, and with lime juice and zest it gives the rice a bright, green, citrus flavour that goes with everything from grilled chicken and black beans to fish tacos and fajitas. The method is what makes the difference between fluffy, separate grains and a sticky lump. The rice is rinsed first to remove the surface starch, which is the cause of stickiness, then briefly fried in a little oil so that each grain is coated, before the water goes in. It is cooked covered on the lowest heat, without stirring or lifting the lid, then left to steam off the heat for ten minutes. The lime and coriander are added at the end, and stirred in gently with a fork, because heat dulls the freshness of both. Long-grain white rice such as basmati or jasmine gives the best result, and the ratio of one part rice to about one and two-thirds parts water is what makes it come out just right.

  • Rinse the rice until the water is clear. The loose starch on the surface is what makes rice clump together.
  • Do not lift the lid while the rice cooks or during the resting time. The steam is doing the cooking.
  • Add the lime and coriander at the end. Both lose their fresh flavour in the heat, and the juice added early can make the rice tough.

item.title: Fried Bologna Sandwich
item.description: Fried bologna sandwich: thick bologna slices fried in butter until browned and blistered, with melted cheese and mustard on toasted white bread.
item.content:encoded:
The fried bologna sandwich is a working-class American lunch that has survived on lunch counters and kitchen tables, especially in the South and Appalachia, because it is cheap, quick and much better than it sounds. Bologna is a cooked, smoked sausage that is sold sliced, and the American version, sometimes spelled baloney, is mild, smooth and slightly sweet. Eaten cold from the packet it is unremarkable, but fried in a hot pan it changes completely. The edges curl and crisp, the surface browns and blisters, and the fat renders and gives it a savoury depth that is closer to bacon than to cold cuts. The one problem is the curl. The slice puffs up in the middle as the casing tightens and the meat swells, and it forms a dome that sits above the pan and cooks unevenly. The answer is to cut a few small slits around the edge of each slice before it goes in, which lets it lie flat. Ask for thick slices, about 6 mm, at the deli counter, as thin ones dry out. Serve it hot on white bread with yellow mustard, mayonnaise and a slice of American cheese melted on top, and add pickles and lettuce if you want them.

  • Slit the edges before frying. It stops the slice from doming, so it lies flat in the pan and browns evenly.
  • Fry until properly browned. Pale bologna tastes the way it does cold, and the browning is what makes it good.
  • Choose thick slices. Thin slices shrink and dry out into leathery discs.

item.title: Peanut Butter and Jelly Sandwich
item.description: Peanut butter and jelly sandwich: soft bread, creamy peanut butter and fruity jelly, with the trick that keeps the bread from going soggy.
item.content:encoded:
The peanut butter and jelly sandwich is as American as anything on the menu, and it has been packed into lunchboxes for more than a century. One of the earliest printed recipes for it appeared in a Boston cooking magazine in 1901, and by the middle of the twentieth century it was the standard school lunch and a staple of military rations. It works because of contrast. The peanut butter is rich, salty and savoury, the jelly is sweet and fruity, and the soft bread is a neutral cushion between them. In the United States, jelly means what the British call jam, a fruit preserve, usually strawberry or grape, while the wobbling gelatine dessert is Jell-O. There is a small technique that improves the result. Spread the peanut butter on both slices of bread, right to the edges, and put the jelly on top of the peanut butter on one of them. The peanut butter forms a barrier that keeps the jelly from soaking into the bread, so the sandwich stays firm even if it is made in the morning and eaten at noon. Use fresh, soft bread, and go easy on the jelly, since too much makes it slide out at the sides. Because peanuts are one of the most common allergens, many schools ban them, and sunflower seed butter is a good substitute.

  • Spread the peanut butter on both slices of bread. It forms a barrier, so the jelly cannot soak into the bread and make the sandwich soggy.
  • Use a light hand with the jelly. A thin layer gives the sweetness you want without leaking out of the sides.
  • Warm the peanut butter for 10 seconds in the microwave if it is cold and stiff. It spreads more easily and does not tear the bread.

item.title: Seven Layer Salad
item.description: Seven layer salad: crisp lettuce, celery, red onion, peas, creamy dressing, cheddar and bacon stacked in a glass bowl and chilled for hours.
item.content:encoded:
The seven layer salad is a fixture of American potlucks, church suppers, picnics and holiday tables, and it is easy to see why. It is built in a clear glass bowl so that the stripes of green lettuce, pale celery, purple onion, bright peas, cheese and bacon show through the sides, and it looks like far more effort than it takes. It is also a dish designed to be made in advance. The layers are assembled with the creamy dressing spread over the top, right to the edges of the bowl, which seals in the vegetables and lets them stay crisp for hours in the fridge, while the dressing slowly seasons the layers below it. It is served without tossing, by digging a big spoon straight down through all of the layers, so that each portion has some of everything. The classic layers are iceberg lettuce, celery, red onion, frozen peas, a mayonnaise dressing, cheddar and crumbled bacon, and the peas can go straight from frozen, since they thaw in the fridge. Cook the bacon until properly crisp, because soft bacon turns chewy and rubbery in the cold. Chilling for at least four hours lets everything come together.

  • Spread the dressing right to the edge of the bowl. It forms a seal that keeps the vegetables crisp and stops the layers oxidising.
  • Add the bacon just before serving if you can. Left on top overnight it softens, but bacon added at the last minute keeps its crunch.
  • Dry the lettuce very well after washing. Wet leaves make the layers watery and thin the dressing.

item.title: Spaghetti Squash
item.description: Spaghetti squash: roasted until tender, forked into golden strands and tossed with garlic butter, Parmesan and parsley. A light pasta alternative.
item.content:encoded:
Spaghetti squash looks like an ordinary yellow winter squash, but its flesh has a party trick. When the squash is cooked and scraped with a fork, the flesh separates into long, thin, golden strands that look like spaghetti, and it is often used as a lighter alternative to pasta, or just as an interesting vegetable side. The flavour is mild and slightly sweet and the texture is tender with a little bite, so it is a blank canvas for other flavours and it takes to garlic, butter and Parmesan very well. Roasting is the best way to cook it, since it concentrates the flavour and dries the surface, whereas boiling or microwaving can leave the strands waterlogged. A few things make a real difference. The squash is cut in half lengthways, but cutting it across in rings gives longer strands, because the strands run in circles around the middle of the squash instead of from end to end. Roasting it cut side down steams the flesh in its own moisture and browns the edges. The cooked squash is scraped while still warm, and then it is best drained briefly, or patted with kitchen paper, so that the dish is not watery. Toss it with garlic butter and cheese while it is hot, and eat it straight away.

  • Cut the squash across into 3 cm rings, not lengthways, if you want long strands, and roast the rings in a single layer for about 25 minutes. The strands run around the squash in circles, so cutting across keeps them whole.
  • Roast it cut side down. The flesh steams in the trapped moisture and the edges brown, which gives more flavour than boiling.
  • Blot the strands on kitchen paper before you toss them. Spaghetti squash holds a lot of water, and a wet base makes the sauce thin.

item.title: Special Burger Sauce
item.description: Special burger sauce: a tangy, creamy, slightly sweet mix of mayonnaise, ketchup, mustard and pickle relish for any burger. Ready in five minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Every great burger chain has a secret sauce, and they all turn out to be variations on the same idea: a creamy, tangy, slightly sweet pink sauce that sits somewhere between mayonnaise and Thousand Island dressing. That combination works for a reason. A burger is rich, salty and meaty, and the sauce needs to cut through it with acidity from pickles and mustard, add a hit of sweetness from ketchup and relish to balance the salt of the cheese and the beef, and bring some creaminess that ties the layers together. The formula here is a mayonnaise base with ketchup, yellow mustard, sweet pickle relish and a splash of dill pickle brine, seasoned with smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder and a pinch of sugar. It needs no cooking and no equipment except a bowl and a whisk, and it takes five minutes. Chilling it for half an hour lets the onion and garlic powders soften and the flavours blend. The proportions are a matter of taste, so make it once by the recipe and then adjust it: more ketchup gives a sweeter, redder sauce, more mustard a sharper one, and a spoonful of finely chopped dill pickle adds crunch. It is worth making a jar, because it goes well with more than burgers. It is good on fries, chicken sandwiches, hot dogs, fried fish, onion rings and as a dip for almost anything crispy.

  • Chop the relish finer if it is chunky. A smooth sauce coats the bun better, and larger pieces slide off the burger.
  • Adjust the pickle brine to change the thickness. A teaspoon at a time thins it for a squeeze bottle without watering down the flavour.
  • Use a good mayonnaise. It is the base of the sauce and its flavour comes through, so a cheap one tastes flat.

item.title: Three Bean Salad
item.description: Three bean salad: green beans, kidney beans and chickpeas in a sweet and tangy vinaigrette with red onion, celery and parsley. Better after chilling.
item.content:encoded:
Three bean salad is an American picnic and barbecue staple, and it deserves its place. It is one of those recipes that depends on a store cupboard and a good dressing, and that improves with time instead of suffering from it. The traditional trio is green beans, red kidney beans and either yellow wax beans or chickpeas, which give a contrast of colour, texture and flavour, from the crisp snap of the fresh green beans to the creamy softness of the tinned pulses. The dressing is what sets it apart from a plain bean salad. It is a sweet and sour vinaigrette made with cider vinegar, a good amount of sugar, oil and seasoning, and it is poured over while the beans are still fresh, so that they take it up. Then the salad is left to chill for hours, and this is when it transforms. The acidity mellows, the beans soak up the flavour and the onion loses its rawness. Since it is served cold, it needs no last-minute work and it holds well at a picnic, and because it is made with beans and oil, it is vegan and gluten free, so almost everyone can eat it. It also makes good use of leftovers, so add sweetcorn, peppers or chopped herbs.

  • Dress the beans while they are still cool but fresh. They take up the dressing better than beans that have been sitting for a while.
  • Plunge the green beans in iced water. It stops the cooking at once and keeps them bright green and crisp.
  • Give it time. The salad is fine after an hour, but the flavour and texture improve markedly if it is left overnight.

item.title: Watermelon Salad
item.description: Watermelon salad: cold watermelon cubes with salty feta, fresh mint, thin red onion, lime and olive oil. A cool, no-cook summer salad.
item.content:encoded:
Watermelon salad is what happens when you stop thinking of watermelon as dessert. The fruit is sweet, watery and cool, and when it meets salty feta, fresh mint, sharp red onion and a squeeze of lime, the whole thing becomes savoury, refreshing and much more interesting than a bowl of plain fruit. The idea has been popular in the United States for years, especially on hot days at barbecues and lunches by the pool, and it echoes an old Mediterranean and Middle Eastern habit of eating watermelon with salty white cheese. It is the contrast that makes it work. Salt heightens the sweetness of the melon, acid sharpens it, and the mint adds a cooling, aromatic note. The red onion should be sliced very thinly, and soaked for ten minutes in cold water, which tames its rawness. Everything depends on the quality of the watermelon. It should be ripe, heavy for its size, with a creamy yellow patch where it lay on the ground, and above all it should be cold. Cut it into large cubes rather than small ones, and dress the salad only at the last moment, because salt draws water out of the fruit and it will slump into a puddle if it sits.

  • Serve it cold, and dress it at the last minute. Salt pulls water from the melon, so a salad that stands turns into a puddle.
  • Pick the melon by weight and sound. A ripe one feels heavy for its size, has a creamy yellow ground spot and sounds hollow when tapped.
  • Use a block of feta in brine rather than pre-crumbled. It is creamier and less salty, and it crumbles on the salad in larger, softer pieces.

item.title: Bath Buns
item.description: Bath buns: soft, lightly sweet yeast buns full of sultanas and peel, topped with crushed sugar that bakes into a crunchy crust.
item.content:encoded:
The Bath bun is one of the oldest named buns in Britain, and it comes from the Georgian spa city of Bath in Somerset, where visitors took the waters in the morning and ate sweet, rich buns with their tea. It is a soft, enriched yeast dough, sweetened with sugar, scented with lemon and full of sultanas and mixed peel, and what marks it out is the topping. Lumps of sugar are roughly crushed and pressed on top of the glazed dough, so that they bake into a crunchy, glittering crust over the soft bun. In the past the topping was caraway comfits, sugar-coated seeds, and sugar lumps replaced them. The bun was sold in vast quantities at the Great Exhibition of 1851, and one story says that the Bath physician William Oliver, who gave his name to the Bath Oliver biscuit, created the plainer biscuit because his patients were gaining weight on the buns. The dough needs some patience, but the technique is not difficult. It rises twice, first as a mass and then as shaped buns, and the second rise gives the light, airy crumb. The buns should be a little rough and uneven in shape, which is part of their charm. Eat them fresh and split, with butter, or with clotted cream and jam.

  • Crush the sugar lumps roughly, into pieces about the size of a lentil. Fine crumbs melt into the glaze, and the crunch is what you want.
  • Judge the dough by feel, not just the clock. It should be soft and slightly tacky, so add only enough flour to stop it sticking to your hands.
  • Do not over-prove the buns. Puffy and soft is right, and buns that have collapsed will bake dense and flat.

item.title: Black and White Cookies
item.description: Black and white cookies: big, soft, cake-like lemon-vanilla cookies iced half in glossy vanilla and half in chocolate. The New York deli classic.
item.content:encoded:
The black and white cookie is a New York icon, a large, round, soft cookie, as much like a small cake as a biscuit, with a smooth fondant-style icing that is half white vanilla and half chocolate, split down the middle. It is sold in delicatessens and bakeries across the city and was made famous outside it by an episode of Seinfeld, in which it became a metaphor for racial harmony. Its origins are usually traced to Hemstrought's Bakery in Utica, in upstate New York, where it was called the half moon, in the early twentieth century. The cookie itself is delicately flavoured with lemon and vanilla, and the batter contains milk, which gives it the soft, cakey crumb instead of a crisp snap. It is scooped, not rolled, and spreads only a little as it bakes, so the finished cookie is domed on top and flat on the bottom. The bottom is what you ice, which gives a level surface for the glaze. The icing is a thick mixture of icing sugar and warm water, with a little golden syrup for shine, and it is spread in two halves, vanilla first and then chocolate. It needs a steady hand, a small offset spatula and a little patience, but the sharp line down the middle is what makes it.

  • Ice the flat underside of the cookie. It gives a level surface, and the domed top ends up as the base of the finished cookie.
  • Keep the icing thick and add water a few drops at a time. If it is too runny it will run off the edge and the two colours will bleed into each other.
  • Ice the vanilla half first and let it set for a minute before the chocolate. A clean, straight line is the mark of a good black and white cookie.

item.title: Buttercream Frosting
item.description: Buttercream frosting: butter beaten pale and fluffy with icing sugar, vanilla and a splash of cream into a smooth, pipeable frosting for 12 cupcakes.
item.content:encoded:
American buttercream is the frosting that most people picture when they think of a birthday cake: sweet, creamy, soft and pale, and piped in swirls. It is also the simplest of all the buttercreams, because it is made with nothing but butter, icing sugar and a little liquid, beaten together, with no cooking, no egg whites and no thermometer. The others, Swiss, Italian and French, are silkier and less sweet, but they involve heating egg whites or sugar syrup, and this is the one you can do in ten minutes with a bowl and a hand mixer. The trick to a good one is in the butter and in the beating. The butter should be properly soft, so that you can press a finger into it without effort, but not oily or melting, and it needs a solid three minutes of beating on its own until it turns pale and fluffy, before any sugar goes in. The sugar is added gradually, in three batches, and then the frosting is beaten for a further few minutes, which lightens the texture by whipping in air. A pinch of salt cuts the sweetness, and a splash of cream or milk makes it spreadable. The quantity here frosts 12 cupcakes generously or fills and covers a two-layer 20 cm cake.

  • Beat the butter on its own first. Three minutes turns it pale and fluffy, and it is this that makes the frosting light instead of dense and greasy.
  • Sift the icing sugar. Lumps are impossible to beat out later and leave the frosting gritty.
  • For chocolate buttercream, replace 40 g of the icing sugar with cocoa powder and add another tablespoon of cream to loosen it.

item.title: Chocolate Babka
item.description: Chocolate babka: buttery yeast dough rolled around a dark chocolate filling, twisted into layers and baked, then brushed with syrup. Two loaves.
item.content:encoded:
Babka is a sweet braided yeast bread that came to the United States with Jewish immigrants from Poland and Ukraine, and in New York bakeries it became something of a cult. The name comes from a word meaning grandmother, said to be a reference to the shape of a woman's skirt, and the original babkas were filled with cinnamon and raisins. It was the chocolate babka that took over, and it became famous well beyond the Jewish community when it was celebrated in an episode of Seinfeld. The technique is as memorable as the filling. A rich, buttery dough is rolled thin and spread with a paste of dark chocolate and butter, then rolled up into a log. The log is cut in half lengthways, exposing the layers, and the two halves are twisted around each other and dropped into a loaf tin, so the finished slice shows a dramatic swirl of dough and chocolate. It takes time, mostly waiting for the dough to rise, but the work is not hard. After baking, the loaves are brushed with a sugar syrup while they are still hot, which gives a glossy top and keeps the crumb moist for days. This recipe makes two loaves, one to eat and one to give away.

  • Let the filling cool until it is just spreadable. If it is too hot it melts into the dough, and if it sets it tears the dough when spread.
  • Use a sharp knife, and cut the log cleanly. A blunt blade drags the filling across the layers and smears the swirl.
  • Brush the syrup on while the loaves are hot. It soaks in and gives the crust its shine, and it keeps the loaves moist for days.

item.title: Coconut Cake
item.description: Coconut cake: two tender coconut milk cake layers brushed with coconut syrup, covered in cream cheese frosting and coated in shredded coconut.
item.content:encoded:
A coconut cake is the sort of cake that gets asked for by name at Easter, weddings, birthdays and family Sundays across the American South, where it is often the centrepiece of the table. A great one is very moist, with a tender crumb that tastes of coconut in every bite, not just in the topping. There are three layers of coconut in this version. The cake itself is made with tinned coconut milk in place of dairy milk, and desiccated coconut is folded into the batter, so that the flavour and the texture run all through the crumb. Each layer is brushed with a syrup of coconut milk and sugar as soon as it comes out of the tin, which soaks in and keeps the cake moist for days. And a cream cheese frosting, lightly tangy to balance the sweetness of the coconut, covers it, and the whole cake is pressed with sweetened flaked coconut. The method is a classic creaming one. The butter and sugar are beaten until pale and light, the eggs are added one at a time, and the flour and coconut milk are added alternately, in three batches, which makes a smoother batter and a more even texture. The layers must be completely cool before frosting, or the frosting will melt and slide.

  • Stir the tin of coconut milk before you measure it. The thick cream rises to the top, and the batter needs the two mixed together.
  • Cool the cakes completely before frosting. A warm cake melts the cream cheese frosting and it slides off the sides.
  • Chill the frosted cake briefly before slicing. The frosting sets and gives clean slices, and the flavours settle.

item.title: Coconut Macaroons
item.description: Coconut macaroons: chewy, golden-tipped mounds of coconut bound with egg white and sugar, baked for 15 minutes and dipped in chocolate. Gluten free.
item.content:encoded:
A coconut macaroon is a simple thing, and a very good one: a small, chewy mound of desiccated coconut held together with egg white and sugar, toasty and golden on the outside, moist and soft within. It should not be confused with the macaron, the delicate almond meringue sandwich cookie of Paris, although the two share a name and a distant ancestry in the almond macaroons that came from Italy to France in the sixteenth century. The British coconut macaroon is the plain cousin, popular for generations in the tea shop and the biscuit tin, and traditionally baked on rice paper so that it did not stick. It has no flour and no fat, which is what makes it naturally gluten free and dairy free, and the whole mixture is made in one bowl and shaped with a spoon. The egg white is whisked first to a light foam, which gives the macaroons some lift and stops them from being dense. Baking them at a moderate temperature browns the tips and leaves the centres soft and chewy. A dip in melted dark chocolate makes them look smarter and adds a bitter note that balances the sweetness of the coconut. Store them in an airtight tin, since they soften quickly in a damp kitchen.

  • Wet your hands before shaping. The mixture is sticky, and damp hands stop it clinging and give tidy, well-packed mounds.
  • Press the mounds firmly together as you shape them. Loosely packed macaroons crumble when you lift them.
  • Check the chocolate label if you need them to be dairy free. Many dark chocolates are, but some contain milk fat.

item.title: Cranberry Orange Bread
item.description: Cranberry orange bread: a moist, tender quick loaf with tart cranberries, orange zest and juice, and a sweet orange glaze. No yeast, no fuss.
item.content:encoded:
Cranberry orange bread is the loaf that turns up all winter in American kitchens, in gift baskets, at holiday breakfasts and on the table at Thanksgiving, and it earns the place because it is such a good match of flavours. The cranberries are sharp and tart and pop as they bake, giving pockets of red and a burst of acidity, while the orange brings sweetness and a bright, floral, citrus scent that lifts the whole loaf. It is a quick bread, which is a name for a bake that is raised with baking powder and bicarbonate of soda rather than yeast, so there is no kneading and no rising time, and the batter goes from bowl to tin in fifteen minutes. The technique is the muffin method: wet and dry ingredients are mixed separately and then combined with a light hand, just until the flour disappears. Overmixing develops the gluten and makes a tough, tunnelled crumb. Both the zest and the juice of the orange go in, since the zest holds the aromatic oils and the juice supplies moisture and gentle acidity, and buttermilk gives the crumb tenderness. Fresh or frozen cranberries both work, and there is no need to thaw the frozen ones. A drizzle of orange glaze on the cooled loaf finishes it.

  • Mix only until the flour disappears. A lumpy batter makes a tender loaf, and overmixing gives a tough, chewy one.
  • Chop the cranberries roughly. Whole berries leave big wet pockets, while chopped ones distribute evenly through the crumb.
  • Cover the loaf with foil if it browns too fast. The long bake gives a dark crust before the middle is cooked.

item.title: Cream Horns
item.description: Cream horns: crisp, flaky puff pastry cones wound round metal moulds, baked golden and piped full of raspberry jam and whipped vanilla cream.
item.content:encoded:
A cream horn is a British bakery classic, a spiral of crisp, flaky, golden puff pastry, filled with a dollop of jam and a swirl of whipped cream, and dusted with icing sugar. It is made by winding thin strips of pastry around a conical metal mould, baking it, sliding out the mould and filling the empty horn, and the contrast between the shatteringly crisp pastry and the soft, cool cream is what makes it so appealing. It has been a fixture of the baker's window for generations, and it was once a mainstay of the school-fête cake stall and the tea shop. Home versions are a good deal easier than they look, mostly because ready-rolled puff pastry does all of the hard work. The only special equipment is a set of cream horn moulds, which are cheap and can be found in kitchen shops and online, and if you do not have them you can make cones from stiff card and foil. The technique matters in two ways. The strips are wound around the mould from the point, overlapping each turn by about a centimetre, so that the layers seal as they bake and do not unravel. And they are filled only just before serving, since pastry left with cream turns soft in an hour.

  • Grease the moulds well, and remove them while the horns are still warm. Cold pastry grips the metal and cracks as you pull it off.
  • Overlap each turn of pastry by about a centimetre. A gap opens up as the pastry puffs in the oven and leaves holes for the cream to leak through.
  • Fill them at the last moment. The crisp pastry is the point, and cream softens it quickly.

item.title: Funnel Cake
item.description: Funnel cake: a thin batter drizzled through a funnel into hot oil in a lacy spiral, fried until golden and crisp and dusted with icing sugar.
item.content:encoded:
A funnel cake is the smell of an American summer: a tangle of crisp, golden, lacy batter, dusted with icing sugar and eaten hot off a paper plate at a state fair, boardwalk or carnival. It is a very old idea. The dish is traced to the Pennsylvania Dutch, who made a similar fried batter cake known as drechderkuche, and it belongs to the wider family of fried dough that includes doughnuts and fritters. The batter is a thin, pourable pancake-style mix of flour, milk, egg, baking powder and a little sugar, and the way it is cooked is what makes it distinctive. It is poured through a funnel, or a squeeze bottle, straight into hot oil, in overlapping circles and loops, forming a web that cooks and sets in about a minute on each side. The result is uneven and crisp at the edges and soft and slightly doughy where the ribbons overlap. The oil temperature is the technique. At 175°C the batter sets at once, and it turns golden without soaking up grease. Cooler oil makes a soggy cake, and hotter oil browns it before the inside cooks. Eat it straight away, while it is still crisp, with a heavy dusting of icing sugar, or topped with strawberries and whipped cream, or chocolate sauce.

  • Check the temperature. At 175°C the batter sets in seconds and stays crisp, whereas cooler oil makes the cake soggy and greasy.
  • Pour close to the surface of the oil. Batter dropped from height splashes, and could burn you.
  • Fry one at a time. A second cake lowers the temperature and makes them stick to each other.

item.title: German Chocolate Cake
item.description: German chocolate cake: three tender chocolate layers with a cooked coconut and pecan caramel frosting. A Texas classic, not German at all.
item.content:encoded:
German chocolate cake has nothing to do with Germany. The name comes from Samuel German, an English-American chocolate maker who developed a mild, sweet dark baking chocolate for the Baker's Chocolate Company in the 1850s, which was named after him as German's Sweet Chocolate. The cake itself took off in 1957, when a Dallas newspaper printed a recipe from a Texas home cook for German's Chocolate Cake, and it became so popular that sales of the chocolate soared. What sets it apart is the frosting.
