It is not a chocolate frosting but a cooked custard of evaporated milk, sugar, egg yolks and butter, thickened on the hob to the consistency of a soft caramel, and then loaded with sweetened coconut and toasted pecans. It is spread between the layers and on top, and traditionally the sides are left bare, so the chocolate cake shows. The cake is mild and tender, made with buttermilk and with whisked egg whites folded in for lightness, and melted chocolate that is only lightly bitter. Any good dark chocolate of 50 to 60 per cent cocoa solids will do in place of the original. It takes time, with three layers to bake and a frosting to cook and cool, but none of the steps is hard.

  • Stir the frosting constantly and keep the heat at medium. The egg yolks scramble if it gets too hot or is left alone, and you want a smooth, golden custard.
  • Fold in the egg whites gently. Beating them in knocks out the air, and the whisked whites are what give the cake its light crumb.
  • Let the frosting cool fully. It thickens as it cools, and hot frosting runs off the cake and soaks in.

item.title: Hawaiian Sweet Rolls
item.description: Hawaiian sweet rolls: soft, fluffy, lightly sweet pull-apart rolls made with pineapple juice and brushed with butter. Perfect for sliders.
item.content:encoded:
Hawaiian sweet rolls are soft, golden, slightly sweet, pull-apart rolls with a tender, feathery crumb and a faint, fruity flavour, and they have become a staple of American cooking, especially for sliders, where their sweetness sets off the saltiness of ham and cheese. They are modelled on the Portuguese sweet bread that immigrants brought to Hawaii in the nineteenth century, a rich, lightly sweet yeast bread that was adapted with local ingredients, and the pineapple juice in the recipe is the local touch. It adds sugar, gentle acidity and a delicate tropical flavour, and helps the rolls stay soft. The method is a basic enriched dough. Bread flour gives the strength and chew, an egg and butter give richness and softness, and a spoonful of instant mashed potato flakes, which is optional, holds moisture in the crumb and keeps the rolls soft for days. The dough is kneaded until smooth and stretchy, left to rise, divided and shaped into balls, then packed close together in a tin so that they rise into each other and bake into a single sheet of rolls that pull apart at the seams. A brush of egg wash gives a shiny top, and butter brushed on after baking keeps the crust soft. Use pineapple juice at room temperature or lukewarm, since a hot liquid will kill the yeast.

  • Use lukewarm juice, not hot. Above about 45°C the yeast begins to die, and the rolls will not rise.
  • Pack the rolls close together. They rise into each other, which gives them their soft sides and makes them pull apart easily.
  • Brush with butter right out of the oven. It is absorbed by the hot crust and keeps it soft, and gives the shiny finish.

item.title: Jaffa Cakes
item.description: Jaffa cakes: small whisked sponges topped with a disc of tangy orange jelly and a shell of dark chocolate. A British teatime favourite, and a cake.
item.content:encoded:
The Jaffa cake has one of the more unusual legal histories in food. In 1991 a UK VAT tribunal had to decide whether it was a cake, which is zero-rated for tax, or a chocolate-covered biscuit, which is not, and the ruling that it was a cake turned partly on the fact that it goes hard when it is stale, where a biscuit goes soft. It is named for the Jaffa orange, and it was first made by McVitie and Price in 1927. It is three layers: a small, light sponge, a disc of orange jelly and a coat of dark chocolate, and the way to make them at home is to treat each layer separately. The sponge is a classic whisked one, made from only eggs, sugar and flour, with no butter or raising agent, where the volume comes from beating the eggs and sugar until they are thick and pale and can hold a ribbon. It bakes in a shallow bun tin in ten minutes. The jelly is made stronger than a packet suggests, with about half the water, and set in a thin sheet in the fridge, so that it can be cut into neat rounds. The chocolate topping is best with a good dark chocolate, spooned on and scored with a fork. Everything takes a while to set, but none of it is difficult, and homemade Jaffa cakes are a real treat.

  • Whisk the eggs and sugar for the full 5 minutes. All of the volume of the sponge comes from the air you beat into them, since there is no raising agent.
  • Make the jelly with half the water on the packet. Made to the instructions it is too soft to cut, and the discs slide off the sponge.
  • Dip the cutter in hot water before you cut the jelly. A warm edge slices through cleanly, and each disc then sits neatly on its sponge.

item.title: Kolaches
item.description: Kolaches: pillowy, lightly sweet yeast rolls with a well in the centre filled with sweet cream cheese or apricot jam. A Czech-Texan bakery classic.
item.content:encoded:
A kolache is a soft, sweet, slightly enriched yeast roll with a well pressed into the top and a spoonful of filling baked in the middle, and it is one of the best-loved pastries in Texas, where it is a morning institution. It came with the Czech immigrants who settled in Central Texas in the nineteenth century, and it is a descendant of the Czech koláč, a round pastry filled with fruit, poppy seed or sweetened cheese. Today Texas kolache bakeries sell them by the dozen, and the town of West calls itself the kolache capital of Texas. There are sweet fillings, such as apricot, prune, poppy seed, cherry and cream cheese, and there are savoury versions wrapped around sausage, which are technically called klobasnek but are usually sold under the same name. The dough is a straightforward enriched one, made with milk, butter, sugar and egg, and it is kneaded until smooth, left to rise, shaped into balls and left to rise again. The indentation is pressed in with your fingers after the second rise, and it must be deep enough to hold the filling, with a raised rim around it. A brush of butter as soon as they come out of the oven softens the crust and makes them glossy.

  • Press the wells deeper than you think you need. The dough puffs up as it bakes and shrinks the hollow, and shallow ones let the filling spill.
  • Do not overfill. A level tablespoon of filling is enough, and more bubbles over the rim and burns on the tray.
  • Brush the rims with butter as soon as they come out of the oven. It keeps the crust soft and gives it a glossy finish.

item.title: Montreal Bagels
item.description: Montreal bagels: small, chewy, slightly sweet, hand-rolled bagels with big holes, boiled in honey water, coated in sesame seeds and baked golden.
item.content:encoded:
Montreal bagels and New York bagels are close relatives, but a Montrealer will tell you at some length that they are not the same thing, and the differences are real. The Montreal bagel is smaller, thinner and denser, with a much larger hole, and it is noticeably sweeter, because the dough contains honey and the bagels are boiled in water that has been sweetened with more. Its dough also contains egg, which gives it a golden colour and a tender chew, and it is traditionally baked in a wood-burning oven, which gives the crust its faint smoky blistering. They are rolled by hand, with the dough formed into a rope and wrapped around the fingers, and the bakeries turn them out through the day and night. The city's two great bagel bakeries, Fairmount, opened in 1919, and St-Viateur, which opened in 1957, are still doing it, and they are as much a part of Montreal as its smoked meat. The technique has three stages. A firm dough is kneaded and left to rise, then shaped into rings, and then the rings are boiled briefly in honey water, which sets the crust and gives the chew, before being coated in sesame or poppy seeds and baked in a very hot oven. Eat them warm from the oven, with cream cheese, or with lox.

  • Make the dough stiff. A soft dough spreads and loses the hole in the boiling water, and a firm one holds its ring shape.
  • Leave a big hole. The dough puffs in the boil and the oven, and a small hole closes up to leave a roll.
  • Do not skip the honey water. It gives the crust its sweetness and a slight shine, and it sets the surface before the bagel goes into the oven.

item.title: Pepperoni Rolls
item.description: Pepperoni rolls: soft, golden, slightly sweet rolls wrapped around sticks of spicy pepperoni and mozzarella. A West Virginia lunch-bucket classic.
item.content:encoded:
The pepperoni roll is a working man's lunch from West Virginia: a soft, slightly sweet bread roll baked around a stick of pepperoni, so that the meat melts and its spicy, orange oil flavours the dough from the inside. It is credited to Giuseppe Argiro, an Italian immigrant baker in Fairmont, who in 1927 began to sell rolls to coal miners, who needed a filling lunch that would not spoil in a lunch bucket and could be eaten with one hand, underground, without any cutlery. It was ideal. The dry, cured pepperoni kept without refrigeration, and the roll wrapped it in bread, making a self-contained meal, and the tradition has never gone away. Today it is sold in gas stations, bakeries and school cafeterias across the state, and often labelled as the state's unofficial food. The bread is a straightforward enriched dough, made with milk, butter and a little sugar, and the sweetness is what balances the salty, spicy sausage. The classic uses a stick of pepperoni, in whole pieces, and many bakers add a little mozzarella, which turns the middle molten. The cheese is not the original way, but it is the way most people ask for now. Pepperoni sticks give the best flavour, and thick slices stacked together work as well.

  • Pinch the seams tightly. If they open in the oven the cheese and oil leak out onto the tray and burn.
  • Cut the pepperoni to fit inside the dough rather than poking out. Exposed ends dry and harden in the heat.
  • Let the rolls cool for 10 minutes before eating. The filling is as hot as molten lava straight from the oven.

item.title: Poached Eggs on Toast
item.description: Poached eggs on toast: soft poached eggs with set whites and runny yolks on thick buttered toast. A British breakfast, and how to get it right.
item.content:encoded:
Poached eggs on toast is one of the most familiar British breakfasts, and one of the trickiest for anyone who has not done it a few times, because the poached egg is where an ordinary cook can come unstuck. A good one has a tender, just-set white that wraps the yolk in a neat, rounded parcel, and a yolk that is warm, thick and runny, that spills over the toast when it is cut. The secret is mainly in the egg. It must be very fresh, because in an old egg the white is thin and watery and spreads into wispy strands in the water, while a fresh egg has a thick white that holds together. It should be cracked into a small cup first, so that it can be slid gently into the pan. The water should be barely simmering, with only the occasional bubble rising, since a rolling boil tears the whites. A splash of vinegar helps the whites to set quickly, and a gentle swirl of the water before the egg goes in encourages it to wrap around itself. Three minutes gives a runny yolk and four a slightly firmer one. Draining the egg on kitchen paper before it goes onto the toast stops the toast becoming soggy, and thick, well-buttered sourdough holds up best.

  • Use the freshest eggs you can find. The white of an old egg is thin and spreads into strings, whereas a fresh one holds its shape.
  • Keep the water at a bare simmer. A rolling boil batters the eggs and tears the whites into ragged shreds.
  • Drain the eggs on kitchen paper. Water dripping onto the toast turns it soggy in seconds.

item.title: Shrewsbury Biscuits
item.description: Shrewsbury biscuits: crisp, buttery, lemon-scented biscuits cut into fluted rounds and sprinkled with sugar. A Shropshire recipe centuries old.
item.content:encoded:
Shrewsbury biscuits, once called Shrewsbury cakes, are among the oldest named biscuits in Britain, and recipes for them appear in English cookery books from the seventeenth century, when they were a fashionable treat. They come from the Shropshire town whose name they bear, and they are a simple, buttery, crisp biscuit, closer to a thin shortbread than to anything else, flavoured with lemon zest and sometimes with nutmeg, caraway or rosewater in the older recipes. The dough is made by the creaming method, with soft butter beaten with sugar, an egg added, and flour worked in until it forms a stiff, pliable dough, which is then chilled, rolled thinly and cut into rounds with a fluted cutter. It is the thickness that decides the result. Rolled to about 4 mm they bake in about ten minutes into biscuits that snap, where thicker ones are cakier and softer. The chilling matters as well, because a cold dough handles easily and holds its shape in the oven. A sprinkle of sugar on top before baking gives a slight sparkle and crunch. They keep very well, which is one reason why they were popular, and they are excellent with tea or as a base for a dessert of cream and berries.

  • Roll the dough to 4 mm. Thicker biscuits are cakey, and thinner ones can burn, so use the edge of a ruler as a guide.
  • Chill the dough properly. A cold dough rolls cleanly and keeps its fluted edge, but warm dough sticks and loses its shape in the oven.
  • Watch the last 2 minutes. They colour quickly, and the best Shrewsbury biscuits are barely golden.

item.title: Yogurt Parfait
item.description: Yogurt parfait: layers of thick honey-vanilla Greek yoghurt, crunchy granola and fresh berries in a tall glass. A fresh, filling ten-minute breakfast.
item.content:encoded:
Parfait is the French word for perfect, and in French cooking it is a frozen dessert of cream, eggs and sugar. In American cafes and diners it came to mean something quite different, a tall glass of yoghurt layered with fruit and granola, and this is now one of the most popular breakfasts and snacks in the United States. It has caught on because it hits every mark. It is fresh, sweet and tangy, crunchy and creamy at the same time, and a good source of protein, and it is quick enough to put together on a weekday morning. The structure is the whole idea. Thick Greek yoghurt gives the creamy base, and it is best sweetened with a little honey and vanilla, which makes it taste more like a dessert. Granola brings the crunch, and berries give brightness and juice. Layering them, instead of stirring them together, keeps the granola crisp and lets each spoonful have a bit of everything. Whatever else you do, keep the granola dry until the last moment, because it softens if it sits in the yoghurt for more than an hour or two, and if you are preparing the parfaits ahead, put the granola on top and add it when you serve. Any berries work well, or use ripe peaches, mango or stewed rhubarb.

  • Use thick, strained Greek yoghurt. Thin yoghurt runs into the berries and makes the granola soggy.
  • Put the granola in at the last minute if you are making the parfaits ahead. It stays crisp for a few hours only, and longer if it is on top.
  • Taste the yoghurt before you layer it. Tart yoghurts and sharp berries may need another spoonful of honey.

item.title: Ambrosia Salad
item.description: Ambrosia salad: mandarin oranges, pineapple, coconut and marshmallows folded into soured cream and whipped cream. The retro Southern potluck dessert.
item.content:encoded:
Ambrosia salad is a dessert masquerading as a salad, a creamy, sweet, cool mixture of tinned fruit, coconut and marshmallows that has been a fixture of potlucks, church suppers and holiday tables across the American South for well over a century. The name is the Greek word for the food of the gods, and the first ambrosias of the nineteenth century were much simpler and more elegant than the one people know today: just layers of sliced oranges and fresh grated coconut, served at Christmas, when oranges were a luxury. The version most Americans grew up with dates from the mid-twentieth century, when tinned mandarins and pineapple, mini marshmallows and whipped topping arrived in the supermarket and were added by home cooks. It is a dessert that some people dismiss and others adore, and this version makes the best of it. Soured cream is folded into fresh whipped cream to cut the sweetness and give the dressing a slight tang, and the fruit is drained very thoroughly, since any surplus juice makes the whole thing runny. The marshmallows soften in the dressing as it chills, which is why it needs at least a couple of hours in the fridge, and some of them dissolve to make it thicker and creamier. Grapes and pecans are optional but add crunch and freshness.

  • Drain the fruit very well and pat it dry. Extra juice thins the dressing and makes a watery salad.
  • Fold in gently. Stirring hard breaks up the segments of mandarin and knocks the air out of the cream.
  • Give it time in the fridge. The marshmallows soften as they chill, and after a couple of hours the salad is creamier and thicker.

item.title: Arctic Roll
item.description: Arctic roll: vanilla ice cream rolled up inside a raspberry jam-spread sponge and frozen until firm. The classic British freezer dessert.
item.content:encoded:
The arctic roll is a British nostalgia dessert, a log of vanilla ice cream wrapped in a thin layer of sponge with a spiral of raspberry jam, sliced into rounds and served, and it was one of the great freezer treats of the 1950s and 1960s, when domestic freezers made frozen desserts a novelty and a Sunday lunch was not complete without one. It became a supermarket staple when it was launched as a frozen product in the 1950s, and for a generation it was simply what a pudding looked like. It is a piece of clever, simple engineering. A thin sponge is baked in a shallow tin, spread with jam and rolled up around a core of softened ice cream, and the whole thing is frozen firm. The sponge is a whisked one, made from eggs, sugar and flour, with no fat, and it is what makes it possible to roll without cracking, as long as it is rolled while still warm and left to cool in the roll. When the ice cream is added, it must be soft enough to shape, but not melted, and the roll must be wrapped tightly and frozen for several hours before slicing. Sliced with a knife dipped in hot water, it gives neat rounds with a spiral of jam, and the whole thing is best served with more raspberry sauce.

  • Roll the sponge while it is hot. It sets in the rolled shape, and unrolls and rerolls without cracking, but a cold sponge splits.
  • Work quickly with the ice cream. It should be soft, not runny, and if it starts to melt, put the roll into the freezer for 10 minutes.
  • Dip the knife in hot water between slices. It cuts through the frozen ice cream cleanly and leaves a neat spiral.

item.title: Banana Cream Pie
item.description: Banana cream pie: sliced bananas layered in thick homemade vanilla custard in a buttery biscuit crust, with whipped cream and chocolate on top.
item.content:encoded:
Banana cream pie is one of the great American diner desserts, a tall slice of soft vanilla custard and sliced banana in a crisp crust under a cloud of whipped cream, and it has been on the pie shelf since bananas became widely available in the United States in the late nineteenth century. What separates a good one from a mediocre one is the custard. It is a real pastry cream, made with milk, egg yolks, sugar and cornflour cooked on the hob until thick, and finished with butter and vanilla off the heat, and it needs to be thick enough to stand up in a slice, silky and rich instead of pudding-like. The key to a smooth result is to whisk constantly, and to bring it to a bubble for a full minute after it thickens, which cooks out the raw flavour of the cornflour and makes sure it will set. The bananas are the other detail. They should be ripe but firm, with just a few spots, since underripe ones are starchy and overripe ones are mushy and turn brown. Tossing the slices in a little lemon juice helps them hold their colour. A crust of crushed biscuits and butter is simple and needs only ten minutes in the oven, and the pie is chilled for several hours to set fully.

  • Whisk the custard constantly and cook it for the full minute after it thickens. It cooks out the starchy taste and makes it set firm.
  • Press cling film directly on the surface of the custard. Otherwise a skin forms, and it leaves rubbery lumps in the filling.
  • Use ripe but firm bananas and slice them just before layering. Slices left standing brown quickly.

item.title: Butterscotch Pudding
item.description: Butterscotch pudding: a silky pudding made from brown sugar and butter cooked to a deep caramel, set with egg yolks and cornflour. Rich and grown-up.
item.content:encoded:
Butterscotch pudding is one of the great American comfort desserts, and one of the first things to disappear from a lunch counter, but the smooth, orange-brown pudding that comes from a packet is only a distant relative of a true butterscotch. Real butterscotch is made from brown sugar and butter cooked together until the sugar is deep, dark and slightly toasty, and it has a flavour that is quite different from caramel, which is made from white sugar and cooked until it is bitter. It is warmer, rounder and more buttery. The technique here starts with the butterscotch itself: butter, dark brown sugar and salt are heated until they bubble and smell like toffee, and cream is poured in to stop the cooking and make a sauce. That sauce is combined with a custard base of milk, egg yolks and cornflour, and cooked until thick, glossy and bubbling. It needs constant whisking, since custard scorches easily, and a full minute of bubbling at the end to cook the cornflour and make sure it sets. The result is a pudding that is dense, silky and dark with a deep flavour, which is served cold, topped with softly whipped cream and a pinch of flaky sea salt. The salt lifts the caramel notes.

  • Cook the sugar and butter until it smells like toffee. Underdone, it tastes only sweet, and overdone, it goes bitter.
  • Add the warm butterscotch to the milk slowly at first. Adding it all at once can scramble the egg yolks.
  • Strain the pudding into the glasses. It catches any small lumps of cooked egg and gives a perfectly smooth finish.

item.title: Chocolate-Covered Strawberries
item.description: Chocolate-covered strawberries: ripe strawberries dipped in glossy dark chocolate and drizzled with white chocolate. An elegant treat in half an hour.
item.content:encoded:
Chocolate-covered strawberries are the simplest dessert that looks as if it took effort, and they are a favourite for Valentine's Day, anniversaries, wedding tables and parties. They are also very easy to get wrong in small ways. The first rule is that the strawberries must be completely dry. Any drop of water that touches melted chocolate makes it seize into a thick, grainy paste that cannot be rescued, and water clinging to the fruit can also cause the chocolate to slide off. So the berries are washed ahead of time and dried very thoroughly on kitchen paper, then left until there is no moisture at all. The second rule is to melt the chocolate gently. Overheated chocolate goes dull and thick, and a bowl over barely simmering water or short bursts in the microwave, with plenty of stirring, keeps it glossy. A teaspoon of oil thins the chocolate slightly and gives a smoother coat. The strawberries are dipped holding the stems, coated two-thirds of the way up and allowed to drip, then set on baking paper, which they release from cleanly once they are cold. A drizzle of white chocolate in a zigzag pattern looks striking. Choose large, firm, ripe, red strawberries with fresh green stems.

  • Dry the strawberries completely. A single drop of water makes melted chocolate seize into a thick paste, and a wet berry will not hold its coating.
  • Melt the chocolate slowly. A little steam is enough to ruin it, and it should stay glossy and smooth.
  • Serve the same day. The berries release juice under the chocolate over time, and the coating goes soft and can leak.

item.title: Nut Roast
item.description: Nut roast: a savoury loaf of ground nuts, chestnuts, mushrooms, sage and cranberries baked golden and sliceable. A vegan Christmas centrepiece.
item.content:encoded:
The nut roast is the traditional British vegetarian Christmas centrepiece, a dense, savoury loaf of ground nuts and vegetables that is meant to sit at the head of the table and be carved in slices with all the trimmings. It has a bad reputation among people who have been served a dry, heavy one, but a good nut roast is moist, well seasoned and full of texture, and it is worth making for its own sake. The mixture is built in layers of flavour. Onion, celery and mushrooms are cooked down until their moisture has evaporated, which concentrates their savoury taste, and garlic, sage, thyme, tomato purée and soy sauce add the depth and umami that meat would supply. A mix of nuts gives richness, with cashews for creaminess, hazelnuts for sweetness and walnuts for bitterness, and they are ground to a coarse crumb, not a paste, so that the roast has texture. Cooked chestnuts add sweetness and a soft, earthy bite, and dried cranberries give sharp, jewel-like bursts of colour. Breadcrumbs and a flax binder hold it together, which means it is vegan, and vegetable stock keeps it moist. The roast is baked covered at first, to steam and set, and then uncovered to brown the top. It should rest for ten minutes before slicing, or it will crumble.

  • Cook the mushrooms until they are dry. Their moisture is the commonest cause of a soggy, crumbly roast, and it takes 8 minutes to drive it off.
  • Do not grind the nuts to a paste. A coarse crumb gives texture and stops the roast from being dense and heavy.
  • Rest the roast for 10 minutes before slicing. It firms up as it cools slightly, and cuts cleanly instead of crumbling.

item.title: Pineapple Fritters
item.description: Pineapple fritters: pineapple rings in a light, crisp batter, deep-fried until golden and rolled in cinnamon sugar. An Aussie chippie favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Pineapple fritters are a fixture of the Australian fish and chip shop, where a golden, battered ring of hot sweet pineapple, rolled in cinnamon sugar and wrapped in paper, is the dessert that follows a dim sim and a serve of chips. It is one of those simple dishes that is much better than the sum of its parts. The hot batter is crisp, light and slightly sweet, and inside is a ring of fruit that has been warmed through until it is soft and jammy, with a sharp acidity that cuts the sweetness and grease. The technique is to make sure that the fruit is very dry. Tinned pineapple rings are easiest, and they must be drained and patted with kitchen paper until their surface is barely damp, or the batter will slide off in the oil. The batter itself is a simple mix of flour, baking powder, sugar, egg and cold milk, and it should be thick enough to coat the fruit in a thin, even layer. It is best used after a ten-minute rest. The oil should be hot, at about 180°C, so that the batter puffs and sets at once, and the fritters should be fried in small batches, for two minutes a side. Roll them in cinnamon sugar while still hot, so that it sticks, and serve at once with ice cream.

  • Dry the pineapple thoroughly, and dust it with flour. Batter slides off wet fruit, and the flour gives it something to grip.
  • Fry in small batches. Too many rings at once lower the oil temperature, and the batter soaks up grease and turns soggy.
  • Roll the fritters in the cinnamon sugar straight away. The sugar sticks only to a hot, freshly fried surface.

item.title: Pumpkin Cheesecake
item.description: Pumpkin cheesecake: a dense, silky baked cheesecake with pumpkin, cinnamon, ginger and nutmeg on a spiced biscuit crust. Thanksgiving in a slice.
item.content:encoded:
Pumpkin cheesecake is the answer to a question that arises every November in the United States: pumpkin pie or cheesecake? It combines the spiced, earthy flavour of pumpkin pie with the dense, tangy, creamy texture of a baked cheesecake, and it is one of the most popular alternatives to the Thanksgiving pie. The base is a crust of crushed biscuits, butter and a little cinnamon, and the filling is a cream cheese custard, loosened with soured cream and lightly thickened with a spoonful of cornflour, and flavoured with pumpkin purée and the warm spices that belong to it: cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg and a pinch of cloves. Like all baked cheesecakes, it must be baked gently and cooled slowly. A high heat makes the eggs puff up and the surface crack, so the oven is set to a moderate 160°C and the cheesecake is baked until the edges are set but the centre still wobbles like jelly, at which point it is switched off and left in the oven with the door ajar for an hour, so that it cools gradually and stays smooth. It then needs to chill for at least six hours, to set and to let the flavours develop, which is why it is a good make-ahead dessert. Use plain pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, and make sure the cream cheese is at room temperature, so that the batter is lump-free.

  • Have everything at room temperature. Cold cream cheese leaves lumps that will not beat out, and cold eggs can make the batter split.
  • Mix on low once the eggs go in. Too much air makes the cheesecake puff up in the oven and crack as it sinks back.
  • Turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. The gradual cooling stops the sudden shrinking that cracks the top.

item.title: Puppy Chow
item.description: Puppy chow: crunchy square cereal coated in melted chocolate and peanut butter, then shaken in icing sugar. A Midwestern party snack.
item.content:encoded:
Puppy chow, also known as muddy buddies, is an American snack made of crisp square cereal coated in melted chocolate and peanut butter and then shaken in a bag of icing sugar until each piece is coated in a sweet, powdery crust. It has nothing whatever to do with dog food, apart from a passing resemblance, and it comes from the Midwest, where it turns up at holiday parties, football games, bake sales and school events, and in Christmas gift tins. The recipe is not a recipe in the usual sense, since it needs almost no cooking, and the entire job is done in a bowl in a few minutes. The chocolate, peanut butter and butter are melted together in short bursts in the microwave, and stirred until smooth, and it is poured over the cereal, which must be folded gently so that the pieces do not break. The coating is what makes it work. The butter in the mixture stops it from setting as hard as chocolate alone, so that it stays a little soft and sticks the icing sugar on. The cereal is then tossed with the icing sugar in a large bag, which coats every piece evenly, and spread out on baking paper to set. Use plain square rice or corn cereal, such as Chex, which are light and crisp and have plenty of surface for the coating to cling to.

  • Fold the cereal gently. It is thin and brittle and breaks into crumbs if you stir it vigorously.
  • Coat the cereal while the chocolate is still warm. Once it hardens, the icing sugar has nothing to stick to.
  • Shake in a bag in 2 batches. Overcrowding the bag means some pieces are bare and others end up in clumps.

item.title: Rhubarb Custard Pie
item.description: Rhubarb custard pie: tart pink rhubarb baked in a sweet, creamy, orange-scented custard inside a flaky butter crust. A Canadian prairie favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Rhubarb custard pie is one of the most beloved pies in Canada, especially on the prairies, where rhubarb grows in nearly every garden and comes up so early in spring that it is often the first fresh fruit of the year. Rhubarb is a vegetable that is eaten as a fruit, with tart, tangy stalks that need a lot of sugar, and it pairs beautifully with the mild, creamy sweetness of a baked custard, which mellows the acidity and turns the whole into something soft and rich. A fruit pie made with rhubarb alone can be watery and sharp, and the custard fixes that. The eggs and flour in the custard bind the juices as they come out of the fruit, so it sets in the oven into a tender wedge rather than a puddle, and a little cream makes it silky. The important detail is the baking. It starts hot, at 200°C, to set the bottom crust before the filling can soak it, and then the oven is turned down to 175°C so that the custard bakes gently, without curdling. The pie is done when the centre is just set and only slightly wobbly, and it must be left to cool for at least two hours, when the custard finishes setting. Cutting a warm rhubarb custard pie gives a runny slice.

  • Cut the rhubarb into even pieces about 2 cm long. Thick stalks take longer to soften, and chunks of different sizes bake unevenly.
  • Start at 200°C for 15 minutes. The initial heat sets the bottom crust before the custard can soak into it and make it soggy.
  • Cool the pie for a full 2 hours. The custard firms up as it cools, and a warm pie cuts into a runny, messy slice.

item.title: Sussex Pond Pudding
item.description: Sussex pond pudding: a suet crust around butter, sugar and a whole lemon, steamed for four hours until it makes its own pond of sticky, tart syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Sussex pond pudding is one of the most unusual and delightful of the old English steamed puddings, a plain suet crust wrapped around a whole lemon, buried in butter and sugar. As it steams, the butter and sugar melt into a rich, golden, caramelised syrup that pools inside the pudding, and when the pudding is cut and turned out, that syrup flows out around it like a pond, which is where the name comes from. The lemon is the surprise. It is pricked all over so that its juice and oils can escape into the syrup, and after four hours of steaming it is soft, sweet and sharp, and can be eaten whole, skin and all, or sliced and shared, so that each person has a piece of the pulp in their bowl. Recipes for the pudding date to the seventeenth century, and it is a very old and very English pudding, from a time when steamed puddings were the everyday sweet dish. The suet pastry is simple to make, and it is the steaming that takes time, at least three and a half hours, and preferably four, in a pan of simmering water that is topped up as it evaporates. The reward is a dessert that nothing else resembles, with a light, tender crust and a sauce that is sweet and sharp, buttery and tart at once. Use a good unwaxed lemon.

  • Seal the lid firmly. If the seam opens during the long steaming, the syrup leaks into the water and the pond is lost.
  • Keep the water at a steady simmer and top it up with boiling water. A pan that boils dry can burn the basin, and cold water halts the cooking.
  • Prick the lemon well. Juice and oils escape into the syrup during steaming, and an unpricked lemon can burst.

item.title: Candied Pecans
item.description: Candied pecans: pecan halves in a whisked egg white, sugar and cinnamon glaze, baked low and slow until crisp. For salads, cheese boards and gifts.
item.content:encoded:
Candied pecans are the sweet, crunchy, cinnamon-spiced nuts that appear at Christmas markets, on salads and cheese boards, in gift jars and at the bottom of a good sundae, and they are among the easiest and most rewarding things to make at home. The commercial ones are often chewy or sticky, but the oven-baked method used here gives a crisp, dry, lightly sugared shell that shatters when bitten. The technique is a very old confectionery idea: a meringue-style coating of whisked egg white, sugar and spices is folded over the nuts, and the nuts are then baked very slowly at a low temperature, which dries the coating rather than browning it, and turns it into a crisp, glassy shell on the surface of each nut. The egg white is what makes the sugar cling, and it means that the coating is thin and light and does not make a sticky clump. Stirring the nuts every fifteen minutes stops them sticking to the tray and to each other. Pecans, native to North America and long a staple of the Southern kitchen, are the classic choice, because their buttery, slightly bitter flavour balances the sugar, but walnuts and almonds work well too. Cool the nuts completely on the tray, when they will finish crisping, and then break them apart.

  • Bake low and slow. A hot oven browns the sugar and makes it taste bitter before the coating has dried.
  • Stir the nuts every 15 minutes. It stops them sticking to the paper, and gives an even coating.
  • Cool them completely before storing. Warm nuts are still soft, and trapped steam makes them sticky.

item.title: Chex Mix
item.description: Chex Mix: crisp square cereals, pretzels and mixed nuts tossed in butter, Worcestershire sauce and savoury seasonings, then baked low until crunchy.
item.content:encoded:
Chex Mix is the American party snack, a bowl of crunchy, savoury, buttery, salty cereal, pretzels and nuts that has been on coffee tables at holiday gatherings, in car snack bags and at game-day tailgates since the 1950s, when the manufacturer of Chex cereals began printing the recipe on the box. It has been made at home ever since, and the homemade version is much better than anything in a bag. The idea is to build a snack with different textures and shapes, so that every handful is a little different. There are three kinds of square cereal, rice, corn and wheat, which absorb the seasoning differently, pretzel sticks for salt and crunch, and mixed nuts for richness. Butter melted with Worcestershire sauce, garlic and onion powder and seasoned salt coats everything, and it needs to be poured over in a thin stream, and stirred very gently so that the cereal does not crumble. What makes it crisp instead of soggy is the baking. It goes into a low oven, at 120°C, for an hour, and is stirred every fifteen minutes, which dries the coating slowly and evenly, and turns the seasoning into a crisp, savoury glaze. It is done when it feels dry and crunchy, and continues to crisp as it cools. Add bagel chips, rye chips or cheese crackers if you like.

  • Pour the butter mixture over slowly, and stir gently. Fast stirring breaks up the square cereal, and pouring it all at once leaves patches uncoated.
  • Stir every 15 minutes and keep the oven low. It dries evenly instead of scorching, and the seasoning does not burn.
  • Let it cool completely on paper. The mix continues to crisp as it cools, and grease drains away.

item.title: Fried Mushrooms
item.description: Fried mushrooms: whole button mushrooms in seasoned flour, egg and crisp panko crumbs, deep-fried until golden. Serve hot with ranch or garlic mayo.
item.content:encoded:
Breaded fried mushrooms are one of the great American bar and diner appetisers, and one of the best ways to change a mushroom's reputation. A whole button mushroom in a crisp, golden crust is a different thing altogether from a soft, sautéed one, because the coating seals the mushroom in as it cooks and the steam keeps it juicy and tender, while the outside becomes crunchy. It is one of the family of breaded and fried vegetables, with onion rings, pickles and zucchini fries, that turns up on pub menus from Wisconsin to Texas. The three-stage coating is the usual way to make it stick: seasoned flour first, which dries the surface and gives the egg something to hold, then beaten egg, then panko breadcrumbs, which are coarser and lighter than ordinary crumbs and fry to a much crisper crust. It is worth pressing the crumbs on firmly, since loose crumbs fall off in the oil. The mushrooms must be dry when they go in, so wipe them with a damp cloth rather than washing them, since mushrooms absorb water like sponges and a wet mushroom makes a soggy coating. The oil should be at 175°C, and the mushrooms fried in small batches for two to three minutes, until they are a deep golden brown. Serve them very hot, with a cool dip.

  • Wipe the mushrooms rather than washing them. They soak up water, and a damp mushroom makes a soggy coating that will not stay on.
  • Press the panko on firmly with your palm. It stops the crumbs falling off in the oil, and gives a thick, even crust.
  • Fry at 175°C in small batches. Cooler oil makes the coating greasy, and crowding lowers the temperature.

item.title: Hot Lemon and Honey
item.description: Hot lemon and honey: fresh lemon juice and a spoonful of honey stirred into hot water, with a slice of ginger. The comforting British home drink.
item.content:encoded:
A mug of hot lemon and honey is the classic British home comfort, the drink that has been made for generations when someone has a cold, when the weather turns, or when it is just the end of a long day. It requires no special skill and only three ingredients, and it is one of those things where getting the details right makes it a good deal better than the drink that most people make. The first detail is the water, which should be hot but not boiling. Water straight from the kettle at 100°C dulls the delicate fragrance of the lemon and the honey, and letting it sit for a minute or so, until it is about 80°C, gives a smoother, brighter drink. The second is the lemon, which must be fresh. The juice from a bottle has a flat, sour taste, and squeezing a fresh lemon gives a fragrant, fruity juice with oils from the zest. A slice of the lemon in the mug adds more aroma. The honey is a matter of taste, and it should be stirred in after the water has cooled slightly, so that it dissolves and keeps its flavour. A few slices of fresh ginger and a cinnamon stick, steeped for a few minutes, make it warming and spicy. It is comforting and soothing, but no drink can cure a cold, so enjoy it for what it is.

  • Let the water cool for a minute after boiling. It gives a fresher, brighter flavour than water at a full boil.
  • Squeeze the lemon fresh. Bottled juice has a flat, harsh taste, and the fresh oil from the zest makes a big difference.
  • Add the honey after the water has cooled slightly. It dissolves easily and keeps its floral flavour.

item.title: Lemon, Lime and Bitters
item.description: Lemon, lime and bitters: lime cordial, fresh lemon and lemonade over ice with a few dashes of Angostura bitters. The Aussie pub soft drink.
item.content:encoded:
Lemon, lime and bitters, or LLB, is the great Australian non-drink drink, the one that gets ordered at the pub, the bowls club, the footy and the barbecue by people who do not want a beer, or who are driving, and it is so much a part of Australian drinking culture that bartenders everywhere in the country will make one without asking for details. It is served in a tall glass over ice, and it is pale pink from a few dashes of Angostura bitters, which are the secret. Bitters are a concentrated infusion of herbs, roots and spices, and although they are technically alcoholic, at about 45 per cent, the few dashes used here contribute a negligible amount, and they give the drink a warm, spicy, aromatic depth that turns sweet lemonade into something more grown-up and refreshing. The rest is simple. Lime cordial gives a sweet, tart, citrus flavour, a squeeze of fresh lemon sharpens it, and lemonade, which in Australia means a clear, fizzy, lemon-flavoured soft drink like the British kind, supplies the sparkle. It is a drink that depends more on balance than on precision, so taste it as you go. Use plenty of ice, and a lemon wheel and a lime wedge to garnish. Leave out the bitters entirely for a completely alcohol-free version.

  • Use plenty of ice and chilled lemonade. The drink is best when it is very cold and lively, and it goes flat and sweet as the ice melts.
  • Add the bitters last, and go by taste. A few dashes give a warm, spicy note, but too many make it taste medicinal.
  • Squeeze the lemon fresh. A little real acidity stops the cordial and lemonade from tasting sugary, and it gives the drink a bright, clean finish.

item.title: Long Island Iced Tea
item.description: Long Island iced tea: vodka, gin, rum, tequila and triple sec with lemon and a splash of cola so that it looks like iced tea. Very strong.
item.content:encoded:
The Long Island iced tea is the cocktail that contains no tea at all. It is a tall, amber-brown drink that looks entirely innocent, and it is made from five different spirits, vodka, gin, white rum, tequila and triple sec, with lemon juice, a little sugar syrup and a splash of cola, which gives it the colour and the name. It is a notoriously strong cocktail, with about three units of alcohol in a single glass, and it is usually said to have been created in 1972 by a bartender named Robert Butt at the Oak Beach Inn on Long Island, New York, in a competition to invent a new cocktail using triple sec, although a Prohibition-era origin in Kingsport, Tennessee, is also claimed. Its appeal is the mix of two things: it tastes like a sweet, sharp, fizzy lemon and cola drink, and it hides the strength very well. That is exactly why it should be handled with care. The spirits are measured in equal parts, 15 ml each, which is less than you might think, and the lemon juice must be fresh, since the sharpness balances the sugar and the alcohol. The cola goes on top, in a small splash, so that it tints the drink without making it too sweet, and it is stirred once and served over plenty of ice. Drink it slowly, and not more than one.

  • Measure the spirits carefully. It is easy to be generous, and this drink is strong even with correct measures.
  • Use fresh lemon juice. The sharpness balances the sugar and the alcohol, and bottled juice makes a flat drink.
  • Add the cola last, in a small splash. Too much cola makes it sweet and hides the citrus, and it kills the fizz.

item.title: Mai Tai
item.description: Mai Tai: aged rum, orange curaçao, almond orgeat and fresh lime juice shaken hard and poured over crushed ice. The tiki classic, tart and nutty.
item.content:encoded:
The Mai Tai is the definitive tiki cocktail, and it is a great deal better than the sweet, fruit-juice-laden versions served at resorts and beach bars. It is generally credited to Victor Bergeron, known as Trader Vic, who is said to have made the first one in 1944 at his restaurant in Oakland, California, for friends from Tahiti, who took a sip and exclaimed, Maita'i roa ae, which means out of this world, or the best. His rival, Donn Beach, has always claimed to have invented it first, and the argument has never been resolved. The original was built simply, with good aged rum, fresh lime juice, orange curaçao, orgeat, which is a sweet almond syrup with a hint of orange flower water, and a little sugar. There was no pineapple juice, no grenadine and no orange juice. What makes it work is the interplay of those flavours. The rum brings depth and a little funk, the lime supplies acidity, the curaçao brings orange, and the orgeat gives a nutty richness and a silky texture that softens the whole drink. It should be shaken hard with ice, then poured, ice and all, into a glass filled with crushed ice, and garnished with a spent lime shell and a big sprig of mint, which you can smell as you drink. Use the best aged rum that you can, since it is the star.

  • Use fresh lime juice, and a good aged rum. There is nothing in the drink to hide either, and it is the quality of both that shows.
  • Shake hard and pour everything into the glass, ice and all. The dilution is part of the recipe.
  • Slap the mint before you use it. The aroma is the first thing you notice as you drink, and it makes a difference to the taste.

item.title: Mimosa
item.description: Mimosa: equal parts chilled fresh orange juice and dry sparkling wine in a flute. The three-minute brunch cocktail.
item.content:encoded:
The mimosa is the brunch cocktail, the drink that seems to appear as soon as the words eggs and Sunday are put together, and it is made from only two ingredients, orange juice and sparkling wine, in roughly equal parts. It is credited to the Ritz Hotel in Paris, where the bartender Frank Meier is said to have created it in 1925, and it was named after the mimosa flower, whose yellow-orange blossom matches the colour of the drink. It is a close relation of the Buck's Fizz, which was invented in London at Buck's Club in 1921, and is made with two parts of Champagne to one part of orange juice. Because there is nothing in a mimosa to hide behind, its success depends entirely on the quality of the two ingredients and on their temperature. The orange juice should be freshly squeezed and pulp-free, since the flavour is brighter and sweeter than anything from a carton, and both it and the wine must be thoroughly chilled, so that no ice is needed and the bubbles last. The sparkling wine should be dry, which means labelled brut or extra dry, because the juice already supplies plenty of sweetness. Prosecco and Cava are perfect and much less expensive than Champagne, and a good mimosa does not need an expensive bottle. Pour the wine first, in a tilted glass, to prevent it from foaming over, and then add the juice.

  • Squeeze the juice fresh, and strain out the pulp. It gives a brighter flavour than carton juice, and the pulp makes the fizz collapse.
  • Choose a dry sparkling wine. A sweet one, added to sweet juice, makes a cloying drink.
  • Pour the wine first and the juice second. The wine foams less this way, and the two mix themselves without stirring.

item.title: Paloma
item.description: Paloma: blanco tequila, fresh grapefruit and lime juice and a splash of soda over ice in a salt-rimmed glass. Mexico's favourite tequila cocktail.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a Mexican bartender what the country's most popular tequila drink is, and the answer will be a Paloma, not a Margarita. It is a long, fizzy, refreshing mix of tequila and grapefruit, and it is everywhere in Mexico, from cantinas and beach bars to family parties. Its name is Spanish for dove, and the story that is most often told credits it to Don Javier Delgado Corona, who ran the bar La Capilla in the town of Tequila, in Jalisco, although no one can be sure. The traditional way to make one is very informal, simply tequila and a grapefruit soda such as Squirt or Jarritos, served over ice in a tall glass with a squeeze of lime, and a pinch of salt. This version is a little more careful. It uses fresh grapefruit juice, plus fresh lime juice and a drop of agave syrup, with soda water to lengthen it, which gives a brighter, drier, more balanced drink, with the pleasing bitterness of grapefruit, without the sweetness of the bottled soda. A rim of flaky salt sets off the citrus and it takes the edge off the bitterness. Choose a blanco tequila made from 100 per cent agave, since its clean, peppery, vegetal flavour is at home with grapefruit, and use a ruby grapefruit for a sweeter, prettier drink.

  • Squeeze the grapefruit and lime juice fresh. Bottled juices are flat, and the drink depends on their bright acidity.
  • Salt only half the rim, or just the outer edge. Salt inside the glass makes every sip taste salty, and some people prefer none.
  • Taste it before you serve it. Grapefruits vary a lot in sweetness, so add a little more agave if it is too bitter, or a squeeze more lime if it is too sweet.

item.title: Popcorn Shrimp
item.description: Popcorn shrimp: bite-size shrimp coated in seasoned flour, egg and panko and deep-fried until golden and crunchy. The seafood-shack snack.
item.content:encoded:
Popcorn shrimp is the fried seafood that people order at beach shacks, chain restaurants and seafood counters, and it is named for its size, since the shrimp are small, and the way that it is eaten, by the handful, out of a paper cone or a basket. It is a natural for home cooking, because once the shrimp are prepared the frying takes barely two minutes. The coating is what defines it. A three-step breading of seasoned flour, beaten egg and panko breadcrumbs gives a thick, crunchy, golden crust that stays crisp long enough to be dipped, and the seasoning of paprika, garlic powder and a little cayenne makes it much more interesting than a plain crumb. The key to success is to make sure that the shrimp are dry. Moisture on the surface stops the flour from sticking, so they should be patted thoroughly with kitchen paper before they are dredged. It is also essential not to overcook them. Small shrimp cook in less than two minutes, and they turn rubbery if they are left longer, so fry them in batches, keep the oil at 180°C, and take them out as soon as they are golden. Serve them at once, with cocktail sauce or tartare sauce and lemon wedges, or toss them in a spicy mayonnaise for a version known as bang bang shrimp.

  • Dry the shrimp very well before coating them. Damp shrimp make the flour go gluey, and the crumbs slide off in the fryer.
  • Do not fry them for more than 2 minutes. Small shrimp overcook very quickly, and they turn rubbery and tough.
  • Fry in batches and keep the oil at 180°C. Crowding lowers the temperature and makes the coating greasy.

item.title: Shrimp Remoulade
item.description: Shrimp remoulade: chilled boiled shrimp in a tangy Creole remoulade of mustard, horseradish and paprika, on shredded lettuce. A New Orleans starter.
item.content:encoded:
Shrimp remoulade is a New Orleans classic, a plate of cold, boiled, plump shrimp coated in a piquant orange-pink sauce and served on a bed of shredded lettuce, and it has been a first course in the restaurants of the French Quarter for more than a century. The sauce is the story. Remoulade is a French idea, a mayonnaise-based sauce with pickles, capers and herbs, but in Louisiana it was transformed by Creole cooks into something bolder and spicier, sharpened with Creole mustard, horseradish and lemon, coloured red with paprika, and given a kick with cayenne and hot sauce. Spring onions, celery and parsley add freshness and crunch. The shrimp are simply boiled in a well-seasoned liquid with lemon, bay leaves and Creole seasoning until just cooked, which takes only two to three minutes, and then cooled quickly in iced water to stop the cooking, since overcooked shrimp turn rubbery and tough. They should be chilled for an hour in the sauce, which is when the flavours blend and the shrimp absorb the seasoning. It is a dish that has to be made ahead, which is what makes it so good for entertaining. Serve on shredded lettuce, with lemon wedges and hot sauce on the side, and plenty of cold beer.

  • Take the shrimp out after 2 to 3 minutes. They keep cooking in the hot water, and once curled tightly into a circle they are overcooked.
  • Cool them in iced water. It stops the cooking at once and keeps the shrimp plump and firm.
  • Dry the shrimp before adding the sauce. Water dilutes the remoulade and makes it thin and pale.

item.title: Thai Fish Cakes
item.description: Thai fish cakes: springy white fish patties with red curry paste, fish sauce, green beans and lime leaf, fried until golden. Serve with sweet chilli.
item.content:encoded:
Thai fish cakes, known as tod mun pla, are one of the best-loved snacks in Thailand and one of the most popular starters on Thai restaurant menus around the world, including in Australia, where they are a fixture of takeaway menus. They are quite unlike a Western fish cake, which is soft, breadcrumbed and mostly potato. A Thai fish cake is made from fish alone, pounded or processed to a sticky paste with red curry paste, and it is springy and bouncy, almost like a fish sausage, and intensely fragrant. The curry paste supplies chilli, lemongrass, galangal and garlic, and fish sauce gives it its savoury depth, while a small amount of sugar and cornflour bind the mixture and help it hold together. The secret to the texture is the processing. The fish is worked in a food processor for a good minute, until the proteins have been broken down and the paste is sticky and elastic, and this gives it the bounce. Finely sliced green beans add colour and a fresh snap, and shredded kaffir lime leaves add an unmistakable citrus fragrance. The patties are shaped with wet hands and shallow fried until golden, which takes only a few minutes. They are served hot, with sweet chilli sauce and a quick cucumber relish, and they make a perfect party canapé.

  • Process the fish for a full minute. It breaks down the proteins and makes the paste sticky, which is what gives the fish cakes their bouncy texture.
  • Wet your hands each time you shape one. The mixture is very sticky and clings to dry fingers.
  • Fry over medium-high heat. Too hot and the outside burns before the middle is cooked, and too cool and they absorb oil.

item.title: Watermelon Agua Fresca
item.description: Watermelon agua fresca: ripe watermelon blended with cold water and lime juice, lightly sweetened and served over ice. Mexico's summer drink.
item.content:encoded:
Agua fresca means fresh water, and it is the name for the light, chilled fruit drinks that are sold from big glass jars called vitroleros at markets, taquerias and street stalls all over Mexico, and one of the most beloved of them is the watermelon version, agua de sandía. It is nothing like a fizzy soft drink or a juice, since it is a very light blend of fruit and water, sweetened very gently, and the aim is to refresh and cool, not to fill you up. Watermelon is ideal for it. It is more than 90 per cent water, and its juice is naturally sweet, fragrant and vividly coloured, which makes it very easy to turn into a drink in less than ten minutes. The fruit is blended with cold water, which dilutes it to the right strength, and it is pressed through a fine sieve for a clear, smooth result, or left unstrained for a more rustic one with a little pulp and fibre. Lime juice is the vital ingredient, because a squeeze of acid brings out the flavour of the fruit and stops it from tasting flat. Sugar or agave is optional, since a ripe watermelon is sweet enough, and most people add only a spoonful. Serve it very cold, over plenty of ice, with mint leaves and a lime wheel. Choose a seedless watermelon that is ripe and heavy for its size.

  • Taste the watermelon first. A ripe one needs very little sugar, and a pale one needs more lime juice instead.
  • Blend just until smooth. Blending for too long warms the mixture and makes it foam.
  • Serve it very cold and stir before pouring. The pulp separates on standing and needs mixing again.

item.title: White Russian
item.description: White Russian: vodka and coffee liqueur over ice, topped with a float of cream that swirls into the dark drink. A smooth three-ingredient cocktail.
item.content:encoded:
The White Russian is a cocktail of only three ingredients, vodka, coffee liqueur and cream, and it is a drink that tastes like a very grown-up milkshake. It is served in a short glass over ice, with the cream poured gently over the top so that it floats, and then either left in layers, to be mixed by the drinker, or stirred gently until it turns a rich, pale coffee colour. It descends from the Black Russian, the same drink without the cream, which is said to have been invented in 1949 by a Belgian bartender named Gustave Tops at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels, for the American ambassador to Luxembourg. The addition of cream came in the 1960s, and the drink was given a huge second life by the 1998 film The Big Lebowski, whose main character, the Dude, drinks nothing else. The recipe depends on proportions and on the ingredients. The standard ratio is two parts of vodka to one part of coffee liqueur and one part of cream, and any variation is a matter of taste. The vodka should be a smooth, clean, good-quality one, and the coffee liqueur is traditionally Kahlúa, although there are many others, some drier and more bitter. Use double cream for a rich, thick float, or whole milk or half-and-half for a lighter drink. It is quick to make, easy to drink and stronger than it seems.

  • Pour the cream over the back of a spoon. It spreads across the surface and floats, where poured straight in it plunges to the bottom and clouds the drink.
  • Use plenty of ice. It keeps the drink cold and gives some dilution, so that the cream and spirits do not feel heavy.
  • Shake it with ice and strain if you like it colder and frothier. The cream turns to a smooth, creamy foam on top.

item.title: Zucchini Fries
item.description: Zucchini fries: zucchini sticks in seasoned flour, egg and a Parmesan and panko crust, baked on a rack until golden and crisp. A lighter snack.
item.content:encoded:
Zucchini fries are one of the best ways of turning a very mild, watery vegetable into something crisp, golden and impossible to leave alone, and they have become a favourite at pubs, party tables and family dinners. Zucchini, called courgette in Britain, is the problem. It is nearly all water, and a coated stick can turn soggy, or slip from its crust, in the oven. There are three things that overcome this. The first is salt. Tossing the sticks with salt and leaving them for ten minutes draws out excess moisture, which is patted away, so the surface is dry and the crust stays put. The second is the coating, a classic three-stage breading of flour, egg and then a mixture of panko breadcrumbs and grated Parmesan, which adds flavour as well as crunch and browns to a deep gold. The third is the baking. The fries are baked on a wire rack, set over a tray, at a high temperature, 220°C, so that hot air circulates around each stick and the underside crisps as well as the top, instead of steaming against the tray. A light spray or drizzle of oil helps the crumbs to colour. They can also be cooked in an air fryer. Serve them hot, with marinara or ranch dressing, and eat them within minutes.

  • Salt the sticks and pat them dry. It draws out moisture that would otherwise make the crust soggy, and it helps the coating to stay on.
  • Bake them on a wire rack. The hot air can reach the underside, and the fries crisp on all sides instead of steaming against the tray.
  • Press the crumbs on firmly. Loose crumbs fall off in the oven, and a firm coating gives a thick, even crust.

item.title: Brunswick Stew
item.description: Brunswick stew: shredded chicken and pork simmered with tomatoes, sweetcorn, butter beans and potato in a tangy, smoky barbecue-style base.
item.content:encoded:
Brunswick stew is the thick, smoky, tomato-red stew of the American South, and it comes with an argument attached. Brunswick County in Virginia and the port of Brunswick in Georgia both claim to have invented it, and both hold cook-offs to prove the point. Early versions were hunters' stews of squirrel or rabbit. Today chicken and pork are standard, cooked until they fall into shreds, with tomatoes, sweetcorn and lima or butter beans. What sets it apart from an ordinary stew is texture. It is cooked down until it can be eaten with a fork, closer to the filling of a wet pulled-pork sandwich than to a soup, and across the barbecue belt it is served as a side beside smoked pork and ribs, often made from the leftovers of the smoker. Recipes disagree about the seasoning. Virginia versions run sweeter and milder, while Georgia and Carolina cooks push the vinegar and the hot sauce. This one lands in the middle: browned chicken thigh and pork shoulder, barbecue sauce for smoke and sweetness, cider vinegar and Worcestershire sauce for tang, and a little hot sauce for warmth. Pork shoulder gives the stew its body, because its collagen melts into the sauce, while thigh meat stays juicy where breast would dry out. Cook it slowly, and expect it to taste better tomorrow.

  • Cut the potatoes small. At 1.5 cm they cook in 20 minutes and break down a little at the edges, which helps to thicken the stew.
  • Brown the meat properly. The dark crust on the pork and chicken, and the browned bits on the base of the pot, are where the smoky, savoury depth comes from.
  • Season at the end. The stew reduces as it cooks, so the vinegar, salt and heat all concentrate. Taste in the last few minutes and correct then.

item.title: Carne Guisada
item.description: Carne guisada: Tex-Mex braised beef stewed with cumin, garlic, green pepper and tomato in a thick brown gravy. Perfect in warm flour tortillas.
item.content:encoded:
Carne guisada, which is simply "stewed meat" in Spanish, is the everyday beef stew of South Texas and northern Mexico, and one of the dishes that define Tex-Mex cooking. Chunks of beef are dredged in seasoned flour, browned, and simmered with onion, green pepper, garlic, tomato and cumin until they collapse into a thick brown gravy that clings to a spoon. It turns up at every meal: rolled into a warm flour tortilla for a breakfast taco, ladled over rice with refried beans at dinner, or scooped up with tortillas at a family table. It is not chilli con carne, which is built on dried chillies and usually eaten from a bowl, and it is not a soup. The gravy should be dark and thick enough to coat the beef, and the flour on the meat does the thickening, so no separate roux is needed. Chuck is the right cut. It is full of connective tissue that dissolves over an hour and a half of gentle simmering, which turns the sauce glossy and leaves the beef soft enough to cut with a spoon. Cumin is the signature spice, with a little chilli powder and oregano behind it, and a fresh jalapeño adds a mild heat. It reheats beautifully, so make it the day before if you can.

  • Do not skip the browning. It builds the deep, savoury flavour of the gravy, and the flour on the beef helps to form the crust.
  • Choose chuck, or another well-marbled braising cut. Lean stewing beef turns dry and stringy before the gravy has thickened.
  • For breakfast tacos, reheat leftover carne guisada with a splash of water and spoon it into flour tortillas with scrambled eggs.

item.title: Dirty Rice
item.description: Dirty rice: Louisiana Cajun rice cooked with browned pork, finely chopped chicken livers, onion, celery, green pepper and warm spices.
item.content:encoded:
Dirty rice is a Cajun staple from southern Louisiana, and the name is a compliment to its colour. Long-grain rice is cooked with browned meat, finely chopped chicken livers and the region's "holy trinity" of onion, celery and green pepper, and the minced liver and dark, savoury fond stain the grains until they look, well, dirty. Its roots are frugal. Cooks in Cajun country made it from the offal of the chicken, the gizzards and livers, stretched with rice to feed a family from very little, and it shows up on Louisiana plates beside fried chicken, as stuffing for a turkey or as a meal in itself. Today it is more often made with pork mince and livers, which is what this recipe does. If you think you dislike liver, this is the dish to try it in. It is finely chopped and cooked until it melts into the pork, so it lends a deep, rich, mineral savour without any of the graininess. The seasoning is a Cajun mix of paprika, cayenne, garlic powder and thyme, and the rice is cooked in stock so that every grain carries the flavour. Finish it with spring onions and parsley for freshness, and pass the hot sauce.

  • Chop the livers as finely as you can, or pulse them in a food processor. Small pieces melt into the meat, while large ones stay grainy.
  • Do not lift the lid while the rice cooks. The steam is what cooks the grains, and letting it out gives you a pan that is hard on top and wet underneath.
  • Brown the pork hard. The crust on the meat and the sticky bits on the pan give the rice its dark colour and roasted flavour.

item.title: Lobster Newburg
item.description: Lobster Newburg: sweet lobster in a silky sauce of butter, sherry, cream and egg yolks with cayenne and nutmeg, served over buttered toast.
item.content:encoded:
Lobster Newburg is one of the great dishes of the American restaurant tradition, a plate of lobster in a rich sauce of cream, egg yolk and sherry that arrived on the tables of grand hotels at the end of the nineteenth century. It is usually traced to Delmonico's in New York in the 1870s. The story goes that a sea captain named Ben Wenberg showed the chefs how he made it, that the dish went on the menu as Lobster à la Wenberg, and that after a falling-out with the owner it was renamed Newburg, with the letters of the name swapped around. Whatever the truth, the recipe has barely changed in a century. The lobster is warmed gently in butter, so that it stays tender, then a splash of sherry or Madeira is boiled down to concentrate its sweetness, and finally cream and yolks are stirred in over low heat until the sauce thickens. That last step is the only tricky part. The yolks thicken the sauce, and if it boils it turns to scrambled egg, so keep the heat low and stir the whole time. A pinch of cayenne and some nutmeg give a warm edge, and a squeeze of lemon lifts the richness. Serve it over buttered toast points, in puff-pastry cases or with plain rice.

  • Keep the heat low once the yolks go in. If the sauce starts to look grainy, lift the pan off the heat and whisk in a spoonful of cold cream to bring it back.
  • Buy cooked lobster meat, or steam two 600 g lobsters for 12 minutes, cool them and pick out the tail and claw meat. Overcooked lobster is rubbery, so warm it rather than cooking it again.
  • Use a real dry sherry or Madeira, not cooking wine. It is the main flavour of the sauce after the lobster.

item.title: Seafood Gumbo
item.description: Seafood gumbo: a dark roux, okra and the Cajun holy trinity simmered in shellfish stock with prawns, crab and oysters, served over steamed rice.
item.content:encoded:
Gumbo is the dish that Louisiana would choose to represent it, and a seafood gumbo is the version of the coast, made with the prawns, crab and oysters of the Gulf. Its flavour begins with the roux, flour and oil stirred over medium heat for about 40 minutes until it turns the colour of dark chocolate. That long stir gives the gumbo its nutty depth and its body, and it cannot be hurried, because a roux that scorches has to be thrown out and started again. The vegetables come next: onion, celery and green pepper, the Cajun holy trinity, which stop the roux cooking and give the pot its sweetness. Okra thickens the gumbo and gives it a silky texture, and a little tomato in the Creole style of New Orleans adds brightness. Cooks argue about whether a real gumbo should be thickened with roux, okra or filé powder made from ground sassafras leaves, and this one uses roux and okra. The stock matters as much as the roux. If you can, simmer the prawn shells for 20 minutes to make a quick shellfish stock, which gives the gumbo a depth that a carton cannot. The seafood goes in at the very end, so that it cooks for minutes rather than hours and stays sweet and tender.

  • Stir the roux the whole time, scraping the corners. It goes from perfect to burnt in seconds once it darkens, so keep the heat at medium and stay with it.
  • Make a quick stock from the prawn shells by simmering them in 1.5 litres of water with a halved onion and a bay leaf for 20 minutes, then strain. It is worth the effort.
  • Add the seafood at the last minute. Prawns need only a few minutes, and gumbo that is cooked too long leaves them tough and dry.

item.title: Santa Maria Tri-Tip
item.description: Santa Maria tri-tip: a beef roast rubbed with salt, pepper and garlic, grilled over charcoal until pink and sliced thin across the grain.
item.content:encoded:
Tri-tip is the barbecue cut of California's Central Coast. It is a triangular piece of beef from the bottom of the sirloin, and for most of the twentieth century it was ground up or sold cheaply, until the butchers and cooks of Santa Maria began to grill it over coals of local red oak. The Santa Maria style is famously simple: a rub of salt, black pepper and garlic powder, nothing more, then fire. The roast is seared over direct heat to build a dark crust and moved to a cooler part of the grill to finish gently, so the middle turns rosy and juicy rather than grey. It is served the traditional way, in thin slices with pinquito beans, fresh tomato salsa and a grilled bread roll. Because tri-tip is lean, it needs watching. Take it off the heat at 52°C / 125°F for medium-rare, since it rises a few degrees as it rests, and it goes dry and chewy beyond medium. The other trick is in the carving. The roast has two muscles with the grain running in different directions, so find the point where the grain changes, cut the roast in two there, and slice each half across the grain. Done right, it eats like a much more expensive steak.

  • Use a thermometer. Tri-tip is lean and the difference between pink and dry is only about 10 degrees, so time alone is not a reliable guide.
  • In the oven, sear the roast in a heavy pan for 3 minutes per side, then roast at 220°C / 425°F (200°C fan) for 18 to 25 minutes to the same temperatures.
  • Slice against the grain and keep the slices thin. Cut with the grain and even a perfectly cooked tri-tip turns chewy.

item.title: Chicken Marbella
item.description: Chicken Marbella: chicken marinated overnight with prunes, green olives, capers, garlic and oregano, then baked until sticky and golden.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken Marbella is the recipe that made The Silver Palate famous. It appeared in the 1982 Silver Palate Cookbook by Julee Rosso and Sheila Lukins, from their New York gourmet shop, and for a generation of American hosts it was the dinner-party dish that could be made a day ahead and would feed a crowd. The idea is Mediterranean: chicken marinated with prunes, green olives, capers, garlic and oregano in red wine vinegar and olive oil, then baked with brown sugar and white wine until the skin is lacquered and the juices are sticky. It is sweet, sharp and salty all at once. The prunes turn soft and jammy, the olives and capers add brine, and the vinegar keeps the sugar from making the dish cloying. The marinade needs time to work. Left overnight, the vinegar and salt season the chicken all the way through and keep it moist, and the garlic and oregano soak into the meat. It travels well, and it is good hot, warm or cold, which makes it the ideal thing to take to a party. Serve it with rice or couscous, to soak up the sauce, and spoon a little of the pan juices over each portion.

  • Do not skip the overnight marinade. It seasons the chicken through to the bone and keeps it moist, and the flavour is much flatter after a short soak.
  • Arrange the chicken in a single layer. If the pieces are piled up, the skin steams instead of turning golden and lacquered.
  • Baste the chicken as it cooks. The sugar in the pan juices caramelises onto the skin and gives it its glossy finish.

item.title: Squash Casserole
item.description: Squash casserole: tender yellow squash and onion in a creamy cheddar and soured cream mix, baked under a crisp, buttery cracker topping.
item.content:encoded:
Squash casserole is a fixture at Southern church suppers, potlucks and Thanksgiving tables, and it is what many cooks in the South do with the glut of yellow summer squash that comes every July. Slices of squash and onion are cooked until tender, drained well, and mixed with cheddar, soured cream and egg, then baked under a crust of crushed butter crackers, which turns golden and crunchy on top while the filling stays soft and creamy. The result is somewhere between a side dish and a comfort food, mild, cheesy and a little sweet from the squash. Everything depends on moisture. Summer squash is more than 90 per cent water, and if it is not cooked and drained properly the casserole turns out soupy. Boil the slices briefly, tip them into a colander, and press them firmly with the back of a spoon to squeeze out the liquid. Courgettes can be used in exactly the same way, and the flavour is nearly the same. The topping is the best part. Crushed round butter crackers mixed with melted butter and a little cheese bake to a crisp, savoury crust that contrasts with the soft filling. Serve it as a side with roast chicken, ham or barbecue, or make it the centre of a vegetable plate.

  • Press the cooked squash hard in the colander. Any water left in it ends up in the dish, and the casserole will be wet.
  • Leave the crackers in coarse crumbs. Crushing them to dust gives a paste, while chunky crumbs bake into a crisp, crunchy topping.
  • Use a sharp, well-flavoured cheddar. The squash is mild and needs the cheese to carry the taste.

item.title: Hasselback Potatoes
item.description: Hasselback potatoes: potatoes sliced thinly almost through, brushed with butter and oil, then roasted until crisp and fanned open.
item.content:encoded:
Hasselback potatoes are a Swedish invention with a restaurant pedigree. The dish, called hasselbackspotatis, is named after Hasselbacken, a restaurant in Stockholm, where trainee chefs are said to have first sliced potatoes this way in the 1950s. The idea is simple and clever. A potato is cut into thin slices along its length, but not quite all the way through, so that it stays in one piece. When it roasts, the slices fan out and the cut edges brown and crisp, while the base stays soft and fluffy. Butter and oil run into the slits as they open and season the potato from within, and a sprinkling of breadcrumbs, which is the traditional Swedish finish, bakes to a crunchy golden crust. You get far more crisp surface than in a plain roast potato, and the fanned shape looks impressive on the plate for very little work. The only skill is the slicing. Set each potato in the hollow of a wooden spoon, or between two chopsticks, and the knife stops before it reaches the base. Choose medium, evenly sized potatoes of a floury or all-purpose variety, such as Maris Piper or Russet, which crisp well and cook through without going soggy. They go with roast chicken, steak or a Sunday roast.

  • Use a wooden spoon or chopsticks as a guide to stop the knife short of the base. A potato cut right through falls apart into slices.
  • Baste twice. Getting the butter and oil between the slices is what makes them crisp and keeps them from drying out.
  • Wait to add the breadcrumbs until the last 10 to 15 minutes. If they go on at the start, they burn before the potatoes are done.

item.title: Turkey Curry
item.description: Turkey curry: leftover roast turkey in a warmly spiced sauce of onion, tomato, mango chutney and apple, softened with coconut cream.
item.content:encoded:
A turkey curry is what a great many British households eat on Boxing Day, when the fridge is full of cold roast turkey and nobody wants another sandwich. It belongs to a long tradition of Anglo-Indian cooking, in which cooked meat is warmed through in a spiced sauce, and it has been a way of using up the Christmas bird since Victorian cookery books first printed recipes for leftover curry. The sauce is what makes it. Onions cooked until soft and golden, garlic and ginger, curry powder fried briefly in the oil to bring out its aroma, then tomatoes and stock. Two very British touches round it out, mango chutney for sweetness and a grated apple that dissolves into the sauce and adds a gentle fruity tartness. Coconut cream softens the heat and gives the curry a silky finish, and a squeeze of lemon at the end lifts everything. Turkey breast is lean and dries out easily, so the meat is added only at the end and warmed through, not simmered, which keeps it tender. Serve with rice, poppadoms and more chutney. It is easily made with leftover roast chicken, ham or lamb, and the sauce freezes well, so it is a useful recipe to know all year round.
