  • Add the turkey at the end. It is already cooked, and a long simmer makes lean breast meat dry and stringy.
  • Fry the curry powder for a minute before adding the liquid. Raw curry powder tastes dusty, and a short fry in the oil brings out its flavour.
  • Taste and balance at the end. If it is too sharp, add a little more chutney, and if it is flat, add more lemon juice or salt.

item.title: Lobster Thermidor
item.description: Lobster thermidor: lobster meat in a creamy sauce of shallot, wine, brandy, mustard and tarragon, piled into the shell and browned under the grill.
item.content:encoded:
Lobster thermidor is the grandest of French lobster dishes and a byword for old-fashioned luxury. It is said to have been created in Paris in 1894, for the first night of Victorien Sardou's play Thermidor, and it has been served at celebration dinners and on restaurant menus since. The lobster is split, the meat removed and cooked in a sauce of shallot, white wine, brandy, mustard and cream, then spooned back into the shell, sprinkled with cheese and browned under the grill until it bubbles. It is a rich dish, and each part is there for a reason. The wine and brandy are reduced to concentrate their flavour and cut the cream, the mustard adds a piquant heat, and the tarragon gives the sauce its unmistakable anise note. The gratin topping seals in the moisture and gives a golden crust, and the shell makes the presentation. The sauce needs to be thick enough to hold on a spoon, because a thin sauce makes the dish soggy. Because the lobster is cooked before it is put in the sauce, it needs only to be warmed through and browned. Buy lobsters that are already cooked, or boil live ones for 12 minutes, and take care to warm the meat gently so it stays tender, not rubbery.

  • Do not overcook the lobster. It is already cooked, so it needs only to be warmed in the sauce, then browned briefly. Long heating makes it rubbery.
  • Reduce the sauce until it is thick. A thin sauce runs out of the shell and makes the gratin soggy.
  • Use fresh tarragon if you can. Its aniseed flavour is the signature of the dish, and dried tarragon is a poor substitute.

item.title: Salmon en Croûte
item.description: Salmon en croûte: a salmon fillet with herby cream cheese and spinach, wrapped in puff pastry and baked golden. A dinner-party centrepiece.
item.content:encoded:
Salmon en croûte is a British dinner-party classic, the fish counterpart to a beef Wellington. It is a whole side of salmon, spread with a herby cream cheese, covered with wilted spinach and wrapped in puff pastry, then baked until the pastry is golden and the salmon underneath is just cooked and moist. It is a favourite for Christmas Eve, Easter and other family gatherings, because it can be assembled the day before, looks impressive, and slices neatly to show the layers of pink, green and gold. The dish has a few traps. Its greatest enemy is moisture, which is what makes the base soggy. Squeeze the cooked spinach as dry as you can, in a clean tea towel if necessary, and let it cool before it goes anywhere near the pastry. Chill the wrapped parcel for 30 minutes before baking, so the butter in the pastry is cold and puffs properly, and bake it on a preheated tray to crisp the underside. Salmon is at its best just cooked, still slightly translucent in the centre, and it carries on cooking as it rests, so take it out when the pastry is golden and let it stand for 10 minutes before you slice it with a serrated knife.

  • Squeeze the spinach until it is really dry. Wet spinach releases water as it bakes and leaves a soggy base.
  • Bake on a tray that has been heating in the oven. The hot metal cooks the pastry underneath at once and gives a crisp base.
  • Check the salmon with a thermometer. At 52°C / 125°F in the thickest part it will finish cooking as it rests, giving moist, just-set fish.

item.title: Hakka Chilli Chicken
item.description: Hakka chilli chicken: crisp battered chicken tossed in a hot wok with peppers, onion, garlic, ginger and green chillies in a glossy soy sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Hakka chilli chicken is the best-known dish of Indo-Chinese cooking, a cuisine that grew out of the Hakka Chinese community of Kolkata and adapted Chinese methods to Indian tastes. Chicken is coated in a light batter and fried until crisp, then tossed in a very hot wok with onion, green pepper, garlic, ginger and slit green chillies in a sauce of soy, chilli sauce, ketchup and vinegar. The result is salty, sour, hot and a little sweet, with a crisp coating that stays crunchy even after it meets the sauce. It has travelled well beyond India. In Canada, especially around Toronto and Brampton, Hakka restaurants are a category of their own, and chilli chicken sits on the menu beside Manchurian dishes and hakka noodles. Two techniques make it work. The first is the batter, where cornflour makes the coating crisp and light and a little flour holds it together. The second is a very hot wok, so that the vegetables sear in a minute and stay crunchy, and the sauce clings to the chicken without soaking it. It is served two ways, dry, as here, or with extra sauce as a gravy, and either goes with egg fried rice or hakka noodles.

  • Fry the chicken twice for extra crunch. Fry it for 4 minutes, rest it for 5, then fry it again for 2 minutes at 190°C / 375°F.
  • Keep the wok very hot and work fast. The vegetables should be seared but still crunchy, and the sauce should reduce to a glaze in a minute.
  • Serve immediately. The coating is at its crispest for the first few minutes, and it softens as the sauce soaks in.

item.title: Chicken Fricot
item.description: Chicken fricot: a comforting Acadian stew of chicken, potatoes, carrots and onion in a savoury broth scented with summer savory.
item.content:encoded:
Fricot is the everyday soup-stew of the Acadians, the French-speaking people of Canada's Maritime provinces, and chicken fricot is the version that is most often cooked. The word comes from the French fricasser, and the dish is in the same family as the fricassées that French settlers carried across the Atlantic in the seventeenth century. It is simple and homely. Chicken is simmered with potatoes, onions and sometimes carrots in a broth that is thin enough to drink from the spoon and full of savour, and it is seasoned with summer savory, the herb of Acadian kitchens, which gives it a peppery, thyme-like taste that nothing else quite matches. A little salt pork or bacon adds smokiness. Recipes vary from village to village in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Some cooks add dumplings or thick strips of dough to make a heartier bowl, and others add a little turnip or leave out the carrots. It is a dish for a cold day, made in a big pot to feed a family, and it is even better the next day. Serve it with bread and butter to mop up the broth.

  • Use summer savory if you can find it. It is the herb that gives the dish its Acadian character, and thyme is the best substitute.
  • For dumplings, mix 150 g of plain flour with 2 teaspoons of baking powder, a pinch of salt and about 100 ml of water. Drop spoonfuls onto the simmering stew for the last 12 minutes and keep the lid on.
  • Keep the simmer gentle. A hard boil makes the chicken stringy and the broth cloudy.

item.title: Stifado
item.description: Stifado: Greek beef stew simmered with small whole onions, red wine, tomato, vinegar, cinnamon, cloves and bay until meltingly tender.
item.content:encoded:
Stifado is the great stew of Greek home cooking, and the rule that defines it is simple: there should be at least as many onions as meat. Small whole onions cook slowly in the pot until they turn silky and sweet, and they melt into a dark red sauce that is glossy with olive oil. The dish takes its name from the Italian stufato, a reminder of the centuries when Venice ruled parts of Greece, and it was originally made with rabbit or hare, which is still cooked on the islands. Beef is the everyday version, and shin or chuck is best because both are rich in connective tissue that softens into a velvety sauce. What separates stifado from other stews is its spicing. Cinnamon, cloves, bay leaf and allspice give it a warm, sweet fragrance that hints at the East, and a splash of red wine vinegar cuts through the richness and stops the onions from making it cloying. In Australia, which has one of the largest Greek communities outside Greece, stifado is a staple of family tables and church festivals, and it is often the first dish that people ask for at a Greek restaurant on a cold night. Serve it with orzo, buttered pasta, crusty bread or roast potatoes to soak up the sauce.

  • Do not skimp on the onions. They are the point of the dish, and they should weigh nearly as much as the beef.
  • Keep the simmer very low and stir gently. A hard boil breaks the onions up, and you want them whole.
  • Make it a day ahead if you can. Like most stews, stifado tastes better after a night in the fridge, when the spices have settled.

item.title: Devilled Sausages
item.description: Devilled sausages: plump sausages simmered in a tangy, lightly spiced sauce of tomato, Worcestershire, mustard and curry powder. A Kiwi classic.
item.content:encoded:
Devilled sausages are a fixture of New Zealand and Australian home cooking, the sort of supper that many people first ate at their grandmother's table. The sausages are browned, then simmered in a sauce that is sweet, sharp and gently hot, made from tomato sauce, Worcestershire sauce, mustard, brown sugar and a spoonful of curry powder. The word devilled has been used in British cooking since the eighteenth century for anything seasoned with pepper, mustard or cayenne, and this is a very Antipodean take on the idea. The sauce is thickened with a spoonful of flour and reduced until it clings to the sausages in a glossy coating, and the onion melts into it and gives it body. It is a dish built for mashed potato, which soaks up the sauce, and for green peas, which give a sweet contrast, and it works just as well with rice or with crusty bread. Choose good-quality thick pork or beef sausages, since the sauce is only as good as the sausage in it. Prick them lightly after browning so the flavours can get in, and simmer them gently so the skins do not split. The whole thing is cooked in one pan in about 45 minutes and costs very little, which is why it has outlasted so many fashions.

  • Simmer the sausages gently. A rolling boil splits the skins and dries the meat out.
  • Adjust the balance at the end. More brown sugar makes it sweeter, and more mustard or vinegar makes it sharper.
  • The dish is good made with thick beef sausages, or with vegetarian sausages. If you use the latter, shorten the simmer to 10 minutes.

item.title: Savoury Mince
item.description: Savoury mince: beef mince simmered with onion, carrot, tomato sauce and Worcestershire in a rich gravy, finished with peas. Spoon over toast or mash.
item.content:encoded:
Savoury mince is one of the most common weeknight dinners in New Zealand and Australia, and it is the sort of dish that nobody writes down because everybody's mother made it. Beef mince is browned with onion and carrot, simmered in a thick brown gravy seasoned with tomato sauce and Worcestershire sauce, and finished with a handful of peas. That is it, and the simplicity is the point. It costs very little, it feeds a family, and it goes a long way, because it can be spooned over thick slices of buttered toast, piled onto mashed potato, used to fill a baked potato, or stuffed into a pie case or pastry. In Britain the same dish appears as mince on toast, and it belongs to the same family as the shepherd's pie filling, although it is thicker and less rich. A few things make it better than the plain version. Browning the mince properly, in a hot pan and in two batches, gives it a deeper savour than steaming it in its own juices. A spoon of flour thickens the gravy without a separate roux, and a splash of Worcestershire sauce adds the depth that people always notice but never identify. Grated carrot melts into the sauce so the mince tastes sweet without extra sugar, and the peas, added at the end, keep their colour and freshness.

  • Brown the mince in batches. In an overcrowded pan it steams and turns grey, and it will not develop the savoury flavour.
  • Grate the carrot finely. It dissolves into the gravy and gives the mince a natural sweetness.
  • Thin the gravy with a splash of stock if it gets too thick as it cooks, or simmer it for a few more minutes if it is too runny.

item.title: Beijing Beef
item.description: Beijing beef: crisp fried strips of beef tossed in a sweet, tangy and mildly hot sauce with peppers and onion. The takeaway favourite at home.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing beef is an American-Chinese restaurant dish that has almost nothing to do with the cooking of Beijing. It was made popular by the Chinese-American takeaway and food-court counters, where its crisp strips of beef in a sweet, sticky and tangy red sauce became a best-seller, and it belongs to the same family as orange chicken and sweet and sour pork. It borrows an old idea from northern Chinese kitchens, the sweet and sour glaze, but its flavour is its own. Thin strips of flank steak are coated in cornflour and egg and fried until crisp, then tossed at the last minute with peppers and onion in a sauce of ketchup, sweet chilli sauce, soy, vinegar and a little brown sugar, with garlic, ginger and dried chilli flakes for heat. The sauce is sticky, bright and somewhere between sweet and hot, and it is meant to cling to the beef. Timing is the trick. Fry the beef in small batches so that it stays crisp, make the sauce while it drains, and toss everything together at the very end, so the coating keeps its crunch. Flank steak is the best cut, because it cooks fast and has a good beefy taste, but it must be sliced very thinly across the grain to stay tender. Serve with steamed rice or fried rice.

  • Slice the beef against the grain, as thinly as you can. Freezing the steak for 20 minutes first makes it much easier to cut.
  • Fry the beef in batches. Crowding the wok lowers the oil temperature and gives you soggy, greasy strips rather than crisp ones.
  • Toss the beef in the sauce at the very last moment and serve straight away. The coating stays crisp for only a few minutes once it is sauced.

item.title: Surf and Turf
item.description: Surf and turf: a seared ribeye steak with a grilled lobster tail brushed with garlic and parsley butter. The steakhouse special at home.
item.content:encoded:
Surf and turf is the celebration meal of the steakhouse menu, a piece of beef served on the same plate as a piece of seafood, usually lobster tail. The pairing became fashionable in American restaurants in the 1960s, when lobster and prime beef were both symbols of a good night out, and it spread across the world. In Australia and New Zealand it goes by the name of reef and beef, and it is a staple of pub and club menus, most often made with prawns. It is a dish with a lot of luxury and very little cooking. A thick ribeye steak seared in a very hot pan needs about 8 minutes, and a lobster tail split lengthways and grilled needs about the same, so both come off the heat together. The garlic butter does the work of tying them together. It melts over the steak and into the lobster meat, and its sharp garlic and lemon cut through the richness of both. Buy lobster tails that are firm, with the shell intact and the meat bright, and thaw frozen ones fully according to the packet. Splitting the tail with kitchen scissors exposes the flesh to the heat and stops it curling. Rest the steak for five minutes before serving so the juices settle.

  • Pat the steaks dry and get the pan very hot. This gives a brown crust instead of a grey, steamed surface.
  • Split the lobster tails through the top shell. The meat lies flat, it cooks evenly, and it is easy to lift from the shell at the table.
  • Do not overcook the lobster. It is done when the meat turns white and firm, and a minute or two longer makes it rubbery.

item.title: Baked Feta Pasta
item.description: Baked feta pasta: a block of feta baked with cherry tomatoes, garlic and olive oil, then mashed into a creamy sauce and tossed with pasta.
item.content:encoded:
Baked feta pasta is the dish that filled kitchens during the spring of 2021, when it went viral on TikTok and there was a shortage of feta in some shops. Its origin is Finnish. The food blogger Jenni Häyrinen shared her uunifetapasta, which means oven feta pasta, in 2019, and it is not hard to see why it caught on. A block of feta is set in a baking dish with a heap of cherry tomatoes, olive oil and garlic, and the oven does the work. The tomatoes split and collapse into a sweet, sticky sauce, the garlic softens and mellows, and the feta turns soft and creamy at the edges without melting away. Then you stir everything together, crush the feta into the tomatoes and toss it through hot pasta, and the result is a creamy, tangy, savoury sauce that needs no cream and almost no effort. The sauce is a balance of sweet and salty, so taste before adding salt, because the feta is already salty. A handful of fresh basil at the end adds a fragrant, peppery lift, and a pinch of chilli flakes gives it warmth. Choose a block of good Greek feta in brine, not the crumbled kind, which does not soften in the same way. Ripe cherry tomatoes make the sweetest sauce.

  • Use a block of feta in brine. Crumbled feta does not soften into the sauce and gives a grainy texture.
  • Do not add salt until you have tasted. The feta and the pasta water already carry a lot of salt.
  • Add a splash of the pasta cooking water to loosen the sauce. Its starch helps the sauce cling to the pasta.

item.title: Chicken Tacos
item.description: Chicken tacos: juicy chicken thighs rubbed with chilli, cumin and lime, seared and chopped, then piled into warm corn tortillas with fresh toppings.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken tacos are the most popular filling in the tacos that people cook at home, and it is easy to see why. They take 30 minutes, need a short list of ingredients and taste far better than anything from a kit. The secret is a simple seasoning of chilli powder, cumin, smoked paprika, garlic and oregano, rubbed over chicken thighs with a squeeze of lime, which soaks in as you heat the pan. Thighs stay juicy and full-flavoured where chicken breast turns dry, and they sear to a deep, spiced crust in about six minutes on each side. Once rested, they are chopped into small pieces that catch the seasoning and cook through evenly. What surrounds the chicken matters just as much. Corn tortillas, warmed in a dry pan until they are soft and just starting to blister, give the taco its taste and its shape, and they are naturally gluten-free. On top go the classic street-taco garnishes: finely chopped white onion and fresh coriander for sharpness, creamy avocado to balance the spice, and a good squeeze of lime. Add a spoonful of salsa if you like some heat. Tacos are eaten in two or three bites, so make more than you think you need.

  • Use thighs rather than breasts. They stay juicy and take up the seasoning well, and they are much harder to overcook.
  • Warm the tortillas and keep them wrapped. Cold corn tortillas crack when folded, and steamed ones stay soft and pliable.
  • Chop the chicken small. Small pieces catch more of the seasoned crust, so each bite has flavour.

item.title: Italian Beef Sandwich
item.description: Italian beef sandwich: chuck roast slow-cooked in a garlicky, herby broth, sliced thin and piled on crusty rolls with giardiniera. A Chicago classic.
item.content:encoded:
The Italian beef sandwich is the signature sandwich of Chicago, and it is a messy, glorious thing. Thin slices of roast beef, soaked in a garlicky, herby broth, are piled into a long, crusty roll and topped with either sweet peppers or hot giardiniera, a pickle of chopped vegetables in oil. It is said to have begun in the 1930s, when Italian-American families in the city fed wedding crowds by slicing cheap cuts of beef very thin and letting them soak up seasoned juices, so a little meat went a long way. Chicago has a language for ordering it. Dry means the beef is drained, wet means it is spooned with extra juice, and dipped means the whole sandwich is dunked in the jus so that the bread is soaked through. Most people go for dipped and eat it leaning over the plate. At home the easiest way to get close is to slow-cook a chuck roast in stock seasoned with garlic, oregano and Italian herbs until it is tender enough to slice thin, then return the slices to the strained cooking liquid. Chuck has plenty of fat and collagen, so the beef stays moist, and the liquid becomes a savoury jus. Serve it on the sturdiest rolls you can find, because a soft roll collapses under the weight of the juice.

  • Slice the beef when it is only just cool. Slightly firm meat cuts far thinner than hot, falling-apart meat, and thin slices are what make the sandwich.
  • Choose sturdy rolls with a crisp crust. Soft rolls turn to mush in the jus, so toast them lightly if they are not very firm.
  • Skim the fat from the jus before you soak the beef. It should taste savoury and clear, not greasy.

item.title: Beef on Weck
item.description: Beef on weck: thinly sliced rare roast beef dipped in jus and piled on a salt and caraway-crusted roll with sharp horseradish. A Buffalo classic.
item.content:encoded:
Beef on weck is the sandwich of Buffalo, New York, and the state of upstate pubs. It is thin slices of rare roast beef, dipped in jus, on a kummelweck roll, which is a soft kaiser-style roll with a crust of coarse salt and caraway seeds, and it is always served with a generous smear of sharp horseradish. The name comes from the German for caraway, Kümmel, and Weck, a regional word for a roll, and the story goes that German bakers in Buffalo in the nineteenth century made the salty rolls to encourage thirsty pub customers to order another beer. It works as a sandwich because of the contrasts. The salt and caraway on the crust are pungent, the beef is tender and mild, the jus is savoury, and the horseradish adds a sharp heat that clears the nose. A good beef on weck should be dripping. The roast is cooked low and slow to a rosy pink, chilled briefly so that it can be sliced paper-thin, and each roll is briefly dipped in the jus before it is filled. Top round or silverside is the traditional cut, because it is lean, and it slices well. At home, a low oven cooks it evenly, and a meat thermometer prevents overcooking.

  • Use a thermometer. The difference between rosy and grey is only a few degrees, and top round dries out quickly.
  • Slice the beef paper-thin. A chilled roast, or a very sharp long knife, gives the thinnest slices, and thin slices are the mark of a good beef on weck.
  • Buy real horseradish, not horseradish sauce. It is much hotter, and the heat is what the sandwich is built around.

item.title: Ham Salad
item.description: Ham salad: finely chopped ham mixed with mayonnaise, mustard, sweet pickle relish and crunchy celery into a creamy spread for sandwiches and crackers.
item.content:encoded:
Ham salad is the classic deli-counter spread of the American Midwest and South, a mix of finely chopped ham, mayonnaise, mustard and sweet pickle relish that turns up at church luncheons, picnics and family gatherings. It began as a way to use up the last of a holiday ham, and Easter leftovers are still the most popular reason to make it. The idea is the same as chicken salad or egg salad: a bland, salty, protein-rich base bound with a creamy dressing and given some crunch and tang. The ham is what sets it apart. It should be chopped very small, or pulsed in a food processor until it is finely minced but still has some texture, so the spread holds together on bread and does not fall out of the sandwich. Sweet pickle relish, in the American style, gives sweetness and acid, celery gives crunch, and a little mustard brings sharpness. The result is a soft, savoury spread that goes into sandwiches, but it is also good on crackers, rolled in lettuce leaves or stuffed into celery sticks. It tastes even better after a night in the fridge, when the flavours have mingled, so it is ideal for making ahead. Choose a good-quality cooked ham with a mild flavour, since the strength of the ham comes through.

  • Chop the ham fine, but do not turn it to a paste. A little texture is what makes the salad pleasant to eat.
  • Leave out the salt. Ham is already salty, and the relish and mustard add more.
  • Make it a day ahead if you can. The flavours meld overnight, and the salad holds its shape better once it has chilled.

item.title: Stuffed Acorn Squash
item.description: Stuffed acorn squash: roasted squash halves filled with quinoa, cranberries, pecans, apple and sage. A hearty, vegan autumn dinner.
item.content:encoded:
Stuffed acorn squash is the dish that turns a fall vegetable into a whole meal, and a good one to serve to a mixed table because it happens to be vegan. Acorn squash has a dark green, ridged skin and pale orange flesh with a mild, nutty sweetness, and the halves are just the right size to be used as edible bowls. Roasting them cut side down at high heat softens the flesh and draws out the sugars, and the shell holds the filling in place. Here, the filling is quinoa cooked in vegetable stock and mixed with a soft-cooked onion and celery, sage and thyme, tart dried cranberries, crunchy toasted pecans and diced apple, and a spoonful of maple syrup ties it all together. It has the flavours of the Thanksgiving table, sweet and savoury, herbal and fruity, and it offers protein from the quinoa and nuts. The squash is roasted first, because it takes longer than the filling to cook, and then stuffed and returned to the oven, so the filling can heat through and the edges can crisp. Look for squash that feel heavy for their size, with a dull skin and no soft spots. Trim a small slice off the rounded side of each half so that it sits flat on the tray without tipping.

  • Roast the squash cut side down first. Trapped steam softens the flesh, and the cut edge caramelises on the hot tray.
  • Toast the pecans in a dry pan for 3 minutes. This brings out their flavour and keeps them crisp in the filling.
  • Use the shell to serve. It is edible, although some people leave it. If the squash are large, cut them into quarters after stuffing to serve as smaller portions.

item.title: Cauliflower Pizza Crust
item.description: Cauliflower pizza crust: riced cauliflower, egg, mozzarella and Parmesan baked until golden and firm, then topped with tomato sauce and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Cauliflower pizza crust is one of the most successful vegetable stand-ins for bread, and it has been around long enough that it has an established method. Riced cauliflower is cooked, squeezed dry, mixed with egg and cheese, patted into a circle and baked until firm, and the result is a crisp-edged, golden base that can carry sauce and toppings. It is gluten-free and much lower in carbohydrate than a wheat crust, which is why it has become popular. It is not the same as a bread base, and it is best to set expectations. The crust is tender, mildly savoury and tastes gently of cauliflower and cheese, and it is eaten with a fork or a folded slice. Everything depends on removing moisture. Cauliflower is more than 90 per cent water, and unless it is steamed and then squeezed hard in a clean tea towel until it is almost dry, the crust will be soggy and will not hold together. The egg binds the mixture, the mozzarella and Parmesan give it flavour and structure, and dried oregano and garlic season it. Bake the crust on its own first until golden and firm, then add the toppings and bake again briefly. If the crust is thin and well browned at the edges, it will hold a slice.

  • Squeeze the cauliflower dry. This step matters more than any other, and a crust made from damp cauliflower will never firm up.
  • Keep the crust thin, about 5 mm. A thick crust stays soft in the middle and will not hold a slice.
  • Bake the crust plain before you add the toppings. This sets it and dries it out, and stops the sauce from making it soggy.

item.title: Cocktail Sauce
item.description: Cocktail sauce: ketchup sharpened with horseradish, lemon juice, Worcestershire and hot sauce. The classic red dip for prawns, oysters and crab.
item.content:encoded:
Cocktail sauce is the red, fiery dip that has been served with chilled shellfish since the early years of the twentieth century, when the prawn cocktail became a fixture on restaurant menus. The name of the sauce comes from the dish, which was a cocktail of shellfish served in a glass, and it has not changed much since. It is ketchup with horseradish, lemon juice and a dash of hot sauce, and it is one of the simplest sauces in the kitchen. What makes it worth making is the freshness of the flavour. Bottled cocktail sauces tend to taste flat and sweet, and a homemade version made with real horseradish has a clean, sharp bite that makes the nose tingle and complements the sweetness of prawns, crab and oysters. Horseradish is the key ingredient, and it is easy to adjust. Two tablespoons gives a gentle kick, and five tablespoons makes a sauce that will make your eyes water, and the flavour develops as it stands, so taste again after it has chilled. Worcestershire sauce adds savoury depth, lemon juice gives it brightness, and a few drops of hot sauce provide a lingering heat. Serve it in a small bowl beside a platter of boiled prawns on ice, alongside oysters on the half shell, or with crab claws, fried calamari or fish fingers. The sauce takes five minutes and keeps well.

  • Use jarred horseradish, not horseradish cream. The plain, grated kind is much hotter, and it gives the sauce its real bite.
  • Let it stand. The heat of horseradish takes some time to develop, so the sauce is hotter after an hour than it is straight after mixing.
  • Stir in a spoonful of chilli sauce for a stronger, hotter version, or a pinch of celery salt for a more savoury one. Taste after each addition.

item.title: Tartar Sauce
item.description: Tartar sauce: mayonnaise with chopped gherkins, capers, shallot, lemon and fresh herbs. The creamy, tangy sauce for fish and chips and fried seafood.
item.content:encoded:
Tartar sauce, called tartare sauce in Britain, is the cool, creamy, sharp partner of fried fish. It is mayonnaise, made lively with chopped gherkins or cornichons, capers, shallot, lemon juice and fresh herbs, and its acidity and crunch cut through the richness of anything deep-fried. French cooks named it sauce tartare and served it with cold meats and raw beef, and in the English-speaking world it moved to fish and chips, fish fingers, crab cakes and fried oysters, where it is now hard to imagine the plate without it. The homemade version is better than any jar for a simple reason: it tastes fresh. Bottled sauces are sweet and one-note, while a sauce made in five minutes has the bite of real capers, the crunch of finely chopped pickles and the freshness of parsley and dill. The key is to chop everything small, so the sauce is even and creamy, and to squeeze the gherkins dry in a paper towel first, so that they do not thin the mayonnaise. Good mayonnaise matters, since it is the base. Use one that you like the taste of, or make your own. Let the sauce rest in the fridge for half an hour, and the flavours will settle and blend. It is excellent with fish, and also good as a spread for a fish finger sandwich or with cold cooked salmon.

  • Chop the pickles and capers finely and squeeze them dry. Large or wet pieces make the sauce watery and lumpy.
  • Taste before adding salt. Capers, cornichons and mayonnaise are all salty already.
  • Use fresh herbs, not dried. Parsley and dill give the sauce its bright colour and clean taste.

item.title: Honey Mustard Dressing
item.description: Honey mustard dressing: Dijon mustard, honey, mayonnaise, lemon and cider vinegar whisked into a golden, creamy dressing for salads and dipping.
item.content:encoded:
Honey mustard is the sweet-and-sharp dressing that sits in the dip cup next to a plate of chicken tenders and on the dressing shelf of nearly every American salad bar, and it is one of the easiest to make at home. It needs only mustard and honey, and the rest is small adjustment. Dijon mustard gives depth and gentle heat, honey gives sweetness and a smooth, syrupy body, and mayonnaise makes it creamy and helps it cling to leaves and chicken. A splash of cider vinegar and lemon juice keeps it lively, so that it does not slide into being cloying, and a spoonful of water loosens it to the right consistency for drizzling. The balance is easy to change. Add more honey for a sweet dip for nuggets, more mustard for a sharper dressing to go with ham and cheese salads, and thin it further for a salad dressing. Wholegrain mustard adds texture, and a pinch of cayenne or a spoonful of hot sauce gives a little warmth. Because it is made in a bowl in a few minutes, it tastes fresher than any bottled version and has no thickeners or additives. It is good on a green salad with chicken, bacon and avocado, as a sauce for roast vegetables, a spread for a turkey sandwich, or as the glaze for salmon or pork chops. Made with honey and mayonnaise, it is not vegan.

  • Warm the honey jar in hot water for a minute if the honey is stiff. Runny honey blends much more smoothly.
  • Thin the dressing gradually. A little water at a time gives you a dip for chicken or a pouring dressing for salad.
  • Use a good Dijon mustard. It is the main flavour, and a mild yellow mustard will make a blander, sweeter dressing.

item.title: Battered Sausage
item.description: Battered sausage: plump pork sausages dipped in a light, crisp batter and deep-fried until golden. The great British chip shop classic.
item.content:encoded:
The battered sausage is a chip-shop staple across Britain, and in the north of England and Scotland it can be as popular as the fish. A pork sausage is dipped in a light batter and fried until the coating puffs, blisters and turns golden and crisp, giving a contrast between a crunchy shell and a juicy, seasoned centre. It is the classic cheap supper from the chippy, wrapped in paper with chips, mushy peas or curry sauce, and eaten from the paper on the way home. The homemade version is easy and much better than a sausage that has spent a while on the hot shelf. The sausages should be cooked through first, since the batter does not cook long enough to do the job, and dried well so that the batter clings. A dusting of flour before dipping is the trick that stops the batter sliding off. The batter itself is very simple, plain flour with a little baking powder, salt and cold sparkling water, or beer, and its lightness comes from the bubbles and from the cold. Mix it just before you use it and do not worry about lumps. The oil must be hot, at 180°C, or the batter will be greasy and heavy. A good thick pork sausage, with plenty of seasoning, is what the batter is there to protect, so choose the best you can.

  • Dry the sausages and roll them in flour before dipping. Without the dusting, the batter slips off and leaves the sausage bare.
  • Keep the batter cold and use it straight away. Its lightness comes from the bubbles in the water, which go flat if it stands.
  • Check the oil temperature. Below 170°C the batter absorbs oil and turns heavy, and above 190°C it browns before it is crisp.

item.title: Gözleme
item.description: Gözleme: hand-rolled, paper-thin dough filled with spinach and feta, folded and griddled until golden and blistered, then brushed with butter.
item.content:encoded:
Gözleme is a Turkish flatbread that has become a fixture of Australian food markets, where you can watch a woman in a headscarf roll the dough paper-thin, fill it, and cook it on a hot plate in front of you. The name comes from the Turkish word göz, meaning eye, and it refers to the way the dough is folded around its filling, and it is one of the best-known snacks of Anatolia. The dough is very simple, made from flour, salt, a little yoghurt, oil and water, and it is rested so that it becomes elastic and can be rolled out extremely thin, almost see-through, with a long rolling pin. Filling is added to half, the dough is folded over, and the parcel is cooked on a griddle called a sac until it blisters and browns. The classic filling is spinach and white cheese, seasoned with onion and pepper, though minced meat, potato and cheese with herbs are also popular. Once it is cooked, the gözleme is brushed with melted butter, which makes it glisten, and cut into squares for eating with a squeeze of lemon. It is a dish that rewards patience with the rolling, because the thinner the dough the crisper and lighter the result. It is a good dish to make with friends, since one person rolls while another cooks.

  • Squeeze the spinach until it is dry. Wet filling steams the dough from the inside and makes the gözleme soggy and hard to seal.
  • Roll the dough as thin as you can. If it springs back, let it rest for 5 minutes and roll again, since resting relaxes the gluten.
  • Keep the heat at medium-high and turn the gözleme once. Too low and it dries out before it browns, and too high and it burns before the dough is cooked.

item.title: Prawn and Avocado Salad
item.description: Prawn and avocado salad: sweet cooked prawns, ripe avocado, cos lettuce, cucumber and tomato in a lime dressing. An Australian summer lunch.
item.content:encoded:
A prawn and avocado salad is the sort of lunch that Australians eat on a hot day, particularly at Christmas, when the table is full of cold prawns and the last thing anyone wants is a hot dinner. It is a combination that suits the climate: sweet, cold prawns from the fish market, creamy ripe avocado, crisp cos lettuce, crunchy cucumber and juicy tomatoes, all in a light lime dressing. It needs no cooking at all when you buy cooked, peeled prawns, and it comes together in fifteen minutes. The salad depends on contrast. The prawns are sweet and slightly springy, the avocado is soft and buttery, the cucumber and lettuce are cold and crisp, and the dressing brings sharpness and freshness. Lime is what lifts it, and a little honey balances the acid without making it sweet, while fresh coriander adds a herbal note. Avocado is a delicate ingredient, and it needs to be ripe but firm, so that it holds in chunks and does not turn to mush. Cut it at the last minute and coat it in dressing, since the lime juice slows the browning. If you are buying whole prawns, peel and devein them yourself and keep the shells for stock. It is a salad that also works as a starter, in lettuce cups, or spooned into a wrap.

  • Dry the prawns before dressing them. Wet prawns water down the dressing and leave the salad sloppy.
  • Add the avocado last and fold gently. It bruises easily, and the lime juice in the dressing slows its browning.
  • Choose avocados that yield slightly to gentle pressure. Rock-hard ones are tasteless, and overripe ones turn to mush.

item.title: Piadina
item.description: Piadina: a thin, soft flatbread from Romagna, cooked on a hot griddle and folded around prosciutto, soft cheese and peppery rocket.
item.content:encoded:
The piadina is the flatbread of Romagna, the part of Emilia-Romagna that runs from Rimini to Ravenna, and it is the local answer to the sandwich. It is a thin, soft, slightly chewy disc, made from flour, lard or olive oil, salt and water, cooked on a hot griddle until it blisters, and folded around a filling. Along the Adriatic coast, kiosks sell them all day, and the classics are prosciutto with soft cheese and rocket, or simply cheese and a little grilled vegetable. It is said to be among the oldest breads in Italy, since it needs no yeast and no oven, and it was originally made on a clay plate over an open fire. The dough is closer to a tortilla than to a pizza base. It is mixed quickly, rested for half an hour so it becomes easy to roll, and rolled thin to about 3 mm. Lard is the traditional fat and it gives a very soft, tender bread, but olive oil makes a good version too. The dough is pricked and cooked in a dry pan on medium-high heat for a minute or two on each side, until it is covered in brown speckles but still supple. Then it is filled while warm so that the cheese softens. The traditional soft cheese is squacquerone, a tangy, spoonable fresh cheese, but stracchino or ricotta are good stand-ins.

  • Rest the dough for the full 30 minutes. It relaxes the gluten, so the dough rolls thin without springing back.
  • Cook on a dry pan, without oil. The blistering and brown speckles come from direct heat, and oil would make it fry and turn crisp.
  • Wrap the cooked piadine in a tea towel as you go. The steam keeps them soft and pliable, ready to fold without cracking.

item.title: Cauliflower Soup
item.description: Cauliflower soup: a smooth, velvety soup of cauliflower, onion and potato simmered in stock and blended with milk, finished with nutmeg and chives.
item.content:encoded:
Cauliflower soup is one of the great vegetable soups, and a good one shows how much a plain white vegetable can taste of. It is smooth, warm and gently nutty, with none of the sharpness that people sometimes fear in cauliflower, because the vegetable is cooked until very soft, and its flavour turns sweet and mild. It is a British favourite for autumn and winter lunches, and it has been made in country kitchens for as long as cauliflower has been grown, often with a little cheese. The technique is easy. A soft, buttered onion gives a sweet base, garlic adds depth, and a small potato is the secret to a velvety body without needing a lot of cream, since its starch thickens and smooths the soup. Cauliflower and stock simmer together for about twenty minutes until tender, then everything is blended, and milk is stirred in to lighten and enrich it. A grating of nutmeg is traditional, because it has a natural affinity with cauliflower and with milk, and white pepper keeps the colour clean. The soup is very good plain, but toppings make it special: a swirl of good olive oil, chopped chives, crisp croutons, toasted almonds, or a few florets roasted until browned. For a richer soup, finish with a spoonful of cream or a handful of grated cheese.

  • Cook the cauliflower until it is really soft. Firm pieces will leave the blended soup slightly grainy.
  • Use a potato for body. It gives the soup a silky, creamy texture without needing much cream.
  • Add the milk after blending and warm the soup gently. Boiling milk can make the soup look grainy and split.

item.title: All-Butter Pie Crust
item.description: All-butter pie crust: flaky, tender pastry made with flour, cold butter, sugar and ice water. Makes a double crust, with blind-baking instructions.
item.content:encoded:
A good pie crust is flaky, tender and tastes of butter, and the all-butter version is the one that most bakers aim for. It has only five ingredients, flour, cold butter, a little salt and sugar, and ice water, but the way they are handled decides the result. Flakiness comes from butter. When cold pieces of butter are left in the dough and it goes into a hot oven, the water in the butter turns to steam and lifts the layers of dough around it, creating the thin, crisp sheets that shatter when you bite them. That is why every rule of pie crust is about keeping the butter cold and the pieces visible: chill the butter, use ice water, work quickly, and stop mixing while the dough still looks a little shaggy. The other rule is to rest it. Chilling for an hour lets the flour absorb the water and relaxes the gluten, so the dough rolls without shrinking back in the oven. A splash of vinegar tenderises the crust by slowing gluten development, and a spoonful of sugar helps it brown. This recipe makes enough for a double-crust pie, and the instructions cover how to roll it, fit it into the tin and blind-bake one crust for custard, cream and no-bake fillings. The second disc can be used for a lattice or a top crust, or frozen for another day.

  • Keep everything cold. If the butter softens, put the bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes before you carry on.
  • Leave visible pieces of butter in the dough. They melt in the oven and leave the flaky layers, and dough with no visible butter is tough and crumbly.
  • Do not stretch the dough into the tin. Stretched pastry snaps back as it bakes and shrinks down the sides.

item.title: Flour Tortillas
item.description: Flour tortillas: soft, stretchy tortillas from flour, baking powder, salt, oil and warm water, rolled thin and cooked on a dry pan until they puff.
item.content:encoded:
Homemade flour tortillas are soft, warm and pliable in a way that most packaged tortillas are not, and they are one of the easiest breads to make. The dough is only flour, baking powder, salt, a little oil and warm water, mixed and kneaded briefly, then divided into balls, rested and rolled out as thin as you can. They are cooked in a hot, dry pan for less than a minute on each side, until they puff up in a few places and develop the brown blisters that give them their flavour. Flour tortillas are the tortilla of northern Mexico and of the American Southwest, where wheat grows better than corn, and they are the traditional wrapper for burritos, fajitas, quesadillas and breakfast tacos. The rest is the essential step. After kneading, the dough needs half an hour under a cloth so that the gluten relaxes, and a tortilla rolled from rested dough stays round and thin, whereas one rolled straight away shrinks back. Warm water helps the dough come together, and the oil, traditionally lard, makes them tender and stops them turning brittle. Once cooked, the tortillas are stacked in a clean tea towel, where they steam a little and stay soft, and they are ready to eat at once or to keep for the next day.

  • Rest the dough for the full 30 minutes. Dough that has not relaxed springs back as you roll and makes small, thick tortillas.
  • Use a hot pan and be quick. A tortilla that stays on the heat for more than a minute or so dries out and turns crisp instead of soft.
  • Roll thinner than you think you need to. The tortilla will puff and thicken as it cooks.

item.title: No-Bake Cookies
item.description: No-bake cookies: oats, cocoa and peanut butter stirred into a boiled sugar, butter and milk mixture and dropped in spoonfuls to set. No oven needed.
item.content:encoded:
No-bake cookies are the cookies that people make in a hurry, because they need no oven, no creaming and no chilling, and they are ready to eat in half an hour. They are also called preacher cookies, boiled cookies and cowpie cookies, and they have been a fixture of American church suppers and school lunchboxes since the middle of the twentieth century. The method is different from a baked cookie. Sugar, butter, milk and cocoa are brought to the boil together and boiled for exactly one minute, which cooks the sugar to the right stage, then peanut butter, vanilla and oats are stirred in and the mixture is dropped in spoonfuls onto paper. As it cools it sets into a chewy, fudgy cookie that tastes of chocolate and peanut butter. The one-minute boil is the only place where things can go wrong. Boil for less than a minute and the cookies will not set, and they stay sticky and soft, while boiling too long makes them dry and crumbly. A timer is worth using. Weather affects them too, since sugar candy sets less well on very humid days, so if it is damp, boil for an extra 15 seconds. Quick-cooking oats are best, because they soak up the syrup and give a soft texture.

  • Time the boil. One minute at a rolling boil is what makes the cookies set, and even 30 seconds less will leave them soft and sticky.
  • Work quickly once the oats go in. The mixture starts to set within a couple of minutes as it cools, and it is harder to shape after that.
  • Use quick oats, not jumbo oats. They absorb the syrup and give the cookies a soft, chewy bite.

item.title: Strawberry Cake
item.description: Strawberry cake: a tender two-layer cake flavoured with real reduced strawberry purée, with a pink strawberry buttercream and fresh berries on top.
item.content:encoded:
Most strawberry cakes owe their pink colour and their flavour to gelatin powder or food colouring, and they taste of artificial fruit. A cake made with real strawberries is a different thing, delicate and fresh, and worth the extra step. The trick is to cook the berries down. Strawberries are mostly water, and if you add the purée to a batter as it is, the cake will be heavy and gummy and taste of very little, so the fruit is simmered until it has reduced by more than half into a thick, jammy concentrate. This gives a natural pink colour and a real strawberry flavour, without adding extra liquid. The cake itself is a soft butter sponge, made by creaming butter and sugar, beating in eggs, and alternating the flour with milk and the cooled reduction. It bakes in two layers, cools completely and is sandwiched with a strawberry buttercream that uses more of the reduction for flavour, and fresh berries on top for a bright finish. The colour is a soft dusty pink, not a bright fondant pink, and that is a good sign. Make the strawberry reduction first, so it has time to cool, and do not frost a cake that is still warm. Frozen strawberries work well too and cook down in the same way, so this is a cake for any time of year.

  • Reduce the purée properly. It should be as thick as jam, with the volume less than half of what you started with, or the cake will be soggy.
  • Cool the purée before it goes into the batter. Hot fruit melts the butter in the mixture and knocks out the air.
  • Let the cake cool completely before you frost it. A warm cake melts the buttercream and slides.

item.title: Cookie Cake
item.description: Cookie cake: one giant, soft and chewy chocolate chip cookie baked in a cake tin and decorated with buttercream. An easy birthday treat.
item.content:encoded:
A cookie cake is a giant chocolate chip cookie made to be sliced like a cake, and it is a favourite birthday treat in the United States, where it is sold in mall cookie shops with a name piped on top. It is also easy to make at home, and it needs no layers, no frosting skills and no special equipment. The dough is a classic soft chocolate chip cookie dough, made with melted butter, so that there is no creaming and no waiting for it to soften, and mixed by hand in one bowl. Brown sugar gives the cookie its chewy centre and caramel flavour, and a little more flour than a normal cookie keeps the cake from spreading too thin. The dough is pressed into a greased 30 cm pizza tray or a 25 cm cake tin and baked until the edges are set and golden and the middle is still slightly soft, because it carries on cooking as it cools. Underbaking a little is the secret to a cookie cake that stays chewy rather than turning hard. Once it is cool, decorate it with piped buttercream, a border, a message or a scattering of sprinkles, or go plain. Serve it cut into wedges, warm with ice cream, or at room temperature with a glass of milk.

  • Take it out when the middle still looks a little soft. It keeps cooking in the hot tin, and an overbaked cookie cake turns hard and dry.
  • Use melted butter and mix by hand. Melted butter gives a chewier, denser cookie than the creamed kind.
  • Do not decorate a warm cake. Buttercream slides off warm dough, so wait until it is completely cool.

item.title: Rugelach
item.description: Rugelach: little crescent pastries of tender cream cheese dough rolled around apricot jam, cinnamon sugar, walnuts and raisins and baked until golden.
item.content:encoded:
Rugelach are the small rolled pastries of Ashkenazi Jewish baking, and they are one of the most loved cookies in New York bakeries and Jewish delis. The name comes from Yiddish and is said to mean little twists, and the pastries are made by rolling a triangle of dough around a sweet filling, into a small crescent. The dough is the marvel: made from equal weights of butter and cream cheese, with flour, it is tender, flaky and slightly tangy, and it rolls out easily when chilled. The classic filling is apricot jam, cinnamon sugar, chopped walnuts and raisins, though chocolate and poppy seeds are popular too. The dough is easy but must be kept cold. The butter and cream cheese are chopped into the flour, the dough is divided and chilled for a couple of hours, and it is rolled into circles that are cut into wedges, filled and rolled from the wide end to the point. Chilling the shaped pastries on the tray for a few minutes before baking helps them hold their shape and keeps the filling from leaking. They are baked until golden, and the jam bubbles out a little and caramelises on the tray, which is part of the charm. Rugelach keep well, and are a good pastry for holidays, and for gifts.

  • Keep the dough cold. If it softens as you roll it, return it to the fridge for 15 minutes, and the pastries will keep their layers.
  • Chop the nuts finely and press the filling down. Large pieces make the dough tear as you roll, and loose filling falls out.
  • Place the point of each wedge underneath the pastry. It stops the rugelach from unrolling in the oven.

item.title: Boston Brown Bread
item.description: Boston brown bread: a dark, moist, steamed loaf of rye, wholemeal flour and cornmeal sweetened with molasses and dotted with raisins.
item.content:encoded:
Boston brown bread is a New England classic, a dark, sticky, steamed loaf that tastes of molasses and is served, in the old tradition, with baked beans on a Saturday night. It is not baked in a dry oven. The batter is poured into a tin, covered tightly and steamed in a pot of simmering water for a couple of hours, which gives it a very moist, dense, almost pudding-like crumb with a smooth, unbroken crust. Its ingredients are the old staples of colonial New England. Rye flour, wholemeal flour and cornmeal are mixed in roughly equal parts, and molasses provides sweetness and the dark colour. Raisins are added for sweetness and texture. Traditional loaves were steamed in empty cans, giving the round slices with a flat top, and you can still buy Boston brown bread in a tin in New England supermarkets. The leavening is only bicarbonate of soda, which reacts with the buttermilk and molasses, so the loaf is dense, not airy. It is served in thick slices, warm or at room temperature, with butter or cream cheese, alongside baked beans and frankfurters, or toasted for breakfast. The method is slow but easy, and nothing needs watching apart from the water level. Top the pot up with boiling water if it drops.

  • Fill the basin only two-thirds full. The batter rises as it steams, and it needs room.
  • Keep the water at a gentle simmer and check it every 30 minutes. If the pot boils dry, the basin cracks and the bread scorches.
  • Use plain molasses, not blackstrap. Blackstrap is very bitter and makes an overpowering loaf.

item.title: Homemade Granola Bars
item.description: Homemade granola bars: chewy bars of toasted oats, almonds, seeds and dried cranberries, held together with honey and peanut butter.
item.content:encoded:
Granola bars became a supermarket staple in the 1970s, and people have been making their own ever since, because a homemade bar is cheaper, less sugary and more flavourful than the packaged version. It is also easy. Rolled oats, nuts and seeds are toasted, mixed with a warm binder of honey, peanut butter, brown sugar and oil, pressed into a tin and baked briefly. The result is a bar that is chewy in the middle and crisp at the edges. Getting a bar that holds together is the main challenge. There are three secrets. First, the binder must be sticky enough, and honey and peanut butter together do the job well. Second, the mixture has to be pressed into the tin very firmly, with the back of a spoon or a flat-bottomed glass, since loose packing means crumbly bars. Third, patience: the bars must cool completely in the tin before they are cut, because it is as they cool that the sugars set and hold everything together. Toasting the oats and nuts first deepens their flavour, and adding dried fruit at the end keeps its chew. The recipe is a template. Swap the almonds for pecans or walnuts, the cranberries for raisins, apricots or dates, or the peanut butter for almond butter. Wrap the bars individually for lunchboxes, hiking trips and breakfasts on the run.

  • Press hard. Firm, even pressure is the difference between bars that hold together and a tin of granola.
  • Cool the bars completely before cutting. They are soft while warm and set as the honey and sugar cool.
  • Cut with a sharp, heavy knife in a sawing motion. If they crumble at the edges, chill them for 20 minutes first.

item.title: Pampushky (Ukrainian Garlic Buns)
item.description: Pampushky: soft, golden yeast buns baked until puffy and brushed while hot with a garlic, dill and oil dressing. The traditional partner for borscht.
item.content:encoded:
Pampushky are the small, round, fluffy yeast buns of Ukraine, and the traditional accompaniment to a bowl of borscht. They are brushed, straight from the oven, with a mixture of garlic, oil, dill and salt that soaks into the crust and perfumes the bread, so that the whole kitchen smells of garlic. The dough is enriched with milk, egg and butter, and it bakes into a tender, golden, slightly sweet bun that stays soft for a day or two. In Ukrainian homes, a basket of pampushky arrives at the table beside the soup, and each guest tears one open and dips it in the broth. The garlic topping is what defines them, and it needs a careful hand. Crushed raw garlic is stirred with sunflower oil, a little water and salt, and left for a few minutes so the flavours blend. Brushing the hot buns lets the oil soak in and mellows the garlic, and covering them with a cloth afterwards keeps the crust soft. Pampushky can also be sweet in some regions, filled with poppy seeds or fruit, but the garlic version is the classic. They are best eaten warm, on the day they are made, and they freeze well, so it is worth making a full batch. The dough is soft and easy to handle, and the buns take two short rises.

  • Brush the topping on while the buns are hot. The oil soaks in, and the heat mellows the raw garlic.
  • Let the dough get properly puffy in both rises. Underproved buns are dense, and overproved ones collapse in the oven.
  • Crush the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt. Chunks burn the mouth, and a paste blends into the oil.

item.title: Zwieback (Mennonite Buns)
item.description: Zwieback: soft, tender double-decker yeast buns from the Mennonite kitchens of the Canadian prairies, with a small ball of dough on a larger one.
item.content:encoded:
Zwieback are the double-decker buns of the Mennonite communities of the Canadian prairies, and they are a fixture of church suppers, weddings, funerals and Sunday tables in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Each bun is made from two balls of dough, a small one set on top of a larger one and pressed down with a floured thumb, so that the finished roll has a distinctive two-tiered shape, with a neat dimple in the middle. The name comes from German and means twice or double, and it should not be confused with the German zwieback, a twice-baked rusk, since these buns are baked only once. The dough is a soft, enriched yeast dough, made with milk, butter and egg, and it is deliberately handled lightly, so the buns are tender and fluffy rather than chewy. They are served warm, split and buttered, with jam or with cold meats, cheese and pickles, and they are a classic part of a Mennonite meal alongside farmer sausage and borscht. Getting the shape right is the fiddly part. The top ball must sit firmly on the base, and you press right through both with a floured thumb or the handle of a wooden spoon until you touch the tray, so the two layers bake together and do not separate. Brush the tops with melted butter as soon as they come out of the oven.

  • Press right through both balls to the tray. If the top ball is only pressed lightly, it slides off as the dough rises.
  • Keep the dough soft. It should be slightly tacky, and adding too much flour makes tough buns.
  • Brush the buns with melted butter straight from the oven for a soft, shiny crust.

item.title: Tofu Scramble
item.description: Tofu scramble: crumbled extra-firm tofu cooked with turmeric, cumin, peppers and spinach into a golden, savoury vegan breakfast.
item.content:encoded:
A tofu scramble is the best-known vegan breakfast, a dish that looks and cooks something like scrambled eggs and has a pleasant savoury taste of its own. Firm tofu is crumbled into a pan with sautéed onion and pepper and cooked until it turns into soft, moist curds, and a pinch of turmeric gives it a golden colour that fools the eye. It is not meant to taste exactly like eggs. Tofu is mild, and it takes on whatever flavours you give it, so the seasoning does the work. Cumin and paprika add warmth and depth, garlic and onion give savour, and nutritional yeast, which is a deactivated yeast sold in flakes, adds a nutty, cheesy taste that makes the whole dish taste richer. A splash of soy sauce brings salt and umami, and a pinch of black salt, if you have it, adds a sulphurous, eggy note. The texture depends on the tofu. Use extra-firm tofu, drain it and press out the water first, since watery tofu steams and turns soggy. Crumble it into irregular chunks, some large and some small, and cook it until the moisture has evaporated and the edges are lightly golden. It is a high-protein breakfast that takes only 20 minutes, and it is very adaptable, so it takes whatever vegetables are in the fridge, and can also go into breakfast burritos or on toast.

  • Press the tofu before cooking. Extra water makes the scramble wet and pale, and pressed tofu browns and takes on the seasoning.
  • Crumble the tofu by hand into uneven pieces. It gives a better texture than mashing it with a fork, which makes it pasty.
  • Add the turmeric with the other spices in oil, not at the end. A minute in the hot oil brings out its colour and softens its raw taste.

item.title: Egg in a Hole
item.description: Egg in a hole: a slice of buttery bread with a hole cut in the middle and an egg fried in the hole. A breakfast ready in a few minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Egg in a hole is one of the great simple breakfasts, a slice of bread with a circle cut from the middle and an egg cracked into the gap, fried in butter until the bread is crisp and golden and the egg is set. It goes by a dozen names. It is egg in a basket, one-eyed Jack, gashouse eggs, bullseye eggs, eggs in a frame, hole in one, and in some parts of the world toad in the hole, which in Britain means sausages in batter. The trick is in the balance between the bread and the egg, and the frying does the work. The bread soaks up butter and turns golden and crisp on the outside while the egg cooks in its own little nest, so that the white sets and the yolk stays runny for dipping. The cut-out circle is not wasted, since it is fried alongside and used to mop up the yolk. It is best made with a thick slice of a sturdy bread, such as sourdough or a good white loaf, because thin bread tears and goes soggy. Cook it over medium heat, not high, so that the bread browns at about the same rate as the egg sets, and the whites do not burn. Turn it gently with a wide spatula, and cook it a minute or two on the second side for a runny yolk, or a little longer for a firm one. It takes ten minutes and one pan.

  • Use medium heat. Higher heat browns the bread before the egg has set, and lower heat makes the bread greasy.
  • Butter both sides of the bread. It gives an even golden crust and stops the egg from sticking.
  • Turn it with a wide spatula and a firm hand, supporting the bread and the egg together, so that the yolk stays whole.

item.title: Lemon Poppy Seed Muffins
item.description: Lemon poppy seed muffins: tall, tender, bakery-style muffins with a bright lemon flavour and crunchy poppy seeds, finished with a lemon glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Lemon poppy seed is one of the great flavour pairings in baking. The lemon gives a clean, fragrant sharpness that keeps a sweet muffin fresh-tasting, and the poppy seeds add a slight crunch and a faintly nutty flavour that make each bite more interesting. A good muffin should be tall, with a domed, golden top, and a crumb that is tender and moist without being heavy. Most of that comes from the technique. Mixing the wet and dry ingredients only until they come together, with a few streaks of flour still visible, keeps the gluten from developing and the muffins from turning tough and rubbery. The lemon flavour comes from three places: zest rubbed into the sugar, which releases the oils and perfumes the whole batter, the juice in the batter, and a glaze on top. Buttermilk gives a tender crumb and a slight tang, and it reacts with the bicarbonate of soda to help the muffins rise. For the tall bakery-style dome, start the oven very hot for the first five minutes, which gives the batter a burst of steam that pushes the tops up, then lower the temperature so that the centres cook through without the tops burning. Oil rather than butter keeps them moist for days. These are easy to make in one bowl, and the batter can be mixed the evening before, and baked in the morning.

  • Do not overmix. Stir just until the flour disappears, and the muffins will be tall and tender instead of tough and tunnelled.
  • Rub the zest into the sugar. The friction releases the lemon oils, and gives far more lemon flavour than stirring the zest in.
  • Start hot and finish cooler. The first 5 minutes at high heat make the tops dome, and the lower temperature finishes the middles without burning the tops.

item.title: Devil's Food Cake
item.description: Devil's food cake: a deep, dark, moist two-layer chocolate cake made with cocoa and hot coffee, covered in rich chocolate fudge frosting.
item.content:encoded:
Devil's food cake is the dark, rich, intensely chocolatey layer cake of American baking, and it is named in contrast to angel food cake, the white, airy, pale cake that is its opposite. The first recipes appeared in cookbooks in the early twentieth century, and the cake has been the choice for birthdays and celebrations since. What sets it apart from an ordinary chocolate cake is the cocoa, in generous quantity, and the way it is used. The batter includes bicarbonate of soda, which reacts with the acidic cocoa and buttermilk to give a tender, soft crumb and, in some cases, a reddish colour, and hot coffee is stirred in at the end to bloom the cocoa, which deepens the chocolate flavour without making the cake taste of coffee. The batter is thin, and it produces a moist, light cake that stays soft for days. Brown sugar adds moisture and a hint of caramel, and buttermilk gives a slight tang that balances the sweetness. The usual frosting is a fudgy chocolate one, made here from melted dark chocolate, butter, icing sugar and soured cream, which gives it a glossy, spreadable texture and a slightly tart edge. Let the layers cool completely before frosting, or the frosting will melt and slide off.

  • The batter is thin. That is right. It makes a moist, tender cake, and adding more flour to thicken it would make it dry.
  • Cool the melted chocolate before beating it into the frosting. Hot chocolate melts the butter and gives a greasy frosting that will not hold.
  • Frost the cake only when it is completely cold. A warm cake melts the frosting and the layers slide.

item.title: Brandy Snaps
item.description: Brandy snaps: thin, golden, lacy tubes of butter, sugar, golden syrup and ginger, rolled around a spoon handle while warm. Best filled with cream.
item.content:encoded:
Brandy snaps are thin, brittle, lace-like biscuits, rolled into tubes while they are still warm and pliable, and they have been a British treat since at least the nineteenth century. They were sold at fairs, and are still associated with the Nottingham Goose Fair and other old English fairgrounds, and in many households they are a Christmas tradition, filled with whipped cream and served with a glass of something festive. Despite the name, the biscuits do not always contain brandy, and the original snaps were called brandy for their crisp snap, or, some say, for a version made with a drop of brandy. The mixture is very simple: equal weights of butter, sugar, golden syrup and flour, with ground ginger and a dash of brandy or lemon juice. It is melted, stirred together, and dropped in small teaspoons onto a tray, where it spreads in the oven into a thin, golden, lacy disc. Then comes the tricky part. The discs must be lifted from the tray and shaped while they are still hot, in the minute or so before they set, and this takes a little nerve and speed. Bake only three or four at a time and roll each one quickly around the handle of a wooden spoon. If they cool and harden before you can shape them, a minute in the oven softens them again. Once cold, they are wonderfully crisp and will keep for weeks.

  • Bake only 3 or 4 snaps at a time. You have less than a minute to roll each one, and a tray of 8 will set before you get to the last.
  • Leave plenty of room. The mixture spreads to about 10 cm, and snaps that touch merge into one large sheet.
  • Fill them only when serving. Cream softens the snaps within an hour, and empty ones keep their crispness for weeks.

item.title: Nettle Soup
item.description: Nettle soup: young spring nettle tops simmered with onion, potato and stock, then blended into a vivid green, velvety soup that tastes like spinach.
item.content:encoded:
Nettle soup is the taste of a British spring, made from the young shoots of stinging nettles that come up in hedgerows, woods and gardens between March and May. Foraging for them has a long history, since nettles were one of the first green vegetables of the year, at a time when stores had run low, and they were traditionally eaten in soups, puddings and teas. The sting disappears completely with cooking, and once it is cooked a nettle tastes like a rich, slightly earthy spinach, with a hint of cucumber and a mineral depth. The soup is very simple. An onion and a potato are simmered in stock to make a base, and the potato gives the soup body without cream. The nettles go in at the end for just a few minutes, so that they stay bright green, and the whole pot is blended until smooth. A little cream and a grating of nutmeg finish it. Collecting the nettles calls for a few precautions. Wear rubber gloves and pick only the top four to six leaves of young plants, before they flower, and always pick from places away from roads, dogs and sprayed fields. Wash them well, and handle them with gloves or tongs until they have been in the boiling stock. Nettles are rich in iron, vitamin C and other nutrients, which is one reason that this soup has always been seen as a spring tonic.

  • Pick only young tops, before the plants flower. Older leaves are tough and can taste bitter, and mature nettles can make the soup gritty.
  • Cook the nettles for only a few minutes. Longer cooking turns them dull and olive green instead of bright.
  • Handle the raw leaves with gloves. Once they have been in the hot stock they are completely safe to touch and eat.

item.title: Stottie Cake
item.description: Stottie cake: a big, flat, chewy round loaf from Newcastle, baked hot and split for sandwiches. The traditional partner for ham and pease pudding.
item.content:encoded:
The stottie cake is the bread of Newcastle and the North East of England, and it is not a cake at all but a large, flat, round loaf that is soft and chewy in the middle and has a pale, floury crust. It is also called a stotty or a stottie, and the name is thought to come from the northern word stot, meaning to bounce, since a well-made one is said to bounce if you drop it on the floor. The bread was traditionally made from leftover bread dough, baked on the bottom of the oven when the fire was hot, and it was a working man's loaf, dense and filling, and cooked to be split open and stuffed. The classic filling is ham and pease pudding, a thick spread of yellow split peas, but it also holds bacon and egg, sausage, cheese and pickle, or a full breakfast. The dough itself is an ordinary white bread dough, made with strong flour, yeast, salt and a little fat, kneaded well and left to rise. What is unusual is the shape. It is shaped into a large flat disc, about 3 cm thick, pricked all over with a fork so it does not puff up, given a short second rise, and baked in a very hot oven. Turning it over halfway through gives an even bake, and a soft, pale crust on both sides. Cool it on a wire rack, and split it horizontally to fill.

  • Prick the dough all over with a fork. It stops the disc from puffing up like a balloon and keeps it flat.
  • Knead the dough well. A stottie should be dense and chewy, and a good 10 minutes of kneading develops the gluten.
  • Turn the loaves halfway through baking. It bakes both sides evenly and gives the traditional soft, pale crust.

item.title: Apple Dumplings
item.description: Apple dumplings: whole apples filled with cinnamon sugar and butter, wrapped in pastry and baked in a bubbling cinnamon syrup. Serve warm with cream.
item.content:encoded:
Apple dumplings are one of the great comforting desserts of American home baking, with strong roots in the German-speaking farm kitchens of Pennsylvania and the Midwest. A whole apple is peeled and cored, the hollow is packed with butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, and the fruit is wrapped in a square of pastry and baked until the crust is golden and the apple has softened right through. The clever part is the sauce. A syrup of brown sugar, butter, water and cinnamon is poured around the dumplings before baking, and as they cook it bubbles up and is absorbed by the pastry, so the outside turns glossy and caramelised while the base soaks up the flavour. What comes out is a pastry-wrapped apple in its own caramel, best eaten warm, with a jug of cream or a scoop of vanilla ice cream beside it. The choice of apple is important. Firm, tart apples, such as Granny Smith, Braeburn or Bramley, hold their shape and balance the sweetness, whereas soft apples collapse into mush. Small ones, about 150 g each, cook through in the time it takes to bake the pastry, and larger ones stay raw in the centre. The pastry can be homemade or ready-made shortcrust or puff, and the dumplings can be assembled a few hours ahead, then baked when the main course is finished.

  • Choose small apples of even size. Large ones do not cook through by the time the pastry is golden, and the centre stays hard.
  • Seal the pastry well. If the seams open, the filling leaks into the sauce and the pastry cooks unevenly.
  • Pour the sauce around the dumplings and not on top. It keeps the pastry crisp on top, and lets the base soak up the syrup.

item.title: Cake Pops
item.description: Cake pops: little balls of crumbled vanilla cake mixed with buttercream, chilled, dipped in melted chocolate and covered in sprinkles, on sticks.
item.content:encoded:
Cake pops turned a party cake into finger food, and since the blogger Bakerella made them famous in the late 2000s they have been a regular at birthday parties, baby showers and bake sales. The idea is that a cake is crumbled into fine crumbs, mixed with just enough frosting to make it hold together, rolled into balls, pushed onto lollipop sticks and dipped in melted chocolate, so that each mouthful is a soft, dense, fudgy truffle of cake inside a crisp shell. They are more forgiving than they look, and they are a good way to use leftover cake, although this recipe includes a simple vanilla cake so you can make them from scratch. The amount of frosting is the key. Too little, and the balls crumble and fall apart, and too much, and they turn greasy and heavy and slide off the stick. Start with a few spoonfuls, and add more only until the mixture holds when squeezed. The other important stage is chilling. The rolled balls must be very firm before dipping, or they fall into the warm chocolate, and the stick must be dipped into a little melted chocolate first, to act as glue, before it is pushed halfway into the ball. Thin the coating with a little coconut oil so that it flows smoothly, and tap off the excess, turning the pop slowly, to avoid cracking.

  • Use as little frosting as you can. The mixture should hold when squeezed, and a greasy mixture makes heavy balls that slip off the stick.
  • Chill the balls until they are hard before dipping. Soft ones fall off the stick or dissolve in the warm chocolate.
  • Dip in a tall narrow glass and keep the chocolate just warm. Chocolate that is too hot makes the balls slide, and too cool makes a thick, lumpy coat.

item.title: Coconut Cream Pie
item.description: Coconut cream pie: a crisp biscuit crust filled with rich coconut custard, topped with whipped cream and toasted coconut. A classic diner pie.
item.content:encoded:
Coconut cream pie is one of the standards of the American diner dessert case, a pie with a tall, creamy, coconut-flavoured custard, a crisp crust and a cloud of whipped cream on top. It is a cream pie, in the family of banana cream and chocolate cream pies, and it depends on a proper cooked custard. Sugar, cornflour and egg yolks are whisked into a mixture of milk and coconut milk and cooked over medium heat, stirring all the time, until it thickens and bubbles, and it has to bubble for a full minute to cook off the raw starch taste and set properly. Butter and vanilla are stirred in at the end for richness. Coconut appears three times, in the coconut milk, in a handful of desiccated coconut stirred into the filling, and in the toasted flakes that finish the top, and that layering gives the pie a deep coconut flavour that does not taste of suntan lotion. The crust here is a biscuit one, simply crushed digestives and melted butter, baked briefly, which is easier and more reliable than pastry and complements the filling well. The pie needs at least four hours in the fridge to set, and it is best made the day before. Cut it with a hot knife, wiping it between slices, for tidy, clean edges.

  • Let the custard bubble for a full minute while you whisk. Undercooked cornflour tastes raw, and the custard will not set firmly.
  • Press cling film on the surface of the hot custard. It stops a skin from forming, and the filling stays smooth.
  • Toast the flaked coconut in a dry pan for 2 minutes until golden. Keep watching, since it burns quickly.

item.title: Lebkuchen
item.description: Lebkuchen: soft, spiced German honey cookies with ground almonds, candied peel and warm Christmas spices, finished with a thin lemon glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Lebkuchen are the spiced honey cakes of the German Christmas, and the biggest name among them is Nuremberg, where they have been baked since at least the fourteenth century, from a recipe developed in the monastery kitchens of Franconia. The dough is sweetened with honey, rather than sugar, and loaded with spices, cinnamon, cloves, ginger, nutmeg, allspice and cardamom, and with ground almonds and candied peel, so that the cookies are soft, moist and chewy, with a rich, warm, complex taste.
