They are traditionally baked in round shapes on thin edible wafers, called Oblaten, that stop them from sticking, and glazed with sugar or dark chocolate, and they are sold at every Christmas market in Germany. Real Nürnberger Lebkuchen has a high proportion of nuts and very little flour, but the home version uses a bit of flour, which makes it much easier to handle. The most important step is the resting time. The dough has to be chilled for a couple of hours, and ideally overnight, so the flour absorbs the honey and the spices mellow. The dough is sticky, so shape the cookies with wet hands. After baking, the cookies are hard, and they soften as they sit, which is why they are traditionally made weeks before Christmas, and kept in a tin with a piece of apple or a slice of bread to mellow.

  • Do not skip the chilling time. The dough is very sticky when it is warm, and resting lets the flour take up the honey so you can shape it.
  • Use wet hands to shape the dough. It clings less to damp skin, and it also keeps the surface of the cookies smooth.
  • Give them time to soften. Lebkuchen taste better after a few days in a tin, when they turn soft and chewy and the spices mellow.

item.title: Rum Balls
item.description: Rum balls: no-bake truffles of crushed biscuits, cocoa, coconut and condensed milk, soaked in rum and rolled in coconut. An Aussie Christmas treat.
item.content:encoded:
Rum balls are a fixture of an Australian Christmas, made in the days before the holiday and handed round on plates and in tins as gifts. They are also popular in New Zealand and Britain. They belong to the family of no-bake sweets, like the chocolate biscuit cake, and are made from what is in the cupboard: crushed plain biscuits, cocoa, desiccated coconut, sweetened condensed milk and a generous splash of dark rum. The mixture is stirred together, chilled until it is firm enough to handle, rolled into small balls and covered in coconut or chocolate sprinkles. The result is a rich, fudgy, boozy little truffle that tastes better after a day or two, when the rum has soaked in and the flavours have blended. The rum is not cooked, so it retains its full strength, and these are not for children. Use a dark or spiced rum, since white rum has little flavour, and add it gradually, because the mixture must be firm enough to roll, and too much liquid makes a sticky paste. A few spoonfuls of the biscuit crumbs can be added if it is too wet. Rolling in a bowl of desiccated coconut, chocolate sprinkles or cocoa gives each ball a different look. Keep them in paper cases in an airtight tin in the fridge, where they last for a couple of weeks. They are also good made with fruit cake or chocolate cake crumbs.

  • Use a dark or spiced rum. Its flavour comes through in the finished balls, while white rum tastes of little.
  • Add the rum gradually and stop when the mixture holds together. Too much liquid makes a sticky paste that cannot be rolled.
  • Make them a day or two in advance. The rum soaks into the crumbs and the flavour deepens with time.

item.title: Chocolate Ganache
item.description: Chocolate ganache: equal parts dark chocolate and hot cream, stirred until glossy. Pour as a glaze, cool for a frosting or whip it light.
item.content:encoded:
Ganache is the simplest of the great French pastry preparations, and one of the most useful. It is made from just two ingredients, chocolate and cream, and the way they are combined and the ratio between them turn it into a glaze, a frosting, a filling for tarts and macarons, or the base of a truffle. It is said to have been discovered by accident in a Paris pastry shop in the middle of the nineteenth century, when an apprentice knocked a pan of hot cream onto a bowl of chopped chocolate, and was called ganache, a word for a fool. The process is very easy. Heat the cream until it is just about to boil, pour it over finely chopped chocolate, leave it for two minutes so the heat can melt it, and stir gently from the centre until it becomes smooth and glossy. The ratio decides the use. Equal weights make a soft ganache that pours as a glaze when warm and thickens as it cools into a spreadable frosting. Two parts chocolate to one part cream set firm enough to roll into truffles, and more cream makes a looser sauce. A small piece of butter stirred in adds a silky gloss, and a pinch of salt sharpens the flavour. Use chocolate of at least 60 per cent cocoa, chopped small so that it melts evenly, and do not overheat the cream, since boiling cream can split the ganache.

  • Chop the chocolate finely. Small pieces melt evenly in the hot cream, whereas large chunks leave the ganache lumpy.
  • If the ganache splits and looks oily, stir in a tablespoon of warm milk or cream, a little at a time, until it comes back together.
  • For truffles, use 300 g of chocolate to 150 ml of cream, chill until firm, scoop and roll in cocoa.

item.title: Baked Alaska
item.description: Baked Alaska: a sponge base topped with a dome of raspberry-ripple vanilla ice cream, covered in meringue and browned in a very hot oven.
item.content:encoded:
Baked Alaska is one of the great showpiece desserts, a dish that seems to contradict itself. A dome of ice cream, sitting on a layer of sponge cake, is covered completely with meringue and put into a scorching oven, and it comes out with a golden, toasted, marshmallowy outside and ice cream that is still frozen in the middle. The secret is the meringue. Whisked egg white is mostly air, and air is a poor conductor of heat, so a thick layer of meringue insulates the ice cream for the few minutes it takes to brown, and the sponge below protects it from the tray. It was made famous at Delmonico's in New York in 1867, where the chef created a dessert called Alaska, Florida to mark the purchase of Alaska by the United States, and it has been a dinner-party favourite in America, Britain and Australia ever since. It is easier than it looks, because most of the work is done ahead. The ice cream is packed into a basin and frozen solid, the meringue is whisked at the last minute, and the assembled dessert is baked for four or five minutes and brought to the table straight away. Every part of the ice cream must be covered, with no gaps, and the meringue must touch the base on all sides. Serve it at once. It cannot wait, and it is at its best in the first few minutes.

  • Freeze the ice cream until it is rock solid. Even a slightly soft centre melts in the hot oven, and the dome will collapse.
  • Cover every bit of the ice cream, and seal the meringue right down to the tray. A gap in the insulation lets the heat in, and the ice cream will run out.
  • Get the oven really hot before the dessert goes in. A fast, high bake browns the meringue before the heat reaches the ice cream.

item.title: Watergate Salad
item.description: Watergate salad: a fluffy, pale green pudding salad of pistachio pudding mix, crushed pineapple, marshmallows and pecans folded into whipped cream.
item.content:encoded:
Watergate salad is one of the retro dishes of the American potluck, a pale green, fluffy, sweet dessert that is called a salad for reasons of tradition, not vegetables. It belongs to the family of fluff and pudding salads that were popular from the 1950s to the 1970s, in which instant pudding, canned fruit, marshmallows and whipped topping were folded together into something creamy and cool. It is known by other names, pistachio delight, green stuff and pistachio pineapple fluff. The name Watergate is usually attributed to the 1970s, when the scandal was in the news, but nobody is quite sure why the dish carries it. It is easy to make, and the method is scarcely a method. Dry instant pistachio pudding mix is stirred straight into a can of crushed pineapple with its juice, which sets and thickens the mixture without any cooking, then whipped cream, mini marshmallows and chopped nuts are folded in. The result is a sweet, creamy, slightly crunchy dish, with the sharp, fruity note of pineapple against the mild pistachio flavour. It is served cold from a big bowl, as a side at a barbecue or a Thanksgiving buffet, or as a dessert. Instant pistachio pudding is an American product. If you cannot get it, use instant vanilla pudding powder with half a teaspoon of almond extract and a drop of green food colouring.

  • Do not drain the pineapple. The juice dissolves the pudding mix and sets it, and drained fruit makes a dry, lumpy salad.
  • Fold gently. Stirring hard knocks the air out of the cream and leaves the dessert flat and runny.
  • Add the marshmallows and nuts just before you chill it. They soften a little as the salad stands, which is part of its charm, and some cooks fold them in just before serving for more bite.

item.title: Mississippi Mud Pie
item.description: Mississippi mud pie: a chocolate cookie crust filled with a dark, gooey, fudgy chocolate and pecan filling, topped with whipped cream and shavings.
item.content:encoded:
Mississippi mud pie is the chocolate lover's dessert of the American South, named for the dark, thick, sticky mud of the Mississippi River banks, which the filling is meant to resemble. It has a crunchy chocolate cookie crust, a deep, dense, fudgy filling somewhere between a brownie and a chocolate pudding, and a heap of whipped cream on top. The exact origins are hard to pin down, but the pie has been a menu fixture in Southern restaurants since at least the 1970s, and it exists in many forms, some with layers of ice cream and some baked like this one. The baked version is made with a mixture of melted butter and dark chocolate, eggs, sugar, a little cocoa and flour, and chopped pecans for crunch, poured into a crust and baked until set at the edges but still gooey in the middle. Underbaking is the point: the centre should wobble slightly when it comes out and set as it cools, giving the pie its soft, fudgy texture. The cookie crust is easy, since chocolate sandwich biscuits are crushed, filling and all, and mixed with melted butter, without any need to roll pastry. Topped with lightly sweetened cream and chocolate shavings, the pie is rich, so cut small slices and serve it cold, with strong black coffee to balance the sweetness.

  • Take the pie out while the middle still wobbles. It continues to set as it cools, and an overbaked pie turns dry and cakey instead of fudgy.
  • Cool the melted chocolate and butter before you whisk in the eggs. If the mixture is too hot, the eggs cook and you will have flecks in the filling.
  • Use a sharp knife dipped in hot water for clean slices. Wipe it between cuts.

item.title: Clotted Cream
item.description: Clotted cream: double cream baked very slowly for twelve hours, then chilled, until it forms a thick, golden, nutty crust. The cream for a cream tea.
item.content:encoded:
Clotted cream is the thick, rich, yellow-crusted cream of Devon and Cornwall, and the crowning glory of the cream tea, spooned onto a warm scone with strawberry jam. Cornwall and Devon disagree about the order, since in Devon the cream goes on first with jam on top, and in Cornwall the jam goes first, and both counties will defend theirs. Cornish clotted cream has had a Protected Designation of Origin since 1998. Traditionally it was made by heating full-cream milk very gently in a shallow pan for many hours, and letting it cool overnight, so the cream rose and thickened into a golden crust, which was skimmed off. At home it is easier to start with double cream and bake it, and the result is remarkably close. A litre of cream is poured into a shallow dish and left in a very low oven for twelve hours, during which the water slowly evaporates and the fat and milk solids concentrate and thicken into a rich, slightly golden layer. It is then chilled overnight, when the crust firms and the cream beneath sets thick. The taste is nutty, sweet and faintly caramelised, unlike whipped cream, and the texture is somewhere between soft butter and thick cream. Use pasteurised double cream with a fat content of at least 48 per cent, since ultra-heat-treated cream does not clot. It needs no work, only patience and a very low oven.

  • Use pasteurised cream, not UHT. UHT cream has been heated so far that it will not clot, and you will get thin, greasy cream instead.
  • A lower oven temperature is better. If your oven will not go below 100°C, set the door ajar with a wooden spoon to keep the heat down.
  • Keep the thin liquid that is left in the dish. It can be used in scones or baking in place of milk or buttermilk.

item.title: Clams Casino
item.description: Clams casino: littleneck clams on the half shell topped with bacon, red pepper, garlic, butter and breadcrumbs and grilled until golden.
item.content:encoded:
Clams casino is one of the classic American seafood starters, a dish of clams on the half shell topped with bacon, peppers and breadcrumbs and grilled until the topping is golden and the clams are just cooked. It is said to have been created in 1917 at the Little Casino in Narragansett Pier, Rhode Island, by a maître d' who wanted something new for a guest, and the casino gave the dish its name. It turned up in steakhouses and Italian-American restaurants across the country, where it is still on the menu next to shrimp cocktail. The recipe has a lovely balance. The clams are sweet, briny and tender, the bacon adds smoke and salt, the red pepper adds sweetness and colour, and the breadcrumbs, butter and garlic give a crisp, savoury crown. The clams have to be small and tender, and the standard is littleneck, which are just big enough to hold a spoonful of topping. They are opened by steaming, which is easy, and then loosened in the shell. Setting the shells on a bed of coarse salt, or crumpled foil, keeps them level so that the butter and juices do not spill. Cook them under a very hot grill for only three or four minutes, because clams turn rubbery when overcooked. Serve at once with lemon wedges.

  • Buy the smallest tender clams you can find, and do not overcook them. They are cooked twice, once in the steam and once under the grill, so keep both short.
  • Set the clams on a bed of coarse salt. It holds the shells level, so the topping and juices stay in place.
  • Chop the bacon and vegetables finely. Large pieces do not stay on the clams and will not cook through in the few minutes under the grill.

item.title: Fried Green Tomatoes
item.description: Fried green tomatoes: slices of firm green tomato dipped in buttermilk and coated in cornmeal and breadcrumbs, then fried until crisp and golden.
item.content:encoded:
Fried green tomatoes are a Southern classic, though their history is less rooted in the South than the popular image suggests. Food historians note that fried green tomatoes were eaten in the Northeast and Midwest, among Jewish immigrants and others, well before they became a symbol of the South, and that they took hold there because the season for ripe tomatoes was short. The film Fried Green Tomatoes, based on Fannie Flagg's novel about the Whistle Stop Cafe, made them famous across the country in 1991. A green tomato is simply an unripe one, and it is firm, tart and slightly bitter, with a texture that stays intact in the frying pan, where a ripe tomato would turn to mush. The slices are salted to draw out some of the moisture, then dipped in egg and buttermilk and coated in a crust of cornmeal, which gives a distinctive crunch and a sweet, toasty flavour. They are fried in a shallow layer of hot oil until crisp and golden, and eaten at once, while the outside is crunchy and the inside is soft and tangy. Serve them with a dipping sauce, such as remoulade, ranch or a spiced mayonnaise, or as a side dish. Select firm, fully green tomatoes, not those on the turn to pink, and slice them evenly so they cook at the same rate.

  • Use firm, entirely green tomatoes. Ripening ones are too soft, and they fall apart in the pan.
  • Salt the slices and pat them dry. It draws out water that would otherwise make the coating soggy.
  • Keep the oil at a steady medium-high heat. If it is too cool, the coating soaks up oil, and if it is too hot, it burns before the tomato has softened.

item.title: Mango Chutney
item.description: Mango chutney: chunks of firm mango simmered with onion, ginger, vinegar, sugar and warm spices until thick and glossy. For poppadoms and curries.
item.content:encoded:
Mango chutney is the sweet, sharp, spiced condiment that sits on the table beside every curry, and the version that most people know is the British take on a much older Indian tradition. Chutneys in India are freshly made pastes and relishes, but the British in India took home the idea of a cooked, preserved fruit chutney, and by the nineteenth century mango chutney was a staple export, known from Bengal to Yorkshire. Made at home, it is much better than most jars, and it is easy. Firm, ripe mangoes are diced and simmered with onion, garlic and ginger in a syrup of sugar and vinegar, with mustard seeds, cumin, chilli and cinnamon, until the fruit is soft and translucent and the liquid has reduced to a thick, glossy glaze. Raisins add sweetness and chew. What matters is the balance, since the sugar and the vinegar need to be in tension, sweet and sour together, with the spices in the background. Choose mangoes that are ripe but still firm, so that they hold their shape in the simmering syrup, and do not use soft, overripe fruit, which turns to mush. Poured into sterilised jars while hot, it keeps for months, and its flavour deepens after a week. Serve it with poppadoms, cheese, cold meats, curries, or in a sandwich with cheddar.

  • Use ripe but firm mangoes. Underripe fruit is sour and stringy, and overripe fruit turns to mush before the syrup has reduced.
  • Stir often as the chutney thickens. The sugar catches on the base of the pan, and burnt chutney has a bitter taste.
  • Test for set by dragging a spoon across the base of the pan. If the trail stays open for a second or two, it is ready.

item.title: Prawn Toast
item.description: Prawn toast: bread spread with a seasoned prawn paste, pressed with sesame seeds and deep-fried until crisp. The Chinese takeaway favourite.
item.content:encoded:
Prawn toast is the classic starter from the Chinese takeaway, a triangle of fried bread topped with a golden layer of prawn paste and crunchy sesame seeds. It began in Hong Kong and Cantonese restaurants, where it was known as hatosi, and it was one of the dishes that Chinese restaurants abroad found the local customers loved, and it now appears on menus across the UK, Australia, Canada and the United States. It is much easier to make at home than it looks. Raw prawns are chopped or pulsed in a food processor to a coarse paste, seasoned with soy sauce, ginger, spring onion and a little sesame oil, and bound with egg white and a spoonful of cornflour, which makes the mixture cling to the bread. The paste is spread thickly on thin white bread, dipped in sesame seeds and fried, paste side down first, in hot oil until crisp. Frying the paste side first is important, since it seals the topping onto the bread, and it stops the prawn from sliding off when the toast is turned. The oil must be hot, at about 180°C, and the pieces should be fried in small batches, so that they stay crisp. Day-old bread is better than fresh, because it is drier and soaks up less oil, and removing the crusts makes neat triangles. Serve hot with sweet chilli sauce.

  • Use day-old bread. It is drier than fresh, so it soaks up less oil and stays crisp.
  • Fry paste side down first. The hot oil sets the topping onto the bread, so it does not slip off when you turn the toast.
  • Keep the paste chunky. Puréeing it smooth gives a rubbery, pasty texture, while a coarser mix is juicier and more tender.

item.title: Pumpkin Spice Latte
item.description: Pumpkin spice latte: hot espresso and steamed milk swirled with real pumpkin purée, sugar, vanilla and pie spice, topped with cream and cinnamon.
item.content:encoded:
The pumpkin spice latte is the drink that turned autumn into a flavour. A coffee chain launched it in 2003, and it grew into a seasonal event so large that the abbreviation PSL has become shorthand for the start of the fall. The recipe is nothing more than a latte flavoured like pumpkin pie, with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg and cloves, although the original had no pumpkin in it at all, and much of the flavour came from syrup. A homemade one is better, and it can be made with real pumpkin purée. The purée gives the drink a natural sweetness, a velvety body and a real vegetable depth, and heating it gently with the milk, sugar and spices lets the flavours blend and infuse. The steps are easy. Milk, pumpkin purée, sugar and spices are warmed in a saucepan, whisked until the pumpkin dissolves and the mixture is steaming, then frothed with a whisk or a blender, and poured over strong coffee. The result is creamy, spiced and not too sweet, and the sweetness can be adjusted to taste. Whole milk gives the creamiest result, but oat milk froths well too. Strong coffee, such as espresso or a very strong brew from a moka pot or AeroPress, keeps the coffee flavour from being lost in the spice. A cloud of whipped cream and a dusting of cinnamon finish it.

  • Use pure pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling. The filling is already sweetened and spiced, and the drink turns out cloying.
  • Keep the heat medium and whisk the whole time. Milk scorches on the base of the pan, and pumpkin sticks to it.
  • Make the coffee strong. A weak brew is lost among the milk and spice, and the drink tastes like pumpkin milk.

item.title: Gimlet
item.description: Gimlet: gin, fresh lime juice and a little sugar syrup, shaken hard and served ice-cold in a coupe. A crisp, tart, clean naval classic.
item.content:encoded:
The gimlet is one of the simplest and most refreshing gin cocktails, a mix of gin and lime that has been served since the age of sail. The most popular story is that it is named after Sir Thomas Gimlette, a surgeon in the Royal Navy in the late nineteenth century, who is said to have added lime cordial to the sailors' gin to encourage them to take their vitamin C and ward off scurvy. Lime cordial, sold as Rose's Lime Juice, was patented in the 1860s and was a fixture on British ships. The gimlet shows up in Raymond Chandler's novel The Long Goodbye, where a character insists that a real gimlet is half gin and half lime cordial and nothing else. That is a sweet drink, and today most bartenders prefer a fresher version, using fresh lime juice and a little sugar syrup in place of the cordial, which gives a brighter, sharper, cleaner taste that lets the gin come through. The drink is built like a daiquiri, a spirit, citrus and sugar in a ratio of about two to one to one, and the balance of sweet and sour is what makes it work. It is shaken hard with ice to chill and dilute it, then strained into a chilled glass. Use a London dry gin, whose juniper and citrus notes are a natural fit with lime, and squeeze the limes just before you make it.

  • Squeeze the lime juice just before you mix. Fresh juice tastes bright and clean, and bottled juice is dull and slightly bitter.
  • For the old-fashioned version, replace the lime juice and syrup with 30 ml of lime cordial and shake with the gin.
  • Shake with plenty of ice for a full 12 seconds. The dilution is part of the recipe, and a drink that is not shaken enough tastes harsh.

item.title: Cuba Libre
item.description: Cuba libre: white rum, cola and a squeeze of fresh lime over ice in a tall glass. It is more than a rum and coke, and the lime makes the difference.
item.content:encoded:
The Cuba libre is the world's best-known rum and cola, and the difference between it and a plain rum and coke is a squeeze of lime, which is what turns a simple mixed drink into a proper cocktail. The name means free Cuba in Spanish, and it comes from the toast raised at the end of the Spanish-American War, around 1900, when American soldiers and Cuban revolutionaries drank in Havana. Cola, still a new drink imported from the United States, was mixed with the local rum, and a squeeze of lime was added, as it was in almost every Cuban drink. It became the national cocktail of the island, and travelled worldwide, and it has been a staple of bars, parties and beaches ever since. It is a highball, built in the glass, and a good one depends on a few simple points. Use a good quality rum, white or golden, since the drink is too simple to hide a poor spirit. Fill the glass with plenty of ice, so the drink stays cold and the ice melts slowly. Use cola that is fresh and fizzy, from a small bottle or can, which holds its bubbles better than a flat two-litre bottle. And squeeze the lime into the drink, then drop the spent shell in, since the oils from the peel add a fragrant, bitter edge that balances the sweetness of the cola. It is not a fancy drink, and that is its charm.

  • Use fresh, cold, fizzy cola from a can or small bottle. Flat cola makes a syrupy drink with no sparkle, and a warm bottle melts the ice too fast and waters down the rum.
  • Drop the squeezed lime into the glass. The peel oils add a fragrant, slightly bitter note that balances the sweetness, and it is the sign of a properly made Cuba libre.
  • Stir gently, once. Vigorous stirring knocks out the bubbles, and the drink turns flat and syrupy before you have finished it.

item.title: Grasshopper
item.description: Grasshopper: green crème de menthe, white crème de cacao and cream, shaken and strained. A minty, chocolatey after-dinner cocktail.
item.content:encoded:
The Grasshopper is a dessert in a glass, a pale green cocktail that tastes like mint chocolate ice cream and is as smooth as cream. It was created at Tujague's, a famous restaurant in New Orleans, in 1918, by the owner Philibert Guichet, who is said to have entered it in a cocktail competition in New York and won second place. It became a fashionable after-dinner drink in the 1950s and 1960s, at the height of the vogue for sweet, creamy cocktails, and it went out of fashion for some time before a revival in recent years. It has three equal ingredients. Green crème de menthe, a peppermint liqueur, gives the mint and the colour, white crème de cacao, a clear chocolate-flavoured liqueur, gives a soft chocolate note, and cream makes it rich and velvety and mellows the two liqueurs. Equal parts is the classic ratio, and the result is very sweet, so many bartenders now use a little less of the liqueurs, or a splash more cream, for a softer, more balanced drink. It must be shaken hard with ice, to chill it, dilute it and make it foamy, and it is best served in a well-chilled coupe. Use white crème de cacao, not brown, or the drink will turn muddy, and add a sprinkle of dark chocolate shavings on top, which sharpens the sweetness.

  • Use white crème de cacao. The brown kind turns the drink a dull khaki, and the pale green colour is part of the appeal.
  • Shake hard for a full 15 seconds. The ice chills and slightly dilutes the drink, and the shaking gives it a light, frothy texture.
  • Taste, and if it is too sweet, reduce the liqueurs to 20 ml each, or add a little more cream. A splash more cream also softens the mint for anyone who finds it too strong.

item.title: Brandy Alexander
item.description: Brandy Alexander: brandy, dark crème de cacao and cream, shaken until frothy and dusted with nutmeg. A rich, smooth, chocolatey after-dinner classic.
item.content:encoded:
The Brandy Alexander is the great cream cocktail of the mid-twentieth century, a smooth, rich mix of brandy, chocolate liqueur and cream that is closer to a dessert than a drink. It is a variation on the earlier Alexander, a gin cocktail with crème de cacao and cream that appeared around the time of the First World War, and when brandy replaced gin the drink became more popular, and was a favourite of the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, in restaurants, hotel bars and living rooms. Its reputation is as an after-dinner drink, and it fits that role beautifully. The brandy brings warmth and a fruity, oaky depth, the dark crème de cacao adds sweetness and chocolate, and the cream turns them into something as smooth and mellow as a milkshake. A dusting of freshly grated nutmeg on top adds a fragrant, spicy note that stops the drink from being flat. The ratio is an equal one, and most bartenders now cut back on the sweetness by using a little more brandy. The drink needs a hard shake with plenty of ice, so that it turns cold, silky and slightly frothy, and it should be strained into a chilled glass and served straight away, since cream does not hold well. Use a good VS Cognac or brandy, and a dark crème de cacao, rather than the clear one, as it adds a deeper chocolate flavour and a more attractive colour.

  • Grate the nutmeg fresh. Pre-ground nutmeg is dull, and the fragrance of freshly grated spice is what lifts the drink, so keep a whole nutmeg and a small grater to hand.
  • Use plenty of ice and shake hard. It makes the drink cold and frothy, and mixes the cream smoothly.
  • For a drier, more brandy-forward drink, use 40 ml of brandy and 20 ml each of the liqueur and cream. Or swap the cream for a scoop of vanilla ice cream and blend it for a milkshake-style version.

item.title: Bramble
item.description: Bramble: gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup over crushed ice, drizzled with blackberry liqueur. A modern British classic that is easy to make.
item.content:encoded:
The Bramble is one of the great modern British cocktails, created in 1984 by the London bartender Dick Bradsell at Fred's Club in Soho, and it has become a standard in bars across the world. Bradsell said that he was inspired by the blackberry picking of his childhood on the Isle of Wight, when he would come home with hands scratched by brambles and stained purple with the fruit. The drink has the simplicity of a classic, and it is built like a gin sour, with gin, fresh lemon juice and sugar syrup, shaken and poured over crushed ice. The distinctive touch is the last step. A measure of blackberry liqueur, crème de mûre, is drizzled over the top of the ice, where it sinks slowly through the drink in dark purple ribbons, so the drink looks as though it is bleeding, and changes colour and flavour as it is drunk. The first sips are sharp and lemony, and the last are sweet and full of blackberry. Crushed ice matters, since it dilutes the drink slowly and keeps it very cold, so if you do not have any, wrap ice cubes in a tea towel and bash them with a rolling pin. Choose a London dry gin with a good juniper backbone, and use fresh lemon juice. A few fresh blackberries and a slice of lemon make the garnish, and a short straw is useful.

  • Use plenty of crushed ice. It keeps the drink cold and dilutes it slowly, and the liqueur sinks through it in ribbons.
  • Pour the crème de mûre slowly, last of all. If it is stirred in, it turns the whole drink a uniform purple, and you lose the effect.
  • Taste, and balance. If the lemon is too sharp for you, add a little more syrup, and if it is too sweet, reduce the liqueur.

item.title: Hugo Spritz
item.description: Hugo spritz: prosecco, elderflower syrup and soda water over ice with fresh mint and lime. A light, floral, fragrant spritz from the Alps.
item.content:encoded:
The Hugo spritz is a light, floral, summery drink from the Italian Alps, and it is a younger and gentler rival of the Aperol spritz. It was created in 2005 by Roland Gruber, a bartender in Naturno, in South Tyrol, the German-speaking region of northern Italy, who originally made it with a syrup of lemon balm and switched to elderflower, which has a more available and delicate flavour. It spread quickly across Austria and Germany and then across Europe, and it has been a summer favourite in Britain, where elderflower is loved. The drink is built in a large wine glass, which gives the aromas room, over ice. Prosecco provides the dry, fruity bubbles, elderflower syrup or cordial adds a perfumed sweetness that smells of a summer hedgerow, soda water lengthens it, and a small handful of fresh mint gives a cooling freshness. A wedge of lime brightens the whole drink. Slap the mint between your palms before it goes in, so that it releases its oils, and push it down among the ice. The ratio is typically three parts prosecco to one of syrup and one of soda, and it can be adjusted to taste, with more syrup for sweetness, or more soda for a lighter, longer drink. It is low in alcohol, refreshing and simple to make in quantity for a party.

  • Use a large wine glass and lots of ice. The size lets the mint and elderflower perfume rise, and the ice keeps the spritz cold without diluting it too quickly.
  • Choose a brut or extra dry prosecco. Elderflower syrup is sweet, and a sweeter wine labelled dry or demi-sec makes the drink cloying.
  • Slap the mint, do not crush it. Bruising the leaves brings out the aroma, whereas muddling releases bitter, grassy flavours. Fresh mint from a pot beats a wilted bunch.

item.title: Pornstar Martini
item.description: Pornstar martini: vanilla vodka, passion fruit liqueur, passion fruit purée and lime, shaken and served with a shot of prosecco on the side.
item.content:encoded:
The Pornstar Martini is Britain's favourite cocktail, and it is one of the best-selling drinks in pubs and bars across the country. It was created in 2002 by the London bartender Douglas Ankrah, at a bar in Knightsbridge, and it caught on, first in the city's cocktail bars and then across the country and the world. It is not a martini in the classical sense, but a fruity, sweet-and-sour drink in a martini glass, and its main flavour is passion fruit, which is tropical, sharp and aromatic. Vanilla vodka and vanilla syrup add a smooth, sweet warmth that softens the tartness, a passion fruit liqueur adds depth, lime juice gives a clean acid edge, and fresh passion fruit purée brings the flavour and the seeds. It is always served with a small glass of chilled prosecco on the side, which is sipped between mouthfuls of the drink, cleansing the palate, and some people pour it in. A half passion fruit floats on top as the garnish, and is scooped up with a spoon. To make it at home, choose ripe, wrinkled passion fruit, which are sweeter, and scoop the pulp with the seeds. Sieving is optional, since the seeds are edible, and many people like their crunch. Shake the drink very hard, with plenty of ice, to make a good foam. If you cannot find vanilla vodka, use plain vodka and a little extra vanilla syrup.

  • Shake for a full 15 seconds with lots of ice. It chills and dilutes the drink and gives it a pale, creamy foam that holds the passion fruit half.
  • Choose wrinkled passion fruit. Smooth ones are underripe and sour, and the wrinkled skin is a sign of sweetness.
  • Taste and adjust. If it is too tart, add a little more vanilla syrup, and if it is too sweet, add a squeeze more lime.

item.title: Stromboli
item.description: Stromboli: rolled pizza dough filled with salami, ham, pepperoni and melted mozzarella, brushed with garlic butter and baked until golden.
item.content:encoded:
Stromboli is an Italian-American invention, a pizza turned inside out. A sheet of pizza dough is layered with cured meats and cheese, rolled up like a Swiss roll and baked until the outside is golden and crisp and the inside is a mass of melted cheese and savoury meat. It is said to have been invented in 1950 by Nazzareno Romano at his restaurant in Essington, near Philadelphia, who named it after the volcanic Italian island of Stromboli, and after a film of the same name that was in cinemas that year, starring Ingrid Bergman. It is often confused with a calzone, but the two are different. A calzone is a folded half-moon with a ricotta filling, and a stromboli is a long rolled loaf, cut into thick slices, and it can carry a much larger amount of filling. It is made from pizza dough, so it is easy to make and you can use a shop-bought ball of dough if you are short of time. What makes a good one is restraint. Overfilling makes the dough burst in the oven and leaves the centre raw and doughy, so leave a clear border, roll tightly and seal the seam well. Slitting the top lets steam escape. A brush of garlic butter after baking gives the crust a glossy, savoury finish. It is best after 10 minutes of rest, when the cheese has stopped flowing, so it cuts cleanly.

  • Do not overfill it. Too much filling bursts through the seam, and the middle of the loaf stays raw and doughy.
  • Pinch the seam firmly and set the loaf seam side down. A loose seam opens in the oven and the cheese leaks onto the tray.
  • Let it rest for 10 minutes before you slice it. Straight from the oven, the cheese is molten and runs out at the first cut.

item.title: Chicken Riggies
item.description: Chicken riggies: rigatoni tossed with chicken, mushrooms and pickled cherry peppers in a spicy tomato cream sauce. A Utica, New York classic.
item.content:encoded:
Chicken riggies is the pasta dish of Utica, New York, and for people in Central New York it is what pizza is to Chicago. It is a big plate of rigatoni, hence the nickname riggies, tossed with chicken, mushrooms, onions and pickled cherry peppers in a spicy tomato and cream sauce. The dish is said to have been created in the 1980s at an Italian-American restaurant in the city, and it spread from there to nearly every restaurant, wedding hall and church supper across the region, each with its own recipe. There are fierce local arguments about the details. Some cooks use a cream sauce, others a plain tomato sauce, and some add a splash of vodka, and the peppers can be hot or sweet, so a home version is really a matter of taste. The pickled cherry peppers give the dish its character, with a tangy, vinegary heat that cuts through the richness of the sauce, and the brine from the jar goes into the sauce too. Rigatoni is the right pasta because its ridges and wide tubes trap the sauce. Cook the chicken in bite-size pieces so that it browns well and stays juicy, and finish the sauce with the pasta water if it is too thick. Serve it with grated Parmesan, extra peppers, and a green salad.

  • Undercook the pasta by 2 minutes. It finishes cooking in the sauce, where it soaks up the flavour and does not turn soft.
  • Add the cherry pepper brine to the sauce. It gives the dish its tangy heat and balances the cream.
  • Choose hot or sweet peppers depending on your taste. Hot ones give the classic kick, and sweet ones are milder and better for children.

item.title: Garbage Plate
item.description: Garbage plate: the Rochester, New York original of home fries and macaroni salad topped with burgers and hot dogs, smothered in meat hot sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The garbage plate is the signature dish of Rochester, New York, and a very generous, very messy one. A plate is piled with home fries and macaroni salad, topped with two kinds of meat, usually cheeseburgers or hot dogs, then covered with a spicy meat sauce, chopped raw onion and yellow mustard, and served with a couple of slices of buttered bread on the side. It began at a Rochester diner, where late-night customers asked for a bit of everything on one plate, and the owner named it after the way it looked. The name Garbage Plate is a registered trademark of the original restaurant, and other places in the city call the same dish a trash plate or a white plate. What defines it is the meat hot sauce, which is not hot in the sense of chilli heat. It is a thin, finely ground beef sauce spiced with cinnamon, allspice, chilli powder and paprika, and it is very different from a chilli or a Bolognese, and it is spooned generously over everything. The macaroni salad is a plain, creamy, slightly tangy one, and the home fries are crisp and salty. The dish is an exercise in abundance, so make each part, and pile it high. It is not health food, and it is not meant to be, and it makes a good meal for a crowd.

  • Cook the meat sauce until the mince is very fine. Breaking it up with a potato masher in the pan gives the smooth, sauce-like texture the dish needs.
  • Boil the potatoes first, then fry them. It cooks the insides through and gives crisp edges, so they stay crunchy under the sauce.
  • Serve the plate at once. Everything is at its best when the fries are still hot and the macaroni salad is cold.

item.title: Runza
item.description: Runza: soft yeast bread pockets filled with seasoned ground beef, cabbage and onion and baked until golden. A Nebraska comfort food.
item.content:encoded:
The runza is the sandwich of Nebraska, a soft yeast bread pocket packed with seasoned ground beef, cabbage and onion, and baked until golden. It came to the Great Plains with the Volga Germans, ethnic Germans who had settled in Russia in the eighteenth century and emigrated to the American Midwest in the late nineteenth century, bringing with them a bread pocket known as a bierock. A fast-food chain named Runza, founded in Lincoln, Nebraska, in 1949, made the name famous, and in Nebraska a runza is as familiar as a hamburger. The filling is simple, humble and very good. Beef is browned with onion and cabbage until the vegetables collapse and the moisture cooks off, and it is seasoned with only salt and pepper, and sometimes caraway. The bread is a soft, lightly enriched dough, with milk, butter and egg, that bakes to a tender, golden crust. What matters is cooking off the liquid in the filling, since wet filling will soak the dough from inside and burst the seams. Let it cool before it goes into the dough, and pinch the seams well. Each pocket is a meal in itself, and they are ideal for freezing and reheating for lunchboxes. Serve with mustard, ketchup or a spoonful of cheese sauce.

  • Cook the filling until it is dry. Wet filling makes soggy dough, and it can burst the seams as the pockets bake.
  • Cool the filling before you use it. Hot filling can start to cook the dough and makes it hard to shape.
  • Pinch the seams firmly and bake seam side down. A loose seam opens in the oven and the filling leaks onto the tray.

item.title: Ragoût de Boulettes
item.description: Ragoût de boulettes: the Québec meatball stew of spiced pork, potatoes and a dark toasted-flour gravy, made for Christmas and New Year.
item.content:encoded:
Ragoût de boulettes is one of the dishes that a Québécois family serves at the Réveillon, the late supper after midnight mass on Christmas Eve, and again at New Year. It is a stew of spiced pork meatballs in a dark, nutty gravy, and it is often cooked in the same pot as a ragoût de pattes, the trotter stew that gives the gravy its body. The seasoning is the same warm mix of cloves, cinnamon and allspice that goes into a tourtière, and it gives the meatballs a fragrance that is closer to a spiced pie than to a meatball in tomato sauce. The gravy is the point of the dish. It is thickened with farine grillée, flour that has been toasted in a dry pan until it turns the colour of peanut butter, which gives it a deep brown colour and a roasted taste that plain flour never gets. Potatoes cook in the stew and thicken it further. The method is simple, but it depends on patience with the flour, which needs stirring the whole time and is spoiled by a moment of neglect. Serve it in deep bowls with good bread to mop up the gravy, and with pickled beetroot or a sharp pickle to cut through the richness. Like most stews it tastes better the next day.

  • Stir the flour the whole time it toasts, over a steady medium heat. Pale flour tastes of paste, and flour that catches turns the gravy bitter.
  • Whisk the toasted flour into cold stock before it goes into the pot. Added dry to hot liquid, it forms lumps that will not break down.
  • Brown the meatballs properly before stewing. The crust holds them together in the gravy and adds to its colour and depth.

item.title: Country Captain
item.description: Country captain: the Georgia chicken braise with curry powder, tomatoes, green pepper and currants, served over rice with toasted almonds.
item.content:encoded:
Country captain is a Southern curry, and one of the oldest. It belongs to Savannah and to the Georgia and South Carolina coast, where the spice trade brought curry powder to the port cities in the nineteenth century, and it is an American way of cooking an Anglo-Indian idea. Nobody agrees on the captain. One story gives him as a British sea captain who brought the recipe home from India, and another as an officer who commanded local troops, the country captains of the East India Company. What the versions share is a chicken braised in a sauce of onion, green pepper, tomatoes and curry powder, with currants stirred in and toasted almonds on top, and it is served over plain white rice. It is gentle rather than hot. The currants add small pockets of sweetness, the green pepper gives the sauce a fresh, slightly bitter edge, and the almonds add crunch. The chicken is floured before it is browned, and the flour thickens the sauce as it cooks, so there is no need to add anything else. It was in American cookbooks by the middle of the nineteenth century, and it has never quite gone out of fashion in the South, where it is still a dish for a Sunday table or a covered-dish supper.

  • Keep the chicken skin above the sauce when it goes back into the pan. Skin that is left dry stays golden, and skin that is submerged turns pale and soft.
  • Use a curry powder that you like. A mild, sweet one gives a gentle sauce, and a hot Madras version makes a brisk one.
  • Toast the almonds separately and add them at the end. They lose their crunch within minutes in the sauce.

item.title: Lomi Lomi Salmon
item.description: Lomi lomi salmon: the Hawaiian luau side of salt-cured salmon, ripe tomatoes, sweet onion and spring onion, massaged together and served cold.
item.content:encoded:
Lomi lomi salmon is a fixture of the Hawaiian luau, the cold, salty and fresh salad that sits beside the rich kalua pork and the poi. Lomi means to massage or to rub in Hawaiian, and the salmon is diced and worked together with the tomatoes and onion by hand, which is where the dish gets its name. Salmon does not live in Hawaiian waters. The fish arrived in the nineteenth century, in barrels of salted salmon that came on trading ships from the North American Pacific coast, and Hawaiian cooks combined it with local tomatoes and sweet onion, and it has been a party dish ever since. The salt cure is the important part. It firms the flesh and seasons it through, and then the fish is rinsed and diced so it is savoury rather than salty. Everything is served cold, often on a bed of ice, because the salad is meant to be refreshing next to hot, smoky meat. It is a simple dish with a great deal of flavour, but it depends on the quality of its three main ingredients. Use salmon that is very fresh, tomatoes that are properly ripe, and a sweet onion, and keep everything well chilled until the moment of serving.

  • Rinse the cured salmon well and taste a piece before you go on. If it is still very salty, rinse it again, because the tomatoes will not balance it.
  • Cut everything into small, even dice about 5 mm across, so that every forkful has a little of each ingredient.
  • Buy the fish from a fishmonger you trust and ask for a piece that is suitable for eating raw. This is not a dish for anyone who is pregnant or has a weakened immune system.

item.title: Mushroom Barley Soup
item.description: Mushroom barley soup: the thick deli soup of pearl barley, browned mushrooms and dried porcini, with carrot, celery, lemon and fresh dill.
item.content:encoded:
Mushroom barley soup came to America with the Jewish immigrants of Eastern Europe, where mushrooms were gathered in the forests, dried for the winter and cooked with barley, the cheapest grain in the pot. It became a mainstay of the delicatessens of New York, served in deep bowls beside a slice of rye, and it was a soup that could sit on the table at a dairy meal because it needed no meat. The soup is thick, brown and savoury, and it depends on two things. The first is the mushrooms. A pack of dried porcini soaked in hot water gives a broth with a deep, almost meaty flavour, and fresh mushrooms cooked until they have lost their water and browned add sweetness and a good texture. The second is the barley. It swells as it cooks and absorbs a great deal of liquid, so the soup thickens as it stands and is often thicker on the second day than the first. Add a little water or stock when you reheat it. A spoonful of tomato paste and a splash of soy sauce give the pot depth without any meat, and lemon juice and dill at the end lift the whole bowl and stop it from tasting heavy.

  • Cook the fresh mushrooms until all the water has gone and they start to brown. This is where the flavour comes from, and pale, wet mushrooms make a bland soup.
  • Keep a jug of hot water or stock nearby. The barley keeps absorbing liquid, and the soup will need loosening when it is reheated.
  • Strain the porcini liquid carefully. Dried mushrooms hold sand, and a gritty spoonful spoils an otherwise good bowl.

item.title: Matzo Ball Soup
item.description: Matzo ball soup: golden chicken soup with fluffy matzo balls, shredded chicken, carrots and dill, the Jewish dish for Shabbat, Passover and sick days.
item.content:encoded:
Matzo ball soup is the best-known dish of the Ashkenazi Jewish kitchen: a clear, golden chicken soup with dumplings made from matzo meal, eggs and fat. It is served for Friday night dinner, at the Passover seder, when the ordinary flour of the year is set aside, and at any time when somebody needs comforting, which is why it is called Jewish penicillin. The matzo balls, or kneidlach, are the subject of an old argument. Some families like them light and fluffy, which are known as floaters, and others like them dense and firm, known as sinkers. Light ones need a gentle hand. The mixture is chilled for an hour so that the matzo meal takes up the liquid and can be shaped, the balls are rolled loosely, without pressing, and they are cooked in a covered pot at a slow simmer. Sparkling water helps, and schmaltz, the rendered chicken fat, gives the balls their traditional flavour, though vegetable oil works well too. Cooking the balls in a separate pot of salted water, rather than in the soup itself, keeps the broth clear. The soup is a plain, generous one: a chicken, some vegetables and a bunch of dill, simmered gently for an hour.

  • Shape the balls loosely with wet hands and do not press them. Packed tightly, they cook into hard sinkers.
  • Cook the matzo balls in salted water and not in the soup. They cloud the broth, and they take up its salt and fat as they swell.
  • Keep the lid on while they simmer. Steam is what puffs them up, and lifting the lid lets it out.

item.title: French Dressing
item.description: French dressing: the sweet and tangy orange-red American salad dressing of oil, vinegar, ketchup, sugar and paprika, shaken in five minutes.
item.content:encoded:
American French dressing has almost nothing to do with France. In the nineteenth century the name simply meant a vinaigrette of oil, vinegar, salt and pepper, but over the following decades it changed into something quite different, an orange-red, sweet and tangy dressing coloured with tomato and paprika and thickened with a great deal of oil. It became the dressing of the American salad bar, of the wedge of iceberg lettuce and the plate of sliced tomato and cucumber, and it was sold in bottles in every supermarket. Making it at home takes five minutes and needs only a jar. The oil and vinegar make the base, ketchup gives the colour and the tomato flavour, sugar softens the sharpness, paprika adds warmth, and a little grated onion and garlic give it savour. It is meant to taste sweet first and tangy after, so do not be tempted to cut back the sugar too far. The proportions here make a dressing that clings to leaves without being heavy, and it is also good as a marinade for chicken, a spread on burgers and a dip for chips. It separates as it stands, which is only the oil and vinegar parting, and a hard shake puts it right.

  • Grate the onion finely so that it melts into the dressing. Chunks of raw onion overpower the other flavours, and they turn harsh and bitter as the dressing stands.
  • Taste the dressing on a leaf, not from the spoon. Dressings taste much stronger on their own than they do once they are spread across a whole bowl of salad.
  • Use a neutral oil. Olive oil turns bitter and heavy when it is shaken into a sweet dressing, and its fruity taste fights with the ketchup and the paprika.

item.title: Béarnaise Sauce
item.description: Béarnaise sauce: the French steak sauce of egg yolks and butter whisked with a reduction of vinegar, wine, shallot and fresh tarragon.
item.content:encoded:
Béarnaise is the sauce for steak in French cooking. It is a cousin of hollandaise, an emulsion of egg yolks and butter, but it is made with a reduction of vinegar, white wine, shallots and tarragon rather than lemon juice, and that gives it its sharp, herbal taste and its slightly wilder character. The name comes from Béarn, the region of south-west France where the future King Henri IV was born. The sauce itself was first served in the 1830s at a restaurant called the Pavillon Henri IV, outside Paris, and it was created there by the chef, who named it in honour of the king. It is a sauce with a reputation for being difficult, but it is not, provided you are patient. The egg yolks are whisked over gently simmering water until they are thick and pale, and the butter is added slowly, so that the emulsion forms and does not break. The heat should always be low, because the yolks scramble if they get too hot. If the sauce splits, a spoonful of cold water whisked in will often bring it back. Béarnaise is at its best over a plain, well-seared steak, but it is also very good with chicken, salmon and asparagus.

  • Keep the water under the bowl at a bare simmer and take the bowl away if it steams too hard. Yolks that get too hot turn to scrambled egg.
  • Add the first of the butter drop by drop. Once the sauce has begun to thicken, the rest can go in more quickly.
  • If the sauce splits, whisk a teaspoon of cold water into a clean bowl, then whisk in the split sauce a little at a time.

item.title: Orzo Salad
item.description: Orzo salad: Greek-style pasta salad of orzo, cucumber, tomatoes, Kalamata olives, red onion and feta in a lemon and oregano dressing.
item.content:encoded:
Orzo is the rice-shaped pasta that the Greeks call kritharaki, which means little barley, and in Greece it is cooked in soups and in baked dishes with meat and tomatoes. The cold orzo salad is more a Greek-American invention, and it takes the flavours of the Greek village salad, cucumber, tomato, red onion, olives and feta, and mixes them through the little pasta with a lemon and oregano dressing. It is a favourite dish for picnics, potlucks and packed lunches, because it keeps well and it tastes as good at room temperature as it does cold. The pasta should be cooked until just tender and rinsed under cold water to stop it cooking further and to wash off the surface starch that would otherwise make it sticky. A splash of olive oil tossed through while it is still damp stops the grains from clumping. Choose ripe tomatoes and a firm, salty feta that comes in brine, because the cheese is not only a garnish, it seasons the salad. The dressing is a simple mixture of olive oil, lemon and oregano, and it is best added while the orzo is still slightly warm, so the pasta soaks up the flavour rather than sitting in a puddle of oil.

  • Drain the orzo very well after rinsing. Water left in the pasta dilutes the dressing and makes the salad taste flat.
  • Salt the dressing lightly. The feta and olives are both salty, so you can taste again after the cheese has gone in.
  • Add the feta last and fold it in gently. Stirred hard, it crumbles into a paste and turns the salad cloudy.

item.title: Cauliflower Rice
item.description: Cauliflower rice: raw cauliflower grated to rice-sized grains and cooked in olive oil with garlic and lemon, a light low-carb side dish.
item.content:encoded:
Cauliflower rice began as a low-carbohydrate trick and turned into a real side dish. A head of cauliflower is chopped or grated into grains the size of rice and cooked briefly in a hot pan, and what comes out is light, mild and pleasantly nutty, with a little of the softness of couscous. It appeared in diet books, then in ordinary kitchens, and in the 2010s supermarkets began selling it in bags, ready to cook. It is not really a substitute for rice, and it does not taste like it, but it does the same job on the plate. It soaks up the sauce of a curry or a stir-fry, it sits under a stew, and it makes a good base for a bowl of roasted vegetables and beans. The cooking is the part that goes wrong. Raw cauliflower has a great deal of water in it, and if it is cooked slowly or crowded in the pan it steams and turns to a wet, grey mush. The answer is a wide pan, a hot flame and only a few minutes, stirring often, so that the moisture cooks off and the grains stay tender with a bit of bite. Salt is important, and so is a squeeze of lemon at the end, which lifts the mild flavour of the vegetable.

  • Pulse in short bursts and stop while the pieces are still distinct. Run continuously, the processor turns the cauliflower into a paste.
  • Use the widest pan you have and do not overcrowd it. A crowded pan traps steam, and steam is what turns the grains soggy.
  • Stop cooking while it still has some bite. It softens further from its own heat on the way to the table.

item.title: Zucchini Fritters
item.description: Zucchini fritters: the Australian café favourite of grated zucchini, feta, spring onion and mint, fried until crisp and served with lemon and yoghurt.
item.content:encoded:
Zucchini fritters are a dish of the Australian brunch table. They appear in cafés from Sydney to Perth, stacked with poached eggs, avocado, smoked salmon, a spoonful of relish or a dollop of yoghurt, and they are also a dish that every home cook with a vegetable garden knows well, since a zucchini plant produces far more fruit than a family can eat. Australians call the vegetable a zucchini, and the British call it a courgette. The fritters are made from grated zucchini bound with egg and a small amount of flour, with feta and mint for salt and freshness and spring onions for sharpness. The one step that matters is salting the zucchini and squeezing it dry. Zucchini is nearly all water, and if the water is left in the mixture, the batter turns loose and the fritters fall apart in the pan and go soggy rather than crisp. Squeeze the grated vegetable hard in a tea towel and you will be surprised how much liquid comes out. Cook the fritters over medium heat, so that they brown and cook through without burning, and do not turn them until they are set. They are good hot from the pan, and also cold in a lunch box.

  • Squeeze the salted zucchini until it is properly dry. It is the most important step, and it stops the fritters from turning to mush.
  • Mix in the flour only at the last moment and stir just until combined, so the batter stays light.
  • Cook them over medium heat. If the pan is too hot the outside burns before the middle has set, and if it is too cool they soak up oil.

item.title: Charcuterie Board
item.description: Charcuterie board: how to build one with cured meats, three cheeses, fruit, nuts, olives, cornichons and bread, and how much to buy for eight.
item.content:encoded:
Charcuterie is the French craft of preparing cured and cooked meats, from the old words for flesh and cooked, and a charcuterie shop sells pâtés, sausages, hams and terrines. The board is a modern idea, and it has become the way to feed a group of people who are having a drink, a table of nibbles that needs no cooking and looks generous. The trick is to think in contrasts. A good board has a few cured meats, such as a thin, silky ham, a firm salami and a coarse saucisson, and three kinds of cheese, one soft, one hard and one blue, so that there is something creamy, something nutty and something sharp. Then come the extras that cut the richness and add texture: grapes or figs for sweetness, cornichons and olives for salt and acid, nuts for crunch, and mustard and honey to spoon on. Bread or crackers carry it all. Take the cheese out of the fridge half an hour before serving, because cold cheese has little flavour, and cut a few slices in advance so guests are not afraid to start. Arrange the food in groups, and leave a small gap between them, and then fill the gaps with fruit and nuts so that the board looks full. The quantities here feed eight as a nibble before a meal.

  • Buy a mix of textures and tastes rather than a large amount of any one thing. Three cheeses, three meats and a few extras are enough for a good board.
  • Give each cheese its own knife. It stops the blue cheese from turning the rest of the board into blue cheese.
  • Add the bread at the last minute or serve it separately. Sliced too early, it dries out and curls at the edges.

item.title: Cowboy Caviar
item.description: Cowboy caviar: the Texas bean and corn salad of black beans, black-eyed peas, sweetcorn, peppers, tomatoes and coriander in a lime vinaigrette.
item.content:encoded:
Cowboy caviar is a cold salad of beans, corn and vegetables in a tangy dressing that is eaten as a dip, scooped up with tortilla chips. It comes from Texas caviar, a dish of black-eyed peas in vinaigrette that is credited to the Texan chef Helen Corbitt, who served it at a New Year's Eve party at the Houston Country Club in 1940 as a way of bringing luck with the peas. The cowboy version adds black beans, sweetcorn, peppers and tomatoes, and it is a fixture of picnics, barbecues, tailgate parties and Super Bowl tables across the United States. It is a good dish for a crowd, because it is made ahead, it costs very little, and it feeds a lot of people. The dressing is what holds it together. It is sharp with lime juice and red wine vinegar, seasoned with cumin and garlic, and it needs an hour in the fridge so that the beans and the vegetables absorb it and the raw onion mellows. Keep the vegetables in small, even dice, so that every scoop has a bit of everything, and add the avocado at the last minute, since it browns and goes soft. The salad is naturally vegan and gluten-free, and it is a fine side dish beside grilled meat as well as a dip.

  • Rinse the tinned beans and peas well. The liquid in the tin is starchy and salty, and it clouds the dressing.
  • Dice the vegetables to about the size of the beans. A dip that is easy to scoop needs pieces that stay on the chip.
  • Keep the avocado for the end. It turns brown and mushy if it sits in the acid for hours.

item.title: Cauliflower Wings
item.description: Cauliflower wings: florets in a crisp panko batter, baked until golden and tossed in buttery buffalo hot sauce, with celery and ranch.
item.content:encoded:
Cauliflower wings are what happens when the buffalo sauce is separated from the chicken. The wings themselves were invented in the 1960s at a bar in Buffalo, New York, and the recipe is now a template. A crisp coating, a hot sauce made with butter, celery and a cool dip on the side, and any food that is firm enough to hold the coating will do. Cauliflower is a very good candidate. It holds its shape in a hot oven, its mild flavour takes up the sauce, and its florets are the right size to eat with the fingers. The wings are baked rather than fried, and the crisp coating comes from a thin batter of flour and milk followed by a roll in panko crumbs, which are coarser and drier than ordinary breadcrumbs, and the oven is very hot. The sauce goes on after the first bake, so the coating has time to set and crisp, and the wings return to the oven for a few minutes so the sauce clings and dries to a sticky glaze. Sauced too early, or left standing too long, the coating turns soft, so serve them straight from the oven. They suit a football match or a party, and they are a good way to eat cauliflower.

  • Dry the florets well after washing. Water on the surface makes the batter slip off.
  • Do not crowd the trays. The florets need room around them so the coating crisps instead of steaming.
  • Toss the florets in the sauce just before the final bake and eat them at once. The longer they stand, the softer the coating becomes.

item.title: Corn Ribs
item.description: Corn ribs: sweetcorn on the cob cut into strips that curl as they roast, tossed with paprika, garlic, butter and Parmesan, and eaten by hand.
item.content:encoded:
Corn ribs are corn on the cob cut into long strips, which curl up in the heat of the oven into shapes that look like a rack of ribs, and they became popular on social media around 2020 before turning up on restaurant menus. The idea is simple. A cob is stood on its end and cut lengthways, through the kernels and the core, into narrow strips, and the strips are seasoned and roasted. The kernels shrink and caramelise, the edges turn golden and slightly chewy, and the pieces are easier to pick up and eat than a whole cob, with no butter running down the chin. They are very good with a smoky, spicy seasoning, and here paprika, garlic and cayenne are mixed with olive oil and finished with melted butter, Parmesan and a squeeze of lime. The cutting is the part that needs care. A cob is hard and round, and a knife can slip, so use a large, sharp knife, cut the cob in half first so that it stands steady on a flat end, and put a damp cloth under the board. Some people soften the cob in the microwave first for a minute. Choose fresh, fat cobs when corn is in season, when the kernels are at their sweetest and the strips will be juicy.

  • Cut the cobs in half before slicing so they stand flat and steady. Keep your fingers clear of the blade and work slowly.
  • Lay the ribs kernels up and in one layer. Overlapping ribs steam instead of roast, and they will not curl.
  • Choose fresh, plump corn. Old cobs have dry kernels that shrivel in the oven and turn tough.

item.title: Blooming Onion
item.description: Blooming onion: a whole sweet onion cut into petals, dredged in seasoned flour and deep-fried until it blooms, served with a creamy dipping sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The blooming onion is one of the great American restaurant appetizers, a whole onion cut into a flower of petals, dipped in batter and deep-fried until it opens out and turns gold, and served in the middle of the table with a dipping sauce. It was made famous by a chain of steakhouses in the late 1980s, and it was so successful that versions of it appeared on menus in pubs and diners across the country, and later around the world. It is worth making at home once, if only for the way it looks when it arrives. The cutting is the key. A large onion is peeled, the top is cut off and the root is left on, and then the onion is cut into wedges from top to bottom, stopping before the root, so it holds together. After a soak in iced water the petals open out, and they are coated in seasoned flour, in egg and milk, and then in flour again, working the coating between the petals with a spoon. In hot oil the onion fries and opens fully. It is a large sweet onion that gives the best result, a Vidalia or another sweet variety, because it fries to a soft, sweet middle. The dipping sauce is a creamy mix of mayonnaise, ketchup, horseradish and spices.

  • Keep the root end whole and stop cutting well short of it. Cut through it and the onion falls apart in the oil.
  • Dry the onion thoroughly after the soak. Water between the petals makes the coating slide off and the oil spit.
  • Hold the oil steady at 175°C / 350°F. Too cool and the onion turns greasy, and too hot and the coating burns before the onion softens.

item.title: Brown Gravy
item.description: Brown gravy: a rich, glossy gravy from a browned butter roux and beef stock with Worcestershire and soy, made without pan drippings in 20 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Brown gravy is the sauce that goes with a mound of mashed potatoes, a meatloaf, a plate of biscuits, a hot roast beef sandwich or a bowl of chips and cheese curds. It is usually made from the drippings of a roast, but there are plenty of times when there are no drippings, and the version here makes a deep, savoury gravy without them. It starts with a roux, which is butter and flour cooked together, and the roux is cooked for longer than it would be for a white sauce, until it turns a nutty brown and smells like toasted biscuits. That colour is the flavour. The more it is cooked, the darker and more roasted the gravy tastes, though it also thickens a little less, so a slightly darker roux needs a slightly longer simmer. Beef stock is whisked in slowly, so that no lumps form, and then Worcestershire sauce and soy sauce add the depth and saltiness that would come from the meat. An onion and garlic seasoning gives it savoury depth without needing to chop and fry an onion. It is the sort of recipe that is worth learning once, because it takes a plain plate of vegetables or potatoes and makes it into a meal, and it takes only twenty minutes.

  • Use hot stock and add it slowly. Cold stock poured onto hot roux makes lumps, and hot stock stirs in smoothly.
  • Cook the roux to the colour of milk chocolate for the deepest flavour, but watch it and stir constantly, because it burns in seconds.
  • Season at the end. The soy sauce and stock are salty, and the gravy reduces as it simmers.

item.title: Royal Icing
item.description: Royal icing: the hard white icing of egg white, icing sugar and lemon juice for piping and flooding biscuits, gingerbread and celebration cakes.
item.content:encoded:
Royal icing is the icing that dries hard. It is made from nothing more than icing sugar, egg white and a few drops of lemon juice, but it can be beaten to a stiff peak for piping fine lines and delicate lace, or thinned with a little water to a smooth flood that sets to a flat, shiny surface. It covers traditional Christmas cakes and wedding cakes, and it is the icing for gingerbread houses, decorated sugar biscuits and the little iced biscuits that are sold at Easter and Christmas. The name is usually explained by the fact that it was the icing used on the cakes of royal families and on grand occasions, and it has been part of English baking for a very long time. The technique needs very little skill, but there are a few rules that decide whether it works. The bowl and beaters must be free from grease, because a trace of fat stops the egg white from building volume and stops the icing from setting hard. The icing sugar must be sifted, or lumps will block a fine piping nozzle. The icing should be kept covered while you work, since it crusts within minutes when the air gets at it. Beat it until it holds a firm, glossy peak, and then thin only the amount that you need for each job.

  • Keep the icing covered with cling film or a damp cloth at all times. It forms a crust in minutes, and the crust makes lumps that block the nozzle.
  • Let the iced biscuits dry uncovered for 6 to 8 hours, or overnight, before stacking or packing them, because they are only dry on the surface at first.
  • Use pasteurised egg white if the icing is for anyone pregnant, elderly or unwell, because the egg is not cooked.

item.title: Sweet Chilli Sauce
item.description: Sweet chilli sauce: the sticky Thai dipping sauce of red chillies, garlic, rice vinegar and sugar, simmered until glossy, for spring rolls.
item.content:encoded:
Sweet chilli sauce is a Thai sauce that has become a British, Australian and New Zealand staple. In Thailand it is served with grilled chicken and with fried snacks, and it is sold in bottles that are found in every supermarket in the English-speaking world. It is sticky, sweet, sharp and gently hot, and its bright red colour and flecks of chilli make it recognisable at once. It is used everywhere. It is the dip for spring rolls, prawn crackers, fish cakes and chicken nuggets, it is poured over a block of cream cheese and served with crackers, and it is a glaze for salmon, wings and pork. The homemade version is quick and much cheaper than the bottle, and you can adjust the heat. It is made by blending fresh red chillies with garlic and rice vinegar, then simmering them with sugar and water until the mixture thickens, and finishing it with a little cornflour so that it has the glossy, clinging texture people expect. The chillies decide the heat. Long, mild red chillies give a gentle sauce, and keeping the seeds or adding a few small hot chillies makes a fierce one. The sauce thickens a great deal as it cools, so stop cooking while it still looks a little thin.

  • Taste one chilli before you begin. Chillies vary a great deal, and the seeds carry most of the heat, so decide how many to keep.
  • Stop simmering while the sauce still looks a little runny. The sugar sets as it cools, and a sauce that looks thick in the pan turns to toffee in the jar.
  • Wear gloves to chop the chillies if you have sensitive skin, and wash your hands well before you touch your eyes.

item.title: Peppercorn Sauce
item.description: Peppercorn sauce: the creamy British pub steak sauce of shallots, green peppercorns, brandy, beef stock, double cream and Dijon, ready in 20 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Peppercorn sauce is the sauce that most people in Britain choose when they order a steak in a pub. It is a British relation of the French sauce au poivre, which goes with steak au poivre, a steak that is pressed with crushed peppercorns before it is fried. The pub version takes the flavour of the pepper into a creamy sauce that is made in a small pan while the steak rests, and it is spooned over the meat and the chips. It is a sauce with three stages. Shallots are softened in butter, then the peppercorns are crushed and cooked with them for a moment, and brandy is added and left to bubble until the sharpness has gone and only the depth of the flavour remains. Beef stock is reduced to concentrate the taste, and cream and a little mustard finish the sauce, so it is smooth, rich and lightly hot. The peppercorns decide the character. Green peppercorns, sold in jars in brine, are soft and mild and taste fresh and slightly floral, while black peppercorns give a stronger, hotter and more traditional flavour. Either way, crush them roughly, since a mix of whole and broken pieces looks and tastes best. It is a quick sauce to make, and it is the kind of thing that turns a plain steak into a treat.

  • Crush the peppercorns roughly with the back of a spoon against the pan. Whole ones are a mouthful, and powdered ones lose their flavour.
  • Reduce the stock before adding the cream. It concentrates the flavour, and the cream can boil without splitting.
  • Stir in the resting juices from the steak just before you serve. They add flavour to the sauce, and it is a habit worth keeping.

item.title: Homemade Ketchup
item.description: Homemade ketchup: thick, glossy tomato ketchup from tomato paste, cider vinegar, brown sugar and warm spices, simmered in 25 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The word ketchup probably comes from kê-tsiap, a word from the Hokkien dialect of southern China for a fermented fish sauce, and the sauce reached Britain in the seventeenth century with sailors and traders. English cooks made their own versions from mushrooms, walnuts and anchovies. Tomatoes did not appear in ketchup until the early nineteenth century, and a recipe published in 1812 by James Mease of Philadelphia is often given as the first, and the sweet, smooth, red tomato ketchup of today grew from that. Making it at home is easier than it sounds, if you begin with tomato paste and not with fresh tomatoes, which have to be cooked down for hours. Tomato paste is already concentrated, so all it needs is thinning with water, then a sweet and sour balance of sugar and vinegar, and the warm spices that give ketchup its familiar background taste, which are allspice, cloves and a little onion and garlic. It simmers in twenty minutes. The result is a ketchup that tastes brighter and more of tomato than a bottle, and that you can change to suit yourself, with less sugar, more vinegar or some smoked paprika. Simmer it slowly and stir often, because it spits, and it catches on the base of the pan as it thickens.

  • Simmer over a low to medium heat and stir often. Ketchup sticks to the base of the pan as it thickens, and a burnt taste cannot be fixed.
  • Let it cool completely before you judge the thickness. It thickens as it cools, and it is easy to overcook a ketchup that looks thin in the pan.
  • Taste it cold, not hot. Warm ketchup tastes sweeter and less sharp, so a small extra splash of vinegar at the end is often needed.

item.title: Homemade Pizza Dough
item.description: Homemade pizza dough: an easy, reliable dough of bread flour, yeast, salt, water and olive oil, risen for an hour, for two crisp, chewy 30 cm pizzas.
item.content:encoded:
A good pizza starts with the dough, and the dough is only flour, water, yeast and salt, with a little olive oil for softness. Its quality depends on how those four things are handled. Strong bread flour, with its higher protein content, gives a dough that stretches thin without tearing and a crust that is chewy rather than crumbly. Kneading develops the gluten that makes it elastic, and a slightly wet dough, one that is a little tacky when you touch it, gives an open, airy crumb and a crisp base. In Naples, where pizza was born, the dough is made with fine 00 flour and baked in a wood-fired oven at 450°C for a minute or two, and no home oven can match that. The answer for the home cook is to heat the oven as high as it will go and to put a heavy baking tray or a pizza stone inside it, so the base meets a very hot surface as soon as the pizza goes in. This dough rises for an hour and can be used at once, but it is also good if it is left in the fridge overnight, when the flavour deepens. It makes two pizzas about 30 cm across, and it can also be shaped into calzones, garlic knots or a flatbread. The whole process takes about half an hour of work.

  • Keep the dough slightly sticky. Extra flour in the kneading makes a dry dough that bakes into a hard, biscuit-like crust.
  • Stretch the dough with your hands, and do not use a rolling pin if you can help it. Stretching keeps the air bubbles in the dough, and rolling squeezes them out.
  • Heat the tray or stone for at least 20 minutes before the pizza goes in. A very hot surface is what gives a crisp base.

item.title: Homemade Moon Pies
item.description: Homemade moon pies: two soft graham-flavoured cookies sandwiched with a marshmallow filling and dipped in chocolate, the old Southern snack.
item.content:encoded:
The moon pie is one of the great snacks of the American South, two round graham cookies with a marshmallow filling, dipped in chocolate, and it is bigger than a hand. It was first made in Chattanooga, Tennessee, in 1917, and the story is that a coal miner asked the baker's salesman for something as big as the moon. It became a cheap and filling lunch for workers, eaten with a bottle of cola, and a whole tradition grew around the pair. There are moon pie festivals in Tennessee, and in Mobile, Alabama, a giant one is lowered from a building at New Year.
