Making them at home is a project, but not a difficult one, and the pies taste fresher and less sweet than the packaged kind. The cookie is soft and cake-like, flavoured with graham crackers and a little honey. The filling is marshmallows melted with butter, which sets to a soft, sticky cream, and the coating is dark chocolate with a spoonful of oil to make it thin and shiny. Work with the marshmallow while it is warm and easy to spread, since it stiffens as it cools, and dip the pies quickly, one at a time, and let them set on a rack. Good ones are soft in the middle, and a few hours after they are made the cookies soften a little from the filling.

  • Work with the marshmallow filling while it is warm. It sets to a sticky mass within minutes, and if it does get stiff, warm it over the water again.
  • Cool the cookies fully before you fill them. Warm cookies melt the marshmallow and slide apart.
  • Add the spoonful of oil to the chocolate. It makes it thin enough to coat evenly and gives a smooth, glossy finish that sets without cracking when you bite it.

item.title: Hamantaschen
item.description: Hamantaschen: the triangular Purim cookies of soft orange butter dough folded around apricot jam, prune or poppy seed filling. Makes 24.
item.content:encoded:
Hamantaschen are the cookies of Purim, the Jewish spring festival that celebrates the rescue of the Jews of Persia from the plot of the wicked Haman, as told in the Book of Esther. The name is Yiddish and is usually translated as Haman's pockets, though some say it means Haman's ears or hat, and the triangular shape is said to recall his three-cornered hat. In Central and Eastern Europe the traditional filling was mohn, a paste of ground poppy seeds, and it is still the classic one, but prunes, apricots, dates, cherry, raspberry jam and, more recently, chocolate spread are all common. The dough is a soft, short cookie dough with butter, sugar, egg and a little orange juice and zest. It needs an hour in the fridge so that it is firm enough to roll and to hold its shape in the oven. The shaping is the part that takes practice. A round of dough is filled with a small spoonful of filling, and three sides are folded up and pinched firmly at the corners, leaving a small opening in the middle so the jam can be seen. Too much filling, or a weak pinch, and the corners spring open in the oven. Use a thick jam, not a runny one, because thin jam boils out and burns on the tray.

  • Use only 1 teaspoon of filling. More than that swells and pushes the corners open, and the filling leaks out and burns.
  • Choose a thick jam or lekvar. Runny jam bubbles out in the oven, and if yours is thin, simmer it until it thickens and let it cool.
  • Pinch the corners hard and press them into the dough. If a triangle starts to unfold, dab a little water on the dough and pinch again.

item.title: Linzer Cookies
item.description: Linzer cookies: buttery almond and cinnamon sandwich cookies with a window in the top, filled with raspberry jam and dusted with icing sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Linzer cookies are small sandwich biscuits from Austria, and they are named after the city of Linz, on the Danube. They are made from a buttery, crumbly dough enriched with ground nuts, almonds in this version, and flavoured with cinnamon and lemon zest, then sandwiched together with raspberry or redcurrant jam. The top biscuit has a small round or star-shaped window cut from its centre, so that the red jam shows, and it is dusted with icing sugar. They are called Linzer Augen, or Linzer eyes, in German, and they are one of the biscuits that fill a Central European Christmas tin, alongside vanilla crescents and spice cookies. They are related to the Linzer torte, a nut pastry with a jam filling that is said to be the oldest cake recipe in the world, and the cookies use the same flavours in a smaller and more delicate form. The dough is short, which is to say that it is rich in butter and low in gluten, so it is soft and breaks easily and needs care. It has to be chilled before it is rolled, and it should be rolled thinly, between sheets of baking parchment, to keep it from sticking. Cut, bake and cool the cookies before you fill them, and assemble them just before serving if you like a crisp bite, or a day ahead for a softer biscuit, in which the jam has softened the dough.

  • Roll the dough between sheets of baking parchment. It is too short and buttery to take much flour, and it tears if it sticks to the bench.
  • If the dough softens as you cut, put the tray in the fridge for 10 minutes. Cold dough holds its shape and bakes into clean edges.
  • Dust the top cookies with icing sugar before you assemble the sandwiches. Once they are filled the sugar melts into the jam where it touches.

item.title: Steak and Eggs
item.description: Steak and eggs: the American diner breakfast of a seared sirloin steak basted in butter with two fried eggs and runny yolks, ready in 20 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Steak and eggs is a breakfast of ranches, diners and steakhouses, and it is a simple one: a steak, cooked hard and fast in a hot pan, with a couple of eggs fried in the same fat. It has a long tradition in the American West, where it was the breakfast of cattle hands who had a long day ahead of them, and it became the way a steakhouse serves breakfast. It is also famous in the space programme. Steak and eggs was the breakfast served to Alan Shepard before his flight in 1961, and it became the traditional launch-day meal for NASA astronauts for decades afterwards. It is a very good breakfast to make at home because it takes twenty minutes and needs almost no ingredients. The steak decides the quality, so choose a sirloin or a rib-eye about 2 cm thick, take it from the fridge a short while before cooking, and pat it dry so that it browns instead of steaming. The pan must be very hot, and the steak should be left alone until a crust has formed. A knob of butter added at the end, with a thyme sprig, is spooned over the meat to baste it, and the same pan cooks the eggs in the fat and juices that are left behind. Rest the steak for five minutes, and eat it with the eggs, some hash browns or toast.

  • Dry the steaks thoroughly. A wet surface steams, and a steak that steams is grey instead of brown.
  • Leave the steaks alone while they sear. Moving them stops the crust from forming, and the crust is where most of the flavour is.
  • Rest the meat before slicing. The juices redistribute, and a steak cut too soon leaves a pool on the plate.

item.title: Creamed Chipped Beef on Toast
item.description: Creamed chipped beef on toast: shreds of dried beef in a thick, peppery white sauce over buttered toast, the old military and diner breakfast.
item.content:encoded:
Creamed chipped beef on toast is one of the oldest breakfasts of the American table, and for a very long time it was the breakfast of the American army, where it was known by a rude nickname that every recruit learned. It is a very simple thing, a white sauce made with butter, flour and milk, with strips of salty dried beef stirred through it, and spooned over toast. The dried beef is sold in small jars or packets in the United States, and it is thin, salty and very concentrated, so a small quantity flavours a great deal of sauce. The white sauce is the whole recipe, and it is worth doing well. The flour and butter are cooked for a minute so the sauce does not taste of raw flour, the milk goes in slowly to avoid lumps, and the sauce is simmered until it coats a spoon. Lots of black pepper is important, since the beef is already salty and needs no other seasoning, and a pinch of nutmeg helps the milk. Rinsing the beef in hot water for a minute removes some of the salt, if the jar is very salty. Outside the United States dried beef is hard to find, and thinly sliced bresaola, cooked salt beef or good ham also works well.

  • Taste the beef before you rinse it. Some brands are very salty, and one minute in hot water saves the sauce from being inedible.
  • Add the milk slowly and whisk as you go. Pouring it in all at once makes lumps that are hard to remove.
  • Season with a lot of black pepper at the end. It is what gives the dish its character, and the dried beef already has plenty of salt.

item.title: Scrapple
item.description: Scrapple: the Pennsylvania Dutch loaf of simmered pork and cornmeal mush with sage and pepper, set overnight then sliced and fried until crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Scrapple is a breakfast meat of Pennsylvania, Delaware and Maryland, and it belongs to the cooking of the Pennsylvania Dutch, the German-speaking settlers who came to the region in the eighteenth century. They were farmers who used every part of the pig when it was killed, and scrapple was the way of using the trimmings and the cooking broth, mixed with cornmeal, spiced, set in a loaf tin and sliced. The German name is panhaas. The mixture is a kind of firm, savoury polenta that is full of shredded pork, and it is seasoned with sage, black pepper and a little nutmeg or cayenne. Once it is cold it can be cut into slices, dusted with flour and fried in a pan until it has a very crisp brown crust, and inside it is soft and creamy, in a mixture of meat and cornmeal. It is served with fried eggs, and with apple butter, maple syrup or ketchup, according to the household. The traditional version uses offal and other parts that are hard to find now, and this one is made with pork shoulder, which gives the same rich flavour with easily bought ingredients. It sets overnight in the fridge, so it is a project for the day before, but it is not difficult, and it keeps well for the days ahead. The frying is the last step, and it should be done in a hot pan with plenty of fat.

  • Whisk the cornmeal into cold broth first. Sprinkled straight into hot liquid it forms lumps that never dissolve.
  • Stir the mush constantly while it thickens and keep the heat low once the pork goes in. Cornmeal mush spits and sticks to the base of the pan.
  • Fry the slices in plenty of hot fat and turn them only once. Moving them tears the crust, and a hot pan gives the crisp edge that is the whole point.

item.title: Fortune Cookies
item.description: Fortune cookies: crisp vanilla and almond cookies baked from a thin batter, folded while hot round a paper fortune into the classic crescent shape.
item.content:encoded:
Fortune cookies are an American invention, though almost everyone thinks of them as Chinese. Historians trace them to Japanese-American bakers in California in the early twentieth century, who made a similar folded wafer, and they spread through the Chinese restaurants of the West Coast, where they became the way to end a meal. In China they are unknown, and most Chinese visitors to the United States are surprised by them. Making them at home is a game more than a recipe, and it is easier than it looks, though it does test your nerve. The batter is a thin one of egg white, sugar, flour and melted butter, the same as the batter used for French tuiles, and it is spread into thin circles on a lined tray and baked until the edges are golden. The discs are soft and flexible for less than a minute once they are out of the oven, and in that time each one has to be lifted, given its fortune, folded in half, and bent over the rim of a glass or mug into its crescent shape. After that they cool and become crisp. The secret is to bake only a few at a time, so that you are never shaping more than you can handle before they harden, and if one sets too soon, a moment in the oven softens it again. Write your own fortunes on strips of paper, and make them as kind or as silly as you like.

  • Bake only one tray at a time and keep the other batter covered. The discs harden in seconds, and shaping more than four at once is impossible.
  • Make the discs thin and even. Thick batter bakes into a cookie that is too soft to fold and never becomes crisp.
  • Wear thin cotton gloves if the discs are too hot to handle. They are very hot when they leave the oven, and gloves save a burnt fingertip.

item.title: Poke Cake
item.description: Poke cake: a vanilla sheet cake pierced with holes, soaked with strawberry jelly, chilled and topped with whipped cream and fresh strawberries.
item.content:encoded:
The poke cake is a modern American classic, and it takes its name from the way it is made. A plain sheet cake is baked and, while it is still warm, it is pricked all over with the handle of a wooden spoon, and a bowl of liquid jelly is poured over the surface so that it runs down into the holes. The cake is chilled until the jelly sets, and it is then covered with whipped cream. What you get when you slice it is a cake with a pattern of bright red streaks running through it, and a texture that is more moist and springy than a plain sponge. It was made popular in the 1970s by the makers of packaged gelatin, whose test kitchens developed it as a way of selling more jelly crystals, and it has been a favourite for potlucks, birthday parties and Fourth of July tables ever since. The strawberry version is the most common, but lime, orange, raspberry and cherry all work, and the colour is a good way to tie a cake to a holiday. It is a good recipe for beginners. The cake itself is plain and forgiving, the poking needs no skill, and the jelly does the decoration. The only requirement is patience, because the cake must chill for several hours before the jelly sets.

  • Poke the holes while the cake is still warm and pour the jelly over slowly, in a few stages. Warm cake soaks up the liquid, and a cold cake sheds it.
  • Make the holes deep, right to the base of the cake, so the jelly runs through the sponge and you get stripes when it is cut.
  • Whip the cream only after the jelly has set, and keep the finished cake in the fridge until it is served. The topping melts and the jelly softens in a warm room.

item.title: Devon Splits
item.description: Devon splits: soft, slightly sweet milk rolls split and filled with clotted cream and strawberry jam, the old Devon and Cornwall cream tea.
item.content:encoded:
Before the scone became the standard cream tea in the West Country, the split was the roll of choice. A Devon split, called a Cornish split on the other side of the Tamar, is a small, soft, slightly sweet white roll made with milk and butter, and it is split open when it is fresh and filled with clotted cream and strawberry jam. Like the scone it has its own controversy. In Devon the cream goes on first and the jam on top, and in Cornwall the jam goes on first and the cream on top, and each side is convinced that the other is wrong. Splits are yeast rolls, so they take longer than a scone, but the method is not difficult, and the reward is a bread that is light, tender and pillowy, and a good match for the dense, nutty cream. The dough is enriched with milk, sugar and butter, and it needs two risings, the first as a whole dough and the second once it has been shaped into rolls. The rolls are best eaten on the day they are made, or even within a few hours of baking, when they are still just warm. The filling is very simple, but do buy the best clotted cream and the best strawberry jam you can find, since there is nowhere for poor ingredients to hide. Dust the tops with icing sugar and serve with tea.

  • Keep the dough soft and slightly tacky. Too much flour when kneading makes a tight, dry roll.
  • Bake them until only pale gold. The rolls are meant to be soft with a thin crust, and a dark bake makes them dry.
  • Fill them when they are warm and fresh, but not hot. Hot rolls melt the clotted cream, and cold ones lose their softness.

item.title: Jamaican Ginger Cake
item.description: Jamaican ginger cake: a dark, moist and sticky loaf of black treacle, muscovado sugar, warm spices and stem ginger that improves after a day.
item.content:encoded:
Jamaican ginger cake is a British lunch box and tea-time classic, a dark, dense, moist loaf that is sold in supermarkets in a foil wrapper and is one of the great keeping cakes. The name comes from the ginger that is grown in Jamaica, which has been prized in Britain for centuries, and from the dark sugar and treacle of the Caribbean, that give the cake its colour and its deep, slightly bitter, sticky sweetness. The recipe is a mixture of the two things that make ginger cakes work: plenty of ground ginger, for a warm, peppery heat, and chunks of stem ginger in syrup for a hot, sweet, fresh bite. Cinnamon and allspice round out the spice, and black treacle and golden syrup give the crumb a dark, sticky finish. It is a cake that is made by melting the sugar, butter and syrups together and mixing them into the flour, so it needs no beating and no creaming, and is easy to make. The batter is loose and pourable, and it bakes slowly at a low temperature so that the middle stays moist. The best part is that it improves with time. Wrapped in baking parchment and foil for a day or two, the top turns sticky and the flavour deepens, so it is worth baking ahead.

  • Do not let the syrup mixture boil. Boiling darkens the sugar and makes a bitter cake, and warm is all it needs.
  • Grease the spoon or measure with a little oil before you weigh the treacle. It slides off cleanly and none of it is left behind.
  • Wrap the cooled cake in parchment and foil and leave it for a day before you cut it. The crumb turns stickier and the spices blend.

item.title: Linzer Torte
item.description: Linzer torte: the Austrian tart of spiced hazelnut shortcrust pastry with a raspberry jam filling and a lattice top, dusted with icing sugar.
item.content:encoded:
The Linzer torte is one of the oldest cakes in the world, and it comes from the Austrian city of Linz. The oldest known recipe for it is in a manuscript that is dated to 1653, and it has been made in Austria ever since. It is not a cake in the modern sense. It is a tart, with a crumbly, buttery pastry that is made with ground nuts, and flavoured with cinnamon, cloves and lemon, filled with a thick layer of raspberry or redcurrant jam and covered with a lattice of the same pastry. It is baked until the pastry is deep golden and the jam beneath has thickened and darkened, and it is dusted with icing sugar. The pastry is very short, which means it is rich in butter and nuts and low in gluten, so it is soft to work with and breaks easily. It is pressed into the tin with the fingers, since it will not roll out without help, and the lattice is cut from strips of the pastry, which is often easier if the dough is chilled before it is cut. Make the torte a day ahead if you can. The flavour improves as the spices and jam soften into the pastry, and the texture becomes softer and more cake-like. It is a Christmas tart in Austria and the rest of Central Europe, but it is good at any time of year with a cup of coffee.

  • Press the pastry into the tin with your fingertips if it will not roll. It is short and fragile, and patching is normal and does not show once it is baked.
  • Use a thick jam. A runny jam bubbles over the lattice and stains the pastry, so simmer a thin one for a few minutes first.
  • Let the torte cool completely in the tin. The pastry is soft when hot and breaks up if you move it too soon.

item.title: Peach Pie
item.description: Peach pie: a double-crust pie of ripe summer peaches with lemon and cinnamon in a flaky all-butter pastry, cooled until the juices thicken.
item.content:encoded:
Peach pie is the pie of high summer, especially in the American South, where Georgia is known as the Peach State. When peaches are at their peak, sweet, fragrant and juicy, they need very little in the way of embellishment, and a pie with a crisp buttery crust and a soft filling of fruit is one of the best ways to eat them. The filling depends on the fruit. Freestone peaches, with flesh that comes away easily from the stone, are the easiest to prepare, and they should be ripe but still firm, so that they hold their shape when baked. They are peeled, which is done by dipping them in boiling water for half a minute and slipping the skins off, then sliced and tossed with sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon and cornflour, which thickens the juices as they cook. The crust is a flaky all-butter pastry, and the secret to it is cold: cold butter, iced water, and a rest in the fridge before it is rolled. The pie bakes at a high temperature at first, to set the pastry, and then at a lower one, to cook the fruit. It must be cooled for at least three hours before it is cut, as the filling is liquid and thickens as it cools. Cut too soon, it runs across the plate.

  • Keep everything for the pastry cold, including the butter, the water and your hands. Warm butter melts into the flour and makes a tough crust.
  • Bake the pie on a hot tray on the middle shelf. The heat from below cooks the bottom crust and stops it turning soggy.
  • Wait until the pie is cool. It is the hardest part of the recipe, but a hot pie is a runny one.

item.title: Blueberry Buckle
item.description: Blueberry buckle: the New England butter cake studded with blueberries under a thick cinnamon crumb topping that buckles as it bakes.
item.content:encoded:
A buckle is one of the old New England fruit desserts, with names that sound like a list of instructions, alongside grunts, slumps, cobblers, pandowdies and bettys. It is a simple butter cake with fruit in it and a crumb topping, and the name is thought to come from the way that the cake buckles and sinks in places as the heavy fruit and crumbs push into the batter while it bakes. Blueberries are the classic fruit, since they grow wild in New England and Maine, and their tart juice bursts in the oven into purple pools among the crumb. The cake itself is moist and tender, made with butter, milk and a modest amount of sugar, and the thick topping of flour, brown sugar, cinnamon and butter bakes into a crisp, sugary crust that is the best part. It is often served for breakfast or with coffee, and it is just as good warm with a scoop of ice cream. The recipe is easy to make. The batter is mixed by hand in a bowl, the blueberries are scattered over the top and the crumb goes on last. Toss the berries in a spoonful of flour first, so that they do not sink to the bottom, and use frozen berries straight from the freezer if fresh ones are out of season. They keep the batter from turning purple.

  • Toss the berries in a little flour before adding them. It absorbs the juice and helps them stay in the cake rather than sinking to the bottom.
  • Leave the topping in large clumps and do not press it down. The clumps bake into a crisp, crunchy crust.
  • Use frozen berries straight from the freezer and do not thaw them. Thawed berries bleed into the batter and stain it a dull grey.

item.title: Sopapillas
item.description: Sopapillas: squares of simple dough fried in hot oil until they puff into hollow pillows, drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Sopapillas are the fried pastry of New Mexico and Texas, and one of the best things on the table of a Mexican or Tex-Mex restaurant. A simple dough of flour, baking powder, salt, shortening and water is rolled thin, cut into squares or triangles and dropped into hot oil, where it puffs up dramatically into a hollow pillow, and it is served hot with a bottle of honey, which is poured into the hollow through a hole torn in the top. In New Mexico they are also served as part of a main meal, stuffed with beans or meat, and the honey and sugar are for dessert. The name comes from the Spanish sopaipa, a fried pastry that came with the Spanish settlers who arrived in the Southwest in the sixteenth century, and the food has changed little since. The puff is the whole point, and it depends on a few things. The dough is rolled to a thickness of about 5 mm, so that there is enough to hold steam. The oil is hot enough to seal the surface at once, about 190°C, and the pieces are dropped in flat and then pushed under the oil, so the steam inside expands the dough and blows them up. Fry them in small batches. They are best when very fresh, because as they cool the steam condenses and the pillow deflates.

  • Keep the oil at 190°C / 375°F. If it is too cool the dough soaks up oil and never puffs, and if it is too hot the outside burns before the middle is cooked.
  • Roll the dough to an even thickness. Thick patches stay doughy and thin ones do not hold enough steam to puff.
  • Fry in small batches and eat the sopapillas as soon as they are ready. They deflate as they cool.

item.title: Spritz Cookies
item.description: Spritz cookies: buttery vanilla and almond cookies pressed through a cookie press into wreaths, trees and stars, and baked until pale golden.
item.content:encoded:
Spritz cookies are the butter cookies of Scandinavian and German Christmas baking, and the name comes from the German word spritzen, to squirt, because the dough is squeezed through a cookie press. The press is a metal tube with a plunger and a set of discs, and each disc makes a different shape: a wreath, a star, a Christmas tree, a flower or a ridged strip. The cookies are called spritsar in Sweden and Spritzgebäck in Germany, and they were brought to the American Midwest by immigrants, where they became a fixture of the holiday cookie tin. The dough is a simple, rich mixture of butter, sugar, egg and flour, flavoured with vanilla and a hint of almond, and it has to be exactly the right consistency. If it is too stiff it will not go through the press, and if it is too soft the shapes spread and lose their pattern. The dough should be about as soft as cool, workable butter. The other rule is to press it onto a cold, ungreased baking tray, with no parchment, because the dough has to stick to the metal for the press to lift away and leave the shape behind. They are baked until pale, with just a faint gold at the edges, since a butter cookie loses its flavour when it browns. They keep well and are very good for gifts.

  • Use cold, ungreased trays. Dough that meets a greased or parchment-lined surface will not stick, and the press pulls the shapes back up.
  • If the dough is too stiff to press, mix in a teaspoon of milk. If it is too soft, chill it for 10 minutes and try again.
  • Bake for the shortest time. The cookies should look pale, and they crisp up as they cool.

item.title: Lefse
item.description: Lefse: the Norwegian Christmas flatbread of mashed potato and flour rolled very thin, cooked on a dry griddle and served with butter and sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Lefse is the soft, thin flatbread of Norway, and for Norwegian families in Norway and in the American Midwest it is the food of Christmas. It is made from mashed potato mixed with a little butter, cream and flour, chilled until firm, rolled out until it is almost transparent and cooked on a dry, hot griddle until it is dotted with pale brown spots. The result is a soft, pliable round, about the size of a dinner plate, that is spread with butter and sprinkled with sugar or cinnamon sugar, rolled up and eaten with the fingers. In Norway the cooking of lefse varies from valley to valley, and there are versions made with flour alone, or cream, or sour milk, but the potato lefse of the immigrant communities in Minnesota and North Dakota is the one best known in America, and there are lefse festivals and clubs. Potatoes came to Norway in the eighteenth century and quickly became the staple food, and the flatbreads followed. The dough is soft and fragile, and it has to be handled with a light touch. Use floury potatoes, put them through a ricer while they are hot so there are no lumps, and chill the dough well so it is firm enough to roll. Roll each piece paper-thin on a well-floured surface, and cook it fast.

  • Rice the potatoes while they are still hot. Lumps do not disappear later, and they tear the thin dough when it is rolled out.
  • Chill the dough well and work with one piece at a time, keeping the rest cold. Warm dough sticks to everything and is hard to lift.
  • Keep the finished lefse covered with a towel. They dry out and turn brittle within minutes in the open air.

item.title: Ladyfingers
item.description: Ladyfingers: light, dry, crisp Italian sponge fingers, or savoiardi, piped from a whisked egg batter, for tiramisu, trifle and dipping in coffee.
item.content:encoded:
Ladyfingers, or savoiardi in Italian, are the long, light, dry sponge biscuits that are dipped in coffee for tiramisu, that line the mould of a charlotte and that give a trifle its base. They are named after the House of Savoy, and the story is that they were first made at the court of the Duke of Savoy in the fifteenth century for a royal visit. They are made from only eggs, sugar and flour, with no butter or raising agent, and all their lightness comes from the eggs, which are separated and whisked to a foam. The yolks are beaten with sugar until pale and thick, the whites are whipped with more sugar to stiff peaks, and the two are folded together with sifted flour with as little stirring as possible. The batter is piped into fingers, dusted with icing sugar twice, which gives them their characteristic slightly crackled and crisp crust, and baked until they are pale gold. The moment of folding is the critical one. If the batter is over-mixed the foam collapses and the fingers spread flat, and if it is under-mixed there are streaks of white in it. Fold with a large spatula and stop as soon as there are no streaks. Homemade ladyfingers are fresher and lighter than shop-bought ones, and they can be dried in a low oven if they are to be soaked for a dessert.

  • Make sure the bowl and whisk are completely clean and dry. A trace of egg yolk or grease in the whites will stop them from whipping.
  • Fold with a large spatula in wide, slow strokes and stop the moment the streaks vanish. Every extra stroke knocks air out of the batter.
  • Dust twice with icing sugar. The first layer dissolves into the batter and the second one forms the fine crackled crust.

item.title: Dirt Cake
item.description: Dirt cake: a no-bake dessert of chocolate cookie crumbs, chocolate pudding and light cream cheese cream, layered like soil with gummy worms on top.
item.content:encoded:
Dirt cake is a dessert for children and for the child in everyone, and it is exactly what the name says. A bowl or a new, clean flowerpot is layered with crushed chocolate sandwich cookies that look like soil, a creamy chocolate pudding and a fluffy cream cheese mixture, and the top is covered with more crumbs and decorated with gummy worms that seem to be crawling out of the earth. It has become a fixture of birthday parties, Halloween, school events and summer picnics across the United States, and it is one of the easiest desserts there is, because it needs no oven, no special skills and nothing more than a food processor or a bag and a rolling pin. The crumbs are made by crushing the cookies whole, including the cream centres, and the filling is a mix of two things. The first is chocolate pudding, made from an instant mix and cold milk, and the second is cream cheese beaten with butter and icing sugar and lightened with whipped cream. The two are folded together, so that the filling is soft, rich and mousse-like, and it sets in the fridge as the crumbs beneath soften slightly and blend into it. Use a big glass bowl so that the layers show, or make it in a clear plastic pot, and add the worms just before it is served so they stay chewy.

  • Crush the crumbs very fine. Big lumps of cookie do not soften, and the dessert loses its soil-like look.
  • Fold the whipped cream in gently, in two batches. It keeps the filling light and airy, and beating it in makes it heavy.
  • Add the worms at the last moment. In the fridge for hours they go hard and dull, and their colours run into the pudding.

item.title: Homemade Peppermint Patties
item.description: Homemade peppermint patties: cool, soft peppermint fondant discs made from icing sugar and syrup, dipped in dark chocolate. Twenty-four sweets.
item.content:encoded:
The peppermint pattie is a classic American sweet: a round, flat disc of soft, white, cool peppermint fondant, coated in dark chocolate. The fondant is the part that surprises people who have never made it, because it is not difficult, and it is made from little more than icing sugar mixed with a little syrup and butter and flavoured with peppermint extract. The dough is kneaded until it is smooth and pliable, like a stiff icing, rolled into small balls and flattened into discs, then chilled or frozen until they are firm enough to dip. The syrup keeps the fondant soft and prevents the sugar from crystallising into a hard candy, and the butter makes it a little creamy. The dipping is a matter of patience, not of skill. The chocolate should be dark, so that its bitterness balances the sweetness of the fondant, and a spoonful of coconut oil makes it melt smoothly and set with a sheen and a clean snap. Each disc is dropped into the melted chocolate, turned over with a fork, lifted out, and tapped on the edge of the bowl to shake off the surplus. The cool, sharp taste of mint against dark chocolate is one of the best combinations in confectionery, and homemade patties make good Christmas presents, with a softer texture than those in the shops. Use a good peppermint extract and add it a drop at a time, because a little goes a long way.

  • Add the milk a teaspoon at a time. The dough goes from crumbly to sticky very quickly, and too much liquid makes a fondant that will not hold its shape.
  • Dip the discs while they are still very cold. Cold fondant does not melt in the warm chocolate, and the coating sets fast.
  • Use a dark chocolate with about 60 per cent cocoa. A milk chocolate is too sweet with the fondant.

item.title: Pecan Turtles
item.description: Pecan turtles: clusters of toasted pecan halves under soft, buttery homemade caramel and melted chocolate, finished with sea salt, for Christmas.
item.content:encoded:
Pecan turtles are a favourite American sweet, and they are named for the way they look. Three pecan halves are laid out on a tray so that their tips meet in the middle, like the head and two legs of a turtle, and a spoonful of soft caramel is set in the centre to form the shell, then covered with chocolate. Each one is a mouthful of toasted nuts, chewy, buttery caramel and smooth chocolate, and a few flakes of sea salt on top make it even better, since they cut the sweetness of the caramel. It is a favourite treat at Christmas, and it is one of the sweets that is sold in old-fashioned candy shops and in boxes of chocolates all over the United States, where the pecan is a native nut and is grown in the southern states. Making the candy at home needs only a little care, and the caramel is the part that needs it. It is made by boiling brown sugar, butter, cream and syrup to 118°C, the firm-ball stage, at which it sets to a soft, chewy texture that holds its shape but does not crack a tooth. A sugar thermometer is the best way of judging this. Toasting the nuts first makes a great difference, bringing out their flavour and keeping them crisp under the caramel. Make the caramel in a heavy pan, and do not stir it after it boils, to stop crystals forming.

  • Use a thermometer and take the caramel off the heat at 118°C. A few degrees less makes it runny, and a few more gives a caramel that sets like a stone.
  • Work fast once the caramel is ready. It thickens as it cools, and if it stiffens in the pan, warm it very gently for a minute.
  • Toast the pecans before you use them. Raw ones taste flat and turn soft under the caramel.

item.title: Chocolate-Covered Cherries
item.description: Chocolate-covered cherries: maraschino cherries wrapped in soft vanilla fondant, dipped in dark chocolate and left with a stem to hold.
item.content:encoded:
Chocolate-covered cherries, also called cherry cordials, are a Christmas and Valentine box chocolate that many people think is too difficult to make at home, and it is not. A single maraschino cherry is wrapped in a layer of soft fondant, made from icing sugar, butter and syrup, and then dipped in melted chocolate. The stem stays on as a handle. The magic happens after they are made. Over a few days, the sugar in the fondant draws moisture from the cherry, and the coating softens and turns into a sweet, thick syrup that surrounds the fruit inside the chocolate shell, which is what gives a cordial cherry its liquid centre. The confectionery trade uses an enzyme called invertase to do the same thing more reliably, but the home method works well if you give the sweets time. They are at their best after about a week in a cool place. The cherries must be very dry before they are wrapped, or the moisture makes the fondant slide off, and the fondant must be pliable, not sticky, or crumbly. Cover the cherry entirely, with no gaps, and seal the chocolate against the stem, or the syrup will leak out. Dark chocolate keeps the sweetness in check, and coconut oil gives the coating a shine. They make an unusual and much-loved present.

  • Dry the cherries thoroughly. Wet cherries make the fondant slippery, and it slides off during dipping.
  • Cover every part of the cherry with fondant, and every part of the fondant with chocolate. A gap in either means the syrup leaks out.
  • Wait about a week before you eat them. The fondant needs the time to soften into a liquid syrup around the cherry.

item.title: Tanghulu
item.description: Tanghulu: skewered strawberries and grapes coated in a clear, glassy, crackling sugar shell, the Chinese candied fruit street snack.
item.content:encoded:
Tanghulu is a traditional snack of northern China, and it is sold on the streets of Beijing in winter, and at temple fairs at the Lunar New Year. The classic version uses hawthorn berries, which are tart and slightly floury, skewered on bamboo sticks and coated in a hard, transparent shell of sugar, which contrasts with the sourness of the fruit. Tradition tells of an emperor of the Song dynasty and a healing tonic of hawthorn and sugar, and the true origin is unknown. In recent years the snack has become well known worldwide, after videos showed the loud crunch that the shell makes when it is bitten, and cooks began to use strawberries, grapes, mandarin segments and cherry tomatoes, which are easier to find than hawthorns. The fruit is not cooked at all. A syrup of sugar and water is boiled to the hard crack stage, about 150°C, and the skewers are dipped in it and twirled, and the syrup sets on the cold fruit in seconds to a thin, glassy layer. It is important to dry the fruit thoroughly, since any moisture on the surface stops the sugar sticking and makes it slide off. It is also important not to stir the syrup once it boils, which causes it to crystallise and turn cloudy. Work quickly and take care, because the sugar is extremely hot and can cause severe burns. Eat the tanghulu soon after they are made, since the shell melts in the humidity of a fridge.

  • Dry the fruit completely with kitchen paper, and use it at room temperature. Wet or cold fruit makes the syrup cloudy and it slides off.
  • Do not stir the syrup after it boils, and do not let sugar crystals form on the sides of the pan. Brush them down with a wet pastry brush if they appear.
  • Handle the syrup with great care and keep children away from the hob. Boiling sugar sticks to the skin and burns badly.

item.title: Edible Cookie Dough
item.description: Edible cookie dough: soft, buttery chocolate chip cookie dough made with heat-treated flour and no raw egg, safe to eat by the spoonful.
item.content:encoded:
Most people have eaten raw cookie dough from the bowl at some time, and most of them have been told not to. The warning is a fair one, but it applies to two ingredients in the dough, not to the dough as a whole. Raw eggs can carry salmonella, and raw flour, which is an agricultural product that has not been treated to kill germs, can carry E. coli, and there have been outbreaks linked to raw flour in several countries. The solution is to make a dough without any egg and to heat-treat the flour first, and this recipe does both. The flour is spread on a tray and baked for a few minutes, until it reaches a safe temperature, and then it is cooled and sifted. There is no egg at all. A spoonful of milk brings the dough together, and the mixture of butter, brown sugar and vanilla tastes exactly like the dough of a chocolate chip cookie. It is best eaten in small amounts, since it is very rich. In the United States shops that sell nothing but edible cookie dough began to open in the 2010s, and the dough has become a flavour of ice cream and of bars and cakes too. This one is quick to make. Heat-treat the flour first, while it cools, beat the butter and sugars, and then mix everything together. Serve it as it is, in a bowl with spoons, or scoop it into balls and roll them in melted chocolate.

  • Do not skip the heat treatment. Raw flour is not safe to eat, and this step is what makes the dough safe.
  • Cool the flour completely before you add it. Warm flour melts the butter and makes the dough greasy.
  • Use mini chocolate chips if you can. They spread through the dough more evenly, and each bite has some.

item.title: Strawberry Jam
item.description: Strawberry jam: bright red jam from ripe strawberries, sugar and lemon juice, boiled to setting point and potted in jars. Makes four 300 ml jars.
item.content:encoded:
Strawberry jam is the first jam that most people ever make, and it is one of the best. The fruit is ripe and sweet, the method is simple, and the result is a bright red preserve that tastes of fresh strawberries far more than anything from a jar in the shops. Strawberries are low in pectin, the natural substance that makes a jam set, so the recipe relies on the pectin in the lemon juice and on cooking the jam to the right temperature, and it needs no added pectin. The berries are first mixed with the sugar and lemon juice and left for an hour, so the sugar pulls out the juice and the fruit holds its shape as it cooks. The mixture is then brought slowly to the boil to dissolve the sugar and boiled hard until it reaches the setting point, 105°C on a thermometer, or when a spoonful on a chilled saucer wrinkles when it is pushed with a finger. This is the crucial test, so do not skip it. Jam that is not boiled long enough is runny, and jam that is boiled for too long becomes dark and sticky and loses its fresh taste. The finished jam is potted into sterilised jars while it is hot and sealed at once. It keeps for a year in a cool, dark cupboard, and is good on toast, scones, in a sponge cake, stirred into yoghurt, or on rice pudding.

  • Choose ripe but firm strawberries. Overripe fruit is low in pectin and gives a soft, syrupy jam.
  • Use a wide pan, not a tall one. A wide pan lets the water evaporate quickly, so the jam reaches setting point before the fruit turns dull.
  • Test the set with a chilled saucer, and take the pan off the heat while you do it. Jam keeps boiling and can pass the point while you are checking.

item.title: Apple Butter
item.description: Apple butter: a dark, thick, spiced spread of apples slowly cooked down with cider, brown sugar, cinnamon and cloves. It contains no butter.
item.content:encoded:
Apple butter is a spread that has no butter in it. The name refers to its smooth, thick texture, which is like that of soft butter, and it is made by cooking apples for hours until they turn dark brown, sweet and concentrated, with cinnamon and cloves added. It is a tradition of the Pennsylvania Dutch, and of the Appalachian region of the United States, where it was made in autumn in big copper kettles, over open fires, and everyone in the community was expected to help with the stirring. The flavour is that of caramelised apples, deep and mellow and spicy, and it is much more intense than applesauce. The method is easy but slow. The apples are first cooked with a little juice or cider until they are soft, puréed, mixed with sugar and spices, and then cooked very slowly, uncovered, in a low oven, which is the least demanding way of doing it, since the oven heats evenly from all sides and there is no risk of scorching on the bottom of a pan. It needs only an occasional stir. The apples reduce to about a third of their volume, and the butter is ready when it holds a mark when a spoon is drawn through it, and a spoonful on a cold plate does not weep liquid. Use a mix of sweet and tart apples and do not peel them, since the skins contain pectin, and they add colour and depth.

  • Use a wide roasting tin, not a deep dish. A large surface lets the water evaporate, and the butter thickens sooner.
  • Stir it every half hour and scrape down the sides. The edges dry out first and can burn if they are ignored.
  • Stop cooking when a spoonful on a cold saucer does not leak liquid around the edge. Apple butter thickens further as it cools.

item.title: Pepper Jelly
item.description: Pepper jelly: the Southern sweet and fiery jelly of red peppers, jalapeños, vinegar and sugar, poured over cream cheese and served with crackers.
item.content:encoded:
Pepper jelly is a Southern pantry staple, a glowing, translucent jelly with small flecks of pepper in it that is sweet at first and hot afterwards. It is made from sweet peppers and hot chillies, cider vinegar and a great deal of sugar, and set with pectin. It is best known as the simplest party appetizer in the American South: a block of cream cheese, with a jar of pepper jelly poured over it, and a box of crackers next to it. The combination of tangy, cool cheese and sweet, hot jelly disappears from the table faster than anything else. It is also used as a glaze on ham, pork and chicken wings, spooned on a cheese sandwich, stirred into a vinaigrette, or spread on a burger. The colour depends on the peppers. Red peppers make a jelly that is a deep red or orange, and green peppers a pale, bright green, and the heat depends on how many jalapeños or other chillies go in and whether their seeds are kept. The main technical point is the set. The jelly is boiled with the sugar and vinegar first and the pectin is stirred in at the end, and it is boiled hard for exactly one minute, and no longer. It may look thin in the pan, but it sets as it cools in the jars over a day. Chop the peppers finely but do not purée them, so that there are small flecks in the jelly.

  • Boil for exactly the time given after adding the pectin. Boiling it longer breaks the pectin down and the jelly will not set.
  • Keep some of the jalapeño seeds if you like a hot jelly. The seeds and the white ribs carry most of the heat.
  • Stir the jelly gently before jarring it. It sets while the pepper flecks float, and stirring keeps them spread throughout.

item.title: Chorizo in Cider
item.description: Chorizo in cider: sliced cooking chorizo simmered in dry cider until it reduces to a sticky, tangy, paprika-red glaze. The Asturian tapas classic.
item.content:encoded:
Chorizo a la sidra is the tapas dish of Asturias, the green, wet region on the northern coast of Spain, where cider is what people drink in the way that others drink wine. In the cider houses, called sidrerías, the cider is poured from a great height into a wide glass to give it air, and plates of chorizo cooked in the same drink are set on the tables. The two are a natural pair. The cider is dry, acidic and lightly fizzy, and it cuts through the smoky, fatty pork sausage, and as the liquid simmers away it reduces to a sticky, tangy, red glaze that coats each slice. The dish is now common in British pubs and gastropubs as well. It is one of the simplest and most flavoursome things that can be served with drinks, and it needs only three ingredients, chorizo, cider and a little garlic, and about twenty minutes. Use cooking chorizo, the semi-cured, soft kind, sold in rings, and not the hard, cured sausage that is sliced and eaten raw. The cooking chorizo releases its paprika-red fat as it fries and takes up the cider as it simmers, and the fat and the cider combine into a sauce. Use dry cider. A sweet one gives a syrupy result that is too sugary. Serve the chorizo hot, in a shallow dish, with plenty of crusty bread to mop up the sauce.

  • Choose dry cider. Sweet cider reduces to a sugary syrup, and the dish loses its balance of fat, smoke and acidity.
  • Use a wide pan so that the cider reduces quickly and evenly. In a narrow pan it takes much longer and the chorizo turns tough.
  • Watch the last few minutes. As the sauce thickens it can catch and burn, and it needs stirring often at the end.

item.title: Fried Cheese Curds
item.description: Fried cheese curds: fresh cheddar curds in a light, crisp beer batter, deep-fried until golden and molten, the Wisconsin bar and fair snack.
item.content:encoded:
Cheese curds are the small, irregular lumps of fresh cheese that form in the vat when milk is turned into cheddar, before the cheese is pressed and aged. Fresh, they are mild, milky and springy, and they squeak against the teeth, and the squeak is how a Wisconsinite knows that the curds are truly fresh. They are eaten as they are, from a paper bag, but the best-loved way of serving them is deep-fried in a batter, which is on the menu of bars, restaurants and county fairs across the state and through the Midwest. The heat melts the cheese inside a crisp coating, and the first bite pulls out a long string of hot cheese. The batter is a simple one of flour, baking powder and seasoning, mixed with cold beer, which makes it light and crisp and gives it a slightly malty flavour. The curds must be at room temperature, and this matters. Cold curds take longer to heat, and the batter overcooks before the cheese has melted, while curds that are at room temperature melt at once. The oil must be very hot, 190°C, so that the coating sets before the cheese leaks out, and the curds are fried in small batches. Eat them at once, because they cool and firm quickly. Ranch dressing is the usual dip, though a marinara sauce or a spicy mayonnaise also goes well.

  • Use the freshest curds you can find, at room temperature. They melt quickly in the hot oil, and the squeaky texture is best when they are just made.
  • Hold the oil at 190°C / 375°F and fry in small batches. Cool oil makes a greasy coating, and a crowded pan drops the temperature.
  • Dust the curds in flour before the batter. It gives the batter something to hold on to, and stops it sliding off.

item.title: Boudin Balls
item.description: Boudin balls: Cajun pork and rice sausage filling rolled into balls without a casing, breaded and fried until crisp outside and moist inside.
item.content:encoded:
Boudin is the fresh sausage of Cajun Louisiana, a soft, spicy mixture of pork, liver, rice and seasonings, stuffed in a casing and eaten hot, with the meal, or straight from a paper bag at a gas station on the highway. In the towns of Acadiana, the region west of New Orleans, people argue about who makes the best. Boudin balls are the second life of the sausage. The filling is taken out of its casing, rolled into balls, coated in flour, egg and breadcrumbs, and fried until it has a crisp brown shell, and inside it is soft, moist and peppery. They are a favourite at tailgate parties and bars, and they are a dish that shows the Cajun way of cooking, which is to make good food from inexpensive cuts. Making them at home starts with a boudin-style filling. Pork shoulder and chicken livers are simmered with onion, pepper, celery and garlic, then chopped finely and mixed with rice, spring onions, parsley and Cajun seasoning. The mixture needs to be moist, sticky and highly seasoned, because the frying and the breadcrumbs dilute the flavour. It needs an hour in the fridge, so that it firms up enough to roll. Serve the balls hot with creole mustard or a remoulade sauce for dipping.

  • Season the filling generously. The rice and breadcrumbs mute the flavour, and a mixture that tastes right raw tastes flat after frying.
  • Chill the mixture well before rolling. A firm mixture holds its shape, and a warm one falls apart in the oil.
  • Fry in small batches at 180°C / 350°F. If the oil is too hot the crust burns before the middle is warm.

item.title: Pizza Rolls
item.description: Pizza rolls: crisp little wonton wrapper parcels of melted mozzarella, pepperoni and pizza sauce, baked until golden and served with marinara.
item.content:encoded:
Pizza rolls are the frozen snack that filled the American after-school hour, small crisp parcels with a molten middle of cheese, tomato and pepperoni, which are usually too hot to eat at the moment they are ready. Making them at home is easy, and it gives you a snack that is fresher and better. The secret is the wrapper. Wonton wrappers, the thin squares of egg dough that are sold in the chilled section of supermarkets, fry and bake to a crisp, blistered, bubbly shell, much like the pastry of the shop-bought ones, and they save you from making pastry. A small piece of mozzarella, a few slices of pepperoni, and a teaspoon of thick pizza sauce make the filling, and it should be a small quantity, since an overfilled parcel bursts. The edges are brushed with egg, so that they seal. The rolls can be fried in hot oil, but baking in a very hot oven with a coating of olive oil gives a crisp, golden roll with a lot less trouble and less oil. They can be filled ahead and kept in the fridge or freezer, then baked when needed, so they are a good party food. Change the filling as you like: sausage, ham and pineapple, mushrooms, or a mix of cheeses.

  • Use only a little filling and seal the edges well. Overfilled parcels burst in the oven, and the cheese runs out and burns on the tray.
  • Keep unused wrappers covered with a damp cloth. They dry out and crack within minutes if they are left in the air.
  • Let the rolls cool for a few minutes before you eat them. The cheese inside is molten and can burn your mouth badly.

item.title: Pork Scratchings
item.description: Pork scratchings: the British pub snack of pork rind simmered, dried in a low oven until hard, then fried until it puffs into crunchy crackling.
item.content:encoded:
Pork scratchings are the pub snack of the English Midlands, where they are sold in bags behind the bar of nearly every pub, and they are the crunchy, salty, savoury partner of a pint of bitter. They are made from the rind of the pig, with a little of the fat still attached, which is cooked, dried and fried, and the result is a light, blistered, brittle piece of crackling with a fat, chewy edge. They are called scratchings in the Black Country and West Midlands, and cracklings in other parts of the country, and every pub has an opinion about the difference between the hard, crunchy, dry type and the softer, fattier kind. Making them at home is a slow process, but not a difficult one. The rind is cut into strips and simmered in salted water to soften it and to draw out some of the fat, then dried in a very low oven for several hours until it is hard and translucent, like amber. This drying step is the important one, since it removes all the moisture, and it is what makes the rind puff when it is fried. The dried pieces look like hard plastic. When they are dropped into oil at 200°C they puff up in seconds into light, crunchy scratchings. Take care during the frying, because any water left in the rind makes the oil spit violently. Dry the pieces well and keep your face away from the pan.

  • Dry the rind until it is hard and glassy. Any softness means moisture, and moisture stops the pieces puffing and makes the oil spit.
  • Fry only a few pieces at a time in a deep pan, with the oil at 200°C / 400°F. They expand to several times their size.
  • Stand back from the pan and use a long-handled slotted spoon. The rind can splutter when it meets the hot oil, so take care.

item.title: Bread and Butter Pickles
item.description: Bread and butter pickles: crisp, sweet-and-sour cucumber and onion slices in a turmeric-gold brine with mustard and celery seeds.
item.content:encoded:
Bread and butter pickles are the sweet pickles of America, thin, crinkled slices of cucumber and onion in a golden brine that is sharp with vinegar, sweet with sugar and scented with mustard seed, celery seed and turmeric. They are the pickle that goes on the burger, the sandwich and the plate of cold chicken. The name is said to come from the 1920s, when a couple who farmed cucumbers in Illinois, the Fannings, are said to have sold the pickles to their neighbours during hard times, when the two things that could be counted on to fill a stomach were bread and butter. They kept on making them, and the name stuck. The main point in making them is the crunch. Cucumbers are more than nine tenths water, and salting the slices draws out a large part of it, so that the pickles stay firm in the brine. The slices are tossed with salt and left for an hour, then rinsed and drained. The brine is heated only until the sugar dissolves and the slices are warmed in it for a minute, no more, since boiling cooks them and turns them soft. The pickles are packed into jars with the hot brine and kept in the fridge, and they are ready to eat after a day or two, though they improve over a week. Use pickling cucumbers, which are small, firm and with few seeds, rather than the large watery kind.

  • Salt the slices for the full hour and drain them well. It is what keeps them crisp, and skipping it gives soft pickles.
  • Do not boil the cucumbers in the brine. Bring the brine back just to a simmer, warm the slices through and take the pan off the heat.
  • Choose small pickling cucumbers and slice them evenly. Large salad cucumbers are watery, and slices of different thickness soften at different speeds.

item.title: Pickled Red Cabbage
item.description: Pickled red cabbage: finely shredded red cabbage, salted overnight and pickled in spiced malt vinegar, the crunchy pickle of the ploughman's lunch.
item.content:encoded:
Pickled red cabbage is one of the oldest British pickles, and it is the crisp, sharp, bright purple accompaniment to cold meat, cheese and pork pies, to the ploughman's lunch, to the Boxing Day cold turkey and to a plate of fish and chips in the north of England. The cabbage is finely shredded, salted overnight to draw out water and keep it crunchy, rinsed, packed into jars and covered with cold spiced vinegar. It is one of the easiest pickles to make and needs no cooking of the cabbage at all. The vinegar is the traditional malt vinegar, which has a dark, malty flavour and a warm acidity that suits the cabbage, and it is spiced with peppercorns, cloves, allspice, mustard seeds, a cinnamon stick and a bay leaf, and sweetened with a little sugar. The vinegar is heated only to dissolve the sugar and infuse the spices, and it is cooled before it is poured over the cabbage, because hot vinegar softens the cabbage, and the pickle should stay crisp. The acid also turns the purple pigments in the cabbage a brilliant ruby red. The pickle is at its best after a week in the jar, when the spices have softened and blended into the cabbage, and it keeps for months in a cool cupboard. It is a good way to preserve a large cabbage, and the jars make useful presents.

  • Rinse the cabbage thoroughly after salting. Any salt left on it makes the pickle harsh, and it taints the vinegar.
  • Let the spiced vinegar cool before it goes on the cabbage. Hot vinegar cooks the cabbage and takes away the crunch.
  • Keep the cabbage under the vinegar. Anything above the liquid discolours and can spoil, so press it down and top up with a little extra vinegar.

item.title: Egg Cream
item.description: Egg cream: the New York soda fountain drink of chocolate syrup, cold milk and seltzer, stirred to a fizzy, foaming head. It has no egg or cream.
item.content:encoded:
The egg cream is the great drink of the New York soda fountain, and it contains no egg and no cream. It is made from three things: chocolate syrup, cold whole milk and seltzer, the fizzy water that in New York comes in a siphon bottle, and what comes out is a cold, chocolatey, bubbly drink with a thick white head of foam, lighter and fizzier than a milkshake and less sweet than a soda. It is linked to Brooklyn and to the Jewish candy stores and delicatessens of the Lower East Side, which were the centre of New York life for immigrants in the early twentieth century, and the classic chocolate syrup for it, Fox's U-bet, was made in Brooklyn. Louis Auster, who ran a candy store in the city, is often credited with inventing it in the 1890s, though there are several stories about how it was made and how it got its name, and none has been proved. The technique matters more than the recipe. The syrup goes into the glass first, then the milk, and the seltzer is poured last, hard, from a height or from a siphon, to raise the foam, and the drink is stirred quickly with a long spoon, so that the syrup is drawn up from the bottom and mixed through. The milk must be very cold, since warm milk does not foam, and the seltzer must be fresh and very fizzy. It should be drunk at once, before the head collapses.

  • Use very cold milk and seltzer. Warm liquids do not foam, and the head disappears in seconds.
  • Pour the seltzer from a height, and pour it fast. The force is what creates the foam, and a gentle pour gives a flat drink.
  • Use plain seltzer or sparkling water and not a flavoured one. The syrup provides the taste, and the water is there only for its bubbles. A bottle that has been open for a day has lost most of its fizz, so open a fresh one.

item.title: Flat White
item.description: Flat white: a double shot of espresso with a little steamed milk and a thin, velvety layer of microfoam. The Australian coffee, stronger than a latte.
item.content:encoded:
The flat white is the coffee that Australia and New Zealand gave to the world, and it is now on the menu of almost every cafe from London to New York. It is made from a double shot of espresso and about 150 ml of steamed milk, in a small ceramic cup of 160 to 180 ml, and it is finished with a thin, glossy layer of microfoam, so fine that it is hardly foam at all and looks and pours like wet paint. The name refers to the flat surface, without the tall, stiff dome of foam that tops a cappuccino. It is stronger than a latte, since there is less milk to the coffee, and smoother than a cappuccino, since the milk is not aerated so much, and the taste of the espresso comes through. Both Australia and New Zealand claim it. A Sydney cafe, Moors Espresso Bar, says it served the first in 1985, and a Wellington cafe, Fidel's, says it made one in 1989, and the argument has run ever since. Making a good one needs an espresso machine with a steam wand, but you can get close at home. Make strong coffee in a moka pot or an AeroPress, heat the milk to 60 to 65°C, no hotter, and froth it with a hand frother held just under the surface for a few seconds. Tap the jug to break up the big bubbles, and swirl it until it is glossy.

  • Do not let the milk go above 65°C. Hotter milk loses its sweetness and the foam turns coarse and dry.
  • Keep the frother just under the surface and stop as soon as the milk has increased by about a third. Too much air gives a stiff foam more like a cappuccino.
  • Use fresh, cold whole milk in a cold jug. It has more time to take in air before it gets hot, and the flavour is sweeter.

item.title: Dalgona Coffee
item.description: Dalgona coffee: instant coffee, sugar and hot water whisked into a thick, glossy, caramel foam, spooned over cold iced milk. The viral whipped coffee.
item.content:encoded:
Dalgona coffee is a drink that became famous almost overnight in the spring of 2020, when millions of people were at home and looking for something to make. It is a coffee with two layers. The bottom is cold milk, poured over ice, and the top is a thick, glossy, caramel-coloured cloud of whipped instant coffee, sugar and hot water, which is spooned on and stirred through as you drink. The name comes from dalgona, a Korean honeycomb toffee that is sold at street stalls, and that the coffee is said to resemble in colour and sweetness, and the drink was popularised on South Korean television before it spread on social media across the world. The idea is not new. In India and Pakistan a beaten coffee, a whipped mixture of instant coffee, sugar and hot water, has been served for many years, and in Greece the frappé is made in the same way. The trick is a simple one. Instant coffee dissolves in hot water and contains the sugar and the compounds that hold air, so that when whipped, the mixture increases in volume and turns pale, thick and stiff. Equal parts of coffee, sugar and hot water is the rule. An electric whisk takes three or four minutes, and a hand whisk takes ten or fifteen and a sore arm, but the result is worth it. The foam holds for a while on the milk, and it can be made ahead and kept in the fridge.

  • Use instant coffee granules or powder and not ground coffee. Only instant will whip, because it dissolves fully and holds the air.
  • Keep the proportions equal, by volume, of coffee, sugar and hot water. Less sugar makes a foam that will not stiffen.
  • Keep whisking until the foam holds a firm peak when you lift the whisk. If it looks like runny latte foam, it needs another minute or two.

item.title: Buck's Fizz
item.description: Buck's Fizz: two parts chilled sparkling wine to one part fresh orange juice, poured into a flute. The British brunch and Christmas morning drink.
item.content:encoded:
Buck's Fizz is the British drink of celebration, served at the wedding breakfast, the birthday brunch, on Christmas morning and on the first day of a holiday. It is two parts chilled sparkling wine to one part fresh orange juice, poured into a flute, and it is light, fruity and very easy to drink. It was created in 1921 at Buck's Club, a gentlemen's club in Clifford Street, London, by the barman Malachi McGarry, and it was named after the club. The original recipe is said to have included a dash of grenadine. Its cousin, the Mimosa, is said to have been created a few years later at the Ritz in Paris, and the two are often confused. The difference lies in the proportions. A Mimosa is half wine and half juice, and a Buck's Fizz has twice as much wine as juice, which makes it drier, fizzier and less sweet. Making it well depends on small things. The orange juice should be freshly squeezed and strained, because it tastes brighter than anything from a carton. Both the wine and the juice must be very cold, which keeps the bubbles lively. The juice goes into the glass first and the sparkling wine is poured slowly over it, down the side of a tilted flute, which preserves the bubbles and mixes the two without stirring. A dry prosecco, cava or crémant suits it perfectly. Champagne is not necessary, since its subtlety is lost under the juice, and a sweet sparkling wine makes the drink cloying.

  • Squeeze the juice fresh and strain it. Carton juice is sweeter and flatter, and pulp makes the bubbles foam up over the rim when the wine is poured in.
  • Keep to the order in the recipe, with the juice first and then the wine, poured slowly down the side of a tilted glass. Pouring the wine first makes it foam, and the two do not mix.
  • Choose a dry sparkling wine, such as prosecco, cava or crémant. A sweet one added to orange juice makes a cloying drink, and there is no need to use champagne.

item.title: Jello Shots
item.description: Jello shots: wobbly, fruity shots of flavoured jelly and vodka, set in small cups and chilled until firm. Twenty-four party shots.
item.content:encoded:
Jello shots are a party staple, small cups of brightly coloured wobbly jelly, made with flavoured jelly crystals, boiling water and vodka, and they are as popular at student parties and weddings as they are at holiday gatherings. The idea of alcoholic jelly is much older than the shot. Recipes for punch jellies made with brandy and rum can be found in cookbooks and bartender's guides of the nineteenth century, when moulded jellies were the height of fashion, and the shot version took its current form in the United States in the second half of the twentieth century. The method is simple, and the only skill is in the proportions. Hot water dissolves the gelatin in the crystals, and then, when the water has cooled slightly, cold vodka is stirred in. The spirit cannot be added to boiling water, because the heat would drive off the alcohol, and there cannot be too much of it, or the jelly will not set. Two parts hot water to one part cold vodka is a good balance in this recipe, and it makes a shot that is set firm enough to hold and strong enough to be noticed. The shots are poured into small plastic cups and chilled for at least two hours. Take care with them. They taste of fruit and disguise the alcohol, so they are stronger than they seem, and each shot holds about 10 ml of vodka, roughly a third of a single measure of spirit.

  • Stir the crystals until they are completely dissolved. Grainy jelly tastes bad and does not set evenly.
  • Cool the hot mixture for a few minutes before adding the vodka. Very hot liquid evaporates alcohol, and the shots come out weaker.
  • Stand the shots up in the fridge on a flat shelf. A tilted tray gives shots that set on a slant.

item.title: Appletini
item.description: Appletini: vodka, sour apple liqueur, cloudy apple juice and lemon juice, shaken until cold and strained into a martini glass.
item.content:encoded:
The Appletini is the vivid green cocktail of the 1990s, and it is one of the drinks that defined the era of the martini bar, when any drink poured into a triangular glass was called a martini. It is said to have been created in 1996 at a Los Angeles restaurant and bar, Lola's, in West Hollywood, by a bartender named Adam Karsten, who made it with vodka and apple liqueur, and it was first known as the Adam's Delicious Martini. It became world famous when it was ordered by the characters of the television series Sex and the City, and it soon appeared on the menu of almost every bar. It has a poor reputation among cocktail experts, because the early ones were made with sickly sweet, artificially flavoured green liqueur and a sour mix, but a well-made one is a very good drink. It should be tart and crisp, with a real apple taste. The way to achieve it is to use good apple liqueur, add a splash of cloudy apple juice for a natural fruit flavour, and balance it with a little fresh lemon juice. Shake it very hard, so that it is very cold and slightly diluted, and strain it into a well-chilled glass. A thin fan of green apple, dipped in lemon juice so it does not brown, is the classic garnish.

  • Use cloudy apple juice and not clear. It has a fuller, fresher apple taste and softens the artificial edge of the liqueur.
  • Shake hard with plenty of ice. The dilution is a part of the recipe, and a drink that is not cold enough tastes sugary.
  • Dip the apple slices in lemon juice and add them at the last minute. Cut apple browns within a few minutes. A Granny Smith gives the brightest green skin and the sharpest taste.

item.title: Last Word
item.description: Last Word: equal parts gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur and fresh lime juice, shaken and strained. An herbal Prohibition-era cocktail.
item.content:encoded:
The Last Word is a cocktail of four ingredients in equal parts, and the four are all strong flavours: gin, which is dry and full of juniper, green Chartreuse, the French herbal liqueur made by monks that tastes of dozens of plants, maraschino liqueur, a bitter-sweet cherry spirit, and fresh lime juice. It should not work, but it does, and the result is one of the most satisfying drinks in the repertoire, herbal, sharp, sweet and a little smoky, with a bright green colour. The Last Word was served at the Detroit Athletic Club in the 1910s and 1920s, and it is said to have been introduced by a vaudeville performer, Frank Fogarty. It disappeared after Prohibition and remained forgotten for decades, until a bartender, Murray Stenson, found the recipe in a 1951 book, Ted Saucier's Bottoms Up, and put it on the menu of the Zig Zag Café in Seattle in 2004. It became one of the cocktails that started the modern craft bar movement, and it led to the invention of a whole family of drinks that use the same equal-parts formula, including the Paper Plane and the Naked and Famous. It needs no skill, only accurate measuring. Use a jigger, because each ingredient is powerful, and any difference throws the balance. Shake it hard until it is very cold and strain it into a chilled coupe.

  • Measure each ingredient exactly. The four flavours are all strong, and a little extra of any one of them takes over the drink. A jigger with clear markings makes this easy, and it is worth owning one.
  • Squeeze the lime juice fresh. Lime juice loses its brightness within a couple of hours, and the drink needs its sharpness to balance the sweet liqueurs.
  • Shake hard for a full 15 seconds. The dilution softens the strong herbal liqueur and makes the drink taste balanced and rounded.

item.title: Penicillin
item.description: Penicillin: blended Scotch, lemon juice and honey-ginger syrup shaken over ice, with a float of smoky Islay whisky. A modern classic.
item.content:encoded:
The Penicillin is a cocktail that was invented in 2005 by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey, a bar in New York, and it has since become one of the most widely copied drinks of the modern cocktail age. It is built on a whisky sour, which is whisky, lemon juice and sweetener, and it adds two ideas. The first is honey and ginger, which are cooked into a syrup, and which suggest the old home remedy for a cold, which is where the name comes from. The second is a float of smoky Islay single malt, which sits on the surface of the drink and gives the nose a great wave of peat smoke each time it is lifted. The base of the drink is a mild blended Scotch, which gives a soft, round, slightly sweet body, and the smoky single malt supplies the character. The sharpness of the lemon and the sweetness of the honey are balanced, and the ginger gives a warm, spicy heat at the back of the throat. The result is a drink that is complex, warming and easy to like, even for people who do not normally enjoy smoky whisky. The syrup takes a few minutes to make, but it keeps for a couple of weeks in the fridge and makes six or more drinks. Shake the drink hard, strain it over a large ice cube, and pour the smoky whisky over the back of a spoon so that it floats. Garnish with a piece of candied ginger.

  • Use a smooth blended Scotch for the base and save the smoky malt for the float. A very peaty base makes the drink harsh and overwhelming.
  • Pour the float slowly over the back of a spoon. It should rest on the surface, where you smell it with every sip, instead of mixing through.
  • Make the syrup with fresh ginger and keep the simmer gentle. Boiling it hard turns the honey bitter and dulls the ginger.

item.title: Black Russian
item.description: Black Russian: vodka and coffee liqueur over ice, stirred in the glass. A dark, sweet, strong two-ingredient after-dinner drink.
item.content:encoded:
The Black Russian is the simplest of the classic cocktails, and it needs only two ingredients, vodka and coffee liqueur, poured over ice in a short glass. It is dark, sweet and strong, with the flavour of coffee and the kick of vodka, and it is one of the drinks that people drink after dinner in place of coffee and dessert. It was created in 1949 in Brussels by Gustave Tops, a bartender at the Hotel Metropole, for Perle Mesta, the American ambassador to Luxembourg, who was known as the hostess with the mostest. The name comes from the vodka, which was thought of as Russian, and from the dark colour, and nothing in it is actually Russian. The drink is the ancestor of the White Russian, which is the same thing with cream added, and which became famous when it was the drink of the Dude in the film The Big Lebowski. The Black Russian was more popular in the 1950s and 1960s, but it has never gone away. The standard proportion is two parts vodka to one part coffee liqueur, which makes it balanced, and not too sweet, though many people prefer it with slightly more liqueur. It is a build drink, and it needs no shaker. The ice goes in the glass, the vodka and liqueur are poured over it, and it is stirred gently for a few seconds until cold. Use a good coffee liqueur, since it supplies all the flavour, and use a large ice cube if you have one, since it melts slowly.

  • Use a good coffee liqueur and do not economise. It gives all the flavour to the drink, and a cheap one is sweet and thin.
  • Use a large ice cube or several big ones. They melt slowly and do not water the drink down before you have finished it. A rocks glass that has been chilled in the freezer also keeps the ice from melting too fast.
  • Adjust the proportions to taste. Less vodka and more liqueur makes a sweeter, more dessert-like drink, and more vodka makes it drier.
